abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level sequence features and interactions give rise to micron-scale structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular decision-making in stress response, signaling, and disease. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework linking intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence grammar to condensate composition, biophysical state, and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists not for lack of data—thousands of studies have generated condensate-component databases, high-content subcellular imaging atlases, proximity-labeling interactomes, cryo-electron tomograms, disease mutation catalogs, and AlphaFold-derived structural ensembles—but because these resources are scattered across incompatible formats, disciplines, and repositories, with no single lab possessing the expertise to harmonize and jointly analyze them. This working group proposes to close that gap through community-scale data synthesis.

We will integrate five previously siloed public data classes: (1) curated condensate-associated protein and sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro); (2) subcellular localization and dynamics imaging (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer); (3) proximity-labeling and interactome datasets defining in vivo condensate composition; (4) biophysical/simulation resources describing IDR sequence patterning (charge, aromaticity, stickers-and-spacers architecture) including coarse-grained simulation parameter sets (e.g., CALVADOS-derived); and (5) disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapping mutations onto IDRs linked to pathological condensate dysregulation. Using graph-based and deep generative models, we will construct a multi-layer network connecting molecular sequence features to condensate proteome composition, imaging-derived morphological/dynamic phenotypes, and organismal disease outcomes. A central analytical goal is to identify emergent “rules”—nonlinear, context-dependent combinations of sequence and interaction features—that predict when and where condensates form, what determines their material properties, and how perturbation (mutation, stress, drug treatment) shifts phenotypic outcomes across cell types.

This effort inherently requires cross-disciplinary integration beyond any single lab: polymer physicists and biophysicists to encode sequence-to-property relationships, cell biologists and imaging scientists to interpret phenotypic datasets, computational/AI scientists to build multi-modal integrative models, and clinical geneticists to connect molecular predictions to disease. NCEMS support is essential to convene this team, provide shared computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous ontologies (protein IDs, imaging metadata, mutation annotations), and establish reproducible, version-controlled pipelines. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, queryable resource (a “Condensate Emergence Atlas”) under FAIR principles, enabling community reuse and extension.

Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across institutions, receiving hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning for biophysical prediction, and open/reproducible science practices, while rotating through partner labs to gain cross-disciplinary fluency. By synthesizing existing but fragmented public data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology—how molecular sequence information encodes emergent cellular organization—while producing a durable, reusable resource and training pipeline for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.
full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level sequence features and interactions give rise to micron-scale structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular decision-making in stress response, signaling, and disease. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework linking intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence grammar to condensate composition, biophysical state, and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists not for lack of data—thousands of studies have generated condensate-component databases, high-content subcellular imaging atlases, proximity-labeling interactomes, cryo-electron tomograms, disease mutation catalogs, and AlphaFold-derived structural ensembles—but because these resources are scattered across incompatible formats, disciplines, and repositories, with no single lab possessing the expertise to harmonize and jointly analyze them. This working group proposes to close that gap through community-scale data synthesis.

We will integrate five previously siloed public data classes: (1) curated condensate-associated protein and sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro); (2) subcellular localization and dynamics imaging (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer); (3) proximity-labeling and interactome datasets defining in vivo condensate composition; (4) biophysical/simulation resources describing IDR sequence patterning (charge, aromaticity, stickers-and-spacers architecture) including coarse-grained simulation parameter sets (e.g., CALVADOS-derived); and (5) disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapping mutations onto IDRs linked to pathological condensate dysregulation. Using graph-based and deep generative models, we will construct a multi-layer network connecting molecular sequence features to condensate proteome composition, imaging-derived morphological/dynamic phenotypes, and organismal disease outcomes. A central analytical goal is to identify emergent “rules”—nonlinear, context-dependent combinations of sequence and interaction features—that predict when and where condensates form, what determines their material properties, and how perturbation (mutation, stress, drug treatment) shifts phenotypic outcomes across cell types.

This effort inherently requires cross-disciplinary integration beyond any single lab: polymer physicists and biophysicists to encode sequence-to-property relationships, cell biologists and imaging scientists to interpret phenotypic datasets, computational/AI scientists to build multi-modal integrative models, and clinical geneticists to connect molecular predictions to disease. NCEMS support is essential to convene this team, provide shared computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous ontologies (protein IDs, imaging metadata, mutation annotations), and establish reproducible, version-controlled pipelines. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, queryable resource (a “Condensate Emergence Atlas”) under FAIR principles, enabling community reuse and extension.

Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across institutions, receiving hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning for biophysical prediction, and open/reproducible science practices, while rotating through partner labs to gain cross-disciplinary fluency. By synthesizing existing but fragmented public data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology—how molecular sequence information encodes emergent cellular organization—while producing a durable, reusable resource and training pipeline for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged as a fundamental organizing principle of the eukaryotic cell, orchestrating processes ranging from ribosome biogenesis and stress granule assembly to transcriptional condensation and DNA damage repair. These membraneless organelles arise through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related phase transitions driven largely by multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA, and folded domains. The mesoscale nature of condensates—bridging molecular sequence information and cellular-scale phenotypes—makes them a paradigmatic system for studying emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences: simple sequence-encoded interaction grammars (charge patterning, aromatic 'stickers,' spacer flexibility) give rise to collective material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that are not trivially predictable from individual molecular features, and these material properties in turn dictate higher-order cellular decisions such as stress adaptation, signal transduction, and disease susceptibility.

Despite a decade of intense investigation, the field lacks a unified predictive framework connecting sequence grammar to condensate phenotype and organismal outcome. This is emphatically not due to insufficient data. The condensate biology community has produced an extraordinarily rich and diverse public data ecosystem: curated sequence and interaction databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro) cataloging thousands of phase-separating proteins; proteome-scale imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer) documenting subcellular localization and dynamics for tens of thousands of proteins; proximity-labeling and interactome studies defining in vivo condensate composition; biophysical and coarse-grained simulation datasets (e.g., CALVADOS parameterizations) encoding sequence-to-phase-behavior relationships; and clinical variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) linking IDR mutations to disease. Each resource, generated by distinct scientific communities using distinct vocabularies, identifiers, and quality standards, offers only a partial view of the sequence-to-phenotype problem. No single dataset—and no single laboratory—possesses the combined expertise in polymer physics, high-content imaging analysis, interactome bioinformatics, and clinical genetics required to integrate them.

This fragmentation represents precisely the kind of long-standing puzzle that community-scale data synthesis is positioned to resolve. The scientific opportunity is significant: condensate dysregulation is implicated in neurodegeneration (TDP-43, FUS, hnRNPA1 aggregation in ALS/FTD), cancer (transcriptional condensates at super-enhancers), and viral infection (replication organelles), such that a predictive sequence-to-phenotype framework would have immediate translational relevance. Moreover, resolving how mesoscale material properties emerge from molecular sequence information addresses a foundational question in NCEMS's scientific vision: how do system properties at one scale (molecular sequence) give rise to unexpected, non-additive properties at another (condensate material state, cellular decision-making)? By synthesizing the fragmented condensate data ecosystem into a harmonized, multi-layer resource, this working group will not only test specific mechanistic hypotheses about sequence-encoded emergence but will also establish a durable community resource and reproducible analytical pipeline that lowers the barrier for future mesoscale synthesis research across other biomolecular systems exhibiting similar multi-scale organization, including membrane-associated assemblies and organelle contact sites.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
We organize the working group's research around three tightly linked questions, each paired with testable hypotheses derived from current biophysical theory and preliminary community data.

RQ1: Can condensate-associated sequence features predict in vivo condensate composition and localization? Building on stickers-and-spacers theory, we hypothesize (H1) that quantitative sequence descriptors—charge patterning (kappa, omega), aromatic sticker density, predicted disorder, and short linear motif content—jointly predict a protein's propensity to partition into specific condensate types (stress granules, nucleoli, paraspeckles) with higher accuracy than any single feature class alone, and that this predictive power will generalize across imaging datasets (HPA, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer) despite differences in cell type and imaging modality. We further hypothesize (H1b) that discrepancies between simulation-predicted phase behavior and observed in vivo localization will be systematically explained by cellular context features (local concentration, competing interactions, post-translational modification sites) recoverable from proteomic and interactome data, revealing where purely biophysical sequence grammar is necessary but not sufficient.

RQ2: What sequence and compositional features determine condensate material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics, multiphase architecture)? We hypothesize (H2) that condensate material state is governed by nonlinear combinations of intra-IDR patterning and interactome-derived valency (number and strength of scaffold-client interactions), such that graph-theoretic properties of the interactome (e.g., network density, degree distribution of scaffold hubs) predict imaging-derived dynamic parameters (FRAP recovery rates, droplet fusion times) better than sequence features alone. This hypothesis directly tests whether the interactome layer contributes emergent information not present in isolated sequence-based models—a signature of genuine multi-scale emergence rather than simple molecular determinism.

RQ3: How do disease-associated mutations in IDRs perturb sequence grammar to shift condensate phenotype and cellular outcome? We hypothesize (H3) that pathological mutations catalogued in ClinVar and COSMIC are enriched at sequence positions predicted by our integrated model to be highly sensitive 'grammar-defining' residues (e.g., aromatic stickers, charge-patterning breakpoints) relative to disease-neutral variants, and that the predicted magnitude of sequence-grammar disruption correlates with reported severity or age-of-onset in relevant neurodegenerative and oncological datasets. A corollary hypothesis (H3b) is that mutations predicted to alter condensate material properties toward pathological hardening (aberrant solidification) versus dissolution will map onto mechanistically distinct disease categories, providing a testable typology of condensate-related pathology.

Across all three questions, our unifying meta-hypothesis is that condensate phenotype and cellular outcome cannot be predicted from any single data layer in isolation; rather, predictive power will emerge specifically from joint, multi-layer integration, and the magnitude of this integration gain—quantifiable through systematic ablation of data layers in our models—constitutes a direct, measurable signature of mesoscale emergence. This framing transforms condensate biology from a collection of disconnected observations into a quantitative test case for how molecular information propagates upward to shape cellular and organismal phenotypes, directly addressing NCEMS's core scientific mission of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale.

[Methods and Approach]
Data Acquisition and Harmonization. We will assemble and harmonize the five public data classes described above. A dedicated data engineering subgroup (co-led by computational and imaging scientists) will construct unified protein-level identifiers (UniProt-anchored crosswalks), standardized ontologies for condensate type and imaging metadata (aligned to Cell Component Ontology terms), and version-controlled ingestion pipelines for each source database, with automated quality-control checks for redundancy, annotation conflicts, and missing metadata. Sequence-derived biophysical descriptors (charge patterning parameters kappa/omega, aromatic sticker density, predicted disorder, short linear motif annotations) will be computed uniformly across all condensate-associated proteins to eliminate cross-database inconsistencies in feature definition.

Multi-Layer Network Construction. We will construct a heterogeneous, multi-layer graph in which nodes represent proteins, sequence features, condensate types, imaging-derived phenotypes, and disease variants, and edges represent empirically observed or predicted relationships (interactome co-membership, imaging co-localization, sequence similarity, mutation-to-domain mapping). This structure explicitly preserves the provenance and data class of each relationship, enabling systematic layer-ablation analyses to quantify integration gain.

Predictive Modeling. Building on this graph, we will develop and benchmark two complementary modeling strategies: (a) graph neural network (GNN) models trained to predict condensate partitioning and material-property phenotypes from multi-layer node/edge features, allowing us to test H1 and H2 through layer-ablation experiments; and (b) deep generative models (variational autoencoders or diffusion-based sequence models) trained on curated phase-separating sequences to learn a latent 'sequence grammar' space, used to score disease variants for predicted grammar disruption (H3). Model performance will be validated using held-out cross-database splits (e.g., training on one imaging atlas, testing on another) to explicitly test generalization across independently generated public datasets—a validation strategy only possible through data synthesis at this scale.

Statistical and Biophysical Validation. Predictions will be benchmarked against existing experimentally measured biophysical parameters (FRAP recovery, saturation concentration, contact-angle measurements curated from literature) and cross-validated against orthogonal coarse-grained simulation outputs (CALVADOS-derived phase diagrams) to ensure biophysical plausibility rather than purely statistical fit. Disease-variant analyses will use permutation-based residue-position enrichment tests comparing pathogenic and benign variant sets.

Working Group Structure and Workflow. The team will be organized into four coordinated subgroups—Data Harmonization, Biophysical Modeling, Imaging/Phenotype Analysis, and Clinical Genetics—with monthly all-hands synthesis meetings and a shared cloud-based computational environment (containerized pipelines, shared compute allocation) to ensure reproducibility. A rotating 'synthesis sprint' model will bring subgroup members together for intensive two-week integration sessions at key milestones (months 6, 12, 18, 24) to jointly resolve cross-layer discrepancies and refine shared models. Trainees will be embedded within and across subgroups, co-supervised by at least two PIs from different disciplinary backgrounds, ensuring genuine cross-disciplinary training rather than siloed contributions.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This working group will produce four concrete deliverables. First, the Condensate Emergence Atlas: a harmonized, queryable, multi-layer public dataset integrating sequence, interactome, imaging, biophysical, and disease-variant information for thousands of condensate-associated proteins, structured for reuse by the broader community. Second, validated predictive models (GNN and generative sequence-grammar models) capable of predicting condensate partitioning, material state, and disease-variant impact from sequence and contextual features, released with full training code and documentation. Third, a quantitative 'integration gain' framework demonstrating, through systematic data-layer ablation, the degree to which condensate phenotype prediction depends on genuine multi-scale emergence rather than single-layer molecular determinism—a generalizable methodological contribution applicable to other mesoscale biological systems. Fourth, a testable typology linking disease-associated IDR mutations to distinct condensate perturbation modes (pathological hardening versus dissolution), generating specific, experimentally testable hypotheses for the broader condensate biology and disease genetics communities.

Scientifically, this project will resolve a long-standing gap between biophysical theory of phase separation and its cellular and organismal consequences, providing the field's first cross-validated, multi-database predictive framework for sequence-to-phenotype prediction in condensate biology. Practically, the Atlas and associated pipelines will serve as a reusable substrate for future hypothesis generation, accelerating discovery well beyond the funding period. Broadly, by explicitly quantifying emergence through data integration rather than assuming it, this project offers a template methodology directly transferable to other NCEMS priority areas—membrane-associated assemblies, cytoskeletal organization, organelle contact sites—where fragmented multi-scale public data currently limit synthesis. The project will also generate peer-reviewed publications and public preprints, disseminated alongside open workshops to train the broader community in multi-layer data synthesis methods.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This project is designed from inception around open, team, and reproducible science principles consistent with NCEMS community standards. All source data are already publicly available; no new experimental data will be generated. All harmonization pipelines, feature-computation scripts, graph construction code, and trained models will be developed in version-controlled public repositories (GitHub, mirrored to Zenodo for permanent archival with DOI assignment) under permissive open-source licenses. We will adopt containerization (Docker/Singularity) to ensure computational environments are fully reproducible across institutions and after the project concludes. Data harmonization crosswalks (identifier mappings, ontology alignments) will be released as standalone, citable community resources, independent of downstream modeling results, to maximize reuse value even for researchers who disagree with our specific modeling choices.

The Condensate Emergence Atlas will be hosted on accessible, queryable infrastructure (documented API and downloadable bulk files) with comprehensive metadata following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles, and will include full data provenance tracking so that every integrated data point can be traced to its original source database and publication. Analysis notebooks will be structured for computational reproducibility using literate programming frameworks and will include unit tests and continuous integration checks to catch pipeline errors as the resource is updated.

We will pre-register core hypotheses and analysis plans (H1–H3) prior to full-scale model training to guard against post hoc overfitting, and will report negative or null results transparently, consistent with rigorous synthesis science practice. All manuscripts arising from this work will be posted as preprints prior to peer review, and the working group commits to responding to community data-correction requests and issue reports through a public tracking system, ensuring the Atlas remains a living, community-maintained resource beyond the initial funding period.

[Budget and Resources]
We request NCEMS support across four categories aligned with the working group's structure. Personnel: partial salary support (2–3 months/year) for four co-PIs spanning biophysics/polymer physics, cell/imaging biology, computational/AI science, and clinical genetics, plus full support for two postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students who will lead day-to-day data harmonization, model development, and cross-disciplinary integration tasks; these trainees will be co-mentored across institutions to ensure genuine cross-disciplinary training. Computational Infrastructure: cloud computing credits and/or high-performance computing allocation sufficient for GNN and generative model training on large-scale multi-layer graphs, plus persistent storage for harmonized datasets and archival deposition costs (Zenodo/DOI, API hosting). Convening Costs: support for two in-person working group meetings (kickoff and mid-project synthesis summit) and quarterly virtual all-hands meetings, plus four two-week 'synthesis sprint' intensive working sessions bringing subgroup members together at rotating host institutions to resolve cross-layer integration challenges. abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level sequence features and interactions give rise to micron-scale structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular decision-making in stress response, signaling, and disease. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework linking intrinsically disordered region (IDR) sequence grammar to condensate composition, biophysical state, and downstream cellular outcomes. This gap persists not for lack of data—thousands of studies have generated condensate-component databases, high-content subcellular imaging atlases, proximity-labeling interactomes, cryo-electron tomograms, disease mutation catalogs, and AlphaFold-derived structural ensembles—but because these resources are scattered across incompatible formats, disciplines, and repositories, with no single lab possessing the expertise to harmonize and jointly analyze them. This working group proposes to close that gap through community-scale data synthesis.

We will integrate five previously siloed public data classes: (1) curated condensate-associated protein and sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro); (2) subcellular localization and dynamics imaging (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer); (3) proximity-labeling and interactome datasets defining in vivo condensate composition; (4) biophysical/simulation resources describing IDR sequence patterning (charge, aromaticity, stickers-and-spacers architecture) including coarse-grained simulation parameter sets (e.g., CALVADOS-derived); and (5) disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapping mutations onto IDRs linked to pathological condensate dysregulation. Using graph-based and deep generative models, we will construct a multi-layer network connecting molecular sequence features to condensate proteome composition, imaging-derived morphological/dynamic phenotypes, and organismal disease outcomes. A central analytical goal is to identify emergent “rules”—nonlinear, context-dependent combinations of sequence and interaction features—that predict when and where condensates form, what determines their material properties, and how perturbation (mutation, stress, drug treatment) shifts phenotypic outcomes across cell types.

This effort inherently requires cross-disciplinary integration beyond any single lab: polymer physicists and biophysicists to encode sequence-to-property relationships, cell biologists and imaging scientists to interpret phenotypic datasets, computational/AI scientists to build multi-modal integrative models, and clinical geneticists to connect molecular predictions to disease. NCEMS support is essential to convene this team, provide shared computational infrastructure for harmonizing heterogeneous ontologies (protein IDs, imaging metadata, mutation annotations), and establish reproducible, version-controlled pipelines. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, queryable resource (a “Condensate Emergence Atlas”) under FAIR principles, enabling community reuse and extension.

Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across institutions, receiving hands-on training in multi-omic data integration, machine learning for biophysical prediction, and open/reproducible science practices, while rotating through partner labs to gain cross-disciplinary fluency. By synthesizing existing but fragmented public data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology—how molecular sequence information encodes emergent cellular organization—while producing a durable, reusable resource and training pipeline for the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level features (disordered sequences, multivalent interactions, post-translational modifications) give rise to organelle-scale material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that in turn shape cellular function and disease. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at each of these scales, the field lacks an integrated, predictive framework linking sequence-encoded biophysics to emergent mesoscale behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists not from lack of data but from its fragmentation across incompatible domains: biophysical LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), disorder and sequence-feature repositories (MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold/ESMFold structural predictions), high-content and super-resolution imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting), single-cell and bulk multi-omics (expression stoichiometry, PTM databases like PhosphoSitePlus), and clinical variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) documenting condensate-associated disease mutations. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, cell imaging analytics, and clinical genomics needed to unify these resources.

This Working Group will address the central question: What sequence-encoded biophysical grammar governs the emergent material properties of condensates, and how do perturbations to this grammar propagate to cellular and organismal phenotypes? We will pursue three synthesis aims. (1) Construct a harmonized cross-database resource linking condensate-forming proteins to quantitative sequence/structural features (charge patterning, aromatic stickers, IDR length, predicted secondary structure) using standardized ontologies, resolving inconsistent annotations across LLPS databases. This project intrinsically requires collaboration beyond any individual lab: biophysicists modeling polymer thermodynamics, structural bioinformaticians curating disorder predictions, cell biologists interpreting high-content imaging phenotypes, and clinical genomicists linking variants to disease—together with data scientists capable of harmonizing heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets into a single predictive framework. NCEMS support is essential to convene this diverse team, provide computational infrastructure for large-scale data harmonization, and establish shared analytical standards. All curated datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows will be released as an open-access resource (GitHub/Zenodo, FAIR-compliant), including a web-based condensate property predictor for community use. The Working Group will embed graduate students and postdocs directly in cross-disciplinary sub-teams, pairing computational trainees with wet-lab-trained condensate biologists, providing structured mentorship in reproducible multi-omic synthesis and building a cohort of researchers fluent in both molecular biophysics and data science—directly advancing NCEMS's mission to train a data-savvy mesoscale biology workforce.

[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level features (disordered sequences, multivalent interactions, post-translational modifications) give rise to organelle-scale material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that in turn shape cellular function and disease. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at each of these scales, the field lacks an integrated, predictive framework linking sequence-encoded biophysics to emergent mesoscale behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists not from lack of data but from its fragmentation across incompatible domains: biophysical LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), disorder and sequence-feature repositories (MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold/ESMFold structural predictions), high-content and super-resolution imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting), single-cell and bulk multi-omics (expression stoichiometry, PTM databases like PhosphoSitePlus), and clinical variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) documenting condensate-associated disease mutations. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, cell imaging analytics, and clinical genomics needed to unify these resources.

This Working Group will address the central question: What sequence-encoded biophysical grammar governs the emergent material properties of condensates, and how do perturbations to this grammar propagate to cellular and organismal phenotypes? We will pursue three synthesis aims. (1) Construct a harmonized cross-database resource linking condensate-forming proteins to quantitative sequence/structural features (charge patterning, aromatic stickers, IDR length, predicted secondary structure) using standardized ontologies, resolving inconsistent annotations across LLPS databases. (2) Train interpretable machine learning models that predict mesoscale material properties (viscosity class, multiphase organization, dynamic exchange rates) from these molecular features, validated against quantitative imaging datasets (FRAP recovery curves, condensate size/number distributions from HPA and OpenCell), enabling discovery of emergent 'grammar rules' not evident from single-protein studies. (3) Map disease-associated mutations (ClinVar, COSMIC) within condensate-relevant sequence regions onto predicted mesoscale property shifts, and cross-reference with single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic data to identify cell-type-specific vulnerabilities where altered condensate stoichiometry may drive pathology (e.g., neurodegeneration, cancer).

This project intrinsically requires collaboration beyond any individual lab: biophysicists modeling polymer thermodynamics, structural bioinformaticians curating disorder predictions, cell biologists interpreting high-content imaging phenotypes, and clinical genomicists linking variants to disease—together with data scientists capable of harmonizing heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets into a single predictive framework. NCEMS support is essential to convene this diverse team, provide computational infrastructure for large-scale data harmonization, and establish shared analytical standards. All curated datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows will be released as an open-access resource (GitHub/Zenodo, FAIR-compliant), including a web-based condensate property predictor for community use. The Working Group will embed graduate students and postdocs directly in cross-disciplinary sub-teams, pairing computational trainees with wet-lab-trained condensate biologists, providing structured mentorship in reproducible multi-omic synthesis and building a cohort of researchers fluent in both molecular biophysics and data science—directly advancing NCEMS's mission to train a data-savvy mesoscale biology workforce.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged as a paradigm-shifting concept in cell biology, revealing that many essential cellular processes—ribonucleoprotein granule assembly, transcriptional condensation, signaling clusters, stress response—arise not from stable macromolecular machines but from dynamic, liquid-like assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These structures are quintessential examples of mesoscale emergence: they exist at a scale intermediate between individual biomolecules and organelles, and their material properties—viscosity, surface tension, internal architecture, exchange dynamics—are not simple sums of molecular components but emergent consequences of collective, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, nucleic acids, and post-translational modifications (PTMs). Understanding how molecular-scale sequence features encode organelle-scale material behavior, and how this behavior dictates cellular phenotype and disease susceptibility, is a central open problem in mesoscale biology and aligns directly with NCEMS's foundational scientific vision.

Over the past decade, an extraordinary volume of public data has accumulated describing condensates at every relevant scale: curated LLPS protein databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro) catalog experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and conditions; disorder and structural prediction resources (MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold/ESMFold) provide sequence-level annotations of IDRs, charge patterning, and structural propensity; high-content and super-resolution imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting) document condensate morphology, localization, and dynamics across thousands of proteins and cell lines; PTM repositories (PhosphoSitePlus) capture modification sites known to modulate phase behavior; and clinical variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) link mutations in condensate-forming proteins to human disease, from ALS/FTD-associated granule dysfunction to oncogenic transcriptional condensate dysregulation.

Despite this wealth of data, no integrated framework exists connecting sequence-encoded biophysical determinants to emergent mesoscale material properties and, ultimately, to cellular and organismal phenotypes. This is not a failure of data generation but of data synthesis: these resources were built by distinct scientific communities—polymer physicists, structural bioinformaticians, cell biologists, and clinical geneticists—using incompatible ontologies, units, and quality standards. A charge-patterning metric computed for one protein family is rarely cross-referenced with FRAP-derived viscosity estimates for the same protein, let alone with disease variant hotspots. This fragmentation has left a fundamental question unanswered: is there a generalizable 'grammar' connecting sequence features to mesoscale material behavior, analogous to the genetic code, and can such a grammar predict when perturbations—mutation, PTM loss, altered stoichiometry—will produce pathological consequences?

Solving this problem exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory. It requires simultaneous fluency in polymer physics theory, large-scale bioinformatic curation, quantitative image analysis, and clinical genomics, along with computational infrastructure to harmonize datasets spanning orders of magnitude in scale and heterogeneous formats. NCEMS's mission to catalyze multidisciplinary synthesis of public molecular and cellular data provides precisely the collaborative structure and infrastructural support needed to unify these fragmented resources into a predictive, generalizable framework—resolving a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology while establishing reusable tools and training pathways for the broader research community.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Central Question: What sequence-encoded biophysical grammar governs the emergent material properties of biomolecular condensates, and how do perturbations to this grammar propagate to cellular and organismal phenotypes?

Aim 1 – Data Harmonization. Question: Can heterogeneous LLPS annotations, generated using disparate experimental and computational methods, be reconciled into a unified, quantitative feature space without loss of biological signal? Hypothesis 1: Despite differing experimental conditions and annotation conventions across PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and MobiDB, condensate-relevant sequence features (charge patterning parameter κ, aromatic sticker density, IDR fraction, predicted secondary structure propensity) can be harmonized into standardized quantitative metrics anchored to UniProt identifiers, revealing that many apparent cross-database discrepancies reflect annotation artifacts rather than true biological variability, and that a consolidated resource will substantially increase statistical power for downstream modeling relative to any single source.

Aim 2 – Predictive Modeling of Emergent Material Properties. Question: Do sequence- and structure-derived features predict emergent mesoscale material properties (viscosity class, multiphase architecture, FRAP-derived exchange dynamics) in a generalizable and interpretable manner, and are these relationships combinatorial rather than additive? Hypothesis 2a: Mesoscale material properties are governed by nonlinear, combinatorial relationships among sequence features—for example, specific ratios of aromatic 'stickers' to charged 'spacers'—such that emergent material behavior cannot be predicted from any single feature considered in isolation, consistent with a grammar-based model of phase separation. Hypothesis 2b: Machine learning models trained on the harmonized, cross-database dataset constructed in Aim 1 will outperform models trained on any individual constituent database in predicting held-out material properties, demonstrating that synthesis itself generates scientific value beyond the sum of its parts. Hypothesis 2c: Interpretable model architectures (e.g., gradient-boosted trees with SHAP attribution, or attention-based sequence models) will recover previously proposed biophysical rules (e.g., stickers-and-spacers framework) while also revealing novel, previously unrecognized feature interactions.

Aim 3 – Disease Mapping and Cellular Vulnerability. Question: Do disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins preferentially localize to sequence regions predicted to control mesoscale material properties, and does resulting predicted property disruption correlate with cell-type-specific disease vulnerability? Hypothesis 3a: Pathogenic variants curated in ClinVar and COSMIC within condensate-associated proteins are significantly enriched, relative to benign variants and random sequence positions, in regions predicted by the Aim 2 models to shift material properties toward pathological extremes (aberrant hardening/aggregation or excessive dissolution). Hypothesis 3b: Cell types exhibiting the highest baseline expression and stoichiometric sensitivity of an affected condensate protein—derived from single-cell transcriptomic atlases—will show preferential association with corresponding disease phenotypes (e.g., neuronal vulnerability for ALS/FTD-linked RNA-binding proteins such as FUS and TDP-43; specific carcinoma subtypes for transcriptional coactivator condensates such as MED1/BRD4), providing a mechanistic bridge from molecular grammar to organismal disease outcome. Collectively, these hypotheses test whether a unifying, data-derived grammar can explain emergence across scales—from sequence to material property to phenotype—and whether such a grammar has practical predictive and translational utility.

[Methods and Approach]
Aim 1 (Months 1–10): We will construct a harmonized relational database anchored on UniProt accessions, integrating PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, MobiDB, and AlphaFold/ESMFold-derived structural predictions. A standardized ontology for condensate-relevant features (κ charge patterning via localCIDER, aromatic sticker density, IDR length/fraction, predicted secondary structure content) will be developed collaboratively by the biophysics and bioinformatics sub-teams, with cross-validation of feature calculations against original source publications. Automated ID-mapping and conflict-resolution pipelines (built in Python/Snakemake) will flag and adjudicate discrepant annotations, with manual curation by domain experts for high-impact edge cases. Output: a versioned, queryable harmonized dataset with full provenance tracking.

Aim 2 (Months 6–20): Using the harmonized feature set, we will extract quantitative mesoscale material property labels from imaging data—FRAP recovery curve fitting (mobile fraction, recovery half-time) from published datasets and OpenCell/HPA image repositories, condensate size and number distributions from high-content imaging, and reported multiphase architecture annotations. We will train and benchmark multiple model classes (gradient-boosted trees, random forests, and graph/sequence-based neural networks) using nested cross-validation stratified by protein family to prevent data leakage from homologous sequences. Model performance will be benchmarked against existing single-purpose predictors (e.g., catGRANULE, FuzDrop, PSPredictor). Interpretability will be assessed via SHAP value analysis and ablation studies to identify emergent, non-additive feature interactions. Independent held-out experimental datasets not used in training will serve as external validation.

Aim 3 (Months 14–28): Disease variants from ClinVar and COSMIC will be mapped onto condensate-relevant protein regions, and in silico mutagenesis will be performed using the Aim 2 models to predict property shifts induced by each variant. Enrichment of pathogenic variants in property-shifting regions will be assessed using permutation-based statistical tests against matched benign variant sets. Predicted molecular vulnerability will be cross-referenced with single-cell expression atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Tabula Sapiens) to construct a cell-type vulnerability index, with mechanistic case studies focused on neurodegeneration (FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1) and cancer (MED1, BRD4, NUP98 fusions).

Team and Timeline: The Working Group comprises co-investigators spanning polymer physics/biophysics, structural bioinformatics, quantitative cell imaging, clinical genomics, and data science, supplemented by embedded graduate students and postdocs assigned to cross-disciplinary sub-teams. An in-person kickoff meeting will establish shared standards; biweekly virtual working sessions and semi-annual hackathons will drive iterative integration across the 30-month project period, with NCEMS-provided computational infrastructure supporting shared data storage, version control, and reproducible pipeline execution (Snakemake/Nextflow, containerized via Docker).

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver: (1) a harmonized, FAIR-compliant, cross-database resource unifying condensate sequence, structural, imaging, and clinical annotations—the first of its kind—immediately reusable by the broader research community; (2) validated, interpretable machine learning models predicting emergent mesoscale material properties from sequence, packaged as an open-access web-based 'condensate property predictor' for hypothesis generation and experimental design; (3) a disease-variant vulnerability atlas linking condensate-disrupting mutations to cell-type-specific pathological risk, generating testable mechanistic hypotheses for neurodegeneration and cancer research communities; and (4) at least three to four peer-reviewed publications spanning methodological (data harmonization standards), discovery (grammar rules of phase separation), and translational (disease mapping) contributions.

Scientifically, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle—whether generalizable sequence-to-material-property rules exist for condensates—by leveraging synthesis at a scale unattainable by any individual laboratory. It will establish reusable ontological and computational standards for condensate data integration that can be extended to future datasets and adopted by database curators (e.g., PhaSepDB, MobiDB) to improve cross-resource interoperability community-wide. Translationally, the disease vulnerability atlas will provide a rational framework for prioritizing variants and cell types for experimental follow-up, accelerating hypothesis-driven wet-lab research in neurodegenerative disease and oncology. Trainees emerging from this Working Group will constitute a cohort fluent in both molecular biophysics and reproducible data science, directly advancing NCEMS's workforce development mission and seeding future collaborative, synthesis-driven research programs in mesoscale biology.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This Working Group is committed to full adherence to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles and NCEMS's community-endorsed open, team, and reproducible science policies. All harmonized datasets, feature-extraction code, trained model weights, and analysis pipelines will be version-controlled in public GitHub repositories with permanent archival snapshots deposited in Zenodo, each assigned a citable DOI. Code will be containerized using Docker/Singularity to guarantee computational reproducibility across environments, and workflows will be implemented in Snakemake/Nextflow to enable end-to-end re-execution by external users. Data provenance—including source database version, curation decisions, and conflict-resolution logic—will be transparently documented via structured metadata and changelogs, allowing full auditability of the harmonization process.

All software will be released under permissive open-source licenses (MIT/BSD), and curated datasets under CC-BY licensing to maximize reuse. Prior to major analyses, we will publicly pre-register model validation strategies (train/test splitting logic, performance metrics, and benchmarking comparators) via an open preprint or protocols repository to guard against overfitting and confirmation bias. Negative and null results—including feature combinations that fail to predict material properties—will be reported alongside positive findings to provide the community with a complete, unbiased view of the sequence-property landscape. The web-based condensate property predictor will be deployed with an open API to enable programmatic access and integration into other tools. Regular working group meetings will include reproducibility checkpoints, where sub-teams independently attempt to reproduce one another's pipeline outputs from raw harmonized data, ensuring internal validation before external release and modeling best practices for trainees in collaborative, reproducible synthesis science.

[Budget and Resources]
We request NCEMS support for a 30-month Working Group comprising five co-investigators (biophysics, structural bioinformatics, quantitative imaging, clinical genomics, and data science/machine learning), each supported at approximately 1 summer month per year to enable sustained engagement. Trainee support includes two full-time postdoctoral researchers (co-mentored across disciplinary sub-teams) and three graduate students (one per major institution/lab), embedded directly in cross-disciplinary pairs to fulfill NCEMS's training mission. A part-time data engineer (0.5 FTE) will support database harmonization infrastructure and pipeline maintenance beyond the expertise typically available in individual labs.

Computational resources include cloud computing credits for large-scale model training (GPU access for deep learning architectures) and data storage for harmonized multi-terabyte imaging and omics datasets, requested through NCEMS's shared computational infrastructure rather than duplicative institutional purchases. We request support for one in-person kickoff meeting (all co-investigators and trainees) and one mid-project synthesis workshop to consolidate cross-aim integration, plus travel for dissemination at one scientific conference per project year. Modest funds are requested for open-access publication fees and Zenodo/GitHub archival costs to support open science commitments.

This project explicitly requires NCEMS-level support rather than standard single-lab R01 mechanisms: no individual laboratory holds the combined domain expertise, cross-institutional data-sharing agreements, or computational infrastructure necessary to harmonize six-plus heterogeneous public databases and train validated predictive models at this scale. NCEMS's convening capacity, shared computational resources, and community-endorsed data standards are the critical enabling factors that transform this from an intractable individual-lab problem into a feasible, high-impact collaborative synthesis project.

Using this atlas, we will address three synthesis-driven questions: (1) What combinations of sequence grammar (charge patterning, aromatic residue spacing, RNA-binding motifs) and interactome topology best predict condensate formation propensity and material state across proteomes? (2) Do condensates exhibit conserved scaling laws or percolation-like thresholds relating molecular valency/concentration to emergent material properties, and are these principles conserved across cell types and species? (3) Can integrated molecular-to-imaging data reveal generalizable ‘emergence signatures’—quantitative markers that predict when a condensate transitions from a passive assembly to one with regulatory or catalytic function at the cellular level?

We will develop novel network-based and generative AI models trained on this synthesized cross-scale dataset, producing publicly available, reproducible pipelines (via containerized workflows and FAIR-compliant repositories) that the community can extend to new proteins or organisms. This project requires NCEMS support because it demands sustained, coordinated data harmonization across incompatible legacy databases maintained by distinct research communities, computational infrastructure for large-scale multi-modal integration, and structured collaboration between biophysics and cell biology groups that rarely co-author work. The initiative will provide hands-on training for graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data science, biophysical modeling, and open-science practices, producing a new generation of scientists equipped to study emergence phenomena computationally. Ultimately, this work will establish generalizable principles governing how molecular-scale interactions generate mesoscale cellular architecture—a foundational advance for predictive cell biology.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged as a central paradigm for understanding how cells organize biochemistry in space and time without membranes. From nucleoli and stress granules to transcriptional hubs and signaling puncta, condensates compartmentalize reactions, buffer concentrations, and enable rapid, reversible responses to cellular cues. Mechanistically, condensate formation is driven by multivalent, often weak interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded multivalent domains, and RNA—interactions that individually appear unremarkable but collectively produce phase-separated states with emergent material properties: viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, and selective permeability. This is a canonical mesoscale emergence problem: properties at the scale of hundreds to thousands of molecules cannot be extrapolated from single-molecule biophysics alone, yet they dictate cellular-scale outcomes including gene regulation, stress adaptation, and disease pathology (e.g., aberrant condensation in neurodegeneration and cancer). Over the past decade, the field has generated an extraordinary volume of public data addressing different facets of this problem. Curated databases such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, and PhaSePro catalog thousands of condensate-associated proteins with experimental annotations. Disorder- and sequence-feature repositories (MobiDB, DisProt) provide residue-level annotations of IDRs, charge patterning, and low-complexity domains. Interactome resources (BioGRID, STRING, RNAct) capture protein-protein and protein-RNA connectivity relevant to multivalent scaffold-client architectures. Imaging consortia (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting) offer proteome-scale subcellular localization and morphology data, while emerging cryo-electron tomography repositories (EMPIAR, CZ Imaging Institute) reveal native, high-resolution architecture of condensates in situ. Despite this wealth of data, no synthesis has integrated sequence grammar, interaction topology, biophysical material properties, and cellular imaging/tomography into a unified, queryable framework. This fragmentation is not a matter of insufficient data but of insufficient integration: each data type is curated by a distinct scientific subculture (biophysics, structural biology, cell biology, computational biology) using incompatible ontologies, units, and quality standards. Consequently, foundational questions remain unresolved—whether sequence-encoded 'grammar' generalizes across proteomes, whether condensates obey universal physical scaling laws, and whether measurable molecular signatures predict functional transition points. Addressing these questions requires exactly the kind of community-scale synthesis NCEMS is designed to catalyze: harmonizing heterogeneous legacy databases, building shared computational infrastructure, and uniting biophysicists, structural biologists, cell biologists, and data scientists who rarely collaborate directly. The significance extends beyond condensate biology narrowly construed; establishing generalizable principles of molecular-to-mesoscale emergence would provide a template for predictive, quantitative cell biology applicable to other self-organizing cellular structures, while directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around three interlocking synthesis-driven research questions, each requiring integration across data modalities that no single dataset or laboratory currently combines. Question 1: What combinations of sequence grammar and interactome topology best predict condensate formation propensity and material state across proteomes? We hypothesize that condensate-forming proteins exhibit statistically distinct, quantifiable sequence signatures—specific patterns of charge blockiness, aromatic residue spacing, and RNA-binding motif density—that interact combinatorially with interactome valency (number and strength of protein-protein/protein-RNA connections) to determine both the likelihood of phase separation and the resulting material state (liquid, gel, solid, or multiphasic). We predict that models integrating sequence and network features will substantially outperform sequence-only or network-only predictors, revealing synergistic, non-additive relationships consistent with emergent behavior. Question 2: Do condensates exhibit conserved scaling laws or percolation-like thresholds relating molecular valency and concentration to emergent material properties, and are these conserved across cell types and species? Drawing on polymer physics and percolation theory, we hypothesize that condensate viscosity, exchange dynamics (as measured by FRAP recovery rates), and multiphasic organization follow predictable scaling relationships with scaffold valency and local concentration, and that these relationships are conserved across human, yeast, and other model organism datasets despite divergent sequences—implying that physical principles, rather than specific sequence identity, govern mesoscale material properties. We further hypothesize the existence of sharp, percolation-like transition thresholds beyond which small increases in valency or concentration produce disproportionate changes in material state, a hallmark of emergent phase transitions. Question 3: Can integrated molecular-to-imaging data reveal generalizable 'emergence signatures' that predict when a condensate transitions from passive assembly to regulatory or catalytic function? We hypothesize that condensates with regulatory or catalytic roles (e.g., transcriptional condensates, stress granules with signaling function) exhibit distinguishing multi-scale signatures—combinations of specific sequence motifs, interactome centrality, characteristic material properties, and imaging-derived morphological features (size, shape irregularity, multiphase substructure visible in cryo-ET)—that differ systematically from condensates that are compositionally similar but functionally passive or purely storage-related. These hypotheses are directly testable using existing public data but require synthesis at a scale and cross-disciplinary depth beyond individual labs: sequence-feature extraction demands computational biophysics expertise, interactome analysis demands network science, material-property interpretation demands soft-matter biophysics, and imaging/tomography interpretation demands structural cell biology. No existing resource links these layers, and hypothesis testing requires simultaneous access to and harmonization of all four data types across shared protein/gene identifiers, organisms, and experimental conditions—precisely the kind of integrative challenge that defines community-scale synthesis science and that motivates our request for NCEMS support.

[Methods and Approach]
Our approach proceeds in four coordinated phases over a two-year Working Group engagement, leveraging in-person and virtual synthesis meetings characteristic of NCEMS working groups. Phase 1 (Months 1–6): Data Harmonization and Atlas Construction. We will systematically extract and cross-reference records from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, and PhaSePro (condensate annotations), MobiDB and DisProt (disorder/sequence features), BioGRID, STRING, and RNAct (interactomes), and Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, and Cell Painting (imaging), alongside cryo-ET datasets from EMPIAR and CZ Imaging Institute. Using UniProt and organism-specific gene identifiers as anchors, we will build a unified relational schema with standardized ontologies for material-property terms (viscosity, FRAP recovery rate, partition coefficient) and imaging metadata. Data quality flags, provenance tracking, and version control will be implemented via a FAIR-compliant database architecture. Phase 2 (Months 4–12): Feature Engineering and Statistical Synthesis. Sequence features (charge patterning via kappa/Omega parameters, aromatic spacing, RNA-binding motif scores) will be computed computationally; interactome features (degree, betweenness centrality, clustering coefficient) will be derived from network analysis; material-property data will be normalized across experimental conditions using meta-analytic techniques to account for cross-study heterogeneity. This phase directly addresses Question 1 through regression and classification models (gradient-boosted trees, random forests) predicting condensate propensity and material state from combined feature sets, with rigorous cross-validation stratified by protein family to avoid data leakage. Phase 3 (Months 10–18): Physical Modeling and Scaling Analysis. To address Question 2, we will apply polymer-physics-informed statistical models to test for scaling relationships and percolation thresholds between valency/concentration metrics and material properties, using comparative analysis across human, yeast, and model organism subsets of the atlas. Bootstrap resampling and Bayesian hierarchical modeling will assess conservation of scaling exponents across species. Phase 4 (Months 14–24): Multi-Modal Emergence Signature Discovery. Addressing Question 3, we will develop graph neural network and generative AI architectures that integrate sequence, interactome, material-property, and imaging-derived morphological features to classify condensates by functional category (regulatory/catalytic vs. passive/storage) as annotated in the literature and imaging databases. Model interpretability methods (SHAP, attention-weight analysis) will identify candidate emergence signatures for experimental follow-up by community collaborators. Throughout, biweekly working group meetings, in-person hackathon-style synthesis workshops hosted at NCEMS, and shared computational infrastructure (cloud computing allocation, containerized environments) will support iterative, transdisciplinary refinement of methods and interpretation, ensuring biophysical plausibility is continuously validated against cell-biological and structural expertise within the team.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver a publicly available, richly annotated Mesoscale Condensate Atlas integrating sequence, interactome, biophysical, and imaging/tomography data—a first-of-its-kind resource enabling future hypothesis generation across the condensate biology community. We expect to produce validated predictive models linking sequence grammar and interactome topology to condensate formation and material state, quantitative evidence for or against conserved scaling/percolation laws governing condensate physics across species, and a novel set of candidate 'emergence signatures' distinguishing functional from passive condensates. These outcomes will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications co-authored across disciplinary lines, open-source software packages, and interactive web-based atlas tools enabling researchers to query cross-modal condensate data without specialized computational expertise. Scientifically, this work will resolve long-standing ambiguity about whether condensate behavior is idiosyncratic per protein or governed by generalizable physical/sequence principles—a foundational question for predictive cell biology and for understanding mesoscale emergence broadly. Translationally, identified sequence-material-function relationships may inform biomarker discovery for condensate-associated diseases (ALS, FTD, certain cancers) and guide synthetic biology efforts to engineer condensates with designed properties. Methodologically, the multi-modal integration pipelines developed here will serve as templates for synthesizing other mesoscale phenomena beyond condensates, directly advancing NCEMS's broader mission. By training graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary synthesis methods, the project will cultivate a cohort of researchers fluent in both wet-lab biophysical reasoning and computational data science—addressing NCEMS's workforce development goals while producing durable, reusable community resources that outlast the funding period itself.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This Working Group is committed to open science as a foundational operating principle, not an afterthought. All harmonized datasets comprising the Mesoscale Condensate Atlas will be deposited in a public, version-controlled repository (e.g., Zenodo or a dedicated NCEMS-hosted data commons) with persistent identifiers, comprehensive metadata, and explicit provenance tracking linking each record to its original source database and access date. All code—including data harmonization scripts, feature-engineering pipelines, statistical models, and machine-learning architectures—will be developed in public GitHub repositories under permissive open-source licenses (MIT or Apache 2.0), with continuous integration testing to ensure functionality is maintained as dependencies evolve. Computational workflows will be containerized (Docker/Singularity) and orchestrated using workflow management systems (Snakemake or Nextflow) to guarantee exact reproducibility of all analyses on independent computing environments, including cloud platforms accessible to the broader community. We will adhere to FAIR data principles throughout, ensuring atlas contents are Findable via searchable indices, Accessible without paywall restrictions, Interoperable through standardized ontologies and file formats, and Reusable through explicit licensing and documentation. Preregistration of key hypotheses (particularly for Questions 2 and 3) will be submitted to a public repository (OSF) prior to confirmatory analyses, distinguishing exploratory from confirmatory findings. All intermediate and final model outputs, including trained model weights and evaluation metrics, will be shared publicly to enable independent verification and extension. We will follow emerging community-created policies on team science, including transparent authorship criteria established at the outset of the collaboration, credit for data generators whose original datasets are synthesized, and structured data/code review checkpoints before public release. Regular synthesis meetings will include explicit reproducibility checks, where team members outside the original analysis pipeline attempt to reproduce key results from shared code and data, catching errors before publication and modeling best practices for trainees.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests NCEMS support for a two-year Working Group comprising approximately 8–10 core investigators spanning soft-matter biophysics, structural/cryo-EM biology, cell biology, and machine learning/data science, plus 4–6 trainees (graduate students and postdocs) embedded across partner labs. Primary budget needs include: (1) Personnel support for a dedicated postdoctoral data scientist (1.0 FTE, two years) to lead database harmonization and pipeline development, ensuring continuity across the distributed team; (2) Partial salary support (0.1–0.2 FTE) for each of 8–10 co-investigators to enable sustained engagement in synthesis meetings, model development, and manuscript preparation beyond typical service commitments; (3) Graduate student/postdoc trainee stipend support (2–3 positions, partial funding) to enable hands-on training in cross-disciplinary synthesis methods; (4) Computational infrastructure costs, including cloud computing credits (AWS/Google Cloud) for large-scale multi-modal data integration, model training (particularly graph neural network and generative AI architectures requiring GPU resources), and public-facing atlas hosting; (5) Travel support for 3–4 in-person working group synthesis meetings/hackathons per year, critical for the iterative, trust-building collaboration required across biophysics and cell biology communities that rarely co-author work; (6) Publication costs including open-access fees for resulting manuscripts and data-descriptor papers. We anticipate leveraging NCEMS-provided shared computational infrastructure and data science support staff where available, reducing redundant institutional overhead. This budget structure reflects the explicit rationale for NCEMS support: the project's scope—harmonizing incompatible legacy databases across four distinct scientific communities, sustaining transdisciplinary collaboration among biophysicists and cell biologists, and building/maintaining shared computational infrastructure and public atlas tools—exceeds what any individual lab's standard R01-style budget could support, justifying the coordinated, center-level investment requested here.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) give rise to material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that cannot be predicted from single-molecule biophysics alone. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data—spanning sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE), structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB, disorder predictors like MobiDB), interactome data (BioGRID, IntAct, STRING), live-cell imaging datasets with FRAP/partition coefficients reported in hundreds of primary papers, and disease-variant repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC)—no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features generate emergent mesoscale properties and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists because no single lab possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, machine learning, and cell biology, nor the bandwidth to curate and harmonize the fragmented, heterogeneous data across dozens of independent studies using inconsistent experimental conditions and metrics.

We propose a Working Group to build an integrated, machine-learning-ready meta-resource and mechanistic model connecting three data tiers: (1) molecular grammar (IDR composition, charge patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs, stoichiometry from proteomics/interactome data), (2) mesoscale material properties (extracted via natural language processing and manual curation from published FRAP recovery curves, partition coefficients, and turbidity/phase diagrams), and (3) cellular/organismal outcomes (localization data from the Human Protein Atlas, disease-associated mutations, and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic correlates of condensate dysregulation in cancer and neurodegeneration cohorts). Using this harmonized dataset, we will develop interpretable machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating sequence, structure, and interaction features) to predict emergent condensate properties from molecular composition, and test whether specific 'grammar motifs' generalize across unrelated protein families and species—a question unanswerable without large-scale cross-dataset synthesis.

The project requires collaboration among biophysicists specializing in LLPS thermodynamics, structural bioinformaticians, data scientists skilled in NLP-based literature mining, cell biologists with condensate imaging expertise, and clinical genomics researchers—expertise no single lab combines. NCEMS support is essential for data harmonization infrastructure, computational resources for large-scale model training, and coordination across geographically distributed teams. All curated datasets, ontologies for condensate property annotation, and trained models will be released as an open, FAIR-compliant resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with reproducible workflows (Snakemake/Nextflow), enabling community reuse. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams, receiving hands-on training in data harmonization, ML model development, and biophysical interpretation—directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop. This synthesis will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology: how simple molecular rules generate the astonishing diversity of condensate behaviors and their roles in health and disease, while establishing a generalizable template for data-driven discovery of emergent properties in other mesoscale biological systems.
