Sequence-centric resources (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE) catalog phase-separating proteins and their sequence features; structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB, DisProt) provide disorder and structural context; interactome databases (BioGRID, IntAct, STRING) capture the multivalent partner networks driving condensation; thousands of primary publications report FRAP recovery curves, partition coefficients, and turbidity/phase diagrams that quantify mesoscale material properties; and clinical repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) plus imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas) link condensate-associated proteins to disease variants and subcellular localization. Yet these resources remain siloed, use inconsistent experimental conditions, nomenclature, and metrics, and have never been harmonized into a single analytical framework capable of testing whether generalizable 'grammar motifs' predict emergent material behavior across unrelated protein families, species, and disease contexts.

This fragmentation is not merely a data-management inconvenience; it reflects a genuine epistemic barrier. No single laboratory possesses simultaneously the LLPS thermodynamics expertise to interpret phase diagrams, the structural bioinformatics skill to encode IDR and PTM features, the NLP and machine learning capacity to mine and harmonize heterogeneous literature-derived measurements, the cell biology expertise to validate emergent predictions against live-cell imaging, and the clinical genomics knowledge to connect condensate dysregulation to disease. The problem is precisely the kind of community-scale synthesis challenge NCEMS was created to address: it requires no new experiments, relies entirely on integrating existing public data, exceeds the capacity of any individual lab or existing bilateral collaboration, and demands convergent expertise from distinct disciplines to yield insights unattainable through disciplinary silos.

Resolving this puzzle would have significance far beyond condensate biology. Establishing a validated, generalizable mapping from molecular sequence grammar to emergent mesoscale material properties would provide a template methodology applicable to other mesoscale phenomena central to NCEMS's mission—such as membrane microdomain formation, cytoskeletal self-organization, and macromolecular complex assembly—thereby advancing the Center's broader scientific vision of understanding emergence across scales of biological organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching question and three tractable sub-questions that collectively require cross-database synthesis and cannot be answered by any single dataset or laboratory in isolation.

Overarching Question: Can a generalizable 'molecular grammar'—defined by IDR sequence composition, charge patterning, PTM occupancy, RNA-binding motifs, and interaction stoichiometry—predict emergent mesoscale material properties of biomolecular condensates and their downstream cellular/disease phenotypes across unrelated protein families and species?

Sub-Question 1 (Molecular-to-Mesoscale Mapping): Do quantitative sequence-derived features (e.g., patterning of aromatic and charged residues, PTM density, disorder content) systematically predict mesoscale material properties (viscosity, surface tension, partition coefficient, aging propensity) extracted from heterogeneous published biophysical measurements? We hypothesize that a constrained set of interpretable sequence-grammar features—rather than full-length sequence identity—will explain a substantial and statistically significant proportion of variance in material properties across condensate systems, reflecting convergent physicochemical rules rather than family-specific idiosyncrasies. This hypothesis is testable only by aggregating material-property measurements across dozens of independently published, non-standardized studies—a synthesis task requiring shared curation standards and NLP-assisted literature mining beyond single-lab capacity.

Sub-Question 2 (Cross-Family and Cross-Species Generalization): Do 'grammar motifs' identified in well-studied model condensate proteins (e.g., FUS, hnRNPA1, DDX4) generalize to predict phase behavior in unrelated, less-studied protein families and non-human species represented in existing databases? We hypothesize that grammar motifs generalize partially: core physicochemical rules (charge patterning, aromatic spacing) will transfer broadly, while RNA-dependent and PTM-dependent modulatory rules will show family- and lineage-specific divergence. Testing this requires integrating sequence and structural databases across taxonomic breadth, which no single existing dataset provides.

Sub-Question 3 (Mesoscale-to-Phenotype Linkage): Do disease-associated mutations and altered post-translational modification states in condensate-forming proteins produce predictable shifts in modeled material properties that correlate with reported cellular localization changes and disease phenotypes (cancer, neurodegeneration)? We hypothesize that pathogenic variants disproportionately cluster in sequence regions our models identify as material-property-determining 'hotspots,' and that predicted property shifts (e.g., increased viscosity, aberrant hardening) correlate with disease-associated aggregation phenotypes reported in imaging and clinical-variant databases.

Collectively, these questions test whether emergence at the mesoscale—the appearance of material properties not predictable from individual molecular features—nonetheless obeys learnable, generalizable rules when sufficient data are integrated. Confirming generalizable grammar motifs would represent a fundamental conceptual advance, establishing that mesoscale material behavior is a tractable, predictable emergent property rather than an intractable case-by-case phenomenon. Rejecting generalization, or finding strong family/species specificity, would itself be a significant and publishable finding, redirecting the field toward context-dependent mechanistic models. Both outcomes require exactly the kind of large-scale, cross-database, multidisciplinary synthesis this Working Group is designed to execute, and neither could be rigorously addressed using any single existing dataset or the resources of one laboratory.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will execute a three-phase synthesis pipeline over the project period, structured around monthly full-group meetings and biweekly subteam sprints.

Phase 1 – Data Harmonization Infrastructure (Months 1–6): We will construct a unified relational schema linking three data tiers. Tier 1 (molecular grammar) will aggregate sequence, disorder, and PTM annotations from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE, MobiDB, DisProt, AlphaFold DB, and PDB, computing standardized features (charge patterning parameters such as kappa/Omega, aromatic residue spacing, PTM site density, RNA-binding motif presence) using established biophysical descriptors. Tier 2 (mesoscale material properties) will be built through a hybrid NLP–manual curation pipeline: a transformer-based literature-mining tool will screen primary LLPS publications to extract FRAP recovery constants, partition coefficients, and turbidity/phase-diagram parameters, with all automated extractions verified by trained curators using a double-annotation protocol with adjudicated discrepancy resolution to ensure data quality. Tier 3 (cellular/disease outcomes) will integrate Human Protein Atlas localization data, ClinVar/COSMIC variant annotations, and publicly available single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic datasets from cancer and neurodegeneration cohorts, cross-referenced to condensate-associated proteins. A shared ontology for condensate property annotation will be co-developed by biophysics and bioinformatics subteams to ensure semantic interoperability across tiers.

Phase 2 – Model Development (Months 5–14): Using the harmonized dataset, we will develop interpretable graph neural network (GNN) architectures in which nodes represent sequence/structural features and interaction partners, and edges represent physicochemical or empirical interaction data. Models will be trained to predict Tier 2 material properties from Tier 1 features, with architecture choices (GNN versus gradient-boosted trees versus attention-based sequence models) benchmarked for both predictive performance and interpretability using SHAP-based feature attribution. Cross-validation will be stratified by protein family and species to directly test generalization (Sub-Question 2). Held-out validation sets will include recently published condensate systems not used in training.

Phase 3 – Phenotype Integration and Validation (Months 12–20): Model-derived material-property predictions will be mapped onto Tier 3 disease-variant and localization data to test Sub-Question 3, using statistical enrichment analyses (e.g., permutation tests for mutation clustering in predicted hotspot regions) and correlation analyses linking predicted property shifts to reported phenotypic outcomes.

Throughout, subteams organized by expertise (biophysics, structural bioinformatics, NLP/ML, cell biology, clinical genomics) will co-lead specific data tiers while participating in cross-cutting integration sprints, ensuring methodological rigor is checked across disciplinary boundaries. All curation decisions, feature engineering choices, and model hyperparameters will be version-controlled and logged for reproducibility.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will produce four concrete deliverables. First, a harmonized, FAIR-compliant meta-database integrating sequence, structural, material-property, and phenotypic data for condensate-forming proteins, filling a critical infrastructure gap for the field. Second, a validated, interpretable machine learning framework capable of predicting emergent mesoscale material properties from molecular sequence grammar, accompanied by explicit quantification of generalization limits across protein families and species. Third, a set of testable mechanistic hypotheses linking specific grammar motifs to disease-associated condensate dysregulation, providing hypothesis-generating value for downstream experimental labs in cancer and neurodegeneration research. Fourth, a generalizable methodological template—spanning literature-mining pipelines, ontology design, and cross-tier data integration—that other NCEMS working groups can adapt to different mesoscale emergence problems.

Scientifically, this project will resolve whether mesoscale material behavior in condensates follows generalizable physicochemical rules or is predominantly context-specific, a question of fundamental importance to the mesoscale emergence framework central to NCEMS's mission. Practically, the resource will accelerate hypothesis generation for the broader LLPS research community, reducing redundant literature curation efforts across dozens of individual labs. Translationally, identification of grammar-motif-disease correlations may inform biomarker or therapeutic target prioritization in condensate-associated pathologies such as ALS, frontotemporal dementia, and specific cancers.

Beyond immediate scientific outputs, the project will demonstrably advance NCEMS's workforce and community goals: trainees will gain rare cross-disciplinary experience spanning biophysics, bioinformatics, and machine learning, while the open-access resource and reproducible workflows will lower barriers for future researchers, including those at institutions with limited computational infrastructure, to engage with mesoscale synthesis science.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This Working Group commits fully to NCEMS's open science principles across data, code, and workflow dimensions. All curated datasets—including harmonized molecular grammar features, extracted mesoscale material-property measurements, and integrated phenotype annotations—will be deposited in Zenodo with persistent DOIs and full metadata compliant with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) standards. The condensate-property annotation ontology developed during Phase 1 will be published as a standalone, versioned community resource to enable consistent future annotation efforts beyond this project.

All code, including NLP extraction pipelines, feature engineering scripts, and machine learning model implementations, will be maintained in public GitHub repositories under permissive open-source licenses, with comprehensive documentation enabling independent reuse. Computational workflows will be containerized and orchestrated using Snakemake or Nextflow to ensure exact reproducibility of data processing and model training pipelines across computing environments, with continuous integration testing to verify pipeline stability as the codebase evolves.

To support reproducible science practices, we will adopt pre-registration of the primary hypotheses and analysis plans described in this proposal via an open repository (e.g., OSF) prior to full-scale model training, distinguishing confirmatory analyses from exploratory findings. Model performance benchmarks, including held-out validation results and generalization tests across protein families and species, will be reported transparently regardless of outcome, including negative or partial-generalization results central to Sub-Question 2.

Data curation protocols, including double-annotation and adjudication procedures for NLP-extracted measurements, will themselves be documented and released, enabling other groups to extend or audit the curation process. Regular working group meetings will include explicit review of open-science compliance milestones, and a designated open-science coordinator within the team will oversee timely deposition of intermediate and final products, ensuring that reproducibility is maintained throughout the project lifecycle rather than addressed only at completion.

[Budget and Resources]
This Working Group requests NCEMS support across four categories consistent with a community-scale synthesis effort. Personnel support will fund a project coordinator/data scientist (50% FTE) to manage cross-tier data harmonization and pipeline maintenance, plus partial salary support (20–30% FTE) for two graduate students and two postdoctoral researchers embedded across subteams, ensuring hands-on training as specified in NCEMS's workforce development goals. Computational resources will include cloud/HPC allocation for large-scale GNN model training, literature-mining NLP pipeline execution, and storage for the harmonized multi-tier database (estimated 5–10 TB), leveraging NCEMS computational infrastructure where available to minimize redundant institutional costs.

Travel and coordination funds will support two in-person Working Group meetings annually to facilitate cross-disciplinary integration that is difficult to achieve remotely, particularly for resolving ontology design disagreements and validating biophysical interpretability of model outputs, plus virtual meeting infrastructure for biweekly subteam sprints given the geographically distributed team spanning biophysics, bioinformatics, cell biology, and clinical genomics expertise across multiple institutions.

Data curation costs will support trained curator time (potentially including undergraduate research assistants under postdoc supervision) for the double-annotation NLP-extraction verification protocol described in Methods, a labor-intensive but essential quality-control step given the heterogeneity of source literature.

Critically, this budget reflects tasks that exceed single-lab capacity: no individual grant currently funds the cross-institutional coordination, shared computational infrastructure, or dedicated curation labor required to harmonize dozens of independent, inconsistently reported datasets. NCEMS support is specifically requested for the coordination infrastructure and computational scale that transforms fragmented public data into a unified, reusable community resource, consistent with NCEMS's mandate to support synthesis work that goes beyond what existing collaborations or individual laboratories can accomplish independently.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) give rise to material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that cannot be predicted from single-molecule biophysics alone. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data—spanning sequence databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE), structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB, disorder predictors like MobiDB), interactome data (BioGRID, IntAct, STRING), live-cell imaging datasets with FRAP/partition coefficients reported in hundreds of primary papers, and disease-variant repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC)—no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features generate emergent mesoscale properties and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists because no single lab possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, machine learning, and cell biology, nor the bandwidth to curate and harmonize the fragmented, heterogeneous data across dozens of independent studies using inconsistent experimental conditions and metrics.

We propose a Working Group to build an integrated, machine-learning-ready meta-resource and mechanistic model connecting three data tiers: (1) molecular grammar (IDR composition, charge patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs, stoichiometry from proteomics/interactome data), (2) mesoscale material properties (extracted via natural language processing and manual curation from published FRAP recovery curves, partition coefficients, and turbidity/phase diagrams), and (3) cellular/organismal outcomes (localization data from the Human Protein Atlas, disease-associated mutations, and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic correlates of condensate dysregulation in cancer and neurodegeneration cohorts). Using this harmonized dataset, we will develop interpretable machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating sequence, structure, and interaction features) to predict emergent condensate properties from molecular composition, and test whether specific 'grammar motifs' generalize across unrelated protein families and species—a question unanswerable without large-scale cross-dataset synthesis.

The project requires collaboration among biophysicists specializing in LLPS thermodynamics, structural bioinformaticians, data scientists skilled in NLP-based literature mining, cell biologists with condensate imaging expertise, and clinical genomics researchers—expertise no single lab combines. NCEMS support is essential for data harmonization infrastructure, computational resources for large-scale model training, and coordination across geographically distributed teams. All curated datasets, ontologies for condensate property annotation, and trained models will be released as an open, FAIR-compliant resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with reproducible workflows (Snakemake/Nextflow), enabling community reuse. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams, receiving hands-on training in data harmonization, ML model development, and biophysical interpretation—directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop. This synthesis will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology: how simple molecular rules generate the astonishing diversity of condensate behaviors and their roles in health and disease, while establishing a generalizable template for data-driven discovery of emergent properties in other mesoscale biological systems.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where local biomolecular interactions give rise to system-level properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that dictate cellular function in transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets, no unified framework connects the molecular determinants of phase behavior (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalent 'sticker-spacer' motifs, post-translational modifications) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences. This gap persists because relevant data are scattered across incompatible resources: sequence/structure databases (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB), condensate-specific repositories (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), post-translational modification atlases (PhosphoSitePlus), protein abundance/localization maps (Human Protein Atlas, PaxDb), and heterogeneous imaging/biophysical measurements (FRAP recovery curves, single-molecule tracking, cryo-electron tomography from EMPIAR). No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, network science, and machine learning required to harmonize these disparate data types into a predictive, mechanistic framework.

This Working Group will assemble condensate biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and machine learning experts to build an integrated, open-access resource—the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA)—that links molecular-scale features to mesoscale phase behavior and cellular outcomes. We will: (1) curate and cross-reference sequence-based determinants (disorder content, charge patterning, aromatic sticker density) with experimentally reported condensate material properties (liquid, gel, solid; FRAP-derived mobile fractions; concentration-dependent phase boundaries); (2) integrate interactome and stoichiometry data to model condensates as emergent network phenomena, testing whether percolation-like thresholds in interaction valency predict phase transition points; (3) incorporate PTM and cellular context data (abundance, localization, cell-type specificity) to explain condition-dependent condensate emergence versus dissolution; and (4) apply supervised and unsupervised machine learning to identify generalizable 'rules' distinguishing functional condensates from aberrant aggregates linked to disease (e.g., neurodegeneration-associated solidification).

A central scientific question we will address: Can mesoscale material properties of condensates be predicted from molecular-scale sequence and interaction features alone, or do emergent properties require irreducible knowledge of cellular context (concentration, crowding, PTM state)? Answering this tests fundamental assumptions about reductionism versus emergence in molecular systems biology.

This project is infeasible for any single lab given the scale of cross-database harmonization, the breadth of required expertise, and the need for standardized ontologies bridging biophysics and cell biology communities. NCEMS support will fund coordinated data-wrangling sprints, shared computational infrastructure, and workshops to establish community standards for condensate data annotation. All curated datasets, harmonization pipelines, and predictive models will be released under FAIR principles via a public repository and interactive web tool. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and machine learning—directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will yield a generalizable framework for predicting mesoscale emergent properties from molecular data, with broad applicability beyond condensates to other emergent cellular phenomena.

[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where local biomolecular interactions give rise to system-level properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that dictate cellular function in transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets, no unified framework connects the molecular determinants of phase behavior (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalent 'sticker-spacer' motifs, post-translational modifications) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences. This gap persists because relevant data are scattered across incompatible resources: sequence/structure databases (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB), condensate-specific repositories (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), post-translational modification atlases (PhosphoSitePlus), protein abundance/localization maps (Human Protein Atlas, PaxDb), and heterogeneous imaging/biophysical measurements (FRAP recovery curves, single-molecule tracking, cryo-electron tomography from EMPIAR). No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, network science, and machine learning required to harmonize these disparate data types into a predictive, mechanistic framework.

This Working Group will assemble condensate biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and machine learning experts to build an integrated, open-access resource—the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA)—that links molecular-scale features to mesoscale phase behavior and cellular outcomes. We will: (1) curate and cross-reference sequence-based determinants (disorder content, charge patterning, aromatic sticker density) with experimentally reported condensate material properties (liquid, gel, solid; FRAP-derived mobile fractions; concentration-dependent phase boundaries); (2) integrate interactome and stoichiometry data to model condensates as emergent network phenomena, testing whether percolation-like thresholds in interaction valency predict phase transition points; (3) incorporate PTM and cellular context data (abundance, localization, cell-type specificity) to explain condition-dependent condensate emergence versus dissolution; and (4) apply supervised and unsupervised machine learning to identify generalizable 'rules' distinguishing functional condensates from aberrant aggregates linked to disease (e.g., neurodegeneration-associated solidification).

A central scientific question we will address: Can mesoscale material properties of condensates be predicted from molecular-scale sequence and interaction features alone, or do emergent properties require irreducible knowledge of cellular context (concentration, crowding, PTM state)? Answering this tests fundamental assumptions about reductionism versus emergence in molecular systems biology.

This project is infeasible for any single lab given the scale of cross-database harmonization, the breadth of required expertise, and the need for standardized ontologies bridging biophysics and cell biology communities. NCEMS support will fund coordinated data-wrangling sprints, shared computational infrastructure, and workshops to establish community standards for condensate data annotation. All curated datasets, harmonization pipelines, and predictive models will be released under FAIR principles via a public repository and interactive web tool. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and machine learning—directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will yield a generalizable framework for predicting mesoscale emergent properties from molecular data, with broad applicability beyond condensates to other emergent cellular phenomena.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged over the past decade as a fundamental organizing principle of cellular biochemistry, compartmentalizing reactions, buffering signaling networks, and responding dynamically to stress without the constraints of lipid membranes. Their formation via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represents a canonical case of mesoscale emergence: molecular-scale interactions among biomolecules—multivalent 'sticker-spacer' motifs within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), aromatic pi-stacking, electrostatic complementarity, and post-translational modifications (PTMs)—collectively give rise to system-level material properties such as viscosity, surface tension, and exchange dynamics that are not trivially predictable from any single molecular feature in isolation. These emergent material properties, in turn, determine higher-order cellular outcomes, including transcriptional bursting, stress granule dynamics, and pathological aggregation implicated in neurodegenerative disease. Understanding how molecular grammar dictates mesoscale phase behavior is therefore not merely a biophysical curiosity but a question central to cellular function and dysfunction. Over the past decade, the field has generated an extraordinary volume of heterogeneous data: sequence and structural resources (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB) characterize disorder and putative sticker motifs; condensate-specific databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE) catalog experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and their reported behaviors; interactome resources (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct) map the physical and functional networks in which condensate components participate; PTM atlases (PhosphoSitePlus) document the modifications known to tune phase behavior; protein abundance and localization maps (Human Protein Atlas, PaxDb) provide cellular context; and imaging/biophysical repositories (FRAP time-series, single-molecule tracking datasets, cryo-electron tomography in EMPIAR) capture the material and structural consequences of condensate formation in situ. Despite this wealth of data, no integrated framework exists that systematically links molecular determinants to emergent material properties and downstream cellular phenotypes. This fragmentation arises because these data types were generated by distinct scientific communities using incompatible vocabularies, formats, and quality standards—biophysicists reporting FRAP mobile fractions rarely cross-reference network topology; structural bioinformaticians annotating IDRs rarely incorporate PTM state; cell biologists documenting condensate function rarely quantify material properties in standardized units. The result is a fundamental knowledge gap: the field lacks a predictive, mechanistic understanding of when and why condensates form, adopt particular material states, and transition between functional and pathological behavior. This gap directly instantiates the emergence problem that motivates NCEMS's mission—understanding how system-level properties arise unpredictably from lower-scale composition—and is precisely the kind of problem that single laboratories, however expert, cannot resolve alone. Solving it requires simultaneous fluency in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, network science, cell biology, and machine learning, combined with the infrastructure to harmonize dozens of disparate public resources. This proposal directly addresses that gap by synthesizing existing condensate-relevant data into an integrated, predictive, and reusable resource, advancing both fundamental understanding of mesoscale emergence and the practical tools needed to anticipate condensate behavior in health and disease.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching scientific question, with four component sub-questions and associated hypotheses that structure the synthesis effort. Overarching question: Can the mesoscale material properties of biomolecular condensates be predicted from molecular-scale sequence and interaction features alone, or do they require irreducible knowledge of cellular context? This question probes whether condensate emergence is fundamentally reducible to molecular grammar or whether higher-scale contextual information constitutes genuinely emergent, non-reducible determinants—a question of broad relevance to molecular systems biology beyond condensates. Sub-question 1 (Sequence-to-material mapping): Do quantifiable sequence features—disorder content, charge patterning (kappa/Omega), aromatic sticker density, and motif spacing—predict experimentally measured material properties (liquid versus gel versus solid state, FRAP-derived mobile fractions, saturation concentrations)? We hypothesize that sticker valency and spacer flexibility jointly predict a continuum of material states, with high sticker density and low spacer flexibility correlating with gel/solid transitions, but that predictive power will be substantially incomplete without concentration and crowding information, revealing a quantifiable 'emergence gap' attributable to context. Sub-question 2 (Network-level percolation): Can condensates be modeled as emergent percolation phenomena in interaction networks, such that measurable thresholds in interactome valency and stoichiometry predict observed phase transition points? We hypothesize that proteins participating in condensates will show interaction network topologies consistent with percolation near critical valency thresholds, and that deviation from predicted percolation thresholds will correlate with additional regulatory inputs (e.g., PTMs, chaperones) not captured by network topology alone. Sub-question 3 (Contextual modulation): Do PTM state, cellular abundance, and subcellular localization data explain condition-dependent condensate emergence and dissolution that sequence and network features fail to capture? We hypothesize that incorporating PTM and abundance data will significantly improve predictive accuracy for condition-specific condensate behavior (e.g., stress-induced assembly, cell-cycle-dependent dissolution) beyond models built from sequence and interactome data alone, providing direct evidence for context-dependent emergence. Sub-question 4 (Functional versus pathological classification): Can machine learning models trained on the integrated dataset distinguish functional, reversible condensates from disease-associated, aberrantly solidified aggregates, and what features most strongly discriminate these classes? We hypothesize that a combination of aging-related biophysical signatures (declining mobile fraction over time), specific low-complexity aromatic-rich kinked segment (LARKS) motifs, and reduced chaperone/network connectivity will jointly discriminate pathological aggregation from functional phase separation, offering candidate biomarkers and intervention points for neurodegenerative disease research. Collectively, these questions test the boundary between molecular reductionism and mesoscale emergence, generating a quantitative, falsifiable account of when molecular-scale information suffices to predict system-level condensate behavior and when it does not—directly advancing NCEMS's core scientific mission.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will proceed through four integrated phases over a proposed two-year period. Phase 1 (Months 1–6): Data harmonization and ontology development. We will systematically extract and cross-reference data from sequence/structure databases (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB), condensate repositories (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), interactome resources (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), PTM atlases (PhosphoSitePlus), abundance/localization maps (Human Protein Atlas, PaxDb), and imaging/biophysical repositories (FRAP datasets curated from primary literature, single-molecule tracking data, EMPIAR cryo-ET entries). A shared identifier-mapping and ontology framework, co-developed with the community during kickoff workshops, will resolve naming inconsistencies (e.g., isoform mismatches, condensate-type taxonomy) and establish standardized units for material property reporting (e.g., normalized mobile fraction, saturation concentration in molar units). This phase directly leverages network science and structural bioinformatics expertise to build a unified relational database, the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA) backend. Phase 2 (Months 4–12): Feature engineering and statistical modeling. Computational biophysicists and structural bioinformaticians will compute sequence-derived features (disorder scores, charge patterning metrics, sticker/spacer annotations via established algorithms) for all curated proteins. Network scientists will construct interactome subgraphs for condensate-associated proteins and compute percolation-relevant metrics (degree distributions, clustering coefficients, valency estimates). These features will be statistically tested against experimentally reported material properties using regression and survival-style analyses to identify significant molecular-to-mesoscale associations, directly addressing sub-questions 1 and 2. Phase 3 (Months 10–18): Machine learning integration and hypothesis testing. Machine learning experts will develop supervised models (gradient-boosted trees, graph neural networks) trained to predict material state and functional/pathological classification from layered feature sets, progressively adding sequence-only, network-augmented, and context-augmented (PTM/abundance/localization) feature blocks. Comparing predictive performance across these nested models provides a quantitative test of the reductionism-versus-emergence hypothesis (sub-question 3) and identifies discriminating features for pathological aggregation (sub-question 4). Unsupervised clustering (UMAP, spectral clustering) will identify novel condensate subtypes not captured by existing taxonomies. Phase 4 (Months 16–24): Validation, community workshops, and dissemination. Predictions will be validated against held-out datasets and, where possible, against independent imaging datasets (e.g., cryo-ET structural signatures) not used in training. Two in-person/hybrid workshops will convene the broader condensate biology community to stress-test the CEA ontology, solicit external data contributions, and co-develop annotation standards for future studies. Throughout, the Working Group will meet biweekly via videoconference, with quarterly in-person data-wrangling sprints hosted by rotating partner institutions to maintain integration momentum and troubleshoot cross-database inconsistencies collaboratively.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will deliver: (1) the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA), a publicly accessible, harmonized database integrating sequence, structural, interactome, PTM, abundance, and biophysical/imaging data for hundreds of condensate-associated proteins, with standardized ontologies enabling future community contributions; (2) validated predictive models quantifying the extent to which molecular-scale features predict mesoscale material properties, and rigorously delineating the contribution of cellular context—directly answering a fundamental question about reductionism versus emergence in molecular systems biology; (3) an interactive web tool enabling researchers to query predicted material behavior for proteins of interest, prioritize candidates for experimental validation, and explore condensate subtype classifications; (4) novel mechanistic hypotheses regarding percolation-like thresholds in condensate networks and discriminating features of pathological aggregation, generating testable predictions for wet-lab follow-up in neurodegeneration and stress-response biology; and (5) a generalizable methodological template for synthesizing molecular-to-mesoscale data that will be transferable to other emergent cellular phenomena (e.g., chromatin organization, membrane microdomains), amplifying NCEMS's broader scientific mission. Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing ambiguity in the condensate field regarding the sufficiency of sequence-based 'molecular grammar' models, informing both basic biology and translational efforts targeting aberrant phase transitions in disease. Methodologically, the harmonization pipelines and ontologies developed here will lower barriers for future data integration efforts across biophysics and cell biology communities. By training embedded graduate students and postdocs across computational and experimental partner labs, the project will directly cultivate interdisciplinary, data-savvy scientists equipped to lead future synthesis research. Broader impacts extend to disease-relevant applications, as the discriminatory features identified for pathological aggregation may inform biomarker development and therapeutic targeting strategies for condensate-linked neurodegenerative disorders.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This Working Group commits fully to open science principles consistent with NCEMS community standards. All curated and harmonized datasets comprising the Condensate Emergence Atlas will be deposited in a public, version-controlled repository (e.g., Zenodo/GitHub with DOI minting) under FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles, using standardized ontologies co-developed during community workshops. All data harmonization scripts, feature-engineering pipelines, and machine learning model code will be released as containerized, executable workflows (using Docker/Singularity and workflow managers such as Snakemake or Nextflow) to ensure computational reproducibility across computing environments. Model training will follow documented, versioned pipelines with fixed random seeds, held-out validation sets, and reported performance metrics, enabling independent replication and benchmarking by external groups. We will pre-register key hypotheses (sub-questions 1–4) and analysis plans via an open platform (e.g., OSF) prior to full-scale modeling to guard against post hoc rationalization. All intermediate and final datasets will include comprehensive metadata documenting provenance, original data sources, transformation steps, and licensing status, ensuring appropriate attribution to original data generators. The interactive web tool will be built on open-source frameworks and hosted with sustainability commitments beyond the funding period, coordinated with NCEMS infrastructure where feasible. Manuscripts arising from this work will be posted as preprints prior to journal submission, and all publications will be open access. Community workshops will be recorded and made publicly available (where consistent with participant consent) to maximize training value beyond the immediate Working Group. We will actively solicit external community feedback on the CEA ontology and database structure through public comment periods, ensuring the resource evolves as a living, community-owned standard rather than a static deliverable, consistent with NCEMS's vision of catalyzing durable, reusable synthesis infrastructure for the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests NCEMS support for a two-year Working Group comprising six to eight investigators spanning condensate biophysics, structural bioinformatics, network science, cell biology, and machine learning, distributed across at least four institutions to reflect geographic, career-stage, and institutional diversity. Budget priorities include: (1) Personnel (approximately 55%): partial salary support for a project coordinator/data scientist to manage cross-database harmonization and infrastructure maintenance, plus stipend support for two embedded graduate students and two postdoctoral trainees who will rotate across partner labs to receive interdisciplinary cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and machine learning. (2) Computational infrastructure (approximately 20%): cloud computing credits or high-performance computing allocation for large-scale feature extraction, network analysis, and machine learning model training, plus costs for sustained hosting of the CEA database and interactive web tool during and immediately after the funding period. (3) Convening and training activities (approximately 15%): two in-person/hybrid data-wrangling sprints and community workshops per year, including travel support for Working Group members and invited external experts/data contributors, to build consensus on ontology standards and stress-test integrated models. (4) Dissemination and open science costs (approximately 10%): preprint and open-access publication fees, repository/DOI costs, and web tool development/maintenance support. NCEMS-specific resources requested include access to shared computational infrastructure, coordination support for cross-institutional data governance agreements, and facilitation of community workshops connecting this Working Group with other NCEMS-funded synthesis efforts addressing related mesoscale emergence questions (e.g., chromatin or membrane microdomain organization), maximizing cross-project synergies. This budget structure reflects the genuinely collaborative, multi-lab nature of the work: no single partner institution possesses the full complement of computational infrastructure, data science personnel, and cross-disciplinary expertise required, justifying the requested shared resources as essential rather than supplementary to project feasibility.
abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where local biomolecular interactions give rise to system-level properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that dictate cellular function in transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets, no unified framework connects the molecular determinants of phase behavior (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalent 'sticker-spacer' motifs, post-translational modifications) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences. This gap persists because relevant data are scattered across incompatible resources: sequence/structure databases (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB), condensate-specific repositories (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), post-translational modification atlases (PhosphoSitePlus), protein abundance/localization maps (Human Protein Atlas, PaxDb), and heterogeneous imaging/biophysical measurements (FRAP recovery curves, single-molecule tracking, cryo-electron tomography from EMPIAR). No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, network science, and machine learning required to harmonize these disparate data types into a predictive, mechanistic framework.

This Working Group will assemble condensate biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and machine learning experts to build an integrated, open-access resource—the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA)—that links molecular-scale features to mesoscale phase behavior and cellular outcomes. We will: (1) curate and cross-reference sequence-based determinants (disorder content, charge patterning, aromatic sticker density) with experimentally reported condensate material properties (liquid, gel, solid; FRAP-derived mobile fractions; concentration-dependent phase boundaries); (2) integrate interactome and stoichiometry data to model condensates as emergent network phenomena, testing whether percolation-like thresholds in interaction valency predict phase transition points; (3) incorporate PTM and cellular context data (abundance, localization, cell-type specificity) to explain condition-dependent condensate emergence versus dissolution; and (4) apply supervised and unsupervised machine learning to identify generalizable 'rules' distinguishing functional condensates from aberrant aggregates linked to disease (e.g., neurodegeneration-associated solidification).

A central scientific question we will address: Can mesoscale material properties of condensates be predicted from molecular-scale sequence and interaction features alone, or do emergent properties require irreducible knowledge of cellular context (concentration, crowding, PTM state)? Answering this tests fundamental assumptions about reductionism versus emergence in molecular systems biology.

This project is infeasible for any single lab given the scale of cross-database harmonization, the breadth of required expertise, and the need for standardized ontologies bridging biophysics and cell biology communities. NCEMS support will fund coordinated data-wrangling sprints, shared computational infrastructure, and workshops to establish community standards for condensate data annotation. All curated datasets, harmonization pipelines, and predictive models will be released under FAIR principles via a public repository and interactive web tool. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and machine learning—directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to develop. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will yield a generalizable framework for predicting mesoscale emergent properties from molecular data, with broad applicability beyond condensates to other emergent cellular phenomena.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-level interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, and RNA give rise to system-level material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, client selectivity) that in turn dictate cellular outcomes such as transcriptional regulation, stress adaptation, and disease pathology. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data, the field remains fragmented: sequence-feature databases (MobiDB, D2P2), curated LLPS protein catalogs (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, PhaSePro, DrLLPS), single-cell condensate imaging repositories (CD-CODE, Human Protein Atlas subcellular data), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), and disease-mutation resources (ClinVar, COSMIG, gnomAD) exist as disconnected silos, each captured by different labs using incompatible vocabularies, scales, and experimental readouts. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, network science, and clinical genomics needed to integrate these resources into a predictive, mechanistic framework linking molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and cellular phenotype. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—biophysicists studying condensate material properties, computational structural biologists, network biologists, cell imaging specialists, and clinical genomicists—to build the first cross-scale, harmonized data resource and predictive model connecting (1) sequence-encoded molecular features (IDR composition, stickers-and-spacers architecture, post-translational modification sites, RNA-binding motifs), (2) network-level context (interactome connectivity, co-condensation partners, stoichiometry), (3) empirically measured mesoscale material properties (FRAP-derived mobility, viscosity, multiphase demixing, aging/hardening propensity compiled from published biophysical studies), and (4) higher-order cellular and organismal outcomes (subcellular localization patterns, stress-responsive condensate remodeling, and disease-associated mutations affecting phase behavior). Using graph-based machine learning and multi-modal data fusion, we will construct a genome-wide predictive atlas of condensate-forming proteins that infers emergent material properties for thousands of uncharacterized proteins, tests whether specific sequence-network signatures predict multiphase organization or aberrant hardening linked to neurodegenerative and oncogenic mutations, and identifies general design principles by which molecular-scale interactions propagate to cellular-scale function. Model predictions will be rigorously validated against independent, held-out public datasets (orthogonal imaging studies, biophysical measurements not used in training) to ensure generalizability rather than dataset-specific overfitting. All harmonized datasets, ontology mappings, code, and trained models will be released as an open, versioned community resource (via NCEMS-supported infrastructure) to enable reuse and extension by the broader condensate biology community. The working group will embed graduate students and postdocs in cross-lab data harmonization, biophysical modeling, and network-based machine learning, providing hands-on training in reproducible, large-scale synthesis science. By resolving inconsistencies across independently generated datasets and establishing shared standards for describing condensate material properties, this project will produce mechanistic insight into why and how mesoscale emergence arises from molecular interactions—addressing a fundamental, long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology that is intractable without cross-institutional, cross-disciplinary data synthesis at NCEMS scale.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence: dilute, individually simple molecular interactions—transient contacts between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent folded domains, and nucleic acids—aggregate into system-level material states (liquid, gel, glass, multiphase) that cannot be trivially predicted from any single interaction alone. These material properties are not epiphenomenal; they causally determine cellular outcomes, including transcriptional condensate dynamics at enhancers, stress-granule-mediated translational repression, nucleolar multiphase architecture, and pathological transitions from liquid to solid-like aggregates implicated in ALS, frontotemporal dementia, and certain cancers. Understanding how molecular grammar—sequence composition, patterning of 'stickers and spacers,' post-translational modification, and RNA-binding capacity—encodes emergent material behavior is therefore a fundamental open question in molecular and cellular biology, squarely within NCEMS's mesoscale mandate.

Over the past decade, the condensate field has generated an extraordinary volume of public data. Sequence-feature resources (MobiDB, D2P2) catalog disorder and low-complexity regions; curated phase-separation databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, PhaSePro, DrLLPS) compile experimentally validated LLPS proteins and their conditions; imaging repositories (CD-CODE, Human Protein Atlas) document condensate morphology and subcellular localization at single-cell resolution; interactome databases (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct) map the network context in which condensate components operate; and clinical genomics resources (ClinVar, COSMIC, gnomAD) catalog disease-associated variants, many of which fall within IDRs of condensate-forming proteins. Individually, each of these resources answers a narrow question. Collectively, they harbor the raw material to answer a much deeper one: what quantitative sequence-to-network-to-phenotype rules govern the emergence of condensate material properties, and how do disease mutations perturb these rules?

This question cannot be answered by any single laboratory or existing bilateral collaboration. It requires simultaneous fluency in biophysical polymer theory, structural bioinformatics, network science, quantitative imaging analysis, and clinical variant interpretation—expertise that is institutionally and disciplinarily dispersed. Moreover, the datasets themselves are not interoperable: they use different protein identifiers, different definitions of 'phase separation,' inconsistent units for material properties (e.g., FRAP recovery half-times versus viscosity estimates versus qualitative droplet/aggregate calls), and largely non-overlapping curation efforts. This fragmentation has left the field with many isolated case studies (e.g., FUS, hnRNPA1, TDP-43) but no systematic, genome-wide, cross-validated framework connecting molecular grammar to mesoscale material behavior and cellular consequence.

The significance of resolving this gap is threefold: scientifically, it will establish general design principles of mesoscale emergence applicable beyond condensates to other supramolecular assemblies; biomedically, it will enable prediction of which uncharacterized disease mutations are likely to perturb condensate material states, prioritizing candidates for mechanistic follow-up; and methodologically, it will produce a reusable harmonization framework and ontology for condensate data that the community urgently lacks. This proposal directly targets NCEMS's founding scientific vision—understanding emergent mesoscale properties and their propagation to cellular outcomes—through exactly the kind of large-scale, cross-disciplinary data synthesis that individual labs cannot undertake alone.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching question and four tractable sub-questions, each paired with a testable hypothesis derived from biophysical theory and prior empirical observation.

Overarching Question: Can a harmonized, multi-database synthesis reveal quantitative molecular grammar rules that predict the emergent material properties of biomolecular condensates and their downstream cellular and disease phenotypes?

Q1 (Sequence-to-material mapping): Do specific sequence-encoded features—sticker density and patterning, IDR charge segregation (kappa), aromatic residue spacing, and RNA-binding motif content—quantitatively predict empirically measured material properties (FRAP mobility, viscosity, propensity for liquid-to-solid transition) across the aggregated biophysical literature?
Hypothesis 1: Condensate material state exists along a predictable continuum governed by sticker valence and patterning regularity, such that proteins with irregularly spaced, high-valence stickers and low net charge segregation will show higher propensity for hardening/aging, independent of protein family, consistent with stickers-and-spacers polymer theory.

Q2 (Network context as a modulator): Does interactome connectivity and co-condensation partner stoichiometry modulate or override sequence-intrinsic predictions of material behavior?
Hypothesis 2: Proteins with high network connectivity and multiple validated co-condensation partners exhibit material properties (e.g., stabilized liquidity, multiphase partitioning) that deviate systematically from predictions based on sequence features alone, indicating that network context is a necessary, non-redundant predictor of emergent mesoscale behavior—directly testing whether emergence at this scale is a property of molecules alone or of molecules-in-context.

Q3 (Multiphase architecture): Can combined sequence and network features distinguish proteins that form single-phase condensates from those that organize into multiphase (core-shell, nested) architectures, as observed in nucleoli and stress granules?
Hypothesis 3: Multiphase architecture is predictable from relative differences in predicted surface tension and homotypic-versus-heterotypic interaction strength between co-localized proteins, such that large predicted immiscibility gaps between interacting partners correspond to empirically documented multiphase organization in imaging datasets.

Q4 (Disease mutation impact): Do disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins preferentially localize to sequence features predicted to control material properties, and can their phenotypic consequence (loss of function versus pathological hardening) be predicted from the integrated model?
Hypothesis 4: Pathogenic mutations catalogued in ClinVar/COSMIC that fall within IDRs of condensate-forming proteins disproportionately alter sticker patterning or charge segregation in directions predicted to increase hardening propensity, distinguishing them from benign population variants in gnomAD at the same loci.

Collectively, these questions test whether mesoscale material emergence is (a) predictable from molecular grammar, (b) contingent on network context, (c) generalizable to complex multiphase architectures, and (d) mechanistically linked to disease. Each question requires cross-referencing at least three independently curated public databases and could not be rigorously addressed using any single existing resource, satisfying the core synthesis-research criterion of this call. Confirmatory and disconfirmatory outcomes are both scientifically informative: a failure of sequence-only models (disconfirming H1 in isolation) would itself be a significant finding, demonstrating that network and cellular context are obligatory components of mesoscale emergence rather than secondary modulators.

[Methods and Approach]
Aim 1 – Data Harmonization and Ontology Development (Months 1–8). We will assemble a unified schema mapping protein identifiers (UniProt-anchored) and standardizing definitions across MobiDB/D2P2 (disorder and PTM annotations), PhaSepDB/LLPSDB/PhaSePro/DrLLPS (LLPS evidence, experimental conditions, positive/negative controls), CD-CODE and Human Protein Atlas (imaging-derived subcellular condensate calls), BioGRID/STRING/IntAct (interaction confidence-weighted networks), and ClinVar/COSMIC/gnomAD (variant pathogenicity and population frequency). A controlled vocabulary for material-property descriptors (e.g., standardizing FRAP half-time, mobile fraction, and qualitative aging descriptors into comparable ordinal and continuous scales) will be developed in consultation with the working group's biophysicists, following FAIR data principles. Curation discrepancies (e.g., conflicting LLPS calls for the same protein across databases) will be resolved via a transparent, documented adjudication protocol rather than silent exclusion.

Aim 2 – Feature Engineering and Sequence-Network Representation (Months 6–14). Sequence features will be computed using established biophysical descriptors (kappa/Omega charge patterning, sticker-spacer decomposition via established stickers-and-spacers algorithms, aromatic/RNA-binding motif density). Network features (degree, clustering coefficient, co-condensation partner enrichment) will be derived from confidence-filtered interactome graphs. These will be fused into a heterogeneous graph representation in which protein nodes carry sequence-derived feature vectors and edges encode interaction/co-condensation evidence weighted by curation confidence.

Aim 3 – Predictive Modeling (Months 10–20). We will apply graph neural network (GNN) architectures alongside interpretable baseline models (gradient-boosted trees, regularized regression) to predict material-property labels from combined sequence-network features, explicitly comparing sequence-only, network-only, and fused models to test Hypotheses 1–3. Model interpretability methods (SHAP values, attention-weight analysis) will identify which features drive predictions, generating mechanistic hypotheses rather than black-box outputs. For Q4, mutation-level features will be recomputed under wild-type and variant sequences to predict differential material-property shifts, benchmarked against curated pathogenic/benign variant sets.

Aim 4 – Validation Against Independent Public Data (Months 18–24). Critically, all models will be validated on held-out data not used in training or feature selection: independent biophysical studies published after initial database compilation, orthogonal imaging datasets, and time-split validation (training on pre-2022 data, testing on 2022–2024 publications) to guard against circularity and dataset leakage. Performance will be benchmarked against naive baselines (disorder-content-only predictors) to demonstrate added value of network integration.

Aim 5 – Community Resource Release (Months 20–24). The harmonized dataset, ontology mappings, trained models, and analysis code will be packaged as a versioned, documented resource with a public API, enabling researchers to query predicted material properties for any human protein.

Throughout, the working group will hold monthly cross-disciplinary synthesis meetings and two in-person hackathons (Months 6 and 18) hosted with NCEMS infrastructure support to resolve integration bottlenecks requiring simultaneous biophysical, computational, and clinical expertise.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will deliver: (1) a first-of-its-kind harmonized, versioned database unifying sequence, network, imaging, biophysical, and clinical variant data for condensate-associated proteins, with a documented ontology resolving cross-database terminological inconsistencies; (2) validated predictive models generating a genome-wide atlas of inferred material properties for thousands of proteins lacking direct biophysical characterization, prioritizing candidates for experimental follow-up by the broader community; (3) mechanistic insight into whether sequence grammar alone, or sequence-network integration, better explains mesoscale material emergence, directly advancing NCEMS's core scientific mission; (4) a prioritized list of disease-associated mutations predicted to perturb condensate material states, informing hypothesis generation in neurodegeneration and cancer biology; and (5) open-source, reusable harmonization and modeling pipelines transferable to other mesoscale synthesis problems beyond condensates.

Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing fragmentation problem that has limited the condensate field to isolated case studies, replacing anecdote with a systematic, falsifiable, quantitative framework. By explicitly testing where sequence-only predictions fail and network context becomes necessary, the project will generate generalizable principles about how mesoscale emergence depends on molecular context—principles likely applicable to other emergent cellular assemblies (e.g., signaling clusters, viral replication compartments).

Broader impacts include establishing reusable data standards for condensate material properties that could be adopted by primary data-generating labs going forward, reducing future fragmentation. Training embedded graduate students and postdocs in cross-database harmonization, graph-based machine learning, and biophysical interpretation will cultivate a cohort of data-savvy scientists equipped to work at the interface of computation and mechanistic biology—directly serving NCEMS's workforce development goals. The resource will lower the barrier for smaller or resource-limited labs to generate testable hypotheses about understudied proteins, democratizing access to synthesis-derived insight.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This working group commits fully to NCEMS's open science and reproducibility standards. All source datasets used are already publicly available; no new experimental data will be generated. All harmonization mappings, ontology definitions, and adjudication decisions for resolving cross-database discrepancies will be documented in a public, version-controlled repository (GitHub, mirrored to Zenodo for permanent DOI-linked archival), ensuring full provenance tracking from raw source database to final harmonized table.

Analysis code, including feature-engineering scripts, model training pipelines, and validation notebooks, will be developed using containerized, environment-locked workflows (Docker/Singularity with pinned dependency versions) to guarantee computational reproducibility across institutions and over time. All code will be released under a permissive open-source license (MIT or Apache 2.0) concurrent with any publication, not after embargo.

Trained models and the resulting predictive atlas will be deposited in a public, queryable database with a documented API, accompanied by comprehensive metadata describing training data provenance, validation performance, and known limitations, to prevent uncritical downstream reuse of predictions outside their domain of validity. Held-out validation datasets and time-split benchmarks will be explicitly flagged and preserved so future researchers can independently verify reported generalization performance rather than relying solely on our internal validation claims.

The working group will adhere to community-endorsed reproducible science practices, including pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans prior to model validation (to avoid post hoc rationalization of results), transparent reporting of negative or disconfirming findings (particularly regarding Hypothesis 1 versus 2), and use of standardized reporting checklists for computational biology analyses. Data and code releases will follow FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable), with persistent identifiers assigned to all major resource components. Regular working group meetings will include an open-science checkpoint to review adherence to these commitments, and a public project website will track resource releases, versioning, and known issues, ensuring the broader community can monitor, reuse, and extend this work throughout and beyond the funding period.

[Budget and Resources]
This synthesis project requires no funding for new data generation, consistent with NCEMS's community-scale synthesis model, and instead focuses resources on personnel time, computational infrastructure, and collaborative convening.

Personnel: The primary budget request supports partial salary (20–30% effort) for five co-investigators spanning biophysics, structural bioinformatics, network science, imaging analysis, and clinical genomics, reflecting the genuinely transdisciplinary nature of the integration task. Two full-time postdoctoral researchers will lead data harmonization and model development respectively, and two graduate student trainees (one per lead institution) will be embedded in cross-lab workflows, receiving structured training in synthesis methodology as a core project deliverable.

Computational Resources: Moderate cloud computing allocation (estimated 50,000 GPU/CPU hours) is requested for graph neural network training, large-scale feature extraction across tens of thousands of proteins, and validation benchmarking. Data storage costs for hosting the harmonized multi-terabyte imaging-linked dataset and versioned model releases are included, leveraging NCEMS-supported infrastructure where available to minimize redundant institutional overhead.

Collaborative Convening: Budget includes support for two in-person working group hackathons (Months 6 and 18) bringing together all co-investigators, postdocs, and students to resolve integration bottlenecks that are difficult to address remotely, plus monthly virtual synthesis meetings requiring minimal additional resources.

Data/Software Access: No proprietary datasets are required; all source databases (MobiDB, PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, BioGRID, ClinVar, etc.) are freely accessible, eliminating licensing costs. Minor funds are requested for software development tools and continued hosting of the public API beyond the funding period's initial release.

Justification for NCEMS-Scale Support: This budget explicitly reflects work that exceeds single-lab capacity—harmonizing five distinct data modalities, sustaining five-discipline collaboration, and maintaining public infrastructure—justifying NCEMS support rather than standard single-investigator funding mechanisms. Resource requests are calibrated to be efficient, leveraging existing free public data and open-source tools wherever possible, concentrating investment in the genuinely scarce resource this problem requires: sustained, structured, cross-disciplinary human collaboration time.

Despite an explosion of condensate-related data, the field remains fragmented: sequence-feature databases (MobiDB, D2P2), curated LLPS protein catalogs (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, PhaSePro, DrLLPS), single-cell condensate imaging repositories (CD-CODE, Human Protein Atlas subcellular data), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), and disease-mutation resources (ClinVar, COSMIG, gnomAD) exist as disconnected silos, each captured by different labs using incompatible vocabularies, scales, and experimental readouts. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, network science, and clinical genomics needed to integrate these resources into a predictive, mechanistic framework linking molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and cellular phenotype. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—biophysicists studying condensate material properties, computational structural biologists, network biologists, cell imaging specialists, and clinical genomicists—to build the first cross-scale, harmonized data resource and predictive model connecting (1) sequence-encoded molecular features (IDR composition, stickers-and-spacers architecture, post-translational modification sites, RNA-binding motifs), (2) network-level context (interactome connectivity, co-condensation partners, stoichiometry), (3) empirically measured mesoscale material properties (FRAP-derived mobility, viscosity, multiphase demixing, aging/hardening propensity compiled from published biophysical studies), and (4) higher-order cellular and organismal outcomes (subcellular localization patterns, stress-responsive condensate remodeling, and disease-associated mutations affecting phase behavior). Using graph-based machine learning and multi-modal data fusion, we will construct a genome-wide predictive atlas of condensate-forming proteins that infers emergent material properties for thousands of uncharacterized proteins, tests whether specific sequence-network signatures predict multiphase organization or aberrant hardening linked to neurodegenerative and oncogenic mutations, and identifies general design principles by which molecular-scale interactions propagate to cellular-scale function. Model predictions will be rigorously validated against independent, held-out public datasets (orthogonal imaging studies, biophysical measurements not used in training) to ensure generalizability rather than dataset-specific overfitting. All harmonized datasets, ontology mappings, code, and trained models will be released as an open, versioned community resource (via NCEMS-supported infrastructure) to enable reuse and extension by the broader condensate biology community. The working group will embed graduate students and postdocs in cross-lab data harmonization, biophysical modeling, and network-based machine learning, providing hands-on training in reproducible, large-scale synthesis science. By resolving inconsistencies across independently generated datasets and establishing shared standards for describing condensate material properties, this project will produce mechanistic insight into why and how mesoscale emergence arises from molecular interactions—addressing a fundamental, long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology that is intractable without cross-institutional, cross-disciplinary data synthesis at NCEMS scale.

title: From Sequence Grammar to Cellular Phenotype: A Multi-Scale Data Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence and Its Disruption in Disease
title_norm: from sequence grammar to cellular phenotype a multiscale data synthesis of biomolecular condensate emergence and its disruption in disease
abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, arising from weak multivalent interactions among biomolecules to produce compartments with system-level functions (e.g., stress granules, transcriptional hubs, nucleoli) that cannot be predicted from single-protein properties alone. Despite an explosion of public data describing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, subcellular localization, and disease-associated mutations, no integrated framework exists linking molecular sequence features to network-level organization to cellular phenotype. This gap persists because the relevant expertise—biophysics of disordered proteins, network science, cell imaging informatics, and clinical genetics—is distributed across disparate communities that rarely collaborate, and because no single lab possesses the computational infrastructure or cross-domain fluency to harmonize these heterogeneous data types at scale.

This Working Group will synthesize five major public resources: (1) sequence-based condensate databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS) and IDR predictors (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) proteome-wide interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct); (3) high-resolution subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, CellPainting); (4) structural and AlphaFold-derived conformational ensembles for disordered/multivalent proteins; and (5) disease-mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-associated proteins. Our central hypothesis is that emergent condensate behavior is governed by a decodable 'grammar' spanning three scales: (a) molecular grammar—sticker-spacer patterning, charge blockiness, and aromatic density within IDRs; (b) network grammar—topological features of interaction hubs (multivalency, promiscuity, community structure) that nucleate condensation; and (c) phenotypic grammar—how these features manifest as condensate size, dynamics, and localization observable in imaging data, and how their disruption by disease mutations produces pathological aggregation or loss-of-function.

The team will integrate machine learning (graph neural networks trained on PPI topology plus sequence embeddings), coarse-grained biophysical simulation benchmarking, and image-derived phenotypic quantification to build predictive models that generalize across protein families and cell types—an analysis impossible without cross-disciplinary data fusion at this scale. Deliverables include: a unified, versioned 'Condensate Emergence Atlas' linking sequence, network, and phenotype data with open APIs; predictive models identifying condensate-prone proteins and mutation-driven emergent dysfunction relevant to neurodegeneration and cancer; and a reproducible open-source pipeline (Snakemake/Nextflow, containerized) for community reuse. The Working Group will comprise biophysicists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomics researchers from institutions varying in size and geography, explicitly recruiting early-career co-PIs and including graduate students/postdocs in every workflow layer, with structured training in reproducible multi-omic synthesis, FAIR data practices, and interdisciplinary communication. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be deposited on public repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Synapse) under NCEMS open science guidelines, enabling the broader community to test, extend, and apply this cross-scale framework to other emergent mesoscale phenomena beyond condensates.
