[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, arising from weak multivalent interactions among biomolecules to produce compartments with system-level functions (e.g., stress granules, transcriptional hubs, nucleoli) that cannot be predicted from single-protein properties alone. Despite an explosion of public data describing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, subcellular localization, and disease-associated mutations, no integrated framework exists linking molecular sequence features to network-level organization to cellular phenotype. This gap persists because the relevant expertise—biophysics of disordered proteins, network science, cell imaging informatics, and clinical genetics—is distributed across disparate communities that rarely collaborate, and because no single lab possesses the computational infrastructure or cross-domain fluency to harmonize these heterogeneous data types at scale.

This Working Group will synthesize five major public resources: (1) sequence-based condensate databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS) and IDR predictors (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) proteome-wide interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct); (3) high-resolution subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, CellPainting); (4) structural and AlphaFold-derived conformational ensembles for disordered/multivalent proteins; and (5) disease-mutation repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) mapped onto condensate-associated proteins. Our central hypothesis is that emergent condensate behavior is governed by a decodable 'grammar' spanning three scales: (a) molecular grammar—sticker-spacer patterning, charge blockiness, and aromatic density within IDRs; (b) network grammar—topological features of interaction hubs (multivalency, promiscuity, community structure) that nucleate condensation; and (c) phenotypic grammar—how these features manifest as condensate size, dynamics, and localization observable in imaging data, and how their disruption by disease mutations produces pathological aggregation or loss-of-function.

The team will integrate machine learning (graph neural networks trained on PPI topology plus sequence embeddings), coarse-grained biophysical simulation benchmarking, and image-derived phenotypic quantification to build predictive models that generalize across protein families and cell types—an analysis impossible without cross-disciplinary data fusion at this scale. Deliverables include: a unified, versioned 'Condensate Emergence Atlas' linking sequence, network, and phenotype data with open APIs; predictive models identifying condensate-prone proteins and mutation-driven emergent dysfunction relevant to neurodegeneration and cancer; and a reproducible open-source pipeline (Snakemake/Nextflow, containerized) for community reuse. The Working Group will comprise biophysicists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomics researchers from institutions varying in size and geography, explicitly recruiting early-career co-PIs and including graduate students/postdocs in every workflow layer, with structured training in reproducible multi-omic synthesis, FAIR data practices, and interdisciplinary communication. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be deposited on public repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Synapse) under NCEMS open science guidelines, enabling the broader community to test, extend, and apply this cross-scale framework to other emergent mesoscale phenomena beyond condensates.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: functional, dynamic compartments—stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P-bodies—arise from weak, multivalent, and often transient interactions among proteins and nucleic acids, yielding system-level properties (viscosity, selective permeability, reaction concentration, dissolution kinetics) that cannot be inferred from any single biomolecule in isolation. Over the past decade, this recognition has catalyzed intense interest across cell biology, biophysics, and medicine, since condensate dysregulation is now implicated in neurodegenerative disease (TDP-43, FUS, hnRNPA1 aggregation in ALS/FTD), oncogenesis (transcriptional condensate hijacking by fusion oncoproteins), and viral replication compartments. Yet our mechanistic understanding remains fragmented along three explanatory scales. At the molecular scale, biophysicists have characterized sequence features of intrinsically disordered regions—sticker-spacer architecture, charge patterning, aromatic residue density—that govern LLPS propensity in vitro. At the network scale, interactome biologists have cataloged multivalent protein-protein interaction hubs and their topological signatures, often without reference to disorder or phase behavior. At the phenotypic scale, imaging consortia have generated proteome-wide subcellular localization atlases capturing condensate morphology, number, and dynamics in living cells, largely disconnected from the sequence and network features that produce them. Meanwhile, disease-genetics repositories document thousands of mutations in condensate-associated proteins, but their functional consequences are rarely interpreted through an emergence lens spanning molecular, network, and phenotypic causation. This fragmentation is not merely a data problem—it reflects a structural gap in scientific community organization: biophysicists modeling IDR sequence grammar, network scientists studying interactome topology, imaging informaticians quantifying phenotype, and clinical geneticists cataloging mutations rarely collaborate, publish in different venues, and use incompatible data standards. No single laboratory possesses the combined domain expertise, computational infrastructure, and cross-disciplinary fluency necessary to harmonize these five heterogeneous public data ecosystems into a unified predictive framework. This is precisely the class of problem NCEMS is positioned to solve: a mesoscale emergence question of high scientific significance, amenable only to community-scale synthesis of existing public data across multiple disciplinary silos. Successfully decoding a cross-scale 'grammar' of condensate emergence would resolve a long-standing puzzle in cell biology—why condensate behavior is so difficult to predict from sequence alone—and would generate a generalizable analytical framework applicable to other emergent mesoscale phenomena (e.g., signaling clusters, chromatin domains, membrane-less organelle biogenesis). The clinical stakes are substantial: a validated cross-scale model linking mutation to network disruption to phenotypic pathology could identify previously unrecognized condensate-disease mechanisms and prioritize candidates for therapeutic intervention in neurodegeneration and cancer, where condensate-modulating small molecules are an emerging drug class. This proposal directly advances NCEMS's mission of catalyzing multidisciplinary synthesis of public molecular and cellular data to answer fundamental emergence questions at the mesoscale, while building infrastructure and training capacity for the broader research community.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group addresses three interlocking research questions that collectively probe how molecular-scale information propagates upward to produce emergent cellular phenotypes, and how this propagation breaks down in disease. RQ1 (Molecular Grammar): What sequence-encoded features of intrinsically disordered regions—sticker-spacer patterning, net charge per residue, charge blockiness (kappa), aromatic/aliphatic density, and predicted conformational ensemble dimensions—best predict a protein's condensate participation across the public condensate databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS)? We hypothesize that a compact, interpretable feature set combining sticker density and charge patterning will outperform sequence-composition-only predictors and will generalize across protein families when trained using transfer learning on large-scale IDR datasets (DisProt, MobiDB). RQ2 (Network Grammar): Do condensate-associated proteins occupy distinctive topological positions within proteome-wide interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), characterized by elevated multivalency (interaction degree), promiscuity (low interaction specificity), and membership in densely connected communities enriched for co-condensing partners? We hypothesize that condensate scaffold proteins form a statistically distinct topological class—hub-like, high-multiplicity nodes bridging otherwise separable network communities—and that this topological signature, combined with molecular grammar features, substantially improves prediction of condensate participation over either feature set alone, indicating non-additive, emergent interplay between sequence and network organization. RQ3 (Phenotypic Grammar and Disease Disruption): Can integrated molecular and network grammar features predict observable condensate phenotypes—size distribution, number per cell, dynamics, and subcellular localization—captured in imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, CellPainting), and does mapping disease-associated mutations (ClinVar, COSMIC) onto this integrated model predict pathological outcomes (aberrant aggregation, loss of condensate function, mislocalization)? We hypothesize that disease mutations disproportionately cluster at positions that simultaneously perturb molecular grammar (e.g., disrupting sticker spacing or altering charge blockiness) and network grammar (e.g., removing or adding interaction interfaces), producing nonlinear, emergent phenotypic consequences that are not predictable from either scale in isolation—consistent with condensate dysfunction as a genuinely emergent, multi-scale disease mechanism rather than a simple loss-of-function at any single scale. A cross-cutting methodological hypothesis underlies all three: that graph neural network architectures jointly trained on sequence embeddings and interaction-network topology will outperform single-modality models in predicting phenotypic outcomes, providing quantitative evidence that emergence in this system is fundamentally a cross-scale, integrative phenomenon requiring data fusion rather than sequential, scale-by-scale analysis. Collectively, these hypotheses will be tested through statistically rigorous, cross-validated model comparisons stratified by protein family and disease category, with explicit benchmarking against null models (e.g., degree-preserving randomized networks, shuffled sequence controls) to ensure that observed cross-scale relationships reflect genuine biological grammar rather than database ascertainment bias—a critical concern given known annotation biases in condensate and interaction databases that the team will explicitly quantify and correct for using bias-aware statistical modeling.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will execute a four-phase synthesis pipeline over the funding period, structured to require sustained cross-disciplinary integration at every stage. Phase 1 (Data Harmonization, Months 1-6): We will construct standardized, version-controlled ingestion pipelines for all five data classes using Nextflow/Snakemake workflows, mapping heterogeneous identifiers (UniProt, Ensembl, gene symbols) onto a unified protein-centric schema. Condensate annotations from PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS will be reconciled against differing curation criteria using a consensus-confidence scoring scheme developed collaboratively by biophysicist and data-science team members. IDR boundaries and disorder scores from DisProt/MobiDB will be recomputed where necessary for consistency. PPI networks from BioGRID, STRING, and IntAct will be integrated into a consensus interactome with edge-confidence weighting, and network features (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient, community membership via Leiden algorithm) computed at proteome scale. Imaging data from Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, and CellPainting will be processed through existing open-source segmentation/feature-extraction tools (CellProfiler, deep-learning localization classifiers) to derive condensate-relevant phenotypic descriptors (puncta count, size distribution, intensity variance, colocalization indices). ClinVar and COSMIC mutations will be mapped onto condensate-protein sequences and, where available, AlphaFold-derived structural models to annotate mutation position relative to sticker/spacer elements and predicted interaction interfaces. Phase 2 (Molecular and Network Grammar Modeling, Months 4-12): Biophysics and computational team members will derive sequence-based features (charge patterning kappa, aromatic density, sticker-spacer periodicity) and benchmark them against coarse-grained LLPS simulation predictions (e.g., using existing HPS-model outputs where available) to validate feature biological plausibility. Network scientists will develop graph neural network (GNN) architectures that embed proteins jointly on sequence-derived embeddings (e.g., ESM-based language model embeddings) and network topology, trained to predict condensate participation and phenotypic descriptors. Phase 3 (Phenotype Integration and Disease Mapping, Months 10-18): Cell biologists and clinical genomics researchers will lead integration of imaging-derived phenotypes and mutation impact scores into the joint model, using multi-task learning to simultaneously predict condensate propensity, phenotypic descriptors, and mutation pathogenicity, with rigorous held-out validation stratified by protein family to test generalization. Statistical rigor will be ensured through nested cross-validation, permutation-based null models controlling for database annotation bias, and pre-registered analysis plans for primary hypotheses. Phase 4 (Atlas Construction and Community Release, Months 16-24): All harmonized data, trained models, and code will be assembled into the versioned, API-accessible 'Condensate Emergence Atlas.' In-person and virtual working meetings (quarterly) will structure cross-disciplinary integration, with dedicated sprints pairing biophysicists with network/data scientists and imaging/clinical experts to co-develop interpretable model outputs, ensuring methodological rigor is maintained across all disciplinary boundaries throughout the project lifecycle.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will deliver: (1) the Condensate Emergence Atlas, a versioned, openly accessible database and API unifying sequence, network, imaging, and mutation data for thousands of condensate-associated proteins; (2) validated, interpretable predictive models linking molecular and network grammar to phenotypic condensate behavior, with quantified generalization performance across protein families and cell types; (3) a mutation-impact scoring framework identifying disease variants likely to disrupt condensate emergence, prioritized for experimental follow-up in neurodegeneration and cancer contexts; and (4) an open-source, containerized analytical pipeline enabling reproducible extension of this framework to new datasets and other emergent mesoscale systems. Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing puzzle—why condensate formation is poorly predicted from single-scale features—by providing quantitative evidence for genuine cross-scale emergence requiring integrated molecular-network-phenotype modeling. This reframes condensate biology from scale-siloed description toward a predictive, generalizable framework, with direct relevance to NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mission. Translationally, prioritized disease mutations and condensate-disruption predictions will provide testable hypotheses for experimental collaborators studying ALS/FTD, cancer, and other condensate-linked pathologies, potentially accelerating identification of therapeutic targets. Methodologically, the GNN-based multi-modal fusion architecture developed here will serve as a template applicable beyond condensates—to any mesoscale system where sequence, network, and phenotype data exist separately but require integration to explain emergent behavior. By training early-career scientists and trainees in cross-disciplinary synthesis methods, FAIR data practices, and reproducible computational workflows, this project builds lasting workforce capacity. The public release of harmonized datasets and models will lower barriers for future research groups, catalyzing downstream studies that neither require nor duplicate the substantial harmonization investment made here, thereby providing outsized, durable impact relative to project cost.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This Working Group commits fully to NCEMS's open science principles across all stages of the project. All data harmonization, feature extraction, model training, and validation code will be developed in public GitHub repositories from project inception, using containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) and workflow managers (Nextflow/Snakemake) to guarantee computational reproducibility across computing environments. Harmonized datasets, intermediate feature matrices, trained model weights, and the final Condensate Emergence Atlas will be deposited in appropriate public repositories (Zenodo for versioned releases and DOIs, Synapse for larger structured datasets, GitHub for code) under permissive open licenses (CC-BY for data, MIT/Apache for code), consistent with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data standards. All primary and secondary source databases used will be explicitly cited and version-pinned to ensure traceability and reproducibility of every downstream analysis. Analysis workflows will be documented with executable notebooks (Jupyter) alongside narrative methods documentation sufficient for independent replication by external researchers. We will pre-register primary hypotheses and analysis plans (e.g., via OSF) prior to full-scale model training to guard against post hoc overfitting and to align with gold-standard reproducible science practices. Team science practices will follow community-endorsed norms for authorship, data/code attribution, and credit-sharing across disciplinary contributors, with an explicit team charter established at project outset covering data governance, publication planning, and conflict resolution. Regular internal reproducibility audits—including independent re-execution of pipelines by team members outside the original analysis subgroup—will be conducted at each project phase milestone. All trainee-led analyses will be developed using the same open, version-controlled infrastructure, ensuring training outcomes directly reinforce open science competencies. Upon completion, we will host a public webinar and tutorial series demonstrating Atlas use and pipeline reuse, explicitly inviting community feedback, contribution, and extension, consistent with NCEMS's goal of enabling durable, reusable community infrastructure rather than one-off analysis products.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests NCEMS support for a two-year Working Group comprising six co-investigators (biophysics, network science, imaging informatics, clinical genomics, computational biology, and data science leads), two funded graduate students, and two postdoctoral researchers, distributed across four institutions varying in size, geography, and research intensity to satisfy NCEMS's diversity and collaborative partnership priorities. Budget categories include: (1) Personnel (approximately 65%): partial salary support for co-PIs' synthesis effort, full support for postdoctoral researchers leading GNN model development and imaging-feature integration, and graduate student support embedded in network-modeling and clinical-mapping subteams; (2) Computational Resources (approximately 15%): cloud computing credits (AWS/GCP) or allocation on NCEMS-affiliated high-performance computing resources for large-scale GNN training, proteome-wide network analysis, and imaging feature extraction, plus data storage and API-hosting costs for the Condensate Emergence Atlas; (3) Working Group Meetings and Travel (approximately 10%): quarterly in-person integration meetings rotating across partner institutions, travel support explicitly prioritizing trainee and early-career participation, and conference dissemination travel; (4) Training and Community Engagement (approximately 5%): development and delivery of tutorial materials, webinars, and a capstone open workshop for the broader research community; (5) Data Curation and Open Science Infrastructure (approximately 5%): dedicated data curator effort for cross-database harmonization quality control, Zenodo/Synapse deposition costs, and reproducibility auditing. This budget structure reflects the genuine multi-lab, multi-disciplinary scale required: no single institution's existing infrastructure or personnel could independently harmonize five heterogeneous public data ecosystems, develop and validate multi-modal GNN architectures, and maintain long-term open community infrastructure. NCEMS support specifically enables the sustained cross-institutional coordination, dedicated computational infrastructure, and trainee integration that distinguish this effort from any single lab's typical funded scope, directly justifying the requested resources as beyond individual-lab capability per NCEMS's core funding criteria.

title: Decoding the Molecular Grammar of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence: A Cross-Scale Data Synthesis of Sequence, Structure, and Material Properties
title_norm: decoding the molecular grammar of biomolecular condensate emergence a crossscale data synthesis of sequence structure and material properties
abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: collective material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, aging into gels or solids) arise from thousands of transient, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs). Despite explosive growth in condensate research, our understanding of how molecular 'grammar' dictates emergent mesoscale behavior remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based phase-separation predictors (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, CD-CODE), cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution imaging datasets depicting condensate ultrastructure (EMDB, EMPIAR), proteomic and interactome studies of condensate composition (BioGRID, IntAct, RNAct), biophysical measurements of material properties (FRAP recovery rates, viscosity, surface tension) buried in supplementary tables of hundreds of papers, and PTM/disease-variant databases (PhosphoSitePlus, ClinVar) linking condensate dysregulation to pathology. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to harmonize these heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets—spanning atomic structure to cellular phenotype—into a unified predictive framework.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and data scientists to construct a curated, interoperable meta-database and companion machine-learning framework—CondensateAtlas—that integrates sequence features (IDR composition, charge patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs), structural/ultrastructural data (condensate size, shape, multiphase organization from imaging archives), interactome-derived compositional networks, and quantitative material-property measurements curated via natural-language-processing-assisted literature mining and manual expert curation. Using this integrated resource, we will (1) test whether sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features quantitatively predict emergent viscoelastic properties across condensate types, (2) identify structural and compositional signatures that distinguish functional liquid-like condensates from pathological solid-like aggregates linked to neurodegenerative and oncogenic variants, and (3) develop generalizable biophysical/ML models capable of predicting mesoscale material behavior from primary sequence and cellular context, tested against held-out experimental datasets. Statistical and generative modeling approaches (Gaussian process regression, graph neural networks trained on interaction networks, physics-informed biophysical polymer models) will be co-developed by computational and wet-lab collaborators to ensure biological interpretability.

This project requires NCEMS support because it depends on cross-institutional data harmonization, standardized ontology development for condensate properties, and computational infrastructure beyond any single lab's capacity, while uniting communities (structural biology, soft-matter physics, cell biology, genomics) that rarely interact directly. The working group will include early-career researchers and trainees who will lead specific data curation and modeling modules, receiving hands-on training in FAIR data practices, reproducible workflow design (Snakemake/Nextflow pipelines), and multidisciplinary team science. All curated datasets, ontologies, trained models, and analysis code will be released as open-access community resources via Zenodo/GitHub, with a living database designed for continuous community contribution. By synthesizing molecular-to-mesoscale data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle—how simple molecular rules generate complex emergent condensate behavior—while generating a foundational, reusable resource for the mesoscale biology community.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles such as nucleoli, stress granules, P-bodies, and paraspeckles—represent one of the most striking examples of mesoscale emergence in cell biology: bulk material properties (viscosity, surface tension, interfacial behavior, and pathological aging into gels or amyloid-like solids) arise from ensembles of weak, transient, multivalent molecular interactions that cannot be predicted from any single interaction in isolation. Since the recognition that liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) underlies condensate assembly roughly a decade ago, the field has produced an explosion of heterogeneous data: thousands of proteins have been catalogued as phase-separating in curated databases (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, CD-CODE); condensate ultrastructure has been visualized at near-atomic and mesoscale resolution via cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution microscopy deposited in EMDB and EMPIAR; compositional interactomes have been mapped via affinity purification-mass spectrometry and proximity labeling in BioGRID, IntAct, and RNAct; quantitative biophysical measurements of condensate viscosity, surface tension, and FRAP recovery kinetics are scattered across supplementary materials of hundreds of individual publications; and disease-relevant post-translational modifications and mutations that perturb condensate material state are annotated in PhosphoSitePlus and ClinVar. Despite this wealth of data, the field lacks a unified, quantitative understanding of the molecular grammar—the specific sequence features, stoichiometries, and modification states—that dictates emergent mesoscale material properties. This gap persists not because of insufficient data, but because the data exist in incompatible formats, scales, and ontologies that no single laboratory has the capacity, expertise, or incentive to harmonize. Structural biologists rarely engage with soft-matter physics formalisms; biophysicists measuring viscosity rarely cross-reference proteomic interactome data; computational biologists building sequence-based predictors seldom incorporate ultrastructural imaging constraints; and clinical genomics databases documenting disease variants are rarely connected to biophysical material-state annotations. This fragmentation represents precisely the kind of long-standing puzzle NCEMS is positioned to address: an emergent, mesoscale phenomenon whose resolution requires synthesizing molecular-to-phenotypic data across historically siloed subfields. The significance of solving this puzzle extends well beyond basic curiosity. Aberrant condensate material properties—particularly pathological liquid-to-solid transitions—are mechanistically implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (ALS, frontotemporal dementia, Alzheimer's disease) and cancer, where mutations in IDR-containing proteins (FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1) alter phase behavior and promote toxic aggregation. A predictive molecular grammar linking sequence, PTM state, and cellular context to emergent material properties would transform our ability to interpret disease variants, design condensate-modulating therapeutics, and engineer synthetic condensates for biotechnology applications. Critically, this synthesis cannot be accomplished by any individual lab: it requires simultaneous fluency in polymer physics, structural biology, proteomics, natural language processing for literature mining, and machine learning, applied across dozens of disparate, non-interoperable public databases. NCEMS's mission to catalyze multidisciplinary teams synthesizing public data to resolve mesoscale emergence questions is uniquely suited to enable this integration, providing the infrastructure, cross-institutional coordination, and community-building support necessary to convert fragmented condensate data into a unified, predictive, and openly reusable scientific resource.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around three interlocking research questions that progress from molecular encoding to mechanistic prediction to translational application, each requiring synthesis of distinct but complementary public data streams. Research Question 1 asks: Do sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features—patterns of charge, aromaticity, and short linear motifs within IDRs—quantitatively predict emergent viscoelastic properties (viscosity, surface tension, relaxation timescales) across diverse condensate types? We hypothesize that despite the biochemical diversity of condensate-forming proteins, a generalizable quantitative relationship exists between sticker valence/patterning and macroscopic material properties, such that features extracted from sequence alone (net charge per residue, kappa charge patterning, aromatic residue spacing, motif density) will explain a significant proportion of variance in curated biophysical measurements (FRAP recovery rates, viscosity, surface tension) once RNA and PTM context are incorporated as covariates. This hypothesis directly tests and extends the stickers-and-spacers theoretical framework from soft-matter physics using empirical data at unprecedented scale, rather than the single-protein-family analyses that have dominated the field to date. Research Question 2 asks: What structural, compositional, and biophysical signatures distinguish functional liquid-like condensates from pathological solid-like or amyloid aggregates associated with neurodegenerative and oncogenic variants? We hypothesize that pathological transitions are associated not merely with individual mutations but with quantifiable shifts in interaction network topology (e.g., increased clustering coefficients or reduced compositional heterogeneity in interactome-derived networks) and with characteristic ultrastructural signatures (altered fibrillar content, reduced internal mixing, multiphase demixing) detectable in cryo-EM and super-resolution imaging datasets. Testing this hypothesis requires cross-referencing PTM/disease-variant databases (PhosphoSitePlus, ClinVar) with condensate compositional and structural archives (EMDB, EMPIAR, BioGRID/IntAct)—an integration no existing single-domain database supports. Research Question 3 asks: Can a generalizable computational model, trained on the integrated sequence-structure-composition-material property dataset, predict emergent mesoscale material behavior from primary sequence and cellular context for condensate systems not used in model training? We hypothesize that hybrid models combining physics-informed polymer theory (providing mechanistic priors and interpretability) with data-driven graph neural networks (capturing higher-order compositional and interaction-network effects) will outperform either purely sequence-based or purely network-based models in predicting held-out experimental material properties, and will generalize better across condensate types than existing single-modality predictors. A secondary, cross-cutting hypothesis is methodological: that natural-language-processing-assisted literature mining, combined with expert curation, can efficiently extract quantitative biophysical measurements currently 'trapped' in supplementary materials at a scale sufficient to power robust statistical and machine-learning analyses—a capability essential not only for this project but as a reusable methodological contribution to the broader mesoscale biology community. Collectively, these questions and hypotheses are deliberately structured so that no single existing dataset or disciplinary perspective can resolve them independently; each requires the simultaneous integration of sequence-level, structural, network-level, and phenotypic/clinical data streams, embodying the community-scale synthesis approach that NCEMS is designed to enable.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds through four integrated work packages executed collaboratively across the Working Group's disciplinary teams. Work Package 1 (Data Harmonization and Ontology Development, months 1-8) will establish a standardized ontology for condensate properties—spanning sequence features, structural descriptors, interactome metrics, and material-property terms—co-developed by structural biologists, biophysicists, and data scientists to ensure semantic interoperability across source databases (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, CD-CODE, EMDB, EMPIAR, BioGRID, IntAct, RNAct, PhosphoSitePlus, ClinVar). Programmatic API-based extraction pipelines will be built in Python/R to pull structured data, while an NLP-assisted literature-mining pipeline (leveraging transformer-based named entity recognition fine-tuned on condensate biophysics terminology) will extract quantitative material-property measurements (FRAP recovery rates, viscosity, surface tension values) from supplementary tables and figures of the primary literature, with extracted values validated through expert manual curation by biophysicist team members. Work Package 2 (CondensateAtlas Database Construction, months 4-14) will integrate harmonized data into a relational/graph-hybrid database architecture, linking sequence records to structural, interactome, and material-property annotations via unique condensate and protein identifiers, with version-controlled schema management enabling continuous community contribution. Work Package 3 (Statistical and Machine-Learning Analysis, months 10-24) directly addresses the three research questions. For RQ1, we will compute stickers-and-spacers sequence descriptors (using established tools such as CIDER, localCIDER) for all curated IDR sequences and apply Gaussian process regression and regularized linear models to test predictive relationships with curated viscoelastic measurements, using cross-validation stratified by condensate family to assess generalizability. For RQ2, interactome-derived compositional networks will be constructed as graphs with proteins as nodes and curated interaction confidence as edge weights; network topology metrics (clustering coefficient, modularity, centrality) will be compared statistically between condensates annotated as liquid-like versus pathologically solid/aggregated, using disease-variant annotations from ClinVar as ground truth labels; parallel image-analysis pipelines will extract quantitative ultrastructural features (shape descriptors, internal texture heterogeneity) from EMDB/EMPIAR datasets for comparison. For RQ3, we will develop and train graph neural network architectures that take as input sequence-derived features and interactome network structure, incorporating physics-informed constraints derived from polymer scaling theory as regularization terms, benchmarking performance against held-out experimental datasets not used in training, and against baseline sequence-only and network-only models. Work Package 4 (Validation, Synthesis, and Dissemination, months 18-30) will synthesize findings across research questions into an integrated predictive framework, validate model predictions against independent experimental datasets identified through literature review, and prepare the database, models, and code for public release. All computational workflows will be containerized (Docker) and orchestrated via Snakemake/Nextflow to ensure reproducibility, with trainees leading discrete curation and modeling modules under joint mentorship from computational and wet-lab co-investigators, supported by regular cross-disciplinary working group meetings and NCEMS-facilitated hackathons for pipeline development and troubleshooting.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver four concrete outcomes. First, CondensateAtlas, a publicly accessible, interoperable meta-database integrating sequence, structural, interactome, material-property, and disease-variant data for hundreds of characterized biomolecular condensates, structured for continuous community contribution and long-term sustainability beyond the funding period. Second, a validated, generalizable computational framework combining physics-informed polymer models with graph neural networks capable of predicting emergent condensate material properties from sequence and cellular context, benchmarked against held-out experimental data and released as open-source, documented software. Third, a novel NLP-assisted literature-mining pipeline for extracting quantitative biophysical measurements from unstructured text and supplementary materials, itself a reusable methodological contribution applicable broadly across mesoscale biology synthesis efforts. Fourth, a mechanistic resolution—supported by cross-scale empirical evidence—of the long-standing question of how molecular-level sequence grammar generates emergent, collective mesoscale material behavior, including identification of structural and compositional signatures distinguishing functional from pathological condensate states. Scientifically, this work will advance fundamental understanding of mesoscale emergence, directly aligned with NCEMS's core mission, by providing the first cross-scale, empirically grounded predictive framework linking molecular sequence to collective material properties. Translationally, the identification of sequence and compositional signatures associated with pathological aggregation has direct relevance for interpreting disease-associated variants in neurodegeneration and cancer, and for guiding future therapeutic strategies targeting condensate material state. Methodologically, the project establishes reusable ontologies, curation pipelines, and modeling frameworks that will accelerate future mesoscale synthesis research well beyond condensate biology, serving as a template for integrating sequence-to-phenotype data in other emergent biological systems. The training component will produce a cohort of early-career researchers fluent in cross-disciplinary data synthesis, reproducible computational workflows, and team science, directly contributing to NCEMS's goal of cultivating a data-savvy scientific workforce.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This project is designed from inception around open science and reproducibility principles consistent with NCEMS community standards. All primary data extracted or harmonized from public sources will retain full provenance metadata linking back to original database entries and literature citations, ensuring transparency and enabling independent verification. The CondensateAtlas database schema, ontology definitions, and all curated datasets will be deposited in open, version-controlled repositories (Zenodo for archival snapshots, GitHub for active development), released under permissive licenses (CC-BY for data, MIT/BSD for code) to maximize reuse. All computational analyses—including NLP extraction pipelines, sequence-feature calculations, network analyses, and machine-learning model training and evaluation—will be implemented as containerized, workflow-managed pipelines (Docker plus Snakemake/Nextflow) with fully documented parameters, enabling exact reproducibility by external users on standard computing infrastructure. Trained model weights, hyperparameters, and evaluation benchmarks will be publicly released alongside detailed model cards describing training data, intended use, and known limitations, following emerging community standards for responsible ML dissemination in biology. The Working Group commits to depositing preprints on bioRxiv prior to journal submission and to publishing in open-access venues wherever feasible. Data and code releases will follow a staged but time-bound embargo policy: internal working group access during active curation phases, followed by public release of each completed module (ontology, database, pipeline, model) upon validation, rather than withholding all resources until final publication, consistent with NCEMS's emphasis on continuous, team-based open science. The database is explicitly architected to support continuous community contribution beyond the funding period, with a governance plan for accepting, validating, and versioning external data submissions, ensuring CondensateAtlas functions as a living, sustainable resource rather than a static deliverable. Reproducibility will be further supported by comprehensive unit testing of all pipeline components, continuous integration testing via GitHub Actions, and detailed README and wiki documentation designed for use by non-expert external users, including trainees and researchers from underrepresented institutions seeking to engage with the resource.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed budget supports a two-and-a-half-year Working Group effort structured around personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination costs. Personnel costs constitute the majority of the budget, supporting partial-effort salary for co-investigators across participating institutions (biophysics, structural biology, cell biology, computational biology/data science), full or partial support for two postdoctoral researchers leading database integration and machine-learning model development respectively, and stipend support for three to four graduate student trainees leading discrete data curation and analysis modules under joint mentorship. A dedicated data curation specialist or research software engineer position is requested to support NLP pipeline development, database architecture, and long-term infrastructure maintenance, reflecting a resource need beyond typical individual lab capacity. Computational resources include cloud computing credits or allocation on high-performance computing infrastructure for graph neural network training, large-scale image analysis of EMDB/EMPIAR datasets, and NLP model fine-tuning, alongside data storage costs for hosting the integrated CondensateAtlas database and associated derived datasets. Travel funds are requested to support two to three in-person Working Group meetings per year, essential for cross-disciplinary synthesis, hands-on trainee mentorship, and hackathon-style pipeline development sessions, alongside travel to relevant scientific conferences for dissemination. Publication costs include open-access publishing fees and preprint server deposition. Modest funds are allocated for external consultation with ontology/database design specialists during early-phase infrastructure development, and for software licensing where necessary for specialized image analysis tools. NCEMS-provided resources—including shared computational infrastructure, data harmonization support staff, project management coordination, and community-science training modules—are integral to feasibility and are explicitly leveraged rather than duplicated within this budget, reflecting the collaborative, Center-supported nature of the proposed work. This budget structure reflects the project's core premise: that meaningful synthesis of this scale and cross-disciplinary scope requires shared infrastructure and coordinated, multi-institutional personnel investment beyond what any single R01-scale or individual laboratory budget could support.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: collective material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, aging into gels or solids) arise from thousands of transient, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs). Despite explosive growth in condensate research, our understanding of how molecular 'grammar' dictates emergent mesoscale behavior remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based phase-separation predictors (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, CD-CODE), cryo-electron tomography and super-resolution imaging datasets depicting condensate ultrastructure (EMDB, EMPIAR), proteomic and interactome studies of condensate composition (BioGRID, IntAct, RNAct), biophysical measurements of material properties (FRAP recovery rates, viscosity, surface tension) buried in supplementary tables of hundreds of papers, and PTM/disease-variant databases (PhosphoSitePlus, ClinVar) linking condensate dysregulation to pathology. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to harmonize these heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets—spanning atomic structure to cellular phenotype—into a unified predictive framework.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and data scientists to construct a curated, interoperable meta-database and companion machine-learning framework—CondensateAtlas—that integrates sequence features (IDR composition, charge patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs), structural/ultrastructural data (condensate size, shape, multiphase organization from imaging archives), interactome-derived compositional networks, and quantitative material-property measurements curated via natural-language-processing-assisted literature mining and manual expert curation. Using this integrated resource, we will (1) test whether sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features quantitatively predict emergent viscoelastic properties across condensate types, (2) identify structural and compositional signatures that distinguish functional liquid-like condensates from pathological solid-like aggregates linked to neurodegenerative and oncogenic variants, and (3) develop generalizable biophysical/ML models capable of predicting mesoscale material behavior from primary sequence and cellular context, tested against held-out experimental datasets. Statistical and generative modeling approaches (Gaussian process regression, graph neural networks trained on interaction networks, physics-informed biophysical polymer models) will be co-developed by computational and wet-lab collaborators to ensure biological interpretability.

This project requires NCEMS support because it depends on cross-institutional data harmonization, standardized ontology development for condensate properties, and computational infrastructure beyond any single lab's capacity, while uniting communities (structural biology, soft-matter physics, cell biology, genomics) that rarely interact directly. The working group will include early-career researchers and trainees who will lead specific data curation and modeling modules, receiving hands-on training in FAIR data practices, reproducible workflow design (Snakemake/Nextflow pipelines), and multidisciplinary team science. All curated datasets, ontologies, trained models, and analysis code will be released as open-access community resources via Zenodo/GitHub, with a living database designed for continuous community contribution. By synthesizing molecular-to-mesoscale data at unprecedented scale, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle—how simple molecular rules generate complex emergent condensate behavior—while generating a foundational, reusable resource for the mesoscale biology community.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membrane-less assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: they arise from collective, multivalent interactions among proteins and nucleic acids, yet exhibit properties (viscosity, selective permeability, catalytic enhancement, signaling thresholds) not predictable from any single component. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across structural biology, proteomics, imaging, and genetics, no unified framework connects molecular-level sequence/structural features to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists because the relevant data are fragmented across disconnected resources—intrinsically disordered region (IDR) predictors (MobiDB, IUPred), condensate component databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, CD-CODE), structural repositories (PDB, AlphaFold DB), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell), single-cell/spatial transcriptomics, and disease-variant catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC). Synthesizing these heterogeneous, multiscale datasets requires expertise spanning biophysics, structural biology, cell biology, computational modeling, evolutionary biology, and clinical genetics—expertise no single lab possesses, and integration efforts that exceed what any two-lab collaboration could reasonably undertake.

This Working Group will construct an open, queryable 'Condensatome' resource and analytical framework that integrates these disparate datasets to answer a fundamental question: What generalizable molecular features—sequence composition, IDR architecture, multivalent interaction motifs, post-translational modification sites, and structural flexibility—predict the emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates (nucleation propensity, material state, compositional selectivity, functional output), and how do disease-associated mutations perturb these emergent properties to drive pathology?

Our approach proceeds in three synthesis phases. First, we will harmonize condensate component annotations, interaction networks, and structural/disorder predictions into a unified schema, applying network-based and machine-learning methods (graph neural networks, multivalency scoring) to identify molecular 'grammars' associated with distinct condensate material states and functions. Second, we will cross-reference these molecular grammars with imaging-derived phenotypic data (condensate size, number, dynamics from public live-cell datasets) and single-cell expression contexts to model how cellular environment (concentration, crowding, post-translational state) modulates emergent phase behavior across cell types. Third, we will overlay disease-variant data to test whether mutations disrupting predicted phase-separation grammar correlate with aberrant condensate formation implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, and stress-granule pathologies, generating testable hypotheses for the broader community.

The Working Group will assemble investigators across career stages and institution types—biophysicists modeling phase behavior, structural biologists curating disorder/structure data, cell biologists with imaging expertise, computational scientists building integrative ML pipelines, and clinical geneticists connecting variants to disease—reflecting the transdisciplinary scope NCEMS uniquely enables. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis workflows will be released as open, versioned, reproducible pipelines (via GitHub/Zenodo) accompanied by tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on data harmonization and modeling subprojects, receiving structured training in FAIR data practices, cross-disciplinary communication, and reproducible computational biology, directly building the data-savvy workforce this call seeks to cultivate while resolving a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.

Our approach proceeds in three synthesis phases. First, we will harmonize condensate component annotations, interaction networks, and structural/disorder predictions into a unified schema, applying network-based and machine-learning methods (graph neural networks, multivalency scoring) to identify molecular 'grammars' associated with distinct condensate material states and functions. Second, we will cross-reference these molecular grammars with imaging-derived phenotypic data (condensate size, number, dynamics from public live-cell datasets) and single-cell expression contexts to model how cellular environment (concentration, crowding, post-translational state) modulates emergent phase behavior across cell types. Third, we will overlay disease-variant data to test whether mutations disrupting predicted phase-separation grammar correlate with aberrant condensate formation implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, and stress-granule pathologies, generating testable hypotheses for the broader community.

The Working Group will assemble investigators across career stages and institution types—biophysicists modeling phase behavior, structural biologists curating disorder/structure data, cell biologists with imaging expertise, computational scientists building integrative ML pipelines, and clinical geneticists connecting variants to disease—reflecting the transdisciplinary scope NCEMS uniquely enables. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis workflows will be released as open, versioned, reproducible pipelines (via GitHub/Zenodo) accompanied by tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on data harmonization and modeling subprojects, receiving structured training in FAIR data practices, cross-disciplinary communication, and reproducible computational biology, directly building the data-savvy workforce this call seeks to cultivate while resolving a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged over the past decade as a fundamental organizing principle of the cell, mediating processes from ribosome biogenesis and stress response to transcriptional control and signal transduction. Membrane-less organelles—nucleoli, stress granules, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, and signaling puncta—form through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related percolation transitions driven by multivalent, often weak and transient interactions among proteins and nucleic acids. The hallmark of condensates as mesoscale emergent phenomena is that their functional properties—material state (liquid, gel, solid), selective permeability, catalytic enhancement, nucleation kinetics, and responsiveness to cellular cues—cannot be predicted from the properties of any single molecular component in isolation. Instead, these properties arise collectively from a combinatorial 'grammar' of interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, short linear motifs, post-translational modification (PTM) sites, and nucleic acid scaffolds. Deciphering this grammar and how it produces emergent mesoscale behavior is one of the central open problems in molecular and cellular biology, with direct relevance to human disease: dysregulated condensate dynamics—aberrant hardening of stress granules, aggregation of FUS or TDP-43, or oncogenic condensate formation—are implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, and viral infection.

Despite intense research interest, the field remains deeply fragmented. Data relevant to condensate biology are distributed across at least seven distinct classes of public resources spanning different scales and modalities: IDR/disorder predictors (MobiDB, IUPred, D2P2); curated condensate component and phase-separation databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, CD-CODE, LLPSDB); atomic structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB); protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, RNAct); subcellular imaging atlases documenting condensate morphology and localization (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell); single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic datasets capturing expression context; and disease-variant catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC, gnomAD). Each resource was built with a different scope, vocabulary, and granularity, and no existing framework harmonizes them into a queryable system capable of testing cross-scale hypotheses linking molecular grammar to emergent function.

This fragmentation is precisely the class of problem NCEMS is designed to solve. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural bioinformatics, imaging analytics, network science, machine learning, and clinical genetics required to integrate these datasets rigorously, nor could a conventional two-lab collaboration reasonably absorb the data engineering, ontology harmonization, and cross-validation burden this synthesis demands. By assembling a transdisciplinary Working Group empowered by NCEMS computational and community infrastructure, this project will produce the first unified, open 'Condensatome' resource linking molecular sequence/structural grammar to emergent mesoscale condensate phenotypes and their perturbation in disease. In doing so, it will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence while establishing reusable synthesis methodology—harmonization schemas, multimodal predictive models, and validation pipelines—broadly applicable across the molecular and cellular sciences, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale and to catalyze data-driven discovery through community-scale synthesis.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Central Question: What generalizable molecular features—sequence composition, IDR architecture, multivalent interaction motifs, PTM sites, and structural flexibility—predict the emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates, and how do disease-associated mutations perturb this mapping to drive pathology? This overarching question decomposes into five interlocking, falsifiable sub-questions and hypotheses.

RQ1 (Molecular Grammar): What combinations of sequence and structural features predict condensate material state and functional class? H1: Condensates will cluster into distinguishable material-state classes (liquid-like, hydrogel, solid aggregate) predictable from quantitative stickers-and-spacers architecture, aromatic/charge patterning metrics (kappa, Omega, FCR, NCPR), and PTM density, and these signatures will generalize across otherwise unrelated protein families that share convergent phase-separation grammar.

RQ2 (Cellular Context Modulation): How does cell-type-specific expression, concentration, macromolecular crowding, and PTM occupancy modulate the phenotypic expression of molecular grammar? H2: The penetrance of a given molecular grammar into observable condensate phenotype is context-dependent, such that scaffold concentration relative to predicted saturation concentration (Csat) and local PTM occupancy will explain a significant fraction of cell-type-to-cell-type variability in condensate size, number, and dynamics beyond sequence features alone.

RQ3 (Network-Level Determinants): Do interactome connectivity patterns and multivalency scores correlate with condensate compositional selectivity, and can they identify previously unannotated condensate components? H3: High-degree, high-clustering-coefficient nodes within condensate-associated interaction subnetworks correspond preferentially to scaffold proteins, whereas peripheral, condition-dependent nodes correspond to client proteins, and this topological signature can predict novel, currently unannotated condensate components with testable specificity.

RQ4 (Disease Perturbation): Do disease-associated variants preferentially localize to residues or motifs predicted to be critical for phase-separation grammar, and do such mutations correlate with reported pathological condensate phenotypes? H4: Pathogenic variants (ClinVar, COSMIC) will be significantly enriched, relative to benign variants (gnomAD), within predicted sticker motifs, PTM sites, and IDR regions of known phase-separating proteins, with the strongest enrichment among variants linked to neurodegenerative and stress-granule-associated pathology.

RQ5 (Integration Value): Does a multimodal predictive model trained on harmonized molecular, network, and phenotypic features outperform single-modality classifiers in predicting condensate material state and disease relevance? H5: Integrative graph neural network models will significantly outperform sequence-only or interaction-only baselines in cross-validated prediction tasks, empirically demonstrating that emergent condensate properties are fundamentally under-determined by any single data modality—validating the mesoscale emergence hypothesis at the level of predictive modeling itself.

Collectively, these hypotheses are falsifiable and will be tested through nested cross-validation, held-out protein-family validation, and benchmarking against well-characterized experimental systems (FUS, hnRNPA1, NPM1, TDP-43, DDX4). The Working Group will generate a ranked, uncertainty-quantified set of testable predictions—candidate scaffold proteins, novel variant-phenotype associations, and a generalizable condensate classification schema—for validation by the broader experimental community, fulfilling NCEMS's mandate to answer novel questions and resolve long-standing puzzles through synthesis rather than new data generation.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds through a governance phase and three sequential, overlapping synthesis phases across a 24-month period, executed by four co-led subteams: Data Harmonization, Molecular Grammar Modeling, Phenotype Integration, and Disease Variant Analysis.

Phase 0 (Months 1–2), Team Assembly and Governance: The Working Group convenes a kickoff workshop to finalize data stewardship protocols, ontology mappings, authorship policies, and subteam charters, establishing shared computational infrastructure (cloud/HPC allocation, version-controlled repositories).

Phase 1 (Months 1–8), Harmonization and Grammar Discovery: We will extract and standardize entries from MobiDB, IUPred, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, CD-CODE, PDB, and AlphaFold DB into a unified relational/graph database keyed to UniProt identifiers and extended Gene Ontology/Condensate Ontology terms. Quantitative descriptors will be computed for each protein, including IDR fraction, charge/aromatic patterning metrics (kappa, Omega, FCR, NCPR), short linear motif enrichment, PTM site density (via PhosphoSitePlus overlay), and AlphaFold-derived structural flexibility (pLDDT-based disorder proxies). Interaction subnetworks from BioGRID, STRING, and IntAct will be constructed for annotated condensate proteins, and topological features (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient) computed. Unsupervised clustering (UMAP/HDBSCAN) and supervised graph neural network classifiers will be trained against literature-curated material-state labels to identify molecular grammar signatures.

Phase 2 (Months 6–16), Phenotype Cross-Referencing: Using existing open-source image analysis pipelines (CellProfiler, deep-learning condensate segmentation tools), we will mine quantitative condensate phenotype metrics (size, number, dynamics) from public imaging datasets (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, published high-content screens). Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data (Tabula Sapiens, Human Protein Atlas RNA-seq) will estimate cell-type-specific expression and approximate Csat ratios. Hierarchical Bayesian and mixed-effects regression models will link molecular grammar features and cellular context variables to observed phenotypic variability across cell types.

Phase 3 (Months 14–22), Disease Variant Overlay: ClinVar, COSMIC, and gnomAD variants will be mapped onto harmonized structural and motif annotations. Permutation-based enrichment tests, stratified by disease category, will evaluate whether pathogenic variants preferentially disrupt grammar-critical residues. Results will generate a ranked hypothesis list of variant-condensate-phenotype associations.

Validation and Synthesis (Months 18–24): All models undergo nested cross-validation, held-out protein-family testing, and benchmarking against well-characterized experimental condensates. Sensitivity analyses will assess robustness to database annotation confidence, and uncertainty quantification will accompany all predictions. A mid-project hybrid synthesis retreat (Month 12) and final synthesis workshop (Month 22) will integrate subteam findings, resolve cross-cutting discrepancies, and finalize the Condensatome resource for public release.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver: (1) the Condensatome, an open, versioned, queryable database and API integrating molecular, network, structural, imaging, and disease-variant data for condensate-associated proteins; (2) validated multimodal predictive models (graph neural network classifiers) linking molecular grammar to material state, compositional selectivity, and disease relevance, released as reproducible pipelines; (3) a ranked, community-facing set of testable hypotheses—candidate novel condensate scaffolds, variant-phenotype associations, and a generalizable condensate classification schema—for experimental validation; and (4) at least three to five peer-reviewed publications spanning methodology, biological discovery, and open resource description, alongside preprints and conference presentations.

Scientifically, this synthesis will resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence by empirically demonstrating whether and how molecular-scale features generalize into emergent, function-relevant condensate behavior across otherwise unrelated protein systems—directly advancing NCEMS's core scientific vision. Practically, it will accelerate hypothesis generation for laboratories studying neurodegeneration, cancer, and stress-response biology by providing pre-computed, statistically validated predictions rather than requiring de novo data integration. Methodologically, the harmonization schema and multimodal modeling framework will be reusable for other mesoscale synthesis efforts beyond condensates (e.g., organelle contact sites, cytoskeletal assemblies), establishing a template for community-scale data synthesis in molecular and cellular biosciences.

Broader impacts include substantial workforce development: embedded trainees will co-author publications, present at NCEMS community events, and gain transferable expertise in FAIR data integration, machine learning, and transdisciplinary team science. By uniting biophysics, structural biology, cell imaging, network science, and clinical genetics around a shared open resource, the project exemplifies the cross-disciplinary, collaborative model of discovery NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This Working Group commits fully to NCEMS's open, team, and reproducible science principles. All harmonized datasets, derived feature tables, and trained models will be deposited in versioned, citable repositories (Zenodo, Figshare) under permissive open licenses (CC-BY for data, MIT/BSD for code), with persistent identifiers (DOIs) assigned at each major release milestone. All analytical code—data harmonization scripts, feature extraction pipelines, graph neural network training routines, and statistical models—will be maintained in public GitHub repositories with continuous integration testing, containerized execution environments (Docker/Singularity), and workflow managers (Snakemake/Nextflow) to ensure computational reproducibility across platforms.

The Condensatome database itself will be released as a queryable, documented public resource with a REST API and accompanying tutorials (Jupyter notebooks), enabling both computational and non-computational researchers to interrogate molecular grammar predictions and disease-variant hypotheses. Data provenance will be tracked at every integration step, with explicit versioning of source databases to ensure downstream reproducibility as upstream resources (e.g., AlphaFold DB, ClinVar) update over time.

Key hypotheses and analysis plans (Phase 1–3 models) will be preregistered via an open preprint prior to full-scale analysis, and all major findings will be released as preprints prior to journal submission to maximize community access and enable rapid feedback. The Working Group will adopt a team-science authorship and contribution policy modeled on CRediT taxonomy to ensure equitable recognition, particularly for trainees and early-career contributors performing substantial data harmonization and modeling work. Regular internal code review, shared documentation standards, and biweekly cross-subteam check-ins will maintain quality control. All materials will be structured to comply with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles, positioning the Condensatome as a durable, community-maintained resource beyond the funding period.

[Budget and Resources]
We request support for a 24-month Working Group comprising five co-investigators (partial effort, 1–2 months/year each) spanning biophysics, structural bioinformatics, cell imaging analytics, computational/network science, and clinical genetics; two postdoctoral researchers (100% effort) leading model development and phenotype integration; three graduate student trainees (50% effort) embedded across subteams for data harmonization, disease-variant analysis, and workflow documentation; and a part-time data engineer (50% effort) supporting database architecture and API development.

Computational resources include cloud or institutional HPC allocation for graph neural network training, large-scale interaction network analysis, and image-derived feature extraction, alongside persistent storage for the harmonized Condensatome database and versioned releases. Budget requests include software licensing (where applicable) and dedicated data storage/backup infrastructure.

Travel funds are requested for two in-person/hybrid Working Group convenings: a Month 1 kickoff workshop to finalize governance and harmonization protocols, and a Month 12 synthesis retreat to integrate cross-phase findings; both include support for trainee participation and travel for geographically distributed team members.

We request NCEMS-provided resources including computational infrastructure consulting, data science/ML methodological support, facilitation for team-science workshops, and support for open-science infrastructure (Zenodo/GitHub organizational accounts, API hosting). NCEMS community engagement support (webinars, cross-Working-Group symposia) will be leveraged to disseminate intermediate findings and recruit external validation partners.

Estimated total budget: approximately $525,000 over 24 months, allocated as roughly 55% personnel (co-investigator effort, postdocs, graduate students, data engineer), 20% computational infrastructure, 10% travel/workshops, and 15% NCEMS-facilitated support services and open-science infrastructure costs, reflecting a lean, synthesis-focused budget appropriate for a data-only, collaborative Working Group.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membrane-less assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: they arise from collective, multivalent interactions among proteins and nucleic acids, yet exhibit properties (viscosity, selective permeability, catalytic enhancement, signaling thresholds) not predictable from any single component. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across structural biology, proteomics, imaging, and genetics, no unified framework connects molecular-level sequence/structural features to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. This gap persists because the relevant data are fragmented across disconnected resources—intrinsically disordered region (IDR) predictors (MobiDB, IUPred), condensate component databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, CD-CODE), structural repositories (PDB, AlphaFold DB), interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct), subcellular imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell), single-cell/spatial transcriptomics, and disease-variant catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC). Synthesizing these heterogeneous, multiscale datasets requires expertise spanning biophysics, structural biology, cell biology, computational modeling, evolutionary biology, and clinical genetics—expertise no single lab possesses, and integration efforts that exceed what any two-lab collaboration could reasonably undertake.

This Working Group will construct an open, queryable 'Condensatome' resource and analytical framework that integrates these disparate datasets to answer a fundamental question: What generalizable molecular features—sequence composition, IDR architecture, multivalent interaction motifs, post-translational modification sites, and structural flexibility—predict the emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates (nucleation propensity, material state, compositional selectivity, functional output), and how do disease-associated mutations perturb these emergent properties to drive pathology?

Our approach proceeds in three synthesis phases. First, we will harmonize condensate component annotations, interaction networks, and structural/disorder predictions into a unified schema, applying network-based and machine-learning methods (graph neural networks, multivalency scoring) to identify molecular 'grammars' associated with distinct condensate material states and functions. Second, we will cross-reference these molecular grammars with imaging-derived phenotypic data (condensate size, number, dynamics from public live-cell datasets) and single-cell expression contexts to model how cellular environment (concentration, crowding, post-translational state) modulates emergent phase behavior across cell types. Third, we will overlay disease-variant data to test whether mutations disrupting predicted phase-separation grammar correlate with aberrant condensate formation implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, and stress-granule pathologies, generating testable hypotheses for the broader community.

The Working Group will assemble investigators across career stages and institution types—biophysicists modeling phase behavior, structural biologists curating disorder/structure data, cell biologists with imaging expertise, computational scientists building integrative ML pipelines, and clinical geneticists connecting variants to disease—reflecting the transdisciplinary scope NCEMS uniquely enables. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis workflows will be released as open, versioned, reproducible pipelines (via GitHub/Zenodo) accompanied by tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on data harmonization and modeling subprojects, receiving structured training in FAIR data practices, cross-disciplinary communication, and reproducible computational biology, directly building the data-savvy workforce this call seeks to cultivate while resolving a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.
