full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (material state, composition, exchange dynamics) arise from combinatorial molecular interactions and cannot be predicted from any single molecule or interaction alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate biology, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based predictors of disorder and multivalency, curated condensate composition databases, protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks, structural ensemble data, single-molecule dynamics measurements, and cellular phenotype datasets have been generated by disconnected communities using incompatible vocabularies and formats. No integrated framework currently links molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and its downstream cellular consequences. This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public resources into a unified, predictive, and mechanistic framework for condensate emergence. We will integrate: (1) sequence-derived features of intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, and multivalent motifs from UniProt, MobiDB, and IDRome conformational ensemble data; (2) curated condensate composition and phase-behavior annotations from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, and CD-CODE; (3) protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction topology from BioGRID, STRING, and RNAct; (4) structural context from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and PDB; (5) subcellular localization and condensate imaging data from the Human Protein Atlas and Allen Cell Explorer; (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived exchange kinetics extracted from published literature and condensate databases; and (7) disease-associated variant data from ClinVar and COSMIC. Using this multi-modal resource, we will address three central questions: First, what combinations of sequence, network topology, and structural features best predict whether a protein participates in condensate formation, and do these features generalize across condensate types (stress granules, transcriptional condensates, nucleoli)? Second, does interactome topology (e.g., hub connectivity, clustering coefficients) correlate with emergent material properties such as liquid-to-solid transitions and exchange dynamics measured by FRAP? Third, can disease-associated mutations be systematically mapped onto this framework to identify variants that specifically perturb condensate emergence, and do such perturbations correlate with altered transcriptional noise or cellular phenotypes documented in single-cell RNA-seq datasets (ENCODE, Human Cell Atlas)? This synthesis requires computational infrastructure and cross-disciplinary expertise—spanning biophysical theory, network science, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics—that no single lab possesses, and it demands harmonization of heterogeneous, differently-curated public databases at a scale only achievable through coordinated collaboration. Deliverables include an open-access, version-controlled integrated database and machine-learning framework (CondensateAtlas), reproducible analysis pipelines, and a predictive model relating molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale phenotype. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in biophysical modeling, network analysis, and open, reproducible data science, directly building the data-savvy interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates—nucleoli, stress granules, transcriptional hubs, and dozens of other membraneless organelles—are now recognized as central organizational units of the cell, compartmentalizing biochemistry without lipid boundaries. Their formation via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related transitions represents a quintessential mesoscale emergent phenomenon: macroscopic properties such as viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability, and component exchange rates arise from thousands of transient, combinatorial, and multivalent molecular interactions, yet cannot be inferred from any single interaction or molecule in isolation. Understanding how molecular-scale 'grammar'—patterns of intrinsic disorder, charge distribution, aromatic stickers, and RNA-binding motifs—gives rise to condensate-scale material behavior, and how that behavior in turn shapes cellular phenotype and disease, is one of the central open problems in mesoscale biology and squarely within NCEMS's scientific vision. Over the past decade, the condensate field has produced an extraordinary volume of public data. Sequence-based resources (UniProt, MobiDB, IDRome) catalog intrinsic disorder and conformational ensembles; condensate-specific databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, CD-CODE) curate experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and their properties; interactome resources (BioGRID, STRING, RNAct) map protein-protein and protein-RNA connectivity; structural databases (AlphaFold DB, PDB) provide atomic and predicted structural context; imaging resources (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Cell Explorer) document subcellular localization and condensate morphology; and clinical genomics repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) catalog disease-associated variants that map onto condensate-forming proteins. Critically, these resources were built by disconnected research communities—biophysicists, structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and geneticists—using incompatible ontologies, identifiers, and quality standards. As a result, no existing framework connects molecular grammar to network topology, structural context, imaging phenotype, and clinical consequence within a single, queryable, predictive system. This fragmentation is not a matter of insufficient effort within any one field; it is a structural problem of disciplinary silos that only cross-domain synthesis can resolve. The scientific stakes are high. Dysregulated condensate emergence is implicated in neurodegeneration (TDP-43, FUS, hnRNPA1 aggregation in ALS/FTD), cancer (transcriptional condensate hijacking by oncogenic fusion proteins), and viral replication (nucleocapsid condensates). A predictive, mechanistic map from sequence and network features to emergent material state and phenotype would transform our ability to anticipate which mutations, expression changes, or interactome perturbations drive pathological condensate behavior—an outcome unreachable by single-database or single-lab analysis. This proposal directly targets NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mandate by synthesizing molecular, network, structural, imaging, and clinical data that individually describe fragments of the condensate emergence problem but collectively, when harmonized, can resolve how lower-scale molecular features generate higher-scale, unpredictable collective behavior. The project's significance lies not merely in aggregating data but in producing a generalizable analytical and conceptual framework—applicable to other mesoscale emergent systems—for linking sequence grammar to network topology, structural ensembles, and phenotype across scales of biological organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group will address three interlocking research questions, each requiring synthesis across data modalities that no single laboratory or database curates in combination. Question 1 (Molecular Grammar of Condensate Participation): What combinations of sequence-derived features (disorder content, charge patterning, aromatic/RGG motif density), interactome topology (node degree, clustering coefficient, community membership), and structural context (predicted local structure, conformational ensemble breadth from AlphaFold and IDRome) best discriminate condensate-forming from non-condensate-forming proteins, and do the discriminative features generalize across condensate types? We hypothesize that no single feature class is sufficient; rather, condensate participation is governed by an interaction between disorder-encoded multivalency and network centrality, such that highly connected 'hub' proteins with moderate disorder content preferentially seed condensates, while client proteins rely more heavily on sequence-encoded stickers. We further hypothesize that stress granules, transcriptional condensates, and nucleoli exhibit partially distinct molecular grammars reflecting their different RNA content and biophysical driving forces, meaning a single universal classifier will underperform relative to condensate-type-aware models. Question 2 (Network Topology and Emergent Material Properties): Does interactome topology—particularly hub connectivity, clustering coefficient, and multivalent binding partner diversity—correlate with emergent material properties such as liquid-to-solid transition propensity and FRAP-derived exchange dynamics (recovery half-time, mobile fraction)? We hypothesize that proteins occupying densely interconnected network neighborhoods with high clustering coefficients exhibit slower exchange dynamics and greater propensity for liquid-to-solid transitions, because dense local connectivity increases the effective valency and residence time of molecular interactions within the condensate, consistent with percolation-theoretic models of phase behavior. We predict this relationship will be modulated by RNA-binding capacity, with RNA-binding hubs showing more tunable, RNA-concentration-dependent dynamics than protein-only hubs. Question 3 (Disease Variants and Condensate Perturbation): Can disease-associated variants from ClinVar and COSMIC be systematically mapped onto condensate-relevant sequence and structural features to identify variants that specifically perturb emergence-relevant properties (e.g., disruption of charge patterning, loss of a multivalent motif, or destabilization of a structured domain adjacent to a disordered driver region), and do such variants correlate with altered transcriptional noise or phenotypic signatures in single-cell RNA-seq data (ENCODE, Human Cell Atlas)? We hypothesize that pathogenic variants cluster non-randomly within condensate-driving sequence elements rather than being uniformly distributed across the protein, and that variants predicted computationally to strengthen aberrant self-association (promoting liquid-to-solid transition) will co-occur with increased transcriptional noise or stress-pathway activation signatures in matched single-cell datasets, providing an orthogonal, population-scale line of evidence linking molecular-level perturbation to cellular-level emergent phenotype. Collectively, these hypotheses are only testable through integration of sequence, network, structural, imaging, biophysical, and genomic data—precisely the kind of community-scale synthesis NCEMS is positioned to enable, and one that requires the combined, non-redundant expertise of biophysicists, network scientists, structural bioinformaticians, cell biologists, and clinical genomicists working from a common, harmonized data resource.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will proceed in four coordinated phases over the funding period. Phase 1 (Data Harmonization, months 1–6): We will construct a unified relational and graph-based data schema mapping UniProt accessions across all source databases, resolving identifier mismatches, differing curation vintages, and inconsistent annotation vocabularies (e.g., divergent definitions of 'client' versus 'scaffold' proteins across PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, and CD-CODE). Sequence features (disorder scores from MobiDB, charge patterning metrics, motif counts) and IDRome conformational ensemble descriptors will be computed or extracted programmatically. Interaction networks from BioGRID, STRING, and RNAct will be merged into a composite weighted graph with topological metrics (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient, community assignment via Louvain/Leiden algorithms) computed under multiple confidence thresholds to test robustness. Structural context will be extracted from AlphaFold DB (per-residue confidence, disorder-structure boundaries) and cross-referenced with PDB entries where available. Imaging annotations (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Cell Explorer) will be mapped to standardized subcellular compartment ontologies. FRAP and single-molecule kinetic parameters will be extracted from condensate databases and augmented via systematic literature mining (semi-automated text extraction with expert curation) to compile a benchmark dynamics dataset. Phase 2 (Predictive Modeling, months 4–14): For Question 1, we will train and cross-validate interpretable machine learning classifiers (gradient-boosted trees, regularized logistic regression, and graph neural networks incorporating network topology directly) to predict condensate participation, using nested cross-validation stratified by condensate type and evaluated with held-out proteins and orthogonal experimental validation sets. Feature importance will be assessed via SHAP analysis to extract interpretable molecular grammar rules. For Question 2, we will use regression and correlation analyses (mixed-effects models accounting for protein family and condensate-type covariates) linking network topology metrics to FRAP-derived dynamics, supplemented by simple biophysical/percolation-theoretic simulations to test mechanistic plausibility of observed correlations. Phase 3 (Variant Mapping, months 10–20): ClinVar and COSMIC variants will be mapped onto condensate-relevant sequence positions and structural contexts; enrichment of pathogenic variants within emergence-relevant regions (disorder segments, motif positions, charge blocks) will be tested via permutation-based null models. Predicted perturbation scores will be correlated with transcriptional noise metrics and stress-response signatures derived from ENCODE and Human Cell Atlas single-cell RNA-seq data using existing processed expression matrices, avoiding any new data generation. Phase 4 (Integration and Validation, months 18–24): All pipelines will be consolidated into the CondensateAtlas framework, with iterative validation against literature-reported experimental findings not used in training, and sensitivity analyses across confidence thresholds and database versions to assess robustness of conclusions.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis will produce four primary deliverables: (1) CondensateAtlas, an open, version-controlled, harmonized database integrating sequence, network, structural, imaging, dynamics, and variant data across thousands of proteins, resolving identifier and ontology conflicts that currently prevent cross-database analysis; (2) a validated, interpretable predictive framework linking molecular grammar and network topology to condensate participation and material state, generalizable across condensate types; (3) a systematic, quantitative map of disease-associated variants predicted to perturb condensate emergence, linked to cellular phenotype signatures, generating testable hypotheses for downstream experimental and clinical research; and (4) reproducible, containerized analysis pipelines and educational tutorials documenting the synthesis workflow. Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing fragmentation in condensate biology by establishing whether molecular grammar rules generalize across condensate types or are context-dependent, and by providing the first cross-scale evidence linking interactome topology to emergent material properties. This advances NCEMS's core mission of understanding mesoscale emergence by demonstrating a generalizable analytical template—linking sequence, network, structure, and phenotype—applicable to other emergent mesoscale systems beyond condensates (e.g., cytoskeletal assemblies, signaling clusters). Clinically, the variant-perturbation map offers a resource for prioritizing candidate pathogenic mechanisms in neurodegenerative disease and cancer genomics. Broader impacts include establishing shared data standards and harmonization protocols that will benefit the condensate research community long after the funding period, lowering barriers for future integrative studies, and providing a public benchmark dataset for emerging machine learning methods in structural and network biology.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group commits fully to NCEMS's open, team, and reproducible science standards. All source data used are already publicly available; no new experimental data will be generated. All harmonization scripts, feature-extraction pipelines, trained models, and statistical analyses will be developed under version control (Git/GitHub) from project inception, with continuous integration testing to ensure reproducibility across computing environments. Computational environments will be containerized (Docker/Singularity) and archived with permanent identifiers (Zenodo/Software Heritage) at each major milestone. The integrated CondensateAtlas database will be released under an open license (CC-BY for annotations, permissive open-source license for code) via a public repository and, where appropriate, deposited with existing community resources (e.g., as a CD-CODE extension or standalone FAIR-compliant repository) to maximize discoverability and reuse. All intermediate and final datasets will be structured according to FAIR principles, with standardized metadata, controlled vocabularies harmonized across source databases, and comprehensive data dictionaries documenting provenance and transformation steps from each original source. Analysis notebooks (Jupyter/R Markdown) will accompany all reported results, enabling line-by-line reproducibility of figures and statistical claims. We will pre-register primary hypotheses and analysis plans for Questions 1–3 via an open preprint server (bioRxiv) prior to full-scale analysis, distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory findings. Regular internal data and code review ('team science' checkpoints) will occur at quarterly Working Group meetings, with external advisory input solicited at the midpoint. All publications arising from this work will be posted as preprints prior to journal submission, and we will actively contribute lessons learned on cross-database harmonization back to the source database maintainers (e.g., PhaSepDB, DrLLPS curators) to improve future interoperability, an explicit commitment to strengthening the broader open data ecosystem rather than merely consuming it.

[Budget and Resources]
This project requests NCEMS support for a two-year Working Group comprising six co-investigators (biophysics, computational structural biology, network science, cell biology, clinical genomics, and data science/bioinformatics leadership), two postdoctoral researchers, and two graduate students distributed across partner institutions. Personnel costs constitute the majority of the budget, supporting dedicated effort for data harmonization, model development, and variant analysis; postdocs and graduate students will be co-mentored across labs to ensure genuine cross-training rather than siloed contributions. Computational resources include cloud/HPC allocation for graph neural network training, large-scale feature extraction across proteome-wide datasets, and permanent hosting of the CondensateAtlas database and associated Zenodo/GitHub archives; we request modest cloud storage and compute credits rather than capital equipment, consistent with a data-synthesis (not data-generation) project. Travel funds are requested for two in-person Working Group meetings (kickoff and midpoint) plus trainee travel to one scientific conference each to present synthesis outcomes, fostering integration and visibility for early-career researchers. A dedicated data curation/software engineering specialist (partial FTE) is requested to lead schema harmonization and pipeline containerization, a resource beyond typical single-lab budgets that is essential given the scale of database integration required. Publication costs cover open-access fees for preprints and journal articles. We specifically request NCEMS-provided support for secure, persistent computational infrastructure and cross-institutional data-sharing agreements, which extend beyond what any single partner lab currently possesses and are essential to enable the multi-database, multi-institution integration central to this proposal. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this Working Group. A detailed budget justification and year-by-year allocation table will be provided in the full budget narrative, with approximately 65% allocated to personnel, 20% to computational infrastructure, 10% to travel/meetings, and 5% to dissemination and open-access costs.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (material state, composition, exchange dynamics) arise from combinatorial molecular interactions and cannot be predicted from any single molecule or interaction alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate biology, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based predictors of disorder and multivalency, curated condensate composition databases, protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks, structural ensemble data, single-molecule dynamics measurements, and cellular phenotype datasets have been generated by disconnected communities using incompatible vocabularies and formats. No integrated framework currently links molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and its downstream cellular consequences. This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, computational structural biologists, network scientists, cell biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public resources into a unified, predictive, and mechanistic framework for condensate emergence. We will integrate: (1) sequence-derived features of intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, and multivalent motifs from UniProt, MobiDB, and IDRome conformational ensemble data; (2) curated condensate composition and phase-behavior annotations from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, and CD-CODE; (3) protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction topology from BioGRID, STRING, and RNAct; (4) structural context from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and PDB; (5) subcellular localization and condensate imaging data from the Human Protein Atlas and Allen Cell Explorer; (6) single-molecule and FRAP-derived exchange kinetics extracted from published literature and condensate databases; and (7) disease-associated variant data from ClinVar and COSMIC. Using this multi-modal resource, we will address three central questions: First, what combinations of sequence, network topology, and structural features best predict whether a protein participates in condensate formation, and do these features generalize across condensate types (stress granules, transcriptional condensates, nucleoli)? Second, does interactome topology (e.g., hub connectivity, clustering coefficients) correlate with emergent material properties such as liquid-to-solid transitions and exchange dynamics measured by FRAP? Third, can disease-associated mutations be systematically mapped onto this framework to identify variants that specifically perturb condensate emergence, and do such perturbations correlate with altered transcriptional noise or cellular phenotypes documented in single-cell RNA-seq datasets (ENCODE, Human Cell Atlas)? This synthesis requires computational infrastructure and cross-disciplinary expertise—spanning biophysical theory, network science, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics—that no single lab possesses, and it demands harmonization of heterogeneous, differently-curated public databases at a scale only achievable through coordinated collaboration. Deliverables include an open-access, version-controlled integrated database and machine-learning framework (CondensateAtlas), reproducible analysis pipelines, and a predictive model relating molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale phenotype. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, receiving cross-training in biophysical modeling, network analysis, and open, reproducible data science, directly building the data-savvy interdisciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based phase-separation predictors (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB), condensate-specific proteomic and interactome maps (CD-CODE, BioGRID, IntAct), structural predictions (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-content imaging atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting), and functional perturbation screens (CRISPR-based condensate disruption studies, disease-mutation databases like ClinVar and COSMIC). The working group will first construct a harmonized meta-database linking condensate-resident proteins across sequence/structural feature sets, experimentally measured or imaging-inferred material properties (FRAP recovery rates, droplet fusion kinetics, aspect ratios extracted from public microscopy datasets), and interactome/expression context. Second, we will cross-reference predicted material-property phenotypes with functional perturbation datasets (e.g., condensate-disrupting mutations linked to disease, optogenetic clustering screens) to test causal links between mesoscale material state and higher-order cellular function, addressing long-standing puzzles such as why chemically similar condensates (e.g., stress granules vs. P-bodies) exhibit distinct dynamics and functional consequences. 

This synthesis is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, quantitative imaging analysis, and cell biology, plus computational infrastructure to harmonize heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets. NCEMS support will enable dataset harmonization workshops, shared computational pipelines, and coordination across geographically distributed labs. [Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—exemplify mesoscale emergence: their material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, component exchange dynamics) arise from collective interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, folded domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications, yet these properties cannot be predicted from single-molecule features alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based phase-separation predictors (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB), condensate-specific proteomic and interactome maps (CD-CODE, BioGRID, IntAct), structural predictions (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-content imaging atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting), and functional perturbation screens (CRISPR-based condensate disruption studies, disease-mutation databases like ClinVar and COSMIC). No integrated framework currently connects molecular grammar to emergent material properties to downstream cellular phenotypes. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell imaging, and machine learning—to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and predictive modeling framework addressing a fundamental question: What combinatorial rules of sequence composition, structural motifs, PTMs, and interaction networks give rise to specific emergent material properties of condensates, and how do these properties causally determine cellular outcomes such as transcriptional bursting, stress granule dynamics, and signaling fidelity? 

The working group will first construct a harmonized meta-database linking condensate-resident proteins across sequence/structural feature sets, experimentally measured or imaging-inferred material properties (FRAP recovery rates, droplet fusion kinetics, aspect ratios extracted from public microscopy datasets), and interactome/expression context. Using this resource, we will train interpretable machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating AlphaFold-derived structural embeddings and disorder/PTM annotations) to predict emergent material properties from molecular features, explicitly testing whether scaling laws or phase diagrams generalize across protein families and cellular contexts. Second, we will cross-reference predicted material-property phenotypes with functional perturbation datasets (e.g., condensate-disrupting mutations linked to disease, optogenetic clustering screens) to test causal links between mesoscale material state and higher-order cellular function, addressing long-standing puzzles such as why chemically similar condensates (e.g., stress granules vs. P-bodies) exhibit distinct dynamics and functional consequences. 

This synthesis is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, quantitative imaging analysis, and cell biology, plus computational infrastructure to harmonize heterogeneous, differently-scaled datasets. NCEMS support will enable dataset harmonization workshops, shared computational pipelines, and coordination across geographically distributed labs. All curated datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned community resource (FAIR-compliant), with tutorials and hackathon-style training events specifically designed to onboard graduate students and postdocs into data-intensive condensate biology, cultivating a new generation of researchers fluent in both wet-lab condensate biophysics and computational data synthesis.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates—liquid-like, membraneless assemblies including nucleoli, stress granules, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and signaling clusters—represent one of the most striking examples of mesoscale emergence in cell biology. Their formation via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) transforms collections of individually soluble biomolecules into compartments with distinct material properties: viscosity, surface tension, interfacial behavior, multiphase (core-shell) architecture, and dynamic component exchange rates. Crucially, these emergent properties are not simple sums of single-molecule biophysical parameters; rather, they arise combinatorially from interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, multivalent motifs, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs), often in a context-dependent and nonlinear fashion. Understanding how molecular 'grammar' encodes emergent mesoscale material states—and how those states causally shape cellular function—constitutes a foundational unsolved problem in molecular and cellular biology, squarely within NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mandate.

Over the past decade, the condensate field has generated an extraordinary volume of public data, yet this data remains scattered across incompatible, purpose-built repositories. Sequence-based predictors (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB) catalog phase-separating proteins and their compositional features but rarely link to measured material properties. Interactome and proteomic resources (BioGRID, IntAct, CD-CODE) document condensate composition and protein-protein interactions but lack systematic material-property annotation. Structural databases (PDB, AlphaFold DB) provide atomic and predicted structural detail but are disconnected from condensate-specific functional context. High-content imaging atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting) contain latent quantitative information—droplet morphology, fusion events, recovery kinetics—that could be mined for material-property proxies but currently sit unexploited outside their original imaging pipelines. Functional perturbation and disease-mutation databases (ClinVar, COSMIC, CRISPR condensate screens) offer causal readouts but are almost never cross-referenced with molecular grammar or material-state predictions. The result is a field rich in data but poor in synthesis: no existing resource or model connects sequence/structural determinants to emergent material properties to downstream cellular phenotype within a unified analytical framework.

This fragmentation has practical and conceptual costs. Practically, researchers cannot currently ask cross-cutting questions such as which sequence or structural features most strongly predict droplet viscosity or fusion propensity across protein families, or whether material-property signatures generalize across cell types and disease contexts. Conceptually, the field lacks a generalizable 'phase-behavior code' analogous to the genetic code or protein-folding rules—despite growing evidence that scaling laws and simple physical parameters (e.g., valency, stickiness, IDR patterning) may approximate condensate behavior in restricted contexts. Resolving why chemically similar condensates (stress granules versus P-bodies) diverge in dynamics and function, and why specific disease mutations alter condensate material state and downstream signaling, requires integrating molecular, structural, imaging, and functional data at a scale and diversity no single laboratory possesses. This proposal directly addresses that gap through a transdisciplinary, data-synthesis-driven Working Group, positioning NCEMS to catalyze a transformative, generalizable framework for mesoscale emergence in condensate biology.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Central Question: What combinatorial rules of sequence composition, structural motifs, PTMs, and interaction-network context give rise to specific emergent material properties of biomolecular condensates, and how do these material properties causally determine higher-order cellular outcomes?

Sub-Question 1 (Molecular Grammar to Material Property): Can interpretable machine learning models, trained on harmonized multi-database features, predict quantitative material properties (viscosity proxies, FRAP recovery rates, fusion kinetics, aspect ratios, multiphase architecture) directly from sequence composition, disorder patterning, folded-domain content, PTM annotations, and AlphaFold-derived structural embeddings?
Hypothesis 1a: Emergent material properties are governed by combinatorial, non-additive interactions among IDR patterning, multivalent motif spacing, and PTM density, such that graph-based models incorporating higher-order feature interactions will substantially outperform models using additive/linear sequence features alone.
Hypothesis 1b: A limited set of generalizable physical scaling parameters (e.g., effective valency, stickiness index, charge patterning) will explain a significant, quantifiable fraction of material-property variance across diverse protein families, indicating partial universality of phase-behavior 'grammar' despite compositional diversity.

Sub-Question 2 (Generalizability Across Contexts): Do molecular-grammar-to-material-property relationships generalize across distinct condensate types (e.g., stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates) and cellular contexts, or are they condensate-specific?
Hypothesis 2: Core physicochemical rules (valency, disorder content, RNA-binding propensity) will generalize across condensate classes, but condensate-specific interactome context (partner protein identity, local concentration, competing interactions) will modulate quantitative material-property outputs, explaining why chemically similar condensates exhibit divergent dynamics.

Sub-Question 3 (Material Property to Cellular Function): Do predicted or measured emergent material properties causally correlate with downstream cellular phenotypes such as transcriptional bursting frequency, stress granule disassembly kinetics, and signaling fidelity, as captured in functional perturbation datasets?
Hypothesis 3: Condensates exhibiting more liquid-like, rapidly exchanging material states will be associated with more dynamic, reversible cellular outputs (e.g., transcriptional bursting, rapid stress granule clearance), whereas condensates with gel-like or multiphase architectures will correlate with more stable, sustained signaling or sequestration outcomes; disease-associated mutations that shift material state toward aberrant rigidity will disproportionately co-occur with loss-of-function or gain-of-toxic-function phenotypes in perturbation datasets.

Sub-Question 4 (Methodological Innovation): Can quantitative material-property proxies be reliably extracted from public high-content imaging datasets (OpenCell, Cell Painting, Human Protein Atlas) not originally designed for biophysical characterization, and do these image-derived proxies correlate with directly measured biophysical parameters from the LLPS literature?
Hypothesis 4: Image-derived morphological and dynamic features (droplet circularity, size distribution, colocalization dynamics) will significantly correlate with literature-reported FRAP and fusion measurements for overlapping proteins, validating imaging atlases as a scalable, underutilized source of material-property information and substantially expanding the effective size and diversity of the training dataset beyond what dedicated biophysics studies alone provide.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses test whether emergent mesoscale material behavior is governed by tractable, generalizable molecular rules, and whether such rules provide causal, mechanistic insight into cellular function and disease—insights unattainable without cross-database synthesis at the scale this Working Group proposes.

[Methods and Approach]
Aim 1: Meta-Database Construction and Harmonization. We will build a unified, relational meta-database linking condensate-resident proteins across five data classes: (i) sequence/compositional features (IDR content, low-complexity regions, charge patterning) from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and LLPSDB; (ii) structural information from PDB and AlphaFold DB, converted into per-residue and per-domain embeddings; (iii) PTM annotations from PhosphoSitePlus and UniProt; (iv) interactome and localization context from BioGRID, IntAct, and CD-CODE; and (v) material-property measurements curated directly from primary literature (FRAP rates, fusion kinetics, aspect ratios) supplemented by features algorithmically extracted from public imaging atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting) using standardized image-analysis pipelines (droplet segmentation, shape descriptors, temporal fusion tracking). A controlled-vocabulary ontology will resolve protein identifiers, condensate-type labels, and experimental-condition metadata across sources, with provenance tracking for every data point.

Aim 2: Predictive Modeling of Emergent Material Properties. Using the harmonized dataset, we will train and benchmark interpretable machine learning architectures—including gradient-boosted trees for baseline feature importance, and graph neural networks (GNNs) that incorporate AlphaFold-derived structural embeddings, disorder annotations, and interaction-network topology—to predict material-property targets. Models will be evaluated via nested cross-validation stratified by protein family and condensate type to test generalizability (Hypothesis 2). SHAP-based feature attribution and ablation studies will identify minimal sufficient feature sets, testing whether simplified physical scaling parameters approximate full-model performance (Hypothesis 1b). Uncertainty quantification (ensemble variance, conformal prediction) will flag low-confidence predictions for prioritized experimental validation by community collaborators.

Aim 3: Linking Material State to Cellular Function. Predicted and literature-derived material-property profiles will be cross-referenced against functional perturbation datasets: CRISPR-based condensate disruption screens, optogenetic clustering studies, and disease-mutation databases (ClinVar, COSMIC). Statistical association tests (mixed-effects models accounting for protein family and condensate-type covariates) and causal-inference approaches (e.g., instrumental-variable analysis using mutation-induced material-property shifts as natural perturbations) will test Hypothesis 3, focusing on case studies contrasting stress granules and P-bodies.

Working Group Process: The team will convene via quarterly in-person/hybrid harmonization workshops and biweekly virtual working sessions, structured around modular sprints (database harmonization, feature engineering, model development, functional validation). Shared computational infrastructure (cloud-based JupyterHub, version-controlled pipelines) hosted with NCEMS support will enable synchronous collaborative development across geographically distributed labs. Task forces led by co-investigators with complementary expertise (biophysics, structural bioinformatics, imaging analysis, machine learning, cell biology) will own specific pipeline modules, with cross-task integration checkpoints every two months to ensure coherence and prevent siloed analysis—directly addressing the multi-lab, multi-expertise requirement that makes this project infeasible for any single group.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver: (1) A publicly released, versioned meta-database integrating sequence, structural, PTM, interactome, imaging-derived, and functional data for condensate-resident proteins—the first resource of its kind bridging molecular grammar to emergent material properties. (2) Validated, interpretable predictive models identifying which molecular features most strongly govern condensate material states, including tests of scaling-law generalizability across protein families and condensate types. (3) Empirical, statistically grounded evidence linking material-property variation to cellular phenotypes (transcriptional bursting, stress granule dynamics, signaling outcomes) and disease-associated mutations, offering mechanistic explanations for long-standing puzzles such as functional divergence among compositionally similar condensates. (4) A validated pipeline demonstrating that public high-content imaging atlases, not originally designed for biophysical study, can be systematically repurposed to extract material-property proxies—a methodological innovation with broad applicability beyond condensate biology.

Scientifically, this work will establish a generalizable framework for mesoscale emergence, directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand how molecular-scale interactions give rise to unexpected higher-order biological properties. It will provide the community with testable, quantitative hypotheses to guide future targeted experiments, reducing costly trial-and-error in condensate engineering and therapeutic targeting (e.g., designing molecules that shift aberrant condensate material states in disease). Broadly, the resource will lower barriers to entry for computational and quantitative researchers to engage with condensate biology, and will serve as a template for synthesis-driven mesoscale research applicable to other emergent cellular phenomena (e.g., cytoskeletal network mechanics, membrane-less organelle competition). By training graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data synthesis, the project will cultivate a cohort of researchers equipped to bridge biophysics, structural biology, and data science—directly fulfilling NCEMS's workforce-development goals while producing durable, reusable community infrastructure.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group is committed to full adherence to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles and NCEMS community standards for open, team, and reproducible science. All harmonized datasets will be deposited in a versioned, publicly accessible repository (e.g., Zenodo with DOI minting, and/or integration with existing community databases such as CD-CODE) under permissive licensing, with complete provenance metadata tracing each data point to its original source, extraction method, and processing pipeline. All code—database harmonization scripts, image-analysis pipelines, machine learning model training and evaluation code—will be maintained in public version-controlled repositories (GitHub/GitLab) with continuous integration testing, containerized environments (Docker/Singularity), and comprehensive documentation to ensure computational reproducibility across platforms and over time.

Model weights, training/validation splits, and hyperparameter configurations will be archived alongside performance benchmarks to enable independent replication and extension by the broader community. We will adopt a pre-registration approach for key hypothesis tests (Aim 3 causal analyses) to enhance rigor and transparency, depositing analysis plans prior to accessing outcome data where feasible. Electronic lab notebooks and shared documentation (e.g., a living project wiki) will record decision rationales, harmonization edge cases, and ontology-mapping choices, ensuring transparency in judgment calls inherent to multi-database integration.

The Working Group will release intermediate products—not just final models—including the harmonized meta-database schema, feature-extraction pipelines for imaging atlases, and benchmark datasets for material-property prediction, explicitly designed for reuse by other researchers tackling related mesoscale questions. Tutorials, annotated Jupyter notebooks, and recorded workshop sessions will be made openly available to maximize training value beyond the immediate team. All publications arising from this work will be deposited as open-access preprints prior to journal submission, and authorship/credit will follow transparent, pre-agreed contributorship guidelines (e.g., CRediT taxonomy) to fairly recognize the diverse, distributed contributions inherent to synthesis science.

[Budget and Resources]
This project requires NCEMS support at a scale exceeding standard individual R01-type funding due to its multi-institutional, multi-domain integration demands. Personnel costs constitute the primary budget component: partial salary support for 5–6 co-investigators (biophysics, structural bioinformatics, imaging analysis, machine learning, cell biology) across 3–4 institutions to coordinate task-force activities; full or partial support for 2 postdoctoral researchers and 3–4 graduate student trainees to execute database harmonization, model development, and functional validation analyses; and a dedicated data engineer/research software engineer to build and maintain shared computational pipelines, ensuring long-term sustainability of the meta-database beyond the funding period.

Computational resources include cloud-computing credits (e.g., AWS/GCP or NCEMS-affiliated HPC allocation) for large-scale image reprocessing, GNN model training, and hosting of the public-facing database and API; costs for data storage (particularly high-resolution imaging data pulled from public atlases) must accommodate multi-terabyte scale. Software licensing needs are minimal given reliance on open-source tools (PyTorch, PyTorch Geometric, scikit-learn, Bioconductor), consistent with open-science commitments.

Travel and workshop funds will support quarterly in-person harmonization workshops (rotating host institutions) and participation in one annual NCEMS-wide symposium to disseminate progress and solicit community feedback. A modest allocation for hackathon-style training events (venue/virtual platform costs, trainee travel support) will directly serve the workforce-development mandate. Requested NCEMS-specific resources include: dedicated data-harmonization and biocuration support staff shared across working groups, access to NCEMS computational infrastructure/consulting for scalable pipeline deployment, and facilitation support for cross-institutional coordination (project management, shared collaborative platforms). These resources are justified because no single lab possesses the combined computational infrastructure, cross-domain expertise, and coordination capacity needed to harmonize five-plus heterogeneous public data ecosystems and validate emergent findings against functional outcomes—precisely the collaborative, beyond-single-lab capability NCEMS is designed to enable.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic mesoscale emergent phenomenon, arising from multivalent, low-affinity interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct biophysical properties and cellular functions. [Abstract]

No single laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, biophysical expertise, and cell biology domain knowledge required to harmonize these heterogeneous, non-standardized datasets—many collected with different assay conditions, buffer compositions, and imaging modalities—into a unified predictive model. This is precisely the kind of large-scale, cross-disciplinary synthesis challenge NCEMS is positioned to catalyze. Our working group will bring together biophysicists specializing in polymer theory of LLPS, structural biologists with cryo-EM/ET expertise, computational biologists skilled in graph-based interactome analysis, and cell biologists studying condensate function in stress response, transcription, and neurodegeneration. Using this integrated resource, we will apply machine learning and biophysical modeling to test three novel hypotheses: (i) whether condensate material properties (liquid vs. gel vs. solid) can be predicted from combinatorial sequence grammar and interactor stoichiometry; (ii) whether condensate emergence thresholds correlate with disease-associated mutations across cancer and neurodegeneration datasets; and (iii) whether evolutionary conservation patterns in IDRs predict condensate functional conservation across species. Deliverables include an open-access, versioned meta-database (deposited via Zenodo/GitHub with full analytical code), a generalizable predictive model of condensate emergence, and reproducible workflows adhering to community open-science standards. The project will directly train 4-6 graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, biophysical modeling, and open science practices through structured hackathons and co-mentorship across participating labs. By synthesizing molecular-scale sequence data with cellular-scale phenotypic outcomes, this working group will resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—how simple sequence and interaction rules generate the emergent complexity of condensate behavior—while establishing a template for future mesoscale synthesis research supported by NCEMS.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged as a central organizing principle of intracellular biochemistry, mediating processes ranging from ribosome biogenesis and stress granule formation to transcriptional bursting and chromatin compartmentalization. These membraneless organelles form through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), a physical process by which multivalent proteins and nucleic acids—often featuring intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—undergo density transitions to create compositionally distinct compartments without a bounding membrane. Condensates constitute a canonical example of mesoscale emergence: they arise from simple, low-affinity molecular interactions yet give rise to complex, functionally consequential material properties (viscosity, surface tension, internal dynamics) that cannot be trivially predicted from the properties of individual constituent molecules alone. Understanding how sequence-encoded molecular grammar produces emergent condensate phenotypes is among the most pressing open questions in modern cell biology, with direct implications for understanding gene regulation, RNA metabolism, and the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases and cancers linked to aberrant condensate solidification. Over the past decade, the condensate field has generated an extraordinary volume of publicly available data. Specialized sequence databases (PhaSepDB, PhaSePro, LLPSDB) catalog thousands of experimentally validated phase-separating proteins alongside computational predictors like CatGRANULE. Proteome-scale interaction and modification databases (BioGRID, STRING, PhosphoSitePlus) document the combinatorial post-translational and interaction landscapes that modulate condensate assembly. Structural and imaging repositories (EMDB, CZI Imaging Data Resource) provide nanoscale and mesoscale visualizations of condensate architecture. Hundreds of published studies report single-molecule and FRAP-based kinetic measurements of condensate material properties, though these remain scattered across supplementary materials in non-standardized formats. Finally, single-cell atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, CCLE) connect condensate-associated protein expression to phenotypic and disease outcomes at cellular resolution. Despite this wealth of data, no integrated framework exists that spans from primary sequence features through biophysical parameters to cellular and organismal phenotype. This fragmentation represents both a scientific gap and a methodological opportunity. Critically, closing this gap exceeds the capacity of any individual laboratory: it requires simultaneous fluency in polymer physics, structural biology, network science, and cell biology, combined with the computational infrastructure to harmonize heterogeneous data types collected under disparate experimental conditions (varying salt concentrations, temperatures, protein constructs, and imaging modalities). This proposal directly targets NCEMS's mission by assembling a transdisciplinary Working Group to perform community-scale synthesis of these existing datasets, generating a unified, versioned meta-resource and predictive modeling framework. In doing so, we will resolve a fundamental puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—the sequence-to-phenotype grammar underlying condensate emergence—while establishing reusable infrastructure and analytical templates for future mesoscale synthesis research across the broader NCEMS community.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching question: Can the emergent material and functional properties of biomolecular condensates be predicted from integrable, multi-scale molecular data, and do deviations from predicted behavior reveal mechanisms of disease? We decompose this into three specific, testable research questions and associated hypotheses. Research Question 1 (Sequence-to-Material-Property Grammar): Can combinatorial sequence features of IDRs—including charge patterning, aromatic residue spacing, motif multivalency—together with interactor stoichiometry from proteome-wide networks, predict a condensate's material state (liquid, gel, or solid) and quantitative biophysical parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity, interfacial tension)? We hypothesize that material state is governed by a generalizable, non-linear combinatorial grammar in which specific sequence motifs interact synergistically with binding partner valency, such that models integrating both sequence and interactome features will significantly outperform sequence-only predictors currently dominant in the field. Research Question 2 (Disease-Associated Emergence Thresholds): Do disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins systematically shift emergence thresholds (e.g., critical concentration, nucleation kinetics) in ways that are predictable from integrated biophysical and genomic data, and do these shifts correlate with phenotypic severity across cancer and neurodegenerative disease datasets? We hypothesize that pathogenic mutations cluster in sequence regions predicted by our integrated model to be most sensitive to perturbation of phase behavior, and that the magnitude of predicted biophysical parameter shift correlates with disease severity metrics extracted from clinical and cell-line datasets. Research Question 3 (Evolutionary Conservation of Condensate Function): Do patterns of evolutionary conservation within IDRs—assessed across orthologous sequences—predict conservation of condensate functional roles (e.g., stress response, transcriptional regulation) across species, and does this conservation follow a modular grammar distinct from conservation patterns in folded domains? We hypothesize that condensate-relevant IDRs exhibit a distinctive mode of evolutionary conservation, preserving compositional and patterning features (rather than strict sequence identity) that correlates with conserved functional outputs, reflecting selection on emergent biophysical properties rather than specific residue identity. These hypotheses collectively probe the extent to which condensate emergence follows learnable, generalizable rules versus idiosyncratic, context-dependent behavior—a question of both fundamental and translational significance. Testing them requires simultaneous access to sequence databases, interactome networks, structural/imaging data, kinetic measurements, and phenotypic/clinical datasets—exactly the kind of cross-domain, cross-scale synthesis that no single laboratory can undertake alone, and that falls squarely within NCEMS's mandate to catalyze community-scale data integration to resolve fundamental mesoscale biological questions. Successful hypothesis testing will yield the first generalizable, cross-validated predictive framework linking molecular sequence grammar to emergent condensate phenotype and disease relevance, directly advancing NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale and their cellular consequences.

[Methods and Approach]
Our approach proceeds in four integrated phases over a two-year Working Group timeline. Phase 1 (Months 1-6): Data Inventory and Harmonization. We will systematically catalog and extract data from PhaSepDB, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, CatGRANULE outputs, BioGRID, STRING, PhosphoSitePlus, EMDB, CZI Imaging Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, and CCLE, alongside systematic literature mining (using text-mining pipelines such as PubTator and custom NLP scripts) to extract FRAP and single-molecule kinetic parameters from supplementary materials of published condensate studies. A working ontology will be developed collaboratively, defining standardized terms for sequence features (charge patterning indices, aromatic spacing metrics), biophysical parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity, surface tension, partition coefficient), and phenotypic descriptors (material state classifications, disease association labels). All datasets will be mapped to this ontology and deposited into a harmonized, relational meta-database using FAIR-compliant schemas (schema.org, Bioschemas). Phase 2 (Months 4-12): Feature Engineering and Integrative Modeling. Computational biologists and biophysicists will jointly develop feature representations spanning sequence-derived descriptors (via established tools including CIDER, localCIDER, and custom pattern-detection algorithms), network-derived features (degree centrality, clustering coefficients from interactome graphs), and structural features derived from cryo-EM/ET and super-resolution datasets. We will apply ensemble machine learning approaches (gradient-boosted trees, graph neural networks) alongside biophysical polymer models (e.g., stickers-and-spacers framework, random phase approximation theory) to predict material state and quantitative biophysical parameters, using nested cross-validation stratified by protein family to avoid data leakage. Phase 3 (Months 10-18): Hypothesis Testing. For Research Question 2, mutation-level data from COSMIC, ClinVar, and neurodegeneration-focused datasets (e.g., ALSoD) will be integrated with our predictive model to assess whether predicted biophysical parameter shifts correlate with disease severity metrics, using mixed-effects regression models accounting for protein family as a random effect. For Research Question 3, orthologous IDR sequences will be retrieved from Ensembl Compara and OrthoDB, and conservation of compositional/patterning features (rather than strict identity) will be quantified using metrics adapted from disorder-aware alignment tools (e.g., a custom implementation building on NAlign and NDD approaches), correlated with functional annotation conservation from Gene Ontology and UniProt. Phase 4 (Months 18-24): Validation, Synthesis, and Dissemination. Model predictions will be validated against held-out experimental datasets not used in training, and cross-checked against emerging community benchmarks. Two in-person/hybrid workshops (Months 6 and 18) and monthly virtual working sessions will structure collaboration, complemented by structured hackathons for trainee-led sub-projects. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be iteratively deposited to GitHub/Zenodo throughout the project, not solely at completion, ensuring continuous open-science engagement and enabling early community feedback and reuse.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will produce four primary deliverables with lasting community value. First, a versioned, FAIR-compliant meta-database integrating sequence, interactome, structural, kinetic, and phenotypic data for condensate-forming proteins, deposited on Zenodo/GitHub with a persistent DOI and full documentation, will serve as a foundational resource for the broader biomolecular condensate research community, reducing duplicative data-wrangling effort across dozens of future studies. Second, a generalizable, cross-validated predictive model linking sequence and interactome features to condensate material properties will advance mechanistic understanding of phase separation and provide a testable framework guiding future experimental design, particularly for under-characterized proteins lacking direct biophysical measurements. Third, quantitative insights linking disease-associated mutations to predicted shifts in condensate emergence thresholds will generate testable hypotheses regarding mechanisms of condensate dysregulation in neurodegeneration and cancer, potentially informing future therapeutic targeting strategies aimed at restoring normal phase behavior. Fourth, evolutionary conservation analyses will clarify whether condensate function is preserved through compositional/patterning grammar rather than strict sequence conservation, reshaping how comparative genomics approaches disordered regions more broadly. Beyond these concrete deliverables, this project will establish a reusable methodological template for mesoscale data synthesis—demonstrating how heterogeneous, non-standardized datasets spanning molecular to cellular scales can be harmonized and jointly modeled—directly supporting NCEMS's broader mission to catalyze synthesis research across the molecular and cellular sciences. The collaborative structure, spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, and cell biology, will model effective transdisciplinary practice for future NCEMS-supported teams. Trainees involved in this project will gain rare, integrative expertise spanning wet-lab-adjacent biophysical reasoning and advanced computational data science, positioning them as leaders in the emerging data-intensive biology workforce that NCEMS aims to cultivate.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This Working Group commits fully to open science principles throughout the project lifecycle, consistent with NCEMS community standards. All harmonized datasets, derived features, and model outputs will be deposited in public repositories (Zenodo for versioned data snapshots with persistent DOIs, GitHub for actively developed code) under permissive open licenses (CC-BY for data, MIT/BSD for code), enabling unrestricted reuse and extension by the broader community. We will adopt FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles from project inception, developing and publishing a shared ontology and metadata schema early in Phase 1 so that intermediate harmonization products are usable by external researchers even before final model completion. Analytical workflows will be implemented using containerized, version-controlled pipelines (Docker/Singularity with Snakemake or Nextflow workflow management) to ensure computational reproducibility across computing environments, with continuous integration testing to verify pipeline stability as code evolves. All machine learning models will be accompanied by detailed model cards documenting training data provenance, performance metrics, known limitations, and intended use cases, following emerging community standards for responsible predictive modeling in biology. We will pre-register our three core hypotheses and primary analytical approach via an open preprint server (bioRxiv) prior to full-scale hypothesis testing in Phase 3, distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory analyses. Regular project updates, including negative or null results, will be shared via a public project website and periodic preprints to counteract publication bias and maximize community value. We will actively engage the broader condensate research community through open working sessions and solicitation of feedback on draft ontology schemas via community platforms (e.g., LLPS community forums, relevant Slack/Discord channels), ensuring our synthesis products reflect broad consensus rather than the perspectives of participating labs alone. All trainee contributions will be explicitly credited through transparent authorship and contribution statements (following CRediT taxonomy), and training materials developed for hackathons will themselves be openly published as reusable educational resources for the wider data science and molecular biology training community.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests support commensurate with NCEMS Working Group funding mechanisms over a 24-month period. Personnel costs constitute the primary budget category, supporting partial salary (20-30% effort) for four co-Principal Investigators representing biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, and cell biology domains, ensuring sustained cross-disciplinary leadership throughout the project. Funding is requested for two full-time postdoctoral researchers with complementary expertise in machine learning/biophysical modeling and database engineering/ontology development, who will serve as project coordinators driving day-to-day data harmonization and analysis. Support for 4-6 graduate student trainees (partial effort, 10-15%) across participating labs will enable distributed sub-project execution and ensure broad training impact consistent with NCEMS workforce development goals. Computational resources include cloud computing credits (AWS/Google Cloud or institutional HPC allocation) for large-scale data processing, machine learning model training, and hosting of interactive database/API infrastructure; we estimate moderate but non-trivial computational needs given the scale of imaging and interactome data involved, necessitating dedicated storage (estimated 5-10TB) and GPU-enabled compute for graph neural network training. Travel funds are requested to support two in-person Working Group workshops (kickoff at Month 1 and mid-project synthesis meeting at Month 12), bringing together all co-PIs, postdocs, and trainees to consolidate ontology decisions, resolve data harmonization conflicts, and plan hypothesis-testing analyses—activities substantially more effective through concentrated in-person collaboration. Additional funds support trainee participation in relevant scientific conferences (e.g., Biophysical Society Annual Meeting, ASCB, ISMB) to disseminate synthesis products and recruit community feedback. A modest allocation is requested for publication costs, including open-access publishing fees and preprint server deposition, consistent with our open science commitments. We will leverage existing institutional resources at participating institutions, including established compute clusters and library/data science support services, to minimize redundant infrastructure costs. This budget reflects an efficient, focused resource allocation appropriate for a synthesis-focused Working Group whose primary deliverables are integrative datasets, analytical code, and predictive models rather than new experimental data generation, aligning with NCEMS's core funding philosophy of supporting high-value synthesis over costly primary data collection.
