This fragmentation represents both a scientific bottleneck and a synthesis opportunity precisely aligned with NCEMS's mission. The unresolved puzzle—how simple, quantifiable molecular features (valency of interaction motifs, patterning of charged and aromatic residues, distribution of post-translational modification sites, RNA-binding motif content) give rise to complex, context-dependent, and functionally consequential condensate behaviors—cannot be solved by any single laboratory or dataset. It demands simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, single-cell genomics, machine learning, and cell biology, applied to already-collected, publicly available data at a scale only achievable through coordinated, cross-institutional synthesis. Furthermore, dysregulation of condensate material properties (aberrant liquid-to-gel-to-solid transitions) is increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative disease, cancer, and viral infection, underscoring the biomedical urgency of decoding these rules. By synthesizing existing data across five previously disconnected domains, this Working Group will establish a generalizable, predictive framework for mesoscale emergence in condensate biology, filling a critical gap in the field and generating a resource and methodology transferable to other emergent phenomena across the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around three interlocking research questions that collectively test whether a generalizable 'molecular grammar' governs condensate emergence and its cellular consequences. Research Question 1 (Sequence-to-Structure Mapping): Can sequence-encoded features—valency of short linear motifs, IDR patterning of charged/aromatic residues, post-translational modification sites, and RNA-binding domains—predict structural and biophysical propensities for phase separation across diverse protein families? We hypothesize that a combinatorial, context-dependent grammar (rather than any single feature in isolation) determines phase separation propensity, and that this grammar is generalizable across unrelated protein families when represented in an appropriately featurized embedding space that integrates disorder annotations, predicted structures, and interaction network topology. Research Question 2 (Structure-to-Mesoscale Emergence): Do specific combinations of molecular grammar features predict not merely binary phase separation propensity but the continuum of emergent material states—liquid, gel, and solid—and their transitions under physiological and stress conditions? We hypothesize that material state transitions are governed by quantifiable shifts in interaction valency and strength (e.g., increased beta-sheet-prone motif content, changes in multivalent scaffold stoichiometry) that can be predicted from integrated structural and imaging data, and that these transitions are detectable as consistent signatures across independent live-cell imaging datasets (OpenCell, LLPSDB) irrespective of the specific protein system studied. Research Question 3 (Mesoscale-to-Phenotype Linkage): Do condensate-associated genes identified through molecular grammar predictions show enrichment in functional perturbation phenotypes—stress granule dynamics, transcriptional output, proteostasis, and neurodegeneration-associated aggregation—consistent with a causal chain from molecular grammar to cellular outcome? We hypothesize that genes predicted to encode high-valency, modification-rich condensate scaffolds will be disproportionately represented among genetic modifiers identified in Perturb-seq and CRISPR screens for stress response and proteostasis phenotypes, establishing a testable, data-driven link between molecular-scale rules and cell-scale emergent function. These hypotheses are directly testable using existing public data: sequence and structural features can be extracted and harmonized across curated databases and predicted structure repositories; material state classifications can be derived from systematic reanalysis of imaging repositories using standardized computer-vision pipelines; and phenotype associations can be tested via integration with functional genomics resources using network and enrichment-based statistical frameworks. Critically, none of these questions can be answered by analyzing any single data class alone—only by simultaneously integrating sequence, structure, imaging, and functional genomic data can we determine whether a unified molecular grammar exists and whether it is causally, not merely correlatively, linked to mesoscale emergence and phenotype. Successful resolution of these questions will directly address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: whether emergent, higher-order cellular organization can be predicted from lower-order molecular rules, and will generate a generalizable methodological template for studying emergence at the mesoscale across other biological systems beyond condensates.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will execute a four-phase, two-year synthesis pipeline built entirely on existing public data. Phase 1 (Months 1–6): Data Harmonization and Ontology Development. We will systematically extract and standardize data from curated LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSepPro), disorder resources (DisProt, MobiDB), structural repositories (PDB, EMDB, AlphaFold/ESMFold models, cryo-ET tomograms), single-cell/spatial atlases (Human Protein Atlas, HuBMAP, Tabula Sapiens), functional screens (Perturb-seq, genome-wide CRISPR datasets, ORFeome libraries), and imaging repositories (OpenCell, LLPSDB). A cross-disciplinary ontology working subgroup will develop standardized vocabularies and metadata schemas to reconcile inconsistent nomenclature (e.g., differing definitions of 'scaffold' versus 'client' proteins, disparate material-state classifications) into a unified, versioned Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase schema. Phase 2 (Months 5–12): Feature Engineering and Multi-Modal Representation Learning. Sequence-based features (motif valency, charge/aromatic patterning via NCPR and kappa metrics, PTM site density, RNA-binding motif content) will be computed using established biophysical algorithms (e.g., CIDER, localCIDER) and merged with structural embeddings derived from AlphaFold/ESMFold predicted contact maps and cryo-ET-derived mesoscale architecture descriptors. These will be encoded into a unified graph representation in which nodes represent proteins/domains and edges represent predicted or empirically observed interactions, forming the substrate for graph neural network (GNN) modeling. Phase 3 (Months 10–18): Predictive Model Development and Validation. We will train multi-modal GNN and complementary transformer-based sequence models to predict (a) phase separation propensity, (b) material state classification (liquid/gel/solid) benchmarked against reanalyzed imaging data using standardized image-processing pipelines (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching kinetics, condensate morphology metrics), and (c) association with functional phenotypes from CRISPR/Perturb-seq datasets via network propagation and enrichment analyses. Models will be validated using held-out data splits stratified by protein family to test generalizability, and cross-validated against independent published experimental findings not used in training. Phase 4 (Months 16–24): Mechanistic Synthesis and Tool Development. Findings across phases will be integrated into a mechanistic framework linking molecular grammar to mesoscale emergence and cellular phenotype, accompanied by an interactive web-based tool allowing users to query predicted condensate properties from arbitrary input sequences. Throughout, the Working Group will convene via quarterly in-person/virtual workshops emphasizing team-science practices, with subgroups (biophysics/structure, single-cell genomics, machine learning, cell biology/imaging) coordinating through shared version-controlled repositories, standardized code review, and joint manuscript preparation. Feasibility is high because all data sources are already public, computational infrastructure needs (GPU clusters for GNN training) are modest and available through NCEMS or institutional HPC resources, and the team's combined expertise directly spans every required methodological domain.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver three primary outcomes. First, an open, harmonized, multi-omic Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase integrating sequence, structural, imaging, single-cell, and functional genomic data under standardized ontologies, designed for sustained community use and expansion beyond the funding period. Second, validated multi-modal predictive models (graph neural networks and sequence-based transformers) capable of predicting condensate formation propensity and material-state transitions directly from protein sequence, accompanied by an interactive, publicly accessible web tool for community-wide query and hypothesis generation. Third, a mechanistic, generalizable framework articulating how specific combinations of molecular features (valency, disorder patterning, PTM sites, RNA-binding motifs) causally propagate to mesoscale emergent properties and downstream cellular phenotypes, including stress granule dynamics and neurodegeneration-associated aggregation. Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing puzzle regarding the predictability of emergent mesoscale organization from molecular-scale rules, providing a template applicable to other emergent phenomena central to NCEMS's mission, such as membrane microdomain formation or chromatin compartmentalization. Broader impacts include acceleration of hypothesis-driven experimental design in condensate biology and biomedicine, particularly for neurodegenerative disease and stress-response pathologies where aberrant phase transitions are implicated. The project directly trains graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, reproducible computational workflows, and collaborative team science, cultivating a cohort of data-savvy scientists equipped to tackle future emergence-related questions. By demonstrating that community-scale data synthesis—rather than new experimentation—can resolve fundamental questions in molecular and cellular biology, this project exemplifies the transformative potential of the synthesis science paradigm that NCEMS champions, while producing durable, reusable community resources with impact extending well beyond the funded period.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This project commits fully to open, team, and reproducible science principles consistent with NCEMS policy. All harmonized datasets, standardized ontologies, extracted features, and metadata schemas will be deposited in the Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase and mirrored on Zenodo with persistent DOIs, ensuring long-term accessibility and citability. All analysis code, including data harmonization pipelines, feature engineering scripts, and graph neural network training/evaluation workflows, will be version-controlled and publicly hosted on GitHub under permissive open-source licenses (MIT/BSD), with continuous integration testing to ensure reproducibility across computing environments. Trained model weights and interactive prediction tools will be released with comprehensive documentation, containerized (Docker/Singularity) for platform-independent reproducibility, and accompanied by executable Jupyter notebooks illustrating key analyses end-to-end. We will adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles throughout, using established minimal-information standards (e.g., MIAPE for structural data, MINSEQE for sequencing-derived datasets) and controlled vocabularies developed in collaboration with existing database curators (PhaSepDB, DisProt, Human Protein Atlas teams) to ensure interoperability with community resources. All intermediate and final results, including negative or null findings, will be reported transparently in preprint form (bioRxiv) prior to journal submission, and all publications will be open access. Team science practices will be formalized through a collaboratively developed data governance and authorship agreement, established at the project's outset, specifying contribution criteria, data usage rights, and credit allocation consistent with community norms for large consortium science. Regular internal reproducibility audits—including independent re-execution of key analyses by team members not involved in original code development—will be conducted at each project phase to verify robustness. Trainees will be directly involved in reproducibility auditing as a core training component, reinforcing best practices in computational rigor. This comprehensive commitment ensures that all synthesis products remain durable, verifiable, and extensible community resources long after the funding period concludes.

[Budget and Resources]
This synthesis project requires modest computational and personnel resources relative to experimental research, consistent with NCEMS's data-synthesis funding model. Personnel costs constitute the primary budget category, supporting two postdoctoral researchers (computational biology/machine learning and structural bioinformatics) and two graduate student trainees (cell biology/genomics and biophysics) across the two-year project period, alongside partial salary support (5–10% effort) for five co-investigating faculty spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell biology, and machine learning. Computational resources include GPU cluster time for graph neural network and transformer model training, cloud storage for hosting harmonized multi-terabyte imaging and structural datasets during processing, and sustained hosting costs for the public-facing Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase and interactive prediction tool, which will be housed on institutional or NCEMS-supported infrastructure to ensure long-term community access. Travel funds are requested to support quarterly in-person Working Group workshops, essential for cross-disciplinary integration, team-science training, and trainee mentorship, as well as travel to relevant scientific conferences (e.g., Biophysical Society, ASCB, ISMB) to disseminate findings and recruit broader community feedback. Modest funds are allocated for open-access publication fees and data deposition costs to ensure compliance with open-science commitments. No funds are requested for new experimental data generation, consistent with NCEMS's synthesis-only funding scope; all budgeted resources support integration, computation, training, and dissemination of existing public data. The requested budget explicitly reflects the collaborative, multi-institutional nature of the work: resources are distributed across partner institutions to support geographically diverse team members, including early-career investigators and researchers from institutions with varying research intensity levels, in direct alignment with NCEMS's goal of assembling teams reflecting diverse career stages, expertise, and institutional contexts. NCEMS-provided shared computational infrastructure and data science consultation services will be leveraged wherever possible to reduce redundant institutional costs and maximize synthesis efficiency.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), RNA, and multivalent interactions generate organelle-like structures with functions not predictable from individual molecular components alone. Despite explosive growth in condensate biology, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based phase separation predictors, structural biology datasets, single-cell spatial atlases, and functional genomic screens exist in isolation, preventing a unified understanding of how molecular grammar dictates emergent mesoscale organization and downstream cellular phenotypes. This proposal assembles a transdisciplinary Working Group—spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell biology, and machine learning—to integrate five classes of publicly available data: (1) curated LLPS driver/scaffold databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSepPro) and disorder annotations (DisProt, MobiDB); (2) structural and interaction data from the PDB, EMDB, and AlphaFold/ESMFold predicted structures, including cryo-ET tomograms of native condensates; (3) single-cell and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, HuBMAP, Tabula Sapiens) capturing condensate-associated protein expression across cell states; (4) high-throughput perturbation datasets (Perturb-seq, genome-wide CRISPR screens, ORFeome overexpression libraries) linking condensate-associated genes to cellular phenotypes; and (5) live-cell imaging repositories (e.g., OpenCell, LLPSDB) documenting condensate dynamics, material properties, and stress responses. No single dataset or lab possesses the breadth needed to bridge molecular sequence features to emergent mesoscale phase behavior and its physiological consequences—this synthesis requires simultaneous fluency in biophysical polymer theory, structural bioinformatics, single-cell genomics, and network-based phenotype mapping. Our central hypothesis is that a generalizable 'molecular grammar'—combinations of valency, disorder patterning, post-translational modification sites, and RNA-binding motifs—predicts not only condensate formation propensity but also material state transitions (liquid-to-gel-to-solid) that underlie both normal cellular function and disease-associated aggregation. We will develop multi-modal graph neural network models trained on integrated sequence-structure-interaction data, validated against independent perturbation and imaging datasets, to predict emergent condensate properties and their causal links to cellular outcomes such as stress granule dynamics, transcriptional condensate function, and neurodegeneration-associated aggregation. The working group will produce: (i) an open, harmonized multi-omic condensate database with standardized ontologies, (ii) predictive models and interactive tools for the community, and (iii) a mechanistic framework connecting molecular-scale grammar to mesoscale emergence and cellular phenotype. All code, harmonized datasets, and trained models will be released under FAIR and open-science principles via community repositories (Zenodo, GitHub, Biomolecular Condensates Knowledgebase). The project will train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data integration, reproducible computational workflows, and collaborative team science, directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to develop while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how simple molecular rules give rise to complex, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in living cells.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation and related processes—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of proteins and nucleic acids give rise to functional subcellular compartments not predictable from any single molecule's properties. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive 'grammar' linking molecular-scale features (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalency, stoichiometry, post-translational modification patterns) to mesoscale material properties (droplet viscosity, multiphase architecture, client selectivity) and ultimately to cellular-scale phenotypes (stress granule dynamics, transcriptional bursting, cell fate transitions). This gap persists because the necessary data are scattered across incompatible resources curated by disconnected communities: biophysicists studying in vitro phase diagrams, cell biologists generating high-content imaging atlases, proteomicists cataloging condensate constituents, evolutionary biologists tracking IDR conservation, and clinical genomicists annotating disease-associated mutations. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these disparate data types into a coherent cross-scale model. This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, computational structural biologists, cell imaging specialists, evolutionary genomicists, and clinical variant scientists to synthesize existing public datasets—including PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and LLPSDB (condensate composition and phase behavior), OpenCell and the Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization imaging), BioGRID/IntAct (interactomes), Human Cell Atlas and single-cell perturbation atlases (transcriptomic consequences across cell states), OrthoDB/Ensembl (cross-species IDR conservation), and ClinVar/COSMIC/gnomAD (disease-linked mutations in condensate-forming proteins)—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Using this integrated dataset, we will: (1) train interpretable machine learning models that map sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features to empirically observed condensate material states and client recruitment specificity; (2) test whether evolutionary conservation patterns of IDR grammar predict functional robustness or tunability of condensate properties across orthologous proteins in diverse species; (3) determine whether disease-associated mutations in condensate scaffolds and clients cluster at predicted grammar 'hotspots' and whether this predicts pathological mesoscale-to-cellular phenotypic outcomes (e.g., aberrant stress granule persistence in neurodegeneration, altered chromatin condensate formation in cancer); and (4) build a generalizable cross-scale predictive framework linking molecular grammar to emergent cellular behavior, tested against independent public single-cell perturbation datasets. This synthesis is intractable for any individual lab given the scale of data harmonization, cross-domain expertise, and computational infrastructure required, and directly requires NCEMS support for data engineering, workshop convening, and shared analytical infrastructure. The Working Group will operate under FAIR and open-science principles, releasing all harmonized datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows via public repositories. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on each data-integration module, receiving structured training in multi-omics data science, biophysical modeling, and collaborative team science, while a rotating visiting-scholar program will recruit early-career researchers from primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions to broaden participation. The project's central deliverable—a public, cross-species 'condensate grammar atlas'—will provide the field's first quantitative bridge between molecular sequence, mesoscale organization, and cellular emergent behavior.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are among the clearest instances of mesoscale emergence in the cell: assemblies such as stress granules, nucleoli, paraspeckles, transcriptional condensates, and heterochromatin domains arise from multivalent, often weak interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, RNA, and DNA, producing collective material properties—viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture, exchange kinetics—that cannot be predicted from any single constituent molecule in isolation. These emergent mesoscale properties in turn govern cellular-scale outcomes, including transcriptional bursting frequency, signal transduction thresholds, stress adaptation, and cell-fate transitions. Understanding how sequence-encoded molecular features give rise to emergent condensate behavior, and how that behavior propagates upward to cellular phenotype, is a central open problem in molecular and cellular biology and lies squarely within NCEMS's mesoscale emergence mission.

Over the past decade, four largely independent research communities have generated rich, complementary datasets bearing on this problem. Biophysicists have built curated databases of condensate-forming proteins and their in vitro phase behavior (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB), capturing critical concentrations, phase diagrams, and material-state annotations. Cell biologists have produced proteome-scale, high-content subcellular localization atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas) documenting which proteins partition into which condensates in living cells. Interactome projects (BioGRID, IntAct) and single-cell perturbation atlases (Human Cell Atlas, Perturb-seq compendia) capture molecular partners and downstream transcriptional consequences of condensate perturbation. Evolutionary genomics resources (OrthoDB, Ensembl) document IDR sequence conservation across species, while clinical variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC, gnomAD) catalog disease-associated mutations in scaffold and client proteins. Each community has independently shown that its data type correlates with some facet of condensate behavior, yet no integrated cross-scale model links molecular grammar to mesoscale material state to cellular phenotype—largely because these resources use incompatible ontologies, identifiers, and measurement units, and reconciling them requires simultaneous biophysical, computational, evolutionary, and clinical expertise that no single laboratory possesses.

This is precisely the class of problem NCEMS is designed to catalyze: a scientifically compelling, cross-scale emergence question that is intractable for any individual lab, requires no new experimentation, and depends on synthesis of heterogeneous public data by a transdisciplinary team. The scientific payoff is substantial. A validated molecular grammar would enable prediction of pathological phase behavior directly from sequence, illuminate why orthologous proteins across species maintain or diverge in condensate-forming capacity, and mechanistically explain why specific disease mutations produce distinct cellular pathologies, such as persistent stress granules in ALS/FTD or aberrant transcriptional condensates in cancer. Beyond this immediate advance, the Working Group instantiates NCEMS's broader goals: it recruits diverse scientific perspectives, trains early-career scientists in cross-domain synthesis, and builds reusable harmonized infrastructure that will serve the condensate field—and mesoscale emergence research generally—well beyond the funding period, establishing a template for how community-scale data synthesis can resolve long-standing puzzles that experimentation alone has been unable to close.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching question—what is the quantitative, cross-scale grammar that links condensate-forming sequence features to mesoscale material properties and cellular phenotypic outcomes?—decomposed into four tractable, data-synthesis-driven sub-questions, each paired with an explicit, falsifiable hypothesis.

RQ1 (Sequence-to-material mapping): Can interpretable machine learning models, trained on harmonized 'stickers-and-spacers' sequence features (aromatic/charged residue patterning, multivalency, IDR length, PTM sites) drawn from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and LLPSDB, predict empirically measured condensate material states (liquid, gel, solid) and client recruitment specificity observed in OpenCell and Human Protein Atlas imaging? Hypothesis 1: A relatively small, conserved set of sticker-spacer patterning features will explain the majority of variance in material state across unrelated protein families, indicating a generalizable—rather than protein-specific—grammar.

RQ2 (Evolutionary tunability): Do cross-species patterns of IDR conservation, extracted from OrthoDB/Ensembl orthogroups, predict whether condensate properties are evolutionarily constrained (robust) or free to diverge (tunable) across orthologs? Hypothesis 2: Grammar features controlling core material properties (e.g., overall stickiness driving phase boundary) will show strong purifying selection, whereas features tuning client selectivity will show lineage-specific diversification, reflecting adaptive repurposing of a conserved biophysical scaffold.

RQ3 (Disease mutation hotspots): Do disease-associated variants curated in ClinVar, COSMIC, and gnomAD cluster within grammar elements predicted by RQ1 to be functionally critical (e.g., sticker residues, multivalent motifs), and does this clustering predict specific mesoscale-to-cellular pathological outcomes documented in single-cell perturbation and imaging atlases? Hypothesis 3: Pathogenic variants will be significantly enriched at predicted grammar hotspots relative to benign population variants (gnomAD), and hotspot location (sticker vs. spacer vs. PTM site) will stratify by disease class—e.g., sticker-disrupting mutations enriched in neurodegeneration-associated aberrant persistence phenotypes, spacer/valency mutations enriched in oncogenic transcriptional condensate dysregulation.

RQ4 (Cross-scale predictive framework): Can a unified computational framework, trained on RQ1–RQ3 outputs, predict cellular-scale transcriptional and phenotypic consequences of condensate perturbation in independent, held-out single-cell perturbation datasets (e.g., Perturb-seq, Human Cell Atlas subsets not used in training)? Hypothesis 4: Grammar-derived features will outperform baseline models using only expression level or annotation-based features in predicting perturbation-induced transcriptional phenotypes, demonstrating that molecular grammar carries emergent, non-redundant predictive information about cellular outcomes.

Collectively, these questions require simultaneous fluency in biophysical phase-behavior data, high-content imaging, comparative genomics, and clinical variant interpretation—expertise distributed across at least five distinct subfields—making this an intrinsically multidisciplinary synthesis problem rather than an extension of any single lab's existing pipeline. Confirmation or refutation of these hypotheses will resolve a long-standing puzzle in the condensate field: whether a truly generalizable molecular grammar exists, or whether condensate behavior is fundamentally idiosyncratic to individual protein systems.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will proceed through four interlocking phases over a two-year project period, each co-led by trainees paired with senior domain experts to ensure both scientific rigor and structured training.

Phase 1 – Data Harmonization Infrastructure (Months 1–6): We will construct a unified relational schema mapping heterogeneous identifiers (UniProt, Ensembl gene IDs, PDB/AlphaFold structures) across all source databases. A shared ontology for condensate material-state terminology will be developed by consensus among biophysicist and cell-biology co-investigators to reconcile inconsistent vocabulary (e.g., 'liquid-like' vs. 'dynamic' vs. 'mobile'). Data engineers (supported by NCEMS computational staff) will build ETL (extract-transform-load) pipelines using Python/Nextflow to ingest PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, BioGRID, IntAct, OrthoDB, Ensembl, ClinVar, COSMIC, and gnomAD into a version-controlled, queryable graph/relational database, with full provenance tracking for every record.

Phase 2 – Sequence-to-Material Modeling (Months 4–12, addressing RQ1): Using harmonized phase-behavior and imaging annotations as labels, we will engineer sticker-spacer feature sets (residue patterning statistics, predicted multivalency, IDR composition biases, annotated PTM sites) and train interpretable models (gradient-boosted trees, sparse regression, and attention-based sequence models with post hoc interpretability via SHAP) to predict material state and client selectivity. Nested cross-validation stratified by protein family will guard against family-level data leakage; performance will be benchmarked against biophysically motivated null models (e.g., simple charge/hydrophobicity patterning).

Phase 3 – Evolutionary and Clinical Integration (Months 8–16, addressing RQ2–RQ3): Orthogroup-level conservation scores for grammar features will be computed across vertebrate and invertebrate lineages using OrthoDB/Ensembl alignments, with dN/dS and feature-specific conservation metrics tested against RQ1 model outputs. Disease-variant enrichment analyses will use permutation-based hotspot statistics comparing pathogenic (ClinVar, COSMIC) versus population (gnomAD) variant distributions across predicted grammar elements, stratified by disease category.

Phase 4 – Cross-Scale Validation (Months 14–22, addressing RQ4): Grammar-derived protein-level features will be integrated as predictors in models trained to forecast transcriptional and phenotypic responses in held-out single-cell perturbation datasets (Human Cell Atlas subsets, public Perturb-seq compendia), with rigorous train/test splits by cell type and perturbation identity to prevent overfitting. Model comparisons will use pre-registered performance metrics and statistical significance testing.

Throughout, biweekly video working sessions and two in-person synthesis workshops (Months 6 and 18) will integrate perspectives across subfields, resolve data-harmonization disagreements, and co-develop manuscripts. All analyses will be conducted in version-controlled, containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) orchestrated via Nextflow to guarantee reproducibility across institutions and computing environments, with computational demands met through NCEMS-supported cloud/HPC allocations.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver: (1) a harmonized, publicly queryable 'condensate grammar atlas' integrating phase-behavior, imaging, interactome, evolutionary, and clinical variant data across thousands of proteins and multiple species—an infrastructure resource with lasting utility far beyond this project; (2) validated, interpretable predictive models linking sequence-encoded grammar to material state and client selectivity, publicly released with full documentation; (3) the first systematic, cross-species map of evolutionary constraint versus tunability in condensate-forming sequence grammar; (4) statistically rigorous evidence on whether disease mutations cluster at predicted functional hotspots, directly informing variant-interpretation pipelines used in clinical genomics; and (5) a validated cross-scale predictive framework connecting molecular grammar to single-cell transcriptional and phenotypic outcomes.

Scientifically, this resolves a long-standing puzzle—whether condensate behavior follows generalizable rules or is irreducibly protein-specific—with direct implications for rational design of condensate-modulating therapeutics in neurodegeneration and cancer, and for predicting phenotypic consequences of novel or engineered IDR sequences. Methodologically, the harmonization pipelines and ontology developed here will serve as reusable infrastructure for future mesoscale emergence syntheses, lowering the barrier for subsequent NCEMS-supported working groups tackling related cross-scale problems (e.g., chromatin organization, membrane-less organelle evolution).

Broader impacts include establishing a reproducible template for transdisciplinary data synthesis in molecular and cellular biology, training a cohort of graduate students and postdocs in multi-omics integration and collaborative team science, and expanding participation of early-career researchers from primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions through the visiting-scholar program. By demonstrating that publicly available data, properly harmonized and analyzed by a diverse transdisciplinary team, can resolve questions intractable to any single lab, this project exemplifies the community-scale synthesis model NCEMS was created to catalyze, while directly advancing understanding of mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group commits to full adherence to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles and NCEMS's community-created open, team, and reproducible science policies. All harmonized datasets, including the integrated relational/graph database schema, will be deposited in open repositories (Zenodo, Open Science Framework, and domain-appropriate archives such as the RCSB/AlphaFold ecosystem where structural data is involved) with persistent DOIs, versioned releases, and complete provenance metadata tracing every record to its original public source. All code—ETL pipelines, feature-engineering scripts, machine learning model training and evaluation code, and statistical analysis workflows—will be developed openly on GitHub under permissive licenses (MIT/BSD) from project inception, not merely at publication, enabling real-time collaboration and community feedback. Computational workflows will be containerized (Docker/Singularity) and orchestrated with Nextflow to ensure exact reproducibility across institutions and computing environments, with all analyses runnable via a single documented pipeline invocation.

Analytical decisions with the potential to introduce bias—cross-validation splitting strategy, hotspot permutation testing procedures, model hyperparameter selection—will be pre-registered on OSF prior to execution of Phases 2–4 to guard against post hoc rationalization. Trained models and their weights will be released alongside model cards documenting training data provenance, intended use, and known limitations. Manuscripts arising from this work will be posted as preprints (bioRxiv) prior to journal submission, and we will pursue publication in venues supporting open peer review where feasible. Data-sharing agreements will respect all upstream licensing terms of constituent databases (e.g., ClinVar and gnomAD usage restrictions), and derived aggregate products will be structured to comply with these terms while maximizing reuse. Regular Working Group meetings will include a standing 'reproducibility check' in which independent team members attempt to rerun each other's pipelines from raw inputs, catching integration errors early and reinforcing a culture of verifiable, team-based science consistent with NCEMS's gold-standard practices.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests NCEMS Working Group support to fund coordination, computational infrastructure, and convening activities that exceed the capacity of any individual laboratory. Personnel support includes a full-time Data Integration Coordinator/postdoctoral scientist (0.75 FTE across two years) to lead cross-database harmonization and pipeline engineering, plus partial salary support (0.2–0.3 FTE each) for two graduate student co-leads embedded in the evolutionary/clinical and cross-scale modeling phases, respectively, providing structured training in multi-omics synthesis. Modest summer-effort support is requested for the five senior co-investigators (biophysics, computational structural biology, cell imaging, evolutionary genomics, clinical genomics) to ensure sustained engagement across the two-year period.

Computational resources include cloud/HPC allocation (estimated 40,000 core-hours) for machine learning model training, permutation-based hotspot statistics, and large-scale single-cell perturbation dataset analysis, along with cloud storage (approximately 10 TB) for harmonized datasets and derived data products. NCEMS shared analytical infrastructure and data-engineering consultation are requested to support schema design and ETL pipeline development during Phase 1.

Convening costs include two in-person synthesis workshops (Months 6 and 18, approximately 12–15 participants each, including trainees and visiting scholars) to resolve cross-domain harmonization decisions and co-develop manuscripts, plus travel support for a rotating visiting-scholar program (two visiting early-career researchers per year from primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions) to participate in working sessions and receive hands-on training.

Additional requested support includes open-access publication fees for at least three manuscripts, data repository deposition costs, and software/license fees for specialized structural and evolutionary analysis tools where not otherwise freely available. All requested resources are directly tied to the cross-database harmonization, cross-disciplinary coordination, and shared computational demands that make this synthesis intractable for any single lab, justifying the need for dedicated NCEMS support rather than existing institutional resources.

[

A critical scientific gap is the lack of a unified, predictive model linking molecular-scale sequence features to mesoscale material properties and cellular-scale phenotypes, primarily because current datasets remain fragmented across incompatible databases. The primary objective is to define a quantitative, cross-scale molecular grammar by harmonizing disparate public databases and training interpretable machine learning models to map sequence features to material states, analyze evolutionary conservation, and map disease mutation hotspots. Integration of disparate phase separation, single-cell, and clinical databases will be achieved by constructing a unified relational schema with mapped heterogeneous identifiers, developing a shared material-state ontology, and utilizing extraction pipelines to ingest data into a version-controlled database. abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation and related processes—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of proteins and nucleic acids give rise to functional subcellular compartments not predictable from any single molecule's properties. Despite intense interest, the field lacks a unified, predictive 'grammar' linking molecular-scale features (intrinsically disordered region composition, multivalency, stoichiometry, post-translational modification patterns) to mesoscale material properties (droplet viscosity, multiphase architecture, client selectivity) and ultimately to cellular-scale phenotypes (stress granule dynamics, transcriptional bursting, cell fate transitions). This gap persists because the necessary data are scattered across incompatible resources curated by disconnected communities: biophysicists studying in vitro phase diagrams, cell biologists generating high-content imaging atlases, proteomicists cataloging condensate constituents, evolutionary biologists tracking IDR conservation, and clinical genomicists annotating disease-associated mutations. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these disparate data types into a coherent cross-scale model. This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, computational structural biologists, cell imaging specialists, evolutionary genomicists, and clinical variant scientists to synthesize existing public datasets—including PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro, and LLPSDB (condensate composition and phase behavior), OpenCell and the Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization imaging), BioGRID/IntAct (interactomes), Human Cell Atlas and single-cell perturbation atlases (transcriptomic consequences across cell states), OrthoDB/Ensembl (cross-species IDR conservation), and ClinVar/COSMIC/gnomAD (disease-linked mutations in condensate-forming proteins)—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Using this integrated dataset, we will: (1) train interpretable machine learning models that map sequence-encoded 'stickers-and-spacers' features to empirically observed condensate material states and client recruitment specificity; (2) test whether evolutionary conservation patterns of IDR grammar predict functional robustness or tunability of condensate properties across orthologous proteins in diverse species; (3) determine whether disease-associated mutations in condensate scaffolds and clients cluster at predicted grammar 'hotspots' and whether this predicts pathological mesoscale-to-cellular phenotypic outcomes (e.g., aberrant stress granule persistence in neurodegeneration, altered chromatin condensate formation in cancer); and (4) build a generalizable cross-scale predictive framework linking molecular grammar to emergent cellular behavior, tested against independent public single-cell perturbation datasets. This synthesis is intractable for any individual lab given the scale of data harmonization, cross-domain expertise, and computational infrastructure required, and directly requires NCEMS support for data engineering, workshop convening, and shared analytical infrastructure. The Working Group will operate under FAIR and open-science principles, releasing all harmonized datasets, trained models, and reproducible workflows via public repositories. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded as co-leads on each data-integration module, receiving structured training in multi-omics data science, biophysical modeling, and collaborative team science, while a rotating visiting-scholar program will recruit early-career researchers from primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions to broaden participation. The project's central deliverable—a public, cross-species 'condensate grammar atlas'—will provide the field's first quantitative bridge between molecular sequence, mesoscale organization, and cellular emergent behavior.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation—represent a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon in which collective molecular interactions give rise to emergent material properties (liquid, gel, solid, multiphase architectures) that are not predictable from any single constituent protein or RNA. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based phase separation predictors, proteomic condensate composition datasets, cryo-electron tomography structural data, live-cell imaging archives, disease mutation catalogs, and functional genomics screens are housed in disconnected repositories, analyzed with incompatible metrics, and rarely cross-validated against one another. No individual laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, computational sequence analysis, cell imaging, evolutionary genomics, and clinical genetics needed to integrate these resources into a unified predictive framework. This proposal establishes a Working Group to synthesize eight major public data classes—LLPSDB and PhaSepDB (experimentally curated phase-separating proteins and conditions), CD-CODE (condensate composition and localization), MobiDB/DisProt (intrinsically disordered region annotations), EMDB cryo-electron tomograms of native condensates, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular imaging, ClinVar/COSMIC disease variants mapped onto disordered regions, multi-species sequence conservation (OrthoDB, UCSC multiz alignments), and DepMap/BioGRID-ORCS functional perturbation screens—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Our central scientific question is: what molecular grammar (sequence patterning of stickers, spacers, charge blocks, and short linear motifs) determines the emergent mesoscale material state and multiphase organization of condensates, and how do these physical properties causally propagate to organelle-level morphology and cell-scale phenotypes, including their disruption in disease? We will apply stickers-and-spacers biophysical theory and modern sequence-to-function machine learning models, trained on the harmonized dataset, to predict material state and client selectivity directly from primary sequence, then validate predictions against orthogonal image-derived morphological signatures (condensate number, size, sphericity, coalescence dynamics) extracted computationally from public imaging archives. We will further test whether disease-associated mutations preferentially alter predicted material properties rather than simple phase separation propensity, and whether evolutionary conservation patterns track functionally important mesoscale properties rather than sequence identity alone. This effort demands NCEMS-scale infrastructure: standardized ontologies for condensate material properties, automated cross-database entity resolution (protein identifiers, cell lines, imaging conditions), and computational pipelines for large-scale image feature extraction—capabilities beyond any single lab or existing bilateral collaboration. The team will unite condensate biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational/AI researchers, evolutionary biologists, and clinical geneticists across institutions varying in size and geography. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across all analytical stages, receiving hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, biophysical modeling, and open-science workflows. All harmonized datasets, trained models, analysis code, and condensate material-property ontologies will be released under FAIR principles via public repositories, providing a durable community resource for predicting and interpreting mesoscale emergence in cell biology and disease.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: assemblies of proteins and nucleic acids that acquire collective material properties—viscosity, surface tension, internal architecture, exchange dynamics—that cannot be inferred from any single molecular constituent. These properties dictate whether a condensate behaves as a dynamic liquid enabling rapid biochemical exchange, a gel that scaffolds signaling, or a pathological solid aggregate implicated in neurodegeneration and cancer. Over the past decade, thousands of studies have cataloged phase-separating proteins, mapped intrinsically disordered regions, imaged condensates across cell types, and linked disease mutations to aberrant assembly. Yet this knowledge remains scattered across at least eight major public resources—LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, MobiDB/DisProt, EMDB, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, ClinVar, COSMIC, OrthoDB, UCSC multiz alignments, DepMap, and BioGRID-ORCS—each built with distinct identifiers, annotation standards, and experimental contexts. Consequently, the field lacks a unified molecular grammar connecting primary sequence features to emergent material state, and lacks systematic tests of whether such physical properties causally propagate to organelle morphology, cellular fitness, and disease phenotypes. Individual laboratories typically specialize in one axis—biophysical theory, structural imaging, sequence bioinformatics, or clinical genetics—and lack the combined capacity to harmonize identifiers across databases, reconcile heterogeneous experimental metrics (e.g., saturation concentration versus qualitative droplet scoring), or extract comparable morphological features from thousands of independently generated micrographs. This fragmentation has stalled progress on a question of fundamental importance to molecular and cellular bioscience: what sequence-encoded rules govern the emergence of distinct material states, and how do these mesoscale properties scale up to influence cellular behavior and disease? Addressing this question requires simultaneous fluency in polymer physics, structural biology, high-throughput imaging analysis, evolutionary genomics, and clinical variant interpretation—an interdisciplinary breadth that no single research group possesses, and that existing bilateral collaborations are not structured to integrate at the scale of eight major data ecosystems. This proposal directly targets the NCEMS mission by synthesizing existing, non-experimental public data to resolve a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology. The condensate field is uniquely positioned for synthesis-driven discovery because the requisite data already exist at scale but have never been cross-validated against one another using a common ontology of material properties. By harmonizing these resources and applying sequence-to-function modeling validated against orthogonal imaging and clinical datasets, this Working Group will produce the first mechanistic, falsifiable framework linking molecular grammar to mesoscale emergent phenotypes, with direct implications for understanding aging-related aggregation disorders, cancer-associated condensate dysregulation, and the evolutionary design principles governing membraneless organelles. The resulting resource will lower the barrier for future researchers to test hypotheses about sequence-encoded emergence without requiring new experiments, fulfilling the Center's vision of catalyzing discovery through data synthesis rather than data generation.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching scientific question and three tractable sub-questions, each paired with falsifiable hypotheses testable through cross-database synthesis rather than new experimentation. Overarching question: What molecular grammar—defined as the sequence patterning of stickers (interaction motifs), spacers, charge blocks, and short linear motifs—determines the emergent mesoscale material state of biomolecular condensates, and how does this grammar causally propagate to organelle-level morphology and cell-scale phenotypes, including disease states? Sub-question 1 (Sequence-to-material-state mapping): Can stickers-and-spacers biophysical theory, trained jointly on LLPSDB/PhaSepDB experimental annotations and MobiDB/DisProt disorder architecture, predict qualitative material state (liquid, gel, solid, multiphase) directly from primary sequence with accuracy exceeding existing phase-separation-propensity predictors that ignore material state entirely? We hypothesize that models incorporating explicit sticker density, spacer flexibility, and charge-block patterning will outperform amino-acid-composition-only predictors, because material state is governed by interaction valence and lattice geometry rather than aggregate hydrophobicity or disorder content alone. Sub-question 2 (Cross-modal validation against imaging phenotypes): Do sequence-predicted material properties correspond to independently measured, image-derived morphological signatures—condensate number, size distribution, sphericity, and coalescence dynamics—extracted computationally from Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell archives and structurally corroborated by EMDB cryo-electron tomograms? We hypothesize that predicted liquid-like sequences will correlate with higher sphericity and coalescence propensity, while predicted gel/solid-like sequences will correlate with irregular morphology and reduced fusion events, providing orthogonal, data-driven validation absent from purely computational predictors. Sub-question 3 (Disease and evolutionary consequence): Do ClinVar- and COSMIC-annotated disease mutations within condensate-forming disordered regions preferentially disrupt predicted material state (e.g., shifting liquid-like sequences toward solid-like behavior) rather than simply abolishing phase separation propensity, and does cross-species conservation (OrthoDB, UCSC multiz alignments) preferentially preserve sticker patterning and material-state-determining residues over bulk sequence identity? We hypothesize that pathogenic variants cluster at positions predicted to be material-state-determining stickers rather than uniformly across disordered regions, and that evolutionary conservation signal is enriched at these same positions, indicating selective pressure to preserve mesoscale physical properties rather than sequence identity per se. A complementary hypothesis, tested using DepMap and BioGRID-ORCS functional screens, posits that genes encoding predicted solid/gel-prone condensate scaffolds will show stronger fitness dependencies in cancer cell lines than liquid-like scaffolds, reflecting reduced buffering capacity of rigid assemblies against perturbation. Collectively, these questions test whether a unifying, sequence-encoded physical grammar—rather than protein-specific idiosyncrasy—explains emergent condensate behavior across scales, from single-molecule interaction motifs to organelle morphology, organismal conservation, and human disease. Confirmation or refutation of these hypotheses requires exactly the kind of large-scale, multi-repository, multi-expertise synthesis that individual laboratories cannot undertake alone, positioning this Working Group to resolve a fundamental open question in mesoscale molecular and cellular biology.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will proceed through four integrated phases over a 24-month period. Phase 1 (Months 1–6): Data Harmonization and Ontology Development. We will construct a unified relational database mapping protein entries across LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, MobiDB/DisProt, UniProt, and OrthoDB using automated entity resolution built on UniProt accession crosswalks and sequence alignment fallback for unmapped entries. A controlled ontology for condensate material state (liquid, gel, solid, multiphase, unclassified) will be developed collaboratively, reconciling heterogeneous experimental descriptors (turbidity assays, FRAP recovery rates, qualitative microscopy calls) into standardized categorical and continuous labels, with inter-annotator agreement metrics reported for transparency. Cell line and imaging condition metadata from Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell will be harmonized using Cellosaurus identifiers. Phase 2 (Months 4–12): Sequence-to-Function Modeling. Using the harmonized labeled dataset, we will implement stickers-and-spacers-informed feature extraction (sticker motif density, spacer length distribution, net charge per residue, charge patterning parameter kappa, short linear motif annotations from ELM) alongside protein language model embeddings (e.g., ESM-2) as complementary representations. Gradient-boosted and deep learning classifiers will be trained to predict material state category, with nested cross-validation stratified by protein family to prevent homology-driven leakage. Model interpretability methods (SHAP values) will identify which sequence features drive material-state predictions, directly testing the molecular grammar hypothesis. Phase 3 (Months 8–18): Cross-Modal Imaging Validation. A computational image-analysis pipeline (built on CellProfiler and deep-learning segmentation models) will extract quantitative morphological features—puncta count, size distribution, sphericity, coalescence frequency where time-series data exist—from publicly archived Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell images for proteins with sequence-based material-state predictions. EMDB tomograms will provide structural corroboration for a curated subset of well-characterized condensates. Correlation and mixed-effects regression analyses will test whether predicted material states align with independent morphological signatures, controlling for imaging modality and cell type as random effects. Phase 4 (Months 14–24): Disease and Evolutionary Analysis. ClinVar and COSMIC variants will be mapped onto disordered regions and material-state-determining positions identified in Phase 2; enrichment of pathogenic variants at sticker positions versus random disordered positions will be tested via permutation analysis. Multi-species alignments (OrthoDB, UCSC multiz) will be used to compute position-specific conservation scores, testing whether material-state-determining residues show elevated conservation beyond background disordered-region conservation. DepMap and BioGRID-ORCS screen data will be integrated to test fitness-dependency hypotheses via differential essentiality analysis stratified by predicted material state. Throughout, biweekly cross-disciplinary working sessions will ensure iterative refinement of the ontology and models as domain experts (biophysicists, structural biologists, imagers, computational biologists, evolutionary geneticists, clinical geneticists) surface discipline-specific caveats, with NCEMS computational infrastructure supporting large-scale image processing and model training beyond individual lab capacity.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver a harmonized, publicly queryable database integrating eight major condensate-relevant repositories under a shared material-property ontology—the first resource of its kind—alongside validated machine learning models predicting condensate material state directly from primary sequence. Expected scientific outcomes include: (1) empirical identification of the sequence features (sticker density, spacer composition, charge patterning) most predictive of material state, advancing stickers-and-spacers theory from qualitative framework to quantitative, testable model; (2) the first large-scale, cross-modal validation of sequence-based material-state predictions against independently derived imaging morphology and structural data; (3) evidence clarifying whether disease mutations act primarily through material-state disruption rather than simple phase-separation abolition, with direct relevance to neurodegenerative disease and cancer mechanisms; and (4) insight into evolutionary constraints on mesoscale physical properties, reframing conservation analysis beyond sequence identity. Beyond specific findings, this project will produce durable community infrastructure: harmonized datasets, trained predictive models, reproducible analysis pipelines, and an open material-property ontology that future researchers can extend without repeating integration labor. This lowers the barrier to entry for mesoscale condensate research, particularly for computational scientists lacking wet-lab access and for groups at less-resourced institutions. The work directly advances NCEMS's mission by resolving a fragmented, long-standing puzzle—why sequence alone has failed to reliably predict condensate behavior—through synthesis rather than new experimentation. Broader impacts include establishing a template for cross-repository synthesis applicable to other mesoscale phenomena, training a cohort of data-savvy trainees fluent in biophysical modeling and open science, and generating testable hypotheses that will seed follow-on experimental studies across the community, amplifying the project's influence well beyond the funding period.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All work will adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and open science principles consistent with NCEMS community standards. The harmonized database, including entity-resolution crosswalks and the condensate material-property ontology, will be deposited in a version-controlled public repository (Zenodo/GitHub) with persistent identifiers, enabling independent verification and reuse. All code—data harmonization scripts, feature extraction pipelines, image analysis workflows, and machine learning model training/evaluation code—will be released under permissive open-source licenses with containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) to ensure computational reproducibility across institutions and hardware. Model weights, hyperparameters, and cross-validation splits will be published alongside detailed model cards documenting training data provenance, known limitations, and intended use, preventing misuse or overinterpretation. Analysis workflows will be implemented in reproducible notebook formats (Jupyter/R Markdown) with continuous integration testing to confirm computational stability as dependencies evolve. Data provenance will be rigorously tracked: every harmonized entry will retain links to original source repository identifiers and access dates, ensuring full traceability back to primary public data. The team will pre-register key hypotheses and analysis plans (Sub-questions 1–3) via OSF prior to large-scale model training to guard against post hoc rationalization. Intermediate outputs—harmonized ontology drafts, validation results, and interpretability analyses—will be shared iteratively through preprints (bioRxiv) rather than withheld until final publication, consistent with team science principles. All working group meetings, decision logs, and ontology governance discussions will be documented in a shared, publicly accessible wiki to model transparent collaborative process for future synthesis teams. Data and code releases will explicitly follow community-created open science policies referenced in the NCEMS charter, including appropriate attribution to original data generators and compliance with any usage restrictions specified by source repositories such as ClinVar and COSMIC.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests support for a two-year Working Group requiring no new data generation, focusing resources on personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative coordination. Personnel costs constitute the primary budget component: partial salary support (20–30% effort) for six co-investigators spanning biophysics, structural biology, imaging analysis, computational/AI methods, evolutionary genomics, and clinical genetics; full support for two postdoctoral researchers leading database harmonization and machine learning model development; and support for three graduate students embedded in imaging pipeline development, evolutionary analysis, and clinical variant mapping, respectively, each receiving structured mentorship across disciplinary boundaries. Computational resources include cloud computing allocation for large-scale image feature extraction from Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell archives (estimated at high-throughput GPU processing for segmentation models) and model training for sequence-based classifiers, alongside data storage for harmonized multi-terabyte imaging derivatives. NCEMS-provided infrastructure—including shared computational clusters, data harmonization tooling, and ontology-development support—will be leveraged to avoid duplicating capacity available centrally, directly justifying the need for Center-level rather than single-lab support. Travel funds are requested for two in-person Working Group meetings annually to conduct intensive cross-disciplinary integration sessions, ontology consensus-building, and trainee mentorship activities, plus conference travel for trainees to present synthesis outcomes. Modest publication costs cover open-access fees for resulting manuscripts and data descriptor papers. No funds are requested for wet-lab experimentation, reagents, or new data collection, consistent with the synthesis-only scope of this project. Cost-sharing is anticipated through in-kind institutional computing resources at participating universities. The requested budget reflects the minimum infrastructure necessary to integrate eight heterogeneous public repositories, train and validate cross-modal predictive models, and sustain a geographically distributed, multi-institutional team over the full analytical lifecycle, while ensuring trainees receive substantive, well-resourced participation throughout.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed by liquid-liquid phase separation—represent a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon in which collective molecular interactions give rise to emergent material properties (liquid, gel, solid, multiphase architectures) that are not predictable from any single constituent protein or RNA. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, the field remains fragmented: sequence-based phase separation predictors, proteomic condensate composition datasets, cryo-electron tomography structural data, live-cell imaging archives, disease mutation catalogs, and functional genomics screens are housed in disconnected repositories, analyzed with incompatible metrics, and rarely cross-validated against one another. No individual laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, computational sequence analysis, cell imaging, evolutionary genomics, and clinical genetics needed to integrate these resources into a unified predictive framework. This proposal establishes a Working Group to synthesize eight major public data classes—LLPSDB and PhaSepDB (experimentally curated phase-separating proteins and conditions), CD-CODE (condensate composition and localization), MobiDB/DisProt (intrinsically disordered region annotations), EMDB cryo-electron tomograms of native condensates, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular imaging, ClinVar/COSMIC disease variants mapped onto disordered regions, multi-species sequence conservation (OrthoDB, UCSC multiz alignments), and DepMap/BioGRID-ORCS functional perturbation screens—into a harmonized, queryable resource. Our central scientific question is: what molecular grammar (sequence patterning of stickers, spacers, charge blocks, and short linear motifs) determines the emergent mesoscale material state and multiphase organization of condensates, and how do these physical properties causally propagate to organelle-level morphology and cell-scale phenotypes, including their disruption in disease? We will apply stickers-and-spacers biophysical theory and modern sequence-to-function machine learning models, trained on the harmonized dataset, to predict material state and client selectivity directly from primary sequence, then validate predictions against orthogonal image-derived morphological signatures (condensate number, size, sphericity, coalescence dynamics) extracted computationally from public imaging archives. We will further test whether disease-associated mutations preferentially alter predicted material properties rather than simple phase separation propensity, and whether evolutionary conservation patterns track functionally important mesoscale properties rather than sequence identity alone. This effort demands NCEMS-scale infrastructure: standardized ontologies for condensate material properties, automated cross-database entity resolution (protein identifiers, cell lines, imaging conditions), and computational pipelines for large-scale image feature extraction—capabilities beyond any single lab or existing bilateral collaboration. The team will unite condensate biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational/AI researchers, evolutionary biologists, and clinical geneticists across institutions varying in size and geography. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across all analytical stages, receiving hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, biophysical modeling, and open-science workflows. All harmonized datasets, trained models, analysis code, and condensate material-property ontologies will be released under FAIR principles via public repositories, providing a durable community resource for predicting and interpreting mesoscale emergence in cell biology and disease.
