full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where interactions among intrinsically disordered regions, multivalent domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications give rise to macroscopic material properties (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) that in turn drive cellular functions such as transcriptional control, stress response, and signal transduction. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across biophysics, structural biology, proteomics, and cell imaging, the field lacks a unified framework connecting molecular-scale determinants to emergent mesoscale behavior and downstream cellular/disease phenotypes. This proposal assembles a Working Group to synthesize disparate public datasets—including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and CD-CODE (condensate composition and in vitro phase behavior), AlphaFold DB and PDB (structural/disorder predictions), Human Protein Atlas and Human Cell Atlas (expression, subcellular localization, single-cell heterogeneity), BioGRID/STRING (interactomes), and ClinVar/COSMIC (disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins)—to build a predictive, cross-scale model of condensate emergence. Our central question: Can molecular-level features (sequence grammar, valency, PTM sites, structural disorder) combined with cellular context (expression stoichiometry, localization, network connectivity) predict which proteins form condensates, the material properties of those condensates, and their functional or pathological consequences when perturbed by disease mutations? This question cannot be addressed by any single lab, as it requires integrating fundamentally different data modalities—biophysical phase diagrams, structural predictions, single-cell transcriptomics/proteomics, network biology, and clinical genomics—each requiring distinct domain expertise (biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and clinical geneticists). The Working Group will develop harmonized ontologies and standardized feature representations across these datasets, construct machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating interactome topology and sequence-based transformers for disorder/valency prediction) to predict condensate propensity and material state, and validate predictions against orthogonal public datasets (e.g., proteome-wide condensate screens, stress granule proteomics). A key innovation is testing whether emergent condensate properties can be predicted purely from public data integration without new wet-lab experiments, and whether disease mutations disrupt predicted phase behavior in ways that explain pathological phenotypes (e.g., ALS-associated FUS/TDP-43 mutations). The team will include biophysicists (LLPS theory), structural biologists (AlphaFold-based feature engineering), computational/systems biologists (network and ML integration), cell biologists (phenotypic validation using public imaging), and clinical genomics experts (mutation-disease linkage), spanning multiple career stages and institutions. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams, receiving training in multi-omics data integration, reproducible computational pipelines, and biophysical modeling. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with a FAIR-compliant condensate feature database, enabling the broader community to test hypotheses about mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. This work directly advances NCEMS's mission by using purely existing data to resolve a fundamental puzzle in emergent cellular organization, requiring collaboration far beyond individual lab capacity, and producing durable, reusable synthesis resources for the field.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged over the past decade as a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence in cell biology—the process whereby collective molecular interactions generate macroscopic properties and functions that cannot be predicted from the behavior of individual biomolecules in isolation. Formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related transitions, condensates such as nucleoli, stress granules, paraspeckles, and transcriptional hubs concentrate specific proteins and nucleic acids into dynamic, membraneless compartments that regulate gene expression, RNA metabolism, signal transduction, and cellular stress responses. Their material properties—viscosity, surface tension, internal architecture, and the propensity to age into solid-like or pathological aggregates—arise from a complex molecular grammar encoded in intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent interaction motifs, RNA-binding domains, and post-translational modifications (PTMs). Despite intensive study, the field lacks a predictive, generalizable framework linking these molecular determinants to emergent mesoscale material behavior and, ultimately, to cellular and organismal phenotypes, including disease.

This gap persists not for lack of data, but because relevant data are fragmented across disconnected repositories, each capturing only one layer of the multi-scale puzzle. In vitro phase separation databases (LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE) catalogue which proteins undergo LLPS under defined conditions but rarely connect these observations to structural, network, or clinical contexts. Structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB) provide residue-level disorder and conformational ensemble predictions but are not systematically cross-referenced with condensate behavior. Proteomic and imaging atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas) document expression and subcellular localization at single-cell resolution but are rarely integrated with biophysical phase behavior data. Interaction databases (BioGRID, STRING) describe network context that governs multivalency and stoichiometry but are seldom incorporated into condensate propensity models. Finally, clinical genomics resources (ClinVar, COSMIC) catalogue disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins (e.g., FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1) without systematic linkage to predicted changes in phase behavior. No existing framework unifies these disparate data modalities into a coherent, cross-scale model of condensate emergence.

This fragmentation represents precisely the kind of long-standing puzzle that NCEMS is positioned to address: a mesoscale phenomenon whose resolution requires synthesizing molecular, structural, cellular, and clinical data that individually reside within distinct scientific communities and expertise domains. No single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in biophysical phase separation theory, structural bioinformatics, single-cell systems biology, network science, and clinical genetics necessary to integrate these datasets meaningfully. Moreover, the scale of harmonization required—reconciling inconsistent nomenclature, experimental conditions, and feature representations across dozens of databases—exceeds the capacity of typical two- or three-lab collaborations and demands a dedicated, resourced Working Group.

Resolving the molecular grammar of condensate emergence has substantial scientific and translational significance. Mechanistically, it would establish generalizable principles connecting sequence-encoded molecular features to emergent material states, advancing fundamental understanding of mesoscale self-organization. Translationally, condensate dysregulation is implicated in neurodegenerative disease (ALS, frontotemporal dementia), cancer, and viral infection, making predictive models of mutation-driven phase behavior disruption directly relevant to understanding disease mechanisms and identifying potential therapeutic vulnerabilities. By building the first cross-scale, data-synthesized model of condensate emergence entirely from public data, this Working Group will generate a durable community resource while directly testing the feasibility of the synthesis-science paradigm NCEMS champions.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Central Research Question: Can integrated, publicly available molecular, structural, cellular, and clinical data be synthesized to predict which proteins form biomolecular condensates, the emergent material properties of those condensates, and the functional or pathological consequences of disease-associated mutations that perturb them?

This overarching question decomposes into four specific, testable sub-questions, each paired with a corresponding hypothesis.

RQ1: Molecular grammar of condensate propensity. Which combinations of sequence-encoded features—IDR content, multivalent motif patterns, RNA-binding domains, PTM site density, and predicted conformational flexibility (from AlphaFold DB)—best discriminate condensate-forming proteins from non-condensate-forming proteins across curated databases (LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE)? Hypothesis 1: A composite grammar score integrating valency, disorder, and PTM density will outperform any single feature class in predicting condensate propensity, and predictive power will further increase when structural context from AlphaFold-derived conformational ensembles is incorporated, reflecting the multivalent, combinatorial nature of phase separation.

RQ2: Cellular context modulates condensate emergence. Does cellular context—expression stoichiometry, subcellular localization, and interactome connectivity (from Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, BioGRID/STRING)—explain variance in condensate formation and localization not accounted for by sequence features alone? Hypothesis 2: Proteins with high network connectivity (hub proteins) and localized co-expression with known scaffold condensate components will show higher observed condensate participation than sequence-based predictions alone would suggest, indicating that mesoscale emergence is co-determined by molecular grammar and cellular network context.

RQ3: Predicting material properties. Can integrated molecular and cellular features predict quantitative material properties of condensates (viscosity, surface tension, multiphase architecture) reported in biophysical databases? Hypothesis 3: Material state (liquid-like versus gel/solid-like) is predictable from a combination of valency, disorder patterning (blockiness versus uniform distribution), and PTM-modulated charge patterning, with graph neural network models incorporating interactome topology outperforming sequence-only transformer models for predicting multiphase architecture.

RQ4: Disease mutations and pathological phase behavior. Do disease-associated mutations (ClinVar, COSMIC) in condensate-forming proteins preferentially localize to predicted phase-separation-driving regions, and do these mutations shift predicted material properties toward pathological (solid-like/aggregation-prone) states? Hypothesis 4: Pathogenic mutations in condensate-associated proteins (e.g., FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1) will be significantly enriched within predicted multivalent or disorder-patterned regions relative to benign variants, and model-predicted shifts toward reduced liquidity will correlate with known disease severity or age-of-onset data where available.

Underlying these specific hypotheses is an overarching meta-hypothesis central to NCEMS's mission: that emergent, mesoscale condensate behavior—previously understood only through targeted wet-lab biophysical experiments—can be substantially predicted through synthesis of existing public data alone, without generating new experimental measurements. Confirming this meta-hypothesis would demonstrate that data synthesis can recover mechanistic insight into emergence phenomena that previously required bespoke experimentation, validating the broader synthesis-science paradigm. Refuting or partially confirming it would still yield valuable insight, precisely delineating which aspects of mesoscale emergence require direct experimental measurement versus which are recoverable from existing community data—a distinction of substantial value for prioritizing future experimental and data-generation efforts across the field.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in four overlapping phases over 24 months, organized around four functional subteams: Data Harmonization; Sequence/Structure Modeling; Network/Systems Modeling; and Validation & Clinical Translation.

Phase 1 (Months 1–6): Data Acquisition and Harmonization. The Working Group will systematically query and download structured data from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE, PDB, AlphaFold DB, Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas, BioGRID, STRING, ClinVar, and COSMIC. A cross-disciplinary harmonization subteam (computational biologists, structural biologists) will develop a shared ontology mapping protein identifiers (UniProt-anchored), condensate types, experimental conditions, and phenotypic annotations across databases, resolving nomenclature inconsistencies and differing confidence metrics. Standardized feature representations will be engineered: sequence-derived features (IDR fraction, disorder profiles from AlphaFold pLDDT, multivalent motif counts, PTM site density from PhosphoSitePlus), structural features (conformational ensemble metrics), cellular features (expression and localization vectors from HPA/HCA), and network features (degree centrality, clustering coefficient from STRING/BioGRID graphs).

Phase 2 (Months 4–12): Model Development. Two complementary strategies will be pursued in parallel: (a) sequence-based transformer models fine-tuned on curated condensate-forming versus non-forming protein sets to predict condensate propensity and material state; (b) graph neural networks (GNNs) incorporating interactome topology alongside node-level sequence/structural features, testing whether network context improves prediction beyond sequence alone. Model architectures, hyperparameters, and train/test splits will be pre-registered, with held-out protein families excluded from training to test generalization rather than memorization.

Phase 3 (Months 10–18): Validation. Predictions will be validated against orthogonal, independent public datasets not used in training, including proteome-wide condensate screens and stress granule/nucleolar proteomic datasets, assessing precision-recall and calibration. Disease-mutation analyses (RQ4) will map ClinVar/COSMIC variants onto predicted phase-separation-driving regions using logistic regression and enrichment statistics, with case studies on FUS, TDP-43, and hnRNPA1 benchmarked against published clinical severity data.

Phase 4 (Months 16–24): Synthesis, Interpretation, and Dissemination. The full team will convene for interpretation workshops translating model outputs into testable biophysical hypotheses. A cell biology subteam will contextualize findings against public imaging datasets to assess phenotypic plausibility, and the group will finalize the harmonized database, models, and manuscripts.

The Working Group will meet biweekly as a full group and weekly within subteams, with in-person workshops at months 1, 9, and 18 to ensure cross-disciplinary integration. Trainees will co-lead subteam analyses under dual-PI mentorship, ensuring cross-disciplinary exposure. NCEMS computational infrastructure (cloud computing, data science personnel) will support harmonization pipelines and GNN/transformer training—resources exceeding what any individual lab currently maintains and central to the feasibility of this synthesis approach.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will produce several concrete, durable outcomes. First, a harmonized, FAIR-compliant Condensate Feature Database integrating molecular, structural, cellular, and clinical annotations for thousands of human proteins, structured for reuse and extension by the broader community. Second, validated predictive models (transformer- and GNN-based) for condensate propensity and material state, released with documented performance benchmarks and limitations, enabling researchers to generate testable hypotheses about understudied proteins without new experiments. Third, a curated catalogue of disease-associated mutations mapped onto predicted phase-separation-relevant regions, highlighting candidate mechanistic links between condensate dysregulation and neurodegenerative or oncogenic phenotypes, informing hypothesis-driven wet-lab follow-up. Fourth, at least two to three peer-reviewed publications reporting the integrated model, its validation, and specific biological insights (e.g., network-context effects on condensate formation; mutation enrichment patterns).

Scientifically, this project will resolve a long-standing puzzle regarding whether mesoscale condensate emergence is predictable from molecular sequence and cellular context alone, directly testing the feasibility of the synthesis-science paradigm for complex emergent phenomena. It will establish methodological precedent—harmonization pipelines and cross-scale modeling strategies—that other mesoscale synthesis projects within NCEMS can adapt. Translationally, mutation-phase behavior linkages may nominate new hypotheses regarding disease mechanism and severity that inform future experimental and therapeutic prioritization in condensate-associated diseases such as ALS and frontotemporal dementia. Broadly, by demonstrating that meaningful mechanistic insight into a complex emergent cellular phenomenon can be derived purely from existing public data integration, this project will provide a template and proof-of-concept for synthesis research across other mesoscale biological systems, reinforcing NCEMS's central scientific mission.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group is committed to full adherence to open, team, and reproducible science principles throughout the project lifecycle. All harmonized datasets, derived feature matrices, and mapping ontologies will be deposited in versioned, citable repositories (Zenodo) with permanent DOIs, accompanied by comprehensive metadata describing provenance, transformation steps, and licensing terms consistent with the original source databases. All analysis code—harmonization scripts, feature engineering pipelines, model training and evaluation code—will be maintained in a public GitHub repository under an open-source license, organized with clear documentation, containerized computational environments (Docker/Singularity), and continuous integration testing to ensure long-term executability by external users.

Trained models will be released with model cards documenting training data, intended use, performance benchmarks, and known limitations, following emerging community standards for responsible ML sharing in biology. Pre-registration of model architectures, train/test splits, and validation criteria (via OSF) will occur prior to Phase 2 model development, guarding against post-hoc overfitting. All intermediate and final datasets will be structured according to FAIR principles, using standard identifiers (UniProt, HGNC, PDB IDs) to maximize interoperability with existing community resources.

The Working Group will follow NCEMS's community-created policies on team science, including transparent authorship criteria established at project outset, documentation of individual and subteam contributions, and structured data/code sharing agreements among institutions. Meeting notes, analysis decisions, and interim findings will be maintained in a shared, version-controlled electronic lab notebook accessible to all members, promoting transparency and easing trainee onboarding. Upon publication, all code and data will be simultaneously released without embargo, and a lightweight web interface will allow non-computational researchers to query the Condensate Feature Database and generate predictions for proteins of interest.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed 24-month Working Group requests support consistent with NCEMS's synthesis-focused funding model, emphasizing personnel time, computational infrastructure, and collaborative convening rather than experimental costs. Primary budget categories include: (1) Personnel support for a dedicated postdoctoral data scientist (1.0 FTE, 24 months) to lead cross-database harmonization and pipeline development, ensuring continuity across subteams; (2) partial salary support (0.1–0.2 FTE each) for five co-investigator PIs spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational/systems biology, cell biology, and clinical genomics, reflecting supervisory and analytical contributions; (3) graduate student and postdoctoral trainee support (approximately 3–4 trainees at 0.25–0.5 FTE across participating labs) embedded within subteams, supporting the training mission of NCEMS; (4) cloud computing resources for GNN and transformer model training, including moderate GPU-hour allocations for structural feature extraction and large-scale interactome graph computation; (5) travel and lodging support for three in-person Working Group workshops (kickoff, midpoint, synthesis/writing) to facilitate the cross-disciplinary integration that virtual meetings alone cannot achieve; and (6) publication and data-deposition costs, including open-access fees and Zenodo/GitHub archival costs.

NCEMS support is essential because this project's scope—harmonizing more than ten distinct database ecosystems, developing and validating novel cross-scale ML architectures, and coordinating five disciplinary perspectives across multiple institutions—exceeds the discretionary resources and existing collaborative infrastructure of any single lab or current collaboration. NCEMS's computational infrastructure and data science support staff will supplement Working Group efforts for intensive harmonization tasks, and NCEMS's convening support will enable the in-person workshops critical for genuine transdisciplinary synthesis rather than superficial data-sharing. This resource structure directly reflects the scale, diversity, and infrastructure requirements characteristic of a true community-scale synthesis project.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where collective molecular interactions produce organelle-like structures with properties (viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability) not predictable from any single protein's biochemistry. Despite thousands of published studies characterizing individual condensates, the field lacks a unified, cross-scale understanding of which sequence features, structural motifs, and interaction network topologies causally determine condensate material properties and downstream cellular outcomes. [Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, where collective molecular interactions produce organelle-like structures with properties (viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability) not predictable from any single protein's biochemistry. This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team—computational biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, network biologists, and machine learning experts—to synthesize existing public datasets into an integrated, multi-scale atlas linking molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale behavior and cellular phenotype. Specific aims include: (1) Curate and harmonize condensate proteomic, sequence, and structural datasets into a standardized ontology capturing IDR composition, multivalency, post-translational modification sites, and predicted AlphaFold conformational ensembles; (2) Develop machine learning models trained on quantitative imaging-derived material property measurements (droplet fusion rates, FRAP recovery kinetics, aspect ratios) to identify sequence/network features predictive of condensate viscoelasticity and stability across previously siloed studies; (3) Integrate condensate composition data with protein interaction networks and single-cell omics to test whether network centrality and connectivity of condensate-resident proteins predict cellular sensitivity to condensate perturbation (e.g., in stress granule dynamics during disease); (4) Build a publicly accessible, version-controlled computational pipeline and interactive database (following FAIR principles) enabling the community to query molecular determinants of mesoscale emergence across cell types and organisms.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it demands reconciling incompatible data formats, resolving conflicting condensate classification schemes across independent labs, and computational infrastructure for cross-referencing structural, network, and imaging data at scale—tasks infeasible for any individual collaboration. The working group will recruit graduate students and postdocs from biophysics, computer science, and cell biology backgrounds, providing hands-on training in reproducible multi-omic data integration, FAIR data stewardship, and emergence-focused hypothesis generation. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analysis code will be released as an open-source resource, establishing a reusable framework for mesoscale emergence research applicable beyond condensate biology to other multi-scale cellular phenomena.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are a paradigmatic instance of mesoscale emergence: collections of proteins and nucleic acids, individually well-characterized biochemically, self-organize through multivalent, often weak and transient interactions into structures with material properties—viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability, aging kinetics—that cannot be predicted from any single component's properties in isolation. These condensates (nucleoli, stress granules, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and many disease-associated aggregates) sit precisely at the compositional and spatial scale NCEMS has identified as foundational: the mesoscale between individual biomolecules and organelles. Over the past fifteen years, the field has produced an extraordinary volume of data characterizing condensates from complementary but disconnected vantage points. Sequence-based resources (DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSePro) catalog intrinsically disordered regions and predicted phase-separation propensity. Proteomic catalogs (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE) enumerate condensate-resident proteins across cell types and species. Structural repositories, including the PDB, cryo-EM/cryo-ET depositions, and AlphaFold-predicted conformational ensembles, offer atomistic and near-atomistic views of condensate-forming domains. Interaction network databases (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct) capture the topology of physical and functional relationships among condensate components. Quantitative imaging repositories (Cell Image Library, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource) contain FRAP curves, droplet fusion kinetics, and size/number distributions that operationally define material properties. Finally, single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic datasets from disease cohorts (ALS/FTD, cancer) document the downstream phenotypic consequences when condensate homeostasis is perturbed. Individually, each resource answers a narrow question. Collectively, they contain the raw material to answer a question no single dataset can: what molecular grammar—sequence composition, multivalency, PTM patterning, structural flexibility, and network embedding—causally determines whether a condensate behaves as a liquid, gel, or solid, and how that material identity propagates to cellular and organismal phenotype. This is precisely the kind of long-standing puzzle envisioned by the NCEMS mission: a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence that is answerable only through synthesis of existing data, not through additional isolated experiments. The scientific barrier is not a lack of data but a lack of integration: incompatible ontologies for describing IDRs, non-overlapping naming conventions for condensates across databases, imaging data reported in heterogeneous units and imaging modalities, and no existing crosswalk between structural, network, and phenotypic layers. Overcoming this barrier requires simultaneous expertise in biophysics, structural biology, computer vision, network science, and systems biology—expertise that does not reside in any single laboratory and that has not previously been assembled around this specific integration problem. The significance extends beyond condensate biology: a validated framework for linking molecular-scale features to emergent mesoscale material properties and cellular outcomes would provide a template applicable to other emergent cellular phenomena that NCEMS aims to catalyze, including cytoskeletal self-organization, membrane-less organelle competition, and multi-protein assembly lines.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching question and three tractable sub-questions, each addressable only through cross-database synthesis. Overarching question: What molecular and network-level features causally determine the material properties of biomolecular condensates, and how do these properties propagate to cellular phenotype and disease susceptibility? Sub-question 1 (Molecular Grammar): Which combinations of IDR sequence features (charge patterning, aromatic residue spacing, PTM site density, multivalency of folded domains) predict condensate material state across independently reported systems? Hypothesis 1: Condensates enriched in regularly spaced aromatic 'stickers' embedded in flexible, low-complexity 'spacers' will exhibit liquid-like behavior (high FRAP recovery, low aspect ratio at fusion) across studies, whereas condensates with irreducible beta-sheet-prone segments or high PTM-mediated crosslinking potential will show gel/solid-like signatures, independent of the specific protein family or reporting laboratory—a pattern currently obscured because no dataset spans enough systems to test it statistically. Sub-question 2 (Network Topology and Robustness): Does the position of a condensate-resident protein within the global protein-protein interaction network predict the cellular sensitivity to condensate perturbation? Hypothesis 2: Proteins with high interaction network centrality and high condensate co-occurrence across cell types constitute 'hub' condensate components whose knockdown or mutation disproportionately destabilizes condensate integrity and produces outsized transcriptomic/phenotypic perturbation, compared to peripheral, low-centrality condensate components—analogous to robustness principles observed in other biological networks but never tested at the condensate-material-property level. Sub-question 3 (Cross-Scale Predictivity and Disease Relevance): Can molecular and network features integrated across datasets predict which condensate perturbations are associated with pathological outcomes (ALS-linked stress granule persistence, cancer-associated transcriptional condensate dysregulation)? Hypothesis 3: Condensates whose material properties (as predicted from Hypothesis 1) sit near liquid-to-solid phase boundaries, and whose components occupy high-centrality network positions (Hypothesis 2), will be disproportionately represented among condensates implicated in disease datasets, reflecting an emergent vulnerability that arises jointly from molecular grammar and network embedding rather than from either factor alone. These hypotheses are deliberately falsifiable and cross-scale: each requires simultaneous access to sequence/structural databases, imaging-derived material property measurements, interaction networks, and phenotypic/disease datasets—a combination that has not been assembled in any prior study. Testing them will determine whether a generalizable, quantitative molecular grammar of condensate emergence exists, or whether material properties are irreducibly system-specific, itself a significant and publishable finding. Successful validation would yield a predictive, mechanistic bridge between molecular composition and mesoscale/cellular emergent behavior; refutation or partial support would sharpen the field's understanding of which features are and are not generalizable, redirecting future hypothesis-driven experimentation. Either outcome constitutes a substantial advance over the current fragmented, single-system literature.

[Methods and Approach]
The project proceeds in four interlocking phases over a two-year working group engagement, structured around quarterly in-person/virtual synthesis meetings and continuous asynchronous collaboration via shared computational infrastructure. Phase 1 (Months 1–6): Data Harmonization and Ontology Development. The team will systematically extract and cross-reference entries from DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE, PhaSePro, BioGRID, STRING, and AlphaFold DB. A controlled vocabulary/ontology will be developed to resolve conflicting condensate nomenclature and classification schemes (e.g., differing definitions of 'client' versus 'scaffold' proteins) across source databases, using protein identifiers (UniProt accessions) as the harmonization backbone. Structural biologists will annotate AlphaFold pLDDT/PAE profiles to identify predicted disorder and conformational heterogeneity for each condensate-associated protein. Phase 2 (Months 4–12): Imaging Data Curation and Feature Extraction. Working with imaging scientists, the team will mine the Cell Image Library, BioImage Archive, and associated publication supplements for quantitative material-property measurements (FRAP recovery half-times and mobile fractions, droplet fusion/relaxation times, aspect ratios, size distributions), applying computer-vision and reanalysis pipelines to standardize measurements originally reported in heterogeneous formats. Where raw images are available, automated segmentation (using existing open-source tools such as CellProfiler or deep-learning segmentation models) will extract features not reported in the original text, subject to careful provenance tracking. Phase 3 (Months 8–18): Model Development and Network Integration. Machine learning experts will develop interpretable models (gradient-boosted trees, attention-based sequence models) trained on the harmonized sequence/structural features to predict imaging-derived material property classes, with rigorous cross-validation stratified by protein family and originating study to avoid data leakage and confounding by laboratory-specific methodology. In parallel, network biologists will compute centrality, modularity, and community-detection metrics on BioGRID/STRING subnetworks restricted to condensate-annotated proteins, testing associations with material property predictions and with phenotypic outcomes drawn from public single-cell RNA-seq/proteomics datasets (e.g., NCBI GEO, PRIDE) from ALS and cancer cohorts using established differential expression and enrichment frameworks. Phase 4 (Months 16–24): Integration, Validation, and Dissemination. All layers will be integrated into a unified relational database and interactive web application, with statistical models validated against held-out condensate systems not used in training. Sensitivity analyses will assess robustness to database version, annotation confidence thresholds, and imaging modality. Throughout, biweekly working sessions will pair trainees with domain-expert mentors on specific integration tasks, and all code will be developed collaboratively on a shared version-controlled repository with continuous integration testing to ensure reproducibility. This phased, iterative approach ensures that data harmonization (the primary bottleneck) is front-loaded, while modeling and biological interpretation proceed on validated, harmonized data rather than provisional extractions.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver: (1) a harmonized, FAIR-compliant multi-modal database linking sequence, structural, imaging-derived material property, network, and phenotypic data for hundreds of condensate systems—the first resource of its kind; (2) validated, interpretable machine learning models identifying sequence and network determinants of condensate viscoelasticity, generalizable across protein families and previously siloed studies; (3) a quantitative test of whether network centrality predicts cellular vulnerability to condensate perturbation, yielding either a novel emergent-robustness principle or a well-characterized boundary condition where such principles fail; (4) an open-source, version-controlled analytical pipeline and interactive query tool enabling the broader community to test new hypotheses about mesoscale emergence without re-performing data integration; and (5) at least three to five peer-reviewed publications co-authored across disciplinary boundaries, alongside preprints and community presentations. Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing fragmentation in condensate biology, converting a large but disconnected literature into a predictive, cross-system framework—directly fulfilling NCEMS's mandate to answer fundamental emergence questions through synthesis rather than new data generation. Methodologically, the harmonization ontology and integration pipeline will be explicitly designed for reuse in other mesoscale emergence contexts (cytoskeletal assembly, membrane-organelle contact sites), amplifying impact beyond condensate biology. Trainees will emerge with rare, high-demand competencies in multi-omic data integration, reproducible computational biology, and cross-disciplinary collaboration, directly serving the goal of training a data-savvy workforce. By resolving conflicting classification schemes and establishing shared standards, this project will also lower the barrier for future data depositors, improving the quality and interoperability of condensate data generated by the broader research community for years to come.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All work will adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and open science principles from inception. Data harmonization scripts, ontology mappings, machine learning training/validation code, and the final integrated database schema will be developed in public GitHub repositories under permissive open-source licenses (MIT/BSD), with continuous integration testing to ensure long-term functionality. All harmonized datasets will be deposited in a persistent, citable repository (e.g., Zenodo or an NCEMS-designated archive) with versioned releases and complete provenance metadata documenting the source database, extraction date, and any transformation applied—critical given that source databases are themselves periodically updated. Analysis workflows will be containerized (Docker/Singularity) and orchestrated via workflow managers (Snakemake/Nextflow) to guarantee computational reproducibility across computing environments. Machine learning models will be released with full training/validation splits, hyperparameters, and evaluation code to enable independent replication and benchmarking by external groups. The interactive web database will be built on open frameworks and hosted with sustainability commitments extending beyond the funding period, with a clear data governance and maintenance plan established during Phase 4. Preprints will be posted to bioRxiv prior to journal submission, and all publications will target open-access venues or include self-archived accepted manuscripts. The team commits to pre-registering key hypotheses and analysis plans (Hypotheses 1–3) via the Open Science Framework prior to finalizing model training, distinguishing confirmatory tests from exploratory analyses. Working group meetings, tutorials, and code walkthroughs will be recorded and shared publicly where appropriate, supporting broader community training. This comprehensive commitment to openness ensures the project's outputs are not merely a static resource but a living, extensible platform that the community can build upon, consistent with NCEMS's emphasis on team science and reproducibility as foundational, not incidental, project deliverables.

[Budget and Resources]
This proposal requests NCEMS Working Group support for a two-year collaborative engagement centered on in-person synthesis meetings, computational infrastructure, and trainee support rather than data generation. Budget priorities include: (1) Personnel—partial salary support for a postdoctoral data integration scientist (0.5 FTE across two years) to lead day-to-day harmonization and pipeline development, and stipend/tuition support for two graduate student trainees (0.25 FTE each) drawn from biophysics and computer science programs, providing hands-on synthesis research training; (2) Working Group Meetings—support for three in-person multi-day synthesis workshops (bringing together the ~8–10 core investigators, postdoc, and trainees) plus travel for early-career participants from diverse institutions, consistent with NCEMS's emphasis on geographic and career-stage diversity; (3) Computational Infrastructure—cloud computing credits (AWS/Google Cloud or institutional HPC allocation) for large-scale image reanalysis, model training, and hosting of the interactive database, plus modest costs for persistent data repository deposition and long-term hosting of the web application; (4) Software Development—limited contractor support for front-end development of the interactive query tool, beyond what trainees and co-PIs can provide; (5) Dissemination—open-access publication fees and preprint server costs. This project explicitly requires no funds for new experimental data generation, consistent with NCEMS's synthesis mandate. The requested resources are scoped tightly to the integration, modeling, and dissemination activities that distinguish this project from what any single laboratory could accomplish: specifically, the computational infrastructure to cross-reference terabyte-scale imaging archives with structural and network databases, and the personnel time required to manually reconcile conflicting ontologies across a dozen independently maintained resources. NCEMS's existing data science and computing resources, along with facilitation support for working group coordination, will be leveraged wherever available to minimize redundant infrastructure costs, and the team will coordinate with NCEMS staff scientists to align data standards with other Center-supported working groups.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related processes—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, arising from collective interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular processes such as transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, our understanding remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based predictors of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent motifs (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, PLAAC, catGRANULE outputs), curated condensate composition and localization databases (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), high-content imaging repositories capturing condensate morphology and dynamics (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Cell Explorer), interactome and PTM databases (BioGRID, STRING, PhosphoSitePlus), and clinical variant repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) linking condensate-associated mutations to disease. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these heterogeneous, multi-scale datasets into a unified predictive framework. This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and clinical geneticists to synthesize these public resources and address a fundamental question: what molecular-level 'grammar'—sequence composition, valency, PTM patterning, and stoichiometry—determines the emergent mesoscale material properties of condensates, and how do these properties causally propagate to higher-order cellular phenotypes and disease states?

Our approach will proceed in three integrated phases. First, we will construct a harmonized, ontology-linked meta-database that cross-references sequence/structural features of condensate-forming proteins with experimentally reported material properties (extracted via text-mining and manual curation from published biophysical assays) and cellular imaging phenotypes. Second, we will apply machine learning and biophysical polymer models to identify generalizable sequence-to-material-property relationships, testing whether emergent condensate behaviors (e.g., liquid-to-gel transitions, multiphase architecture) can be predicted purely from primary sequence and interactome context, independent of any single protein family. Third, we will link these mesoscale signatures to organismal and disease-relevant outcomes by integrating single-cell transcriptomic stress-response datasets (GEO, Human Cell Atlas) and disease variant databases, testing whether condensate-destabilizing mutations converge on shared material-property signatures across neurodegenerative and cancer-associated proteins.

This project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: it requires no new experiments, relies entirely on integration of existing public datasets across previously unlinked disciplines, and demands collaborative infrastructure beyond any individual lab's capacity, including standardized data harmonization pipelines, shared computational resources, and cross-domain expertise. All curated datasets, ontologies, and analysis code will be released as open-source, FAIR-compliant resources through NCEMS infrastructure, accompanied by a public database and interactive visualization tool for the condensate research community. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across sub-teams (data curation, ML modeling, biophysical validation, phenotype integration), receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and open data science practices, directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce central to NCEMS's mission while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how molecular-scale interactions generate emergent, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in cells.

Dysregulation of condensate material states is now implicated in neurodegeneration (FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1 aggregation), oncogenesis (MED1/BRD4 condensates at super-enhancers), and viral replication factories, positioning condensate biophysics as a critical node connecting molecular sequence information to organismal disease phenotypes.

Each resource captures a different scale of the emergence problem—molecular sequence, biophysical behavior, cellular phenotype, or organismal outcome—yet they remain siloed, using incompatible ontologies, identifiers, and metadata standards. Consequently, even though the raw information needed to derive a predictive 'molecular grammar' of condensate emergence already exists in public repositories, no unified analysis has systematically linked sequence-encoded features to mesoscale material properties and then to cellular and disease phenotypes.

Bridging these datasets requires simultaneous fluency in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, high-content imaging analysis, machine learning, and clinical genetics—expertise that is rarely, if ever, housed within a single laboratory. The scientific payoff of solving this integration problem is substantial: a validated sequence-to-material-property-to-phenotype framework would transform condensate biology from a largely descriptive, case-by-case discipline into a predictive science, enabling rational design of condensate-modulating therapeutics and providing a template for studying emergence at other biological scales. This proposal directly matches NCEMS's mission of mesoscale emergence synthesis: it uses exclusively existing public data, demands cross-disciplinary collaboration exceeding single-lab capacity, and targets a long-standing puzzle—how molecular-scale heterogeneity gives rise to reproducible, functionally consequential mesoscale organization—through community-scale data integration rather than new experimentation. By formalizing this grammar, the project will also generate reusable infrastructure (ontologies, harmonized databases, prediction models) of lasting value to the broader molecular and cellular biosciences community, catalyzing future synthesis efforts on emergent phenomena beyond condensates.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching question and three tractable sub-questions, each paired with a testable hypothesis derived from existing biophysical theory and preliminary community data.

Overarching Question: What sequence-encoded molecular grammar—composition, valency, patterning, and post-translational modification (PTM) state—determines the emergent mesoscale material properties of biomolecular condensates, and how do these properties causally propagate to cellular and organismal phenotypes?

Sub-question 1 (Sequence-to-Material-Property Mapping): Can mesoscale material properties (viscosity, surface tension, liquid-to-gel transition propensity, multiphase architecture) be predicted from primary sequence features and interactome context alone, independent of protein family identity? Hypothesis 1: Condensate material state is governed by generalizable 'sticker-and-spacer' grammar (patterning of aromatic/charged residues, IDR length, PTM density) such that machine learning models trained on cross-family sequence and interactome features will predict material properties with accuracy comparable to family-specific models, revealing conserved physical principles that transcend individual protein identity. We further hypothesize that PTM patterning (particularly phosphorylation clusters) acts as a tunable rheostat shifting condensates along the liquid-to-gel continuum, detectable as a quantitative interaction between PhosphoSitePlus-annotated PTM density and reported viscosity/FRAP recovery metrics.

Sub-question 2 (Material Property-to-Phenotype Propagation): Do specific mesoscale material signatures correspond to distinct cellular functional outcomes (e.g., transcriptional condensates favor low-viscosity liquid states enabling rapid exchange, while stress granules and pathological aggregates favor higher-viscosity, gel-like states)? Hypothesis 2: Cellular imaging phenotypes (condensate number, size distribution, dynamics from Human Protein Atlas and Allen Cell Explorer) will cluster into a small number of recurrent 'material-phenotype archetypes' that correlate with functional annotation (transcriptional, translational, stress-response) independent of the specific proteins involved, indicating that material state, not molecular identity, is the primary determinant of functional role.

Sub-question 3 (Disease Convergence Hypothesis): Do disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins converge on shared material-property perturbations across otherwise unrelated diseases? Hypothesis 3: Pathogenic variants curated in ClinVar and COSMIC that map onto condensate-forming regions will disproportionately shift predicted material properties toward aberrant gelation/solidification, and this convergence will be detectable across neurodegenerative (FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1) and oncogenic (MED1, EWS-FLI1) protein sets despite their distinct biological contexts, supporting a unifying 'aberrant hardening' model of condensate-linked pathology.

These hypotheses are individually falsifiable through statistical and machine-learning analyses of existing data, and collectively they interrogate the causal chain from sequence to mesoscale material state to cellular function to organismal disease—the defining structure of an emergence problem. Critically, none of these questions can be answered by mining a single database or by any one disciplinary lens: they require simultaneous, harmonized access to sequence/structural, biophysical, imaging, interactome, and clinical data streams, and the interpretive expertise to connect them. This is precisely the kind of multi-scale, cross-disciplinary synthesis question that individual labs are structurally unable to pursue but that a coordinated NCEMS Working Group is uniquely positioned to resolve.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will execute a three-phase, 24-month workplan structured around monthly cross-team synthesis meetings and shared computational infrastructure hosted on NCEMS servers.

Phase 1 – Harmonized Meta-Database Construction (Months 1–8): We will build a unified, ontology-linked resource integrating (a) sequence/structural features from UniProt, AlphaFold DB, PLAAC, and catGRANULE; (b) curated condensate composition/localization records from PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and CD-CODE; (c) quantitative material property measurements (viscosity, surface tension, FRAP recovery rates, saturation concentrations) extracted through a combination of automated text-mining (using large language model-assisted literature parsing) and expert manual curation from primary biophysical publications; (d) interactome and PTM annotations from BioGRID, STRING, and PhosphoSitePlus. A standardized condensate-protein identifier crosswalk and controlled vocabulary (aligned with Gene Ontology and the emerging Condensate Ontology) will resolve naming inconsistencies across sources. Data provenance, curation confidence scores, and version control will be tracked via a FAIR-compliant relational database with a documented schema.

Phase 2 – Sequence-to-Material-Property Modeling (Months 6–16): Using the harmonized database, we will apply (i) supervised machine learning (gradient-boosted trees, sequence-based transformer embeddings) to predict material property classes from sequence and interactome features, employing family-blind cross-validation to test generalizability (Hypothesis 1); (ii) biophysical polymer models (stickers-and-spacers, random-phase approximation extensions) to interpret ML-derived feature importance in mechanistic terms; and (iii) unsupervised clustering of imaging-derived phenotypic features from Human Protein Atlas and Allen Cell Explorer to identify recurrent material-phenotype archetypes (Hypothesis 2). Model performance will be benchmarked against held-out experimentally characterized condensates and evaluated using rigorous statistical criteria (nested cross-validation, permutation testing, false discovery correction).

Phase 3 – Phenotype and Disease Integration (Months 14–24): We will map ClinVar and COSMIC variants onto condensate-relevant protein regions, using Phase 2 models to predict the material-property consequences of each variant, and test for convergence of predicted perturbations across neurodegenerative and oncogenic protein sets (Hypothesis 3). Single-cell transcriptomic stress-response datasets (GEO, Human Cell Atlas) will be integrated to examine whether cells harboring predicted condensate-destabilizing genotypes show convergent stress-response transcriptional signatures.

Team Structure and Workflow: Sub-teams will focus on (1) data curation/harmonization, (2) ML/biophysical modeling, (3) imaging phenotype analysis, and (4) clinical/disease integration, with cross-team liaisons ensuring methodological consistency. Bi-weekly working sessions, shared GitHub repositories, and containerized (Docker/Singularity) analysis pipelines will ensure reproducibility. An external advisory panel of condensate biologists and clinical geneticists will review progress at 6 and 18 months to validate biological plausibility and disease relevance of findings.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will deliver: (1) a publicly accessible, harmonized meta-database linking sequence, material property, imaging, interactome, and disease-variant data for condensate-forming proteins, with an interactive web visualization tool; (2) validated, family-agnostic machine learning models predicting mesoscale material properties from sequence and interactome context, released as open-source, documented software packages; (3) a mechanistic, testable framework identifying recurrent 'material-phenotype archetypes' linking condensate physical state to cellular function; and (4) a disease-convergence atlas mapping pathogenic variants onto predicted material-property perturbations across neurodegenerative and oncogenic contexts.

Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology—whether generalizable sequence rules govern condensate material behavior—and establish a template for connecting molecular-scale information to mesoscale emergent properties and macroscale phenotypes. The predictive framework will generate specific, experimentally testable hypotheses (e.g., candidate PTM sites or sequence motifs whose perturbation should shift material state), catalyzing new experimental programs across the field and reducing costly trial-and-error in future condensate and drug-discovery research.

Broader impacts include establishment of reusable infrastructure (ontologies, curated datasets, prediction models) that will accelerate future synthesis studies on other emergent mesoscale phenomena, directly advancing NCEMS's core scientific vision. The project will train graduate students and postdocs in interdisciplinary, data-intensive synthesis science, producing a cohort of researchers fluent in biophysics, computational biology, and open science practices. By demonstrating that fundamental emergence questions can be resolved through rigorous integration of existing public data rather than new experimentation, this project will serve as a proof-of-concept for community-scale synthesis as a discovery paradigm in the molecular and cellular biosciences, with anticipated dissemination through high-impact publications, community workshops, and a sustained open-access resource for the condensate biology community.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All aspects of this project will adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and open, team, and reproducible science principles consistent with NCEMS community policies. The harmonized meta-database, including all curation decisions, provenance metadata, and confidence scores, will be deposited in a public repository (e.g., Zenodo/Figshare with a persistent DOI) and mirrored on NCEMS infrastructure, with a machine-readable schema and controlled vocabulary documented for reuse by the broader community. All code—data harmonization scripts, machine learning pipelines, polymer modeling implementations, and visualization tools—will be version-controlled on a public GitHub repository under a permissive open-source license (MIT/BSD), with containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) to ensure exact computational reproducibility across platforms.

Analytical workflows will be implemented as modular, well-documented Jupyter notebooks and workflow management pipelines (Snakemake/Nextflow), enabling independent replication of every reported result from raw public data through final figures. We will adopt pre-registration of key hypotheses and analysis plans (Phase 2 and 3 models) via the Open Science Framework prior to model training, mitigating overfitting and confirmation bias risks inherent in large-scale data synthesis. Model performance metrics, including negative and null results, will be reported transparently to avoid publication bias.

An interactive, public-facing web application will allow external researchers to query the meta-database, visualize predicted material properties for proteins of interest, and download underlying data and code. Data curation protocols and ontology mappings will be published as a standalone methods resource to enable extension by other groups. The Working Group will convene at least one open community workshop to solicit feedback on the database schema and prediction models prior to final release, ensuring the resource meets the needs of the broader condensate and cell biology communities and exemplifies team science conducted transparently and reproducibly.

[Budget and Resources]
This project requests NCEMS support for a 24-month Working Group comprising 6–8 co-investigators spanning biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, cell biology, and clinical genetics, plus embedded trainees. Requested resources include: (1) Personnel—partial salary support (2.4 person-months/year) for each co-PI, full support for two postdoctoral researchers specializing in machine learning and biophysical modeling, and two graduate research assistants engaged in data curation and imaging phenotype analysis; (2) Computational Resources—cloud/high-performance computing allocation for large-scale text-mining, machine learning model training, and polymer simulations, plus data storage for the harmonized meta-database and associated version-controlled archives; (3) NCEMS Infrastructure Support—access to shared data harmonization pipelines, ontology development consultation, and web application hosting for the public visualization tool; (4) Travel—funds for quarterly in-person Working Group meetings (rotating host institutions) and trainee participation in one NCEMS-sponsored training workshop and one scientific conference per year to present synthesis results; (5) Curation and Text-Mining Costs—support for manual literature curation and validation of automated text-mining extraction of material property data from legacy biophysical publications, including expert-hours for quality control; (6) External Advisory Panel—modest honoraria for two annual review sessions with condensate biology and clinical genetics experts to validate biological plausibility of findings.

This budget reflects the minimum resources necessary to sustain a genuinely multidisciplinary, multi-institutional collaboration integrating five distinct data ecosystems—resources and coordination needs that substantially exceed what any single laboratory's standard R01-type funding could support. NCEMS's shared computational infrastructure and community-building support are essential enabling factors, as they provide the harmonization tools, storage capacity, and cross-institutional coordination mechanisms required for this scale of synthesis. Cost-sharing will be pursued through in-kind contributions of existing lab-specific software tools and preliminary curated datasets from participating investigators, maximizing the efficiency of NCEMS-provided resources.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related processes—are a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, arising from collective interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce compartments with distinct material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that in turn shape cellular processes such as transcription, stress response, and signaling. Despite explosive growth in condensate research, our understanding remains fragmented across disconnected data silos: sequence-based predictors of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent motifs (UniProt, AlphaFold DB, PLAAC, catGRANULE outputs), curated condensate composition and localization databases (PhaSePro, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE), high-content imaging repositories capturing condensate morphology and dynamics (Human Protein Atlas, Allen Cell Explorer), interactome and PTM databases (BioGRID, STRING, PhosphoSitePlus), and clinical variant repositories (ClinVar, COSMIC) linking condensate-associated mutations to disease. No single lab possesses the expertise or bandwidth to integrate these heterogeneous, multi-scale datasets into a unified predictive framework. This proposal assembles a Working Group of biophysicists, structural biologists, computational biologists, cell biologists, and clinical geneticists to synthesize these public resources and address a fundamental question: what molecular-level 'grammar'—sequence composition, valency, PTM patterning, and stoichiometry—determines the emergent mesoscale material properties of condensates, and how do these properties causally propagate to higher-order cellular phenotypes and disease states?

Our approach will proceed in three integrated phases. First, we will construct a harmonized, ontology-linked meta-database that cross-references sequence/structural features of condensate-forming proteins with experimentally reported material properties (extracted via text-mining and manual curation from published biophysical assays) and cellular imaging phenotypes. Second, we will apply machine learning and biophysical polymer models to identify generalizable sequence-to-material-property relationships, testing whether emergent condensate behaviors (e.g., liquid-to-gel transitions, multiphase architecture) can be predicted purely from primary sequence and interactome context, independent of any single protein family. Third, we will link these mesoscale signatures to organismal and disease-relevant outcomes by integrating single-cell transcriptomic stress-response datasets (GEO, Human Cell Atlas) and disease variant databases, testing whether condensate-destabilizing mutations converge on shared material-property signatures across neurodegenerative and cancer-associated proteins.

This project exemplifies community-scale synthesis: it requires no new experiments, relies entirely on integration of existing public datasets across previously unlinked disciplines, and demands collaborative infrastructure beyond any individual lab's capacity, including standardized data harmonization pipelines, shared computational resources, and cross-domain expertise. All curated datasets, ontologies, and analysis code will be released as open-source, FAIR-compliant resources through NCEMS infrastructure, accompanied by a public database and interactive visualization tool for the condensate research community. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across sub-teams (data curation, ML modeling, biophysical validation, phenotype integration), receiving cross-training in wet-lab condensate biology, computational biophysics, and open data science practices, directly cultivating the data-savvy, interdisciplinary workforce central to NCEMS's mission while resolving a long-standing puzzle: how molecular-scale interactions generate emergent, functionally consequential mesoscale organization in cells.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (viscosity, selective permeability, reaction enhancement) arise from ensembles of weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, and RNA. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at multiple scales—proteomic composition (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS), sequence/disorder features (DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt), high-throughput in vitro phase diagrams, super-resolution and live-cell imaging (Cell Image Library, IDR/BioImage Archive), disease variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC), and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas)—these resources remain siloed within disciplinary boundaries (biophysics, structural biology, cell imaging, genetics, computational biology). No integrated framework currently links molecular-grammar features of condensate-forming proteins to their higher-order mesoscale material properties and ultimate cellular/phenotypic consequences, including disease-associated dysregulation.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and analytical framework: the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA). Our central scientific question is: What sequence-encoded and network-level features predict the emergent material and functional properties of condensates across scales, and how do disease-associated mutations perturb this sequence-to-phenotype mapping? We will pursue three synthesis aims: (1) Integrate sequence/disorder databases with biophysical phase-behavior datasets to derive quantitative 'condensate grammars'—stoichiometric and compositional rules linking IDR patterning, charge blockiness, and multivalency to phase diagram parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity); (2) Cross-reference these molecular grammars with public imaging datasets to test whether in vitro biophysical predictors explain observed in-cell condensate morphology, dynamics, and localization across cell types; (3) Map disease-associated variants (ALS, FTD, cancer) onto condensate-forming proteins to determine whether mutations systematically shift emergent mesoscale properties in ways that correlate with pathological cellular phenotypes from public multi-omic disease datasets.

This project is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics/phase-separation theory, machine learning on heterogeneous imaging/sequence data, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics, plus harmonization of incompatible data formats and scales across at least six major public repositories. NCEMS support will fund a coordinated data harmonization pipeline, shared computational infrastructure, and recurring cross-disciplinary working sessions to reconcile conflicting metrics of 'phase separation propensity' across source databases. All harmonized datasets, predictive models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with FAIR metadata standards, accompanied by interactive tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, co-developing cross-training modules in biophysics, imaging analytics, and genomics, and co-authoring resulting publications and open-source software—directly cultivating a new generation of data-savvy researchers equipped to study emergence phenomena at the mesoscale.
