[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (viscosity, selective permeability, reaction enhancement) arise from ensembles of weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, and RNA. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at multiple scales—proteomic composition (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS), sequence/disorder features (DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt), high-throughput in vitro phase diagrams, super-resolution and live-cell imaging (Cell Image Library, IDR/BioImage Archive), disease variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC), and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas)—these resources remain siloed within disciplinary boundaries (biophysics, structural biology, cell imaging, genetics, computational biology). No integrated framework currently links molecular-grammar features of condensate-forming proteins to their higher-order mesoscale material properties and ultimate cellular/phenotypic consequences, including disease-associated dysregulation.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and analytical framework: the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA). Our central scientific question is: What sequence-encoded and network-level features predict the emergent material and functional properties of condensates across scales, and how do disease-associated mutations perturb this sequence-to-phenotype mapping? We will pursue three synthesis aims: (1) Integrate sequence/disorder databases with biophysical phase-behavior datasets to derive quantitative 'condensate grammars'—stoichiometric and compositional rules linking IDR patterning, charge blockiness, and multivalency to phase diagram parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity); (2) Cross-reference these molecular grammars with public imaging datasets to test whether in vitro biophysical predictors explain observed in-cell condensate morphology, dynamics, and localization across cell types; (3) Map disease-associated variants (ALS, FTD, cancer) onto condensate-forming proteins to determine whether mutations systematically shift emergent mesoscale properties in ways that correlate with pathological cellular phenotypes from public multi-omic disease datasets.

This project is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics/phase-separation theory, machine learning on heterogeneous imaging/sequence data, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics, plus harmonization of incompatible data formats and scales across at least six major public repositories. NCEMS support will fund a coordinated data harmonization pipeline, shared computational infrastructure, and recurring cross-disciplinary working sessions to reconcile conflicting metrics of 'phase separation propensity' across source databases. All harmonized datasets, predictive models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with FAIR metadata standards, accompanied by interactive tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, co-developing cross-training modules in biophysics, imaging analytics, and genomics, and co-authoring resulting publications and open-source software—directly cultivating a new generation of data-savvy researchers equipped to study emergence phenomena at the mesoscale.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are among the clearest examples of mesoscale emergence in cell biology: macroscopic material properties—viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability, and catalytic enhancement—arise from ensembles of weak, multivalent, and often transient interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, and nucleic acids. Over the past decade, condensates have been implicated in transcriptional regulation, stress response, RNA metabolism, and signaling, while their dysregulation is increasingly linked to neurodegenerative disease (ALS, FTD), cancer, and viral infection. Yet a fundamental gap persists: we lack a predictive, quantitative 'grammar' that connects primary sequence features of condensate-forming proteins to the emergent mesoscale properties of the assemblies they form, and further, to the cellular and organismal phenotypes that result when this grammar is perturbed by disease mutations.

The scientific community has generated an extraordinary, but fragmented, public data landscape relevant to this problem. Sequence and disorder databases (DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt) catalog IDR boundaries, charge patterning, and predicted disorder propensity for thousands of proteins. Condensate-specific repositories (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro) aggregate experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and, in many cases, quantitative phase-behavior parameters such as saturation concentration and droplet viscosity. Imaging repositories (Cell Image Library, BioImage Archive, IDR) house super-resolution and live-cell microscopy data documenting condensate morphology, dynamics, and subcellular localization across diverse cell types and stimuli. Clinical and variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC, gnomAD) catalog disease-associated mutations in condensate-forming proteins, while large-scale atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas) provide single-cell expression context. Each of these resources, taken alone, illuminates only one scale of the emergence problem—sequence, biophysics, cell biology, or pathology—and each employs incompatible metrics, ontologies, and quality standards. No existing framework integrates them into a single analytical pipeline capable of testing whether sequence-encoded molecular grammar predicts mesoscale material behavior, and whether that behavior in turn predicts cellular and disease phenotypes.

This gap represents precisely the kind of fundamental, cross-scale question that motivates NCEMS's mission. Condensates sit squarely at the mesoscale boundary between biomolecules and organelles, and their study requires synthesis across composition (multivalent interaction networks), space (subcellular localization and morphology), time (dynamics and aging of condensates), and phenotype (cellular and disease outcomes). Addressing this question is not merely of academic interest: a validated sequence-to-phenotype mapping would enable prediction of pathogenicity for novel variants in condensate-forming proteins, rational design of condensate-modulating therapeutics, and a generalizable framework for studying emergence in other mesoscale biological systems. Critically, no single laboratory possesses the combined expertise in polymer physics, structural bioinformatics, quantitative imaging analytics, and clinical genomics, nor the resources to harmonize six or more large, heterogeneous public repositories, that this synthesis demands. This proposal directly answers NCEMS's call for community-scale synthesis of existing data to resolve a long-standing, cross-disciplinary puzzle in molecular and cellular bioscience.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Central Question: What sequence-encoded and network-level features predict the emergent material and functional properties of biomolecular condensates across scales, and how do disease-associated mutations perturb this sequence-to-phenotype mapping?

This overarching question is decomposed into three tractable, hypothesis-driven sub-questions, each corresponding to a synthesis aim.

Sub-question 1 (Molecular Grammar): Can quantitative rules linking IDR sequence features—charge patterning/blockiness, aromatic residue spacing, multivalency of short linear motifs, and predicted disorder content—be derived that predict in vitro phase-behavior parameters (saturation concentration, dense-phase viscosity, and Flory-Huggins-type interaction parameters) across proteins cataloged in PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, and PhaSePro? Hypothesis 1: Condensate-forming proteins exhibit statistically distinct, quantifiable sequence 'grammars' (e.g., patterned charge blocks combined with periodic aromatic 'stickers') that explain a significant proportion of variance in reported phase-separation propensity and material properties, independent of protein family, and these grammars generalize across independently curated databases despite differing experimental assays.

Sub-question 2 (Molecular-to-Cellular Bridge): Do in vitro biophysical predictors derived in Aim 1 explain condensate morphology, number, size, dynamics (recovery after photobleaching, fusion behavior), and subcellular localization as observed in public live-cell and super-resolution imaging datasets across diverse cell types and stress conditions? Hypothesis 2: Proteins predicted to have low saturation concentration and high predicted viscosity in vitro will form fewer, larger, and less dynamic condensates in cells, but this relationship will be modulated systematically by cellular context (e.g., RNA concentration, crowding, partner protein co-expression) recoverable from paired transcriptomic/proteomic data, indicating that mesoscale emergence in cells is a joint function of intrinsic sequence grammar and extrinsic cellular environment.

Sub-question 3 (Phenotype-to-Disease Bridge): Do disease-associated mutations (ALS/FTD-linked variants in FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1; cancer-associated variants in condensate-forming transcription factors and coactivators) systematically shift predicted mesoscale properties (e.g., increased aggregation propensity, aberrant hardening, altered client recruitment) in directions that correlate with pathological cellular phenotypes reported in multi-omic disease datasets? Hypothesis 3: Pathogenic variants disproportionately alter sequence features implicated in the Aim 1 grammar (particularly increasing aromatic stickiness or disrupting charge patterning that normally maintains liquid-like behavior), producing a predictable shift toward pathological solid-like or aggregation-prone states, and the magnitude of this shift correlates with disease severity or age-of-onset metrics where available.

Collectively, these hypotheses test whether emergence at the mesoscale is governed by generalizable, quantifiable rules that propagate predictably from sequence to material property to cellular phenotype to disease outcome—a multi-scale causal chain that no existing single-discipline study has been positioned to test. Confirmation, partial confirmation, or refutation of these hypotheses will each yield significant scientific insight: confirmation would establish a predictive framework applicable to uncharacterized proteins and variants; refutation or context-dependence would reveal the limits of sequence-based prediction and highlight the necessity of cellular context, motivating new synthesis and experimental directions. Both outcomes advance fundamental understanding of mesoscale emergence and directly serve NCEMS's mission of resolving long-standing puzzles through data synthesis.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will execute a three-aim synthesis pipeline, each building on harmonized data infrastructure developed collaboratively across partner labs.

Aim 1 – Deriving Condensate Grammars: We will assemble a unified protein-sequence dataset by cross-referencing PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, and PhaSePro with disorder and domain annotations from DisProt, MobiDB, and UniProt. A harmonization pipeline (built in Python/Snakemake for reproducibility) will resolve identifier mismatches, reconcile differing experimental definitions of 'phase separation propensity,' and compute standardized sequence features (charge patterning via kappa/Omega metrics, aromatic residue spacing, predicted multivalent motif counts using established IDR-analysis tools). These features will be regressed against reported phase-diagram parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity, critical temperature where available) using interpretable machine learning approaches (regularized regression, gradient-boosted trees with SHAP-based feature attribution) to preserve biophysical interpretability alongside predictive power. Cross-validation will be stratified by source database to explicitly test generalizability across independently generated datasets.

Aim 2 – Linking Grammar to Cellular Morphology: Using condensate-associated proteins from Aim 1, we will query imaging metadata from the BioImage Archive, IDR, and Cell Image Library, applying existing open-source image-analysis pipelines (e.g., CellProfiler, deep-learning segmentation models) to extract quantitative morphological and dynamic descriptors (droplet count, size distribution, circularity, FRAP recovery rates, fusion propensity) at scale. These descriptors will be statistically linked to Aim 1 grammar-derived predictions using mixed-effects models that incorporate cell type, stress condition, and expression level (drawn from Human Protein Atlas/Human Cell Atlas) as covariates, testing whether intrinsic sequence-based predictions retain explanatory power once cellular context is modeled.

Aim 3 – Mapping Disease Variants: Pathogenic and benign variants in condensate-forming proteins will be extracted from ClinVar, COSMIC, and gnomAD, mapped onto sequence positions relevant to the Aim 1 grammar, and scored for predicted shifts in phase-behavior parameters. These predicted shifts will be correlated with available clinical/phenotypic metadata (age-of-onset, disease severity classifications) and, where available, disease-relevant transcriptomic signatures.

Throughout, the Working Group will convene recurring (monthly virtual, semi-annual in-person) cross-disciplinary working sessions to resolve data-harmonization conflicts, validate biophysical interpretations against imaging and clinical expertise, and co-develop the integrated Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA) database and web-accessible query interface. A dedicated data-integration coordinator (postdoctoral scientist) will maintain version-controlled harmonization scripts and metadata schemas (following FAIR principles) shared via a common repository accessible to all partner labs, ensuring methodological consistency and reproducibility across the distributed team.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will produce four primary deliverables. First, the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA): an open, versioned, queryable database integrating sequence, biophysical, imaging, and disease-variant data for condensate-forming proteins, accompanied by harmonization pipelines reusable by the broader community. Second, a validated quantitative 'condensate grammar' model predicting phase-behavior parameters from sequence features, with documented performance and interpretability metrics. Third, an empirically grounded assessment of how well in vitro biophysical predictors generalize to in-cell condensate behavior across cell types, clarifying the role of cellular context in mesoscale emergence—a question of substantial current debate in the field. Fourth, a disease-variant scoring framework linking mutations to predicted mesoscale property shifts, offering a novel, testable resource for interpreting variants of uncertain significance in ALS/FTD and cancer genes.

Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing gap between biophysical theory of phase separation and cell-biological/clinical observation, providing the field's first cross-scale, multi-database validated framework for mesoscale emergence in condensates. It will generate testable predictions for future targeted experiments, thereby seeding new hypothesis-driven research beyond the synthesis effort itself. Methodologically, the harmonization pipelines and interpretable ML approaches developed here will serve as a template for integrating heterogeneous mesoscale datasets in other emergence contexts (e.g., cytoskeletal assemblies, membrane microdomains), directly advancing NCEMS's broader analytical mission. Practically, the CEA and its variant-scoring tool have translational relevance for prioritizing disease variants and guiding condensate-targeted therapeutic development. Finally, by embedding trainees across labs and disciplines, this project will produce a cohort of early-career scientists fluent in biophysics, imaging analytics, and genomics—directly building the data-savvy, cross-disciplinary workforce NCEMS aims to cultivate.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group is fully committed to open, team, and reproducible science consistent with NCEMS community standards. All harmonized datasets, derived features, trained models, and analysis code will be version-controlled in public GitHub repositories and archived with permanent DOIs via Zenodo at each major milestone, ensuring long-term accessibility independent of any single institution. Data harmonization scripts, feature-extraction pipelines, and statistical models will be containerized (Docker/Singularity) and orchestrated via Snakemake or Nextflow workflows to guarantee computational reproducibility across computing environments and by external users. All shared data products will adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles, with structured metadata schemas co-developed by the team and mapped to existing ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology, Sequence Ontology, Protein Ontology) to maximize interoperability with other synthesis efforts.

The Condensate Emergence Atlas itself will be released as a public, web-accessible resource with an open API, enabling programmatic querying by the broader research community, not merely static data download. Interactive tutorials and Jupyter notebooks will accompany each analytical pipeline, lowering barriers to reuse by researchers outside the original Working Group, including those at institutions with less computational infrastructure. All pre-registration of hypotheses, analysis plans, and interim findings will be posted to a project OSF (Open Science Framework) page prior to finalization, and preprints will be deposited on bioRxiv concurrent with journal submission. Authorship and contribution will follow CRediT taxonomy standards to transparently credit the diverse disciplinary contributions inherent to this synthesis effort. Regular internal data-audit checkpoints will verify that all harmonization decisions are documented and traceable, ensuring that any researcher can reconstruct the full analytical chain from raw public data to final published conclusions.

[Budget and Resources]
This Working Group requests NCEMS support for personnel, computational infrastructure, and collaborative convening costs over a two-year period. Personnel: one full-time postdoctoral Data Integration Coordinator (responsible for harmonization pipeline development, database maintenance, and cross-lab coordination) and partial graduate student/postdoc effort (approximately 25% FTE each) embedded across four to five partner labs to conduct aim-specific analyses and receive cross-training. Computational resources: cloud computing credits and storage allocation sufficient to host large-scale imaging data extraction, machine learning model training, and the public-facing CEA database/API infrastructure, along with software licensing for specialized image-analysis tools where necessary (preference given to open-source alternatives). Convening costs: support for semi-annual in-person working group meetings (essential for resolving complex cross-disciplinary data-harmonization conflicts and co-designing the integrated framework) and monthly virtual working sessions, including travel support prioritized for trainees and early-career participants to maximize training impact.

Additional requested resources include modest funds for data-archiving fees (Zenodo/institutional repository costs beyond free tiers), publication open-access fees to ensure all outputs are freely available, and support for developing and disseminating training materials (tutorials, workshops) at relevant scientific conferences to broaden community engagement with the CEA resource. Existing institutional computational infrastructure at partner labs (local GPU clusters for imaging analysis, existing database licenses) will be leveraged in-kind to reduce direct costs where possible. This budget reflects the minimum infrastructure necessary to accomplish a synthesis project that is explicitly beyond the scope of any individual lab's existing resources: sustained data harmonization across six-plus repositories, shared computational infrastructure for community-facing tool deployment, and dedicated coordination effort to maintain scientific and technical coherence across a geographically and disciplinarily distributed team.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective properties (viscosity, selective permeability, reaction enhancement) arise from ensembles of weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded domains, and RNA. Despite an explosion of public data describing condensates at multiple scales—proteomic composition (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS), sequence/disorder features (DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt), high-throughput in vitro phase diagrams, super-resolution and live-cell imaging (Cell Image Library, IDR/BioImage Archive), disease variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC), and single-cell transcriptomic/proteomic atlases (Human Protein Atlas, Human Cell Atlas)—these resources remain siloed within disciplinary boundaries (biophysics, structural biology, cell imaging, genetics, computational biology). No integrated framework currently links molecular-grammar features of condensate-forming proteins to their higher-order mesoscale material properties and ultimate cellular/phenotypic consequences, including disease-associated dysregulation.

This Working Group will assemble biophysicists, structural biologists, imaging scientists, computational biologists, and clinical genomicists to synthesize these disparate public datasets into a unified, queryable resource and analytical framework: the Condensate Emergence Atlas (CEA). Our central scientific question is: What sequence-encoded and network-level features predict the emergent material and functional properties of condensates across scales, and how do disease-associated mutations perturb this sequence-to-phenotype mapping? We will pursue three synthesis aims: (1) Integrate sequence/disorder databases with biophysical phase-behavior datasets to derive quantitative 'condensate grammars'—stoichiometric and compositional rules linking IDR patterning, charge blockiness, and multivalency to phase diagram parameters (saturation concentration, viscosity); (2) Cross-reference these molecular grammars with public imaging datasets to test whether in vitro biophysical predictors explain observed in-cell condensate morphology, dynamics, and localization across cell types; (3) Map disease-associated variants (ALS, FTD, cancer) onto condensate-forming proteins to determine whether mutations systematically shift emergent mesoscale properties in ways that correlate with pathological cellular phenotypes from public multi-omic disease datasets.

This project is infeasible for any single lab: it requires simultaneous expertise in polymer physics/phase-separation theory, machine learning on heterogeneous imaging/sequence data, structural bioinformatics, and clinical genetics, plus harmonization of incompatible data formats and scales across at least six major public repositories. NCEMS support will fund a coordinated data harmonization pipeline, shared computational infrastructure, and recurring cross-disciplinary working sessions to reconcile conflicting metrics of 'phase separation propensity' across source databases. All harmonized datasets, predictive models, and analysis code will be released as an open, versioned resource (via Zenodo/GitHub) with FAIR metadata standards, accompanied by interactive tutorials. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across partner labs, co-developing cross-training modules in biophysics, imaging analytics, and genomics, and co-authoring resulting publications and open-source software—directly cultivating a new generation of data-savvy researchers equipped to study emergence phenomena at the mesoscale.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: the collective behavior of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) gives rise to structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that are not predictable from any single molecular feature alone. Despite an explosion of publicly available data describing condensates at multiple scales—sequence-based IDR predictions (e.g., DisProt, MobiDB), condensate composition databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB), in vitro phase diagrams, cryo-electron tomography of native condensate architecture, live-cell imaging with FRAP and single-molecule tracking (Allen Cell Institute, JUMP Cell Painting), proteome-wide interactome maps (BioGRID, STRING), and disease-associated mutation catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC)—these resources remain fragmented across incompatible formats, model organisms, and measurement scales. No unified framework currently links molecular-scale ‘grammar’ (sequence composition, valency, PTM state) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences (transcriptional output, stress granule dynamics, disease phenotypes).

This Working Group will synthesize these disparate public datasets into an integrated, multiscale resource and predictive framework for condensate emergence. Specifically, we will: (1) harmonize sequence/structural features (charge patterning, aromatic stickers, IDR length, PTM sites) across thousands of condensate-forming proteins; (2) integrate in vitro biophysical phase-diagram data with in-cell imaging-derived material property proxies (droplet size distributions, FRAP recovery rates, coalescence kinetics) to build a cross-scale property atlas; (3) apply machine learning and polymer physics-informed models to identify molecular determinants that predict emergent mesoscale behavior across condensate types (stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P-bodies); and (4) test whether disease-associated mutations systematically perturb predicted material properties, linking molecular lesions to mesoscale dysfunction and cellular phenotype.

This project is inherently a community-scale synthesis effort: no single lab possesses simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural biology, live-cell imaging analytics, proteomics, and machine learning required to integrate these heterogeneous datasets meaningfully. The Working Group will unite biophysicists specializing in phase separation theory, structural biologists working with cryo-ET/EM datasets, cell biologists with quantitative imaging expertise, computational biologists skilled in ML and network analysis, and data scientists focused on ontology harmonization—drawn from institutions varying in size, geography, and research intensity. NCEMS support is essential to provide the computational infrastructure, data harmonization pipelines, and cross-disciplinary coordination needed to reconcile disparate data modalities (sequence, structure, dynamics, phenotype) under shared ontologies and metadata standards.

All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analytical workflows will be released as an open, reproducible resource (via FAIR-compliant repositories and containerized pipelines), enabling the broader community to query condensate emergence principles across new protein systems. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across subteams, receiving hands-on training in data harmonization, multiscale modeling, and interdisciplinary science communication. By revealing generalizable rules connecting molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale material properties, this synthesis will resolve a long-standing puzzle in cell biology—how simple molecular interactions robustly generate complex, functional mesoscale architectures—and establish predictive tools for understanding condensate dysregulation in disease.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged over the past decade as a fundamental organizing principle of the cell, mediating processes ranging from transcriptional regulation and RNA metabolism to stress response and signal transduction. These membraneless organelles form via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), driven by multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), folded oligomerization domains, nucleic acids, and post-translationally modified residues. Critically, condensates are archetypal mesoscale phenomena: their defining material properties—viscosity, surface tension, internal molecular exchange rates, and aging behavior—are emergent, arising from collective polymer physics rather than being reducible to any single biomolecule's properties. Understanding how molecular-level 'grammar' (sequence patterning, valency, PTM state, RNA content) dictates emergent mesoscale material behavior, and how that behavior in turn shapes cellular and organismal phenotypes, represents one of the most compelling open problems in molecular and cellular biology. This problem sits precisely at NCEMS's core scientific mission: elucidating emergent properties at the mesoscale and their influence on higher-order cellular outcomes. The field has produced an extraordinary wealth of public data spanning every relevant scale. Sequence-based resources (DisProt, MobiDB, CIDER) catalog IDR composition and predicted phase-separation propensity for thousands of proteins. Curated condensate databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro) compile experimentally validated condensate-forming proteins, their partners, and in vitro phase diagrams. Structural resources including cryo-electron tomography datasets reveal native condensate architecture at nanometer resolution. Quantitative live-cell imaging repositories (Allen Cell Institute, JUMP Cell Painting Consortium) provide FRAP recovery curves, single-molecule tracking trajectories, and droplet morphology metrics across thousands of conditions. Proteome-scale interactome maps (BioGRID, STRING, IntAct) delineate the multivalent protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks that underlie condensate composition. Finally, disease-mutation catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC) document how sequence lesions in condensate-forming proteins associate with neurodegenerative disease, cancer, and developmental disorders. Despite this abundance, these resources remain siloed: they use incompatible ontologies, span disparate model organisms and cell types, and capture fundamentally different observables (sequence, structure, dynamics, phenotype) without a shared framework for cross-referencing. Consequently, even though the field increasingly recognizes that condensate material properties are functionally consequential—altered viscosity and aging are implicated in ALS, FTD, and cancer—no systematic, quantitative map exists linking molecular grammar to mesoscale material behavior across condensate types. This gap persists not for lack of data but for lack of synthesis: reconciling sequence-level predictions with biophysical measurements and cellular imaging phenotypes requires simultaneous fluency in polymer physics, structural biology, quantitative imaging, and machine learning that no single laboratory possesses. Resolving this puzzle would transform our conceptual understanding of subcellular self-organization and provide the mechanistic foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting condensate dysregulation in disease, fulfilling NCEMS's mandate to catalyze community-scale synthesis addressing fundamental mesoscale emergence questions.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This Working Group is organized around one overarching question and four tractable sub-questions, each addressable through synthesis of existing public data rather than new experimentation. Overarching Question: What generalizable molecular grammar rules govern the emergence of mesoscale material properties in biomolecular condensates, and how do disruptions to this grammar propagate to cellular dysfunction and disease? Sub-Question 1 (Molecular Feature Harmonization): Can sequence-derived features—charge patterning (kappa, Omega), aromatic 'sticker' density, IDR length and disorder score, and annotated PTM sites—be harmonized across heterogeneous databases (DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS) into a unified feature space applicable to thousands of condensate-forming proteins spanning diverse organisms? We hypothesize that despite inconsistent annotation practices, a core set of physicochemical descriptors can be reliably extracted and normalized, revealing conserved sequence grammars shared across condensate classes. Sub-Question 2 (Cross-Scale Property Atlas): Can in vitro phase-diagram data (saturation concentration, critical temperature) be quantitatively integrated with in-cell imaging proxies (droplet size distributions, FRAP recovery half-times, coalescence kinetics) to construct a unified atlas of condensate material properties? We hypothesize that in vitro and in-cell material property proxies are correlated but systematically offset due to cellular crowding and active regulation, and that this offset itself is informative of in vivo regulatory mechanisms. Sub-Question 3 (Predictive Molecular-to-Mesoscale Models): Do polymer physics-informed machine learning models trained on harmonized sequence features and the cross-scale property atlas accurately predict emergent material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) across distinct condensate types, including stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, and P-bodies? We hypothesize that a shared set of molecular determinants—valency of stickers, spacer length and flexibility, and PTM-modulated charge patterning—will predict material properties across condensate classes better than condensate-specific models, reflecting a conserved biophysical logic underlying mesoscale emergence, while condensate-specific modulators (e.g., RNA scaffolds in stress granules, rRNA in nucleoli) will explain residual variance. Sub-Question 4 (Disease Mutation Perturbation): Do disease-associated mutations catalogued in ClinVar and COSMIC systematically and predictably perturb the molecular features that our models identify as material-property determinants, and do these perturbations correlate with reported cellular phenotypes? We hypothesize that pathogenic mutations in condensate-forming proteins disproportionately alter sticker valency or charge patterning in ways that predictably shift material properties toward pathological hardening (aberrant solidification) or destabilization, and that the magnitude of predicted property perturbation correlates with disease severity or age of onset where such clinical metadata exist. Collectively, these questions test the central hypothesis that mesoscale material properties of condensates are emergent yet predictable outcomes of quantifiable molecular grammar, and that this grammar is conserved sufficiently across condensate types and organisms to enable a generalizable, transferable predictive framework—directly addressing NCEMS's mission to resolve long-standing puzzles regarding emergence at the mesoscale through data synthesis rather than new experimentation.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will execute a four-phase synthesis pipeline over a two-year period, structured around monthly full-group meetings and biweekly subteam sprints. Phase 1: Data Acquisition and Ontology Harmonization (Months 1–6). We will systematically compile datasets from DisProt, MobiDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, PhaSePro, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, ClinVar, COSMIC, the Allen Cell Institute imaging repository, and JUMP Cell Painting. A dedicated ontology-harmonization subteam, led by our data science co-investigators, will develop a controlled vocabulary and metadata schema (extending existing MIAPPE/FAIR frameworks) to reconcile inconsistent protein identifiers, condensate-type labels, organism annotations, and measurement units. All raw and harmonized data will be version-controlled and deposited in a project data lake with full provenance tracking. Phase 2: Cross-Scale Feature and Property Extraction (Months 4–12). Sequence-based features (charge patterning parameters kappa/Omega, aromatic stickers, PTM sites, IDR length) will be computed using established tools (CIDER, localCIDER) applied uniformly across the harmonized protein set. In parallel, biophysical subteams will extract quantitative material-property proxies from in vitro phase diagrams (saturation concentration, critical temperature) and from in-cell imaging datasets (droplet size distributions via image segmentation pipelines, FRAP recovery kinetics via curve-fitting, coalescence rates via time-lapse tracking). Structural biologists will contribute cryo-ET-derived architectural metrics (internal density, mesh spacing) where available. All extracted properties will populate a relational cross-scale property atlas linking each protein/condensate entry to its molecular features and multiscale material-property measurements. Phase 3: Predictive Model Development (Months 10–18). Using the harmonized atlas, we will train polymer physics-informed machine learning models (e.g., graph neural networks incorporating stickers-and-spacers formalism, gradient-boosted models with physics-derived features) to predict mesoscale material properties from molecular grammar. Models will be validated using held-out condensate types and cross-organism generalization tests, with performance benchmarked against physics-based null models (e.g., Flory-Huggins predictions). Feature importance and interpretability analyses (SHAP values, ablation studies) will identify dominant molecular determinants across condensate classes. Phase 4: Disease Mutation Analysis (Months 16–24). Disease-associated mutations from ClinVar and COSMIC affecting condensate-forming proteins will be mapped onto harmonized sequence features, and predicted material-property shifts will be computed using the Phase 3 models. These predictions will be cross-referenced with available phenotypic annotations to test correlations between predicted biophysical perturbation and clinical severity. Throughout, statistical rigor will be ensured via pre-registered analysis plans, cross-validation with held-out data partitions, and sensitivity analyses accounting for database-specific biases (e.g., overrepresentation of well-studied proteins). Working Group coordination will leverage NCEMS computational infrastructure (shared cloud compute, containerized environments) and dedicated project management support to synchronize contributions across seven to nine geographically distributed labs with complementary expertise.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis effort will yield four principal deliverables: (1) a harmonized, FAIR-compliant multiscale database linking molecular sequence features, biophysical phase-diagram parameters, and in-cell material-property proxies for thousands of condensate-forming proteins; (2) validated, interpretable machine learning models predicting emergent mesoscale material properties from molecular grammar, generalizable across condensate types and organisms; (3) a mechanistic map connecting disease-associated mutations to predicted material-property perturbations, generating testable hypotheses for follow-up mechanistic studies; and (4) open-source, containerized analytical pipelines enabling the community to apply this framework to newly characterized proteins and condensates. Scientifically, this work will resolve a fundamental puzzle regarding how simple, quantifiable molecular interactions robustly generate complex, functional mesoscale architecture—directly advancing NCEMS's mission to understand emergent properties at the mesoscale. The predictive framework will provide the field with its first cross-condensate, cross-scale quantitative model of phase-separation-driven material behavior, shifting the field from qualitative, case-by-case characterization toward generalizable, predictive biophysics. Translationally, the disease-mutation analysis will generate prioritized candidate mechanisms linking specific mutations to condensate dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease and cancer, informing future therapeutic targeting of aberrant phase behavior. Broader impacts include establishing reusable data-harmonization standards and ontologies for the phase-separation community, likely adopted by future database curation efforts. The project will train an interdisciplinary cohort of graduate students and postdocs in data synthesis, multiscale modeling, and cross-disciplinary collaboration, cultivating a data-savvy workforce equipped to tackle future mesoscale emergence questions. Dissemination through peer-reviewed publications, preprints, conference presentations, and public seminars will maximize scientific and societal reach.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
This Working Group is committed to open science as a foundational operating principle, not an afterthought. All harmonized datasets—including unified feature tables, cross-scale property atlas entries, and mutation-perturbation predictions—will be deposited in FAIR-compliant public repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Dryad, and domain-specific archives such as the LLPS community databases) with persistent identifiers and comprehensive metadata documenting provenance, harmonization decisions, and version history. All code, including data harmonization scripts, feature-extraction pipelines, and machine learning model training and evaluation workflows, will be version-controlled in public GitHub repositories under permissive open-source licenses, with containerized environments (Docker/Singularity) ensuring computational reproducibility across platforms. Trained models will be archived with accompanying model cards detailing training data, performance metrics, known limitations, and intended use cases to prevent misuse or overinterpretation. We will adhere to community-endorsed reproducible science practices, including pre-registration of major analysis plans prior to model validation, transparent reporting of negative or null results, and explicit documentation of database-specific biases and limitations. Regular data and code releases will occur at defined milestones (Months 6, 12, 18, 24) rather than only at project completion, enabling ongoing community feedback and early reuse. The Working Group will designate a data-stewardship lead responsible for ensuring compliance with FAIR principles and NCEMS open-science policies throughout the project lifecycle. Analytical workflows will be documented using literate programming approaches (Jupyter/R Markdown notebooks) to maximize transparency and pedagogical value for future users, including trainees outside the immediate Working Group. Finally, all publications arising from this work will be deposited as open-access preprints prior to journal submission, and we will organize a capstone open workshop, coordinated through NCEMS, to disseminate the harmonized resource and train external researchers in its use, ensuring the synthesis products achieve maximal community reuse and long-term sustainability beyond the funding period.

[Budget and Resources]
This Working Group requests NCEMS support for a two-year project structured around personnel, computational infrastructure, and coordination costs essential for community-scale synthesis. Personnel costs constitute the primary budget component, supporting two full-time postdoctoral researchers (one with expertise in polymer physics/machine learning, one in imaging analytics/data harmonization) and partial graduate student support (four students at 25% effort across partner labs) to execute data harmonization, feature extraction, and model development tasks. Modest salary support (5–10% effort) is requested for each of the six to eight co-investigator faculty to enable sustained cross-disciplinary coordination, subteam leadership, and quality control across the harmonization and modeling phases. Computational resources include cloud-computing credits for large-scale image processing (droplet segmentation, FRAP curve-fitting across thousands of imaging datasets) and machine learning model training (graph neural network training requiring GPU resources), alongside data storage costs for the project's harmonized data lake, estimated based on the multi-terabyte scale of aggregated imaging and structural datasets. We request NCEMS-provided access to shared computational infrastructure and data harmonization pipeline templates where available, reducing redundant infrastructure development costs. Travel funds are requested to support two in-person Working Group summits (kickoff and mid-project), critical for establishing shared analytical standards and troubleshooting cross-disciplinary integration challenges that are difficult to resolve remotely, plus trainee travel to present synthesis outcomes at relevant conferences (e.g., Biophysical Society, ASCB). A modest allocation supports publication costs (open-access fees) and workshop logistics for the capstone dissemination event. Given the community-scale nature of this synthesis—requiring simultaneous integration of sequence, structural, imaging, and clinical mutation data by a distributed, multidisciplinary team—this budget reflects resource needs substantially beyond what any single laboratory's existing grant funding could support, justifying dedicated NCEMS Working Group investment in personnel, computation, and cross-institutional coordination infrastructure.

Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence: the collective behavior of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent domains, RNA, and post-translational modifications (PTMs) gives rise to structures with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) that are not predictable from any single molecular feature alone. Despite an explosion of publicly available data describing condensates at multiple scales—sequence-based IDR predictions (e.g., DisProt, MobiDB), condensate composition databases (PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB), in vitro phase diagrams, cryo-electron tomography of native condensate architecture, live-cell imaging with FRAP and single-molecule tracking (Allen Cell Institute, JUMP Cell Painting), proteome-wide interactome maps (BioGRID, STRING), and disease-associated mutation catalogs (ClinVar, COSMIC)—these resources remain fragmented across incompatible formats, model organisms, and measurement scales. No unified framework currently links molecular-scale ‘grammar’ (sequence composition, valency, PTM state) to emergent mesoscale material properties and their downstream cellular consequences (transcriptional output, stress granule dynamics, disease phenotypes).

This Working Group will synthesize these disparate public datasets into an integrated, multiscale resource and predictive framework for condensate emergence. Specifically, we will: (1) harmonize sequence/structural features (charge patterning, aromatic stickers, IDR length, PTM sites) across thousands of condensate-forming proteins; (2) integrate in vitro biophysical phase-diagram data with in-cell imaging-derived material property proxies (droplet size distributions, FRAP recovery rates, coalescence kinetics) to build a cross-scale property atlas; (3) apply machine learning and polymer physics-informed models to identify molecular determinants that predict emergent mesoscale behavior across condensate types (stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P-bodies); and (4) test whether disease-associated mutations systematically perturb predicted material properties, linking molecular lesions to mesoscale dysfunction and cellular phenotype.

This project is inherently a community-scale synthesis effort: no single lab possesses simultaneous expertise in polymer physics, structural biology, live-cell imaging analytics, proteomics, and machine learning required to integrate these heterogeneous datasets meaningfully. The Working Group will unite biophysicists specializing in phase separation theory, structural biologists working with cryo-ET/EM datasets, cell biologists with quantitative imaging expertise, computational biologists skilled in ML and network analysis, and data scientists focused on ontology harmonization—drawn from institutions varying in size, geography, and research intensity. NCEMS support is essential to provide the computational infrastructure, data harmonization pipelines, and cross-disciplinary coordination needed to reconcile disparate data modalities (sequence, structure, dynamics, phenotype) under shared ontologies and metadata standards.

All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analytical workflows will be released as an open, reproducible resource (via FAIR-compliant repositories and containerized pipelines), enabling the broader community to query condensate emergence principles across new protein systems. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded across subteams, receiving hands-on training in data harmonization, multiscale modeling, and interdisciplinary science communication. By revealing generalizable rules connecting molecular grammar to emergent mesoscale material properties, this synthesis will resolve a long-standing puzzle in cell biology—how simple molecular interactions robustly generate complex, functional mesoscale architectures—and establish predictive tools for understanding condensate dysregulation in disease.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—exemplify mesoscale emergence, arising from collective interactions among proteins and nucleic acids to produce organelle-like structures with distinct biochemical and mechanical properties. Despite an explosion of condensate-related data across genomics, proteomics, structural biology, and live-cell imaging, the field lacks a unified, quantitative framework linking molecular sequence features to network-level interactions and ultimately to cellular-scale phenotypes. Individual labs have generated fragmented insights—biophysicists characterize intrinsically disordered region (IDR) grammar in vitro, cell biologists document condensate dynamics via imaging, and systems biologists map protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks—but no systematic integration exists to explain why some proteins condense in some cellular contexts and not others, or how emergent condensate properties (e.g., material state, composition, responsiveness) scale with underlying molecular features and network topology.

This Working Group proposes to synthesize five previously siloed classes of public data: (1) sequence-based IDR and low-complexity domain predictions (e.g., from MobiDB, PONDR-derived datasets); (2) curated condensate/LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro) cataloguing experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and their in vitro conditions; (3) genome-scale PPI and co-expression networks (BioGRID, STRING, ProteomeHD); (4) quantitative single-cell imaging and localization atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas subcellular imaging, LLPSDB-linked microscopy) capturing condensate morphology, number, and dynamics; and (5) proteomic abundance and post-translational modification datasets (PhosphoSitePlus, PaxDb) that modulate condensation propensity in vivo. By harmonizing these disparate data types—spanning sequence, network, image, and abundance modalities—we will build predictive, mechanistic models of condensate emergence that no single dataset or disciplinary approach could achieve alone.

Our central hypothesis is that condensate emergence is governed by a combinatorial 'molecular grammar' operating simultaneously at three scales: intra-protein (IDR patterning, valency of interaction motifs), inter-protein (network connectivity, co-condensation partners), and cellular (local concentration, PTM state, compartment identity). We will use graph neural networks and multi-modal representation learning to integrate these layers, testing whether emergent condensate properties (size, number, material state, responsiveness to stress) can be predicted from lower-scale features, and identifying network motifs or sequence grammars that generalize across protein families and cell types. Validation will leverage held-out experimental datasets and cross-species comparisons (yeast, human, plant) to test universality of discovered rules.

This project requires collaboration among condensate biophysicists, network biologists, imaging data scientists, and machine learning experts—expertise no single lab possesses collectively—and NCEMS support for compute infrastructure, data harmonization workshops, and cross-database ontology alignment. The Working Group will include graduate students and postdocs in hands-on data integration, model-building, and reproducible workflow design, producing open-source pipelines, harmonized datasets, and a public condensate-emergence prediction resource. All code, integrated datasets, and models will be released under FAIR and open-science standards, providing a template for mesoscale emergence research broadly.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged over the past decade as a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence in cell biology—the process by which weak, multivalent interactions among proteins and nucleic acids give rise to organelle-like structures with properties (viscosity, surface tension, selective permeability, biochemical activity) that cannot be predicted from any single molecular component in isolation. These membraneless compartments, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), underlie critical cellular functions including stress response, transcriptional regulation, RNA metabolism, and signal transduction, and their dysregulation is implicated in neurodegenerative disease, cancer, and viral infection. Understanding how condensates emerge—why particular proteins condense under particular cellular conditions, and how their emergent material and functional properties scale from molecular features—represents one of the most compelling open questions in molecular and cellular bioscience, and a quintessential test case for the mesoscale emergence framework that motivates NCEMS.

Over the last decade, the field has generated an extraordinary wealth of public data addressing different facets of this problem, yet these data remain disciplinarily siloed. Structural and sequence biologists have annotated intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and low-complexity domains genome-wide, and in vitro biophysicists have characterized phase behavior, valency, and stickers-and-spacers grammar for hundreds of individual proteins, depositing results in specialized databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSePro). Independently, systems biologists have mapped genome-scale protein-protein interaction and co-expression networks (BioGRID, STRING, ProteomeHD) that capture higher-order connectivity but rarely intersect with condensate-specific annotations. Meanwhile, imaging-focused cell biologists have produced quantitative, proteome-wide subcellular localization atlases (OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas) documenting condensate morphology and dynamics at single-cell resolution, and proteomics groups have cataloged abundance and post-translational modification landscapes (PhosphoSitePlus, PaxDb) known to modulate condensation propensity in vivo. Each of these data classes captures a different scale of organization—molecular sequence, network topology, cellular phenotype, or biochemical state—but no existing framework integrates them to explain condensate emergence as a multi-scale phenomenon.

This fragmentation is not merely an inconvenience; it represents a fundamental barrier to scientific progress. Sequence-level 'molecular grammar' models developed in vitro cannot explain why the same protein condenses in one cell type or compartment but not another. Network-based approaches ignore the sequence-encoded biophysics that determine which interactions are condensation-competent. Imaging atlases document phenotypic diversity in condensate behavior without a mechanistic account of its molecular origins. Bridging these scales requires simultaneous access to, and computational integration of, all five data classes—a task far beyond the scope, expertise, or resources of any single laboratory, and one for which the necessary cross-database ontology alignment, harmonization infrastructure, and multi-modal modeling expertise has not previously been assembled. By synthesizing these public resources within a unified computational framework, this Working Group will address a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale biology and establish a generalizable template for studying emergence across scales of biological organization, directly advancing NCEMS's scientific mission to understand how new system-level properties arise from the composition, spatial, temporal, energetic, and informational organization of molecular constituents.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Central Research Question: Can the emergent, cellular-scale properties of biomolecular condensates be predicted and mechanistically explained by integrating molecular sequence features, protein interaction network topology, and in vivo biochemical state, using only existing public data? We decompose this overarching question into three tightly linked sub-questions, each paired with a testable hypothesis.

RQ1 (Intra-protein scale): What sequence-encoded features of IDRs and low-complexity domains determine a protein's intrinsic phase-separation propensity, and do these features generalize across protein families and species? H1: Condensation propensity is governed by a quantifiable, compositional and patterning-based 'sticker-spacer' grammar (e.g., density and spacing of aromatic/charged residues, sequence charge decoration, motif valency) that is conserved across eukaryotic proteomes and predictive of experimentally validated LLPS behavior independent of overall disorder content.

RQ2 (Inter-protein/network scale): How does a protein's position within genome-scale interaction and co-expression networks influence its participation in condensate formation, and do condensate-forming proteins occupy distinctive topological niches (e.g., hub status, community structure, multivalency of partners)? H2: Proteins that participate in condensates preferentially occupy highly connected, modular network positions enriched for co-condensing partners, and network-derived 'co-condensation motifs' can predict condensate membership even for proteins lacking canonical IDR signatures, reflecting emergent network-level determinants of phase behavior not captured by sequence alone.

RQ3 (Cellular/phenotypic scale): How do cellular context variables—local protein abundance, post-translational modification state, and subcellular compartment identity—modulate whether and how condensates form, and can these variables explain condition-specific and cell-type-specific condensate heterogeneity observed in imaging atlases? H3: Condensate emergence is a threshold-dependent, context-gated phenomenon in which sequence- and network-encoded propensity is necessary but not sufficient; PTM state and local concentration act as tunable 'switches' that determine whether latent phase-separation potential is realized in a given cellular context, and these switches are predictable from proteomic and phosphoproteomic data.

Integrative Hypothesis: We hypothesize that condensate emergence is best modeled not as a property of any single scale but as an emergent output of a multi-scale, combinatorial 'molecular grammar'—a joint function of intra-protein sequence features, inter-protein network context, and cellular biochemical state—such that predictive power for cellular-scale phenotypes (condensate size, number, material state/viscosity, and stress-responsiveness) increases significantly when data from all three scales are integrated compared to any single-scale model. Furthermore, we hypothesize that a subset of these multi-scale grammar rules will be evolutionarily conserved across yeast, human, and plant proteomes, reflecting a generalizable design principle of mesoscale emergence, while other rules will be lineage- or cell-type-specific, reflecting evolutionary tuning of condensate function.

These questions and hypotheses are specifically structured to require synthesis: none can be rigorously tested using a single existing database or within the expertise of a single discipline. Testing H1 requires biophysical and sequence-analytic expertise; H2 requires network biology and graph-theoretic methods; H3 requires proteomics and quantitative imaging analysis; and the Integrative Hypothesis requires machine learning expertise capable of multi-modal data fusion. Success will be measured by (a) statistically significant improvement in predictive accuracy for held-out condensate phenotypes when integrating multi-scale data versus single-scale baselines, and (b) identification of specific, mechanistically interpretable grammar rules validated across independent, cross-species datasets.

[Methods and Approach]
Phase 1: Data Acquisition, Curation, and Harmonization (Months 1-6). We will systematically acquire and harmonize five public data classes: (1) IDR/low-complexity annotations from MobiDB, PONDR-derived datasets, and DisProt; (2) experimentally validated LLPS protein data from PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and PhaSePro, including in vitro condition metadata; (3) PPI and co-expression networks from BioGRID, STRING, and ProteomeHD; (4) quantitative imaging data from OpenCell and Human Protein Atlas subcellular atlases; (5) abundance/PTM data from PaxDb and PhosphoSitePlus. A central challenge is identifier and ontology mismatch across databases; we will develop a unified ontology and cross-reference mapping pipeline anchored on UniProt accessions, with automated reconciliation scripts and manual curation for ambiguous cases, conducted through dedicated data harmonization workshops bringing together all Working Group members and NCEMS data science staff.

Phase 2: Feature Engineering and Exploratory Analysis (Months 4-10). For each protein, we will construct a multi-scale feature vector: (a) sequence-derived features (IDR length/fraction, charge patterning [kappa, SCD], aromatic residue density and spacing, motif counts); (b) network features (degree, betweenness, clustering coefficient, community membership, fraction of condensate-annotated neighbors); (c) cellular/biochemical features (abundance, PTM site count and type, compartment annotation). Exploratory statistical analyses (correlation, enrichment, dimensionality reduction) will characterize univariate and pairwise relationships between features and condensate phenotypes prior to integrative modeling.

Phase 3: Multi-Scale Model Development (Months 8-18). We will develop graph neural network (GNN) architectures in which protein interaction networks form the graph structure, node features encode sequence and biochemical properties, and the model is trained to predict condensate phenotypes (binary condensation status, material state classification, size/number metrics from imaging data) in a multi-task learning framework. We will complement GNNs with multi-modal representation learning (contrastive/fusion-based architectures) combining imaging-derived embeddings with sequence and network embeddings, benchmarked against single-scale baselines to directly test the Integrative Hypothesis.

Phase 4: Validation and Generalization Testing (Months 14-22). Models will be validated using held-out experimental data and cross-validation stratified by protein family and species to avoid leakage. Cross-species generalization will be tested by training on human/yeast data and evaluating on plant proteome data (and vice versa). Interpretability methods (attention analysis, SHAP values, subgraph extraction) will extract human-readable 'grammar rules' for mechanistic interpretation and future experimental hypothesis generation.

Phase 5: Synthesis, Dissemination, and Resource Building (Months 18-24). We will consolidate harmonized datasets, trained models, and analytical pipelines into an open-access, queryable condensate-emergence prediction resource, accompanied by reproducible, containerized, version-controlled workflows and manuscripts describing discovered grammar rules.

Working Group Structure: The team comprises condensate biophysicists (sequence grammar expertise), network biologists (graph-theoretic analysis), imaging data scientists (quantitative phenotyping), and machine learning experts (multi-modal integration), with graduate students/postdocs embedded across sites conducting hands-on integration work, supported by quarterly in-person/virtual workshops coordinated through NCEMS.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver: (1) a harmonized, cross-referenced multi-scale dataset integrating sequence, network, imaging, and proteomic data for thousands of proteins across human, yeast, and plant proteomes—an enduring, reusable community resource; (2) validated, interpretable predictive models establishing quantitative, mechanistically grounded rules for condensate emergence, benchmarked against single-scale approaches and tested for cross-species generalization; (3) open-source software pipelines for data harmonization and multi-modal graph-based modeling, generalizable to other mesoscale emergence questions beyond condensates; (4) peer-reviewed publications reporting discovered grammar rules, methodological innovations, and benchmark comparisons; (5) a public, queryable web resource enabling researchers to obtain predicted condensation behavior and mechanistic annotations for any protein of interest; and (6) trained graduate students and postdocs equipped with transdisciplinary skills in data synthesis, network science, and machine learning. Scientifically, this work will resolve a long-standing puzzle regarding context-dependent condensate formation, providing the field's first quantitative, multi-scale account of why condensation is realized in some cellular contexts and not others. Methodologically, it establishes a reusable synthesis framework—spanning sequence, network, image, and abundance data—that can be adapted to other mesoscale emergence phenomena central to NCEMS's mission. Practically, the predictive models and resource will guide more efficient, hypothesis-driven experimental design, reducing costly trial-and-error in condensate biology and informing mechanistic understanding of condensate-linked diseases such as neurodegeneration and cancer. By assembling biophysicists, network biologists, imaging scientists, and machine learning experts around a shared, previously intractable problem, this project exemplifies the transdisciplinary, data-synthesis approach NCEMS is uniquely positioned to catalyze.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All data harmonization scripts, feature engineering pipelines, trained models, and analysis code will be released publicly on GitHub under a permissive open-source license (MIT/Apache 2.0), with full version control and containerization (Docker/Singularity) to ensure computational reproducibility. Harmonized, cross-referenced datasets will be deposited in community repositories (Zenodo/Dryad) with persistent DOIs, adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles and using stable identifiers (UniProt accessions) to enable long-term interoperability with source databases. Analysis workflows will be implemented in reproducible pipeline frameworks (e.g., Snakemake/Nextflow) with documented parameters and environment specifications. We will pre-register core hypotheses and analysis plans prior to model training to distinguish confirmatory from exploratory findings, and we will follow emerging community standards for reporting AI/ML models in biology (e.g., TRIPOD-AI-inspired reporting) to ensure transparency regarding training data, validation splits, and performance metrics. Preprints will be posted on bioRxiv concurrent with journal submission to accelerate community access. Prior to public release, datasets, code, and models will undergo internal reproducibility review by a designated Working Group member and, where applicable, NCEMS reproducibility support staff, verifying that pipelines execute correctly from raw public inputs to reported results. We will develop and openly host tutorial materials (annotated Jupyter notebooks, workflow documentation) to onboard trainees and the broader community into multi-scale data synthesis methods, consistent with NCEMS's mandate to train a data-savvy workforce. Working Group meetings, interim results, and workshop materials will be shared through NCEMS community channels to maximize transparency, enable community feedback, and model team-science best practices throughout the project lifecycle.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed budget supports a lean, focused Working Group over a 24-month period. Personnel costs include partial salary support for two postdoctoral researchers (one focused on network/graph modeling, one on multi-modal machine learning integration) and two graduate students embedded at partner institutions to conduct hands-on data harmonization and model development, providing direct hands-on training. Partial effort (5-10% academic-year equivalent) is requested for four co-PIs spanning condensate biophysics, network biology, imaging data science, and machine learning, reflecting the genuinely cross-disciplinary nature of the work. Computational resources include cloud/HPC allocation for training graph neural network and multi-modal models on large-scale interaction and imaging-derived datasets, along with data storage for harmonized multi-terabyte imaging and proteomic datasets; we request NCEMS-supported compute infrastructure and data science staff time to assist with cross-database ontology alignment, a task requiring specialized informatics expertise beyond the Working Group's core disciplinary training. Two in-person data harmonization and model-building workshops are budgeted (hosting/travel for ~10 participants each), supplemented by regular virtual working sessions, to ensure tight integration across geographically distributed team members. Additional funds support publication costs (open-access fees), web hosting and maintenance for the public prediction resource, and dissemination travel to present results at relevant scientific conferences. We request NCEMS support specifically for: (1) compute infrastructure beyond individual lab capacity; (2) data science/ontology alignment personnel time; (3) workshop coordination and logistics; and (4) reproducibility review services—resources and expertise that collectively exceed what any single lab or existing collaboration could provide, justifying the need for NCEMS Working Group support.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of proteins and nucleic acids give rise to new functional compartments with properties absent from their individual components. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets across biophysics, structural biology, proteomics, and cell imaging, no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features (sequence composition, disorder, post-translational modifications, multivalent interaction motifs) predict emergent mesoscale properties (condensate material state, size, dynamics, composition) and how these in turn shape cellular and organismal phenotypes. This gap persists because the relevant data are fragmented across incompatible repositories—biophysical LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), intrinsic disorder predictors (MobiDB, DisProt), structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB), interactome and proximity-labeling datasets (BioPlex, OpenCell, BioID studies), single-cell and super-resolution imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Cell Image Library), and disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC)—each curated by distinct research communities with disparate ontologies and quality standards. Synthesizing these resources into a coherent, queryable framework is beyond the scope of any single laboratory and requires sustained collaboration among biophysicists, structural biologists, cell biologists, computational scientists, and clinical genomicists.

This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team to build an integrated, open-access Mesoscale Condensate Atlas that links molecular sequence/structural features to emergent biophysical properties and downstream cellular outcomes. We will pursue three synthesis aims: (1) Harmonize existing LLPS, disorder, PTM, and interaction datasets into a standardized, machine-readable ontology, enabling systematic cross-referencing of condensate-forming proteins with their sequence-encoded valency, stickers-and-spacers architecture, and structural context. (2) Develop and validate machine learning and biophysical polymer models trained on this harmonized dataset to predict emergent condensate properties (formation propensity, viscosity, multiphase organization) directly from primary sequence and structural features, benchmarking against published in vitro and in-cell phase diagrams. (3) Connect predicted mesoscale properties to higher-order cellular phenotypes by integrating single-cell transcriptomic, proteomic, and imaging datasets, testing whether condensate material properties predicted from sequence correlate with transcriptional output, stress granule dynamics, or disease-associated mutation burden across public disease-variant repositories.

This effort satisfies NCEMS's synthesis mandate: it uses exclusively existing public data, requires integration across fundamentally distinct data modalities and expert communities, and promises insights—a predictive, generalizable grammar linking molecular sequence to emergent mesoscale behavior—unattainable by any single lab. The working group will include investigators from biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, and clinical genetics across multiple institutions and career stages, with explicit mechanisms for including early-career and underrepresented researchers. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analytical pipelines will be released as open, versioned, reproducible resources (via GitHub, Zenodo, and community platforms), accompanied by tutorials and hackathons that train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data synthesis, machine learning, and biophysical modeling—directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to build while addressing a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.
