[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless assemblies formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represent a paradigmatic case of mesoscale emergence, where collective behaviors of proteins and nucleic acids give rise to new functional compartments with properties absent from their individual components. Despite an explosion of condensate-related datasets across biophysics, structural biology, proteomics, and cell imaging, no unified framework exists to explain how molecular-scale features (sequence composition, disorder, post-translational modifications, multivalent interaction motifs) predict emergent mesoscale properties (condensate material state, size, dynamics, composition) and how these in turn shape cellular and organismal phenotypes. This gap persists because the relevant data are fragmented across incompatible repositories—biophysical LLPS databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), intrinsic disorder predictors (MobiDB, DisProt), structural resources (PDB, AlphaFold DB), interactome and proximity-labeling datasets (BioPlex, OpenCell, BioID studies), single-cell and super-resolution imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Cell Image Library), and disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC)—each curated by distinct research communities with disparate ontologies and quality standards. Synthesizing these resources into a coherent, queryable framework is beyond the scope of any single laboratory and requires sustained collaboration among biophysicists, structural biologists, cell biologists, computational scientists, and clinical genomicists.

This Working Group will assemble a transdisciplinary team to build an integrated, open-access Mesoscale Condensate Atlas that links molecular sequence/structural features to emergent biophysical properties and downstream cellular outcomes. We will pursue three synthesis aims: (1) Harmonize existing LLPS, disorder, PTM, and interaction datasets into a standardized, machine-readable ontology, enabling systematic cross-referencing of condensate-forming proteins with their sequence-encoded valency, stickers-and-spacers architecture, and structural context. (2) Develop and validate machine learning and biophysical polymer models trained on this harmonized dataset to predict emergent condensate properties (formation propensity, viscosity, multiphase organization) directly from primary sequence and structural features, benchmarking against published in vitro and in-cell phase diagrams. (3) Connect predicted mesoscale properties to higher-order cellular phenotypes by integrating single-cell transcriptomic, proteomic, and imaging datasets, testing whether condensate material properties predicted from sequence correlate with transcriptional output, stress granule dynamics, or disease-associated mutation burden across public disease-variant repositories.

This effort satisfies NCEMS's synthesis mandate: it uses exclusively existing public data, requires integration across fundamentally distinct data modalities and expert communities, and promises insights—a predictive, generalizable grammar linking molecular sequence to emergent mesoscale behavior—unattainable by any single lab. The working group will include investigators from biophysics, structural biology, computational biology, and clinical genetics across multiple institutions and career stages, with explicit mechanisms for including early-career and underrepresented researchers. All harmonized datasets, trained models, and analytical pipelines will be released as open, versioned, reproducible resources (via GitHub, Zenodo, and community platforms), accompanied by tutorials and hackathons that train graduate students and postdocs in cross-disciplinary data synthesis, machine learning, and biophysical modeling—directly cultivating the data-savvy workforce NCEMS aims to build while addressing a long-standing puzzle in mesoscale emergence.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) have emerged as a fundamental organizing principle of the cell, compartmentalizing biochemistry without membranes and driving processes ranging from transcriptional regulation and stress response to RNA metabolism and signal transduction. Condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: individual proteins and nucleic acids, none of which possess phase-separation capacity in isolation in most cases, collectively give rise to a new physical state—a dense liquid, gel, or solid phase—with material properties (viscosity, surface tension, exchange dynamics) and functional consequences (concentrating enzymes and substrates, sequestering toxic species, buffering fluctuations) that cannot be predicted by summing molecular parts. Understanding how sequence-encoded molecular grammar—patterns of aromatic 'stickers', charged blocks, disordered 'spacers', multivalent binding motifs, and post-translational modifications—dictates emergent mesoscale behavior is one of the central unresolved questions in modern cell biology, with direct relevance to neurodegenerative disease, cancer, and viral replication, where condensate dysregulation is increasingly implicated. Over the past decade, the field has generated an extraordinary wealth of public data addressing pieces of this puzzle. Biophysical databases such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS catalog experimentally validated phase-separating proteins and their solution behaviors. Intrinsic disorder resources (MobiDB, DisProt) and structural repositories (PDB, AlphaFold DB) provide sequence-to-structure mappings essential for identifying stickers-and-spacers architectures. Interactome and proximity-labeling datasets (BioPlex, OpenCell, BioID) reveal the compositional networks that define condensate identity in cells, while super-resolution and single-cell imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Cell Image Library) capture condensate morphology, dynamics, and subcellular localization at scale. Disease-variant databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) link condensate-forming proteins to pathogenic mutations, many of which cluster in disordered, phase-separation-prone regions. Despite this abundance, no synthesis has integrated these disparate data modalities into a unified, queryable resource capable of testing sequence-to-emergence hypotheses across scales. Each data type is curated by a distinct scientific community using incompatible ontologies, quality metrics, and file formats, and the inferential leap from molecular sequence feature to emergent mesoscale property to cellular phenotype requires biophysical, computational, and cell-biological expertise that rarely coexists within a single laboratory. This fragmentation is precisely the kind of long-standing puzzle NCEMS is positioned to solve: the underlying data already exist in sufficient quantity and quality to support rigorous cross-scale inference, but the synthesis task—harmonizing ontologies, building shared computational infrastructure, and validating predictive models against independent phenotypic data—demands sustained, well-resourced, multidisciplinary collaboration. By resolving this gap, our Working Group will establish a generalizable, mechanistic understanding of how molecular-scale information gives rise to mesoscale material states and, in turn, to cellular and disease phenotypes—directly advancing NCEMS's scientific vision of emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences and creating a durable community resource for the broader condensate biology field.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our Working Group is organized around three interlocking research questions that map directly onto the molecular-to-mesoscale-to-cellular hierarchy central to NCEMS's scientific vision. Research Question 1 (Molecular Grammar): Can sequence-encoded features—amino acid composition, disorder propensity, valency of stickers, spacer chemistry, and post-translational modification sites—be harmonized across independently curated databases into a unified feature space that reliably distinguishes condensate-forming from non-condensate-forming proteins? We hypothesize that a composite, cross-database feature representation will substantially outperform any single existing predictor because current tools are each trained on partial, non-overlapping subsets of validated condensate proteins and fail to capture combinatorial sticker-spacer interactions that only become apparent when biophysical, structural, and proteomic evidence are jointly considered. Research Question 2 (Sequence-to-Emergence Prediction): Do quantitative mesoscale properties of condensates—phase boundary position, material state (liquid, gel, solid), internal viscosity, and propensity for multiphase (core-shell) organization—follow a predictable, generalizable relationship with underlying sequence and structural features, and can this relationship be captured by biophysically informed machine learning models trained on harmonized data? We hypothesize that stickers-and-spacers polymer theory, when parameterized with empirically harmonized valency and patterning metrics rather than idealized sequences, will yield models that generalize across protein families and outperform purely data-driven black-box predictors, revealing conserved biophysical rules that recur across otherwise unrelated condensate systems (e.g., stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs). Research Question 3 (Mesoscale-to-Phenotype Linkage): Do sequence-predicted mesoscale material properties correlate with higher-order cellular and organismal outcomes, including transcriptional output at condensate-associated loci, stress granule dynamics under proteostatic stress, and the mutational burden of disease-associated variants in phase-separating domains? We hypothesize that proteins predicted to form more viscous or solid-like condensates will show enrichment for disease-associated missense mutations within their sticker regions, consistent with the hypothesis that aberrant hardening of condensates is a recurrent pathogenic mechanism in neurodegeneration and cancer, and that this relationship will be detectable only when biophysical predictions are integrated with population-scale variant data and single-cell phenotypic readouts. Collectively, these questions test the overarching hypothesis of the Working Group: that a generalizable 'sequence-to-emergence grammar' exists, linking molecular composition to emergent mesoscale material properties and thereby to cellular phenotype and disease risk, and that this grammar is only discoverable through synthesis of currently siloed public datasets rather than through any single experimental or computational study. Each research question is explicitly designed to require cross-disciplinary synthesis: Question 1 demands biophysical and bioinformatic expertise to reconcile database ontologies; Question 2 requires polymer physicists and machine learning scientists working alongside structural biologists to ensure model interpretability; and Question 3 requires cell biologists and clinical genomicists to validate computational predictions against orthogonal phenotypic and disease data. This structure ensures that the Working Group's activities are not merely additive but generate emergent insight—an understanding of condensate biology unattainable from any single data modality or disciplinary perspective alone, directly fulfilling NCEMS's mandate to address fundamental emergence phenomena through community-scale data synthesis.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will execute a three-year, three-aim synthesis pipeline built entirely on publicly available data, structured to maximize cross-disciplinary integration at each stage. Aim 1 (Data Harmonization, Months 1–12): We will systematically extract records from PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, MobiDB, DisProt, PDB, AlphaFold DB, BioPlex, OpenCell, and relevant BioID studies, mapping each to a common protein identifier scheme (UniProt-anchored) and constructing a unified ontology for condensate-relevant features (valency counts, disorder scores, PTM annotations, structural confidence metrics). We will adapt and extend existing bio-ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology, Protein Ontology) rather than building de novo, ensuring interoperability with community standards. A dedicated data curation subgroup, including a research data scientist and domain-expert postdocs, will implement automated ETL (extract-transform-load) pipelines in Python/Snakemake, with manual curation checkpoints for conflicting annotations, and will document all harmonization decisions in a transparent, versioned data dictionary. Aim 2 (Predictive Modeling, Months 6–24): Using the harmonized dataset, we will develop two complementary modeling approaches: (a) biophysically grounded stickers-and-spacers polymer models parameterized directly from empirical sequence-patterning metrics, implemented via established coarse-grained simulation frameworks (e.g., HOOMD-blue, LAMMPS with existing condensate-tuned force fields), and (b) supervised machine learning models (gradient-boosted trees and sequence-based deep learning architectures, e.g., transformer embeddings from ESM or similar public protein language models) trained to predict phase behavior, viscosity, and multiphase organization from harmonized features. Model performance will be benchmarked via held-out cross-validation against independently published in vitro and in-cell phase diagrams, with explicit interpretability analyses (SHAP values, learned attention weights) to extract generalizable sequence rules rather than opaque predictions. Aim 3 (Phenotype Integration, Months 18–36): We will link Aim 2 model outputs to single-cell transcriptomic (e.g., Human Protein Atlas single-cell data), proteomic, and super-resolution imaging datasets (Cell Image Library) to test correlations between predicted material properties and transcriptional/phenotypic readouts. In parallel, we will cross-reference predicted sticker regions with ClinVar and COSMIC variant data to quantify disease-mutation enrichment within predicted phase-separation-critical residues, using statistical enrichment tests (Fisher's exact, permutation-based null models controlling for gene length and mutation rate background). Throughout, the Working Group will convene via quarterly in-person/hybrid workshops and monthly virtual subgroup meetings, with shared computational infrastructure (cloud-based JupyterHub, GitHub organization) enabling real-time collaborative analysis across institutions. An external advisory panel of condensate biology, biophysics, and clinical genetics experts will review progress at 12 and 24 months to ensure scientific rigor and course-correct as needed. All statistical analyses will follow pre-registered analysis plans deposited on OSF prior to phenotype-correlation testing in Aim 3, minimizing confirmation bias in this exploratory-yet-hypothesis-driven synthesis effort.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver four concrete outcomes. First, the Mesoscale Condensate Atlas: a harmonized, versioned, publicly queryable database integrating sequence, structural, interactome, imaging, and disease-variant data for all known and candidate condensate-forming proteins, released with a stable API and community governance plan for long-term maintenance. Second, validated predictive models—both biophysical polymer models and machine learning classifiers—capable of predicting condensate formation propensity and material state directly from primary sequence, benchmarked openly against existing tools and released as reusable software packages. Third, a set of peer-reviewed publications establishing whether a generalizable sequence-to-emergence grammar exists, including quantitative evidence linking predicted mesoscale properties to cellular phenotypes and disease-mutation enrichment, directly resolving a long-standing conceptual gap in condensate biology. Fourth, a trained cohort of graduate students and postdocs fluent in cross-disciplinary data synthesis, biophysical modeling, and machine learning, prepared to extend this framework to new condensate systems and disease contexts. Scientifically, this work will reframe condensate biology around a predictive, mechanistic framework rather than case-by-case empirical characterization, with immediate applications to identifying disease-relevant condensate-hardening mutations and prioritizing therapeutic targets in neurodegeneration and cancer. Methodologically, the harmonization ontology and ETL pipelines developed here will serve as a template for future mesoscale synthesis efforts across other emergent cellular systems, directly supporting NCEMS's broader mission. Community-wide, the open Atlas and associated tools will lower barriers to entry for smaller labs and researchers from underrepresented institutions to engage in condensate research without requiring specialized biophysical infrastructure, broadening participation in this rapidly growing field. By demonstrating that rigorous, hypothesis-driven synthesis of fragmented public data can resolve a fundamental emergence question beyond the reach of any single laboratory, this project exemplifies the transformative potential of the community-scale synthesis paradigm NCEMS was created to catalyze.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group commits fully to open, team, and reproducible science practices consistent with NCEMS policy and broader community standards (e.g., FAIR data principles, TOP Guidelines). All harmonized datasets produced in Aim 1 will be deposited in versioned form on Zenodo with persistent DOIs, accompanied by a comprehensive data dictionary documenting every harmonization and curation decision, enabling full provenance tracing back to original source databases. All code—ETL pipelines, polymer simulation configurations, machine learning training scripts, and statistical analysis notebooks—will be maintained in a public GitHub organization under permissive open-source licensing (MIT/BSD), with continuous integration testing to ensure long-term functionality, and mirrored to Zenodo at each major release for citable, immutable snapshots. Analysis workflows will be containerized (Docker/Singularity) and orchestrated via Snakemake or Nextflow to guarantee computational reproducibility across computing environments. Following community-endorsed practices, we will pre-register statistical analysis plans for hypothesis-testing components (Aim 3 phenotype correlations) on OSF prior to execution, clearly distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory analyses. All manuscripts will be posted as preprints (bioRxiv) prior to journal submission, and we will pursue publication in venues supporting open peer review where feasible. Trained predictive models will be shared via standard model repositories (e.g., Hugging Face for language-model-based classifiers) with clear documentation of training data, intended use, and known limitations to prevent misuse or over-extrapolation. The Working Group will adopt a contributor-credit framework (e.g., CRediT taxonomy) to ensure equitable attribution across the multidisciplinary team, particularly for early-career contributors performing substantial data curation or software development work. Governance of the Atlas post-funding will be established through a community advisory board, with a clear versioning and update policy to incorporate new public data releases, ensuring the resource remains a living, sustained community asset rather than a static deliverable—directly fulfilling NCEMS's expectation that synthesis outputs remain openly available and reproducible well beyond the funding period.

[Budget and Resources]
The requested budget supports a three-year Working Group comprising six co-investigators (biophysics, structural biology, computational biology/machine learning, cell biology, and clinical genomics), each contributing partial effort (10–20% FTE), plus dedicated personnel: two postdoctoral researchers (one biophysical modeling-focused, one machine learning/data engineering-focused) at 100% FTE, two graduate research assistants (50% FTE) drawn from partner institutions to maximize training reach, and a part-time data curation specialist (50% FTE) responsible for ontology harmonization and database maintenance. Personnel costs constitute the majority of the budget, reflecting the labor-intensive nature of cross-database harmonization and model validation. Computational resources include cloud computing credits (AWS/Google Cloud) for large-scale machine learning training and coarse-grained polymer simulations, plus subscription costs for high-performance JupyterHub infrastructure enabling real-time multi-institutional collaborative analysis. Travel funds are budgeted for two in-person all-hands workshops per year (Years 1–2) and one capstone symposium (Year 3), plus travel support for trainees to present at relevant conferences (e.g., Biophysical Society, ASCB). A dedicated line item supports two open-access hackathons (Year 2 and Year 3) training external graduate students and postdocs in the harmonized data infrastructure and modeling pipelines, including modest stipends for participant travel to broaden accessibility for trainees from underrepresented institutions. Publication costs cover open-access fees and preprint server deposition. Data and software archiving costs (Zenodo storage tiers, GitHub organization maintenance) are included as a minor but essential recurring cost. We request NCEMS support specifically for the coordination infrastructure—shared computational environments, cross-institutional personnel, and convening costs—that no single participating laboratory currently possesses or could independently fund, consistent with NCEMS's requirement that supported projects demonstrably exceed the capacity of existing individual collaborations. Matching in-kind contributions from participating institutions include existing laboratory computing infrastructure, partial faculty salary support, and access to institutional high-performance computing clusters, ensuring cost-effective use of NCEMS funds while maximizing sustainable, collaborative research output.

title: Predicting Emergent Mesoscale Biomolecular Condensate Behaviors from Public Multimodal Molecular and Cellular Data
title_norm: predicting emergent mesoscale biomolecular condensate behaviors from public multimodal molecular and cellular data
abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak, multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites can generate dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, compositions, and cellular functions. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some molecular assemblies form reversible, functional condensates, while others transition into aberrant, persistent, or disease-associated states? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from publicly available molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and perturbation phenotypes.

This working group will integrate existing public datasets spanning scales from sequence to cell state. Data sources will include curated condensate and phase-separation databases, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification repositories, protein-RNA interaction maps, affinity and proximity interaction datasets, spatial proteomics, public live-cell imaging datasets, CRISPR perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic atlases, and disease-variant resources. We will harmonize these datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph linking condensate-associated biomolecules to physicochemical features, interaction topology, cell-type context, subcellular localization, perturbation outcomes, and reported material or dynamical properties.

The central scientific question is: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts give rise to distinct mesoscale condensate phenotypes, including nucleation propensity, compositional selectivity, fusion dynamics, stress responsiveness, and pathological persistence? To answer this, the project will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-based models that distinguish condensate classes and identify higher-order feature combinations not apparent from individual datasets. Particular emphasis will be placed on emergent properties that cannot be inferred from single molecules alone, such as multicomponent interaction density, RNA-dependent buffering, post-translational modification logic, and context-specific rewiring during stress, differentiation, or disease.

This effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or infrastructure to synthesize the relevant public data types at community scale. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, network theorists, machine-learning researchers, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS workshops will enable consensus building around condensate ontologies, metadata standards, uncertainty scoring, benchmark datasets, and reproducible analytical workflows.

Expected outcomes include: an open condensate emergence knowledge graph; benchmark datasets for predicting mesoscale condensate behaviors; interpretable models identifying molecular and contextual rules of condensate formation and maturation; and community guidelines for integrating heterogeneous condensate data. The project will train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows through team-based data synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-disciplinary short courses on open science, graph analytics, and AI-assisted biological discovery. All code, harmonized metadata, model outputs, tutorials, and manuscripts will be released publicly under open licenses.

By synthesizing diverse public data rather than generating new experiments, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: how do molecular-scale features collectively produce emergent mesoscale organization that shapes cellular behavior? The resulting framework will advance predictive understanding of condensates and provide a reusable model for studying emergence across other subcellular systems.

The resulting framework will advance predictive understanding of condensates and provide a reusable model for studying emergence across other subcellular systems.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates organize the intracellular environment without delimiting membranes, concentrating selected proteins, RNAs, and metabolites into dynamic mesoscale assemblies such as nucleoli, stress granules, P bodies, transcriptional hubs, DNA repair foci, and signaling clusters. These assemblies exemplify emergence because their properties arise from collective, weak, multivalent interactions that are not obvious from the behavior of individual molecules. Condensates can buffer biochemical noise, accelerate reactions, compartmentalize RNA metabolism, coordinate stress adaptation, and tune gene expression. However, similar molecular ingredients can also produce persistent aggregates, toxic inclusions, or pathological states associated with neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, and developmental disorders. A central unresolved problem in molecular and cellular biosciences is therefore to identify the rules that distinguish reversible, functional condensates from aberrant or disease-associated assemblies. Existing studies have revealed important contributors, including intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity sequence motifs, folded interaction domains, RNA scaffolds, post-translational modifications, charge patterning, aromatic residues, and local concentration thresholds. Yet these features are insufficient when considered in isolation. The same protein may form distinct condensates across cell types, stress conditions, developmental stages, or disease contexts. Similarly, condensate material properties depend on multicomponent interaction networks, RNA abundance, protein stoichiometry, enzymatic modification states, molecular crowding, subcellular localization, and active cellular processes. This complexity has created a fragmented literature in which mechanistic insights from biophysics, cell biology, proteomics, genomics, imaging, and clinical genetics are rarely synthesized at community scale. The timing is ideal for a coordinated synthesis effort. Public resources now include curated condensate and phase-separation databases, protein sequence and disorder annotations, post-translational modification catalogs, protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction maps, proximity labeling datasets, spatial proteomics atlases, public live-cell and fixed-cell imaging repositories, CRISPR perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic atlases, and disease-variant databases. Individually, these resources answer narrow questions; integrated, they can reveal higher-order principles of mesoscale emergence. No single laboratory can harmonize these heterogeneous data types, establish community metadata standards, evaluate uncertainty across evidence sources, and develop interpretable models that connect molecular features to cellular phenotypes. NCEMS is uniquely suited to support this work because the project directly addresses emergence at the mesoscale, uses only existing public data, requires a multidisciplinary working group, and will create reusable open infrastructure for the broader community. The proposed synthesis will transform condensate biology from a collection of case studies into a predictive, comparative science. By linking molecular composition, interaction topology, cellular context, perturbation response, imaging-derived dynamics, and disease relevance, we will identify combinations of features that produce emergent condensate behaviors. This knowledge will advance fundamental understanding of cellular organization, provide mechanistic hypotheses for disease-associated phase transitions, and establish a generalizable framework for studying other mesoscale systems, including cytoskeletal assemblies, membrane contact sites, chromatin domains, and organelle subcompartments.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching question is whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from publicly available molecular, network, imaging, perturbation, and cellular-context data. We will focus on five interrelated questions that define a tractable synthesis program. First, what combinations of sequence, structural, physicochemical, and regulatory features distinguish condensate-forming molecules from closely related non-condensate molecules? Second, how do interaction-network properties, including multivalency, modularity, hub status, RNA dependence, and proximity relationships, contribute to nucleation, compositional selectivity, and recruitment hierarchy? Third, how do cell state, cell type, stress condition, subcellular localization, and molecular abundance alter condensate behavior? Fourth, which publicly observable signatures distinguish reversible functional condensates from persistent, aberrant, or disease-associated assemblies? Fifth, can interpretable models identify higher-order rules that generalize across condensate classes while preserving class-specific mechanisms? We hypothesize that condensate phenotypes are predictable only when molecular features are interpreted in a network and cellular context. Specifically, we hypothesize that nucleation propensity emerges from a combination of intrinsic multivalency, local concentration, disorder-mediated interaction potential, and context-dependent availability of scaffold partners. We further hypothesize that compositional selectivity is governed by interaction-network topology and molecular grammar, including domain-motif compatibility, RNA-binding specificity, charge patterning, and post-translational modification states. We expect that condensates with similar visible morphologies may arise from distinct feature combinations, requiring model classes that allow multiple mechanistic routes to the same phenotype. We also hypothesize that pathological persistence reflects a shift in the balance among reversible weak interactions, stabilizing crosslinks, impaired clearance, altered RNA buffering, disease variants, and stress-induced rewiring. This hypothesis predicts that disease-associated condensates will show enriched combinations of aggregation-prone sequence features, disrupted modification sites, altered interaction neighborhoods, reduced dynamic exchange signatures, and perturbation phenotypes linked to proteostasis, RNA metabolism, or stress granule regulation. A final methodological hypothesis is that knowledge-graph representations combined with interpretable machine learning will outperform single-dataset or single-feature models because condensate emergence is relational and multiscale. Graph models can represent molecules, condensates, cell types, perturbations, phenotypes, variants, and evidence sources as connected entities, while uncertainty-aware learning can incorporate heterogeneous evidence quality. We will evaluate these hypotheses through benchmark prediction tasks: identifying condensate-associated biomolecules, classifying condensate type, predicting stress responsiveness, inferring recruitment to known condensates, distinguishing functional versus pathological annotations, and predicting imaging-derived dynamic features when available. We will also test whether model explanations recover known biological principles and reveal plausible new feature combinations. The intended product is not a black-box classifier but a community-vetted set of predictive rules, uncertainty estimates, and benchmark datasets that clarify how molecular-scale information gives rise to mesoscale organization.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will be conducted by an NCEMS working group using only existing publicly available data. The team will include expertise in condensate cell biology, biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, spatial omics, live-cell imaging, clinical genetics, knowledge representation, network science, machine learning, biostatistics, data curation, and open-source software engineering. The work will proceed in four integrated aims. Aim 1 will establish community standards for condensate data harmonization. During NCEMS-supported workshops, participants will define controlled vocabularies for condensate identity, molecular role, evidence type, cellular context, perturbation, material property, and uncertainty. We will align these terms with existing ontologies wherever possible, including gene, protein, cell type, disease, subcellular localization, phenotype, and experimental-assay ontologies. Data will be assigned evidence scores reflecting source reliability, assay type, replication, species, cell type, and whether observations are endogenous, overexpression-based, in vitro, or computationally inferred. Aim 2 will build an open condensate emergence knowledge graph. Public datasets will be harvested from condensate databases, UniProt, Gene Ontology, DisProt, MobiDB, AlphaFold annotations, PhosphoSitePlus where license-compatible, BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, POSTAR, ENCODE, spatial proteomics repositories, Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, CRISPR screen repositories, single-cell atlases, ClinVar, gnomAD, GWAS Catalog, and disease-focused variant resources. We will not generate new experimental data. Data will be mapped to stable identifiers, provenance-tracked, versioned, and represented as typed relationships among molecules, RNAs, interactions, condensates, contexts, perturbations, phenotypes, variants, and publications. Aim 3 will derive quantitative features and benchmark labels. Feature sets will include disorder content, low-complexity motifs, charge patterning, aromaticity, prion-like domains, domain-motif architecture, predicted structure confidence, post-translational modification density, RNA-binding evidence, protein and RNA abundance, interaction degree, network clustering, proximity enrichment, localization specificity, perturbation phenotypes, disease-variant burden, and imaging-derived descriptors when available. Benchmark tasks will be split by condensate, protein family, publication, and species to reduce leakage and overoptimistic performance. Negative and unknown classes will be treated carefully using positive-unlabeled learning and sensitivity analyses. Aim 4 will develop interpretable predictive models. We will compare regularized generalized models, gradient-boosted trees, graph neural networks, matrix factorization, heterogeneous network propagation, causal discovery-inspired analyses, and Bayesian hierarchical models. Interpretability will be emphasized through feature attribution, rule extraction, counterfactual analyses, uncertainty calibration, and expert review. Model performance will be evaluated using held-out benchmarks, cross-dataset validation, temporal validation based on publication date, and recovery of well-established biological mechanisms. Trainees will participate in data-curation sprints, code review, reproducible workflow development, and cross-disciplinary analysis teams. Milestones include a draft ontology and data inventory by month 6, a public beta knowledge graph by month 12, benchmark datasets and baseline models by month 18, refined predictive models by month 24, and community guidelines, tutorials, and manuscripts by month 30.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce four primary outcomes. First, we will release an open, versioned condensate emergence knowledge graph that connects biomolecules, RNAs, molecular features, interactions, cell states, perturbations, imaging observations, disease variants, and reported condensate behaviors. Second, we will create benchmark datasets for predicting condensate association, condensate class, stress responsiveness, compositional recruitment, dynamic behavior, and pathological persistence. Third, we will develop interpretable computational models that identify combinations of molecular and contextual features associated with emergent mesoscale phenotypes. Fourth, we will publish community guidelines for condensate metadata, evidence scoring, uncertainty reporting, and reproducible integration of heterogeneous public datasets. The scientific impact will be a shift from descriptive cataloging of condensates toward predictive and comparative principles of mesoscale cellular organization. The models will help distinguish features that are individually correlated with phase separation from feature combinations that are collectively predictive in specific cellular contexts. This distinction is essential for explaining why similar molecular assemblies can be adaptive in one setting and pathological in another. The project will also provide mechanistic hypotheses for disease-associated variants, stress granule persistence, altered RNA buffering, and condensate remodeling during differentiation or stress. Broader impacts include reusable data infrastructure, open training materials, and a community model for synthesis research in molecular and cellular emergence. The knowledge graph and workflows will be extensible to other mesoscale systems, including chromatin compartments, cytoskeletal assemblies, and membrane-associated signaling clusters. By involving trainees, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, database curators, computational scientists, and experimental domain experts, the working group will broaden participation in data-intensive molecular bioscience and train a workforce fluent in open, reproducible, AI-assisted synthesis.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open science principles from inception through publication. All nonrestricted harmonized metadata, knowledge-graph schemas, analysis workflows, benchmark definitions, model code, documentation, tutorials, and manuscript-associated outputs will be deposited in public repositories under permissive licenses, such as CC BY for documentation and MIT or Apache 2.0 for software. Data releases will use stable version identifiers and digital object identifiers, enabling reproducible citation and long-term reuse. Each dataset ingested into the knowledge graph will retain provenance, source links, license information, processing history, identifier mappings, evidence scores, and uncertainty annotations. Reproducibility will be implemented technically and socially. Computational workflows will be scripted using open tools, containerized with Docker or Apptainer, and orchestrated with reproducible workflow systems such as Snakemake or Nextflow. Continuous integration tests will verify schema validity, identifier consistency, data transformations, and model execution on representative subsets. Analyses will be documented in executable notebooks and command-line workflows, with random seeds, software versions, and parameter files archived for each release. Benchmark splits will be frozen and publicly documented to prevent data leakage and facilitate fair comparison by external researchers. The working group will establish transparent governance for contributions, authorship, conflict resolution, and community feedback. Regular open office hours, issue trackers, and public documentation will allow researchers outside the funded team to suggest datasets, report errors, and contribute improvements. Preprints will be posted before journal submission, and publications will be accompanied by reproducibility packages. Training activities will include short courses on FAIR data, knowledge graphs, uncertainty-aware curation, interpretable machine learning, and responsible use of AI. These practices will ensure that the project is not merely open at the end, but reproducible, inspectable, and reusable throughout its life cycle.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires community-scale coordination, shared cyberinfrastructure, structured synthesis meetings, and trainee participation beyond the capacity of any individual laboratory. Funds will support working group convenings, data-synthesis sprints, trainee travel, software and data-engineering effort, cloud computing, documentation, and dissemination. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase experimental reagents, perform new imaging, or conduct new wet-lab assays. The largest resource need is personnel time for harmonizing heterogeneous public datasets, building the knowledge graph, implementing reproducible workflows, and developing benchmark models. We anticipate support for a part-time project manager or data coordinator, trainee stipends for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows contributing to curation and analysis, and limited software-engineering consultation. Meeting funds will enable in-person and hybrid NCEMS workshops that bring together experts from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and public data resources. These meetings are critical for ontology development, evidence scoring, benchmark design, model interpretation, and community guideline writing. Computing resources will include NCEMS-supported collaborative cloud workspaces, version-controlled repositories, storage for processed public datasets, and scalable analysis environments for graph analytics and machine learning. We will leverage existing public databases, institutional high-performance computing where available, open-source software, and NCEMS collaborative infrastructure to maximize cost efficiency. Dissemination resources will support public tutorials, webinars, documentation, preprint preparation, and long-term archiving of releases. The budget is therefore tightly aligned with NCEMS priorities: catalyzing a multidisciplinary team, synthesizing existing public data, advancing mesoscale emergence science, training data-savvy researchers, and producing open resources that outlast the award period.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak, multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites can generate dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, compositions, and cellular functions. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some molecular assemblies form reversible, functional condensates, while others transition into aberrant, persistent, or disease-associated states? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from publicly available molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and perturbation phenotypes.

This working group will integrate existing public datasets spanning scales from sequence to cell state. Data sources will include curated condensate and phase-separation databases, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification repositories, protein-RNA interaction maps, affinity and proximity interaction datasets, spatial proteomics, public live-cell imaging datasets, CRISPR perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic and proteomic atlases, and disease-variant resources. We will harmonize these datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph linking condensate-associated biomolecules to physicochemical features, interaction topology, cell-type context, subcellular localization, perturbation outcomes, and reported material or dynamical properties.

The central scientific question is: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts give rise to distinct mesoscale condensate phenotypes, including nucleation propensity, compositional selectivity, fusion dynamics, stress responsiveness, and pathological persistence? To answer this, the project will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-based models that distinguish condensate classes and identify higher-order feature combinations not apparent from individual datasets. Particular emphasis will be placed on emergent properties that cannot be inferred from single molecules alone, such as multicomponent interaction density, RNA-dependent buffering, post-translational modification logic, and context-specific rewiring during stress, differentiation, or disease.

This effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or infrastructure to synthesize the relevant public data types at community scale. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, network theorists, machine-learning researchers, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS workshops will enable consensus building around condensate ontologies, metadata standards, uncertainty scoring, benchmark datasets, and reproducible analytical workflows.

Expected outcomes include: an open condensate emergence knowledge graph; benchmark datasets for predicting mesoscale condensate behaviors; interpretable models identifying molecular and contextual rules of condensate formation and maturation; and community guidelines for integrating heterogeneous condensate data. The project will train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows through team-based data synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-disciplinary short courses on open science, graph analytics, and AI-assisted biological discovery. All code, harmonized metadata, model outputs, tutorials, and manuscripts will be released publicly under open licenses.

By synthesizing diverse public data rather than generating new experiments, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: how do molecular-scale features collectively produce emergent mesoscale organization that shapes cellular behavior? The resulting framework will advance predictive understanding of condensates and provide a reusable model for studying emergence across other subcellular systems.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, lipids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications generate dynamic compartments whose properties cannot be inferred from any single component. Yet a central puzzle remains unresolved: why do the same scaffold proteins form distinct condensate states across cell types, stresses, developmental programs, and disease contexts, and when do these states become adaptive versus pathological? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, cellular, and imaging datasets to identify generalizable rules linking molecular composition to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will integrate diverse resources including Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive datasets, Cell Painting profiles, ProteomeXchange and PRIDE proteomics, GEO and SRA transcriptomics, public phosphoproteomics and ubiquitinomics, RBP and RNA interactome datasets, PhaSepDB and DrLLPS condensate annotations, AlphaFold-derived structural features, DepMap perturbation screens, and public stress-response and neurodegeneration datasets. The project will address three questions: (1) Which combinations of molecular features predict condensate formation, morphology, dynamics, and localization across cellular contexts? (2) Which context variables, such as phosphorylation state, RNA abundance, expression stoichiometry, and stress history, explain apparent contradictions in published condensate behavior? (3) Which emergent condensate states are associated with beneficial stress adaptation, impaired proteostasis, altered signaling, or cell vulnerability? We will build an open condensate synthesis atlas that harmonizes heterogeneous public datasets into a FAIR knowledge graph connecting molecules, interactions, modifications, imaging phenotypes, perturbations, and cellular outcomes. Analytical innovations will include multimodal representation learning for combining images and omics, graph-based causal discovery to separate correlates from candidate drivers, biophysically informed machine learning features such as disorder, multivalency, charge patterning, and interaction valence, and community benchmark tasks for predicting condensate localization and phenotype transitions. NCEMS support is essential because the work requires coordination beyond any single laboratory: cell biologists and biophysicists to define condensate states, imaging scientists to standardize visual phenotypes, proteomic and transcriptomic experts to harmonize context-specific molecular measurements, computational scientists to develop scalable integrative models, and statisticians to establish uncertainty-aware cross-dataset inference. The Working Group will include researchers across institution types, career stages, and geographic regions, with dedicated roles for graduate students and postdoctoral scholars in data curation, reproducible workflow development, and collaborative model benchmarking. Trainees will participate in NCEMS-supported hackathons and short courses on open data integration, image analysis, graph machine learning, and team science. All code, harmonized metadata, analysis workflows, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly through version-controlled repositories and community-governed standards. The anticipated outcome is a predictive, reusable framework for understanding condensates as emergent mesoscale systems, transforming fragmented public data into testable principles for how molecular interactions scale into cellular organization and phenotype.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are dynamic, membrane-less mesoscale assemblies that organize biochemical reactions, buffer molecular noise, regulate gene expression, and respond to environmental change. Their formation is commonly associated with multivalent interactions, intrinsically disordered regions, nucleic acids, post-translational modifications, and local concentration thresholds, yet these ingredients do not provide a complete predictive theory. The same scaffold protein can assemble into liquid-like droplets, gel-like networks, solid aggregates, nuclear bodies, cytoplasmic stress granules, nucleolar subdomains, or disease-associated inclusions depending on cell type, stress exposure, RNA milieu, protein stoichiometry, modification state, and interaction history. This context dependence is a central example of emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences: condensate properties arise from collective interactions among components and cannot be inferred from any single molecule in isolation. Despite rapid progress, the field remains fragmented. Imaging studies document condensate morphology, localization, and dynamics, but often lack deep molecular measurements. Proteomic and transcriptomic studies measure expression, modification, and interactome state, but frequently lack quantitative imaging phenotypes. Databases such as PhaSepDB and DrLLPS curate condensate-associated molecules, while Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, GEO, SRA, DepMap, public phosphoproteomics, ubiquitinomics, RBP interactome resources, AlphaFold-derived structural predictions, and disease-focused repositories contain complementary information. However, differences in metadata structure, cell lines, perturbations, imaging modalities, feature definitions, and quality metrics impede synthesis. As a result, published claims sometimes appear contradictory: proteins reported as stress granule components in one context may be diffuse, nucleolar, chromatin-associated, or aggregation-prone in another; phosphorylation may dissolve one condensate while stabilizing another; and disease-linked variants may either increase assembly, impair clearance, or alter material state. A community-scale synthesis is now timely and necessary. The volume and diversity of public molecular, cellular, and imaging data have reached a scale that can support cross-context inference, but no individual laboratory has the expertise or coordination capacity to harmonize these resources into a coherent, reusable framework. This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by using only existing public data, integrating multiple modalities, focusing on mesoscale emergence, and assembling a transdisciplinary team of cell biologists, biophysicists, imaging scientists, omics experts, computational modelers, statisticians, and trainees. The work will convert dispersed public observations into generalizable principles linking molecular composition, biophysical features, cellular context, emergent condensate state, and phenotypic consequence. Its significance extends beyond condensate biology. Condensates participate in transcription, RNA metabolism, signaling, DNA repair, proteostasis, stress adaptation, development, viral infection, cancer, and neurodegeneration. A predictive synthesis atlas will help distinguish adaptive cellular organization from pathological transitions, identify hidden context variables that explain inconsistent findings, and provide benchmark datasets for future mechanistic and computational research. By emphasizing open science, uncertainty-aware inference, and trainee-centered team science, the Working Group will establish a model for how public data synthesis can reveal emergent biological rules.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The Working Group will address three integrated scientific questions. First, which combinations of molecular and contextual features predict condensate formation, morphology, dynamics, and localization across cell states? We hypothesize that condensate behavior is best predicted by multivariate feature constellations rather than by single determinants such as intrinsic disorder or expression level alone. Specifically, we expect predictive models to require joint representation of protein concentration, RNA abundance, interaction valence, charge patterning, aromatic and polar residue distribution, low-complexity sequence architecture, predicted structural accessibility, post-translational modification status, subcellular localization, cell cycle state, and stress history. We further hypothesize that imaging-derived morphology features, including puncta number, size distribution, texture, coarsening patterns, compartmental proximity, and colocalization signatures, will reveal latent condensate states that are not captured by current binary annotations of condensate membership. Second, which context variables explain apparent contradictions in the literature and public datasets? We hypothesize that many inconsistencies arise from unmodeled cellular context rather than irreproducibility. For example, phosphorylation may either inhibit or promote condensation depending on whether it disrupts electrostatic attraction, creates a new binding site, changes localization, or alters client recruitment. RNA may buffer condensation at one concentration but promote crosslinking at another. Expression stoichiometry may determine whether a scaffold forms a functional compartment, remains soluble, or transitions toward aberrant aggregation. Cell type-specific proteomes, stress duration, recovery phase, metabolic state, and proteostasis capacity may shift phase boundaries and material properties. We will test whether harmonized context variables improve cross-dataset transferability and reduce unexplained discrepancies among studies. Third, which emergent condensate states are associated with beneficial stress adaptation, impaired proteostasis, altered signaling, or cell vulnerability? We hypothesize that adaptive condensates occupy a distinct region of a multidimensional state space characterized by reversible assembly, context-appropriate client enrichment, preserved proteome balance, and recovery-associated dissolution. In contrast, pathological or vulnerability-associated states will show features such as excessive persistence, altered material signatures, enrichment for aggregation-prone proteins, disrupted RNA processing, impaired ubiquitin-proteasome or autophagy markers, abnormal phosphorylation patterns, and association with reduced cell fitness in perturbation screens. The proposal will also test methodological hypotheses. We hypothesize that multimodal representation learning will outperform single-modality models for predicting condensate localization and phenotype transitions; that graph-based models incorporating molecular interactions, modifications, imaging phenotypes, and perturbation outcomes will identify candidate drivers more robustly than correlation networks; and that explicit uncertainty modeling will distinguish well-supported rules from dataset-specific artifacts. These hypotheses align with the NCEMS emphasis on emergent properties because they ask how mesoscale condensate states arise from interacting molecular systems and how those states influence higher-order cellular outcomes. The questions are designed for synthesis rather than new data generation: all tests will use public images, annotations, omics profiles, perturbation screens, and curated condensate resources. Success will be measured by predictive performance on held-out datasets, reproducible identification of context variables explaining discrepancies, biologically interpretable rules validated through independent public datasets, and community adoption of the resulting atlas and benchmarks.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will proceed through coordinated workstreams that transform heterogeneous public data into an integrated, analyzable, and reusable condensate synthesis atlas. Workstream 1 will define scope, metadata standards, and controlled vocabularies. Cell biologists and biophysicists will refine a condensate state ontology covering localization, morphology, dynamics, reversibility, material proxy, scaffold-client relationships, stress condition, and cellular outcome. The ontology will map to existing identifiers including UniProt, Ensembl, Gene Ontology, Cell Ontology, Sequence Ontology, PSI-MOD, Experimental Factor Ontology, and BioSample metadata. Workstream 2 will acquire and harmonize public datasets. Imaging sources will include Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, and Cell Painting collections. Molecular sources will include ProteomeXchange, PRIDE, GEO, SRA, public phosphoproteomics and ubiquitinomics studies, RBP and RNA interactome datasets, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, AlphaFold-derived features, STRING or BioGRID interactions, DepMap dependency screens, and stress-response, cancer, and neurodegeneration datasets. No new experimental data will be generated. Dataset inclusion will require public accessibility, reusable licensing where possible, sufficient metadata, and documented quality metrics. Workstream 3 will extract standardized features. For proteins and RNAs, we will compute or retrieve expression, abundance, stoichiometry, disorder, low-complexity content, prion-like domains, charge patterning, aromaticity, multivalency, predicted structural exposure, interaction degree, motif composition, modification sites, variant annotations, and RNA-binding evidence. For images, we will use reproducible segmentation and feature extraction pipelines based on established tools such as CellProfiler, scikit-image, napari-compatible workflows, and deep learning embeddings. Features will include puncta count, size, intensity, shape, texture, compartment localization, colocalization, cell-to-cell variability, and perturbation response. Workstream 4 will construct a FAIR knowledge graph connecting molecules, complexes, RNAs, modifications, conditions, imaging phenotypes, perturbations, diseases, and outcomes. The graph will support provenance tracking, uncertainty labels, evidence weights, and versioned updates. Workstream 5 will develop integrative models. Multimodal representation learning will combine image embeddings, omics profiles, structural features, and graph neighborhoods to predict condensate state labels and continuous phenotypes. Graph neural networks and probabilistic graphical models will identify context-dependent associations, while causal discovery methods and perturbation-aware analyses will prioritize candidate drivers over passive correlates. Models will be trained with nested cross-validation, leave-dataset-out testing, cell-type-stratified splits, negative control tasks, and calibration analyses to reduce overfitting and quantify uncertainty. Workstream 6 will implement community benchmarks. Benchmark tasks will include predicting condensate localization from molecular features, predicting image-derived condensate morphology from omics context, classifying adaptive versus vulnerability-associated states, and identifying context variables that reconcile conflicting public reports. Performance metrics will include area under precision-recall curves, balanced accuracy, calibration error, uncertainty coverage, transfer performance, and biological interpretability. The Working Group will meet virtually monthly and in NCEMS-supported in-person workshops and hackathons. Trainees will co-lead curation sprints, workflow implementation, documentation, and benchmark evaluation. Milestones include a data inventory by month 3, ontology and pilot graph by month 6, initial multimodal models by month 12, public benchmark release by month 18, and final atlas, manuscripts, tutorials, and community recommendations by month 24.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open condensate synthesis atlas that integrates public imaging, omics, structural, interaction, perturbation, and disease-context datasets into a coherent knowledge graph. The atlas will enable researchers to query how proteins, RNAs, modifications, cell types, stresses, and perturbations relate to emergent condensate states and downstream cellular outcomes. A second outcome will be a set of validated computational models and benchmark tasks for predicting condensate localization, morphology, context-dependent transitions, and adaptive versus pathological associations. These resources will provide a rigorous foundation for comparing future algorithms and for identifying where public data are sufficient or insufficient for inference. Scientifically, the project will generate generalizable rules for condensate emergence, including feature combinations that distinguish reversible organization from persistent or vulnerability-associated states. It will clarify why apparently similar scaffold proteins behave differently across conditions and why the same protein may produce divergent phenotypes in different cellular contexts. By integrating DepMap, stress-response, proteostasis, and neurodegeneration datasets, the project will identify condensate signatures associated with cell fitness, impaired protein homeostasis, altered signaling, and disease vulnerability. The broader impact is a reusable synthesis framework for mesoscale cell biology. The project will demonstrate how community-scale integration of public data can transform fragmented observations into predictive principles without generating new experimental data. It will support NCEMS goals by advancing emergence-focused biology, catalyzing cross-disciplinary collaboration, training data-savvy trainees, and producing open resources that lower barriers for investigators at diverse institutions. The resulting atlas, workflows, and training materials will serve as a template for synthesis studies of other mesoscale systems such as cytoskeletal assemblies, membraneless organelles, signaling clusters, and organelle contact sites.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow gold-standard open, team, and reproducible science practices. All harmonized metadata, derived features, code, workflows, model outputs, benchmark definitions, documentation, and manuscripts will be released publicly, subject only to the terms of the original public datasets. Data products will be deposited in stable repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, GitHub, and institutional archives, with digital object identifiers and clear versioning. Code will use permissive open-source licenses, while metadata and derived annotations will use community-appropriate open licenses when allowed. Reproducibility will be built into the workflow architecture. Data ingestion, quality control, feature extraction, graph construction, model training, and evaluation will be implemented with containerized and workflow-managed pipelines using tools such as Docker or Apptainer, Snakemake or Nextflow, and continuous integration testing. Each analysis will include machine-readable provenance, parameter files, software versions, random seeds, and data access dates. Benchmark datasets will include fixed training, validation, and held-out evaluation splits, plus documentation of known biases and limitations. Open governance will be established through a Working Group charter covering authorship, decision-making, conflict resolution, data stewardship, trainee credit, and inclusive participation. Community feedback will be solicited through public issue trackers, virtual office hours, hackathons, and preprint releases. Tutorials, example notebooks, and teaching modules will be developed for trainees and external users, including participants from minority-serving institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, and resource-limited research environments. The group will report negative results, uncertainty estimates, and failed modeling strategies where informative, reducing publication bias and improving reuse. These practices ensure that the project is not merely open at the end, but transparent, reproducible, and community-governed throughout its life cycle.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis across domains, institutions, and data types that exceed the capacity of a single laboratory. Funds will primarily support Working Group coordination, trainee participation, data engineering, collaborative meetings, and open dissemination rather than new experiments. Personnel resources will include partial support for a project data scientist or research software engineer to maintain ingestion pipelines, knowledge graph infrastructure, reproducible workflows, and benchmark releases. Graduate students and postdoctoral scholars from participating laboratories will receive travel and short-term effort support for curation sprints, model benchmarking, documentation, and training activities. Meeting resources will include two in-person NCEMS workshops, quarterly virtual synthesis meetings, focused hackathons, and trainee-led technical clinics on image analysis, omics harmonization, graph machine learning, causal inference, and reproducible workflow design. Travel funds will prioritize participation by early-career researchers, investigators from geographically diverse institutions, minority-serving institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, and groups not traditionally represented in computational cell biology. abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, lipids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications generate dynamic compartments whose properties cannot be inferred from any single component. Yet a central puzzle remains unresolved: why do the same scaffold proteins form distinct condensate states across cell types, stresses, developmental programs, and disease contexts, and when do these states become adaptive versus pathological? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, cellular, and imaging datasets to identify generalizable rules linking molecular composition to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will integrate diverse resources including Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive datasets, Cell Painting profiles, ProteomeXchange and PRIDE proteomics, GEO and SRA transcriptomics, public phosphoproteomics and ubiquitinomics, RBP and RNA interactome datasets, PhaSepDB and DrLLPS condensate annotations, AlphaFold-derived structural features, DepMap perturbation screens, and public stress-response and neurodegeneration datasets. The project will address three questions: (1) Which combinations of molecular features predict condensate formation, morphology, dynamics, and localization across cellular contexts? (2) Which context variables, such as phosphorylation state, RNA abundance, expression stoichiometry, and stress history, explain apparent contradictions in published condensate behavior? (3) Which emergent condensate states are associated with beneficial stress adaptation, impaired proteostasis, altered signaling, or cell vulnerability? We will build an open condensate synthesis atlas that harmonizes heterogeneous public datasets into a FAIR knowledge graph connecting molecules, interactions, modifications, imaging phenotypes, perturbations, and cellular outcomes. Analytical innovations will include multimodal representation learning for combining images and omics, graph-based causal discovery to separate correlates from candidate drivers, biophysically informed machine learning features such as disorder, multivalency, charge patterning, and interaction valence, and community benchmark tasks for predicting condensate localization and phenotype transitions. NCEMS support is essential because the work requires coordination beyond any single laboratory: cell biologists and biophysicists to define condensate states, imaging scientists to standardize visual phenotypes, proteomic and transcriptomic experts to harmonize context-specific molecular measurements, computational scientists to develop scalable integrative models, and statisticians to establish uncertainty-aware cross-dataset inference. The Working Group will include researchers across institution types, career stages, and geographic regions, with dedicated roles for graduate students and postdoctoral scholars in data curation, reproducible workflow development, and collaborative model benchmarking. Trainees will participate in NCEMS-supported hackathons and short courses on open data integration, image analysis, graph machine learning, and team science. All code, harmonized metadata, analysis workflows, model outputs, and documentation will be released openly through version-controlled repositories and community-governed standards. The anticipated outcome is a predictive, reusable framework for understanding condensates as emergent mesoscale systems, transforming fragmented public data into testable principles for how molecular interactions scale into cellular organization and phenotype.
