full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies whose properties cannot be predicted from any single component: multivalent interactions among proteins, RNA, metabolites, and post-translational modifications generate emergent material states that influence transcription, translation, stress adaptation, and disease. Yet a central unresolved question remains: what generalizable molecular rules determine whether a condensate becomes adaptive, inert, or pathological in living cells? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available data to build the first community-scale, cross-system atlas linking condensate composition and predicted material properties to cellular outcomes. We will focus on stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, DNA-repair foci, and disease-associated protein assemblies, asking whether shared mesoscale design principles govern their formation, dynamics, and phenotypic consequences across cell types and perturbations. The project will integrate existing datasets spanning BioID/APEX proximity proteomics, affinity purification mass spectrometry, fluorescence recovery and single-particle imaging, immunofluorescence image repositories, RNA-binding maps, post-translational modification databases, protein disorder and phase-separation predictors, CRISPR/RNAi perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomics, and disease variant resources. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize heterogeneous public data into interoperable condensate-centered knowledge graphs, with standardized metadata describing cell type, perturbation, assay modality, temporal scale, and measured phenotype. We will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-inference approaches to identify emergent features that best predict condensate behavior, including compositional diversity, interaction valency, sequence disorder, charge patterning, RNA dependence, modification state, molecular crowding proxies, and connectivity to signaling or proteostasis pathways. A central innovation is to move beyond cataloging condensate components toward modeling condensates as mesoscale systems whose collective features explain higher-order outcomes such as stress survival, transcriptional bursting, genome stability, viral replication, and neurodegenerative toxicity. This synthesis effort requires NCEMS support because the relevant data are distributed across communities that rarely interact: cell biologists studying membraneless organelles, proteomics experts, biophysicists modeling phase behavior, image analysts, systems biologists, RNA biologists, and disease geneticists. The scope exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory, as success depends on coordinated curation standards, shared computational infrastructure, cross-domain model evaluation, and community agreement on what constitutes comparable evidence for condensate state and function. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-science initiatives, with leadership opportunities for early-career scientists. Trainees will participate in hackathon-style data integration sprints, reproducible workflow development, and cross-training modules in condensate biology, FAIR data practices, image analysis, graph learning, and interpretable AI. All outputs will be openly released, including curated datasets, metadata templates, analysis notebooks, benchmark tasks, interactive visualization tools, and a living condensate knowledge graph under permissive licenses. The expected outcome is a predictive and reusable framework for identifying when molecular composition gives rise to emergent mesoscale states that alter cell physiology. By synthesizing public data across scales, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular science, generate testable hypotheses for the broader community, and establish open analytical strategies for studying emergence in complex cellular assemblies.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are central examples of emergence in molecular and cellular biology. They arise when many weak, multivalent interactions among proteins, nucleic acids, metabolites, ions, and post-translational modifications generate mesoscale assemblies with properties not evident from individual components alone. Condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, DNA-repair foci, heterochromatin domains, and disease-associated protein assemblies influence gene expression, RNA metabolism, proteostasis, genome integrity, antiviral defense, and cell survival. Their relevance extends from normal physiology to cancer, neurodegeneration, viral infection, developmental regulation, and stress adaptation. Yet the field lacks generalizable rules connecting molecular composition to material state and cellular phenotype. A protein may promote adaptive stress granule assembly in one context, become toxic in another, and appear inert in a third. This context dependence is precisely the type of mesoscale emergence that NCEMS is designed to address. The current literature contains extensive public data relevant to condensate biology, but these data are fragmented across communities, formats, scales, and assumptions. Proximity proteomics maps list candidate components of membrane-less compartments; affinity purification studies reveal interaction networks; FRAP and single-particle tracking quantify dynamics; fluorescence imaging repositories capture morphology and localization; RNA-binding maps define transcript associations; phosphoproteomic and other modification resources record regulatory state; CRISPR and RNAi screens connect genes to phenotypes; single-cell transcriptomics captures cell-state variation; and human variant databases link sequence changes to disease. Individually, these datasets have advanced local understanding. Collectively, they provide an unprecedented opportunity to infer cross-system principles of condensate organization, but only if harmonized through a community-scale synthesis effort. The significance of this Working Group is twofold. First, it addresses a fundamental scientific question: which collective molecular features predict whether a condensate will behave as adaptive, neutral, or pathological in living cells? This question cannot be answered by cataloging components alone. It requires integrative modeling of compositional diversity, interaction valency, intrinsic disorder, charge patterning, RNA dependence, modification state, dynamic exchange, and connectivity to cellular pathways. Second, it will create reusable public infrastructure for condensate-centered data synthesis. The field currently lacks shared metadata standards for comparing condensate evidence across assays, cell types, perturbations, time scales, and phenotypic readouts. Without such standards, results remain difficult to reproduce, compare, or use in predictive models. This project is well matched to NCEMS because it focuses on emergent mesoscale properties, uses only existing public data, requires collaboration across multiple disciplines, and will produce open, reproducible resources. The scope exceeds any single laboratory: expertise is needed in condensate cell biology, proteomics, biophysics, RNA biology, image analysis, systems biology, graph learning, disease genetics, metadata standards, and open-science practice. By convening a diverse Working Group, NCEMS can catalyze a synthesis that transforms scattered datasets into a coherent framework for understanding how molecular interactions generate cellular-scale outcomes.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This project is organized around one overarching question: what emergent molecular and mesoscale features determine whether biomolecular condensates produce adaptive, inert, or pathological cellular outcomes? We will address this question through four linked research questions. First, are there shared compositional signatures that distinguish functional condensates from condensates associated with cellular toxicity or disease? We hypothesize that adaptive condensates are enriched for balanced interaction architectures, including mixtures of scaffold and client proteins, regulated RNA interactions, reversible post-translational modifications, and pathway-specific control nodes, whereas pathological assemblies show higher aggregation propensity, reduced exchange capacity, altered charge patterning, and disproportionate enrichment of low-complexity or prion-like domains. Second, can material state be predicted from integrated public molecular features? We hypothesize that no single feature, such as intrinsic disorder or phase-separation propensity, is sufficient. Instead, predictive power will emerge from combinations of features: multivalent interaction density, sequence grammar, RNA-binding capacity, phosphorylation and methylation status, abundance, stoichiometric imbalance, and local network topology. These combinations should predict measured or inferred states such as liquid-like exchange, gel-like persistence, solid-like accumulation, and mixed or aging-dependent behavior. Third, do condensates across distinct biological systems share common mesoscale design principles despite differences in composition? We hypothesize that stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, and DNA-repair foci occupy partially overlapping regions of a multidimensional design space. For example, stress-responsive condensates may share high regulatory reversibility and signaling connectivity, while constitutive nuclear condensates may show more stable compositional cores and stronger coupling to chromatin or RNA biogenesis. Disease-associated assemblies may represent excursions from these functional regions, caused by mutations, altered expression, proteostasis decline, or disrupted post-translational regulation. Fourth, which condensate features best explain higher-order cellular phenotypes? We hypothesize that phenotypic consequences are determined by both intrinsic condensate properties and cellular context. A condensate’s impact on stress survival, transcriptional bursting, genome stability, viral replication, or neurodegenerative toxicity should depend on its material state, persistence, recruitment or exclusion of key enzymes, RNA selectivity, and coupling to signaling, proteostasis, and metabolic pathways. The Working Group will test these hypotheses using public data synthesis rather than new experiments. We will define evidence classes for condensate membership, material state, and phenotype; construct condensate-centered knowledge graphs; and train interpretable models that predict outcomes across held-out condensate classes, cell types, and perturbations. We will evaluate whether models trained on one condensate family generalize to another, thereby directly testing for shared emergent rules. We will also identify cases where models fail, because such failures may reveal biological exceptions, missing data types, or incompatible assay assumptions. The final product will not be a static catalog but a hypothesis-generating framework. It will nominate molecular features and regulatory mechanisms that distinguish adaptive condensation from maladaptive assembly, prioritize disease variants likely to alter condensate behavior, and define benchmark questions that the broader community can refine through future experimental and computational work.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will implement a synthesis-only, data-driven strategy with no generation of new experimental data. In phase 1, we will inventory and prioritize public datasets relevant to six condensate classes: stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, DNA-repair foci, and disease-associated protein assemblies. Data sources will include PRIDE, MassIVE, BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, Human Protein Atlas, Cell Painting and image repositories, OpenCell, ENCODE, GEO, SRA-derived processed resources, DepMap, GenomeRNAi, PhosphoSitePlus, UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, LLPS databases, RNA-binding resources, ClinVar, gnomAD, OMIM, and disease-specific variant collections. Inclusion criteria will require public accessibility, clear provenance, reusable licensing where possible, and sufficient metadata to map observations to genes, proteins, cell types, perturbations, assays, and phenotypes. In phase 2, we will harmonize datasets using standardized identifiers and metadata templates. Proteins will be mapped to UniProt and gene identifiers; RNAs to Ensembl or RefSeq; cell lines and cell types to Cellosaurus and Cell Ontology; perturbations to controlled vocabularies; and phenotypes to structured ontologies where feasible. Each observation will be assigned evidence attributes, including assay modality, confidence score, biological context, temporal scale, and directionality. Condensate membership will be represented probabilistically rather than as a binary label, allowing proximity proteomics, imaging colocalization, literature-curated membership, and perturbation evidence to contribute differently. In phase 3, we will build a condensate-centered knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, sequence features, modifications, RNAs, cellular contexts, material-state measurements, perturbations, and phenotypes. Feature engineering will quantify compositional diversity, scaffold-client balance, interaction valency, network centrality, disorder, low-complexity content, charge patterning, aromatic and polar residue grammar, predicted phase-separation propensity, RNA-binding density, modification burden, abundance, disease variant load, and pathway connectivity. Imaging-derived public features will include size, number, shape, intensity, colocalization, and dynamics when available. FRAP and single-particle tracking data will be normalized into comparable exchange and mobility descriptors with explicit uncertainty. In phase 4, we will develop interpretable machine-learning and network-inference models. Candidate approaches include regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, graph neural networks with explainability constraints, Bayesian hierarchical models, matrix factorization, and causal discovery methods appropriate for observational data. Models will be evaluated through nested cross-validation, held-out condensate families, held-out cell types, and temporal or perturbation splits. Benchmark tasks will include predicting condensate membership, material-state class, response to perturbation, and phenotypic outcome. Interpretability will be emphasized through feature attribution, stability selection, counterfactual analysis, and expert review. In phase 5, Working Group meetings and data sprints will integrate domain expertise with computational development. Subteams will focus on metadata standards, proteomics integration, imaging features, biophysical descriptors, RNA and modification features, disease variants, and trainee-led reproducible workflows. Milestones include a public data inventory by month 3, harmonized pilot datasets by month 6, a beta knowledge graph by month 12, benchmark models by month 18, and final open resources, manuscripts, and training materials by month 24.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will produce the first open, cross-system atlas linking biomolecular condensate composition, predicted material state, and cellular phenotype across public datasets. The primary scientific outcome will be a set of empirically supported rules describing how collective molecular features generate mesoscale behavior. We expect to identify feature combinations that distinguish adaptive, reversible condensates from persistent or toxic assemblies; define shared and condensate-specific regions of design space; and reveal how cellular context modifies condensate outcomes. These results will directly address a fundamental question in emergence: how do many weak molecular interactions produce higher-order cellular properties that are not predictable from individual components alone? The project will also deliver reusable community infrastructure. Outputs will include harmonized datasets, metadata standards, evidence scoring schemes, a condensate-centered knowledge graph, benchmark prediction tasks, interpretable modeling workflows, visualization tools, and documentation. These resources will enable researchers to compare condensate evidence across assay types, prioritize variants or perturbations likely to alter condensate behavior, and formulate experimentally testable hypotheses without duplicating curation effort. The impact will extend across cell biology, biophysics, systems biology, RNA biology, proteomics, disease genetics, and data science. For disease research, the framework may help explain why mutations in RNA-binding proteins, nucleolar factors, transcriptional regulators, or DNA-repair proteins cause pathology only in particular cellular contexts. For basic biology, it will clarify whether condensates obey shared design principles or represent unrelated assemblies with superficially similar appearances. For method development, the project will establish analytical strategies for modeling emergent mesoscale systems from heterogeneous public data. NCEMS support will amplify these impacts by enabling a community-scale collaboration that includes research-intensive institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, early-career scientists, and trainees. The resulting open resources and trained participants will strengthen the future workforce in data-savvy molecular and cellular science.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices from inception. All datasets used will be publicly available, and no new experimental data will be generated. We will maintain a public project repository containing data inventories, metadata templates, curation protocols, code, workflow documentation, issue tracking, and meeting summaries when appropriate. Derived datasets will include source citations, accession numbers, processing histories, license information, version numbers, and machine-readable provenance. When redistribution restrictions apply, we will release scripts and manifests that allow users to reconstruct derived resources from original public sources. Analytical workflows will be implemented in reproducible environments using containerization, workflow managers, and version-controlled notebooks. Model training and evaluation will include fixed data splits, documented hyperparameters, random seeds, uncertainty estimates, and complete reporting of negative or inconclusive results. The knowledge graph will use persistent identifiers and community ontologies whenever possible, supporting interoperability with existing molecular databases. All software will be released under permissive open-source licenses, and curated data products will be released under appropriate open data licenses consistent with source restrictions. We will create benchmark tasks with transparent evaluation metrics so that the broader community can compare new methods fairly. Governance will emphasize community participation and accountability. The Working Group will establish authorship, contribution, code review, data review, conflict resolution, and trainee mentoring policies at the outset. We will use contributor taxonomies to recognize curation, software, analysis, visualization, project management, and training contributions. Trainees will receive structured instruction in FAIR data principles, reproducible computing, responsible AI, metadata design, and collaborative software development. Public webinars, tutorials, and documentation will lower barriers for researchers at institutions with varied computational resources. By making all outputs findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable, and extensible, the project will ensure that NCEMS investment creates durable infrastructure for synthesis research beyond the initial Working Group.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because this project requires coordinated synthesis across data types, disciplines, and institutions rather than the resources of a single laboratory. Requested resources will support Working Group convenings, trainee participation, collaborative data sprints, computational infrastructure, project coordination, open-resource dissemination, and accessibility. In-person meetings at NCEMS will be used for high-value activities that cannot be accomplished efficiently by isolated teams: establishing consensus metadata standards, resolving cross-domain evidence definitions, designing benchmark tasks, evaluating preliminary models, and training participants across disciplinary boundaries. Virtual meetings will maintain momentum through monthly subteam check-ins and quarterly full-group integration sessions. Budget priorities include travel and lodging for investigators, trainees, and participants from under-resourced institutions; modest support for trainee time devoted to curation and reproducible workflow development; cloud computing or shared server resources for large-scale graph construction, image feature integration, and model training; software engineering assistance for public release of the knowledge graph and visualization tools; and publication, archiving, and outreach costs. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data. The team will leverage existing public infrastructure, including molecular databases, imaging repositories, proteomics archives, public code libraries, institutional high-performance computing where available, and open-source data science platforms. NCEMS resources will provide the neutral convening environment needed to align communities that rarely collaborate, including condensate biologists, proteomics experts, biophysicists, image analysts, RNA biologists, systems modelers, and disease geneticists. The Working Group will include senior investigators, early-career faculty, graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, data scientists, and educators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data initiatives. This structure will maximize scientific rigor while advancing NCEMS priorities for diverse participation and workforce development. The anticipated investment will yield durable public products: curated datasets, reusable workflows, training modules, benchmark models, an interactive knowledge graph, and manuscripts that define community standards for condensate synthesis research.

title: A Cross-Scale Public Data Synthesis to Predict When Biomolecular Condensates Emerge and Control Cellular Phenotypes
title_norm: a crossscale public data synthesis to predict when biomolecular condensates emerge and control cellular phenotypes
abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates are paradigmatic mesoscale structures: they emerge from weak, multivalent molecular interactions yet can reorganize signaling, transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and disease phenotypes. Despite thousands of studies, the field lacks a predictive synthesis explaining why the same protein can form a condensate in one cellular context but remain diffuse in another, or when condensate formation produces measurable cellular outcomes. This working group will integrate publicly available molecular, imaging, and functional genomic data to answer a central question: What combinations of molecular grammar, cellular state, and interaction context are sufficient to predict the emergence and phenotypic consequences of biomolecular condensates?

We will build an open, cross-scale Condensate Emergence Atlas by harmonizing existing datasets that are currently siloed across disciplines. Molecular features will be extracted from public protein sequence resources, AlphaFold structures, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification databases, RNA-binding datasets, protein-protein interaction maps, and condensate-specific repositories such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and curated literature-derived annotations. Mesoscale localization and morphology will be synthesized from public imaging resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, and published high-content microscopy datasets. Cellular state and outcome layers will incorporate public transcriptomics, proteomics, stress-response time courses, Perturb-seq and CRISPR screen datasets, DepMap dependencies, and disease-associated variant resources.

The project will develop reusable analytical strategies for emergence research. [Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates are paradigmatic mesoscale structures: they emerge from weak, multivalent molecular interactions yet can reorganize signaling, transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and disease phenotypes. Despite thousands of studies, the field lacks a predictive synthesis explaining why the same protein can form a condensate in one cellular context but remain diffuse in another, or when condensate formation produces measurable cellular outcomes. This working group will integrate publicly available molecular, imaging, and functional genomic data to answer a central question: What combinations of molecular grammar, cellular state, and interaction context are sufficient to predict the emergence and phenotypic consequences of biomolecular condensates?

We will build an open, cross-scale Condensate Emergence Atlas by harmonizing existing datasets that are currently siloed across disciplines. Molecular features will be extracted from public protein sequence resources, AlphaFold structures, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification databases, RNA-binding datasets, protein-protein interaction maps, and condensate-specific repositories such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and curated literature-derived annotations. Mesoscale localization and morphology will be synthesized from public imaging resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, and published high-content microscopy datasets. Cellular state and outcome layers will incorporate public transcriptomics, proteomics, stress-response time courses, Perturb-seq and CRISPR screen datasets, DepMap dependencies, and disease-associated variant resources.

The project will develop reusable analytical strategies for emergence research. First, we will create controlled vocabularies and probabilistic labels for condensate presence, morphology, dynamics, and cellular context, explicitly representing uncertainty across datasets. Second, we will use interpretable machine learning and graph-based models to connect molecular features, interaction networks, RNA context, post-translational modifications, and cell-state variables to observed mesoscale condensate formation. Third, we will test whether inferred condensate states explain higher-level cellular outcomes, such as stress survival, transcriptional rewiring, growth defects, and disease variant impact, beyond predictions from single-molecule properties alone. The central deliverable will be a set of open models that distinguish generalizable principles from dataset-specific artifacts and generate prioritized, experimentally testable hypotheses for the broader community.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the combined expertise or infrastructure to integrate image analysis, protein biophysics, RNA biology, cell biology, network science, functional genomics, and open-science software engineering at this scale. The working group will include condensate biologists, computational biophysicists, bioimage analysts, data curators, machine-learning researchers, cell-state and genomics experts, and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS working sessions will be used to establish shared data standards, perform collaborative model benchmarking, train graduate students and postdocs in reproducible synthesis workflows, and engage community stakeholders who maintain relevant public resources.

All products will follow open science principles: curated metadata, harmonized feature tables, analysis notebooks, containerized workflows, model code, benchmark datasets, and interactive visualizations will be released publicly with clear documentation and community contribution mechanisms. By transforming fragmented public observations into a predictive framework, this project will address a fundamental mystery in molecular and cellular sciences: how molecular-scale properties combine with cellular context to generate emergent mesoscale organization and cell-level consequences.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences. They arise when proteins, RNAs, and other macromolecules engage in many weak, dynamic, and context-dependent interactions that collectively generate mesoscale assemblies with properties not predictable from any single molecule alone. Condensates organize transcriptional hubs, stress granules, nucleoli, signaling clusters, DNA repair foci, germ granules, and pathological aggregates. Their formation can concentrate enzymes and substrates, buffer molecular noise, alter reaction kinetics, sequester regulators, remodel chromatin, and change cell fate decisions. Yet the field lacks a general predictive framework for when a condensate will appear, what morphology or dynamics it will adopt, and whether its formation will measurably influence cellular phenotypes. This gap is especially important because the same protein may form puncta in one cell type, stress condition, or perturbation background, but remain diffuse in another, suggesting that condensate emergence depends on cross-scale combinations of sequence grammar, structure, valency, post-translational modification, RNA availability, interaction networks, concentration, and cell state. A decade of intensive condensate research has generated a rich but fragmented public data landscape. Condensate-specific resources such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and literature-derived databases capture proteins and conditions associated with phase separation, but their annotations vary in evidence type, experimental context, and confidence. Public sequence, structure, disorder, motif, RNA-binding, post-translational modification, and protein interaction resources provide molecular predictors, but they are rarely integrated with cell biological observations. Imaging repositories such as the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, and high-content microscopy studies contain large-scale measurements of subcellular localization and punctate morphologies, but these data are not consistently labeled as condensate-related and often lack harmonized metadata describing cell state, stress, or perturbation context. Functional genomics resources, including Perturb-seq, CRISPR screens, DepMap dependencies, transcriptomic time courses, proteomic atlases, and disease variant catalogs, capture higher-level cellular outcomes but are seldom connected to mesoscale condensate states. The proposed working group addresses a fundamental NCEMS theme: how molecular-scale components generate emergent mesoscale structures that influence cellular phenotypes. The significance is both conceptual and practical. Conceptually, the project will test whether condensate emergence can be explained by general principles that operate across systems, or whether each condensate class is governed by idiosyncratic rules. Practically, it will provide a public synthesis resource and computational models that help researchers prioritize proteins, variants, cell states, and perturbations most likely to alter condensate behavior. Because the necessary evidence spans protein biophysics, RNA biology, bioimage analysis, systems biology, machine learning, disease genomics, and open data engineering, this synthesis exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory. NCEMS support is essential to convene the multidisciplinary expertise, shared infrastructure, community standards, and trainee-centered collaborative environment required to transform disconnected public observations into a rigorous, reusable framework for mesoscale emergence.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The central research question is: What combinations of molecular grammar, interaction context, and cellular state are sufficient to predict the emergence of biomolecular condensates and their phenotypic consequences? We will organize the working group around four linked questions. First, which molecular features are reproducibly associated with condensate formation across public datasets after accounting for study design, evidence type, and annotation uncertainty? Candidate features include intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity composition, aromatic and charged residue patterning, prion-like domains, folded interaction modules, short linear motifs, predicted multivalency, AlphaFold-derived accessibility, RNA-binding propensity, nucleic acid context, and post-translational modification sites. Second, how do cellular context variables modulate these molecular propensities? We will assess whether protein abundance, RNA abundance, cell type, stress condition, cell-cycle state, perturbation background, localization compartment, interaction partners, and signaling states explain why the same molecule condenses in some settings but not others. Third, do mesoscale condensate states improve prediction of cellular outcomes beyond models that use molecular features alone? Relevant outcomes include stress survival, transcriptional rewiring, growth defects, dependency phenotypes, changes in protein localization, altered RNA metabolism, and disease variant impact. Fourth, which inferred principles are robust across datasets and organisms, and which are artifacts of imaging modality, curation bias, cell line, or experimental condition? Our primary hypothesis is that condensate emergence is predictable from a limited set of cross-scale feature combinations rather than from single attributes such as disorder or low-complexity sequence alone. Specifically, we hypothesize that proteins with moderate-to-high interaction valency, context-specific concentration increases, accessible motif architecture, appropriate RNA or partner availability, and regulatory modification sites will show the strongest probability of condensate formation. A second hypothesis is that cellular state variables are not merely covariates but gating factors: molecularly competent proteins will remain diffuse unless abundance, binding partners, RNA pools, stress signaling, or compartmental constraints cross threshold-like regimes. This hypothesis directly addresses emergence because it predicts nonlinear transitions from diffuse molecular distributions to mesoscale organization. A third hypothesis is that condensate-associated phenotypes are most detectable when condensates occupy network control points, such as transcriptional regulators, RNA-binding hubs, stress-response factors, or proteins with high disease-variant burden. In these cases, condensate state should add explanatory power to models of expression changes, viability, and variant pathogenicity. A fourth hypothesis is that uncertainty-aware synthesis will reveal both strong general principles and domain-specific classes, including RNA-rich granules, transcriptional condensates, signaling clusters, and pathological assemblies with distinct feature weights. The project is intentionally designed to produce falsifiable outputs. If cross-scale models do not outperform molecular-only baselines, the result will constrain claims about general condensate grammar and identify where current public data are insufficient. If they do, the working group will define interpretable combinations of features and contexts that predict emergence, while generating prioritized hypotheses for independent experimental communities to test using their own systems.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will use only existing publicly available data and will not generate new experimental data. We will build the Condensate Emergence Atlas through five coordinated workstreams conducted during NCEMS-facilitated working sessions and virtual sprints. Workstream 1 will define data standards and evidence vocabularies. The team will harmonize terms for condensate presence, absence, morphology, compartment, dynamics, perturbation, cell type, stress condition, assay type, and evidence strength. Because public annotations vary in reliability, labels will be probabilistic rather than binary where appropriate, distinguishing direct phase-separation assays, endogenous imaging, overexpression puncta, literature inference, and computational prediction. Workstream 2 will assemble molecular and interaction features. Protein identifiers will be mapped across UniProt, Ensembl, HGNC, RefSeq, and model-organism resources. Features will include amino-acid composition, low-complexity and intrinsically disordered regions, sequence patterning, short linear motifs, prion-like domains, folded domains, AlphaFold structural properties, solvent accessibility proxies, RNA-binding evidence, post-translational modification sites from public databases, protein abundance, and protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction network measures. Condensate annotations will be integrated from PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, public literature tables, and related repositories. Workstream 3 will synthesize image-derived mesoscale phenotypes. Public images and feature tables from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, and published high-content datasets will be mined for localization, puncta number, size, intensity, texture, compartment enrichment, and condition-specific changes. Where reusable segmentations or feature tables exist, we will use them directly; where public images are available with permissive reuse, we will apply standardized open-source image analysis workflows. Manual review by domain experts will create benchmark subsets, but no new imaging data will be produced. Workstream 4 will connect condensate states to cell-state and functional outcomes. Public transcriptomics, proteomics, stress-response time courses, Perturb-seq, CRISPR screens, DepMap dependencies, disease variant resources, and pathway annotations will be linked through common gene, protein, cell-line, and condition identifiers. Workstream 5 will develop and benchmark models. Baseline models will include regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, and calibrated classifiers. Graph neural networks or heterogeneous graph models will integrate proteins, RNAs, interactions, modifications, compartments, cell states, and outcomes. Interpretable methods, including SHAP analysis, feature ablation, counterfactual prediction, partial dependence, and subgroup-specific models, will identify candidate mechanisms rather than only maximize accuracy. Rigor will be ensured through predefined train-test splits by dataset, protein family, cell type, and publication source; negative-control labels; batch-effect assessment; leakage checks; uncertainty propagation; and comparison with molecular-only baselines. Deliverables will include harmonized tables, benchmark label sets, reusable workflows, trained models, model cards, and a public interactive Atlas. Trainees will participate in data curation, coding, benchmarking, documentation, and cross-disciplinary interpretation under mentorship from experts in condensate biology, bioimage informatics, biophysics, genomics, network science, and open-source software.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver an open Condensate Emergence Atlas that links molecular features, public imaging phenotypes, cell-state variables, interaction networks, and functional outcomes for condensate-associated and comparison proteins. The Atlas will provide harmonized identifiers, controlled vocabularies, uncertainty-aware labels, curated benchmark sets, reproducible feature matrices, and interactive visualizations that allow users to explore when and where condensate-like mesoscale states occur. We will also deliver interpretable predictive models that estimate condensate emergence probability across cellular contexts and test whether inferred condensate states improve prediction of stress responses, transcriptional changes, growth phenotypes, disease variant effects, and genetic dependencies. Scientific impact will arise from replacing fragmented, anecdotal, and assay-specific observations with a community-scale synthesis capable of distinguishing general principles from dataset-specific artifacts. The work will clarify whether condensate behavior is primarily encoded by molecular grammar, gated by cellular state, shaped by interaction networks, or driven by combinations of all three. It will identify proteins and variants whose predicted condensate behavior is most context-sensitive, generating prioritized hypotheses for experimental laboratories without requiring this working group to produce new data. Methodological impact will extend beyond condensates. The uncertainty-aware ontology, cross-scale data integration strategy, imaging-to-function linkage, and benchmarking framework will be reusable for other emergent mesoscale systems, including cytoskeletal assemblies, membrane-less organelles, signaling nanodomains, and chromatin compartments. Broader impacts include training graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in data synthesis, reproducible computational biology, team science, and responsible use of AI. By including investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, data-resource teams, and multiple career stages, the project will broaden participation in high-impact synthesis research and create durable community infrastructure aligned with NCEMS goals.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All project products will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science practices consistent with NCEMS expectations. We will release the Condensate Emergence Atlas, metadata schemas, controlled vocabularies, probabilistic labels, feature tables, benchmark datasets, model code, documentation, and analysis notebooks through public repositories with persistent identifiers. Code will be developed in version-controlled repositories using issue tracking, pull requests, continuous integration, automated testing, and transparent contribution guidelines. Computational environments will be containerized using Docker or Apptainer and described with machine-readable workflow specifications such as Snakemake, Nextflow, or equivalent open workflow systems. Where data licenses permit redistribution, processed datasets will be deposited in repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, or domain-specific archives; where redistribution is restricted, scripts will retrieve data from original sources and record provenance, access dates, versions, and transformations. Reproducibility will be strengthened through data and model cards documenting source datasets, inclusion criteria, known biases, uncertainty estimates, intended uses, limitations, and ethical considerations. Model evaluation will include locked benchmark splits, negative controls, leakage detection, calibration metrics, and sensitivity analyses. We will preregister core benchmarking decisions within the project repository before final model comparison to reduce analytical flexibility. All publications will be open access when possible, and preprints will be posted before or at submission. Community engagement will be supported through public webinars, tutorials, example notebooks, and mechanisms for external users to submit corrections or new public dataset links. Trainees will receive structured training in FAIR data principles, reproducible workflows, responsible machine learning, metadata curation, and collaborative software development. The project will not claim ownership of underlying public data; instead, it will add value through harmonization, provenance-preserving synthesis, transparent uncertainty representation, and reusable analytical infrastructure that the broader molecular and cellular sciences community can inspect, extend, and critique.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested because the project requires coordinated expertise, shared cyberinfrastructure, and sustained working-group time beyond the capacity of any single laboratory or bilateral collaboration. Funds will support in-person and virtual working sessions that convene condensate biologists, computational biophysicists, RNA biologists, bioimage analysts, systems biologists, machine-learning researchers, data curators, software engineers, and trainees. Travel funds will prioritize broad participation across geographic regions, institution types, and career stages, including investigators from primarily undergraduate institutions and trainees who would otherwise lack access to synthesis-center activities. Personnel support will include partial effort for a project coordinator or data scientist to maintain timelines, organize metadata standards, manage repositories, document workflows, and ensure that working-group outputs remain interoperable and reproducible. Computational resources will be used for public data ingestion, image-feature extraction from openly available datasets, graph construction, model training, benchmarking, storage of processed feature tables, and hosting of prototype interactive visualizations. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase experimental reagents, recruit human subjects, or perform new wet-laboratory assays. The working group will leverage existing public databases, open-source software, institutional computing resources, and NCEMS collaborative infrastructure. Budget categories will include travel and lodging for workshops, trainee participation and short-term synthesis residencies, modest cloud or high-performance computing costs, software engineering and data curation effort, accessibility support for hybrid meetings, publication and data deposition fees, and outreach or training materials. NCEMS resources are essential not merely as funding but as convening infrastructure: neutral facilitation, standards development, collaborative project management, and training in open synthesis practices will enable a genuinely community-scale effort. The anticipated return on investment is high because the project transforms already-funded public datasets into durable models, reusable workflows, and community benchmarks that will accelerate many future experimental and computational studies.

Stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, Cajal bodies, nuclear speckles, DNA repair foci, and transcriptional condensates are not merely passive aggregates. They concentrate selected molecules, exclude others, alter reaction rates, buffer noise, tune gene expression, and coordinate cellular responses to stress, development, infection, and damage. Their properties arise from many weak, multivalent, context-dependent interactions among folded domains, intrinsically disordered regions, short linear motifs, RNA-binding modules, nucleic acids, and modifying enzymes. These assemblies therefore embody the NCEMS mission: understanding how new system-level properties appear across scales of composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion. A persistent barrier is that condensate biology remains fragmented. Individual studies have revealed important principles, including the roles of low-complexity sequence, charge patterning, aromatic residues, RNA valency, phosphorylation, methylation, ATP-dependent remodeling, molecular crowding, and network architecture. However, many observations are condensate-specific, cell-type-specific, or assay-dependent. Proteins that phase separate in vitro may not form condensates in vivo; condensates that appear compositionally similar can have distinct material states; and assemblies that support normal stress adaptation can transition toward pathological persistence or cytotoxic aggregation in neurodegeneration, cancer, and viral infection. The field lacks a rigorous synthesis that distinguishes general design principles from context-specific mechanisms and from artifacts of measurement. This proposal addresses that gap using only existing public data. The timing is ideal. Over the past decade, public resources have accumulated across multiple relevant scales: curated phase-separation and condensate databases, proteome-wide disorder and domain annotations, RNA-binding and transcript feature maps, interactomes from affinity purification, proximity labeling, yeast two-hybrid screens, crosslinking mass spectrometry, perturbation transcriptomics and proteomics, post-translational modification atlases, high-content microscopy screens, single-cell data, disease variant catalogs, and literature-mined condensate annotations. It also requires community consensus on how to describe condensate identity, material state, perturbation context, and uncertainty. By convening a diverse working group across institution types and career stages, NCEMS will enable an integrative framework for predicting when molecular features and cellular contexts produce reversible functional condensates versus aberrant states. The resulting synthesis will advance fundamental molecular and cellular science while establishing reusable infrastructure for future studies of mesoscale emergence.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will pursue one overarching question: which combinations of molecular features, interaction networks, cellular contexts, and perturbations determine emergent condensate identity, material state, and downstream cellular function? Question 1 asks whether condensate membership can be predicted from proteome-scale and transcriptome-scale features. We hypothesize that condensate enrichment is not determined by any single feature, such as intrinsic disorder, but by a multivalent architecture combining disordered regions, folded interaction domains, short linear motifs, RNA-binding capacity, charge patterning, aromatic and polar residue content, post-translational modification sites, expression level, and interaction-network position. We further hypothesize that different condensate classes use partly shared design logic but distinct feature weights; for example, stress granules may be more dependent on RNA-binding and stress-regulated phosphorylation, whereas transcriptional condensates may rely more heavily on activation domains, chromatin contacts, and coactivator networks. Question 2 asks whether public datasets contain sufficient information to infer emergent material states such as liquid-like, gel-like, solid-like, reversible, persistent, or aging-prone assemblies. We hypothesize that material state can be predicted probabilistically from sequence grammar, valency, interaction strength, RNA stoichiometry, modification state, and chaperone or remodeling factor connectivity. We expect that disease-linked or aberrant condensate states will occupy recognizable regions of this feature space, characterized by increased aggregation propensity, altered charge or aromatic patterning, disrupted modification sites, expanded repeat domains, or loss of regulatory interactions. Question 3 asks how cellular context and perturbation reshape condensate behavior. We hypothesize that context acts through measurable axes, including cell type, stress modality, developmental state, expression dosage, metabolic state, signaling pathway activation, and availability of RNA or chromatin substrates. Perturbations such as kinase inhibition, stress exposure, viral infection, gene knockdown, mutation, or drug treatment should shift condensate phenotypes in ways that are predictable from network proximity to scaffold molecules, client molecules, modifiers, and dissolution factors. Question 4 asks whether mesoscale condensate predictions explain higher-level cellular outcomes. We hypothesize that condensate identity and material state mediate measurable functional consequences, including translational repression, mRNA stabilization or decay, ribosome biogenesis, DNA damage signaling, enhancer activity, antiviral response, and cytotoxicity. We will test whether models incorporating mesoscale condensate variables outperform models using molecular abundance or interaction data alone. A methodological hypothesis underlies all four questions: harmonized knowledge graphs and reproducible image-analysis pipelines can convert heterogeneous public studies into reliable benchmark datasets with explicit uncertainty. Rather than seeking a single universal condensate rule, we will build interpretable, uncertainty-aware models that identify robust mechanisms, condensate-specific exceptions, and data gaps. These hypotheses are falsifiable using held-out datasets, cross-study validation, negative controls, and comparison with known non-condensate proteins, unrelated cellular structures, and perturbations not expected to affect condensate formation.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will be organized as an NCEMS working group with coordinated subteams for data curation, ontology development, image analysis, graph integration, predictive modeling, causal analysis, and training. No new experimental data will be generated. All inputs will be publicly available and will include phase-separation and condensate resources such as LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, CD-CODE, RNA granule annotations, and manually curated literature tables; protein sequence and structure annotations from UniProt, AlphaFold, Pfam, InterPro, MobiDB, DisProt, PLAAC, IUPred, and low-complexity predictors; RNA-binding and transcript resources from ENCODE, POSTAR, CLIPdb, RBPbase, RNAcentral, and transcript feature databases; protein interaction and proximity resources from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, HuRI, CORUM, OpenCell, BioPlex, proximity-labeling datasets, and crosslinking mass spectrometry repositories; post-translational modification resources from PhosphoSitePlus, dbPTM, PRIDE, MassIVE, and ProteomeXchange; perturbation resources from GEO, SRA, ArrayExpress, PRIDE, DepMap, LINCS, Perturb-seq, and CRISPR screens; imaging data from the Cell Image Library, Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, and high-content screen repositories; and disease resources including ClinVar, OMIM, DisGeNET, gnomAD, COSMIC, and neurodegeneration variant datasets. Aim 1 will construct an open, versioned condensate knowledge graph. We will map identifiers across proteins, genes, RNAs, variants, publications, cell types, organisms, treatments, assays, and phenotypes. The team will develop a condensate-state ontology covering assembly identity, localization, morphology, dynamics, material descriptors, perturbation context, evidence type, and confidence. Existing ontologies such as Gene Ontology, Cell Ontology, Experimental Factor Ontology, Protein Ontology, Sequence Ontology, and OBO Foundry resources will be reused whenever possible. Evidence will be annotated with provenance, assay type, directionality, uncertainty, and potential bias. Aim 2 will create benchmark feature matrices and phenotype labels. Quantitative molecular features will include disorder, charge patterning, stickers and spacers, prion-like composition, domain valency, motif counts, RNA-binding potential, expression abundance, modification-site density, disease-variant burden, and network centrality. Imaging subteams will develop reproducible workflows using tools such as CellProfiler, ilastik, napari, scikit-image, DeepCell, and segmentation models adapted to public images. Extracted features will include condensate count, size, circularity, localization, intensity, colocalization, dissolution kinetics where time series exist, and cell-to-cell heterogeneity. Aim 3 will build interpretable predictive models. We will compare penalized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, graph neural networks, Bayesian hierarchical models, and calibrated ensemble methods. Models will be evaluated with nested cross-validation, cross-dataset validation, organism and cell-type holdouts, label-noise models, and negative controls. Interpretability methods will identify molecular and network features associated with specific condensate classes and material states. Aim 4 will test functional mediation using existing perturbation datasets. Causal inference approaches, including directed acyclic graphs, propensity weighting, difference-in-differences, mediation analysis, and network intervention models, will assess whether predicted condensate changes help explain transcriptomic, proteomic, imaging, or fitness outcomes. Working-group meetings will be used for ontology consensus, model comparison, reproducibility audits, trainee hackathons, and preparation of community standards.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver scientific, methodological, and community impacts directly aligned with NCEMS priorities. Scientifically, we expect to produce the first cross-scale predictive framework linking molecular features, interaction architecture, cellular context, condensate phenotypes, material state, and downstream function across major classes of membraneless organelles. The framework will identify which principles generalize across condensates and which are specific to stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, nuclear speckles, DNA damage foci, or disease-associated assemblies. We expect to clarify why some molecular mixtures form reversible, adaptive, functional states whereas others become persistent, aberrant, or cytotoxic. Methodologically, the working group will produce an open condensate knowledge graph, harmonized benchmark datasets, ontology terms for mesoscale phenotypes, reproducible image-analysis workflows, trained predictive models, uncertainty estimates, and negative-control sets. These resources will enable rigorous comparison of competing models and reduce overinterpretation of isolated phase-separation assays. The synthesis will also provide practical tools for prioritizing candidate scaffold proteins, client molecules, regulatory modifications, disease variants, and perturbations likely to alter condensate behavior, while explicitly labeling predictions that require future experimental validation outside the scope of this project. The broader impact will be a reusable model for community-scale synthesis in molecular and cellular biosciences. By integrating public data rather than generating new experiments, the project will increase the value of existing investments in proteomics, imaging, sequencing, structural prediction, perturbation screening, and curated databases. The team will train graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and undergraduate participants in collaborative data science, responsible AI, ontology-based curation, uncertainty-aware modeling, and open-source software development. Participation by primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data infrastructure groups, and research-intensive universities will broaden access to synthesis biology and recruit diverse talent into mesoscale cell biology. Final products will support both discovery and education: publications describing design principles, public tutorials, reusable notebooks, community standards, and an extensible data infrastructure for future NCEMS working groups studying emergence.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Open science is central to the project design. All non-restricted inputs will come from publicly available repositories, and all derived datasets, code, models, documentation, tutorials, and standards will be released under open licenses. The working group will follow FAIR principles by assigning persistent identifiers, preserving provenance, documenting metadata, using interoperable ontologies, and depositing outputs in stable repositories such as Zenodo, GitHub, GitLab, Figshare, BioImage Archive, and appropriate domain repositories. The condensate knowledge graph will be versioned, with each release accompanied by machine-readable metadata, changelogs, data dictionaries, provenance records, and quality-control summaries. Reproducibility will be enforced through containerized workflows, scripted analyses, continuous integration, workflow managers, and environment files. Image-analysis and modeling pipelines will be implemented as reusable notebooks and command-line workflows with test datasets, unit tests, validation reports, and documented parameters. Model training will use predefined data splits, held-out benchmarks, cross-study validation, calibration metrics, and transparent reporting of failures as well as successes. We will publish negative controls, uncertainty estimates, missingness patterns, and evidence grades so that users can judge where predictions are reliable. To support responsible AI, we will document training data composition, known biases, label uncertainty, model limitations, and appropriate use cases. Community governance will include an open contributor guide, code of conduct, authorship and credit policy, issue tracker, and regular public updates. Working-group outputs will be shared early through preprints, open seminars, and public release candidates to invite feedback before final publication. Trainees will receive structured training in reproducible analysis, collaborative coding, data ethics, metadata standards, and review of computational workflows. The group will avoid proprietary dependencies whenever possible and will ensure that all workflows can run on accessible computing infrastructure. Because the project synthesizes existing data, special attention will be given to respecting original data licenses, properly crediting source investigators, and linking all derived claims to evidence provenance. These practices will make the project transparent, reusable, extensible, and consistent with NCEMS expectations for open, team-based, reproducible synthesis science.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested for activities that enable community-scale synthesis rather than new experimental data generation. Funds will support three in-person working-group meetings over two years, regular virtual coordination, trainee participation, collaborative software development, data curation, cloud or high-performance computing time for image processing and model training, and dissemination of open resources. No budget line will support new wet-lab experiments, sample collection, proprietary datasets, or unpublished private data. Travel support is essential because the project depends on consensus building among experts who do not normally work together: condensate biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics specialists, microscopy analysts, ontology engineers, graph database developers, machine-learning researchers, causal inference experts, data librarians, and open-science trainers. Meeting funds will prioritize participation by graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career investigators, researchers from minority-serving institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, and institutions with limited travel resources. Each meeting will have concrete deliverables: first, ontology and data-inventory consensus; second, benchmark dataset and model-comparison review; third, community standards, manuscript integration, and sustainability planning. Computational resources will be used for public image retrieval, segmentation, feature extraction, graph construction, model training, validation, and web-accessible documentation. Software support will maintain versioned repositories, automated testing, container builds, user documentation, and public tutorials. Modest trainee support will fund cross-site analysis sprints, mentoring groups, and short virtual workshops in reproducible pipelines, responsible AI, and biological interpretation of condensate data. Participating laboratories will contribute in-kind expertise, existing code, curated domain knowledge, institutional computing access where available, and mentorship time. NCEMS coordination is uniquely necessary because the project requires neutral convening, shared governance, sustained collaboration, and synthesis infrastructure beyond any single laboratory or bilateral collaboration. The requested resources will transform scattered public datasets into durable community products: an open knowledge graph, harmonized benchmarks, reusable analysis workflows, predictive models, training materials, and consensus standards that will remain valuable after the award period.

abstract_original:
Membraneless organelles such as stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, and transcriptional condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: dynamic assemblies arise from many weak molecular interactions yet produce higher-order cellular outcomes including RNA regulation, signaling, genome organization, and stress adaptation. Despite extensive studies of individual condensates, the field lacks a predictive, systems-level understanding of why some molecular mixtures form reversible functional assemblies whereas others yield aberrant, disease-linked states. This working group will synthesize existing public data to answer a central question: which combinations of molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and perturbations determine emergent condensate identity, material state, and downstream cellular function?

The project will integrate publicly available datasets spanning scales that are rarely analyzed together. These will include protein and RNA sequence features; curated phase-separation and condensate-partitioning databases; affinity-purification, proximity-labeling, and crosslinking mass spectrometry interaction maps; single-cell and bulk transcriptomic/proteomic perturbation datasets; microscopy image repositories reporting condensate number, size, localization, and dynamics; post-translational modification datasets; and disease-variant resources. We will harmonize these data into an open, versioned knowledge graph linking molecules, interaction motifs, cellular conditions, condensate phenotypes, and functional outcomes. The synthesis will explicitly address data heterogeneity by developing shared ontologies for condensate states, experimental conditions, and mesoscale phenotypes, enabling comparison across laboratories, organisms, cell types, and stress conditions.

Analytically, the group will combine biophysics, cell biology, network science, machine learning, and causal inference. We will build interpretable models that predict condensate membership and emergent material behavior from multivalent interaction architecture, intrinsically disordered region properties, RNA-binding features, modification states, and network topology. We will then test whether these mesoscale predictions explain higher-level outcomes such as translational repression, RNA stabilization, DNA damage response, or cytotoxic aggregation using only existing perturbation and imaging datasets. A major methodological product will be an open workflow for extracting quantitative condensate phenotypes from public microscopy images and connecting them to molecular datasets through reproducible pipelines. Rather than generating new experiments, the working group will produce benchmark datasets, uncertainty estimates, negative controls, and community standards for evaluating claims about biomolecular condensates.

This effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory currently spans the required expertise in condensate biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, image analysis, data curation, graph modeling, and open-science software engineering. The proposed team will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, national data infrastructure groups, and minority-serving institutions, with trainees embedded in cross-site analysis teams. NCEMS working-group meetings will enable iterative synthesis, ontology development, model comparison, and community consensus building that would not arise from a conventional bilateral collaboration.

The expected outcome is a predictive framework for condensate emergence that distinguishes general design principles from condensate-specific mechanisms. By integrating public data across molecular, mesoscale, and cellular levels, the project will clarify how weak interactions collectively generate organized subcellular states and how those states influence cell fate. All harmonized datasets, code, trained models, documentation, and tutorials will be released publicly under open licenses. Trainees will receive hands-on training in reproducible data science, collaborative software development, responsible AI, and team-based synthesis biology. The project will therefore advance a fundamental question in molecular and cellular sciences while creating reusable community resources for studying emergent mesoscale organization.
