[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, metabolites, and membranes produce dynamic compartments whose collective properties cannot be inferred from any single component. Despite thousands of public datasets on protein localization, phase separation, RNA binding, perturbation phenotypes, and disease variation, a central question remains unresolved: what molecular and cellular contexts determine when condensates form, what material states they adopt, and whether they buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build and test an integrative, predictive framework for condensate emergence across human cells and model organisms.

The project will assemble a community-scale team spanning molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure. The group will integrate existing public resources including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold and protein language model embeddings, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, public stress-response transcriptomics, CRISPR perturbation screens from DepMap and BioGRID ORCS, and ClinVar/gnomAD disease variant annotations. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will harmonize these heterogeneous datasets into a FAIR, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular state, mesoscale morphology, dynamics, and phenotypic outcomes.

The core scientific innovation is to treat condensates not merely as lists of phase-separating proteins, but as emergent systems whose properties depend on multivalent molecular grammar, expression stoichiometry, post-translational modification potential, RNA context, interaction network topology, and cellular stress history. We will develop transparent AI and statistical models to predict three linked outcomes: condensate membership, emergent material or morphological class, and downstream cellular consequence after perturbation. By comparing predictions across stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P bodies, nuclear speckles, and disease-associated aggregates, we will test whether shared rules govern distinct condensate systems or whether each represents a context-specific emergent regime. A special focus will be placed on long-standing puzzles, including why proteins with similar intrinsically disordered regions produce different condensate behaviors, why some condensates are protective while others become pathological, and how disease mutations shift mesoscale organization without necessarily altering canonical molecular function.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis beyond the scope of any single laboratory: cross-dataset ontology alignment, image-derived feature extraction, multimodal model development, biological interpretation across condensate classes, and community governance for reusable data products. Working-group meetings will produce shared standards for condensate metadata, benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, and open tutorials. Trainees from diverse institutions will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams and trained in data integration, responsible AI, reproducible workflow design, and collaborative synthesis science.

All outputs will be released openly, including curated datasets, code, model cards, workflow containers, documentation, and interactive visualization tools. The expected outcome is a generalizable synthesis framework for predicting how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale condensate behavior and cellular phenotypes, providing a foundational resource for emergence-focused molecular and cellular biology.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are dynamic mesoscale assemblies formed through multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, nucleic acids, lipids, metabolites, and membranes. They include stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, transcriptional hubs, heterochromatin-associated compartments, signaling clusters, and disease-linked aggregates. These structures exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences because their morphology, dynamics, composition, material state, and physiological consequence arise from collective interactions rather than from a single molecule or pathway. Condensates can accelerate reactions, sequester biomolecules, organize gene expression, buffer stress, and coordinate cell fate decisions; however, similar molecular ingredients can also produce pathological solidification, aberrant sequestration, and toxic gain of function in cancer, neurodegeneration, viral infection, and developmental disease.

A central barrier in the field is that condensate knowledge remains fragmented across disciplinary and data silos. Biophysical databases curate phase-separating proteins and in vitro observations, whereas cell biological resources capture localization, imaging phenotypes, and perturbation responses. RNA biology datasets map RNA-binding proteins and transcript targets, while proteomics repositories quantify abundance, post-translational modifications, and stress-dependent remodeling. Structural and sequence resources describe intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, charge patterning, aromatic residues, prion-like regions, folded interaction modules, and predicted conformations. Clinical variant databases catalog mutations that may alter condensate behavior without abolishing canonical enzymatic or binding functions. These data are publicly available, but they are not harmonized into a framework capable of explaining how molecular grammar gives rise to mesoscale organization and cellular phenotype.

This gap is especially important because the dominant paradigm often treats condensates as lists of components or binary phase-separation labels. Such representations obscure the contextual determinants of emergence: expression stoichiometry, RNA availability, network connectivity, post-translational modification state, subcellular location, cell type, stress history, and energetic environment. They also make it difficult to distinguish protective condensates from maladaptive aggregates or to infer why homologous proteins and proteins with apparently similar disordered regions can show different condensate behaviors. Resolving these puzzles requires community-scale synthesis that integrates molecular biophysics, imaging, omics, perturbational genomics, disease genetics, and machine learning.

This project directly aligns with the NCEMS mission by using only publicly available data to answer fundamental questions about emergent mesoscale biological properties. The proposed atlas will transform dispersed observations into a FAIR, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph and predictive modeling resource. By linking molecular features to mesoscale material and morphological states, and then to cell-level phenotypes, the working group will generate a reusable framework for studying emergence across scales of composition, space, time, information, and cellular function. The project is beyond the capacity of any individual laboratory because it requires ontology alignment, large-scale image feature extraction, multimodal model development, biological interpretation across condensate systems, and community governance. NCEMS support will enable a transdisciplinary synthesis team to establish shared standards, train data-savvy trainees, and produce open resources that accelerate discovery across molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching research question is: what combinations of molecular grammar, cellular context, and interaction-network architecture determine the emergence of biomolecular condensates, their mesoscale material states, and their downstream cellular consequences? We will address this question through three linked aims that treat condensate formation, condensate state, and phenotype as coupled emergent outcomes rather than independent observations.

Question 1 asks which molecular and contextual features predict condensate membership across diverse biological systems. We hypothesize that condensate membership is best predicted by combinations of multivalent interaction features rather than by intrinsic disorder alone. Relevant features include low-complexity sequence composition, charge patterning, aromatic and sticker-spacer architecture, RNA-binding domains, modular folded interaction domains, prion-like regions, predicted structural disorder, post-translational modification potential, protein abundance, subcellular localization, RNA target abundance, and protein-protein interaction degree. We further hypothesize that distinct condensate classes use partially overlapping molecular grammars: for example, stress granules and P bodies will emphasize RNA-binding and translation-related features, whereas nucleoli and transcriptional condensates will show stronger coupling to ribonucleoprotein biogenesis, chromatin association, and transcriptional regulatory networks.

Question 2 asks what determines emergent material and morphological state. Public imaging and curated databases distinguish liquid-like, gel-like, solid-like, punctate, spherical, irregular, fibrillar, reversible, and stress-dependent states, but these labels are inconsistent and incomplete. We hypothesize that material and morphological state arise from nonlinear interactions among molecular grammar, concentration, stoichiometry, modification state, RNA context, and network topology. Proteins with similar intrinsically disordered regions may diverge in behavior because of differences in interaction valency, sequence patterning, folded-domain scaffolding, RNA binding specificity, local abundance, and recruitment to preexisting cellular structures. We predict that graph-based and multimodal models will identify condensate state features that are not visible from sequence alone but emerge when expression, localization, interaction partners, and stress condition are integrated.

Question 3 asks when condensates buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress. We hypothesize that protective condensates are characterized by reversible assembly, enrichment for adaptive stress-response functions, and network positions that sequester or reorganize vulnerable factors without collapsing essential processes. In contrast, pathological or maladaptive condensates will be associated with high-risk sequence features, disease variants that alter interaction valency or charge patterning, persistent localization changes, impaired clearance pathways, and perturbation phenotypes indicating reduced viability, altered transcriptional programs, or proteostasis failure. We will test whether disease mutations shift predicted material state and network influence even when canonical molecular functions remain intact.

A cross-cutting hypothesis is that condensate systems occupy a limited number of emergent regimes defined by molecular grammar, mesoscale state, and phenotypic consequence. Some rules may generalize across stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated assemblies, while others will be context-specific. The project will therefore compare shared versus specialized predictors, quantify uncertainty, and identify cases where existing public data are insufficient. The result will be a falsifiable, community-extensible model of condensate emergence.

[Methods and Approach]
The working group will conduct a synthesis-only project using existing public datasets; no new experimental data will be generated. The project will be organized into five coordinated work packages led by cross-disciplinary subteams including molecular biophysicists, cell biologists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, machine-learning researchers, network scientists, database engineers, and trainees.

Work Package 1 will define metadata standards, ontologies, and inclusion criteria. We will map condensate names, aliases, organisms, cell types, experimental conditions, stressors, localization terms, material-state descriptors, and evidence types using controlled vocabularies where possible, including Gene Ontology, Cell Ontology, PSI-MI, Sequence Ontology, Disease Ontology, and OBO Foundry resources. Ambiguous labels such as granule-like, aggregate-like, and phase-separated will be assigned evidence codes and uncertainty scores. The group will produce a community condensate metadata schema suitable for future reuse.

Work Package 2 will assemble the condensate-emergence knowledge graph. Core sources will include LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, UniProt, AlphaFold structures, protein language model embeddings, ENCODE eCLIP and RNA-binding protein datasets, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, PhosphoSitePlus where licensing permits, GEO and Expression Atlas stress-response transcriptomics, DepMap and BioGRID ORCS CRISPR screens, STRING and BioGRID interactions, ClinVar, gnomAD, OMIM annotations where accessible, and disease-variant effect predictors. Nodes will represent genes, proteins, isoforms, domains, motifs, RNAs, interactions, modifications, cell states, condensate classes, images, perturbations, variants, and phenotypes. Edges will encode evidence provenance, condition, confidence, and source version.

Work Package 3 will extract features across modalities. Sequence features will include disorder, low complexity, charge patterning, aromatic content, sticker-spacer metrics, prion-like regions, domain architecture, predicted structure, and embeddings from protein language models. Contextual features will include abundance, stoichiometry, tissue and cell-type expression, stress inducibility, RNA targets, localization patterns, interaction-network centrality, modification-site density, and variant burden. Imaging subteams will use established, reproducible computer-vision workflows and foundation-model embeddings to quantify puncta number, size, shape, texture, spatial distribution, co-localization, and condition-dependent relocalization from public microscopy images.

Work Package 4 will develop transparent predictive models for three outcomes: condensate membership, material or morphological class, and phenotypic consequence after perturbation. We will compare interpretable statistical models, gradient-boosted trees, graph neural networks, multimodal representation learning, and calibrated ensemble approaches. Training and evaluation will use nested cross-validation, organism-aware and condensate-class-aware data splits, negative-set sensitivity analyses, batch-effect diagnostics, and external validation on held-out databases. Model interpretation will use feature attribution, counterfactual analyses, pathway enrichment, and expert review.

Work Package 5 will synthesize biological insight through comparative case studies of stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, transcriptional condensates, and disease-linked aggregates. Working-group meetings will be structured around data harmonization sprints, model review sessions, biological interpretation workshops, and trainee-led reproducibility checks. Milestones include a public schema and pilot graph by month 6, benchmark datasets by month 12, first-generation models by month 18, cross-condensate comparative analyses by month 24, and final atlas release with tutorials by month 30.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open, FAIR, versioned condensate-emergence atlas linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, mesoscale morphology, material state, perturbation phenotypes, and disease variation. This resource will convert fragmented public datasets into a coherent synthesis platform that can be queried by molecule, condensate class, cell state, stress condition, phenotype, or variant. The atlas will include provenance-rich annotations, uncertainty estimates, reusable benchmarks, and interactive visualizations.

The project will also deliver predictive and interpretable models for three coupled outcomes: whether a protein or RNA is likely to participate in a condensate, what mesoscale state or morphology is expected under defined contexts, and whether perturbation is predicted to buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress. These models will not be treated as black boxes; they will be accompanied by model cards, performance reports, feature-attribution summaries, and documented limitations. The resulting predictions will identify candidate general rules of condensate emergence as well as context-specific regimes that differ among stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated assemblies.

Scientifically, the work will address long-standing puzzles in condensate biology, including why similar disordered proteins behave differently, why some condensates remain reversible while others mature into pathological assemblies, and how disease variants alter mesoscale organization without eliminating canonical function. Methodologically, the project will establish a transferable synthesis strategy for connecting molecular-scale data to mesoscale emergent states and cellular outcomes. Community impact will include new metadata standards, curated benchmark datasets, open tutorials, and trainee training in collaborative data science. Because the work uses public data only and requires broad expertise, it is well matched to NCEMS priorities and will provide a foundation for future emergence-focused discovery across molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will operate under open, team, and reproducible science principles from inception. All public datasets used in the project will be documented with source identifiers, access dates, licenses, versions, preprocessing steps, and provenance metadata. Derived datasets will be released in FAIR formats through appropriate repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, GitHub, and domain repositories when available. The knowledge graph will be distributed in interoperable formats including RDF, JSON-LD, TSV edge lists, and graph database dumps, accompanied by a data dictionary and ontology mappings.

All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories using issue tracking, code review, continuous integration, and semantic versioning. Reproducible workflows will be implemented with portable workflow tools such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or equivalent systems, and computational environments will be distributed as containers. Analyses will include executable notebooks, scripted pipelines, test datasets, and automated checks that allow external users to reproduce tables, figures, model training, and benchmark evaluations. Model releases will include trained weights where licensing permits, hyperparameters, training data summaries, model cards, intended-use statements, known biases, and uncertainty-calibration results.

Governance will be transparent and inclusive. The working group will adopt community participation guidelines, authorship and contribution policies based on CRediT taxonomy, data-use expectations, and a code of conduct. Trainees will participate in reproducibility rotations in which they rerun analyses developed by another subteam, document failure points, and improve tutorials. Public webinars and hackathon-style annotation sprints will invite feedback from the condensate, RNA biology, proteomics, imaging, and machine-learning communities.

Because no new experimental data will be generated, reproducibility will focus on traceable data transformation, robust model evaluation, and clear reporting of uncertainty. Negative results, failed harmonization attempts, and data gaps will be documented to prevent duplication and guide future community efforts.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested to enable a synthesis effort that exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. Funds will prioritize working-group coordination, trainee participation, computational synthesis, open-science infrastructure, and community dissemination rather than experimental data generation. No budget will be used for new wet-lab experiments, sample collection, animal work, or proprietary data acquisition.

Major cost categories include travel and lodging for two in-person NCEMS working-group meetings per year, with funds reserved to support participants from geographically diverse institutions, minority-serving institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, and early-career laboratories. Additional support will cover monthly virtual coordination, facilitation, documentation, and accessibility services such as captioning. Trainee support will provide partial salary or stipends for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams responsible for data harmonization, image feature extraction, knowledge-graph construction, benchmark development, and reproducibility testing.

Computational resources will support cloud storage, secure shared workspaces, graph database hosting, workflow execution, image-processing pipelines, and model training using publicly available datasets. The project will preferentially use open-source tools and institutional or NCEMS-provided cyberinfrastructure to maximize cost efficiency. Funds are also requested for data curation support, ontology alignment, software engineering, user-interface development for interactive visualization, and long-term archiving of releases with persistent identifiers.

The working group will leverage substantial existing resources: public repositories including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, ENCODE, BioImage Archive, ProteomeXchange, DepMap, BioGRID ORCS, ClinVar, and gnomAD; participating investigators' expertise in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, AI, network science, and FAIR data systems; and NCEMS infrastructure for collaborative synthesis science. The requested support will create the structured time, shared standards, trainee training environment, and interoperable computational products necessary to deliver a community-scale atlas.

[
  "Within the domain of molecular and cellular biology, biomolecular condensates are studied to understand their emergence, material states, dynamics, and phenotypic consequences. However, the specific contexts that determine when condensates form, their adopted material states, and whether they buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress remain unresolved due to fragmented data that obscures necessary determinants like stoichiometry and network connectivity. To determine the combinations of molecular grammar, cellular context, and interaction-network architecture that drive condensate emergence, this study utilizes a secondary data synthesis approach employing foundation-model embeddings and graph neural networks. Diverse public databases will be harmonized into a versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph where nodes represent biological entities and edges encode interactions, conditions, and evidence provenance. By modeling condensates as context-dependent emergent systems rather than static component lists, this research will elucidate why structurally similar proteins exhibit different behaviors and how protective condensates transition into pathological aggregates."
abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, metabolites, and membranes produce dynamic compartments whose collective properties cannot be inferred from any single component. Despite thousands of public datasets on protein localization, phase separation, RNA binding, perturbation phenotypes, and disease variation, a central question remains unresolved: what molecular and cellular contexts determine when condensates form, what material states they adopt, and whether they buffer, transmit, or amplify cellular stress? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build and test an integrative, predictive framework for condensate emergence across human cells and model organisms.

The project will assemble a community-scale team spanning molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure. The group will integrate existing public resources including LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold and protein language model embeddings, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, public stress-response transcriptomics, CRISPR perturbation screens from DepMap and BioGRID ORCS, and ClinVar/gnomAD disease variant annotations. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will harmonize these heterogeneous datasets into a FAIR, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular state, mesoscale morphology, dynamics, and phenotypic outcomes.

The core scientific innovation is to treat condensates not merely as lists of phase-separating proteins, but as emergent systems whose properties depend on multivalent molecular grammar, expression stoichiometry, post-translational modification potential, RNA context, interaction network topology, and cellular stress history. We will develop transparent AI and statistical models to predict three linked outcomes: condensate membership, emergent material or morphological class, and downstream cellular consequence after perturbation. By comparing predictions across stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, P bodies, nuclear speckles, and disease-associated aggregates, we will test whether shared rules govern distinct condensate systems or whether each represents a context-specific emergent regime. A special focus will be placed on long-standing puzzles, including why proteins with similar intrinsically disordered regions produce different condensate behaviors, why some condensates are protective while others become pathological, and how disease mutations shift mesoscale organization without necessarily altering canonical molecular function.

NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis beyond the scope of any single laboratory: cross-dataset ontology alignment, image-derived feature extraction, multimodal model development, biological interpretation across condensate classes, and community governance for reusable data products. Working-group meetings will produce shared standards for condensate metadata, benchmark datasets, reproducible workflows, and open tutorials. Trainees from diverse institutions will be embedded in cross-disciplinary subteams and trained in data integration, responsible AI, reproducible workflow design, and collaborative synthesis science.

All outputs will be released openly, including curated datasets, code, model cards, workflow containers, documentation, and interactive visualization tools. The expected outcome is a generalizable synthesis framework for predicting how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale condensate behavior and cellular phenotypes, providing a foundational resource for emergence-focused molecular and cellular biology.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions, yet their organizing principles remain difficult to generalize across cell types, stresses, and organisms. A central unresolved question is: which combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and environmental perturbations cause condensates to transition from adaptive, dynamic assemblies to dysfunctional states that alter gene expression, signaling, or viability? This working group will synthesize publicly available data to build a predictive, open atlas linking condensate composition, material properties, spatial organization, and cellular outcomes. The project will integrate existing datasets from proteomics of stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated aggregates; fluorescence imaging and image-derived phenotypes from resources such as the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting, and Image Data Resource; public perturbation data including CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, LINCS, DepMap, and stress-response transcriptomics; and curated databases of intrinsically disordered regions, post-translational modifications, RNA-binding proteins, phase-separation assays, protein interaction networks, and disease variants. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize heterogeneous datasets into a common representation of condensate-associated mesoscale states. We will develop graph- and representation-learning approaches that combine molecular features, interaction topology, localization patterns, perturbation responses, and phenotypic readouts to identify recurrent ‘condensate state modules.’ These modules will be tested computationally for conservation across organisms, sensitivity to stress, enrichment for disease variants, and association with emergent cellular phenotypes such as translational repression, transcriptional bursting, DNA damage response, senescence, or toxicity. A key innovation is to move beyond cataloging condensate components toward identifying emergent state rules: for example, whether specific combinations of low-complexity sequence composition, RNA abundance, phosphorylation potential, network centrality, and local concentration predict reversible assembly versus persistent pathological aggregation. The project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, proteomics, microscopy, RNA biology, network science, machine learning, ontology development, and open-science infrastructure. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data resources, and computational biology groups, with structured roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will receive hands-on training in FAIR data curation, reproducible workflow design, cloud-based analysis, image feature extraction, and interpretable AI. Deliverables will include an openly accessible condensate-state knowledge graph, reusable analysis pipelines, benchmark datasets for predicting condensate behavior, community-developed metadata standards for condensate-related public data, and a synthesis manuscript defining cross-system principles of condensate emergence. By transforming dispersed public datasets into a unified framework, this project will address a fundamental mystery in molecular and cellular biosciences: how collective mesoscale assemblies acquire properties not predictable from individual molecules alone, and how those emergent properties propagate upward to shape cellular physiology and disease.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences. They arise when proteins, RNAs, and other macromolecules form dynamic mesoscale assemblies through many weak, multivalent interactions. Stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs, DNA repair foci, signaling clusters, and disease-associated aggregates share features of concentration, selective permeability, exchange, and context-dependent material behavior, yet they produce distinct cellular outcomes. Their properties cannot be inferred from any single component alone; rather, they reflect collective effects of sequence grammar, RNA abundance, post-translational modification, interaction network topology, local concentration, cellular state, and environmental perturbation. Understanding these rules is central to NCEMS priorities because condensates occupy the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles and influence higher-order outcomes including gene regulation, translation, genome stability, stress adaptation, senescence, neurodegeneration, cancer fitness, and cell death. Despite rapid progress, the field lacks a general synthesis framework. Existing studies often focus on one condensate class, organism, stress condition, assay, or molecular feature. Public datasets are abundant but fragmented across proteomics repositories, imaging resources, transcriptomic perturbation studies, CRISPR screens, disease variant databases, phase-separation assay compilations, and curated annotations of intrinsically disordered regions, RNA-binding proteins, post-translational modifications, and protein interactions. This fragmentation limits discovery of cross-system principles. For example, stress granule components enriched for low-complexity domains may also participate in transcriptional condensates, but the conditions that favor reversible adaptive assembly rather than persistent toxic aggregation remain unclear. Similarly, phosphorylation, methylation, or ubiquitination may dissolve one condensate while stabilizing another, depending on interaction topology and cellular context. A synthesis approach is therefore needed to distinguish universal rules from system-specific mechanisms. The proposed working group will address this gap by integrating only publicly available molecular, imaging, perturbational, and phenotypic data into a unified public atlas of condensate-associated mesoscale states. The project is significant because it moves beyond cataloging components toward identifying state modules: recurrent combinations of molecular features, localization patterns, network relationships, perturbation responses, material-property annotations, and cellular phenotypes. Such modules will enable computational tests of whether condensate behaviors are conserved across organisms, predictable across cell types, and associated with disease risk or cellular dysfunction. This work cannot be accomplished by a single laboratory. It requires coordinated expertise in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, biophysics, machine learning, network science, ontology engineering, cloud computing, and open-science governance. NCEMS support is essential to convene this community, harmonize data standards, support trainees, and sustain reproducible synthesis workflows. By transforming dispersed public resources into an interoperable knowledge graph and benchmark datasets, the project will provide a foundation for predictive condensate biology and for future experimental prioritization without generating new data.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching research question is: what combinations of molecular features, cellular context, environmental perturbations, and interaction architecture give rise to emergent condensate states that shape cellular phenotypes? We will organize the working group around four linked questions. First, are there recurrent condensate state modules across stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, DNA damage foci, signaling assemblies, and pathological aggregates? We define a state module as a reproducible pattern combining component composition, sequence features, RNA association, post-translational modification potential, spatial localization, interaction topology, perturbation sensitivity, and downstream phenotype. Our first hypothesis is that apparently diverse condensates can be mapped to a smaller set of conserved modules, such as RNA-buffered reversible stress assemblies, chromatin-tethered transcriptional hubs, ribonucleoprotein storage bodies, repair-associated foci, and low-solubility aggregation-prone states. Second, which molecular and contextual features predict adaptive versus dysfunctional condensate behavior? Our second hypothesis is that no single feature, such as intrinsic disorder or low-complexity content, is sufficient. Instead, state transitions are predicted by feature combinations: sticker-and-spacer sequence grammar, local RNA concentration, phosphorylation or methylation capacity, network centrality, valency, chaperone connectivity, subcellular compartment, stress duration, and expression level. We specifically predict that reversible adaptive assemblies will show balanced multivalency, enriched regulatory modification sites, and strong links to stress-response or RNA-processing networks, whereas persistent dysfunctional assemblies will show aggregation-prone sequence composition, reduced regulatory connectivity, disease-variant enrichment, and association with toxicity or loss of fitness. Third, how do mesoscale condensate states propagate upward to cellular outcomes? Our third hypothesis is that condensate modules mediate phenotypes through identifiable functional axes, including translational repression, transcriptional bursting, chromatin reorganization, DNA damage signaling, proteostasis burden, antiviral response, senescence, and apoptosis. Integrating Perturb-seq, CRISPR fitness, LINCS, DepMap, stress-transcriptome, and image-based phenotyping data will test whether module membership predicts cellular responses better than individual gene annotations. Fourth, how transferable are condensate rules across organisms, cell types, and perturbations? Our fourth hypothesis is that core physical and network principles are conserved, while phenotype coupling is context-dependent. For example, RNA-binding and low-complexity features may predict assembly in yeast, flies, mammals, and plants, but the resulting viability, transcriptional, or stress-response phenotypes will depend on cell state, tissue identity, and buffering networks. Methodologically, we ask whether graph-based representation learning and interpretable models can synthesize heterogeneous public data into reliable predictions with quantified uncertainty. We hypothesize that knowledge-graph embeddings, multimodal variational representations, and transparent rule-learning models will outperform single-modality baselines while remaining interpretable enough for biological use. Collectively, these questions directly address emergence: how collective mesoscale properties arise from molecular interactions and how those properties become causal predictors of cellular physiology and disease.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will use no new experimental data. The working group will synthesize existing public resources through coordinated data curation, ontology development, multimodal modeling, and community validation. In year one, we will inventory and prioritize datasets covering condensate composition, imaging, perturbation, molecular features, and phenotypes. Core sources will include proteomic studies of stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, DNA repair foci, and disease aggregates; Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting, BioImage Archive, and Image Data Resource microscopy data; CRISPR and RNAi screens, Perturb-seq, LINCS, DepMap, GEO and SRA stress-response transcriptomics; and curated resources such as DisProt, MobiDB, Pfam, UniProt, PhosphoSitePlus, BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, ENCORI, RBP databases, phase-separation assay catalogs, ClinVar, gnomAD, OMIM, and cancer variant repositories. Inclusion criteria will require public accessibility, documented provenance, reusable licensing or terms, and sufficient metadata for mapping to genes, proteins, cell types, organisms, perturbations, or phenotypes. We will harmonize identifiers using HGNC, UniProt, Ensembl, NCBI Taxonomy, Cell Ontology, Gene Ontology, Sequence Ontology, Disease Ontology, Experimental Factor Ontology, and OBO Foundry standards. A condensate-state metadata schema will capture assembly type, evidence source, assay modality, cell type, stress condition, timescale, localization, composition, material-property annotation, perturbation, and measured phenotype. The central integrative product will be a condensate-state knowledge graph linking molecules, RNAs, modifications, domains, sequence features, interactions, images, perturbations, conditions, condensate classes, and outcomes. Imaging specialists will extract or reuse image-derived features, including subcellular localization, puncta number, size, intensity, texture, colocalization, and cell morphology, using reproducible workflows based on open tools such as CellProfiler, scikit-image, ilastik, napari, and deep-learning feature extractors where pretrained models are appropriate. Proteomics and transcriptomics teams will reprocess or normalize published tables when raw data are available, while preserving original accession links and uncertainty estimates. Computational teams will develop complementary models. Graph neural networks and knowledge-graph embeddings will infer latent relationships among condensate components, conditions, and phenotypes. Multimodal representation learning will combine sequence, network, expression, perturbation, and image features. Interpretable models, including sparse regression, generalized additive models, random forests with SHAP analysis, and rule-learning approaches, will identify feature combinations associated with reversible assembly, persistent aggregation, stress sensitivity, disease variants, and cellular outcomes. Models will be benchmarked against held-out condensate classes, organisms, cell types, and perturbations to test transferability. Negative and ambiguous examples will be curated to reduce confirmation bias, including proteins with disordered regions that do not localize to condensates and condensates lacking canonical low-complexity components. The working group will meet through NCEMS-supported in-person synthesis workshops, monthly virtual analysis sprints, trainee hackathons, and focused subgroup meetings. Milestones include a data inventory and schema by month six, a prototype knowledge graph by month twelve, benchmark datasets by month eighteen, predictive models by month twenty-four, community feedback release by month thirty, and final atlas, manuscripts, tutorials, and standards by month thirty-six.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open, versioned atlas of emergent condensate states that links public molecular, imaging, perturbational, and phenotypic evidence in a computable framework. The atlas will include a condensate-state knowledge graph, harmonized benchmark datasets, reusable image and omics processing workflows, trained baseline models, uncertainty annotations, and documentation sufficient for reuse by cell biologists, biophysicists, computational scientists, and trainees. Scientifically, we expect to identify recurrent state modules that generalize across condensate classes and reveal which feature combinations distinguish adaptive, reversible assemblies from persistent or dysfunctional states. These modules will generate testable predictions about how RNA abundance, sequence grammar, post-translational modifications, network position, expression level, and cellular stress jointly shape mesoscale behavior and downstream outcomes. The project will advance the molecular and cellular sciences by reframing condensates as emergent states rather than isolated structures or lists of components. It will provide a synthesis-based answer to a long-standing puzzle: why similar molecules can form beneficial condensates in one context and harmful assemblies in another. Impact will extend to disease biology by identifying module enrichment for neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, and developmental disorders, and to methods development by providing benchmark datasets for interpretable AI in mesoscale cell biology. NCEMS support will also catalyze a durable interdisciplinary community, connecting investigators across research-intensive institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data resources, and computational groups. Trainees will gain practical skills in FAIR data integration, reproducible workflows, cloud analysis, and collaborative team science. The final products will enable future experimental laboratories to prioritize mechanisms and perturbations, while demonstrating how public-data synthesis can reveal emergent principles that are invisible in single datasets.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow gold-standard open, team, and reproducible science practices aligned with NCEMS expectations. All derived datasets, metadata schemas, code, workflows, benchmark splits, model cards, documentation, and manuscripts will be made publicly available under permissive licenses whenever source-data terms allow. The knowledge graph and benchmark releases will be deposited in stable repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, GitHub, the Open Science Framework, and appropriate domain archives, with digital object identifiers and semantic versioning. We will not redistribute restricted primary data when terms prohibit it; instead, we will provide accession links, transformation scripts, metadata, and reproducible instructions. Reproducibility will be built into the workflow architecture. Analyses will use containerized environments with Docker or Apptainer, workflow managers such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or CWL, and continuous integration tests for data validation and model execution. Computational notebooks will be paired with scripted pipelines to avoid irreproducible point-and-click analyses. Provenance will be captured using machine-readable metadata, checksums, data dictionaries, and change logs. Models will include training data descriptions, hyperparameters, benchmark partitions, limitations, uncertainty estimates, and bias assessments. Open governance will include a data-use and authorship policy, a contribution guide, code of conduct, decision logs, and transparent criteria for dataset inclusion, exclusion, and evidence grading. Community engagement will occur through public webinars, issue trackers, standards workshops, and trainee-led tutorials. We will invite external feedback from condensate researchers, data-resource maintainers, ontology developers, and computational biologists before major releases. Training activities will emphasize responsible reuse of public data, limitations of machine learning, FAIR principles, accessible documentation, and inclusive collaboration. These practices will ensure that the atlas is not only a static product but a sustainable community resource that can be audited, extended, and reused after NCEMS support ends.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested because the project requires coordinated synthesis infrastructure, working-group convening, trainee participation, and shared computational resources beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. The budget will prioritize people, collaboration, computing, and open dissemination rather than experimental materials, because no new experimental data will be generated. Major cost categories will include personnel support for a project coordinator or data scientist, partial trainee support for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows contributing to curation and analysis, and stipends for participants from primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and other resource-limited settings to ensure broad participation. Travel funds will support annual NCEMS in-person synthesis meetings, focused subgroup workshops, and trainee hackathons, with remote participation options to reduce barriers and broaden access. Computational resources will include cloud storage, scalable compute for image feature extraction and graph learning, secure collaborative workspaces, and software engineering support for workflow deployment, documentation, and public release. Funds will also support open-science dissemination, including repository fees if needed, DOI-minted data releases, website hosting, tutorial development, captioning for webinars, and community standards meetings. The working group will leverage extensive existing resources: public databases and archives, open-source software, institutional high-performance computing, national data-resource expertise, and NCEMS coordination infrastructure. Expertise will be organized into thematic cores for biological interpretation, data curation and ontology, imaging and phenotyping, omics and perturbation analysis, network science and machine learning, open science, and training. The proposed resource plan is feasible because it uses public datasets and established tools while reserving NCEMS funds for the activities that make synthesis possible: harmonization, collaboration, benchmarking, trainee development, and durable community infrastructure. Budget review milestones will be tied to public deliverables, including the schema, prototype graph, benchmark datasets, model releases, training modules, and final atlas.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates are a defining mesoscale phenomenon: dynamic assemblies arise from many weak molecular interactions, yet display emergent properties such as selective partitioning, viscoelasticity, spatial organization, and regulatory influence on transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and signaling. Despite rapid progress, a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and cellular contexts determine when condensates form adaptive regulatory hubs versus pathological or dysfunctional assemblies? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and perturbational data to build an open, cross-scale atlas linking condensate composition and physicochemical features to cellular outcomes across organisms, cell types, stresses, and disease states.

The project will integrate existing datasets from public repositories including the Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, Cell Painting and fluorescence microscopy datasets, PRIDE and MassIVE proteomics studies, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic and chromatin datasets, DepMap and CRISPR perturbation screens, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold structural models, and published condensate interactomes. We will harmonize heterogeneous data describing protein localization, intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA-binding capacity, expression stoichiometry, interaction networks, and perturbation phenotypes. Using graph-based data integration, weakly supervised computer vision, representation learning, and interpretable machine learning, we will identify combinations of molecular features and environmental conditions that predict emergent condensate behaviors such as stress-induced assembly, nucleolar or nuclear body reorganization, granule persistence, and links to phenotypes including growth, differentiation, viral response, neurodegeneration, and cancer vulnerability.

The core scientific goal is to move beyond single-condensate case studies toward general principles of mesoscale emergence. We will test three synthesis questions: (1) Are there conserved molecular “design rules” that distinguish reversible functional condensates from persistent disease-associated assemblies? (2) How do changes in expression, modification state, and interaction-network topology combine nonlinearly to produce condensate formation or dissolution? (3) Can condensate-level properties explain cellular phenotypes that are not predictable from individual protein abundance or interaction data alone? The resulting models will generate community-testable hypotheses, such as specific combinations of low-complexity domains, RNA availability, phosphorylation sites, and network position that confer context-dependent condensate behavior.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, standardize, and analyze the breadth of imaging, proteomic, structural, genomic, and perturbation data needed to infer general principles of condensate emergence. [Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates are a defining mesoscale phenomenon: dynamic assemblies arise from many weak molecular interactions, yet display emergent properties such as selective partitioning, viscoelasticity, spatial organization, and regulatory influence on transcription, RNA metabolism, stress responses, and signaling. Despite rapid progress, a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and cellular contexts determine when condensates form adaptive regulatory hubs versus pathological or dysfunctional assemblies? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and perturbational data to build an open, cross-scale atlas linking condensate composition and physicochemical features to cellular outcomes across organisms, cell types, stresses, and disease states.

The project will integrate existing datasets from public repositories including the Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, Cell Painting and fluorescence microscopy datasets, PRIDE and MassIVE proteomics studies, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic and chromatin datasets, DepMap and CRISPR perturbation screens, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold structural models, and published condensate interactomes. We will harmonize heterogeneous data describing protein localization, intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA-binding capacity, expression stoichiometry, interaction networks, and perturbation phenotypes. Using graph-based data integration, weakly supervised computer vision, representation learning, and interpretable machine learning, we will identify combinations of molecular features and environmental conditions that predict emergent condensate behaviors such as stress-induced assembly, nucleolar or nuclear body reorganization, granule persistence, and links to phenotypes including growth, differentiation, viral response, neurodegeneration, and cancer vulnerability.

The core scientific goal is to move beyond single-condensate case studies toward general principles of mesoscale emergence. We will test three synthesis questions: (1) Are there conserved molecular “design rules” that distinguish reversible functional condensates from persistent disease-associated assemblies? (2) How do changes in expression, modification state, and interaction-network topology combine nonlinearly to produce condensate formation or dissolution? (3) Can condensate-level properties explain cellular phenotypes that are not predictable from individual protein abundance or interaction data alone? The resulting models will generate community-testable hypotheses, such as specific combinations of low-complexity domains, RNA availability, phosphorylation sites, and network position that confer context-dependent condensate behavior.

This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can curate, standardize, and analyze the breadth of imaging, proteomic, structural, genomic, and perturbation data needed to infer general principles of condensate emergence. The working group will assemble cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, data curators, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, and trainees from research-intensive, primarily undergraduate, and minority-serving institutions. NCEMS working group meetings will enable consensus development on metadata standards, benchmark tasks, uncertainty reporting, and interpretable modeling strategies.

All products will follow open science principles: harmonized datasets, code, model weights, workflows, documentation, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories with reproducible containers and community governance. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary analysis sprints, receive training in FAIR data stewardship, image analysis, network science, and responsible AI, and co-lead open tutorials for the broader community. By synthesizing existing public data at community scale, this project will provide a predictive framework for how molecular features give rise to emergent mesoscale condensate states and how those states shape cellular function.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences because their properties cannot be inferred by examining any single molecule in isolation. Through multivalent protein-protein, protein-RNA, RNA-RNA, and post-translationally regulated interactions, condensates produce mesoscale assemblies with selective permeability, dynamic exchange, viscoelastic material states, spatial patterning, and context-dependent regulatory effects. These assemblies include nucleoli, stress granules, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, DNA damage foci, signaling clusters, and viral replication compartments. They influence gene expression, RNA processing, protein homeostasis, cell-cycle control, immune signaling, and stress adaptation. However, the same molecular logic that enables rapid and reversible organization can also support aberrant persistence, gelation, aggregation, or mislocalized regulatory activity in neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, and developmental disorders.

Despite extensive case studies, the field lacks a synthesis-level framework for predicting when condensate emergence is adaptive, neutral, or harmful. Current knowledge is fragmented across imaging datasets, proteomic studies, LLPS annotations, disease genetics, chromatin and transcriptomic resources, perturbation screens, structural predictions, and curated literature databases. Individual laboratories often focus on one condensate, molecule, organism, or assay type, making it difficult to distinguish general principles from system-specific observations. Public datasets now provide an unprecedented opportunity to integrate molecular features, cellular context, and phenotype at community scale. Yet these resources remain heterogeneous in metadata standards, spatial resolution, perturbation descriptions, cell-type coverage, and evidence quality.

This proposal directly addresses NCEMS priorities by using only publicly available data to investigate a fundamental mesoscale emergence problem: how weak molecular interactions and cellular contexts combine to generate condensate states with higher-order cellular consequences. Condensates sit squarely between biomolecules and organelles, making them ideal systems for understanding emergent properties across composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion. Their behavior reflects nonlinear relationships among intrinsic disorder, low-complexity sequence grammar, folded interaction domains, RNA availability, local concentration, stoichiometry, post-translational modification, molecular crowding, network topology, and cellular stress state.

The significance is both conceptual and practical. Conceptually, the project will move the field from descriptive catalogs toward predictive design rules for condensate emergence. Practically, it will create reusable resources that connect condensate composition and physicochemical features to phenotypes such as proliferation, differentiation, antiviral response, stress survival, and disease vulnerability. By integrating image-derived phenotypes, perturbation outcomes, structural features, proteomics, transcriptomics, and interaction networks, the working group will test whether condensate-level variables explain cellular outcomes beyond individual protein abundance or pairwise interactions.

NCEMS support is essential because the required synthesis exceeds the scope of any single laboratory. The project requires coordinated expertise in cell biology, biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, structural bioinformatics, disease genomics, data curation, statistics, and machine learning. It also requires consensus standards for evidence grading, metadata harmonization, benchmark tasks, model evaluation, and uncertainty reporting. The resulting atlas and workflows will accelerate discovery, train data-savvy scientists, and establish an open foundation for future experimental and computational studies of mesoscale emergence.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching objective is to identify general principles that explain how molecular features and cellular contexts produce emergent condensate behaviors and downstream cellular outcomes. We will organize the working group around three tightly linked synthesis questions.

Question 1 asks whether conserved molecular design rules distinguish reversible functional condensates from persistent disease-associated or dysfunctional assemblies. We hypothesize that reversible condensates are enriched for balanced combinations of intrinsic disorder, modular folded interaction domains, regulated RNA-binding capacity, dynamic post-translational modification sites, and interaction-network positions that permit rapid assembly and disassembly. In contrast, disease-associated assemblies will show signatures of excessive valence, altered sequence grammar, mutation-driven exposure of low-complexity regions, disrupted phosphorylation or methylation control, increased aggregation propensity, or reduced availability of disassembly mechanisms such as chaperones, helicases, and degradation pathways. This hypothesis will be tested across curated condensate classes, disease-linked proteins, proteomic interactomes, AlphaFold-derived structural features, DisProt annotations, LLPS databases, and disease genetics resources.

Question 2 asks how expression, modification state, interaction topology, and cellular environment combine nonlinearly to drive condensate formation or dissolution. We hypothesize that condensate emergence is governed by context-dependent thresholds rather than additive molecular features. A protein may be condensate competent only when expression stoichiometry, RNA abundance, phosphorylation state, binding-partner availability, and stress-induced localization changes jointly cross a phase-boundary-like regime. Public perturbation datasets allow this hypothesis to be tested by comparing cell types, stresses, drug treatments, CRISPR perturbations, viral infection states, and disease contexts. We will evaluate whether graph-based and representation-learning models identify combinations of features that predict stress granule induction, nucleolar reorganization, nuclear body formation, transcriptional hub assembly, or granule persistence better than linear or single-feature models.

Question 3 asks whether condensate-level properties explain cellular phenotypes not predictable from individual proteins alone. We hypothesize that emergent condensate features, including compositional diversity, interaction valence, spatial co-localization, material-state proxies, RNA association, and regulatory network centrality, will improve prediction of growth effects, differentiation markers, transcriptional programs, antiviral response, proteostasis stress, and cancer dependency. This would support a central premise of emergence: higher-order mesoscale states carry explanatory information beyond their parts.

We will also test methodological hypotheses relevant to synthesis science. First, weakly supervised computer vision can extract condensate-relevant phenotypes from heterogeneous public imaging data even when labels are incomplete or inconsistent. Second, graph representations linking proteins, RNAs, modifications, cell types, perturbations, localizations, and phenotypes will support transferable models across condensate classes. Third, interpretable models with uncertainty estimates will produce biologically meaningful hypotheses rather than opaque predictions. Candidate outputs include ranked feature combinations, context-specific condensate state maps, and predictions of which perturbations shift assemblies from reversible to persistent states.

These questions are designed to be feasible with existing data, but ambitious enough to require NCEMS-enabled collaboration. They are not a request for new experimental data. Instead, the group will synthesize public evidence to generate benchmarked, community-testable predictions and establish a shared conceptual vocabulary for condensate emergence across molecular and cellular systems.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will proceed through four integrated work packages, all based exclusively on public data. Work Package 1 will establish a condensate evidence framework and harmonized metadata model. We will curate condensate-associated proteins, RNAs, complexes, localizations, perturbations, cell types, organisms, disease states, and assay evidence from LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, UniProt, Gene Ontology, Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, Cell Painting resources, ENCODE, GEO, PRIDE, MassIVE, DepMap, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, OpenTargets, AlphaFold, and published condensate interactomes. Each record will receive provenance, license, organism, cell type, perturbation, assay type, confidence, and evidence-grade annotations. A controlled vocabulary will distinguish direct phase-separation evidence, imaging co-localization, biochemical enrichment, genetic association, physical interaction, and inferred condensate membership.

Work Package 2 will derive molecular, cellular, and imaging features. Molecular features will include intrinsic disorder, low-complexity and prion-like sequence content, charge patterning, aromatic and sticker-spacer grammar, domain architecture, predicted aggregation propensity, AlphaFold confidence and interface features, RNA-binding motifs, post-translational modification sites, disease variants, and conservation. Network features will capture multivalency, hub status, modularity, community membership, shortest-path proximity to chaperones or RNA-processing factors, and condensate-specific interactome structure. Contextual features will include transcript and protein abundance, cell-type specificity, stress condition, chromatin state, perturbation identity, and pathway activity. Imaging features will be extracted from public microscopy datasets using weakly supervised segmentation, localization classification, texture analysis, object morphology, puncta number, intensity distribution, co-localization, and Cell Painting embeddings. Quality control will flag batch effects, inconsistent labels, low-resolution data, and incompatible perturbation metadata.

Work Package 3 will integrate features using graph-based data synthesis and interpretable machine learning. We will construct a heterogeneous knowledge graph connecting proteins, RNAs, condensates, features, cell types, perturbations, diseases, images, omics profiles, and phenotypes. Graph neural networks, matrix factorization, contrastive representation learning, random forests, generalized additive models, and Bayesian hierarchical models will be compared on benchmark tasks. Tasks will include predicting condensate membership, stress-induced assembly, persistent versus reversible behavior, disease association, and perturbation phenotypes. We will use nested cross-validation, held-out condensate classes, held-out cell types, external dataset validation, permutation controls, negative-control proteins, and calibration curves. Interpretability will rely on feature attribution, Shapley-value summaries, counterfactual analyses, sparse models, and uncertainty estimates.

Work Package 4 will synthesize biological principles and deliver community resources. The working group will meet through NCEMS-supported in-person workshops, virtual analysis sprints, and trainee-led hackathons. Subgroups will focus on metadata, imaging, proteomics, RNA and chromatin context, perturbation screens, modeling, and interpretation. Milestones include a versioned data dictionary by month 3, a prototype atlas by month 9, benchmark models by month 15, biological synthesis manuscripts by month 20, and a public release with tutorials by month 24. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, predictions will be explicitly framed as community-testable hypotheses for future studies.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open Data-Synthesis Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Emergence that links condensate composition, molecular features, cellular context, perturbations, images, and phenotypes across public datasets. The atlas will include harmonized annotations, confidence scores, evidence provenance, feature matrices, image-derived embeddings, network representations, model outputs, and interactive visualizations. It will provide the community with a common resource for asking when, where, and why condensates form and how they influence cell state.

Scientifically, the project is expected to produce generalizable design principles for mesoscale emergence. We anticipate identifying feature combinations that distinguish reversible functional condensates from persistent or disease-associated assemblies; context thresholds that explain stress-induced assembly or dissolution; and condensate-level variables that improve prediction of cellular phenotypes beyond single-gene or pairwise-interaction models. These outputs will advance understanding of transcriptional regulation, RNA metabolism, stress responses, viral replication, proteostasis, neurodegeneration, and cancer dependency.

Methodologically, the project will establish benchmark tasks for condensate prediction, uncertainty-aware models for heterogeneous public data, and reusable workflows for integrating imaging, proteomics, transcriptomics, structure, disorder, perturbation, and disease resources. These methods will be transferable to other mesoscale systems such as signaling clusters, cytoskeletal assemblies, membrane-less organelles, and subcellular reaction hubs.

The broader impact aligns strongly with NCEMS goals. The working group will stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration among experimental biologists, quantitative scientists, data curators, and trainees from diverse institutions. It will train graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in FAIR data stewardship, responsible AI, image analysis, graph science, and reproducible team science. By producing open resources rather than private datasets, the project will lower barriers for researchers at primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and laboratories without large computational infrastructure. The final deliverables will enable hypothesis generation, model comparison, classroom use, and future experimental validation by the broader molecular and cellular biosciences community.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, reproducible, and team-based science practices from inception. All data inputs will be publicly available and will be documented with persistent identifiers, accession numbers, download dates, licenses, processing scripts, and provenance records. We will not generate new experimental data. Derived datasets will be released under permissive licenses when source licenses allow, with clear separation between redistributed data, feature tables, metadata, and pointers to restricted third-party resources. The atlas will follow FAIR principles: findable through indexed repositories, accessible through standard file formats and APIs, interoperable through controlled vocabularies and identifiers, and reusable through documentation and evidence grading.

All code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories using issue tracking, code review, continuous integration, and documented contribution guidelines. Workflows will be implemented with reproducible workflow systems such as Snakemake, Nextflow, or equivalent notebook pipelines, packaged in containers, and accompanied by environment files. Model training will include fixed random seeds, documented splits, benchmark definitions, hyperparameter records, evaluation metrics, and uncertainty estimates. Model weights, feature matrices, and trained embeddings will be deposited in public repositories when feasible. Interactive visualizations will provide confidence labels and links back to original sources rather than presenting predictions as definitive biological facts.

Reproducibility will be strengthened through independent reruns by multiple subgroup members, preregistered benchmark tasks, negative controls, ablation analyses, held-out validation, and transparent failure reporting. The working group will produce a living data dictionary, metadata schema, tutorials, and example analyses. Trainees will co-lead documentation sprints and open workshops on condensate data integration, image analysis, graph modeling, and responsible AI. Governance will include inclusive authorship policies, a code of conduct, transparent decision records, and community feedback mechanisms. These practices will ensure that outputs remain usable, auditable, extensible, and trustworthy after the NCEMS-supported working group period ends.

[Budget and Resources]
The requested resources are designed to support synthesis, collaboration, training, and open dissemination, not new experimental data generation. NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated curation, standardization, computational analysis, and consensus building across domains that exceed the capacity of any single laboratory. Major resource categories include working group convening, trainee participation, cyberinfrastructure, data curation, dissemination, and project coordination.

Working group convening will support two in-person NCEMS meetings per year for approximately 18 to 24 participants, supplemented by monthly virtual meetings and focused analysis sprints. Travel support will prioritize broad participation across research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national laboratories, and geographically diverse sites. Funds will also support invited expertise in microscopy standards, proteomics metadata, RNA biology, biophysics, machine learning, and open science governance.

Trainee resources will support graduate students and postdoctoral researchers as active analysts rather than observers. Trainees will receive travel support, short-term synthesis fellowships, cloud-computing credits, and structured mentoring. They will contribute to benchmark construction, data harmonization, model development, documentation, and public tutorials. This directly advances NCEMS goals for training a data-savvy molecular and cellular biosciences workforce.

Cyberinfrastructure needs include shared cloud storage, scalable compute for image feature extraction and graph learning, container registries, workflow execution, web hosting for the atlas, and long-term archival deposition. Data curation resources will support part-time professional curation assistance, metadata harmonization, ontology mapping, quality-control audits, and user documentation. Dissemination resources will support open-access publication fees, community webinars, tutorial development, and maintenance of public repositories.

A feasible two-year budget would allocate approximately 35 percent to convening and travel, 25 percent to trainee support, 20 percent to cyberinfrastructure and compute, 10 percent to curation and project management, and 10 percent to dissemination and sustainability. No funds will be used for new experiments, sample collection, proprietary data acquisition, or closed software dependencies. Existing institutional computing, public repositories, and participant expertise will provide matching intellectual and infrastructure support.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that concentrate proteins, RNAs, chromatin regions, and small molecules without delimiting membranes. They regulate translation, transcription, RNA processing, ribosome biogenesis, DNA repair, signaling, and stress adaptation. Their formation is governed by multivalent weak interactions, intrinsically disordered regions, nucleic acid scaffolds, post-translational modifications, and context-dependent changes in concentration, crowding, energy availability, and cellular state. These features make condensates exemplary systems for NCEMS: molecular properties combine across space, time, information, and energy to generate emergent material states that cannot be inferred from single components alone. A major unresolved problem is that condensates can be beneficial, neutral, or pathological. Stress granules may support survival during transient stress but also become persistent assemblies linked to neurodegeneration. Nucleoli are essential for growth control but reorganize in cancer and viral infection. DNA damage foci organize repair factors but may also reflect genome instability. Transcriptional hubs can coordinate gene expression yet may be disrupted by oncogenic fusions or repeat expansions. The field has identified many condensate components, sequence motifs, and phase-separation mechanisms, but lacks a general predictive framework for when assemblies form, dissolve, mature, localize, or impair cellular function. Public data now create an unprecedented opportunity for synthesis. Thousands of studies have deposited proteomics, transcriptomics, genome-wide perturbation screens, imaging datasets, interaction maps, proximity labeling results, disease variant catalogs, and curated sequence annotations relevant to condensates. However, these resources are distributed across incompatible repositories, use heterogeneous metadata, and measure different biological scales. Imaging datasets often contain rich mesoscale phenotypes that remain unquantified beyond original study goals. Perturbation screens identify regulators but are rarely connected to sequence grammar, interaction networks, or disease mutations. Multi-omics resources capture expression and modification states but are not systematically linked to condensate morphology or material behavior. Consequently, data exist to answer integrative questions, but no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise, curation capacity, or community reach to synthesize them. This Working Group will address that gap by building a public, interoperable, and predictive synthesis of condensate biology. The project is significant for molecular and cellular biosciences because it transforms condensates from descriptive phenomena into testable emergent states with measurable inputs, phenotypes, and outcomes. It will clarify conserved principles, such as the contribution of interaction valence, disordered region patterning, RNA binding, and network centrality, while also identifying context-specific exceptions across organism, cell type, stress, and disease. The work directly aligns with NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data, catalyzing a multidisciplinary community, focusing on mesoscale emergence, developing innovative AI and data science strategies, training data-savvy trainees, and releasing reusable resources. The expected knowledge base and analytic workflows will enable researchers to interpret condensate experiments, prioritize disease variants, design perturbation hypotheses, and benchmark computational models of emergent cellular organization.
