The overarching question is which combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and perturbation history are sufficient to predict emergent biomolecular condensate states and their downstream cellular consequences. We define condensate state as an integrated phenotype encompassing assembly propensity, number, size distribution, morphology, subcellular localization, molecular composition, dynamics, reversibility, maturation, and association with adaptive or dysfunctional outcomes. The Working Group will organize its synthesis around four interlocking research questions. First, what molecular grammar predicts condensate participation and state transitions? We hypothesize that condensate formation is best predicted not by any single property, such as intrinsic disorder, but by combinations of disordered region patterning, aromatic and charged residue distribution, low-complexity motifs, RNA binding domains, oligomerization domains, post-translational modification sites, nucleic acid features, and expression abundance. We further hypothesize that adaptive and reversible condensates will be enriched for regulatory features that tune interaction valence, including phosphorylation, methylation, acetylation, alternative splicing, and stress-responsive expression changes. Second, how does interaction network topology shape emergent condensate behavior? We hypothesize that condensates differ systematically in the topology of their component networks. Reversible assemblies will show modular, redundant, and dynamically rewired interaction structures, whereas persistent or pathological condensates will be associated with high-valence hubs, prion-like domains, disease mutations that increase interaction strength, and network bottlenecks that reduce dissolution capacity. We will test whether protein-protein, protein-RNA, and proximity networks improve predictions beyond sequence features alone. Third, how do cell type, organism, and environmental perturbation alter the mapping between molecular grammar and mesoscale phenotype? We hypothesize that the same molecular components can produce distinct condensate outcomes depending on concentration, RNA availability, proteostasis state, metabolic stress, cell cycle phase, chromatin context, and organismal background. This predicts that multimodal models incorporating transcriptomic, proteomic, and perturbation metadata will outperform context-free models. It also predicts discoverable conserved rules for core behaviors, such as stress-induced assembly, overlaid with context-specific modifiers. Fourth, which condensate features predict cellular adaptation versus dysfunction or disease association? We hypothesize that acute, reversible changes in condensate number and localization will correlate with adaptive stress responses, whereas persistent enlargement, altered material maturation, reduced reversibility, abnormal recruitment of RNA or repair factors, and disease-variant enrichment will predict impaired growth, toxicity, transcriptional dysregulation, genome instability, or neurodegenerative phenotypes. These questions will be evaluated with explicit, pre-specified validation strategies. Models trained on one subset of organisms, condensate classes, or perturbation types will be tested on held-out datasets from independent studies. Competing hypotheses will be compared through ablation analyses that remove feature classes, negative controls using non-condensate proteins and random networks, and calibration tests that assess whether predictions are reliable across data sources. The result will be not only a ranked list of predictors, but a rigorous assessment of which rules generalize, which are context dependent, and where public data remain insufficient.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will use only existing publicly available data and will proceed through coordinated Working Group activities supported by NCEMS workshops, virtual sprints, trainee exchanges, and shared computational infrastructure. The team will include experts in condensate cell biology, molecular biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, genomics, microscopy, network science, statistics, machine learning, ontology development, and open-source software engineering. Aim 1 will create a condensate knowledge graph. We will curate public records from resources such as UniProt, Ensembl, Gene Ontology, DisProt, MobiDB, PhosphoSitePlus where licensing permits, BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, POSTAR, ENCODE, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting collections, Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, GEO, SRA, DepMap, BioGRID ORCS, OMIM, ClinVar, gnomAD, COSMIC, and organism-specific databases. Entities will include genes, proteins, isoforms, RNAs, condensate classes, sequence features, post-translational modifications, interactions, perturbations, microscopy phenotypes, cell types, stresses, diseases, and publications. Each edge will include provenance, evidence type, organism, experimental context, confidence, and licensing metadata. We will map terms to community ontologies and extend them only where condensate-specific descriptors are missing. Aim 2 will extract standardized mesoscale phenotypes from public microscopy data. We will inventory fixed-cell and live-cell datasets containing stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, DNA repair foci, transcriptional hubs, nuclear speckles, paraspeckles, and related assemblies. Reusable workflows will perform image quality control, channel harmonization, segmentation, object tracking when time series exist, batch correction, and feature extraction. Phenotypes will include condensate count, area, intensity, circularity, texture, spatial clustering, distance to organelle or nuclear landmarks, co-localization, fusion or coalescence signatures, appearance and dissolution rates, and recovery proxies when appropriate metadata are available. Methods will combine classical image analysis, foundation models for microscopy, active learning, and human-in-the-loop validation by domain experts. Aim 3 will integrate molecular, contextual, network, and image-derived features into interpretable predictive models. We will benchmark graph neural networks, gradient-boosted trees, generalized additive models, Bayesian hierarchical models, matrix factorization, and multimodal contrastive learning. Interpretability will be prioritized through feature attribution, rule extraction, counterfactual testing, uncertainty quantification, and biologically constrained model comparisons. Models will predict condensate membership, class, assembly under stress, reversibility, localization, maturation, perturbation sensitivity, and disease association. Aim 4 will validate and generalize. We will use nested cross-validation, leave-study-out validation, leave-condensate-class-out validation, and held-out disease or perturbation datasets. Negative controls will include matched non-condensate proteins, permuted interaction networks, and randomized labels preserving study structure. Sensitivity analyses will evaluate missing data, publication bias, imaging batch effects, and species-specific annotation quality. Deliverables will be released iteratively: data dictionaries and schemas in months 1 to 6, first knowledge graph and image pipeline in months 6 to 12, benchmark models in months 12 to 20, and final integrated resource, manuscripts, and training materials by month 24.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce four major outcomes. First, it will deliver a public condensate knowledge graph that integrates molecular features, interactions, perturbations, imaging phenotypes, cellular contexts, and disease associations with transparent provenance. This resource will allow investigators to query relationships that are currently scattered across publications and repositories, such as which phosphorylation sites, RNA partners, or disease variants are associated with altered stress granule reversibility. Second, it will provide reusable, benchmarked microscopy workflows for extracting mesoscale condensate phenotypes from public images. These tools will increase the value of existing imaging investments and establish community standards for comparing condensate morphology and dynamics across studies. Third, it will generate interpretable multimodal models that identify predictive rules for condensate emergence, state transitions, and cellular outcomes. The models will distinguish general principles from context-specific modifiers, helping resolve why similar molecular components can support adaptive assemblies in one setting and pathological persistence in another. Fourth, it will create benchmark datasets and training modules that support education in data synthesis, open science, AI, and mesoscale cell biology. The broader impact is a shift from cataloging condensate components toward predicting emergent cellular organization. The framework will help researchers prioritize experiments without generating new data within this project, interpret disease mutations in disordered or RNA-binding proteins, identify potential regulators of reversible assembly, and evaluate how stress, cell type, and expression state reshape mesoscale behavior. By linking molecular grammar to cellular outcome, the project will advance NCEMS goals of understanding emergence across scales and developing synthesis methods that are reusable beyond condensates. The Working Group will also broaden participation by engaging trainees and investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and data-resource communities, thereby building a more diverse workforce capable of collaborative, computationally enabled molecular and cellular science.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Open science is central to the project design. All datasets, code, workflows, model outputs, documentation, and training materials produced by the Working Group will be released through public repositories under permissive licenses whenever source-data licenses allow. We will use GitHub or GitLab for version-controlled development, Zenodo or Figshare for citable releases, and appropriate biological repositories for derived tables, metadata, and image annotations. The knowledge graph will include persistent identifiers, source citations, license information, evidence codes, processing dates, and machine-readable provenance so that every integrated assertion can be traced back to public data. Reproducibility will be supported through containerized workflows using Docker or Apptainer, workflow managers such as Nextflow or Snakemake, pinned software environments, automated tests, continuous integration, and executable notebooks. Major analyses will be accompanied by data manifests and checksums. Models will be released with training data splits, hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, uncertainty estimates, and model cards describing intended use, limitations, bias risks, and inappropriate applications. Imaging pipelines will include benchmark examples, quality-control reports, and instructions for applying the tools to new public datasets. The Working Group will establish community governance for terminology, schema changes, issue tracking, and contribution review. Quarterly open virtual meetings will solicit feedback from condensate researchers, data-resource curators, tool developers, and trainees. Preprints, protocols, and manuscripts will be shared openly, and negative or inconclusive synthesis results will be reported to avoid biasing the field toward successful predictions only. Training materials will include modular tutorials on knowledge graphs, microscopy feature extraction, multimodal machine learning, uncertainty-aware validation, and reproducible team science. These materials will be designed for graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and faculty at institutions with varied computational infrastructure, supporting NCEMS goals for open, collaborative, and inclusive data-savvy workforce development.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is requested because the project requires sustained coordination, shared infrastructure, and community participation beyond the capacity of a single laboratory or existing collaboration. Funds will be allocated to four integrated resource categories. First, Working Group meetings will support two in-person synthesis workshops per year at NCEMS or partner sites, plus monthly virtual coordination meetings. Travel support will prioritize broad participation across geographic regions, institution types, career stages, and disciplines, including investigators from primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource communities. Second, trainee participation will be supported through graduate student and postdoctoral fellow travel, short collaborative visits, hackathon participation, and mentored leadership roles in data curation, workflow development, model benchmarking, and documentation. These investments directly support training in open, team-based, computational molecular and cellular science. Third, computational and data-management resources will support secure cloud or center-provided storage for public datasets, containerized workflow execution, model training, image-processing tasks, knowledge graph hosting, persistent web documentation, and citable archival releases. The project will not request funds for new experimental data generation, wet-lab reagents, animal work, new imaging, or proprietary data acquisition. Fourth, modest support will be used for open-source software engineering, accessibility of training materials, community outreach, and publication or repository costs when not otherwise covered. The Working Group will leverage substantial existing resources, including public databases, institutional computing allocations, open-source image-analysis and machine-learning libraries, established ontology standards, and participating investigators expertise. NCEMS adds unique value by providing neutral convening power, synthesis-focused project management, interdisciplinary matchmaking, training infrastructure, and expectations for open, reproducible team science. Budget decisions will be reviewed by the project steering committee to ensure alignment with milestones, equity goals, and open science deliverables. This resource plan is feasible, cost-conscious, and tightly aligned with the NCEMS mandate to synthesize existing public data rather than generate new experimental measurements.

abstract_original:
Membraneless biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and DNA damage foci exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, chromatin, metabolites, and post-translational modifications produce collective material states that regulate cellular physiology. Despite intense study, a central puzzle remains unresolved: why do some condensates form adaptive, reversible mesoscale assemblies whereas others transition into pathological or dysfunctional states? We propose a community-scale synthesis project to develop a predictive, publicly available framework linking molecular features to emergent condensate behaviors and downstream cellular outcomes across organisms, cell types, stresses, and disease contexts.

This Working Group will integrate existing public data spanning complementary modalities: protein and RNA sequence features; intrinsically disordered region annotations; post-translational modification databases; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction resources; proximity labeling datasets; CRISPR and RNAi perturbation screens; single-cell and bulk transcriptomics; proteomics; live-cell and fixed-cell imaging repositories; and curated disease mutation databases. Rather than generating new experimental data, the project will harmonize and reanalyze these resources to ask: which combinations of molecular grammar, interaction network topology, expression context, and environmental perturbation are sufficient to predict condensate assembly, dissolution, localization, material maturation, and cellular consequences?

The analytical strategy will combine expertise from molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, image analysis, machine learning, network science, and open-source software engineering. We will first create an interoperable condensate knowledge graph connecting molecular components, sequence features, interaction evidence, perturbations, imaging-derived phenotypes, and cellular outcomes using transparent provenance standards. Second, we will develop reusable computer vision workflows to extract mesoscale condensate phenotypes from public microscopy data, including size distributions, number, spatial organization, coalescence signatures, and temporal reversibility where time-lapse data exist. Third, we will train interpretable multimodal AI models to identify predictive rules for condensate emergence and state transitions, explicitly testing whether conserved mesoscale behaviors can be inferred from molecular features across different biological contexts. Finally, we will perform cross-dataset validation using held-out perturbation and disease datasets to identify general principles and context-specific exceptions.

NCEMS support is essential because this synthesis exceeds the scope of a single laboratory: it requires coordinated data curation across many repositories, shared standards for condensate phenotypes, integration of heterogeneous molecular and imaging data, and sustained collaboration among experimentalists, computational scientists, statisticians, and trainees. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource communities, with explicit roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in data stewardship, reproducible workflow development, and collaborative team science.

All outputs will follow open science principles. We will release curated datasets, ontologies, analysis notebooks, trained models, image-analysis pipelines, and benchmark tasks through public repositories with documented metadata and community governance. The project will also produce training modules on multimodal biological data synthesis, interpretable AI, and reproducible mesoscale cell biology. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent predictive resource, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular properties generate emergent condensate states and how those states influence cellular adaptation, dysfunction, and disease.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and DNA repair foci exemplify emergence in cell biology: collective mesoscale assemblies arise from multivalent molecular interactions and generate new spatial, kinetic, and regulatory properties not predictable from individual components alone. Despite intense study, the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when specific proteins and RNAs will form condensates, how condensate material properties vary across cellular contexts, and which emergent assemblies causally influence cell state. This Working Group will synthesize publicly available datasets to answer a central question: what combinations of molecular features, interaction network architecture, expression stoichiometry, and cellular context predict the emergence and functional consequences of mesoscale condensates in human cells?

The project will integrate existing public resources that are individually powerful but rarely analyzed together: subcellular localization images from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, and Cell Painting datasets; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction maps from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, ENCODE, POSTAR, and published AP-MS, BioID, and CLIP-seq studies; sequence-derived features including intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, charge patterning, prion-like domains, and multivalent motifs; transcriptomic and proteomic abundance data from GTEx, DepMap, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, and single-cell atlases; and public perturbation datasets including CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, stress-response time courses, and drug response studies. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will create harmonized, FAIR data products linking molecular composition, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, interaction networks, and cellular outcomes.

Our analytical strategy will combine computer vision, network science, statistical physics-inspired descriptors, and interpretable machine learning. First, we will use reproducible image-analysis pipelines to extract condensate-related phenotypes from public microscopy data, including puncta number, size distributions, co-localization, spatial organization, and context-dependent relocalization. Second, we will build multilayer interaction and feature networks capturing sequence grammar, binding multiplicity, RNA association, abundance, and compartmental localization. Third, we will train and benchmark models that predict condensate membership, condition-specific assembly, and emergent mesoscale phenotypes from molecular and network features. Finally, we will connect predicted condensate states to cellular outcomes such as stress survival, transcriptional reprogramming, proliferation, and disease-associated vulnerability using public perturbational and phenotypic datasets.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it is beyond the scope of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in condensate biology, cell imaging, RNA biology, proteomics, biophysics, machine learning, network theory, and open-science software engineering. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data repositories, with active roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will receive hands-on training in reproducible workflows, metadata harmonization, image analysis, machine learning, and collaborative team science.

Expected outputs include an open atlas of predicted and observed human condensate-forming systems, validated computational workflows, benchmark datasets for community model development, and testable hypotheses about how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale organization and higher-order cell behavior. By transforming fragmented public data into an integrated predictive framework, this project will address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how dynamic molecular interactions generate emergent cellular organization.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are dynamic, mesoscale assemblies that concentrate proteins, RNAs, and other macromolecules without requiring delimiting membranes. They include stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, transcriptional hubs, DNA repair foci, and signaling clusters. These systems are central examples of biological emergence because their properties arise from collective interactions among many components rather than from any single molecule. Condensates can create new reaction environments, alter diffusion and encounter rates, buffer molecular noise, reorganize genomes and transcriptomes, and switch cellular programs during stress, development, infection, and disease. Yet the field still lacks a predictive theory that links molecular-scale features to mesoscale assembly and then to cellular consequences. Most current knowledge comes from focused studies of individual condensates or purified components, which are essential but insufficient for identifying generalizable rules across cell types, compartments, and physiological contexts. Public data now provide an unprecedented opportunity to solve this problem through synthesis. Imaging repositories contain millions of cellular images reporting protein localization, punctate morphology, co-localization, and stress-induced relocalization. Proteomic and transcriptomic resources quantify abundance, isoforms, tissue specificity, and cellular state. Interaction databases capture protein-protein, protein-RNA, and proximity relationships. Sequence databases allow systematic annotation of intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, prion-like regions, charge patterning, aromatic and charged residues, modular binding motifs, and post-translational modification sites. Perturbation datasets report the consequences of gene knockouts, knockdowns, overexpression, drug treatment, stress exposure, and disease-associated mutations. However, these resources are fragmented, use heterogeneous identifiers and metadata, and have rarely been analyzed together with condensate emergence as the organizing question. This proposal directly aligns with NCEMS priorities by addressing emergence at the mesoscale between biomolecules and organelles, using only publicly available data, and requiring a multidisciplinary synthesis team. The proposed Working Group will integrate public imaging, proteomic, interaction, transcriptomic, sequence, and perturbation datasets into a unified framework for predicting condensate formation and function in human cells. The project is significant for three reasons. First, it addresses a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how do distributed molecular interactions give rise to spatially organized, dynamic cellular structures with new regulatory capacities? Second, it will provide practical predictive tools to identify candidate condensate components, context-dependent assemblies, and perturbations likely to disrupt mesoscale organization. Third, it will transform condensate biology from a collection of compelling examples into a comparative, quantitative, and reproducible science. By synthesizing existing data rather than generating new experiments, the Working Group will leverage past public investments, identify gaps in current resources, and produce community assets that individual laboratories cannot readily create. The effort will also train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in data integration, machine learning, image analysis, network biology, reproducible workflows, and collaborative team science. The resulting framework will help explain how molecular composition, stoichiometry, interaction topology, and cellular context combine to generate emergent organization and phenotypic outcomes.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The Working Group will address one overarching research question: what combinations of molecular features, interaction network architecture, expression stoichiometry, localization, and cellular context predict the emergence and functional consequences of biomolecular condensates in human cells? This question will be decomposed into four integrated aims. Aim 1 asks which molecular features distinguish observed or predicted condensate components from non-condensate proteins and RNAs. We hypothesize that condensate membership is best predicted by combinations of multivalent interaction capacity, intrinsically disordered region content, low-complexity sequence grammar, charge patterning, RNA-binding potential, oligomerization domains, and regulated post-translational modification sites rather than by any single feature alone. Aim 2 asks how network architecture contributes to mesoscale assembly. We hypothesize that condensate-forming systems occupy distinctive positions in multilayer molecular networks, including high local clustering, modular hubs, repeated weak interactions, protein-RNA bridges, and context-specific proximity edges. We further hypothesize that emergent assemblies arise when sequence-encoded interaction potential is matched by sufficient abundance and stoichiometric balance among scaffolds, clients, and regulatory factors. Aim 3 asks how cellular context influences condensate formation and material-like phenotypes. We hypothesize that the same molecule may be diffuse, punctate, coarsened, dispersed, or relocalized depending on cell type, stress state, developmental state, cell-cycle phase, mutation status, and drug exposure. Context dependence will be captured by integrating public transcriptomic, proteomic, microscopy, and perturbation data, allowing prediction of condition-specific assembly rather than static condensate membership. Aim 4 asks which condensate states are associated with functional outcomes such as stress survival, transcriptional reprogramming, proliferation, antiviral response, neurodegeneration, cancer vulnerability, and DNA damage repair. We hypothesize that emergent condensate phenotypes will explain variation in cellular outcomes beyond what is explained by expression level or single-gene essentiality alone. In particular, perturbations that alter scaffold abundance, multivalent binding, RNA association, or condensate-localized regulatory enzymes will have disproportionate effects on cell-state transitions. A cross-cutting methodological question is how to define and benchmark condensate phenotypes from public data without generating new experiments. We will use curated positive sets from established condensates, literature-mined annotations, public localization evidence, and image-derived puncta features, while maintaining uncertainty labels to avoid overconfident classifications. Negative and ambiguous examples will be selected carefully from proteins with repeated diffuse localization, incompatible compartmental localization, or insufficient evidence. We will test whether interpretable models can recover known condensate principles and reveal new, testable hypotheses. The strongest support for our hypotheses would be models that generalize across repositories, cell types, and condensate classes; identify biologically meaningful feature interactions; predict condition-specific relocalization; and connect mesoscale phenotypes to perturbational outcomes. Alternative outcomes are scientifically valuable: failure of general models may indicate that condensates are governed by class-specific rules, organelle-specific environments, or missing metadata, thereby refining the theory of mesoscale emergence.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will proceed through coordinated synthesis, analysis, benchmarking, and dissemination activities over a two-year Working Group timeline. No new experimental data will be generated. In Phase 1, the group will inventory, prioritize, and harmonize public datasets. Imaging sources will include the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting resources, and condition-specific microscopy datasets from published studies. Molecular interaction sources will include BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, ENCODE, POSTAR, CLIP-seq compendia, AP-MS, BioID, TurboID, and proximity-labeling datasets. Abundance and state data will come from GTEx, DepMap, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, Human Proteome Map resources, public single-cell atlases, stress time courses, drug response datasets, CRISPR screens, and Perturb-seq studies. Data will be mapped to stable identifiers including UniProt, Ensembl, HGNC, RefSeq, and RNA identifiers, with provenance recorded for every assertion. Phase 2 will generate condensate-relevant features. Sequence features will include disorder, low-complexity regions, prion-like domains, charge distribution, aromatic and cationic residue patterning, short linear motifs, domain architecture, predicted phase-separation propensity, RNA-binding potential, and post-translational modification density. Interaction features will include degree, weighted clustering, centrality, multilayer community membership, edge confidence, protein-RNA connectivity, scaffold-client ratios, and proximity versus direct-binding distinctions. Abundance features will include expression level, dynamic range, tissue specificity, cell-line variability, stress responsiveness, and estimated stoichiometry. Phase 3 will extract mesoscale phenotypes from public images using reproducible computer vision workflows. We will use established tools such as CellProfiler, scikit-image, napari plugins, and deep-learning segmentation models when appropriate. Features will include puncta count, area, intensity, circularity, size distributions, spatial clustering, nuclear versus cytoplasmic partitioning, co-localization, organelle proximity, and condition-dependent relocalization. A curated subset will be manually reviewed by domain experts to estimate label quality and calibrate uncertainty. Phase 4 will build predictive and explanatory models. Baseline models will include regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, and support vector methods. More integrative models will include graph machine learning, multilayer network embeddings, and interpretable ensemble models. We will benchmark predictions for condensate membership, condensate class, condition-specific assembly, image-derived phenotypes, and links to cellular outcomes. Performance will be evaluated with nested cross-validation, repository-held-out validation, condensate-class-held-out validation, cell-type-held-out validation, precision-recall analysis for imbalanced classes, calibration curves, and sensitivity analyses for dataset bias. Interpretability methods will include feature importance, SHAP-style attribution, network module enrichment, partial dependence, and counterfactual feature perturbation. Phase 5 will connect condensate predictions to functional outcomes using public perturbation data. We will test whether predicted scaffold or client status, network position, stoichiometric imbalance, and image-derived condensate phenotypes improve models of gene essentiality, stress survival, transcriptional programs, drug sensitivity, and disease-associated vulnerability. The Working Group structure is essential: condensate biologists will define biological questions and annotations; imaging scientists will guide phenotype extraction; RNA biologists and proteomics experts will evaluate molecular evidence; biophysicists will develop emergence-inspired descriptors; data scientists will build reproducible pipelines; and open-science specialists will ensure FAIR products. Regular virtual meetings, NCEMS-hosted synthesis workshops, trainee-led hackathons, and community feedback sessions will maintain integration across disciplines.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver four major outcomes. First, we will produce an open atlas of observed and predicted human condensate-forming systems, linking proteins, RNAs, sequence features, interaction evidence, localization patterns, image-derived mesoscale phenotypes, abundance contexts, and perturbational outcomes. Second, we will release benchmark datasets for community model development, including curated positive, negative, and uncertain labels; standardized feature matrices; harmonized imaging phenotypes; and held-out validation splits. Third, we will provide validated computational workflows for extracting condensate-relevant phenotypes from public images, constructing multilayer interaction networks, and predicting context-dependent assembly. Fourth, we will generate ranked, testable hypotheses about uncharacterized condensates, context-specific relocalization events, disease-relevant vulnerabilities, and molecular features that control emergent organization. The scientific impact will be broad. For condensate biology, the project will move the field from anecdotal and condensate-specific knowledge toward comparative and predictive principles. For molecular and cellular biology, it will clarify how molecular composition, network topology, abundance, and cell state combine to produce mesoscale structures with new functions. For data science, it will establish reusable strategies for integrating images, sequences, interaction networks, and perturbation profiles. For NCEMS, the project directly addresses emergence at the mesoscale and demonstrates how synthesis of public data can reveal principles that are inaccessible to individual laboratories. The effort will also identify systematic gaps in public metadata, imaging conditions, perturbation coverage, and annotation standards. Trainees will gain experience in collaborative synthesis, reproducible computational biology, machine learning, and open software development. The final products will support future experimental studies without depending on new data generation during the funded project.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group will operate under open, team, and reproducible science principles consistent with NCEMS expectations. All derived datasets, metadata mappings, feature tables, model inputs, benchmark splits, analysis workflows, documentation, and manuscripts will be made publicly available, subject only to the licenses and use conditions of the original public resources. Code will be developed in public version-controlled repositories using issue tracking, code review, continuous integration, unit tests, and tagged releases. Workflows will be implemented with reproducible workflow managers such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or equivalent tools and packaged in containers using Docker or Apptainer to ensure portability across local, cloud, and NCEMS computing environments. Data products will follow FAIR principles. Each dataset will include persistent identifiers, machine-readable metadata, provenance records, data dictionaries, source citations, license information, uncertainty annotations, and clear versioning. Harmonized identifiers will be traceable to original public sources so users can audit every transformation. We will deposit stable releases in appropriate repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, GitHub, Open Science Framework, or domain-specific archives recommended by NCEMS and community partners. Analytical notebooks will be executable and paired with lightweight example datasets, while full-scale workflows will be documented for high-performance or cloud execution. Reproducibility will be built into governance. Each analysis will have a designated lead, independent reviewer, and trainee co-owner. Major results will require reproduction by at least one team member not involved in the original implementation before dissemination. Model performance reports will include negative results, failure modes, uncertainty estimates, bias assessments, and limitations associated with uneven repository coverage. Preprints and publications will be open access whenever feasible. Community engagement will include open webinars, documentation sprints, and feedback periods for benchmark labels and atlas structure. Trainees will receive structured instruction in responsible data reuse, metadata standards, reproducible workflow design, collaborative coding, and transparent authorship practices.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained coordination across disciplines, institutions, repositories, and trainee groups rather than isolated analysis by a single laboratory. Funds and Center resources will be allocated to six categories. First, personnel support will provide partial effort for a project coordinator or data steward responsible for meeting logistics, metadata tracking, provenance documentation, community communication, and release management. Second, trainee support will enable graduate students and postdoctoral fellows to participate in synthesis sprints, lead reproducible workflow modules, receive cross-disciplinary mentoring, and present results. Third, travel and meeting support will fund NCEMS-hosted in-person working sessions, hybrid participation, trainee hackathons, and targeted workshops with external repository experts and community advisors. Fourth, computational resources will support secure storage of derived public datasets, image feature extraction, workflow testing, model training, versioned releases, and cloud or high-performance computing access where needed. Fifth, open-science dissemination funds will support data deposition, documentation, web hosting for the atlas interface, tutorial materials, open-access publication costs when necessary, and community webinars. Sixth, accessibility and inclusion funds will support remote participation, captioning, childcare or dependent-care supplements where allowed, and participation by investigators from primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and institutions with limited computational infrastructure. The Working Group will leverage substantial existing resources at no data-generation cost: public repositories provide the primary data; participating laboratories contribute domain expertise, existing software, and mentoring capacity; repository partners contribute knowledge of standards and data provenance; and NCEMS provides the convening environment, synthesis expertise, collaboration infrastructure, and open-science guidance. The budget will not include experimental reagents, animal costs, sequencing, microscopy acquisition, or other new data generation. Feasibility will be maintained by phased milestones: dataset inventory and governance in months 1 to 3, harmonized feature products in months 4 to 9, image and network pipelines in months 6 to 15, predictive models in months 12 to 21, and public atlas release, manuscripts, and training materials in months 18 to 24.
abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional hubs, and DNA repair foci exemplify emergence in cell biology: collective mesoscale assemblies arise from multivalent molecular interactions and generate new spatial, kinetic, and regulatory properties not predictable from individual components alone. Despite intense study, the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when specific proteins and RNAs will form condensates, how condensate material properties vary across cellular contexts, and which emergent assemblies causally influence cell state. This Working Group will synthesize publicly available datasets to answer a central question: what combinations of molecular features, interaction network architecture, expression stoichiometry, and cellular context predict the emergence and functional consequences of mesoscale condensates in human cells?

The project will integrate existing public resources that are individually powerful but rarely analyzed together: subcellular localization images from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, and Cell Painting datasets; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction maps from BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, ENCODE, POSTAR, and published AP-MS, BioID, and CLIP-seq studies; sequence-derived features including intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, charge patterning, prion-like domains, and multivalent motifs; transcriptomic and proteomic abundance data from GTEx, DepMap, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, and single-cell atlases; and public perturbation datasets including CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, stress-response time courses, and drug response studies. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will create harmonized, FAIR data products linking molecular composition, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, interaction networks, and cellular outcomes.

Our analytical strategy will combine computer vision, network science, statistical physics-inspired descriptors, and interpretable machine learning. First, we will use reproducible image-analysis pipelines to extract condensate-related phenotypes from public microscopy data, including puncta number, size distributions, co-localization, spatial organization, and context-dependent relocalization. Second, we will build multilayer interaction and feature networks capturing sequence grammar, binding multiplicity, RNA association, abundance, and compartmental localization. Third, we will train and benchmark models that predict condensate membership, condition-specific assembly, and emergent mesoscale phenotypes from molecular and network features. Finally, we will connect predicted condensate states to cellular outcomes such as stress survival, transcriptional reprogramming, proliferation, and disease-associated vulnerability using public perturbational and phenotypic datasets.

This synthesis requires NCEMS support because it is beyond the scope of a single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in condensate biology, cell imaging, RNA biology, proteomics, biophysics, machine learning, network theory, and open-science software engineering. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data repositories, with active roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will receive hands-on training in reproducible workflows, metadata harmonization, image analysis, machine learning, and collaborative team science.

Expected outputs include an open atlas of predicted and observed human condensate-forming systems, validated computational workflows, benchmark datasets for community model development, and testable hypotheses about how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale organization and higher-order cell behavior. By transforming fragmented public data into an integrated predictive framework, this project will address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: how dynamic molecular interactions generate emergent cellular organization.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: weak, multivalent molecular interactions produce mesoscale assemblies with properties not predictable from individual components alone, including selective partitioning, altered reaction kinetics, and coordinated cellular responses. Despite rapid growth in condensate research, the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when a protein or RNA will participate in condensates, what mesoscale state will emerge, and how that state influences cellular phenotypes. This working group will synthesize publicly available datasets to answer a central question: which molecular features and cellular contexts jointly determine emergent condensate behavior and downstream cell-state outcomes? We will integrate complementary public resources spanning molecular sequence, structure, localization, interaction, and phenotype. Data sources will include condensate and phase-separation databases, AlphaFold and Protein Data Bank structural models, UniProt and RNAcentral annotations, BioGRID and STRING interaction networks, OpenCell and Human Protein Atlas subcellular localization images, BioImage Archive datasets of stress granules and nuclear bodies, PRIDE proteomics, ENCODE and GEO transcriptomic data, LINCS perturbational signatures, and genome-scale CRISPR or RNAi screens from DepMap and related repositories. The project will not generate new experimental data; instead, it will harmonize heterogeneous public datasets into an open, versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph linking molecular features to mesoscale assemblies and phenotypic consequences. The working group will develop transparent analytical strategies combining computer vision, protein language models, graph machine learning, causal inference, and physical feature engineering. Image-based models will quantify condensate morphology, number, size distributions, coarsening, and spatial relationships across published microscopy datasets. Sequence and structure models will extract multivalency, disorder, charge patterning, interaction motifs, RNA-binding potential, and post-translational modification sites. Network and perturbation analyses will test whether emergent condensate states mediate cellular outcomes such as stress resistance, transcriptional repression, cell-cycle arrest, viral infection response, or cancer dependency. Rather than producing a black-box predictor alone, the group will compare mechanistic hypotheses: whether condensate emergence is best explained by intrinsic molecular grammar, cellular concentration and stoichiometry, interaction-network topology, post-translational regulation, or combinations of these factors. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise or coordination capacity to integrate high-content imaging, proteomics, structural bioinformatics, RNA biology, soft-matter physics, machine learning, and causal modeling at community scale. The proposed team would include molecular and cell biologists studying condensates, computational biologists, biophysicists, statisticians, imaging scientists, database curators, and trainees from research-intensive and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS working-group meetings will enable consensus on metadata standards, benchmarking tasks, uncertainty reporting, and interpretable model evaluation. All code, workflows, harmonized metadata, trained models, and derived feature tables will be released under open licenses through reproducible containers and public repositories. Trainees will lead cross-institutional analysis modules, participate in data-integration hackathons, and receive training in open, team-based synthesis science. The expected outcomes are a reusable public atlas of condensate-associated molecular and cellular features, validated predictive models for emergent mesoscale organization, and testable hypotheses explaining how condensates convert molecular interactions into higher-order cellular phenotypes. By transforming fragmented public data into a coherent synthesis framework, this project will address a fundamental puzzle in cell biology and provide a community resource for predicting emergent organization across the molecular-to-cellular scale.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are dynamic, membrane-less mesoscale assemblies formed through multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, nucleic acids, metabolites, and post-translationally modified macromolecules. Stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs, DNA repair foci, centrosomal condensates, heterochromatin domains, and signaling clusters illustrate how molecular-scale interactions can generate higher-order cellular properties, including compartmentalized chemistry, selective molecular partitioning, buffered biochemical noise, altered reaction rates, mechanical organization, and coordinated stress responses. These features make condensates a central model system for emergence in the molecular and cellular sciences, directly aligned with the NCEMS vision of understanding how unexpected system properties arise across scales of composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion. Despite intense experimental and theoretical progress, the field faces a fundamental unresolved problem: condensate participation and behavior remain difficult to predict from molecular properties alone. Proteins with similar disorder content may differ in condensate propensity; condensates with similar components may exhibit distinct material states; and perturbing the same component may yield different phenotypes depending on cell type, stress, concentration, or interaction context. Current knowledge is fragmented across specialized databases, individual imaging studies, structural repositories, proteomics experiments, transcriptomic perturbation datasets, and genome-scale screens. As a result, hypotheses about condensate grammar, concentration thresholds, network topology, RNA scaffolding, post-translational regulation, and disease relevance are often evaluated in isolation rather than through community-scale synthesis. This proposal addresses that gap by integrating publicly available data into a coherent, reusable framework for predicting emergent condensate states and their cellular consequences. The project is timely because several enabling resources now exist at sufficient scale: curated condensate and phase-separation databases, AlphaFold structural predictions, protein disorder and motif annotations, public interactomes, high-content localization images, BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, PRIDE proteomics, ENCODE and GEO expression profiles, LINCS perturbational signatures, and DepMap dependency screens. Each resource captures a partial view of condensate biology. Synthesized together, they can support mechanistic comparisons that no single dataset can answer. The significance is both conceptual and practical. Conceptually, the working group will test whether emergent condensate organization is primarily encoded by intrinsic biomolecular features, imposed by cellular context, shaped by network architecture, regulated by modifications, or produced by combinations of these determinants. Practically, the resulting atlas, benchmarks, models, and workflows will help researchers identify candidate condensate regulators, interpret disease-associated variants, prioritize perturbations, and connect mesoscale organization to cellular phenotypes. The project meets NCEMS requirements because it will generate no new experimental data, requires coordinated expertise beyond any individual laboratory, integrates multiple public data modalities, develops innovative analytical strategies, trains data-savvy trainees, and produces open, reproducible community resources. By converting dispersed public observations into mechanistic synthesis, the project will advance a predictive science of mesoscale cellular organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The working group will address one overarching question: which molecular features and cellular contexts jointly determine whether a protein or RNA participates in a biomolecular condensate, what emergent mesoscale state forms, and how that state influences cellular outcomes? This question will be divided into four linked aims that connect molecular determinants to mesoscale organization and phenotype. Aim 1 asks whether condensate membership can be predicted from intrinsic molecular grammar. We hypothesize that condensate-associated proteins and RNAs are enriched for combinations of disordered regions, low-complexity domains, charge patterning, aromatic and cationic residues, short linear motifs, modular interaction domains, RNA-binding capacity, multivalent binding sites, and post-translational modification sites. We further hypothesize that no single feature is sufficient across condensate classes; instead, distinct molecular grammars underlie stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional condensates, nuclear speckles, P bodies, and signaling condensates. Aim 2 asks how cellular context modifies this intrinsic propensity. We hypothesize that concentration, stoichiometry, cell type, subcellular localization, RNA abundance, stress condition, and modification state determine whether a potentially condensate-forming molecule crosses an effective assembly threshold. This aim explicitly tests the long-standing puzzle of why proteins with similar sequence features assemble in one context but remain diffuse in another. Aim 3 asks whether public imaging data can reveal reproducible emergent condensate states. We hypothesize that condensates occupy a low-dimensional phenotypic space defined by number, size distribution, roundness, density, coarsening behavior, fusion-like morphology, subcellular positioning, proximity to organelles or chromatin, and response to perturbation. We predict that these image-derived states will not map one-to-one to named condensates but will reveal shared physical and functional regimes across biological systems. Aim 4 asks how condensate states mediate downstream cellular phenotypes. We hypothesize that condensate effects on stress survival, transcriptional repression or activation, cell-cycle progression, antiviral response, DNA damage repair, and cancer dependency are mediated by network position and selective partitioning of key regulators. We will compare competing causal models in which phenotypes are driven by intrinsic properties of individual proteins, abundance changes, interactome rewiring, post-translational regulation, or emergent mesoscale state. The group will develop explicit, falsifiable predictions for each model. For example, if intrinsic molecular grammar dominates, models trained on sequence and structure should generalize across cell types. If cellular context dominates, the same molecular features should require expression, localization, and perturbation variables for accurate prediction. If network topology is central, condensate components should occupy interaction positions that amplify perturbation effects. If post-translational regulation controls state transitions, modification-site features and kinase or phosphatase perturbations should improve prediction of context-specific assembly. These hypotheses will be evaluated through transparent benchmark tasks, uncertainty-aware modeling, cross-dataset validation, and mechanistic interpretation rather than through black-box classification alone.

[Methods and Approach]
This synthesis project will use only existing publicly available data and will be organized as a coordinated NCEMS working group with expertise in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, structural bioinformatics, imaging, soft-matter physics, statistics, machine learning, knowledge representation, and open science. The workflow will have five integrated components. First, we will build a versioned condensate-emergence knowledge graph. Nodes will represent proteins, RNAs, complexes, condensates, cell types, perturbations, imaging phenotypes, molecular features, interactions, publications, and cellular outcomes. Edges will encode evidence for participation, localization, binding, regulation, perturbation response, and phenotype. Public resources will include condensate and phase-separation databases, UniProt, RNAcentral, AlphaFold, Protein Data Bank, BioGRID, STRING, OpenCell, Human Protein Atlas, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, ENCODE, GEO, LINCS, DepMap, and related CRISPR or RNAi screens. Harmonization will use persistent identifiers, evidence codes, provenance fields, ontology terms, license tracking, and confidence scores. Second, we will engineer interpretable molecular and contextual features. Protein and RNA features will include disorder, low-complexity composition, prion-like domains, charge patterning, aromaticity, sticker-and-spacer metrics, domain architecture, short linear motifs, predicted binding sites, RNA-binding potential, structural confidence, solvent exposure, multimerization potential, and modification-site density. Contextual features will include expression, protein abundance, localization, cell type, stress or perturbation condition, interaction partners, pathway membership, and network centrality. Third, imaging scientists and trainees will curate public microscopy datasets and apply reproducible computer-vision pipelines to quantify condensate number, size, intensity, shape, texture, spatial distribution, colocalization, and condition-dependent changes. Segmentation will combine established tools with foundation models where appropriate, followed by manual review of benchmark subsets and uncertainty estimation. Fourth, the group will develop predictive and explanatory models. Baseline models will include logistic regression, random forests, gradient boosting, and generalized additive models. Advanced models will include protein language model embeddings, graph neural networks, multimodal representation learning, and causal discovery or mediation analyses. Performance will be evaluated with pre-registered benchmark tasks: predicting condensate membership, condensate class, image-derived state, perturbation sensitivity, and downstream phenotype. Validation will use held-out condensate classes, held-out cell types, temporal splits by publication date, and negative-control labels to reduce leakage. Fifth, hypothesis comparison will be central. We will construct nested models representing intrinsic grammar, concentration and stoichiometry, network topology, post-translational regulation, and combined mechanisms. Model comparison will use cross-validated predictive performance, calibration, feature attribution, ablation, stability across datasets, and biological plausibility. NCEMS support will enable quarterly virtual meetings, two in-person synthesis workshops, focused data-integration hackathons, trainee-led analysis sprints, and community review of metadata standards and benchmark definitions. No new experimental data will be generated; all outputs will derive from public datasets and publicly released computational analyses.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce four major outcomes. First, we will release an open condensate-emergence knowledge graph that integrates public molecular, imaging, structural, proteomic, transcriptomic, interaction, and perturbation data with consistent provenance and uncertainty annotations. This resource will allow researchers to query relationships among molecular features, condensate classes, cellular contexts, and phenotypic consequences. Second, we will deliver a public atlas of condensate-associated features and image-derived mesoscale states, including standardized measurements of condensate morphology, abundance, spatial organization, and perturbation response across published datasets. Third, we will provide benchmark datasets and validated predictive models for condensate participation, condensate class, emergent image state, and downstream cell-state outcome. These models will be interpretable, uncertainty-aware, and accompanied by explicit documentation of limitations and biases. Fourth, we will generate testable mechanistic hypotheses about how molecular grammar, abundance, interaction topology, RNA scaffolding, and post-translational regulation combine to produce emergent condensate behavior. The impact will extend beyond condensate biology. By demonstrating how heterogeneous public resources can be synthesized into a mechanistic framework, the project will establish analytical strategies applicable to other mesoscale systems, including cytoskeletal assemblies, signaling clusters, chromatin domains, organelle contact sites, and membrane-associated molecular platforms. The work will address a central NCEMS goal by explaining how molecular-scale interactions generate unexpected cellular-scale properties. It will also provide practical value for disease biology, because aberrant condensates are implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, developmental disorders, and stress-related pathology. The working group will train graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and undergraduate participants in collaborative data synthesis, reproducible computation, benchmark construction, and cross-disciplinary communication. By transforming fragmented public observations into reusable community infrastructure, the project will accelerate discovery and create a foundation for predictive, open, data-driven cell biology.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow gold-standard open, team, and reproducible science practices from the outset. All derived metadata, feature tables, benchmark labels, analysis workflows, trained models, documentation, and manuscripts will be released publicly under permissive open licenses whenever permitted by source-data terms. The knowledge graph will preserve provenance for every assertion, including source repository, accession, publication, version, processing date, evidence type, and confidence score. Data products will be versioned through public repositories and archived with persistent identifiers using platforms such as Zenodo, GitHub, institutional repositories, and community biological databases. Reproducibility will be ensured through containerized workflows, environment files, workflow managers, automated tests, continuous integration, and executable notebooks. Each major analysis will include a machine-readable manifest describing inputs, parameters, software versions, and outputs. Benchmark tasks will be specified before model evaluation, and results will include calibration, uncertainty estimates, negative controls, missing-data assessments, and sensitivity analyses. To promote transparency, the group will publish model cards and dataset cards documenting intended uses, limitations, known biases, data coverage gaps, and ethical or licensing constraints. Open governance will be central. The working group will develop community guidelines for condensate metadata, imaging feature reporting, evidence grading, and benchmark evaluation through NCEMS-supported meetings and public comment periods. Authorship, contribution tracking, conflict resolution, and trainee leadership policies will be established at project launch using contributor-role taxonomies. Trainees will receive hands-on training in reproducible coding, FAIR data principles, responsible machine learning, open peer review, and collaborative software development. No unpublished experimental data will be required, and the project will not generate new experimental measurements. By making the complete synthesis pipeline public and reusable, we will allow independent researchers to reproduce, critique, extend, and apply the resource to new questions in mesoscale cellular organization.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because this project requires coordination, synthesis infrastructure, and transdisciplinary collaboration beyond the capacity of a single laboratory or conventional bilateral collaboration. Requested resources will support a two-year working group structure centered on community meetings, trainee engagement, computation, data stewardship, and open dissemination. Major cost categories include personnel effort for a part-time project coordinator or data curator, trainee stipends for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows leading cross-institutional analysis modules, travel and lodging for two in-person NCEMS synthesis workshops, virtual meeting support, cloud or high-performance computing for image processing and multimodal model training, software engineering assistance for workflow packaging, and publication or repository costs for open dissemination. NCEMS facilities and coordination will be used to convene investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, data-science groups, imaging centers, and biological domain laboratories. The working group will include senior and early-career condensate biologists, RNA biologists, biophysicists, structural bioinformaticians, computational biologists, statisticians, machine-learning researchers, imaging scientists, database curators, and trainees. Existing public datasets and open-source tools will be leveraged to control costs and maximize return on investment. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase experimental reagents, maintain animal colonies, or support new wet-lab assays. Computing needs will focus on storage of harmonized public metadata, processing of public microscopy images, extraction of sequence and structural features, graph construction, model training, and reproducible workflow execution. The project will reduce duplication by using established repositories, ontologies, and software wherever possible. NCEMS investment will yield durable community assets: a maintained knowledge graph, reusable workflows, benchmark tasks, trained models, documentation, and a cohort of trainees experienced in synthesis science. This resource-centered budget aligns directly with the NCEMS mission to catalyze collaborative data synthesis, promote open science, and train the future data-savvy workforce.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates exemplify mesoscale emergence: thousands of weak molecular interactions can collectively produce spatially organized, dynamic compartments that alter signaling, transcription, RNA metabolism, and stress responses without membrane boundaries. Yet a central unresolved question remains: when do molecular features such as intrinsic disorder, multivalency, post-translational modification, RNA binding, and interaction-network topology combine to generate a condensate state with predictable cellular consequences? This working group will synthesize public molecular, imaging, proteomic, and functional genomics data to derive generalizable rules linking molecular composition to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular phenotypes.

We will integrate existing datasets from Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, ENCODE, DepMap, BioGRID, STRING, UniProt, AlphaFold, DisProt, PhosphoSitePlus, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, and publicly available single-cell transcriptomic and perturbation screens.
