The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource teams, with intentional participation by early-career scientists, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows. NCEMS convening infrastructure will enable sustained cross-disciplinary synthesis, community standards for condensate data annotation, and collaborative benchmarking of computational models.

Deliverables will include an open Condensate Emergence Atlas; reproducible workflows for data harmonization, image-derived localization feature extraction, and multimodal modeling; benchmark datasets for predicting condensate membership and context-dependent function; and community-authored guidelines for integrating condensate-related public data. Trainees will participate in hackathons, model-building sprints, and team-science workshops focused on reproducible analysis, FAIR data practices, and responsible AI. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent mesoscale synthesis framework, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how do distributed molecular interactions give rise to emergent cellular organization and function?

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are among the clearest examples of emergence in the molecular and cellular sciences. They arise when many individually weak, transient interactions among proteins, nucleic acids, metabolites, and post-translational modifications collectively produce mesoscale compartments with properties not predictable from isolated molecular components alone. These membraneless assemblies, including nucleoli, stress granules, P bodies, transcriptional hubs, DNA repair foci, nuclear speckles, paraspeckles, and signaling condensates, organize biochemical reactions in space and time. Their material properties, molecular exchange rates, and stimulus responsiveness influence transcription, RNA processing, genome maintenance, proteostasis, innate immunity, and cell fate. Aberrant condensate regulation is implicated in cancer, neurodegeneration, viral infection, and developmental disorders, making condensates both a fundamental biological problem and a translationally important class of cellular states. Despite rapid progress, the field lacks a general synthesis framework for predicting when molecular features combine to produce a functional condensate state in a specific cellular context. Many studies have identified individual drivers of phase separation, such as intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, multivalent folded interaction modules, RNA binding, prion-like sequences, aromatic residues, charged blocks, and modification-sensitive motifs. However, these features are neither necessary nor sufficient in isolation. Some highly disordered proteins do not form condensates, many condensate residents are structured clients, and the same protein can behave as a scaffold in one cell type or perturbation state and as a passive client in another. This gap reflects the core challenge of emergence: condensate behavior depends on nonlinear combinations of molecular composition, concentration, binding valency, interaction-network architecture, RNA availability, post-translational modification state, subcellular localization, and cellular stress history. Public data now provide an unprecedented opportunity to address this challenge through synthesis rather than new experimentation. Protein localization images, proteomes, phosphoproteomes, interaction networks, sequence annotations, predicted structures, disorder databases, RNA-binding catalogs, chromatin and transcriptomic maps, genetic dependency screens, perturbation screens, and disease-variant resources exist at scales that no single laboratory could generate. Yet these resources remain fragmented by identifier systems, cell-type coverage, imaging standards, metadata quality, and disciplinary conventions. NCEMS is uniquely suited to catalyze the multidisciplinary synthesis required to convert these public resources into mechanistic insight. This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by focusing on mesoscale emergent properties, using only publicly available data, requiring a diverse working group, and producing open resources, workflows, benchmarks, and training opportunities. The significance is twofold. Scientifically, the project will test whether condensate membership and functional impact can be predicted from integrated multiscale features better than from any single data type. Practically, it will establish a reusable Condensate Emergence Atlas that enables the community to compare condensates across cell types, perturbations, disease contexts, and molecular mechanisms using transparent, reproducible, and extensible methods.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address one overarching question: what combinations of molecular features and cellular context generate emergent biomolecular condensate states with predictable functional consequences? We will organize the project around four connected research questions and associated hypotheses. Question 1 asks which multiscale features distinguish condensate scaffolds, context-dependent clients, and non-condensate proteins across human cell types. Hypothesis 1 is that condensate scaffolds are not defined by intrinsic disorder alone, but by specific combinations of disorder architecture, interaction valency, expression level, subcellular concentration, RNA-binding capacity, and network centrality. We predict that integrated models will outperform models based solely on disorder, low-complexity sequence, or known phase-separation annotations. Question 2 asks whether public imaging and proteomic data can reveal emergent condensate behaviors that are invisible in single-protein annotations. Hypothesis 2 is that image-derived localization features, including puncta size distributions, nuclear-cytoplasmic partitioning, spatial co-localization, texture, and cell-to-cell variability, will identify cooperative recruitment thresholds and stimulus-dependent phase switching. These emergent properties should be most detectable when imaging features are combined with phosphoproteomic, transcriptomic, and interaction-network information. Question 3 asks how cell type and cellular state rewire condensate composition and function. Hypothesis 3 is that the same molecular component can occupy different condensate roles depending on expression stoichiometry, RNA abundance, modification state, and availability of binding partners. We expect to identify cell-type-specific condensate modules linked to transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, DNA damage response, and stress adaptation, including modules that are stable across cell types and modules that are highly context dependent. Question 4 asks whether condensate-associated mesoscale states map onto higher-order cellular outcomes such as proliferation dependency, stress resistance, transcriptional programs, and disease phenotypes. Hypothesis 4 is that proteins occupying network positions that bridge condensate modules will be enriched for genetic dependencies, disease mutations, cancer vulnerabilities, and perturbation-sensitive expression programs. These proteins may represent disease-sensitive regulatory nodes whose importance emerges from cooperative network organization rather than from individual molecular annotations. Methodologically, we hypothesize that interpretable multimodal learning, graph-based inference, and transparent benchmarking can produce generalizable rules without requiring new experimental data. The project will explicitly test competing explanations. For example, if condensate prediction is driven mainly by database curation bias, models trained on one data source should fail when evaluated on independent imaging or perturbation datasets. If condensate behavior is a simple consequence of protein abundance, expression-only models should perform as well as integrated models. If mesoscale organization has independent explanatory value, then multimodal models incorporating localization, interaction topology, modifications, and cell-state data should improve prediction of functional phenotypes after controlling for abundance, essentiality, and annotation density. These hypotheses are designed to yield falsifiable results, benchmarkable computational products, and community-relevant biological insights into emergence.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will be conducted as an NCEMS working group using only existing publicly available data and no new experimental data generation. The team will include experts in condensate cell biology, polymer biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, computational imaging, structural bioinformatics, graph theory, machine learning, functional genomics, data engineering, and open-science training. Work will proceed in four coordinated phases. Phase 1 will define the data model, inclusion criteria, and community annotation standards. We will compile known and candidate condensate components from PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, UniProt, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, BioImage Archive, and the primary literature represented in public databases. Each protein will be mapped to stable identifiers and annotated for condensate type, evidence level, subcellular compartment, cell type, perturbation context, and scaffold or client status when available. Negative and uncertain examples will be curated carefully to avoid treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence. Phase 2 will harmonize molecular and cellular features. Sequence and structure features will include intrinsic disorder, low-complexity regions, prion-like domains, charged blocks, motif density, folded-domain valency, AlphaFold confidence and predicted interaction surfaces, RNA-binding annotations, and disease variants. Network features will be derived from BioGRID, STRING, CORUM, ENCODE, and public RNA-protein interaction resources, including degree, clustering, modularity, betweenness, community membership, and local multivalency. Proteomic features will include abundance, phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, and stimulus-responsive modification from PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, PhosphoSitePlus, and related repositories. Imaging features will be extracted from public microscopy resources using reproducible segmentation and feature-extraction workflows to quantify puncta, texture, co-localization, spatial heterogeneity, and cell-to-cell variability. Functional features will include DepMap dependencies, CRISPR and RNAi perturbation results, transcriptomic signatures, single-cell expression context, stress-response programs, and disease associations. Phase 3 will develop and benchmark models. We will compare interpretable baselines, including logistic regression, random forests, gradient-boosted trees, network propagation, graph embeddings, and multimodal deep learning where justified. Model tasks will include predicting condensate membership, scaffold versus client roles, condensate class, cell-type-specific localization, modification-sensitive switching, and association with dependency or disease phenotypes. Evaluation will use held-out datasets, cross-database validation, cell-type-stratified splits, perturbation-aware splits, calibration analysis, feature ablation, and uncertainty quantification. Interpretability methods, including SHAP analysis, sparse rules, network module enrichment, and counterfactual feature tests, will identify candidate rules rather than black-box predictions alone. Phase 4 will synthesize results into the Condensate Emergence Atlas, benchmark datasets, manuscripts, training modules, and guidelines. NCEMS support will enable quarterly virtual meetings, two in-person synthesis workshops, trainee hackathons, cross-team code review, and engagement with data-resource maintainers to ensure feasibility, rigor, and long-term reuse.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open Condensate Emergence Atlas linking human condensate-associated proteins to molecular features, interaction topology, imaging phenotypes, modification states, cell-type contexts, functional genomics outcomes, and disease associations. This atlas will transform fragmented public resources into a coherent synthesis framework for studying mesoscale emergence. A second outcome will be a set of benchmark datasets and transparent prediction tasks for condensate membership, scaffold-client classification, context-dependent localization, and functional impact. These benchmarks will allow the community to compare analytical methods rigorously and avoid overinterpreting models trained on inconsistent annotations. A third outcome will be a collection of reproducible workflows for data harmonization, image-derived feature extraction, network construction, multimodal modeling, and visualization. Scientifically, the project will produce generalizable and falsifiable rules describing how intrinsic disorder, multivalency, RNA binding, post-translational modification, abundance, and network architecture combine to generate condensate states. We expect to identify conserved condensate modules, cell-type-specific rewiring events, and disease-sensitive regulatory nodes whose functional importance emerges from mesoscale organization. The project will also clarify where current public data are insufficient, generating a community roadmap for future data deposition and annotation standards without producing new experimental data under this award. Broader impact will arise through NCEMS-enabled team science, training, and open dissemination. Graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and early-career researchers will gain experience in public-data synthesis, responsible AI, FAIR data practices, reproducible workflows, and collaborative authorship. Participation by research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and public data-resource teams will broaden access to cutting-edge synthesis science. Ultimately, the project will provide conceptual and computational infrastructure for predicting how distributed molecular interactions give rise to emergent cellular organization and phenotype.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science principles from inception. All data used will be publicly available, and every dataset will be documented with source accession, license information, download date, version, preprocessing steps, and known limitations. Harmonized data products will be released under permissive licenses when compatible with source terms, with clear provenance so users can trace each feature to its origin. Code will be developed in public repositories using issue tracking, pull requests, peer code review, continuous integration, environment files, containerized workflows, and archived releases with persistent digital object identifiers. Analyses will be implemented as reproducible pipelines using workflow managers and executable notebooks where appropriate. Model training and evaluation will include fixed data splits, versioned benchmarks, random seeds, performance metrics, calibration plots, uncertainty estimates, and documentation of failed or inconclusive analyses. To reduce bias and improve interpretability, we will report annotation density, missingness, database overlap, class imbalance, cell-type representation, and sensitivity to alternative negative sets. Open-science governance will be established at the first NCEMS convening. The working group will create authorship, contribution, data-use, and conflict-resolution policies aligned with community standards for inclusive team science. Trainees will be credited for code, curation, analysis, visualization, and writing contributions through contributor taxonomies. Preprints, manuscripts, benchmark descriptions, tutorials, and workshop materials will be made openly available. The Condensate Emergence Atlas will include a public web interface, downloadable tables, application programming interfaces when feasible, and user documentation suitable for both computational and experimental biologists. Community feedback will be solicited through webinars, GitHub discussions, and coordination with database maintainers. These practices will ensure that the project is not only open at publication, but reproducible, inspectable, reusable, and extensible throughout its life cycle.

[Budget and Resources]
The budget will support a synthesis-focused working group rather than experimental data generation. No funds will be used for new wet-lab experiments, sample collection, or proprietary data acquisition. Requested resources will prioritize personnel coordination, trainee participation, data engineering, computing, convening, and open dissemination. Personnel support will include partial salary or stipend effort for a project manager or data coordinator, graduate student and postdoctoral trainee time for curation and analysis, and limited software engineering support for the atlas, pipelines, documentation, and releases. Travel and convening funds will support two in-person NCEMS synthesis workshops, regular virtual meetings, trainee hackathons, model-building sprints, and participation by collaborators from geographically diverse institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource teams. Computing funds will support cloud or high-performance computing for public image processing, network construction, multimodal model training, benchmark evaluation, storage, backups, and public hosting of data products. Dissemination funds will support web deployment, digital object identifier registration, tutorial development, open-access publication fees where necessary, and community webinars. NCEMS resources are essential because the project requires sustained cross-disciplinary coordination, neutral convening infrastructure, synthesis expertise, training support, and open-science guidance that exceed the capacity of a single laboratory or informal collaboration. The center will enable shared governance, milestone tracking, integration across disciplinary languages, and engagement with external stakeholders. In-kind resources from participating institutions will include faculty effort, existing computational infrastructure, access to public-domain expertise, trainee mentoring, and established relationships with public databases. Major milestones will include a harmonized data model by month 6, first benchmark release by month 12, preliminary integrated models by month 18, public atlas beta release by month 24, and final atlas, workflows, guidelines, and manuscripts by the end of the award period.

Their material properties range from liquid-like droplets with rapid molecular exchange to viscoelastic gels and persistent solid-like aggregates. This continuum is central to normal physiology and disease, because the same physicochemical principles that promote rapid, reversible compartmentalization can also favor pathological maturation in neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, and age-associated proteostasis decline. Proteomics studies identify candidate condensate clients and interaction partners, but often lack direct material-state annotations. Genetic screens reveal phenotypic dependencies, yet their relationship to condensate architecture remains underexplored. Question 1 asks which conserved and context-specific molecular signatures predict condensate formation across organisms, cell types, and condensate classes. We hypothesize that condensate formation is not explained by intrinsic disorder alone, but by higher-order combinations of intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity sequence grammar, modular interaction domains, RNA-binding capacity, charge patterning, aromatic and polar residue distribution, expression level, subcellular localization, and local interaction-network density. We further hypothesize that drivers, clients, and regulators occupy distinguishable positions in a joint feature space: drivers will show multivalent interaction potential and context-dependent nucleation capacity, clients will show enriched partitioning motifs without autonomous phase separation, and regulators will show modification, chaperone, helicase, kinase, phosphatase, or RNA-processing functions that alter condensate assembly thresholds. Question 2 asks how molecular and regulatory features shape emergent material states. We hypothesize that liquid-like, gel-like, and solid-like condensate states arise from different balances among transient sticker-spacer interactions, RNA scaffolding, electrostatic complementarity, saturation concentration, molecular crowding, ATP-dependent remodeling, and post-translational modification. Specifically, phosphorylation, methylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, SUMOylation, and disease-associated sequence variants will have predictable but context-dependent effects on material state by modulating interaction valence, charge distribution, binding kinetics, and recruitment of remodeling factors. We expect that transitions toward persistent or pathological states will be associated with particular combinations of prion-like low-complexity domains, impaired clearance pathways, high local concentration, aging or stress contexts, and network proximity to proteostasis and RNA-metabolism modules. Question 3 asks how condensate state transitions influence higher-order cellular outcomes. We hypothesize that condensate phenotypes mediate links between molecular perturbations and cellular functions such as transcriptional bursting, splice isoform regulation, stress-granule dynamics, nucleolar activity, signaling responsiveness, DNA-damage repair, and neuronal vulnerability. Rather than treating condensates as binary present or absent entities, we will model condensate state as a latent mesoscale variable connecting molecular features to phenotypic consequences. This approach will allow us to test whether similar material states converge on similar cell-level outcomes despite different molecular compositions, and whether distinct condensate classes share transferable organizing principles. A cross-cutting methodological question is how to infer robust rules from heterogeneous public data with uneven quality and strong publication bias. We hypothesize that transparent data harmonization, uncertainty-aware machine learning, causal discovery constrained by biological knowledge, and benchmark datasets with negative and ambiguous examples will outperform single-modality predictors. The Working Group will explicitly evaluate alternative explanations, including dataset ascertainment bias, expression confounding, protein abundance effects, and circularity from literature-derived labels. Successful hypotheses will generate testable, community-validated rules that explain how molecular-scale features produce mesoscale condensate properties and how those properties affect cellular function.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will be conducted entirely through synthesis of existing public data and will not generate new experimental data. The Working Group will first assemble a Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph that harmonizes entities, evidence, and relationships across molecular, mesoscale, and cellular scales. Data sources will include LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, PhasePro, UniProt, Pfam, InterPro, MobiDB, DisProt, AlphaFold-derived structural annotations, RNA-binding protein catalogs, PTM resources such as PhosphoSitePlus and dbPTM where licensing permits, BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, CORUM, ENCODE, GEO, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, DepMap, GenomeRNAi, CRISPR screen repositories, single-cell atlases, ClinVar, gnomAD, DisGeNET, and curated literature corpora. Identifiers will be mapped through stable accessions, and metadata will capture species, cell type, perturbation, stress condition, assay type, evidence strength, and provenance. Aim 1 will define molecular signatures of condensate formation. We will create positive, negative, and uncertain benchmark sets by integrating curated condensate proteins, matched non-condensate controls, and unlabeled candidates. Sequence features will include disorder, low complexity, prion-like composition, charge patterning, sticker-spacer motifs, aromaticity, domain valence, RNA-binding motifs, predicted structure, evolutionary conservation, abundance, localization, and expression context. Network features will quantify centrality, modularity, interaction density, co-complex membership, and proximity to RNA, chromatin, signaling, and proteostasis modules. Models will include regularized regression, gradient boosting, graph neural networks, and Bayesian hierarchical models, with interpretation through SHAP values, feature ablation, partial dependence, and stability selection. Generalization will be tested by leave-one-condensate-class, leave-one-species, and leave-one-dataset validation. Aim 2 will infer determinants of material state. Public microscopy images and videos will be analyzed using reproducible computer-vision workflows to extract condensate number, size, circularity, fusion behavior, texture, spatial distribution, and recovery-like dynamics when time series or FRAP data are available. Literature-mined material-state labels will be linked to molecular features, PTMs, variants, stress conditions, and remodeling factors. We will model material state as an ordinal and probabilistic outcome, explicitly retaining ambiguous labels. Causal discovery will be applied cautiously using directed acyclic graph assumptions informed by known biology, perturbation screens, and temporal metadata. Aim 3 will connect condensates to cellular function and disease. We will integrate CRISPR and RNAi phenotypes, transcriptomic responses, proteomic changes, localization shifts, and disease variants with condensate-state predictions. Network propagation and mediation models will test whether predicted condensate state explains links between molecular perturbation and phenotypic outcome. Working Group activities will include quarterly virtual meetings, two in-person synthesis workshops, themed data sprints, trainee-led benchmark hackathons, and external community review sessions. Feasibility will be ensured by staged milestones: months 1 to 6 data inventory and schema; months 7 to 12 first knowledge-graph release; months 13 to 18 benchmark models; months 19 to 24 imaging and causal analyses; months 25 to 30 phenotype integration; months 31 to 36 final releases, manuscripts, tutorials, and community handoff.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce five major outcomes. First, it will deliver an open Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph linking proteins, RNAs, domains, sequence features, PTMs, variants, interactions, localization patterns, imaging phenotypes, condensate classes, environmental contexts, and cellular outcomes. Second, it will provide curated benchmark datasets for condensate formation, driver-client-regulator classification, material-state prediction, and condensate-associated phenotypes, including negative and uncertain examples needed for rigorous model evaluation. Third, it will generate transparent predictive models that estimate condensate propensity and material state while reporting confidence, applicability domain, and likely sources of bias. Fourth, it will identify candidate organizing rules, such as combinations of multivalent domains, RNA-binding features, charge patterning, PTM sites, network position, and cellular context that distinguish reversible functional compartments from persistent or disease-associated assemblies. Fifth, it will produce reusable workflows, tutorials, and training materials for community-scale molecular and cellular data synthesis. Scientifically, the work will advance understanding of mesoscale emergence by explaining how collective molecular interactions generate compartments with new material and functional properties. It will address long-standing debates about whether condensates are primarily governed by sequence grammar, interaction networks, expression and localization, RNA scaffolding, active remodeling, or cellular stress state by testing these factors in integrated models rather than isolated case studies. The framework will guide future experimental design by prioritizing hypotheses and highlighting under-sampled condensate classes, organisms, cell types, and conditions, while all data generation remains outside this synthesis award. The impact extends beyond condensate biology. The knowledge-graph schema, bias-aware benchmark design, image-analysis workflows, and causal modeling strategies will be adaptable to other emergent mesoscale systems, including cytoskeletal assemblies, membrane contact sites, chromatin hubs, and signaling clusters. The project will train graduate students and postdocs in collaborative, reproducible, data-intensive bioscience and will establish a durable community resource aligned with NCEMS goals for synthesis-driven discovery.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group will implement open science as a core research strategy rather than an end-stage dissemination activity. All non-restricted curated data, metadata, schemas, ontologies, code, computational environments, model outputs, documentation, and tutorials will be released through public repositories such as GitHub or GitLab, Zenodo, Figshare, BioStudies, and appropriate domain archives, with persistent identifiers and clear versioning. The Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph will use open formats, stable identifiers, machine-readable provenance, evidence codes, and community ontologies where available, including Gene Ontology, Sequence Ontology, Cell Ontology, PSI-MI, EDAM, and OBO-aligned terms. Data ingestion scripts will preserve links to original public sources and licenses, and each derived dataset will include a data card describing origin, inclusion criteria, transformations, quality filters, known biases, and recommended uses. Reproducibility will be supported through containerized workflows using Docker or Apptainer, environment files, workflow managers such as Snakemake or Nextflow, executable notebooks, continuous integration tests, and archived releases. Model development will follow transparent machine-learning practices: preregistered benchmark splits where feasible, separation of training and test sets by dataset or biological class, reporting of negative results, uncertainty estimates, calibration, feature importance, and sensitivity analyses. We will explicitly track publication bias, missingness, label ambiguity, and circularity between literature-mined labels and model features. Community governance will include a steering committee with representatives from condensate biology, computational biology, imaging, trainees, and open-source software. External users will be invited to submit issues, annotations, benchmark challenges, and feature requests. Authorship and contribution policies will be established at project launch using CRediT roles and inclusive team-science guidelines. Trainees will receive training in responsible data reuse, software sustainability, documentation, reproducible workflows, and ethical use of AI-assisted literature mining. All manuscripts will be posted as preprints, and final products will be released under permissive licenses whenever source licenses allow. The result will be a transparent, reusable, and community-maintained synthesis platform that enables verification, extension, and reuse by the broader molecular and cellular sciences community.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the proposed synthesis exceeds the coordination, expertise, and cyberinfrastructure capacity of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. Requested resources will support a three-year Working Group organized around intensive collaboration, data harmonization, trainee training, and open resource development. The largest cost category will be personnel effort for shared synthesis infrastructure: a part-time project coordinator to manage meetings, milestones, documentation, and community engagement; a data scientist or knowledge-graph engineer to implement data ingestion, identifier mapping, provenance tracking, and releases; and partial trainee support for graduate students and postdocs leading benchmark construction, imaging workflows, and reproducible tutorials. These roles are necessary to convert heterogeneous public datasets into reliable community resources rather than one-off analyses. Travel and meeting funds will support two in-person synthesis workshops at NCEMS or affiliated facilities, with equitable participation from investigators at research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and geographically dispersed institutions. Workshops will be complemented by quarterly virtual meetings, focused data sprints, trainee hackathons, and open community feedback sessions. Funds will also support trainee travel awards, accessibility needs, and participation by early-career scientists who would otherwise lack resources to join a national synthesis effort. Computational resources will include cloud storage, scalable compute for image processing and machine-learning benchmarks, repository hosting, persistent identifiers, and long-term archiving of releases. No funds will be used for new wet-lab experiments, new microscopy, sequencing, proteomics, or other primary data generation. Budgeted software activities will rely primarily on open-source tools, with limited funds for security, testing, documentation, and sustainability. NCEMS intellectual resources are equally important: facilitation of team science, guidance on FAIR data practices, support for reproducible workflows, and connection to a broader synthesis community studying emergence. The project will leverage in-kind contributions from participating laboratories, including domain expertise, existing code, public-data familiarity, mentoring time, and institutional computing where available. Budget success will be evaluated by timely knowledge-graph releases, completed benchmark datasets, trained trainees, documented workflows, community uptake, and peer-reviewed synthesis manuscripts.
abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are a defining mesoscale feature of cellular organization, yet the field lacks generalizable rules explaining why some molecular assemblies become dynamic functional compartments while others transition toward persistent aggregates or disease-associated states. This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, genetic, and phenotypic datasets to answer a central question in emergence biology: what combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and network architecture give rise to condensates with distinct material properties and downstream cellular outcomes? The project will not generate new experimental data. Instead, it will integrate existing resources including LLPS and condensate databases, protein sequence and intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification datasets, protein interaction networks, public affinity-purification and proximity-labeling proteomics, microscopy image repositories, CRISPR and RNAi perturbation screens, single-cell transcriptomic atlases, and disease-variant databases. By linking molecular composition to mesoscale condensate behavior and cell-level phenotypes, the project will directly address NCEMS priorities in understanding emergent properties between biomolecules and organelles. The Working Group will develop an open, extensible Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph connecting proteins, RNAs, modifications, interaction motifs, environmental conditions, localization patterns, condensate classes, and phenotypic consequences. This resource will support three analytical aims. First, we will identify conserved and context-specific molecular signatures that predict condensate formation across cell types and organisms, distinguishing drivers, clients, and regulators. Second, we will infer how multivalent interactions, disorder, RNA binding, charge patterning, and post-translational modification jointly shape emergent material states such as liquid-like dynamics, gelation, and solidification. Third, we will connect condensate state transitions to higher-order cellular outcomes, including stress response, transcriptional regulation, RNA metabolism, signaling, and neurodegenerative disease phenotypes. Methodologically, the team will combine network science, interpretable machine learning, causal discovery, natural-language mining of the literature, and computer vision applied to public microscopy images. A major innovation will be the development of benchmark datasets and transparent models that predict condensate behavior from molecular and contextual features while quantifying uncertainty and dataset bias. This synthesis effort requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the expertise or coordination capacity to harmonize heterogeneous public datasets spanning biophysics, cell biology, genomics, proteomics, imaging, and clinical genetics. The Working Group will include condensate biologists, protein biophysicists, RNA biologists, data scientists, image analysts, network theorists, and experts in open scientific software from diverse institutions and career stages. Trainees will participate through structured data-synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow workshops, cross-lab mentoring, and leadership roles in benchmark construction and software documentation. All products will follow open science principles: curated datasets, metadata standards, code, workflows, model outputs, and tutorials will be released through public repositories with persistent identifiers and community governance. The expected outcome is a predictive, community-validated framework for explaining how molecular-scale features generate mesoscale condensate properties and how those properties influence cellular function. This will transform a fragmented literature into a reusable synthesis platform, resolve long-standing debates about determinants of condensate specificity and pathological maturation, and train a new cohort of scientists in collaborative, data-intensive molecular and cellular biology.

Membraneless organelles formed by biomolecular condensation exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites produce dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, biochemical activities, and cellular consequences. Yet a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and environmental contexts determine whether a condensate becomes adaptive, inert, or pathological? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, biophysical, and phenotypic datasets to derive generalizable rules connecting condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes. The project will focus on stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated assemblies involving proteins such as FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1, MED1, NPM1, G3BP1, and DDX family helicases.

The effort will integrate existing data from public repositories including BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting datasets, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, ENCODE, DepMap, and disease variant resources such as ClinVar and gnomAD. No new experimental data will be generated.

The primary scientific objective is to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from combinations of molecular grammar, network context, and cellular state. Specifically, we will ask: (1) Which sequence, structural, and interaction features best distinguish condensates with liquid-like, gel-like, or solid-like behaviors? (2) How do post-translational modifications and RNA abundance shift mesoscale material states? (3) Which condensate properties are associated with downstream cellular phenotypes such as stress resilience, altered transcription, impaired translation, cytotoxicity, or disease vulnerability? (4) Are there conserved cross-organelle principles that explain why some condensates buffer cellular noise whereas others amplify pathological transitions?

Methodologically, the group will develop an open, reproducible computational framework combining ontology-driven data harmonization, probabilistic graphical models, multimodal representation learning, interpretable machine learning, and network-based causal discovery. A key deliverable will be a community-curated condensate knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, condensate types, material properties, perturbations, cell states, and phenotypes. We will benchmark predictive models across independent datasets and prioritize interpretable rules rather than black-box correlations, enabling the field to evaluate proposed principles of condensate emergence.

This project requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise and data integration exceed the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, computational biologists, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, database curators, and trainees from diverse institution types and geographic regions. NCEMS will provide the collaborative infrastructure needed to establish shared standards, resolve conflicting annotations, train early-career scientists in synthesis science, and produce community resources. All workflows, harmonized metadata schemas, analysis notebooks, models, and derived datasets will be released openly under FAIR principles. [Abstract]
Membraneless organelles formed by biomolecular condensation exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites produce dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, biochemical activities, and cellular consequences. Yet a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and environmental contexts determine whether a condensate becomes adaptive, inert, or pathological? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, biophysical, and phenotypic datasets to derive generalizable rules connecting condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes. The project will focus on stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated assemblies involving proteins such as FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1, MED1, NPM1, G3BP1, and DDX family helicases.

The effort will integrate existing data from public repositories including BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting datasets, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, ENCODE, DepMap, and disease variant resources such as ClinVar and gnomAD. We will harmonize heterogeneous data types spanning protein sequence features, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modifications, RNA-binding properties, interaction networks, in vitro phase-separation measurements, live-cell condensate imaging, FRAP-derived dynamics, perturbational transcriptomics, proteomics, genetic dependency profiles, and disease-associated mutations. No new experimental data will be generated.

The primary scientific objective is to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from combinations of molecular grammar, network context, and cellular state. Specifically, we will ask: (1) Which sequence, structural, and interaction features best distinguish condensates with liquid-like, gel-like, or solid-like behaviors? (2) How do post-translational modifications and RNA abundance shift mesoscale material states? (3) Which condensate properties are associated with downstream cellular phenotypes such as stress resilience, altered transcription, impaired translation, cytotoxicity, or disease vulnerability? (4) Are there conserved cross-organelle principles that explain why some condensates buffer cellular noise whereas others amplify pathological transitions?

Methodologically, the group will develop an open, reproducible computational framework combining ontology-driven data harmonization, probabilistic graphical models, multimodal representation learning, interpretable machine learning, and network-based causal discovery. A key deliverable will be a community-curated condensate knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, condensate types, material properties, perturbations, cell states, and phenotypes. We will benchmark predictive models across independent datasets and prioritize interpretable rules rather than black-box correlations, enabling the field to evaluate proposed principles of condensate emergence.

This project requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise and data integration exceed the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, computational biologists, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, database curators, and trainees from diverse institution types and geographic regions. NCEMS will provide the collaborative infrastructure needed to establish shared standards, resolve conflicting annotations, train early-career scientists in synthesis science, and produce community resources. All workflows, harmonized metadata schemas, analysis notebooks, models, and derived datasets will be released openly under FAIR principles. By transforming fragmented public data into testable rules of mesoscale organization, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how collective molecular interactions generate emergent compartments that shape cell fate.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that arise when many weak interactions among proteins, RNAs, nucleic acids, and small molecules collectively generate compartments without delimiting membranes. These membraneless organelles, including stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, Cajal bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated ribonucleoprotein assemblies, concentrate specific biochemical activities while excluding others. They are therefore central examples of emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences: properties such as viscosity, fusion, aging, selective permeability, buffering capacity, and pathological hardening cannot be inferred from any single molecule alone but arise from composition, stoichiometry, molecular valence, environmental state, and network context. Understanding these emergent rules is a foundational challenge for cell biology.

The field has advanced rapidly. Public studies have identified proteins and RNAs enriched in condensates, mapped intrinsically disordered regions and low-complexity domains, measured in vitro phase separation, quantified condensate dynamics by microscopy and FRAP, cataloged post-translational modifications, and linked condensate disruption to neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, developmental regulation, and stress responses. However, these data remain fragmented across repositories, organismal systems, cell types, perturbations, assay modalities, and vocabularies. One study may describe a condensate as liquid-like from rapid recovery after photobleaching, another may report gel-like behavior from slow fusion kinetics, and another may infer solid-like aggregation from disease mutations or detergent insolubility. Without synthesis, the field cannot distinguish universal principles from assay-specific observations.

This gap is especially consequential because condensates can be beneficial, neutral, or harmful depending on context. Stress granules may protect cells transiently but seed pathological TDP-43 or FUS aggregates under chronic stress. Transcriptional condensates can enhance gene regulation yet may be hijacked by oncogenic fusions. Nucleoli organize ribosome biogenesis and stress sensing but change material state during aging, infection, and proteotoxic stress. P bodies and RNA granules regulate mRNA turnover and translation while responding dynamically to nutrient and signaling cues. The same molecular grammars that enable adaptive compartmentalization may also permit aberrant phase transitions.

A public-data synthesis is timely because the necessary resources now exist at community scale. BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, GEO, ENCODE, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, AlphaFold, DepMap, ClinVar, and gnomAD collectively capture molecular features, imaging phenotypes, interaction networks, cellular states, and human variation. Yet no individual laboratory has the disciplinary breadth, curation capacity, and computational infrastructure to integrate these data into generalizable rules. NCEMS is uniquely suited to convene a working group that combines condensate biology, biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, imaging, statistics, machine learning, ontology design, and open science. The proposed synthesis directly addresses the NCEMS mission by using only existing public data to uncover how molecular interactions generate emergent mesoscale compartments that influence cellular outcomes.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching question is: what combinations of molecular composition, biophysical state, and cellular context determine whether a biomolecular condensate produces adaptive, inert, or pathological cellular outcomes? We will address this question through four integrated research questions designed to yield testable, interpretable principles of mesoscale emergence.

Question 1 asks which molecular features distinguish liquid-like, gel-like, and solid-like condensate behaviors across organelles and experimental systems. We hypothesize that material state is not determined by disorder content alone but by a multivariate molecular grammar combining intrinsically disordered region architecture, aromatic and charged residue patterning, prion-like domains, RNA-binding domains, multivalent interaction motifs, structured oligomerization elements, predicted surface exposure, and interaction-network valence. Specifically, we predict that rapidly exchanging liquid-like condensates will be enriched for reversible electrostatic and cation-pi interaction grammars, whereas gel-like or solid-like states will show higher density of beta-prone low-complexity regions, persistent homotypic contacts, disease-enriched mutations, or network motifs that promote kinetic trapping.

Question 2 asks how post-translational modifications, RNA abundance, and environmental context shift condensate material state. We hypothesize that phosphorylation, methylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, SUMOylation, PARylation, and proteolytic cleavage act as context-dependent switches that alter molecular valence, charge patterning, and scaffold-client relationships. We further hypothesize that RNA has biphasic effects: moderate RNA concentrations promote assembly and fluidity by bridging RNA-binding proteins, while excessive or depleted RNA can dissolve condensates or promote less dynamic states depending on transcript length, structure, abundance, and sequence composition. Cell stress, osmolarity, ATP availability, cell-cycle phase, and differentiation state are expected to modulate these relationships.

Question 3 asks which condensate features predict downstream phenotypes, including stress resilience, transcriptional rewiring, translational repression, altered proteostasis, genetic dependency, cytotoxicity, and disease vulnerability. We hypothesize that adaptive condensates are characterized by reversible assembly, high client exchange, regulated dissolution, and enrichment for pathways that buffer fluctuations in RNA metabolism, signaling, or proteostasis. In contrast, pathological transitions will be associated with reduced reversibility, persistent sequestration of essential factors, accumulation of aggregation-prone disease variants, impaired chaperone or helicase activity, and transcriptomic or proteomic signatures of stress amplification.

Question 4 asks whether conserved cross-organelle principles explain why some condensates buffer cellular noise while others amplify pathological transitions. We hypothesize that condensates behave as mesoscale control nodes whose outcomes depend on the balance between scaffold valence, client diversity, energetic remodeling, and quality-control capacity. A central prediction is that the same features that increase compartment robustness, such as high multivalency and cooperative recruitment, create vulnerability to hysteresis and irreversible state changes when regulation fails. This synthesis will test these hypotheses by integrating independent public datasets and evaluating whether learned rules generalize across condensate classes, cell types, perturbations, and disease contexts.

[Methods and Approach]
This working group will execute a three-year synthesis project using only publicly available data. The first phase will define scope, standards, and provenance. We will focus on stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated assemblies centered on FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1, MED1, NPM1, G3BP1, DDX helicases, and related scaffolds and clients. A cross-disciplinary curation team will establish a condensate ontology that harmonizes terms for organelle identity, molecular role, assay type, perturbation, cell state, material property, and phenotype. Public datasets will be inventoried from BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Cell Painting resources, GEO, ENCODE, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, AlphaFold, DepMap, ClinVar, gnomAD, and relevant interaction databases. Each dataset will receive machine-readable metadata describing source, license, organism, cell type, measurement modality, normalization, uncertainty, and limitations.

The second phase will generate harmonized feature layers. Protein features will include disorder predictions, low-complexity regions, prion-like domains, charge patterning, aromatic and polar residue content, RNA-binding domains, predicted structures, known and predicted interaction interfaces, post-translational modification sites, disease variants, and evolutionary conservation. RNA features will include abundance, localization, length, structure proxies, repeat content, and binding partners. Network features will capture protein-protein, protein-RNA, genetic interaction, regulatory, and pathway relationships. Imaging-derived features will include condensate number, size, shape, intensity, colocalization, fusion, persistence, cell-to-cell variability, and, where available, FRAP recovery parameters. Existing image analyses will be reused when available; otherwise, public images will be reanalyzed with reproducible segmentation workflows without generating new experimental data. Phenotype layers will include transcriptomic responses, proteomic changes, Cell Painting profiles, genetic dependencies, disease associations, and cellular stress outcomes.

The third phase will integrate these layers into a community-curated condensate knowledge graph. Nodes will represent molecules, modifications, variants, RNAs, condensate types, assays, perturbations, cell states, material properties, and phenotypes; edges will encode evidence-weighted relationships and provenance. We will apply probabilistic graphical models to represent uncertainty and missingness, multimodal representation learning to combine sequence, structure, network, imaging, and omics information, and interpretable machine-learning models to predict material state and phenotype. Candidate methods include regularized generalized linear models, random forests with feature attribution, gradient boosting with monotonic constraints where justified, graph neural embeddings benchmarked against simpler baselines, Bayesian hierarchical models, and causal discovery approaches constrained by perturbational data and known biology.

Model evaluation will emphasize rigor and generalization. We will predefine training, validation, and holdout partitions by dataset, condensate class, cell type, and protein family to prevent information leakage. Performance will be assessed using calibrated probabilities, area under precision-recall curves for imbalanced labels, cross-dataset transfer, negative controls, permutation tests, sensitivity analyses, and expert review of inferred rules. Conflicting annotations will be tracked rather than erased, and uncertainty will be propagated into conclusions. Quarterly working-group meetings, focused hackathons, trainee-led analysis sprints, and external advisory reviews will ensure feasibility, community input, and iterative refinement.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver four major products. First, we will produce a FAIR, community-curated condensate knowledge graph integrating public molecular, biophysical, imaging, perturbational, phenotypic, and disease-variant evidence. This resource will make fragmented condensate data searchable, interoperable, and reusable, with explicit provenance and uncertainty. Second, we will generate benchmark datasets and reproducible workflows for predicting condensate material states and cellular phenotypes from molecular grammar, network context, and cell state. Third, we will provide interpretable rules that identify combinations of features associated with liquid-like dynamics, gelation, solidification, reversibility, stress resilience, cytotoxicity, and disease vulnerability. Fourth, we will publish synthesis papers and living documentation that define data standards and best practices for condensate informatics.

The scientific impact will be broad. By comparing stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and pathological assemblies within a single analytical framework, the project will distinguish condensate-specific mechanisms from general mesoscale principles. It will clarify why similar proteins and interaction motifs can support adaptive organization in one context and pathological aggregation in another. It will also provide hypotheses that experimental laboratories can test using their own future studies, while the proposed NCEMS project itself will not generate new experimental data.

The community impact will align strongly with NCEMS priorities. The working group will require expertise beyond any single lab, recruit diverse participants across disciplines and institution types, and train graduate students and postdocs in synthesis research, open science, data harmonization, machine learning, and biological interpretation. More broadly, the project will create a reusable model for studying emergence in cell biology by showing how public data can be synthesized into mechanistic, predictive, and interpretable mesoscale rules.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science practices from inception. All derived data products, metadata schemas, code, workflows, notebooks, model specifications, benchmarks, and documentation will be released through public repositories such as GitHub or GitLab for active development, Zenodo or Figshare for versioned archival releases, and appropriate domain repositories for tabular and image-derived outputs. We will not redistribute restricted raw data; instead, we will provide accession identifiers, provenance records, transformation scripts, and derived features consistent with source licenses. All project outputs will use permissive open licenses whenever allowed, such as CC BY for documentation and data products and MIT, BSD, or Apache licenses for software.

Reproducibility will be engineered into the workflow. Analyses will be implemented with workflow managers such as Snakemake, Nextflow, or equivalent systems; software environments will be captured with containers and lockfiles; and all major results will be generated by executable notebooks or scripted pipelines. We will maintain data dictionaries, ontology mappings, quality-control reports, model cards, and dataset cards that document intended use, limitations, biases, missingness, and uncertainty. Continuous integration tests will check schema validity, pipeline execution on small test datasets, and reproducibility of benchmark outputs.

The working group will adopt transparent governance. Curation decisions, annotation conflicts, and model assumptions will be recorded in public issue trackers. Authorship, contribution, and decision-making policies will be established at project launch using community-centered team science guidelines. Trainees will receive structured training in FAIR data, reproducible coding, responsible use of AI, statistical validation, and collaborative software development. Preprints, open peer review when possible, public tutorials, and community webinars will ensure that results are rapidly accessible and that external researchers can critique, reuse, and extend the resources.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because this synthesis requires coordinated expertise, shared infrastructure, facilitated collaboration, and trainee engagement that exceed the capacity of any single laboratory or existing bilateral collaboration. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data. abstract_original:
Membraneless organelles formed by biomolecular condensation exemplify mesoscale emergence: weak multivalent molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites produce dynamic compartments with distinct material properties, biochemical activities, and cellular consequences. Yet a central unresolved question remains: which molecular features and environmental contexts determine whether a condensate becomes adaptive, inert, or pathological? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, biophysical, and phenotypic datasets to derive generalizable rules connecting condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes. The project will focus on stress granules, nucleoli, P bodies, transcriptional condensates, and disease-associated assemblies involving proteins such as FUS, TDP-43, hnRNPA1, MED1, NPM1, G3BP1, and DDX family helicases.

The effort will integrate existing data from public repositories including BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting datasets, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Gene Expression Omnibus, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, MobiDB, AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, ENCODE, DepMap, and disease variant resources such as ClinVar and gnomAD. We will harmonize heterogeneous data types spanning protein sequence features, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modifications, RNA-binding properties, interaction networks, in vitro phase-separation measurements, live-cell condensate imaging, FRAP-derived dynamics, perturbational transcriptomics, proteomics, genetic dependency profiles, and disease-associated mutations. No new experimental data will be generated.

The primary scientific objective is to determine whether emergent condensate behaviors can be predicted from combinations of molecular grammar, network context, and cellular state. Specifically, we will ask: (1) Which sequence, structural, and interaction features best distinguish condensates with liquid-like, gel-like, or solid-like behaviors? (2) How do post-translational modifications and RNA abundance shift mesoscale material states? (3) Which condensate properties are associated with downstream cellular phenotypes such as stress resilience, altered transcription, impaired translation, cytotoxicity, or disease vulnerability? (4) Are there conserved cross-organelle principles that explain why some condensates buffer cellular noise whereas others amplify pathological transitions?

Methodologically, the group will develop an open, reproducible computational framework combining ontology-driven data harmonization, probabilistic graphical models, multimodal representation learning, interpretable machine learning, and network-based causal discovery. A key deliverable will be a community-curated condensate knowledge graph linking molecules, interactions, condensate types, material properties, perturbations, cell states, and phenotypes. We will benchmark predictive models across independent datasets and prioritize interpretable rules rather than black-box correlations, enabling the field to evaluate proposed principles of condensate emergence.

This project requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise and data integration exceed the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will bring together cell biologists, biophysicists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, computational biologists, machine-learning researchers, statisticians, database curators, and trainees from diverse institution types and geographic regions. NCEMS will provide the collaborative infrastructure needed to establish shared standards, resolve conflicting annotations, train early-career scientists in synthesis science, and produce community resources. All workflows, harmonized metadata schemas, analysis notebooks, models, and derived datasets will be released openly under FAIR principles. By transforming fragmented public data into testable rules of mesoscale organization, this project will address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology: how collective molecular interactions generate emergent compartments that shape cell fate.
