full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and chromatin can generate dynamic compartments with system-level effects on transcription, signaling, stress adaptation, and disease phenotypes. Yet the field lacks a general, data-driven framework for predicting when condensate formation produces functional cellular outcomes rather than passive molecular co-localization. This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, genomic, and phenotypic data to answer a fundamental question: what combinations of molecular features, cellular context, and environmental state make condensates causally associated with emergent cellular behavior? We will integrate existing datasets spanning curated condensate atlases, proteome-wide phase-separation measurements, intrinsically disordered region annotations, protein-RNA and protein-protein interaction networks, post-translational modification databases, ENCODE and 4D Nucleome chromatin datasets, public live-cell and fixed-cell microscopy repositories, Perturb-seq and CRISPR-screen datasets, single-cell transcriptomic atlases, and stress-response phenotyping resources. The project will focus initially on three well-studied but mechanistically unresolved condensate classes: transcriptional condensates, stress granules, and DNA-damage-associated repair foci. These systems provide rich public data and represent distinct emergent outcomes across information processing, cellular adaptation, and genome maintenance. The working group will develop an open analytical framework that links molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular outcome. First, we will harmonize heterogeneous public datasets into a community-accessible knowledge graph connecting condensate components, biophysical features, interaction partners, cell types, perturbations, imaging phenotypes, and downstream molecular responses. Second, we will use interpretable machine learning and network-based causal inference to identify feature combinations that distinguish functional condensate-associated states from nonfunctional co-assemblies. Third, we will test whether shared design principles emerge across condensate classes, including thresholds in multivalency, RNA dependence, post-translational modification state, chromatin context, and stress history. The expected product is not new experimental data, but a reusable synthesis platform, benchmark datasets, predictive models, and testable hypotheses that can guide future experimental studies. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory has the breadth of expertise needed to integrate biophysics, cell biology, microscopy, genomics, computational biology, machine learning, and open-science infrastructure at this scale. The working group will include condensate biologists, quantitative microscopists, RNA and chromatin experts, systems biologists, data scientists, biostatisticians, and trainees from research-intensive universities, minority-serving institutions, and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS convening resources will enable iterative community curation, shared standards for condensate-relevant metadata, cross-training workshops, and sustained collaboration across disciplines. All code, workflows, harmonized metadata, knowledge graph schemas, model outputs, and tutorials will be released through open repositories under permissive licenses, with reproducible computational environments and community documentation. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will lead subprojects in data integration, model interpretation, and open workflow development, receiving training in team science, FAIR data practices, and AI-assisted synthesis. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a cross-scale predictive framework, this project will advance a central goal of NCEMS: explaining how emergent mesoscale organization gives rise to higher-order cellular function.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences because their defining properties cannot be inferred from any single molecule in isolation. Weak, multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered protein regions, folded interaction domains, RNA, DNA, chromatin, metabolites, and post-translational modifications can generate mesoscale assemblies with selective permeability, altered reaction kinetics, spatial memory, and regulated material states. These emergent properties influence transcriptional bursting, RNA metabolism, signal amplification, stress adaptation, DNA repair, and pathological aggregation. However, a central unresolved problem remains: many condensate-like puncta are observed by microscopy or inferred from molecular colocalization, but only a subset measurably changes cellular function. The field lacks a general framework for distinguishing condensates that are causally linked to higher-order cellular outcomes from assemblies that are correlative, passive, or experimentally incidental. This gap limits mechanistic interpretation, disease translation, and rational perturbation of condensate biology. The timing is ideal for a synthesis-centered solution. Over the last decade, public repositories have accumulated diverse condensate-relevant datasets, including curated component atlases, proteome-scale phase-separation assays, disorder and low-complexity annotations, protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction maps, phosphorylation and other modification resources, public microscopy images, chromatin conformation maps, enhancer and transcription factor occupancy data, single-cell transcriptomic atlases, CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq experiments, and stress-response phenotyping datasets. Individually, these resources have advanced specific subfields. Collectively, they contain latent information about cross-scale relationships between molecular features, mesoscale organization, cellular state, and phenotypic outcome. Yet their integration is impeded by inconsistent nomenclature, heterogeneous metadata, variable imaging descriptors, incompatible perturbation annotations, and disciplinary separation among biophysicists, genomicists, microscopists, and computational scientists. This proposal directly addresses NCEMS priorities by using only publicly available data to study emergent mesoscale biological organization through a collaborative, transdisciplinary synthesis effort. We focus on three condensate classes that are experimentally rich but mechanistically unresolved: transcriptional condensates, stress granules, and DNA-damage-associated repair foci. These systems span distinct biological functions: information processing at regulatory chromatin, adaptive remodeling of translation and RNA metabolism during stress, and genome maintenance through spatial coordination of repair machinery. They also provide complementary data modalities and perturbation contexts, enabling rigorous comparative analysis. By asking which design principles are shared and which are context-specific, the working group will move beyond cataloging condensates toward predicting emergent function. The significance extends beyond condensate biology. A reusable framework for integrating molecular composition, mesoscale imaging, regulatory genomics, and cellular phenotypes will provide a model for synthesis research on other emergent cellular structures, including signaling clusters, cytoskeletal assemblies, membrane-less organelles, and chromatin domains. The project will also establish community standards for condensate-relevant metadata, benchmark datasets for interpretable machine learning, and transparent workflows for causal hypothesis generation. These products will transform fragmented public data into actionable knowledge and will train a diverse cohort of scientists in open, reproducible, AI-enabled synthesis methods aligned with the NCEMS mission.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching research question is: what combinations of molecular features, cellular context, environmental state, and mesoscale organization predict when a biomolecular condensate is functionally associated with emergent cellular behavior? We define emergent cellular behavior as a reproducible higher-order outcome, such as altered transcriptional dynamics, stress survival, translational control, DNA repair efficiency, cell-cycle progression, or disease-associated phenotypic state, that arises from collective organization of many components rather than from the independent action of a single molecule. We will address this question through four linked research questions. First, which molecular features best distinguish functional condensate-associated states from nonfunctional or weakly functional co-assemblies? We hypothesize that functional states are enriched for specific combinations of multivalency, intrinsically disordered region architecture, low-complexity sequence grammar, RNA-binding capacity, modular interaction domains, and regulated post-translational modifications. We further hypothesize that no single feature is sufficient across condensate classes; instead, emergent function depends on feature combinations that produce tunable interaction networks and state-dependent material properties. Second, how does cellular context alter the relationship between condensate formation and outcome? We hypothesize that the same component can participate in different functional regimes depending on cell type, cell-cycle phase, chromatin accessibility, RNA abundance, signaling state, metabolic status, and stress history. For transcriptional condensates, chromatin context and enhancer-promoter topology are predicted to be decisive modifiers. For stress granules, pre-stress translational state, RNA composition, and stress duration are predicted to determine whether assemblies are adaptive or pathological. For DNA repair foci, lesion type, replication status, and repair-pathway availability are predicted to determine functional consequences. Third, are there shared design principles across transcriptional condensates, stress granules, and repair foci? We hypothesize that all three systems exhibit threshold-like transitions in network connectivity and regulatory modification state, but differ in the dominant control variables that tune those thresholds. We expect transcriptional condensates to be especially sensitive to chromatin-bound valency and transcription factor residence time, stress granules to RNA-dependent percolation and translation initiation inhibition, and repair foci to damage-induced recruitment cascades and ubiquitin or phosphorylation signaling. Fourth, can public perturbation and phenotypic datasets support causal prioritization rather than simple association? We hypothesize that integrating CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, public imaging perturbations, and known pathway interventions with molecular interaction networks will identify candidate causal nodes and state variables whose alteration changes both condensate organization and downstream cellular outcome. The project will explicitly distinguish prediction from causal inference. Predictive models will estimate the probability that a condensate-associated state corresponds to a functional outcome. Causal graphical and network approaches will identify perturbation-supported relationships that are consistent with functional influence. We will treat causal claims conservatively, ranking hypotheses by evidence strength and identifying where public data are insufficient. The final hypothesis is methodological: a harmonized knowledge graph, interpretable machine learning, and community curation can reveal cross-scale principles that are inaccessible to single datasets or single laboratories. Success will be measured by reproducible prediction across held-out datasets, interpretable feature sets that align with known biology, and new, testable hypotheses prioritized for future experimental validation outside the scope of this synthesis project.

[Methods and Approach]
This working group will conduct a synthesis project using only existing, publicly available data. No new experimental data will be generated. The project will proceed through four integrated workstreams coordinated through NCEMS-supported meetings, shared repositories, and trainee-led analysis teams. Workstream 1 will identify, evaluate, and harmonize public datasets. Core resources will include condensate component databases, proteome-wide phase-separation and aggregation screens, UniProt and disorder annotations, low-complexity and prion-like domain predictors, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, RNA-binding protein atlases, CLIP-seq resources, PhosphoSitePlus and related post-translational modification databases, ENCODE, 4D Nucleome, Gene Expression Omnibus, Sequence Read Archive, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting and other public imaging repositories, DepMap, CRISPR screen compendia, Perturb-seq datasets, Human Cell Atlas resources, and stress-response phenotyping datasets. Inclusion criteria will prioritize public accessibility, clear provenance, reusable licensing, sufficient metadata, and relevance to transcriptional condensates, stress granules, or DNA repair foci. Workstream 2 will build a condensate knowledge graph. Nodes will include proteins, RNAs, genomic loci, chromatin states, cell types, perturbations, stresses, modifications, interactions, imaging phenotypes, and cellular outcomes. Edges will encode evidence-backed relationships such as component membership, physical interaction, regulatory modification, co-localization, perturbation effect, transcriptional response, and phenotype association. Evidence provenance, assay type, organism, cell line, condition, and confidence will be represented explicitly. Community curation sprints will refine ontologies for condensate-relevant metadata, including assembly type, material-state evidence, stress condition, temporal scale, and functional readout. Workstream 3 will develop predictive and interpretable models. Features will be derived at multiple scales: molecular sequence and domain composition, disorder and charge patterning, RNA-binding and nucleic-acid dependence, network centrality and modularity, post-translational modification state, chromatin accessibility and contact frequency, expression level, cell state, perturbation context, and imaging descriptors such as puncta number, size, intensity, texture, colocalization, and dynamics where available. Models will include regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, graph neural networks where justified, and simpler baseline models. Interpretability will be emphasized through feature attribution, sparse models, partial dependence, counterfactual analysis, and subgroup evaluation. Performance will be assessed using held-out datasets, leave-one-condensate-class-out tests, external repository validation, calibration metrics, and negative controls composed of co-localizing but nonfunctional assemblies where public evidence supports that classification. Workstream 4 will apply causal and comparative synthesis methods. We will integrate perturbation data using network propagation, causal graphical modeling, Mendelian-style perturbation logic where applicable to CRISPR screens, and triangulation across independent modalities. Evidence will be graded by reproducibility across datasets, directionality of perturbation effects, temporal plausibility, and agreement between imaging and molecular readouts. Comparative analyses will identify design principles shared across the three condensate classes and principles that are class-specific. The working group structure will include domain subteams for transcription, stress granules, and DNA repair; cross-cutting teams for data engineering, imaging analysis, statistical modeling, and open science; and trainee cohorts that rotate across subteams. Quarterly virtual meetings, two annual in-person synthesis workshops, code-review sessions, and community feedback webinars will ensure methodological rigor, interdisciplinary interpretation, and feasibility within the NCEMS working group model.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce six major outcomes. First, we will release a community-accessible condensate knowledge graph linking molecular features, interaction networks, chromatin and RNA context, imaging phenotypes, perturbations, cell states, and cellular outcomes. Second, we will provide benchmark datasets for transcriptional condensates, stress granules, and DNA-damage-associated repair foci, including transparent labels, metadata, provenance, and evidence grades. Third, we will deliver interpretable predictive models that estimate when condensate-associated organization is likely to be functionally linked to emergent cellular behavior. Fourth, we will identify candidate cross-class design principles, including thresholds in multivalency, RNA dependence, modification state, network connectivity, chromatin context, and stress history. Fifth, we will generate prioritized, testable hypotheses for future experimental studies, clearly distinguishing strongly supported causal candidates from associations requiring validation. Sixth, we will provide reusable open workflows, tutorials, and metadata templates that can be adapted to other mesoscale cellular systems. The scientific impact will be substantial because the project addresses a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology: why some biomolecular condensates have clear functional consequences whereas others appear to be passive or context-dependent assemblies. By integrating public data across scales, the working group will move the field from descriptive catalogs toward predictive, mechanism-informed synthesis. The broader impact aligns closely with NCEMS goals. The project will demonstrate how AI, data science, and community curation can extract new biological insight from existing resources without generating new experimental data. It will stimulate collaboration across biophysics, cell biology, genomics, microscopy, statistics, and machine learning, while engaging scientists from research-intensive institutions, minority-serving institutions, and primarily undergraduate institutions. Trainees will gain practical experience in team science, FAIR data practices, reproducible workflows, and interpretable AI. The resulting platform will support future experimental design, disease interpretation, and broader studies of emergence at the mesoscale between molecules and organelles.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Open science is central to the project design. All datasets used will be publicly available, and every derived data product will retain machine-readable provenance linking back to original repositories, accession numbers, processing dates, licenses, and transformation steps. We will not redistribute restricted data or data with unclear reuse permissions. Harmonized metadata, knowledge graph schemas, controlled vocabularies, benchmark labels, model inputs, trained model outputs, and documentation will be deposited in open repositories such as GitHub or GitLab for development and Zenodo or Figshare for versioned archival release. Code will be released under a permissive open-source license, and data products will use community-appropriate open licenses whenever allowed by source terms. Reproducibility will be implemented through containerized computational environments, scripted workflows, workflow managers such as Snakemake or Nextflow where appropriate, pinned package versions, continuous integration tests, and automated generation of analysis reports. Major figures, tables, benchmark results, and model evaluations will be reproducible from public inputs through documented pipelines. We will maintain a public project website containing tutorials, data dictionaries, onboarding materials, meeting summaries, and contribution guidelines. Model transparency will be emphasized. We will publish feature definitions, training and validation splits, negative-control strategies, calibration results, subgroup performance, uncertainty estimates, and known limitations. Where machine learning models are complex, simpler baseline models and interpretable summaries will be released alongside them. Causal inferences will be explicitly labeled as hypothesis-generating unless supported by convergent perturbation evidence. Team science practices will follow community standards for authorship, contribution tracking, inclusive participation, and conflict resolution. Trainees will receive structured instruction in FAIR principles, responsible AI use, reproducible coding, data ethics, and collaborative software development. Community engagement will include open webinars, documentation sprints, and feedback periods before major data releases. These practices will ensure that the project is not only scientifically rigorous but also reusable, extensible, and trustworthy for the broader molecular and cellular biosciences community.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the proposed synthesis exceeds the scope of a single laboratory and requires coordinated expertise, convening infrastructure, data engineering, computational resources, and sustained cross-disciplinary training. The budget will be organized around activities that directly enable public data synthesis and community-scale collaboration, with no funds requested for new experimental data generation. The largest resource need is personnel time for data harmonization, software development, statistical modeling, and trainee-led synthesis. Funds will support graduate students and postdoctoral fellows who will curate datasets, construct the knowledge graph, implement reproducible workflows, perform model evaluation, and prepare tutorials. Limited staff support for a data scientist or research software engineer will ensure robust infrastructure, documentation, and long-term usability. A second category is convening and collaboration. NCEMS resources will support two annual in-person working group meetings, quarterly virtual synthesis meetings, focused hackathons, and community curation workshops. Travel support will prioritize participation by trainees, early-career researchers, scientists from minority-serving institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, and geographically distributed collaborators. These meetings are necessary to align biological definitions, resolve metadata standards, review model interpretation, and integrate perspectives from condensate biology, microscopy, chromatin biology, RNA biology, systems biology, and machine learning. A third category is computation and data stewardship. Funds will support cloud or high-performance computing time for processing public imaging, genomics, graph, and perturbation datasets; storage for harmonized derived products; container registries; archival deposition; and web documentation. Computational plans will emphasize efficient reuse of public data, transparent provenance, and cost control through shared workflows. Additional modest funds will support open-science dissemination, including tutorial development, webinar hosting, accessibility improvements, and publication charges where necessary for open access. The requested resources will create durable community assets: a public condensate knowledge graph, benchmark datasets, validated workflows, predictive models, and trained researchers. NCEMS is uniquely suited to provide the neutral convening environment, synthesis culture, open-science expectations, and multidisciplinary network required for this project to succeed.

This effort requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the scope of any single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, bioimage analysis, machine learning, ontology development, and open-science infrastructure. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data repositories, and computational biology centers, with trainees embedded in cross-institutional analysis teams. Graduate students and postdocs will receive hands-on training through hackathons, reproducible workflow workshops, FAIR data curation sprints, and mentored team-authored publications.

All harmonized metadata, code, workflows, trained models, benchmark datasets, and interactive visualizations will be released openly under community-approved licenses using reproducible containers and version-controlled repositories. By transforming fragmented public observations into a predictive synthesis of condensate emergence, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale cellular organization and higher-order cellular phenotypes.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are among the clearest examples of emergence in molecular and cellular bioscience. Proteins, RNAs, and metabolites interact through weak, multivalent, and often transient contacts, yet their collective behavior produces mesoscale structures with properties not evident from isolated components: selective partitioning, local reaction acceleration or repression, stress buffering, RNA triage, transcriptional organization, and pathological solidification. Condensates such as nucleoli, stress granules, P-bodies, paraspeckles, transcriptional hubs, heterochromatin bodies, and disease-associated aggregates occupy the NCEMS target scale between individual biomolecules and organelles. They also bridge composition, space, time, energy, information flow, and motion, because their assembly depends on molecular grammar, concentration, post-translational regulation, cellular stress, and nonequilibrium processes.

Despite rapid progress, the field still lacks a predictive synthesis. Many proteins have been cataloged as phase-separating or condensate-associated, and many public studies describe condensates under particular stresses, mutations, or cell types. However, observations remain fragmented across incompatible databases, imaging formats, annotations, perturbation assays, and conceptual vocabularies. A protein may be reported as liquid-like in one system, gel-like in another, and aggregate-prone in disease, but the public record rarely connects those outcomes to expression stoichiometry, RNA context, modification state, interaction partners, cell identity, and downstream phenotype. This prevents rigorous answers to a fundamental emergence question: when do molecular-scale features become sufficient to predict mesoscale condensate state and cellular consequence?

The opportunity is timely because public data now span the necessary scales. Condensate and phase-separation resources summarize components and experimental evidence. Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, and published microscopy datasets contain rich subcellular localization and puncta phenotypes. ENCODE, GEO, Expression Atlas, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, DepMap, BioGRID, IntAct, POST-translational modification databases, RNA-binding protein maps, eCLIP datasets, and Perturb-seq studies provide molecular abundance, interaction, perturbation, and viability context. Advances in image foundation models, self-supervised representation learning, knowledge graphs, graph neural networks, causal inference, and interpretable biophysical modeling make it feasible to synthesize these resources without generating new experimental data.

This project is significant because it transforms condensate biology from descriptive catalogs toward predictive, testable principles. It will identify combinations of sequence features, interaction networks, RNA abundance, modification potential, and cellular state that forecast dispersed, liquid-like, gel-like, and aggregate-like outcomes. It will clarify which rules generalize across condensate classes and which are context-specific. It will also reveal when condensates produce beneficial adaptation versus pathological dysfunction. The work is inherently beyond one laboratory: it requires molecular biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, proteomics, bioimage informatics, machine learning, ontology engineering, and open-science infrastructure. NCEMS is uniquely suited to convene this community-scale synthesis, support shared standards, train trainees in data-intensive team science, and generate a durable public atlas for the broader molecular and cellular sciences community.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address one central scientific question: which combinations of molecular features, cellular contexts, and perturbation histories are sufficient to predict the emergent formation, dissolution, material state, and functional consequences of biomolecular condensates? We will decompose this into five linked research questions that directly test mechanisms of mesoscale emergence using only public data.

Question 1: What molecular grammars predict condensate participation across classes? We hypothesize that condensate membership is best predicted not by any single feature, such as intrinsic disorder, but by multivalent combinations of low-complexity motifs, folded interaction domains, charged patterning, aromatic and polar residue composition, RNA-binding capacity, oligomerization potential, and post-translational modification sites. We further hypothesize that different condensate classes use partially distinct grammars: stress granules and P-bodies will be enriched for RNA-binding and translation-related features, nucleoli for ribosome biogenesis and RNA polymerase I-associated features, transcriptional condensates for activation domains and chromatin contacts, and disease aggregates for altered solubility and impaired quality-control interactions.

Question 2: How does cellular context alter condensate state? We hypothesize that expression stoichiometry, RNA abundance, cell type, stress exposure, developmental state, and proteostasis capacity determine whether the same molecular components remain dispersed, assemble reversibly, mature into gels, or become aggregate-like. Thus, molecular grammar provides a latent interaction potential, whereas cellular context determines whether that potential crosses a mesoscale transition boundary.

Question 3: Can imaging-derived phenotypes serve as quantitative readouts of material state? We hypothesize that public microscopy contains recoverable signatures of condensate state, including puncta number, size distribution, circularity, fusion or coarsening proxies, subcellular localization, colocalization, intensity heterogeneity, and persistence across treatments. Although most public images were not collected for material-state inference, harmonized computer-vision features should distinguish dispersed, liquid-like, gel-like, and aggregate-like regimes when combined with literature annotations and perturbation metadata.

Question 4: Which perturbations reveal causal regulators of condensate transitions? We hypothesize that genetic knockouts, knockdowns, CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq profiles, stress-response datasets, kinase and phosphatase perturbations, and disease mutations can be integrated as natural experiments. These data will identify regulators whose effects are not explained by abundance alone, including chaperones, RNA helicases, translation factors, nucleocytoplasmic transport factors, and modification enzymes that control condensate dissolution, maturation, or toxicity.

Question 5: When do condensate transitions affect cellular outcomes? We hypothesize that emergent condensate states mediate measurable phenotypes, including transcriptional rewiring, translation repression, RNA stabilization or decay, proteostasis burden, altered signaling, and cell viability. We predict that some condensate features are adaptive within bounded stress regimes but become deleterious when transitions are prolonged, irreversible, or mismatched to cell state.

Together these hypotheses establish a rigorous synthesis framework: molecular features define interaction potential; cellular context modulates transition thresholds; perturbations expose causal control points; imaging provides mesoscale phenotypes; and downstream omics and fitness data reveal biological consequence.

[Methods and Approach]
We will implement a three-year, NCEMS-enabled synthesis workflow organized around data harmonization, phenotype extraction, predictive modeling, and community validation. No new experimental data will be generated. All analyses will use existing public resources, including PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS, condensate-specific literature tables, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, ENCODE, GEO, SRA-derived expression compendia with open processed outputs, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, DepMap, BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, POST-translational modification resources, UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, Pfam, InterPro, eCLIP and RNA interactome datasets, Perturb-seq studies, and public disease-mutation resources.

Aim 1 will create a FAIR condensate ontology and harmonized evidence model. A curation team spanning cell biology, biophysics, RNA biology, and ontology engineering will define controlled terms for condensate identity, component role, evidence type, assembly condition, material-state descriptor, perturbation, cell type, organism, and cellular outcome. Terms will map to Gene Ontology, Cell Ontology, Experimental Factor Ontology, PSI-MI, OBO Foundry resources, and community image metadata standards. We will record provenance, assay type, uncertainty, and evidence strength, enabling analyses that distinguish direct condensate evidence from inferred association.

Aim 2 will build a multiscale condensate knowledge graph. Nodes will represent proteins, RNAs, genes, motifs, domains, modifications, interactions, cell types, stresses, images, perturbations, condensates, phenotypes, and publications. Edges will encode experimentally supported relations such as binds, modifies, localizes to, partitions into, regulates, changes abundance under, and affects viability. Feature layers will include sequence grammar, disorder, low-complexity regions, charge patterning, prion-like domains, RNA-binding motifs, abundance, stoichiometry, interactome connectivity, modification sites, disease variants, and perturbation signatures.

Aim 3 will extract mesoscale phenotypes from public imaging. We will benchmark segmentation using Cellpose, ilastik, StarDist, Segment Anything-derived tools, and domain-adapted image foundation models. Quality-controlled pipelines will quantify puncta count, area, intensity, shape, texture, spatial distribution, colocalization, nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, and treatment response. Datasets with insufficient resolution or metadata will be flagged rather than overinterpreted. Expert annotators and trainees will create validation labels for representative condensate classes, emphasizing transparent uncertainty.

Aim 4 will develop predictive and interpretable models. Baseline statistical models will test individual hypotheses and provide interpretable coefficients. Random forests, gradient boosting, graph neural networks, variational embeddings, and multimodal transformers will integrate graph, sequence, expression, proteomic, perturbation, and image features. We will use blocked cross-validation by study, cell type, condensate class, and stress condition to test generalization. Calibration curves, uncertainty estimates, ablation studies, negative controls, and data-leakage audits will be required before model release.

Aim 5 will infer candidate causal relationships and synthesize principles. We will integrate perturbation datasets using causal graphical models, difference-in-differences where applicable, mediation analysis, and target-trial emulation concepts. Results will be reviewed in iterative working-group meetings, hackathons, and curation sprints. Deliverables will include benchmark datasets, a public knowledge graph, reproducible workflows, trained models, an interactive condensate emergence map, and community-authored synthesis papers.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver the first community-scale public-data atlas linking molecular features, cellular context, perturbation responses, imaging phenotypes, and functional outcomes for biomolecular condensates. The primary outcome will be an interactive condensate emergence map that predicts transitions among dispersed, liquid-like, gel-like, and aggregate-like states across condensate classes, cell types, stresses, and disease contexts. The map will expose both generalizable principles and exceptions, enabling users to ask why a component behaves differently across cellular environments.

Scientific products will include a FAIR condensate ontology, a provenance-rich knowledge graph, harmonized benchmark datasets, validated image-analysis workflows, interpretable predictive models, and synthesis manuscripts addressing condensate grammar, context-dependent material transitions, perturbation-defined regulators, and links to cellular phenotypes. These resources will allow the field to move beyond binary labels such as phase-separating versus non-phase-separating toward quantitative, context-aware predictions of emergent mesoscale organization.

The broader impact is substantial. For molecular and cellular biology, the project will clarify how weak molecular interactions generate higher-order cellular functions. For disease biology, it will help distinguish adaptive condensate assembly from toxic maturation in neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, and stress pathology. For data science, it will establish transferable methods for integrating images, omics, sequence features, perturbations, and literature evidence into mechanistic knowledge graphs. For workforce development, trainees will learn open, collaborative, reproducible synthesis science through cross-institutional teams. The project aligns directly with NCEMS goals by using only public data, addressing emergence at the mesoscale, requiring multidisciplinary collaboration, developing innovative analytical strategies, and creating open resources that no single laboratory could produce.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The working group will operate under open, team, and reproducible science principles from project launch. All nonrestricted derived data, metadata schemas, curation guides, ontologies, code, workflows, trained model weights, benchmark splits, documentation, and visualization tools will be released publicly under permissive community-appropriate licenses, such as CC BY 4.0 for documentation and metadata and MIT or Apache 2.0 for software. We will respect source repository licenses and data-use conditions and will publish clear provenance for every imported record.

Analyses will be version controlled in public repositories with issue tracking, code review, continuous integration, and archived releases through Zenodo or equivalent repositories with persistent identifiers. Computational workflows will be implemented in reproducible systems such as Nextflow, Snakemake, CWL, Docker, Apptainer, and Conda, with executable notebooks used only when paired with tested pipeline code. Data products will follow FAIR principles, include machine-readable metadata, and use established identifiers for genes, proteins, cell types, publications, datasets, and assays.

Reproducibility safeguards will include preregistered analysis plans for major modeling comparisons, locked benchmark datasets, blinded or held-out validation tasks, leakage checks, negative controls, calibration reporting, uncertainty estimates, and model cards describing intended use and limitations. Image-analysis outputs will include quality metrics and flags for datasets unsuitable for specific inferences. Curation decisions will be auditable, with evidence grades and multiple-reviewer reconciliation for high-impact annotations.

Community engagement will include public webinars, documentation sprints, office hours, and open calls for feedback from condensate biologists, repository scientists, computational researchers, and trainees. Preprints and publications will use transparent contributorship statements. This open-science structure will ensure that the atlas is not merely a static product but a reusable, extensible foundation for future synthesis research in mesoscale emergence.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordinated synthesis infrastructure, cross-disciplinary convening, trainee participation, and shared computational resources beyond the capacity of any one laboratory. Funds will support four categories: working-group collaboration, personnel effort, computation and data infrastructure, and dissemination and training. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data.

Working-group collaboration will include two in-person NCEMS synthesis meetings per year, quarterly virtual workshops, focused hackathons, ontology sprints, and trainee-led analysis retreats. Travel support will prioritize participation from minority-serving institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, early-career investigators, repository scientists, and trainees who would otherwise lack resources for sustained collaboration. Meeting time will be structured around deliverables: ontology releases, benchmark freezes, model evaluations, manuscript outlines, and community demonstrations.

Personnel resources will include partial support for a project coordinator, data curator, research software engineer, and trainee analysts embedded in cross-institutional teams. The coordinator will manage milestones, inclusive communication, authorship tracking, and reporting. Curators will harmonize metadata and evidence annotations. Software engineering support will ensure robust pipelines, public documentation, containers, application programming interfaces, and interactive visualization tools. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will receive stipends or travel supplements to participate in hackathons, workshops, and mentored publications.

Computational resources will cover cloud storage, high-performance computing time, graphics processing units for image and graph model training, repository hosting, persistent identifiers, and security-compliant data management. Because public microscopy and omics datasets are large and heterogeneous, shared NCEMS cyberinfrastructure will prevent duplication of effort across institutions.

Dissemination resources will support public webinars, tutorials, community documentation, accessibility-compliant web interfaces, preprint preparation, conference workshops, and long-term archiving of datasets and workflows. NCEMS investment will therefore create durable public goods: trained people, interoperable standards, reusable software, benchmark datasets, and a predictive atlas for condensate emergence.

Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions and reorganize cellular biochemistry without membrane boundaries. Although thousands of proteins and RNAs have been implicated in condensates, a central puzzle remains unresolved: when do condensates act as adaptive organizers that buffer cellular stress, and when do they become amplifiers of dysfunction leading to altered signaling, growth, or disease phenotypes? [Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates have emerged as a central paradigm for understanding cellular organization at the mesoscale, the scale between individual macromolecules and membrane-bounded organelles. Stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs, P bodies, heterochromatin domains, synaptic assemblies, and many RNA-protein granules concentrate selected molecules, exclude others, and alter reaction kinetics without lipid membranes. These assemblies arise from multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered protein regions, folded domains, nucleic acids, post-translational modifications, and cellular physicochemical conditions. Their formation is therefore a powerful example of emergence: local molecular features and network interactions generate collective material states and biochemical functions that are not obvious from any single component. Despite rapid progress, condensate biology remains fragmented. Public databases catalogue thousands of condensate-associated proteins, RNAs, and experimental observations, but annotations differ in terminology, evidence strength, organism, cell type, perturbation, and assay type. Some studies infer phase separation from in vitro droplet assays, others from live-cell microscopy, proteomics, genetics, or perturbational phenotypes. The field also lacks consistent distinctions among liquid-like phase separation, gelation, aggregation, clustering, and functional compartmentalization. This heterogeneity has produced a long-standing puzzle: similar molecular features can support adaptive stress buffering in one context yet correlate with pathological hardening, altered signaling, toxicity, or cancer dependency in another. Public data now make a synthesis approach timely and necessary. Resources such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE, UniProt, AlphaFold, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, PhosphoSitePlus, dbPTM, ENCODE, eCLIP, RBP compendia, ProteomeXchange, PRIDE, Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, LINCS, DepMap, Human Protein Atlas, and published high-content imaging screens collectively span sequence, structure, disorder, RNA binding, post-translational regulation, localization, stress response, morphology, transcriptional state, pathway activity, and fitness. However, these data are distributed across incompatible formats and scales. No single laboratory can integrate, curate, benchmark, and interpret these resources with the breadth of expertise required. This proposal aligns directly with NCEMS priorities by using only existing public data to address a fundamental question in molecular and cellular emergence: how do molecular composition, material state, and network context combine to produce cellular outcomes? The project will synthesize heterogeneous datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph and use interpretable modeling to identify principles that distinguish beneficial condensate organization from maladaptive dysfunction. The work requires a community-scale, transdisciplinary Working Group including condensate biophysicists, cell biologists, RNA biologists, proteomics specialists, bioimage analysts, network theorists, ontology developers, machine-learning researchers, and trainees. By converting a scattered literature and data landscape into a reusable predictive framework, the project will advance mesoscale cell biology, support rigorous open science, and train data-savvy scientists in collaborative synthesis.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The Working Group will address one overarching question: can emergent cellular outcomes be predicted from condensate composition, material state, and network context more accurately than from molecular components considered independently? This question will be decomposed into four linked research questions. First, which molecular features consistently predict condensate participation and apparent material behavior across public datasets? We will evaluate sequence disorder, prion-like composition, low-complexity regions, charge patterning, aromatic and cation-pi motifs, RNA-binding domains, folded multivalent domains, predicted structural surfaces, post-translational modification sites, expression level, localization, and interaction valency. Second, which contextual variables determine whether a condensate is reversible and adaptive or persistent and potentially dysfunctional? We will test stress type, duration, cell type, disease mutation, pathway state, RNA abundance, phosphorylation or methylation status, chaperone association, and proximity to signaling or transcriptional networks. Third, do mesoscale features such as droplet number, size distribution, circularity, fusion behavior, internal mobility proxies, recruitment selectivity, and hardening explain downstream transcriptomic, proteomic, signaling, and fitness phenotypes beyond protein-level features alone? Fourth, can a harmonized ontology and evidence model resolve contradictions across databases and publications by separating evidence for phase separation, molecular clustering, aggregation, localization, and functional compartmentalization? Hypothesis 1 is that condensate formation and material state are governed by feature combinations rather than by single markers. For example, intrinsic disorder or low complexity alone will be insufficient; predictive signal will improve when disorder is combined with charge patterning, RNA-binding capacity, multivalent interaction domains, expression level, post-translational regulation, and network connectivity. Hypothesis 2 is that adaptive condensates occupy specific network positions that buffer perturbations. These assemblies will be enriched for reversible interactions, stress-responsive modifications, dynamic RNA exchange, chaperone connectivity, and links to pathways that restore homeostasis. In contrast, condensates associated with dysfunction will show signatures of irreversible or slowly reversible assembly, altered valency due to mutation or modification, reduced turnover, abnormal recruitment of essential regulatory proteins, and proximity to disease or fitness-dependency modules. Hypothesis 3 is that mesoscale condensate descriptors mediate the relationship between molecular perturbation and cellular phenotype. Models including imaging-derived morphology and inferred material state will predict pathway activation, transcriptional response, translation repression, growth phenotype, or viability better than models using only sequence, expression, or interaction data. This hypothesis directly tests emergence by asking whether properties at the mesoscale have explanatory value independent of lower-scale components. Hypothesis 4 is that many apparent conflicts in condensate biology arise from incompatible annotations and assay contexts. A shared ontology incorporating evidence provenance, assay type, cellular condition, temporal scale, and confidence will reveal when studies are truly contradictory versus when they describe different mesoscale phenomena. Together, these hypotheses are falsifiable using public data and will generate benchmark tasks for the community: predicting condensate association, predicting material-state class, predicting reversibility under stress, and predicting cellular phenotypic impact.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will be organized as a two-year NCEMS Working Group with coordinated synthesis sprints, virtual analysis meetings, trainee-led benchmark teams, and community review sessions. No new experimental data will be generated. Aim 1 will build a harmonized condensate knowledge graph. We will ingest public resources including PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE, UniProt, AlphaFold and predicted structural models, InterPro, Pfam, MobiDB, DisProt, PhosphoSitePlus, dbPTM, ENCODE, eCLIP, RBP compendia, BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, CORUM, ProteomeXchange, PRIDE, Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, Human Protein Atlas, LINCS, DepMap, and relevant published high-content imaging datasets. Entities will include proteins, RNAs, condensates, cell types, perturbations, stress conditions, assays, images, molecular features, interactions, modifications, pathways, and phenotypes. Edges will encode provenance, evidence type, confidence, species, cellular context, and temporal information. Ontology developers and domain experts will extend existing standards where possible rather than creating isolated vocabularies. Aim 2 will standardize feature extraction. Protein features will include disorder, low-complexity composition, charge patterning, motif density, domain architecture, predicted multivalency, structural accessibility, mutation burden, abundance, localization, interaction degree, and post-translational modification potential. RNA features will include length, abundance, modification evidence, binding partners, localization, and predicted structural or repetitive elements. Imaging features will be derived only from available public images and published segmentations where licensing permits. Using reproducible bioimage workflows, we will quantify condensate count, size, shape, intensity, coarsening proxies, colocalization, spatial distribution, and condition-dependent changes. Where raw images are not reanalyzable, curated published measurements will be encoded with evidence tags. Aim 3 will develop interpretable predictive models. Baseline models will test individual feature classes. Integrated models will use regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, calibrated classifiers, graph neural networks where appropriate, and interpretable graph embeddings. Performance will be evaluated with nested cross-validation, species-aware and study-aware data splits, external holdout datasets, calibration metrics, uncertainty estimates, and negative-control labels. Model explanations will use feature attribution, pathway enrichment, counterfactual analyses, and subgraph inspection. Aim 4 will test emergence and causal structure. We will compare models that include only molecular features with models that add mesoscale morphology, material-state annotations, and network position. Mediation and causal-inference approaches, including directed acyclic graphs, propensity weighting, sensitivity analyses, and perturbational transcriptomic comparisons, will ask whether condensate-level variables explain cellular outcomes beyond confounding by expression, essentiality, localization, or study bias. Aim 5 will create community benchmarks and validation by synthesis. The group will define gold, silver, and uncertain labels for phase separation, clustering, aggregation, reversibility, and functional compartmentalization. Benchmarks will be released with frozen training and test splits, clear evaluation metrics, and documentation. Feasibility is supported by the maturity of the public resources, the complementary expertise of the proposed Working Group, and the NCEMS environment for collaborative cloud-based synthesis.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will produce five major outcomes. First, it will deliver an open, versioned condensate knowledge graph linking molecular features, public imaging observations, experimental context, material-state annotations, network properties, and cellular phenotypes. Second, it will produce a community-reviewed ontology and evidence framework that clarifies distinctions among phase separation, clustering, aggregation, gelation, localization, and functional compartmentalization. Third, it will release benchmark datasets and transparent predictive models for condensate participation, material state, stress reversibility, recruitment selectivity, and phenotypic impact. Fourth, it will generate mechanistic hypotheses about how mesoscale assemblies regulate transcription, translation, signaling, proteostasis, and cell viability. Fifth, it will train graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and early-career scientists in collaborative synthesis, FAIR data stewardship, bioimage analysis, graph modeling, interpretable machine learning, and responsible AI. The scientific impact will be to move condensate biology from cataloguing components toward explaining emergent function. If the hypotheses are supported, the field will gain evidence that mesoscale condensate descriptors provide explanatory and predictive power beyond the properties of individual molecules. If the hypotheses are not supported, the project will still provide a rigorous negative result by identifying limits of current public data and specifying which missing measurements most constrain understanding. The work will benefit molecular and cellular biosciences broadly because condensates intersect with gene regulation, RNA metabolism, stress adaptation, development, neurodegeneration, viral infection, and cancer. The project will also advance methodology for NCEMS-relevant synthesis science by demonstrating how heterogeneous molecular, imaging, network, and phenotypic data can be integrated into reproducible, interpretable, community-governed resources. The expected long-term impact is a reusable framework for predicting when mesoscale molecular organization produces adaptive cellular behavior and when it contributes to pathological or maladaptive outcomes.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
All project activities will follow open, team-based, and reproducible science principles. The Working Group will create a public project repository at the start of the award, with governance documents, contribution guidelines, code of conduct, data-use policies, issue tracking, meeting notes, and decision logs. Curated datasets, ontologies, knowledge-graph schemas, extracted features, benchmark splits, model code, workflow definitions, trained models, documentation, and visualization tools will be released under permissive licenses whenever allowed by source databases. All derived resources will include persistent identifiers, semantic versioning, provenance metadata, source citations, and machine-readable data dictionaries. Reproducibility will be built into the computational infrastructure. Analyses will be implemented in containerized environments using workflow managers such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or equivalent open systems. Notebooks will be paired with executable scripts, automated tests, continuous integration, and archived software environments. Model development will include preregistered benchmark definitions, frozen training and test partitions, explicit exclusion criteria, uncertainty quantification, and reporting of failed models as well as successful ones. To reduce bias, we will document label provenance, assay context, organism, cell type, publication source, and evidence strength. We will actively assess study-level leakage, class imbalance, database redundancy, and overrepresentation of well-studied proteins. Community engagement will occur through open webinars, hackathons, trainee synthesis sprints, public documentation reviews, and benchmark challenges. Trainees will receive structured instruction in FAIR principles, responsible AI, reproducible bioimage analysis, ontology curation, and ethical data reuse. Manuscripts and preprints will be accompanied by executable workflows and archived releases in repositories such as Zenodo, GitHub, institutional repositories, or NCEMS-supported platforms. The final products will not be static supplements but living community resources with transparent governance for updates, corrections, and extension by future researchers.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires structured team science, cross-domain coordination, shared computational infrastructure, and sustained community governance beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. Requested resources will support Working Group meetings, data harmonization, cloud computing, trainee participation, software engineering, ontology development, community engagement, and dissemination. Approximately one third of the budget will support personnel effort for a project coordinator, data curator, part-time research software engineer, and trainee stipends. These roles are critical for maintaining schedules, enforcing metadata standards, building reproducible workflows, curating evidence, and ensuring that trainees from research-intensive universities, minority-serving institutions, and primarily undergraduate institutions can participate equitably. Approximately one quarter will support in-person and virtual Working Group activities, including two annual synthesis meetings, focused analysis sprints, hybrid participation infrastructure, accessibility accommodations, and travel awards for early-career researchers and participants from under-resourced institutions. Another portion will support cloud computing, storage, database hosting, workflow execution, image reanalysis, model training, and interactive visualization. Funds will also support open-science dissemination, including persistent data archiving, documentation, community webinars, benchmark challenge hosting, and publication costs where necessary. NCEMS resources will provide additional value through facilitation of team science, access to collaborative cyberinfrastructure, guidance on FAIR and reproducible practices, and connection to a broader community studying emergence in molecular and cellular systems. The Working Group will leverage substantial in-kind contributions from participating investigators, including domain expertise, existing code, previously curated datasets, mentoring time, and institutional computational resources. The project will not request funds for new experiments, sample collection, proprietary data acquisition, or instrument use. Budget decisions will be reviewed by a steering committee with trainee representation to ensure alignment with milestones, equity goals, open-science commitments, and NCEMS priorities.
abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from multivalent molecular interactions and reorganize cellular biochemistry without membrane boundaries. Although thousands of proteins and RNAs have been implicated in condensates, a central puzzle remains unresolved: when do condensates act as adaptive organizers that buffer cellular stress, and when do they become amplifiers of dysfunction leading to altered signaling, growth, or disease phenotypes? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, transcriptomic, and phenotypic datasets to identify generalizable principles linking condensate composition and material state to higher-order cellular outcomes.

The project will use only existing public data, integrating resources such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, CD-CODE, UniProt, AlphaFold structures, post-translational modification repositories, ENCODE and RNA-binding protein datasets, ProteomeXchange stress-response proteomics, Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, LINCS perturbational transcriptomics, DepMap fitness screens, and published high-content imaging screens. We will construct an open, versioned knowledge graph connecting condensate-associated proteins and RNAs to sequence features, predicted disorder, interaction valency, post-translational modifications, localization, microscopy-derived condensate morphology, stress conditions, pathway activity, and cellular phenotypes. Using interpretable machine learning, network modeling, and causal-inference strategies, we will test whether specific combinations of molecular features and network positions predict emergent condensate behaviors such as nucleation, fusion, hardening, reversibility, recruitment selectivity, and downstream effects on transcription, translation, signaling, and cell viability.

The central scientific question is whether mesoscale condensate properties can be predicted from integrated molecular features and, in turn, whether those properties explain cellular-scale outcomes better than the properties of individual molecules alone. This directly addresses emergence across scales: local molecular interactions give rise to condensate material states, which then reshape information flow, biochemical reaction organization, and cellular decisions. The project will also resolve a long-standing inconsistency in the field by harmonizing heterogeneous condensate annotations, imaging measurements, and experimental contexts into a shared ontology that distinguishes evidence for phase separation, clustering, aggregation, and functional compartmentalization.

NCEMS support is essential because the work exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory. The Working Group will bring together condensate biophysicists, cell biologists, RNA biologists, proteomics experts, bioimage analysts, data scientists, network theorists, ontology developers, and trainees from research-intensive universities, minority-serving institutions, and primarily undergraduate institutions. NCEMS will enable structured team science, dataset harmonization, cloud-based analysis, benchmark development, and community governance for open resources.

All outputs will follow open science principles: curated datasets, ontologies, code, workflows, trained models, documentation, and interactive visualization tools will be released publicly with reproducible computational environments. Trainees will participate in cross-disciplinary synthesis sprints, receive training in FAIR data practices, bioimage analysis, graph machine learning, and responsible AI, and co-lead benchmark challenges. The expected outcome is a community resource and predictive framework that transforms condensate biology from a catalog of components into a mechanistic, data-driven understanding of how mesoscale assemblies generate emergent cellular functions.
