[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs, and signaling clusters exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: multivalent molecular components collectively generate mesoscale material states, spatial organization, and cellular phenotypes that are not predictable from any single molecule alone. Despite rapid progress, a central unresolved question remains: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts determine whether condensates assemble, dissolve, mature, or become pathological, and how do these emergent mesoscale states influence cell-level outcomes? We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, perturbational, and phenotypic datasets into a predictive, open framework for condensate emergence across human cells. The project will integrate existing resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource microscopy datasets, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, BioGRID/IntAct protein interaction networks, LLPSDB/DrLLPS/PhaSepDB condensate annotations, DepMap and genome-scale CRISPR perturbation data, AlphaFold structural predictions, post-translational modification databases, and public transcriptomic and stress-response datasets. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize these heterogeneous resources to create a community-curated atlas linking sequence composition, disorder, multivalency, interaction topology, expression stoichiometry, localization dynamics, perturbation sensitivity, and cellular phenotypes. The scientific goal is to identify generalizable rules by which molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale condensate behaviors and higher-order cellular consequences. We will develop interoperable analytical workflows that combine computer vision for condensate morphology and dynamics, graph learning on interaction and co-localization networks, biophysical feature extraction from sequence and structure, and causal inference from genetic and pharmacological perturbation datasets. These methods will be used to test three linked hypotheses: first, that condensate-forming systems occupy distinct regions of a multiscale feature space defined by disorder, valency, interaction network architecture, and regulated modifications; second, that emergent condensate material states can be inferred from public static and live-cell imaging signatures when integrated with molecular context; and third, that specific condensate state transitions predict downstream phenotypes such as stress tolerance, transcriptional reprogramming, cell-cycle arrest, or loss of viability. This effort requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory: it demands expertise in cell biology, soft-matter biophysics, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, database curation, and open-source software engineering, as well as coordinated community standards for condensate data representation. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data repositories, with balanced participation across career stages. Trainees will participate in hackathons, reproducible workflow development, cross-disciplinary journal clubs, and team-authored data papers, gaining practical training in synthesis biology, FAIR data practices, and responsible AI. Deliverables will include an open condensate synthesis atlas, reproducible analysis pipelines, benchmark datasets for machine learning, community metadata standards, and testable predictions for future experimental studies. By transforming fragmented public data into a unified framework, this project will advance a mechanistic understanding of how molecular interactions generate emergent mesoscale organization and how that organization shapes cellular behavior.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies formed through networks of weak, multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, nucleic acids, metabolites, and membranes. They concentrate biochemical activities, organize reaction spaces, buffer molecular noise, and respond rapidly to stress. Examples include nucleoli, stress granules, P-bodies, paraspeckles, transcriptional condensates, postsynaptic densities, DNA repair foci, and signaling clusters. These systems are central to NCEMS priorities because they exhibit emergent properties: collective material states, spatial patterns, dynamic exchange rates, compositional selectivity, aging behavior, and phenotypic effects that cannot be inferred from isolated components alone. Understanding condensates therefore requires synthesis across molecular composition, interaction topology, physical chemistry, cellular context, and phenotype. Despite intense study, the field lacks general rules for predicting condensate assembly and state transitions in living cells. Many proteins contain intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity sequences, modular interaction domains, folded oligomerization interfaces, or post-translational modification sites that can promote phase separation or clustering. However, these features are neither necessary nor sufficient in isolation. Cellular concentration, RNA abundance, partner availability, competitive interactions, chaperone activity, ATP-dependent remodeling, stress history, and cell type all influence whether a condensate forms, dissolves, hardens, or becomes pathological. The same component can participate in productive ribonucleoprotein granules in one context and aberrant aggregates in another. This context dependence has created a long-standing puzzle: how do molecular-scale properties combine with cellular environments to produce reproducible mesoscale states and cell-level outcomes? The opportunity for synthesis is exceptional. Public resources now contain proteome-wide localization images, affinity purification and proximity-labeling proteomics, curated protein interaction networks, genome-scale perturbation screens, transcriptomes across cell states, post-translational modification catalogs, structural predictions, disease annotations, and specialized condensate databases. Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell provide spatial maps of thousands of proteins. BioImage Archive and the Image Data Resource include microscopy studies of stress granules, nucleoli, nuclear bodies, transcriptional hubs, and signaling condensates. PRIDE and ProteomeXchange contain compositional datasets for condensates and stress-responsive complexes. BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, and related resources describe interaction networks. LLPSDB, DrLLPS, and PhaSepDB curate condensate-associated molecules. DepMap and public CRISPR screens provide perturbational links to viability, stress responses, cell-cycle progression, and transcriptional phenotypes. AlphaFold, UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, PhosphoSitePlus, and dbPTM support extraction of structural, disorder, motif, and regulatory features. Yet these resources remain fragmented, with incompatible metadata, uneven annotation, and limited cross-scale integration. This Working Group will transform dispersed data into a community-scale synthesis framework for condensate emergence. The project is significant because it addresses a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biosciences: how do interacting molecular parts generate new mesoscale properties that shape cellular behavior? It is feasible because it uses only publicly available data and builds on mature repositories and analytical methods. It requires NCEMS because no single laboratory can integrate the necessary expertise in condensate biology, soft-matter physics, proteomics, imaging, machine learning, network science, data standards, and open-source infrastructure. The resulting atlas and models will provide a reusable foundation for mechanistic discovery, hypothesis generation, and future experimental prioritization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching research question is: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts determine emergent biomolecular condensate states, and how do those states influence cellular outcomes? We will operationalize condensate state as a multidimensional phenotype including assembly propensity, subcellular localization, size and number distributions, shape, circularity, intensity enrichment, coarsening or fusion behavior, molecular exchange where available, compositional complexity, stress responsiveness, reversibility, maturation, and association with cell viability or transcriptional programs. Rather than treating condensates as a binary class, the Working Group will model them as dynamic mesoscale states emerging from molecular, network, and environmental variables. Question 1 asks whether condensate-forming systems occupy reproducible regions of multiscale feature space. We hypothesize that condensate-associated proteins and RNAs are not defined by a single property such as intrinsic disorder, but by combinations of disorder patterning, aromatic and charged residue grammar, short linear motifs, modular domains, oligomerization capacity, RNA-binding potential, post-translational modification density, expression concentration, and interaction network architecture. We further hypothesize that different condensate classes, such as stress granules, nucleoli, P-bodies, transcriptional condensates, and signaling clusters, can be distinguished by feature combinations reflecting different physical organizing principles, including polymer-polymer phase separation, bridging-induced clustering, gelation, surface condensation, and active remodeling. Question 2 asks whether public imaging datasets contain sufficient information to infer condensate material or functional state when interpreted in molecular context. We hypothesize that image-derived features, including puncta size distributions, spatial dispersion, intensity heterogeneity, shape anisotropy, fusion signatures, temporal persistence, recruitment kinetics, and co-localization patterns, encode latent state variables associated with liquid-like, gel-like, solid-like, scaffolded, or actively maintained condensates. Static images alone are insufficient for definitive material classification, but integration with live-cell imaging, perturbation metadata, component identities, and biophysical annotations will permit probabilistic inference of mesoscale state. Question 3 asks which condensate transitions predict downstream cellular phenotypes. We hypothesize that specific state transitions, such as failure to assemble stress granules, persistent maturation of ribonucleoprotein granules, altered nucleolar organization, or hyperstabilization of transcriptional hubs, are predictive of stress sensitivity, translational repression, transcriptional rewiring, DNA damage responses, cell-cycle arrest, senescence, neurodegeneration-associated toxicity, or loss of viability. We will distinguish correlation from plausible causation by triangulating independent data types: perturbation screens, time-resolved transcriptomics, proteomic remodeling, drug treatments, stress conditions, and disease-associated variants. Question 4 addresses generalizability and limits. We ask which rules are conserved across cell lines, compartments, stresses, and condensate families, and which are context specific. We hypothesize that a core set of multivalency and network features predicts assembly across systems, whereas state transitions and phenotypic consequences depend strongly on expression stoichiometry, cell type, regulatory modifications, and stress duration. Question 5 is methodological: how can heterogeneous public datasets be represented so that condensate emergence becomes computable by the community? We hypothesize that a shared data model linking molecules, interactions, images, perturbations, contexts, and phenotypes will enable reproducible benchmarking and accelerate discovery. Together, these hypotheses connect molecular-scale variables to emergent mesoscale organization and cellular function in a testable, synthesis-driven framework.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will be conducted as an NCEMS Working Group using only existing publicly available datasets. The work plan has five integrated aims. Aim 1 will assemble and harmonize a condensate synthesis corpus. We will ingest condensate annotations from LLPSDB, DrLLPS, PhaSepDB, PhaSePro, UniProt, and the literature-linked records in public repositories. Molecular features will be collected from UniProt, Ensembl, AlphaFold, MobiDB, DisProt, InterPro, Pfam, ELM, PhosphoSitePlus, dbPTM, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, CORUM, DepMap, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, GEO, SRA-derived expression matrices where processed data are available, and public stress-response transcriptomic studies. The group will define inclusion criteria, provenance records, licensing status, confidence scores, and controlled vocabularies for condensate type, assay modality, cell line, perturbation, stress condition, and phenotype. Aim 2 will extract multiscale molecular and network features. Sequence-based workflows will compute intrinsic disorder, low-complexity architecture, charge patterning, prion-like composition, aromatic residue patterning, short linear motifs, RNA-binding propensity, domain valency, predicted oligomerization interfaces, post-translational modification density, and disease variant burden. Structure-informed workflows will use AlphaFold confidence, solvent exposure, multimerization evidence, and interface annotations. Network workflows will quantify degree, clustering, betweenness, modularity, bipartite RNA-protein connectivity, co-complex membership, interaction confidence, and condition-specific rewiring. Expression and proteomic data will estimate concentration, stoichiometry, and stress-dependent abundance changes. Aim 3 will develop imaging-derived state representations. Using publicly available microscopy from Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, and IDR, we will apply standardized segmentation and feature extraction with CellProfiler, scikit-image, ilastik, napari plugins, and deep learning models such as Cellpose or Segment Anything variants where appropriate. We will quantify puncta number, area, circularity, intensity enrichment, texture, spatial distribution, compartmental localization, co-localization, temporal persistence, fusion events, dissolution kinetics, and cell-to-cell heterogeneity. Human-in-the-loop curation will produce benchmark subsets, with uncertainty labels for ambiguous cases. Aim 4 will build predictive and causal models. Supervised models will classify condensate membership and state using interpretable machine learning, including regularized regression, random forests, gradient boosting, graph neural networks, and multimodal representation learning. Unsupervised and semi-supervised models will identify latent condensate state manifolds across molecular and imaging features. Causal inference workflows will combine CRISPR knockout and CRISPR interference screens, drug perturbations, stress-response datasets, and expression changes using do-calculus-inspired graphical models, propensity score approaches, mediation analysis, and robustness checks across datasets. We will emphasize interpretability, uncertainty quantification, external validation, and negative controls. Aim 5 will coordinate synthesis, training, and community review. The Working Group will convene quarterly virtual meetings, two annual in-person synthesis workshops, focused hackathons, and trainee-led analysis sprints. Subteams will include condensate cell biologists, soft-matter physicists, proteomics experts, imaging scientists, computational biologists, machine learning researchers, network scientists, data curators, and software engineers. Feasibility will be ensured through staged milestones: first-year data model and pilot atlas, second-year multimodal models and benchmark release, third-year integrative predictions, standards papers, and community tutorials.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open, community-curated condensate synthesis atlas that links molecular features, interaction networks, localization patterns, imaging phenotypes, perturbational sensitivities, and cellular outcomes across human condensate systems. The atlas will convert fragmented public resources into an interoperable knowledge base with provenance, uncertainty estimates, and reusable identifiers. A second outcome will be a set of benchmark datasets for machine learning and statistical modeling of condensate assembly, state transitions, and phenotypic consequences. These benchmarks will include positive, negative, and uncertain examples, documented sampling biases, train-test splits designed to evaluate generalization across condensate families and cell contexts, and baseline model performance. A third outcome will be reproducible workflows for feature extraction, image analysis, graph modeling, multimodal integration, and causal inference from perturbation data. Scientifically, the project will deliver candidate rules connecting molecular-scale properties to emergent mesoscale behavior. We expect to identify combinations of disorder grammar, valency, network topology, modification potential, and expression stoichiometry that predict condensate classes more accurately than any single feature. We also expect to infer probabilistic condensate state signatures from public imaging and to nominate state transitions that predict stress tolerance, transcriptional reprogramming, cell-cycle arrest, or viability loss. These predictions will be explicitly framed as testable hypotheses for future experimental work, not as claims derived from new data generation. The broader impact is a shift in condensate biology from case-by-case description toward predictive synthesis. The project will help resolve long-standing uncertainty about why some condensates are adaptive, reversible, and regulated, whereas others become persistent or pathological. It will provide reusable data standards for the field, improve the value of existing public datasets, and create training pathways for graduate students and postdocs in FAIR data integration, responsible AI, collaborative software development, and team science. Because the Working Group will include research-intensive institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and data repositories, the project will broaden participation and distribute synthesis capacity beyond traditional disciplinary boundaries.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science practices from inception. All derived datasets, metadata schemas, analysis workflows, trained models, benchmark definitions, documentation, and manuscripts will be released publicly under permissive licenses whenever compatible with source repository terms. Code will be developed in public GitHub or GitLab repositories with issue tracking, code review, continuous integration, versioned releases, and archived snapshots deposited in Zenodo with persistent digital object identifiers. Workflows will be implemented using reproducible workflow managers such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or CWL and distributed through containers using Docker, Apptainer, or Bioconda environments. Computational notebooks will be paired with executable scripts and automated tests to avoid non-reproducible point-and-click analysis. Data products will follow FAIR principles. Each record in the condensate atlas will include source identifiers, accession numbers, licensing information, processing history, cell type, perturbation, assay modality, confidence level, and uncertainty annotations. We will use community ontologies where possible, including Gene Ontology, Cell Ontology, Protein Ontology, Sequence Ontology, PSI-MI, OBO Foundry terms, and imaging metadata standards such as OME-NGFF. Where condensate-specific vocabulary is lacking, the Working Group will propose minimal metadata standards through open community consultation. Reproducibility will be assessed through independent reruns of workflows by trainees at different institutions, blinded reanalysis of benchmark subsets, comparison of alternative feature extraction pipelines, and model evaluation on held-out datasets from distinct repositories. Machine learning models will include data sheets, model cards, documented intended uses, known biases, and uncertainty measures. We will avoid overclaiming by reporting negative results, ambiguous annotations, and dataset limitations. Team practices will include a collaboration agreement, authorship and contribution policies based on CRediT taxonomy, inclusive meeting norms, accessible documentation, and trainee mentorship plans. Regular public webinars, tutorials, hackathon materials, and data papers will ensure that outputs are usable by both computational and experimental condensate communities.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires coordination, synthesis infrastructure, and cross-disciplinary training beyond the resources of a single laboratory. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data. The budget will support Working Group meetings, trainee participation, data curation, software engineering, computation, dissemination, and community engagement. Approximately one third of requested resources will support personnel effort for synthesis activities: a part-time project manager, data curator, research software engineer, and trainee fellows drawn from participating laboratories. These roles will maintain the atlas, harmonize metadata, implement workflows, coordinate versioned releases, and ensure that trainees receive structured mentorship. Approximately one quarter will support collaborative activities, including two annual in-person NCEMS synthesis workshops, quarterly virtual meetings, focused hackathons, and travel awards prioritizing graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and early-career investigators. Approximately one fifth will support computational resources, including cloud computing credits, storage for derived image features and processed tables, workflow execution, model training, and backup infrastructure. The project will use public repositories rather than private data stores, but temporary compute and storage are needed for harmonization and reproducible analysis. Remaining funds will support outreach, documentation, publication costs for open-access data and methods papers, accessibility services, and community standardization activities. NCEMS resources will provide the neutral convening environment required to align investigators from cell biology, biophysics, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, database curation, and software engineering. Center staff support in team science, open science, data management, and reproducible workflow design will reduce duplication and accelerate progress. Participating institutions will contribute faculty expertise, trainee time, existing computational tools, and access to institutional cyberinfrastructure. Public repositories and standards groups will contribute domain knowledge and pathways for long-term sustainability. By concentrating funds on synthesis, coordination, and training rather than new data generation, the budget directly matches NCEMS priorities and maximizes the scientific return from existing public molecular and cellular datasets.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs, and signaling clusters exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: multivalent molecular components collectively generate mesoscale material states, spatial organization, and cellular phenotypes that are not predictable from any single molecule alone. Despite rapid progress, a central unresolved question remains: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts determine whether condensates assemble, dissolve, mature, or become pathological, and how do these emergent mesoscale states influence cell-level outcomes? We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, perturbational, and phenotypic datasets into a predictive, open framework for condensate emergence across human cells. The project will integrate existing resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource microscopy datasets, PRIDE and ProteomeXchange proteomics, BioGRID/IntAct protein interaction networks, LLPSDB/DrLLPS/PhaSepDB condensate annotations, DepMap and genome-scale CRISPR perturbation data, AlphaFold structural predictions, post-translational modification databases, and public transcriptomic and stress-response datasets. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the group will harmonize these heterogeneous resources to create a community-curated atlas linking sequence composition, disorder, multivalency, interaction topology, expression stoichiometry, localization dynamics, perturbation sensitivity, and cellular phenotypes. The scientific goal is to identify generalizable rules by which molecular-scale properties give rise to mesoscale condensate behaviors and higher-order cellular consequences. We will develop interoperable analytical workflows that combine computer vision for condensate morphology and dynamics, graph learning on interaction and co-localization networks, biophysical feature extraction from sequence and structure, and causal inference from genetic and pharmacological perturbation datasets. These methods will be used to test three linked hypotheses: first, that condensate-forming systems occupy distinct regions of a multiscale feature space defined by disorder, valency, interaction network architecture, and regulated modifications; second, that emergent condensate material states can be inferred from public static and live-cell imaging signatures when integrated with molecular context; and third, that specific condensate state transitions predict downstream phenotypes such as stress tolerance, transcriptional reprogramming, cell-cycle arrest, or loss of viability. This effort requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory: it demands expertise in cell biology, soft-matter biophysics, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, network science, database curation, and open-source software engineering, as well as coordinated community standards for condensate data representation. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data repositories, with balanced participation across career stages. Trainees will participate in hackathons, reproducible workflow development, cross-disciplinary journal clubs, and team-authored data papers, gaining practical training in synthesis biology, FAIR data practices, and responsible AI. Deliverables will include an open condensate synthesis atlas, reproducible analysis pipelines, benchmark datasets for machine learning, community metadata standards, and testable predictions for future experimental studies. By transforming fragmented public data into a unified framework, this project will advance a mechanistic understanding of how molecular interactions generate emergent mesoscale organization and how that organization shapes cellular behavior.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology: weak, multivalent molecular interactions generate mesoscale compartments with material properties and regulatory functions that cannot be inferred from single molecules alone. Yet the field lacks generalizable, data-driven rules connecting protein sequence features, interaction networks, subcellular organization, environmental context, and cellular consequences. We propose an NCEMS Working Group to synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, proteomic, and perturbation datasets to answer a central question: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts give rise to emergent condensate organization, and when do these mesoscale assemblies produce measurable cellular phenotypes? This project will use only existing public data, integrating resources including the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive microscopy datasets, BioPlex and STRING interaction maps, LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, AlphaFold structural predictions, post-translational modification databases, stress-response transcriptomic atlases, and DepMap/GenomeCRISPR perturbation screens. The working group will build an open, harmonized condensate-centric knowledge graph linking protein sequence grammar, intrinsically disordered regions, predicted interaction interfaces, multivalent binding motifs, localization patterns, condensate annotations, stress conditions, interaction partners, evolutionary conservation, and phenotypic effects of perturbation. We will then develop interpretable machine learning and network-based synthesis methods to identify mesoscale organizing principles that explain why some proteins form dynamic cellular bodies, why some condensates are robust or stress-sensitive, and which condensate components are most likely to control higher-order cellular outcomes such as viability, transcriptional state, signaling adaptation, or proteostasis. The project is intentionally beyond the scope of a single laboratory because it requires expertise in cell biology, phase separation biophysics, protein disorder and structural bioinformatics, microscopy image analysis, graph machine learning, causal inference, database engineering, and open-science workflow development. NCEMS support is essential to convene a geographically and institutionally diverse team, including researchers from R1 universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and data-science groups, to establish shared standards for integrating heterogeneous condensate-related data. Trainees will receive hands-on training through hackathon-style synthesis sprints, reproducible workflow development, image-derived feature extraction, graph analytics, and collaborative manuscript preparation. Expected outcomes include: an open FAIR database of condensate-associated molecular and cellular features; reusable pipelines for harmonizing public imaging, proteomic, and perturbation data; predictive models for condensate propensity and functional impact; and a community-authored framework defining testable principles of condensate emergence. By synthesizing existing data across molecular, mesoscale, and cellular scales, this working group will address a long-standing puzzle in cell biology: how dynamic molecular collectives become functional cellular structures. The resulting resource will enable the broader community to prioritize mechanisms, reinterpret existing experiments, and design future studies of emergent mesoscale organization without generating new experimental data during the funded synthesis effort.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies formed through networks of weak, transient, and multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, nucleic acids, metabolites, and post-translationally modified molecular surfaces. Examples include nucleoli, stress granules, P bodies, nuclear speckles, transcriptional hubs, centrosomal assemblies, and signaling clusters. These structures are central to current questions in emergence because their properties cannot be predicted by enumerating individual molecular components alone. Condensates display collective behaviors such as selective molecular partitioning, maturation, fusion, dissolution, viscoelasticity, buffering, reaction acceleration, and environment-dependent switching. They influence transcription, RNA processing, stress adaptation, DNA repair, signaling, proteostasis, and cell fate, and their dysregulation is implicated in cancer, neurodegeneration, viral infection, developmental disorders, and aging. Despite intense experimental progress, the field lacks generalizable rules that connect molecular composition to mesoscale organization and cellular phenotype. Current knowledge is fragmented across specialized databases, imaging repositories, proteomic interaction maps, structural predictions, disorder annotations, stress-response atlases, and perturbation screens. Individual studies often characterize one condensate, one protein family, one stress condition, or one imaging modality. As a result, it remains unclear which sequence features, interaction architectures, localization patterns, environmental cues, and network positions distinguish condensate scaffolds from clients, functional condensates from incidental assemblies, and adaptive mesoscale states from pathological or deleterious states. This knowledge gap is precisely suited to the NCEMS mission. Publicly available data now provide an unprecedented opportunity to synthesize information across scales. Protein sequence resources capture low-complexity regions, aromatic and charged motifs, prion-like domains, short linear motifs, RNA-binding domains, and intrinsically disordered regions. AlphaFold and related structural predictions provide putative folded domains, interface features, and conformational context. Interaction maps from BioPlex, STRING, IntAct, and related resources reveal multivalent network neighborhoods. LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, UniProt, PhosphoSitePlus, dbPTM, the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, the Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, DepMap, GenomeCRISPR, and transcriptomic stress atlases capture complementary information on condensate association, localization, dynamics, perturbation effects, and cellular context. However, these resources differ in identifiers, evidence standards, imaging metadata, cell types, perturbation designs, and ontology usage. No single laboratory is positioned to harmonize these data types, build shared analytical standards, and extract broadly useful principles. The proposed Working Group will address this need through a collaborative, community-scale synthesis effort that uses no new experimental data. By integrating molecular features, subcellular organization, interaction networks, environmental context, and phenotypic consequences into a condensate-centric knowledge graph, we will transform scattered observations into an analyzable representation of emergent mesoscale biology. The significance extends beyond condensates. The project will establish a model for how synthesis science can bridge biomolecular mechanisms and cellular outcomes, train data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists, and create open resources that enable the community to formulate and test mechanistic hypotheses about emergence.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The Working Group will focus on a central scientific question: what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts give rise to emergent condensate organization, and when do these mesoscale assemblies produce measurable cellular phenotypes? This question will be divided into four tractable aims that can be answered through synthesis of existing public data. Aim 1 asks which molecular grammars distinguish condensate scaffolds, clients, regulators, and non-condensate controls. We hypothesize that condensate scaffolds are not defined by intrinsic disorder alone, but by combinations of disordered regions, repeated short linear motifs, folded interaction domains, charge patterning, aromatic or polar residue enrichment, RNA or DNA binding capacity, and post-translational modification sites that together create tunable multivalency. We further hypothesize that clients share localization and interaction features with scaffolds but have fewer independent interaction modules and lower network centrality within condensate-associated neighborhoods. Aim 2 asks how protein interaction networks and subcellular localization jointly predict mesoscale assembly. We hypothesize that condensate-forming systems occupy distinctive network positions characterized by local interaction density, modularity, enrichment for weak and transient interactions, and context-sensitive connections that change during stress, cell cycle progression, differentiation, or signaling. We predict that proteins with similar molecular grammars will form different mesoscale structures depending on their interaction partners, concentration proxies, localization constraints, and cellular state. Aim 3 asks why some condensates are robust across cell types and conditions, whereas others are stress-sensitive, transient, or disease-associated. We hypothesize that robust condensates contain multiple redundant scaffolding mechanisms and conserved interaction architectures, while stress-sensitive condensates depend on switch-like features such as phosphorylation, methylation, ATP-dependent remodeling, RNA availability, oxidative state, or rapid transcriptional responses. We expect that comparative synthesis across imaging, proteomic, and transcriptomic data will reveal context-dependent thresholds for assembly and dissolution. Aim 4 asks which condensate components exert causal influence on higher-order cellular outcomes. We hypothesize that phenotypically influential components are those that couple mesoscale organization to essential cellular processes, such as ribosome biogenesis, transcriptional regulation, RNA metabolism, DNA damage response, signaling adaptation, and proteostasis. These proteins should show convergence among condensate annotation, centrality in interaction networks, stress-responsive regulation, evolutionary conservation, disease association, and sensitivity in CRISPR or RNAi perturbation screens. A cross-cutting methodological hypothesis is that interpretable graph-based machine learning, combined with careful evidence scoring and causal-inference-inspired triangulation across independent datasets, can identify robust organizing principles despite heterogeneity in public data. The project will not claim that public data alone prove physical mechanism for every protein. Instead, it will generate well-supported, reproducible, and explicitly uncertainty-aware rules that explain observed patterns and prioritize mechanisms for future experimental testing by the broader community after the synthesis effort. Success will be measured by the ability of these rules to predict held-out condensate annotations, explain image-derived mesoscale features, stratify stress-responsive assemblies, and identify perturbation-sensitive components more accurately than sequence-only, disorder-only, or interaction-only baselines.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will be conducted as an NCEMS Working Group organized around integrated data, modeling, and interpretation sprints. All analyses will use only publicly available data and will generate no new experimental measurements. First, we will assemble a condensate-centered data inventory and evidence framework. Core sources will include LLPSDB, PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, DisProt, UniProt, Gene Ontology, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive, BioPlex, STRING, IntAct, CORUM, AlphaFold structure predictions, PhosphoSitePlus, dbPTM, PRIDE-derived proteomics where publicly accessible, stress-response transcriptomic atlases from GEO, Expression Atlas, and ArrayExpress, DepMap, GenomeCRISPR, and published genome-wide CRISPR or RNAi screens. Metadata will be harmonized using stable identifiers, including UniProt accessions, Ensembl gene IDs, HGNC symbols, Cellosaurus cell line identifiers, PSI-MI interaction terms, Gene Ontology cellular component terms, and OME-compatible imaging metadata where available. Each assertion will be assigned provenance, evidence type, organism, cell type, condition, assay, and confidence. Second, we will construct an open knowledge graph linking proteins, domains, motifs, intrinsically disordered regions, predicted structural features, post-translational modifications, interaction partners, condensate annotations, localization phenotypes, stress conditions, disease associations, and perturbation outcomes. Database engineers and ontology specialists will implement schema design, identifier reconciliation, versioning, and programmatic access. The graph will support transparent queries, such as identifying proteins with arginine-glycine motifs, nuclear speckle localization, phosphorylation changes under stress, and essentiality in transcription-dependent cell lines. Third, we will derive feature sets spanning molecular, network, imaging, and phenotypic scales. Sequence features will include disorder propensity, charge patterning, low-complexity composition, repeat content, prion-like scores, motif density, domain architecture, predicted binding interfaces, and conservation. Network features will include degree, betweenness, clustering, community membership, condensate-neighborhood enrichment, and context-specific interaction evidence. Imaging features will include localization class, puncta-like patterns, compartment co-localization, intensity heterogeneity, cell-to-cell variability, and where public images permit, segmentation-derived mesoscale descriptors obtained with existing open tools. Perturbation features will include viability effects, dependency profiles, transcriptomic signatures, stress-response changes, and pathway-level phenotypes. Fourth, we will build interpretable predictive and explanatory models. Baselines will include logistic regression, random forests, gradient-boosted models, and network propagation. Graph neural networks and heterogeneous graph embeddings will be used only when interpretable feature attribution and rigorous validation are possible. Models will be trained for scaffold-client classification, condensate-association prediction, stress sensitivity, localization pattern prediction, and phenotypic impact. Validation will use held-out datasets, leave-one-condensate-out tests, leave-one-database-out tests, negative control proteins matched for expression and localization, and sensitivity analyses for annotation bias. Causal-inference-inspired triangulation will compare independent evidence streams rather than infer causality from one dataset. Finally, biological interpretation will occur through cross-disciplinary synthesis meetings involving condensate biologists, biophysicists, structural bioinformaticians, image analysts, network scientists, data engineers, trainees, and open-science specialists. The Working Group will produce community-vetted rules, uncertainty estimates, reusable workflows, and manuscripts.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver four major outcomes aligned with NCEMS goals. First, we will release a FAIR, condensate-centric knowledge graph that integrates public molecular, structural, interaction, imaging, stress-response, and perturbation data with transparent provenance and evidence scoring. This resource will enable researchers to query relationships among sequence grammar, mesoscale localization, context, and phenotype without recreating complex data harmonization pipelines. Second, we will provide reusable open workflows for identifier mapping, condensate annotation harmonization, feature extraction from protein sequences and structures, network analysis, public microscopy metadata processing, image-derived mesoscale feature extraction where feasible, and integration of perturbation screens. Third, we will produce interpretable predictive models that identify candidate scaffolds, clients, stress-sensitive assemblies, robust condensate modules, and components likely to control cellular phenotypes. These models will be benchmarked against simple baselines and accompanied by uncertainty estimates to support responsible use. Fourth, the Working Group will generate a community-authored conceptual framework describing testable rules of condensate emergence, including how multivalent molecular features interact with localization, concentration proxies, post-translational regulation, network topology, and cellular state. The scientific impact will be substantial. The project addresses a long-standing puzzle in cell biology: how dynamic molecular collectives become functional cellular structures. It will transform condensate research from a collection of case studies into a comparative, data-driven synthesis across molecular and cellular scales. The broader impact includes democratizing access to integrated condensate knowledge, supporting laboratories that lack large-scale computational infrastructure, and creating training experiences for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in team science, reproducible data science, biological interpretation, and open software development. The resource will help the community prioritize future experiments, reinterpret existing datasets, identify disease-relevant condensate mechanisms, and develop general strategies for studying emergence in mesoscale molecular systems.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Open science is central to the project design rather than an end-stage dissemination activity. All code, workflows, data schemas, documentation, benchmark definitions, and derived nonrestricted datasets will be released under permissive open licenses through public repositories such as GitHub, Zenodo, and institutional or NCEMS-supported archives. The Working Group will follow FAIR principles by using persistent identifiers, machine-readable metadata, clear provenance, standardized ontologies, and versioned releases. Because the project synthesizes public data from multiple sources, each source will be documented with license status, access date, citation, processing steps, and any restrictions on redistribution. When source licenses prevent redistribution of full data, we will release transformation scripts, metadata, identifiers, and instructions that enable reproducible reconstruction by authorized users. Reproducibility will be ensured through containerized computational environments, workflow managers such as Snakemake or Nextflow, version-pinned dependencies, automated tests, continuous integration, and archived releases linked to manuscripts. Analyses will include negative controls, data leakage checks, holdout validation, sensitivity analyses, and explicit reporting of missingness and uncertainty. Model cards will describe intended uses, limitations, training data, bias risks, validation procedures, and appropriate interpretation of predictions. The Working Group will adopt an open-team-science governance plan with clear authorship policies, contribution tracking, meeting notes, decision logs, and mechanisms for resolving disagreements. Trainees will be included as full contributors and will receive training in reproducible coding, responsible AI, metadata standards, workflow documentation, collaborative software engineering, and ethical data reuse. Community engagement will include public tutorials, virtual workshops, issue trackers for data corrections, and periodic open feedback sessions. Manuscripts will be posted as preprints when appropriate, and final publications will be open access where feasible. These practices will make the synthesis transparent, reusable, extensible, and trustworthy for the broader molecular and cellular biosciences community.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the proposed synthesis requires coordinated expertise, shared infrastructure, and sustained collaboration beyond the capacity of any single laboratory. Requested resources will support Working Group convening, trainee participation, data engineering, computational infrastructure, and open dissemination. The largest cost category will be personnel and participation support for a distributed team including senior investigators, early-career researchers, graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, database engineers, image-analysis specialists, and data-science contributors from R1 universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and computational groups. Support will enable compensated trainee effort for workflow development, curation, benchmarking, documentation, and collaborative manuscripts, ensuring that training is embedded in productive research. Travel and meeting funds will support two in-person synthesis meetings per year at NCEMS or affiliated sites, supplemented by monthly virtual working sessions and short hackathon-style sprints. These meetings are necessary for ontology alignment, cross-disciplinary interpretation, model validation, and community consensus on evidence standards. Computational resources will include cloud or center-supported storage and compute for processing public imaging metadata, building the knowledge graph, running feature extraction pipelines, training interpretable models, maintaining container registries, and hosting documentation. Funds will also support software sustainability activities, including repository maintenance, user tutorials, help-desk issue triage, and long-term archiving of releases. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase experimental reagents, or conduct new wet-lab assays. NCEMS resources are uniquely appropriate because the Center provides a synthesis-focused environment, expertise in AI and data science, open-science infrastructure, and convening power for multidisciplinary teams studying emergence. The Working Group will leverage existing public data assets and institutional in-kind expertise, while NCEMS support will supply the coordination, training structure, computational backbone, and community legitimacy needed to transform fragmented condensate data into a durable, reusable resource for mesoscale molecular and cellular science.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates are mesoscale assemblies that emerge from weak multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, and metabolites, yet their cellular consequences remain difficult to predict: under what conditions do condensates buffer perturbations, amplify stress signals, sequester regulatory factors, or drive pathological transitions? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and phenotypic data to identify generalizable rules connecting condensate composition and material state to cellular stress responses and fate decisions. The central hypothesis is that condensate function is not encoded by individual components alone, but emerges from network-level features such as interaction valency, compositional diversity, RNA coupling, post-translational modification state, and subcellular context. The project will provide a reusable framework for synthesizing heterogeneous data on mesoscale cellular organization, while producing testable principles for how emergent condensate properties shape higher-order cellular behavior. By transforming fragmented public data into predictive, interpretable models, this working group will help resolve a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular sciences: how dynamic molecular assemblies acquire system-level functions that cannot be inferred from their individual components alone.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are dynamic mesoscale assemblies that concentrate proteins, RNAs, metabolites, and signaling factors without requiring delimiting membranes. They include stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs, DNA damage foci, postsynaptic densities, heterochromatin domains, and viral replication compartments. These structures arise through weak multivalent interactions, intrinsically disordered regions, structured domain contacts, RNA scaffolding, post-translational modifications, and local biochemical environments. They exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biology because their material properties, spatial organization, and regulatory consequences cannot be predicted from any single component in isolation. Instead, condensate behavior depends on collective molecular features operating across scales of composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion. Despite rapid progress, the field faces a central unresolved problem: the same apparent mechanism, phase separation or related associative assembly, can produce opposing cellular outcomes. Condensates can protect cells by buffering toxic proteins, storing untranslated mRNAs, or organizing repair factors. They can also amplify stress pathways, trap regulators, alter transcriptional programs, and mature into aberrant gel-like or solid-like states associated with neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, and aging. This ambiguity limits the ability to predict whether a condensate observed under stress is adaptive, neutral, maladaptive, or disease-promoting. Current knowledge is fragmented across imaging studies, proteomic surveys, transcriptomic perturbations, structural databases, protein interaction resources, and curated phase-separation repositories. Most datasets were generated for distinct purposes, use different metadata standards, and measure different scales of organization. Yet together they contain an unprecedented opportunity for synthesis. Public resources now capture protein localization dynamics, condensate morphology, RNA-binding maps, post-translational modification sites, stress-specific transcriptomic responses, genetic dependencies, protein structures and predicted structures, interaction networks, and phenotypic consequences of perturbations. No individual laboratory can harmonize and interpret this landscape alone. Progress requires a transdisciplinary working group that integrates cell biology, biophysics, RNA biology, microscopy, data science, network science, statistics, and responsible artificial intelligence. This proposal directly aligns with NCEMS priorities by using only publicly available data to address a fundamental question about mesoscale emergence: how do dynamic molecular assemblies acquire system-level functions that shape cellular decisions under stress? The work will not generate new experimental data. Instead, it will transform dispersed public datasets into an open condensate-to-phenotype atlas and a suite of interpretable analytical models. The scientific significance is twofold. First, it will identify generalizable rules linking condensate composition and material state to buffering, amplification, sequestration, relocalization, and pathological transition. Second, it will establish reusable standards, benchmark tasks, and computational workflows for synthesis research on mesoscale cellular organization. By clarifying when condensates stabilize cellular systems and when they drive state transitions, the project will advance understanding of stress biology, disease mechanisms, and the broader principles of emergent cellular organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The working group will address three integrated research questions designed to move the field from cataloging condensate components toward predicting emergent cellular consequences. Question 1 asks which molecular and mesoscale features best predict condensate behaviors such as assembly, dissolution, fusion, hardening, selective recruitment, exclusion, spatial relocalization, and stress-dependent persistence. We hypothesize that these behaviors are predicted more accurately by network-level and polymer-physics-inspired features than by membership in curated condensate lists alone. Key predictors will include interaction valency, intrinsically disordered region architecture, charge patterning, aromatic and polar residue composition, short linear motifs, RNA-binding capacity, RNA abundance and structure, post-translational modification density, oligomerization state, and subcellular context. We further hypothesize that image-derived descriptors, including number, size distribution, circularity, texture, coalescence, intensity partitioning, and spatial proximity to organelles, will provide essential mesoscale information not captured by molecular annotations. Question 2 asks when condensates act as robust buffers versus switch-like amplifiers of stress-response pathways. We define buffering as reduced sensitivity of downstream molecular or phenotypic outputs to perturbation, such as stabilization of translation, sequestration of misfolded proteins, or preservation of cell viability. We define amplification as nonlinear propagation of stress signals, such as abrupt transcriptional activation, kinase pathway reinforcement, cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, senescence, or inflammatory signaling. We hypothesize that buffering is favored by high compositional diversity, reversible interaction networks, broad client capacity, and rapid exchange dynamics, whereas amplification is favored by scaffold dominance, positive feedback through post-translational modifications, recruitment of signaling enzymes, and slow material maturation. We will test whether condensates occupy identifiable regimes along axes of reversibility, selectivity, connectivity, and stress coupling. Question 3 asks whether conserved mesoscale organizational principles explain why similar molecular components produce divergent outcomes across cell types, organisms, and perturbations. We hypothesize that divergent outcomes arise when conserved condensate modules are embedded in different cellular contexts, including distinct RNA expression landscapes, kinase and phosphatase activities, proteostasis capacity, metabolic state, chromatin environment, and baseline stress tolerance. Thus, the effect of a component such as G3BP1, TDP-43, FUS, DDX proteins, nucleophosmin, Mediator subunits, or DNA repair proteins cannot be inferred without modeling the surrounding molecular ecosystem. Across these questions, the central hypothesis is that condensate function emerges from multiscale organization rather than from individual components. This hypothesis yields testable predictions. First, multimodal models integrating sequence, interaction, RNA, post-translational, imaging, and phenotype data will outperform single-modality models in predicting condensate behavior and cellular outcome. Second, interpretable model features will reveal recurrent organizational motifs associated with buffering, amplification, sequestration, and pathological maturation. Third, causal-inference approaches applied to public perturbation datasets will identify context-dependent mediators linking condensate-associated molecular features to stress decisions. These hypotheses are well suited to NCEMS synthesis because they require harmonization of heterogeneous public datasets, collaborative expertise beyond any single laboratory, and transparent analytical frameworks that generate broadly reusable community resources.

[Methods and Approach]
This project will operate as a 24-month NCEMS working group organized around data harmonization, feature extraction, model development, community benchmarking, and synthesis. No new experimental data will be generated. In months 1 to 6, the group will create an inventory of relevant public datasets and define shared metadata standards. Core data sources will include Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource, PRIDE, GEO, SRA, LINCS, DepMap, Protein Data Bank, AlphaFold, BioGRID, IntAct, POSTAR, ENCODE, PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS. We will prioritize datasets linked to heat shock, oxidative stress, nutrient limitation, osmotic stress, viral infection, proteotoxic stress, and DNA damage. Metadata will capture cell type, organism, perturbation, time point, assay modality, imaging conditions when available, molecular identifiers, stress ontology terms, and phenotypic endpoints. In months 4 to 12, we will build a harmonized condensate-to-phenotype atlas. Protein and RNA identifiers will be mapped across UniProt, Ensembl, HGNC, RefSeq, and RNAcentral where appropriate. Molecular features will include predicted disorder, low-complexity regions, charge patterning, prion-like domains, folded domains, multivalent interaction motifs, AlphaFold-derived structural confidence and interfaces, known and predicted RNA-binding capacity, post-translational modification sites from PRIDE and related resources, and interaction-network metrics from BioGRID and IntAct. RNA features will include binding evidence, expression, localization, and regulatory annotations from POSTAR, ENCODE, GEO, and SRA. Phenotypic features will include transcriptional signatures, viability, dependency scores, pathway activation, cell-cycle effects, and stress-response gene modules from LINCS, DepMap, and public expression studies. In months 6 to 16, a computer-vision subteam will extract standardized mesoscale descriptors from public microscopy datasets. Workflows will use reproducible segmentation and feature-extraction pipelines based on open tools such as CellProfiler, scikit-image, napari, and deep-learning models where appropriate. Outputs will include condensate count, area, volume when available, shape, texture, intensity enrichment, colocalization, spatial dispersion, organelle proximity, temporal dynamics, and confidence metrics. Human review and uncertainty estimates will be incorporated for benchmark image subsets. In months 10 to 22, data scientists, statisticians, and domain experts will develop a cross-dataset knowledge graph linking molecules, condensates, stressors, cell types, features, and outcomes. Analytical strategies will include interpretable machine learning, graph representation learning, generalized additive models, causal discovery with careful sensitivity analysis, negative controls, and cross-validation by dataset, cell type, and perturbation. Benchmark prediction tasks will include predicting stress-induced assembly, dissolution, material-state proxy, client recruitment, pathway activation, and cell-fate outcome. Model interpretation will emphasize robust, biologically plausible features rather than black-box performance alone. Working group activities will include quarterly virtual meetings, two in-person synthesis workshops, focused data sprints, open code reviews, and trainee-led benchmarking challenges. Expertise will include condensate cell biology, protein biophysics, RNA regulation, microscopy, systems biology, statistics, AI, and data stewardship, with participation from research-intensive institutions, primarily undergraduate institutions, and geographically diverse teams.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The primary outcome will be an open condensate-to-phenotype atlas that integrates molecular, imaging, network, structural, RNA, post-translational, perturbational, and phenotypic evidence across public resources. This atlas will convert fragmented observations into a searchable framework for asking how condensate organization relates to stress decisions across cell types, organisms, and perturbations. A second outcome will be a set of standardized image-derived mesoscale descriptors and metadata templates that enable comparison of condensate properties across repositories and studies. A third outcome will be a knowledge graph, benchmark datasets, and interpretable predictive models for condensate assembly, dissolution, recruitment, buffering, amplification, and pathological transition. Scientifically, the project will produce candidate rules for when condensates stabilize cellular systems versus when they drive switch-like responses or maladaptive states. These rules will be explicitly testable by the broader community using future experiments, but the proposed working group itself will remain a synthesis project using only existing public data. Methodologically, the project will demonstrate how computer vision, network science, causal inference, protein biophysics, RNA biology, and responsible AI can be combined to understand mesoscale emergence. The anticipated impact extends beyond condensate biology. The atlas, standards, and workflows will provide a reusable template for synthesis studies of other mesoscale assemblies, including cytoskeletal structures, membrane contact sites, signaling clusters, chromatin compartments, and organelle subdomains. The project will also train graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in reproducible data integration, image analytics, metadata curation, benchmark design, and collaborative team science. By enabling investigators to move from component lists to predictive organizational principles, this working group will address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology and advance the NCEMS mission to reveal emergent properties at the mesoscale.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Open science will be embedded in every phase of the project. All curated datasets, metadata schemas, controlled vocabulary mappings, derived features, analysis notebooks, model code, benchmark definitions, evaluation results, and visualization tools will be released through public repositories with persistent identifiers. Code will be maintained on GitHub or an equivalent public platform, archived through Zenodo, and distributed under a permissive open-source license. Data products will be deposited in appropriate community repositories when possible and indexed through a project portal with clear documentation, provenance records, and citation guidance. The group will follow FAIR principles: outputs will be findable through persistent identifiers and rich metadata, accessible through open repositories, interoperable through community identifiers and ontologies, and reusable through explicit licenses and documentation. Reproducibility will be supported through containerized workflows, version-controlled environments, executable notebooks, workflow managers, and continuous integration tests for core pipelines. Each analysis will record dataset version, preprocessing decisions, feature definitions, model parameters, random seeds, and evaluation splits. Benchmark tasks will include transparent training, validation, and held-out testing partitions, with procedures to prevent data leakage across related datasets. Model performance will be reported with uncertainty estimates, subgroup analyses, and negative controls. The working group will adopt open team science practices, including shared governance, documented authorship criteria, rotating leadership opportunities, and inclusive meeting norms. Synthesis sprints and code reviews will be open to trainees and external community observers when feasible. Training modules will cover reproducible workflows, microscopy metadata standards, responsible AI, data ethics, uncertainty communication, and limitations of inference from observational public data. Because the project uses only existing public data, privacy and human-subjects risks are minimal, but the group will respect repository terms of use and carefully document any restrictions. The goal is not only to publish results, but to create a durable, inspectable, and extensible community resource.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the proposed synthesis effort requires coordination, infrastructure, and community engagement beyond the capacity of a single laboratory or existing collaboration. Requested resources will support working group convening, data stewardship, trainee participation, computational analysis, dissemination, and inclusive collaboration. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data, purchase experimental reagents, or conduct new wet-laboratory assays. The largest budget category will be personnel and trainee support. Funds will support partial effort for a project coordinator or data steward responsible for metadata harmonization, repository tracking, documentation, meeting logistics, and release management. Stipends or salary support will enable graduate students and postdoctoral fellows to participate in benchmarking, image-analysis pipelines, knowledge-graph construction, and reproducibility testing. Participation from trainees at primarily undergraduate institutions and institutions with fewer computational resources will be prioritized. A second category will be collaborative meetings. Funds will support two in-person synthesis workshops hosted through NCEMS, quarterly virtual working sessions, focused data sprints, accessibility services, and travel support for geographically diverse participants, early-career researchers, and contributors from under-resourced institutions. These meetings are central to integrating expertise from condensate biology, biophysics, RNA biology, microscopy, statistics, AI, and systems biology. A third category will be computing and data infrastructure. Resources will support cloud storage, scalable image processing, knowledge-graph hosting, model training, container registries, and web-based visualization. NCEMS cyberinfrastructure and staff consultation will be critical for ensuring secure, reproducible, and sustainable workflows. A fourth category will be dissemination and training. Funds will support public tutorials, documentation, virtual workshops, benchmark challenge administration, conference presentations, and open-access publication costs where allowable. Existing public databases, open-source software, institutional computational resources, and participant expertise will provide substantial in-kind support. NCEMS investment will transform these distributed assets into a coordinated community-scale synthesis program with lasting public value.
