This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can assemble the needed expertise in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, quantitative imaging, biophysics, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure, nor can it coordinate the community standards required to make heterogeneous public data interoperable. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, data science centers, and experimental condensate laboratories, with active roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will participate in reproducible workflow development, image-analysis hackathons, model benchmarking, and community annotation jamborees. All outputs will be open: curated datasets, metadata standards, analysis notebooks, trained models, uncertainty estimates, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories. The expected outcome is a reusable predictive framework for mesoscale emergence in RNP condensates, providing testable hypotheses for the broader community and a model for synthesis-driven discovery in molecular and cellular biology.

[Background and Significance]
Ribonucleoprotein condensates are dynamic, membraneless cellular assemblies formed through multivalent interactions among RNAs, RNA-binding proteins, intrinsically disordered regions, structured domains, post-translational modifications, and environmental cues. Stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, nuclear speckles, paraspeckles, and related assemblies exemplify mesoscale emergence: molecular-scale properties combine nonlinearly to produce compartment-like behaviors that cannot be inferred from any single component. These condensates influence mRNA storage and decay, translation initiation, ribosome biogenesis, splicing, innate immune signaling, proteostasis, and cell survival. Aberrant condensate regulation has been implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, developmental disorders, and stress adaptation, making the ability to predict condensate behavior a fundamental and biomedical priority.

Despite rapid progress, the field remains fragmented. Individual studies have identified condensate markers, stress-dependent recruitment patterns, RNA-protein interactions, and biophysical determinants such as low-complexity domains, charge patterning, aromatic residues, prion-like domains, RNA valency, and phosphorylation. However, conclusions often differ across cell types, perturbations, imaging modalities, and annotation schemes. Public repositories now contain extensive but heterogeneous data relevant to condensate biology, including microscopy images, proteomic interaction maps, CLIP-seq datasets, RNA localization atlases, genetic perturbation screens, single-cell expression profiles, and sequence-based predictions of disorder, structure, and phase-separation propensity. These resources have not yet been synthesized into an interoperable framework capable of linking molecular features to condensate assembly, condensate morphology, dynamics, compositional specificity, and downstream cell-state outcomes.

This gap is well suited to the NCEMS mission because RNP condensates occupy the mesoscale between individual biomolecules and organelles, and their emergent properties shape higher-order cellular function. Understanding how condensate number, size distribution, spatial positioning, exchange kinetics, and compositional heterogeneity arise from molecular and network context requires synthesis across scales of composition, space, time, information, and motion. It also requires expertise spanning RNA biology, condensate biophysics, quantitative cell imaging, proteomics, network science, machine learning, causal inference, and open-data engineering. The proposed working group will integrate only publicly available datasets and will not generate new experimental data, directly aligning with NCEMS requirements for synthesis research.

The significance of this project is both conceptual and practical. Conceptually, it will test whether generalizable rules govern RNP condensate emergence across diverse cellular contexts or whether each condensate class follows distinct principles. Practically, it will provide the community with harmonized metadata standards, curated datasets, reproducible image-analysis pipelines, interpretable predictive models, and prioritized testable hypotheses for future experimental validation by independent investigators. By transforming scattered public datasets into a cross-scale atlas and predictive framework, the project will address a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences: how many weak and context-sensitive molecular interactions produce robust, regulated, and sometimes pathological mesoscale cellular structures.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The central research question is: what molecular, biophysical, network, and cellular-context features predict the emergent assembly, composition, dynamics, and cell-state consequences of human RNP condensates? This question will be decomposed into four linked subquestions that are specific, testable, and appropriate for synthesis using public data.

Question 1: Which molecular features predict condensate membership and condensate specificity? We hypothesize that condensate association is best predicted by combinations of features rather than single properties. Specifically, proteins enriched in RNP condensates will show context-dependent combinations of intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity sequence, prion-like domains, RNA-binding domains, short linear motifs, post-translational modification sites, and favorable charge or aromatic patterning. RNAs enriched in condensates will show higher effective valency through transcript length, structure, repeat content, modification status, abundance, and binding-site multiplicity for condensate-associated RNA-binding proteins. We further hypothesize that different condensate classes use partially overlapping feature grammars: stress granules will emphasize translational repression and RNA-binding valency, P-bodies will emphasize decay and repression networks, nucleoli will emphasize ribosome biogenesis and rRNA processing, and nuclear speckles will emphasize splicing and transcription-coupled RNA processing.

Question 2: Which molecular and cellular-context features predict mesoscale condensate phenotypes? We hypothesize that condensate number, size, circularity, texture, fusion behavior, dissolution kinetics, and organelle proximity can be predicted from a combination of component concentration, interaction-network topology, perturbation type, stress duration, cell type, and biophysical sequence features. We expect nonlinear thresholds: small changes in expression, phosphorylation, RNA abundance, or stress intensity may produce abrupt changes in mesoscale morphology, consistent with emergent assembly.

Question 3: Do condensate mesoscale properties help explain downstream cell states beyond molecular composition alone? We hypothesize that quantitative condensate features extracted from public images will improve prediction of phenotypes such as translational arrest, cell survival under stress, antiviral signaling, proteostasis dysfunction, drug sensitivity, and genetic dependency. For example, persistent large stress granules may associate with impaired recovery and proteotoxic vulnerability, whereas rapid dissolution may associate with adaptive stress resilience.

Question 4: Which inferred relationships are likely causal rather than merely correlative? We hypothesize that integrating perturbation screens, time-resolved imaging, drug treatments, genetic dependencies, and prior biological constraints will identify candidate causal paths from molecular perturbation to condensate phenotype to cell-state consequence. The project will distinguish direct component effects from indirect effects mediated by global stress, expression level, cell-cycle state, or imaging bias.

Together, these hypotheses advance beyond cataloging condensate components. They ask whether a cross-scale, interpretable model can predict emergent mesoscale behavior from public multi-omic and imaging data. Success will be measured by out-of-dataset generalization, robustness to missing data, biological interpretability, and production of ranked mechanistic hypotheses that can guide future experiments.

[Methods and Approach]
The working group will execute a coordinated synthesis workflow organized into five integrated aims. Aim 1 will assemble and harmonize public datasets. Imaging sources will include the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Allen Cell Explorer, Image Data Resource, Cell Painting resources, and published live-cell stress-granule and condensate studies with reusable images or feature tables. Molecular sources will include BioGRID, IntAct, STRING where license-compatible, AP-MS and proximity-labeling datasets, condensate-enrichment proteomics, ENCODE, POSTAR, eCLIP and CLIP-seq compendia, APEX-seq, RNA localization datasets, DepMap, genome-scale CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, drug-response repositories, UniProt, AlphaFold-derived structural predictions, MobiDB, DisProt, PhosphoSitePlus where license-compatible, and sequence-derived feature resources. Only existing publicly available data will be used.

Aim 2 will create harmonized metadata and ontologies for condensate identity, cell type, perturbation, stress condition, time point, imaging modality, molecular assay, quality metric, and measured mesoscale phenotype. The group will map terms to established identifiers whenever possible, including Cell Ontology, Gene Ontology, Sequence Ontology, PSI-MI, Experimental Factor Ontology, UniProt accessions, HGNC identifiers, and OBI assay terms. Community annotation jamborees will resolve ambiguous condensate labels and define confidence tiers for component membership, localization, and perturbation-response evidence.

Aim 3 will extract comparable quantitative features from public images. Reproducible computer-vision workflows will segment nuclei, cytoplasm, condensate puncta, and relevant organelle markers using established tools such as CellProfiler, ilastik, napari plugins, StarDist, Cellpose, and deep-learning models benchmarked on public annotations. Features will include puncta count, size distribution, intensity, circularity, texture, colocalization, cell-to-cell heterogeneity, spatial relationship to nuclei or organelles, and time-dependent assembly or dissolution when live-cell data are available. Quality control will flag batch effects, resolution limits, overexpression artifacts, antibody quality concerns, and inconsistent stress conditions.

Aim 4 will integrate molecular, imaging, and phenotype features using interpretable computational models. Baseline statistical models will establish transparent benchmarks. Graph machine-learning models will represent proteins, RNAs, interactions, sequence features, localization evidence, perturbations, and phenotypes as typed nodes and edges. Physics-informed models will encode principles of multivalency, concentration dependence, charge patterning, and interaction strength. Causal discovery will combine perturbation directionality, time ordering, prior knowledge, and negative controls to infer candidate paths from molecular features to condensate states to cellular outcomes. Model performance will be evaluated by cross-validation stratified by condensate class, cell type, laboratory source, and data modality, with special emphasis on external generalization.

Aim 5 will convene the NCEMS working group through in-person synthesis meetings, virtual sprints, trainee-led hackathons, and model benchmarking challenges. Team members will include experts in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, quantitative imaging, biophysics, machine learning, network science, ontology development, and open-science infrastructure from diverse institution types. The project is feasible because it relies on mature public repositories and established computational tools, yet requires NCEMS coordination to integrate heterogeneous resources at community scale.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver four major outcomes. First, it will produce a curated, versioned, cross-scale atlas of human RNP condensates linking proteins, RNAs, sequence features, interaction evidence, imaging-derived mesoscale phenotypes, perturbations, stress contexts, and cellular outcomes. This atlas will make dispersed public data findable, interoperable, and reusable for the condensate community.

Second, the working group will generate harmonized metadata standards and controlled vocabularies for condensate synthesis research. These standards will improve comparability across imaging studies, proteomic datasets, RNA localization experiments, and perturbation screens, thereby reducing one of the main barriers to cumulative progress in the field.

Third, the project will produce predictive and interpretable models of condensate assembly and consequence. Rather than simply classifying known components, models will identify feature combinations and network contexts that predict condensate specificity, morphology, dynamics, and links to phenotypes such as stress adaptation, translational arrest, antiviral response, proteostasis failure, and cell viability. Ranked predictions will provide testable hypotheses for the broader community, including candidate regulators, condition-specific recruitment mechanisms, and condensate features most strongly associated with maladaptive cell states.

Fourth, the project will establish a reusable model for synthesis-driven discovery in mesoscale cell biology. The workflows developed here can be adapted to other emergent assemblies, including signaling clusters, cytoskeletal compartments, chromatin bodies, and membrane-associated biomolecular condensates. The broader impact includes accelerating discovery without new data generation, increasing the value of public investments in molecular and cellular datasets, and training a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in open, reproducible, AI-enabled data synthesis. By meeting the NCEMS emphasis on emergence, collaboration, public data, and workforce development, this working group will provide both scientific insight and durable community infrastructure.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will operate under open, team, and reproducible science principles from inception. All derived datasets, metadata schemas, analysis code, trained models, model cards, documentation, and visualization tools will be released publicly, subject only to the licenses and use restrictions of source repositories. Data products will be deposited in appropriate community repositories such as Zenodo, Figshare, GitHub, GitLab, BioStudies, or related archives, with persistent identifiers and versioned releases. Large processed image features and graph data will be distributed in open formats such as OME-Zarr, AnnData, Parquet, JSON-LD, and standard network exchange formats.

Reproducibility will be ensured through containerized workflows, explicit environment files, workflow managers such as Nextflow, Snakemake, or CWL, continuous integration tests, provenance tracking, and standardized quality-control reports. Each major analysis will include executable notebooks and command-line workflows that reproduce figures, tables, benchmark results, and model outputs from documented inputs. The group will implement data and code review before public release, including checks for identifier consistency, license compatibility, missing metadata, leakage between training and test sets, and robustness of conclusions to alternative preprocessing choices.

The project will also promote transparent and equitable collaboration. Authorship, contribution tracking, decision-making processes, and conflict-resolution expectations will be established in a shared collaboration agreement. Trainees will receive visible credit through dataset descriptors, software releases, preprints, conference presentations, and coauthored manuscripts. Community annotation events and benchmarking challenges will invite participation beyond the core working group, including researchers at primarily undergraduate institutions and minority-serving institutions.

To maximize reuse, the group will create tutorials, template workflows, and interactive dashboards that allow users to query condensate components, compare conditions, inspect model explanations, and download uncertainty-aware predictions. Preprints and final manuscripts will be posted open access. The final deliverables will comply with FAIR principles and will be designed so that independent researchers can audit, reproduce, extend, and challenge the models.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the proposed work requires sustained coordination, computing, training, and community synthesis beyond the capacity of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. The requested budget will support working-group meetings, trainee participation, data-engineering effort, cloud and high-performance computing, open-science dissemination, and community engagement. No funds will be used to generate new experimental data.

Approximately 30 percent of the budget will support personnel time for a project manager or data-science coordinator, part-time research software engineering, and trainee stipends for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows contributing to curation, workflow development, image analysis, benchmarking, and documentation. These roles are critical for transforming heterogeneous public data into reliable, reusable synthesis products.

Approximately 25 percent will support NCEMS-hosted in-person synthesis meetings, including travel for investigators and trainees from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and data science centers. Meetings will be structured around ontology development, image-analysis sprints, model integration, interpretation of results, and manuscript preparation. Virtual meetings will occur monthly to maintain momentum.

Approximately 20 percent will support cloud computing, storage, and data-transfer costs for public microscopy images, feature extraction, graph construction, model training, and interactive dashboards. The project will preferentially use open-source tools and NCEMS-supported cyberinfrastructure when available to reduce cost and improve sustainability.

Approximately 15 percent will support training activities, including hackathons, annotation jamborees, reproducible-workflow workshops, and trainee-led benchmarking challenges. These activities directly address NCEMS goals of training the next generation of data-savvy molecular and cellular scientists.

The remaining 10 percent will support dissemination, accessibility, and sustainability, including repository fees, persistent identifiers, website and dashboard hosting, documentation, tutorial development, and open-access publication costs where needed. Major milestones will include a metadata standard and pilot atlas in year one, integrated predictive models and benchmark reports in year two, and final public releases, manuscripts, and community training materials by project completion.

abstract_original: Membraneless ribonucleoprotein condensates such as stress granules, P-bodies, nucleoli, and nuclear speckles are archetypal mesoscale systems: they emerge from many weak molecular interactions yet shape translation, RNA fate, signaling, and cell survival. Despite extensive public data, the field lacks a unified, predictive framework explaining when specific RNAs and proteins form condensates, how condensate composition varies across cellular contexts, and which mesoscale properties causally associate with downstream cellular phenotypes. This working group will synthesize existing public datasets to answer a central question: what molecular, biophysical, and network features predict the emergent assembly, composition, dynamics, and cellular consequences of human RNP condensates? The project will integrate only publicly available data, including fluorescence imaging datasets from the Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Explorer, and published live-cell stress-granule studies; proteomic and interactome data from BioGRID, IntAct, AP-MS, proximity-labeling, and condensate-enrichment studies; RNA localization and RNA-protein interaction data from ENCODE, POSTAR, CLIP-seq, APEX-seq, and subcellular fractionation studies; perturbation and phenotype data from DepMap, genome-scale CRISPR screens, Perturb-seq, and drug-response repositories; and sequence-derived features such as intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, prion-like domains, charge patterning, RNA-binding motifs, post-translational modification sites, and predicted structures. The synthesis will produce a cross-scale atlas linking molecular features to mesoscale condensate behaviors and cellular outcomes. We will develop harmonized ontologies for condensate identity, experimental perturbation, stress condition, cell type, and measured mesoscale phenotype, then use computer vision to extract comparable features from public images, including condensate number, size distribution, shape, colocalization, dissolution kinetics, and spatial relationship to organelles. These features will be integrated with molecular interaction networks and perturbation phenotypes using interpretable graph machine learning, causal discovery, and physics-informed models of multivalent assembly. The goal is not simply to classify condensate components, but to identify generalizable rules explaining how emergent mesoscale properties arise from molecular composition and how these properties influence higher-order cell states such as translational arrest, antiviral response, proteostasis failure, and stress adaptation. This project requires NCEMS support because no single laboratory can assemble the needed expertise in condensate biology, RNA biology, proteomics, quantitative imaging, biophysics, machine learning, network science, and open-science infrastructure, nor can it coordinate the community standards required to make heterogeneous public data interoperable. The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, data science centers, and experimental condensate laboratories, with active roles for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Trainees will participate in reproducible workflow development, image-analysis hackathons, model benchmarking, and community annotation jamborees. All outputs will be open: curated datasets, metadata standards, analysis notebooks, trained models, uncertainty estimates, and interactive visualizations will be released through public repositories. The expected outcome is a reusable predictive framework for mesoscale emergence in RNP condensates, providing testable hypotheses for the broader community and a model for synthesis-driven discovery in molecular and cellular biology.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates are a central example of emergence in molecular and cellular biology: multivalent interactions among proteins and RNAs generate mesoscale compartments whose properties cannot be inferred from any single component alone. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some molecular assemblies reproducibly form functional condensates in living cells, while compositionally similar systems remain diffuse, aggregate pathologically, or reorganize only under specific cellular states? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available data to derive generalizable rules linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and emergent condensate behavior. The project will integrate existing datasets spanning scales: protein sequence features and low-complexity domains from UniProt and AlphaFold; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks from BioGRID, STRING, ENCODE, eCLIP, and POSTAR; subcellular localization and protein abundance from the Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell; perturbation and morphology profiles from Cell Painting, LINCS, and image repositories such as the BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource; and transcriptomic and stress-response datasets from GEO, SRA, and single-cell atlases. No new experimental data will be generated. The central scientific question is: what combinations of molecular grammar, interaction topology, expression stoichiometry, and cellular state predict the emergence, material behavior, and functional consequences of mesoscale condensates? To address this, the team will build an open, harmonized condensate knowledge graph linking molecular components to imaging phenotypes, perturbations, disease associations, and cell-state variables. We will develop interpretable machine-learning models and causal network analyses to identify thresholds and nonlinear interactions that distinguish functional condensate formation from non-condensing assemblies or pathological aggregates. A major analytical innovation will be the integration of foundation-model-derived image embeddings with molecular interaction and sequence embeddings, allowing condensate-like mesoscale phenotypes to be compared across cell types, perturbations, laboratories, and imaging modalities. The project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, phase separation biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, artificial intelligence, statistics, network science, and open-science software engineering. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource centers, with graduate students and postdoctoral fellows embedded in all stages of data curation, model development, reproducibility assessment, and community dissemination. Training activities will include hands-on workshops in FAIR data integration, reproducible workflow construction, biological image analysis, and responsible AI for molecular and cellular synthesis. Expected products include a public condensate data atlas, reproducible computational pipelines, benchmark datasets for predicting condensate emergence, interactive visualization tools, and community guidelines for annotating mesoscale cellular structures from heterogeneous public data. By synthesizing diverse existing datasets, this project will generate testable principles for how molecular-scale interactions give rise to emergent mesoscale cellular organization and how those mesoscale states influence cellular phenotypes. The resulting framework will advance fundamental understanding of cellular organization, provide reusable infrastructure for the broader community, and establish a model for open, collaborative synthesis research in emergent molecular and cellular systems.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates, including nucleoli, stress granules, P bodies, transcriptional hubs, nuclear speckles, paraspeckles, and signaling clusters, exemplify emergence at the mesoscale. They arise through collective, multivalent interactions among proteins, RNAs, chromatin, metabolites, and membranes, producing compartments with material properties, exchange kinetics, biochemical selectivity, and regulatory functions that are not predictable from isolated molecules alone. Condensates organize reactions, buffer molecular noise, tune gene expression, and enable rapid adaptation to stress. Conversely, dysregulated condensate formation is implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, viral infection, developmental disorders, and aging. Understanding when and why condensates form, dissolve, harden, fuse, or acquire specific functions is therefore a fundamental problem in molecular and cellular bioscience with broad biomedical relevance. Despite major advances in phase separation biophysics, a predictive cell biological framework remains incomplete. Current models emphasize sequence features such as intrinsically disordered regions, low-complexity domains, aromatic and charged residues, prion-like motifs, RNA binding domains, and modular interaction domains. However, many proteins with similar molecular grammar do not form visible condensates, while some condensates form only under specific transcriptional, metabolic, osmotic, cell-cycle, or stress conditions. Cellular concentration, stoichiometry, post-translational modification, RNA availability, molecular crowding, active transport, and network topology can shift systems across thresholds. The central gap is that condensate emergence is a multiscale property, yet most available studies examine one condensate, one protein, one cell type, or one perturbation at a time. This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by synthesizing public data to reveal principles of emergence across scales of composition, space, time, information, and motion. The opportunity is timely because the community has generated extensive public resources that have not yet been integrated for this question. Sequence and structural repositories capture molecular features for nearly all human proteins. Interaction databases contain protein-protein and protein-RNA networks. Proteomic atlases quantify abundance and localization. Imaging repositories increasingly provide high-content phenotypes across perturbations, cell lines, and microscopy modalities. Transcriptomic and single-cell atlases define cellular states and stress responses. Separately, these resources are valuable; together, they can expose nonlinear combinations of molecular grammar, interaction topology, and cell context that predict mesoscale organization. The proposed Working Group is necessary because no single laboratory can harmonize these heterogeneous datasets, develop cross-modal analytical methods, interpret condensate biology, and produce community standards. The project requires coordinated expertise in phase separation, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, machine learning, statistics, network science, ontology development, and reproducible software engineering. It will use only existing publicly available data and will generate no new experimental data. By creating a public condensate knowledge graph, benchmark datasets, interpretable predictive models, and community annotation guidelines, the project will transform fragmented observations into a reusable synthesis platform. The work will clarify how molecular-scale interactions generate mesoscale cellular structures and how those structures influence cellular phenotypes, thereby advancing fundamental understanding of emergent biological organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching research question is: what combinations of molecular features, interaction networks, expression stoichiometry, localization, and cellular state predict the emergence, material behavior, and functional consequences of biomolecular condensates? We will address this question through four linked aims that convert heterogeneous public data into testable, generalizable principles. The first question asks which molecular grammars distinguish condensate-associated proteins and RNAs from compositionally similar non-condensing molecules. We hypothesize that condensate competence is not determined by any single feature, but by combinations of disorder, motif valence, charge patterning, aromatic residue distribution, RNA binding capacity, predicted structure, post-translational modification sites, and evolutionary conservation. We further hypothesize that these features differ among condensate classes: for example, stress granules, transcriptional condensates, and nuclear speckles will show distinct grammars reflecting different interaction chemistries and functions. The second question asks how interaction network topology controls condensate emergence. We hypothesize that condensate-forming systems occupy identifiable regions of protein-protein and protein-RNA networks characterized by high multivalency, modularity, local clustering, hub participation, and enrichment for weak but numerous interactions. We expect functional condensates to show network architectures that permit reversible assembly and compositional selectivity, whereas pathological aggregates will show signatures of excessive self-association, impaired chaperone connectivity, or loss of regulatory edges. The third question asks how cellular context shifts assemblies across emergent thresholds. We hypothesize that the same molecular system can be diffuse, condensed, or aggregated depending on concentration, stoichiometric imbalance, RNA abundance, cell-cycle state, stress exposure, metabolic state, and perturbation history. We predict that transcriptomic and proteomic state variables will identify switch-like regions in which small changes in abundance or modification potential produce large changes in mesoscale morphology. These thresholds are expected to be nonlinear and context dependent, explaining why studies of isolated components often fail to predict behavior in living cells. The fourth question asks how condensate emergence relates to cellular function and disease-relevant phenotypes. We hypothesize that condensate states mediate links between molecular perturbations and cell-level outcomes such as transcriptional reprogramming, stress tolerance, altered morphology, senescence, antiviral response, and toxicity. We will test whether imaging phenotypes and perturbational transcriptomic signatures can distinguish adaptive condensate remodeling from maladaptive aggregation or failure to assemble. Methodologically, we hypothesize that cross-modal integration will outperform single-modality prediction. Specifically, models combining protein sequence embeddings, structural features, interaction network embeddings, transcriptomic state vectors, and foundation-model-derived image embeddings will more accurately predict condensate presence, class, material behavior, and perturbation sensitivity than models using molecular features alone. We also hypothesize that interpretable machine learning and causal network analyses can identify not only predictive features, but candidate mechanisms, including threshold variables and interaction motifs. These hypotheses are designed for synthesis research: they rely entirely on public datasets, demand transdisciplinary collaboration, and will yield community benchmarks that allow the field to evaluate competing models of mesoscale emergence.

[Methods and Approach]
The Working Group will execute an integrated synthesis workflow organized around data acquisition, harmonization, knowledge graph construction, modeling, validation, and dissemination. No new experimental data will be generated. In phase one, we will assemble a public data inventory and define inclusion criteria. Condensate annotations will be drawn from published condensate resources, curated literature, Gene Ontology cellular component terms, UniProt annotations, Human Protein Atlas localization data, OpenCell localization and abundance measurements, and image repositories including BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource. Molecular features will be extracted from UniProt, AlphaFold, Pfam, InterPro, MobiDB, phosphosite and modification resources, and sequence-based predictors of disorder, low-complexity regions, charge patterning, prion-like domains, coiled coils, RNA binding domains, and short linear motifs. Protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions will be integrated from BioGRID, STRING, IntAct, ENCODE, eCLIP, POSTAR, and related public sources. Cellular state and perturbation information will be collected from GEO, SRA, LINCS, DepMap, Cell Painting datasets, single-cell atlases, and stress-response compendia. In phase two, we will harmonize identifiers, ontologies, metadata, and quality measures. Entities will be mapped to stable identifiers for genes, proteins, RNAs, cell lines, tissues, perturbations, imaging assays, and disease terms. We will document provenance, license status, uncertainty, assay type, organism, cell state, and evidence level. The condensate knowledge graph will link components, molecular features, interactions, abundance, localization, perturbations, imaging phenotypes, transcriptomic states, diseases, and literature evidence. Because public datasets vary in quality and bias, we will implement confidence scoring, batch annotation, missingness characterization, and sensitivity analyses. In phase three, we will develop multimodal representations. Sequence and structure embeddings will be derived from publicly available protein language models and AlphaFold features. Network embeddings will capture local clustering, centrality, modularity, and community context. Transcriptomic and perturbational profiles will be reduced using robust latent factor models. Imaging data will be represented using both curated morphological features and foundation-model-derived embeddings, with careful attention to cross-laboratory and cross-modality normalization. In phase four, we will build interpretable predictive and causal models. Supervised models will predict condensate association, condensate class, stress responsiveness, pathological aggregation risk, and morphology-associated outcomes. Candidate methods include regularized generalized linear models, gradient boosted trees, graph neural networks, multimodal transformers, and Bayesian hierarchical models. Interpretability will be assessed using feature attribution, partial dependence, counterfactual perturbation, and rule extraction. Causal discovery and network propagation analyses will identify candidate threshold variables and mediator pathways linking molecular perturbations to mesoscale phenotypes. Validation will rely on rigorous held-out evaluation across cell types, laboratories, perturbation classes, and databases. Negative and ambiguous examples will be explicitly modeled to reduce circularity. Benchmark splits will test generalization to unseen proteins, unseen condensate classes, and unseen cellular states. Reproducibility will be ensured through containerized workflows, versioned datasets, code review, independent reruns by partner laboratories, and public benchmark leaderboards. Working Group meetings will coordinate curation sprints, modeling jamborees, trainee workshops, and community feedback sessions.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will produce five major outcomes. First, we will release a public condensate data atlas that harmonizes molecular components, sequence and structural features, interaction networks, localization, abundance, perturbations, imaging phenotypes, transcriptomic states, disease links, and evidence provenance. Second, we will deliver an open condensate knowledge graph with programmatic access, interactive visualization, and documented confidence scores, enabling researchers to explore cross-scale relationships that are currently dispersed across many databases. Third, we will generate benchmark datasets and reproducible workflows for predicting condensate association, condensate class, context-dependent assembly, and aggregate-like versus functional mesoscale phenotypes. Fourth, we will produce interpretable models that identify candidate rules, thresholds, and nonlinear interactions governing emergent condensate behavior. Fifth, we will publish community guidelines for annotating condensate-like mesoscale structures from heterogeneous public data, including standards for uncertainty, negative examples, imaging metadata, and evidence strength. The scientific impact will be a shift from case-by-case descriptions of condensates to a predictive, synthesis-based framework for mesoscale emergence. The project will clarify why some multivalent molecular systems form functional compartments, why others remain diffuse, and why some become pathological under specific cellular states. It will connect molecular grammar and interaction topology to imaging phenotypes and cellular outcomes, creating testable hypotheses for the broader community without generating new data. The infrastructure will be reusable beyond condensates, serving as a model for integrating public molecular, cellular, and imaging data to study emergent biological organization. The workforce impact will include intensive training of graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, and early-career scientists in FAIR data integration, responsible AI, image analysis, network science, reproducible workflows, and collaborative team science. By including research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and data-resource centers, the Working Group will broaden participation and create durable cross-disciplinary partnerships aligned with NCEMS goals.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The project will follow open, team, and reproducible science practices from inception. All derived data products, metadata schemas, code, model weights when licensing permits, notebooks, documentation, benchmark splits, and analysis workflows will be deposited in public repositories such as GitHub, Zenodo, Figshare, and appropriate biological data archives. Releases will use persistent identifiers, semantic versioning, machine-readable provenance, and permissive licenses compatible with source database requirements. The knowledge graph will record the origin, date accessed, license, transformation steps, evidence level, and confidence score for each assertion, allowing users to trace every conclusion back to public sources. Reproducibility will be built into the workflow architecture. Analyses will be implemented in scripted pipelines using workflow managers such as Snakemake or Nextflow, containerized with Docker or Apptainer, and executed in continuous integration environments for automated testing. We will maintain locked software environments, data dictionaries, unit tests, validation reports, and reproducibility checklists. Independent reruns by at least two partner sites will be required before major releases. Model development will include pre-specified evaluation metrics, held-out benchmark sets, documentation of data leakage risks, and reporting of uncertainty and failure modes. To promote inclusive community governance, the Working Group will maintain a public project roadmap, issue tracker, contribution guidelines, code of conduct, authorship and credit policy, and transparent decision-making procedures. Community feedback will be solicited through virtual town halls, conference workshops, and open review of annotation guidelines. Trainees will be embedded in curation, software development, quality control, and dissemination, receiving credit through citable data products and software contributions. The project will not generate new experimental data, but it will make existing public data more reusable by harmonizing identifiers, improving metadata, documenting biases, and creating benchmarks. These practices will ensure that NCEMS investment produces durable, inspectable, extensible resources that the molecular and cellular bioscience community can reuse and improve.

[Budget and Resources]
The budget will support a community-scale synthesis effort that cannot be accomplished by a single laboratory or standard bilateral collaboration. Funds will be directed toward Working Group coordination, trainee participation, data engineering, computational analysis, open-source software development, and dissemination. The requested budget is therefore tightly aligned with NCEMS priorities: it enables multidisciplinary collaboration, synthesis of public data, open and reproducible infrastructure, broad participation, and trainee-centered workforce development. The project will deliver durable public products that outlast the award period and provide a foundation for future community synthesis efforts in emergent molecular and cellular systems.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates are a central example of emergence in molecular and cellular biology: multivalent interactions among proteins and RNAs generate mesoscale compartments whose properties cannot be inferred from any single component alone. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some molecular assemblies reproducibly form functional condensates in living cells, while compositionally similar systems remain diffuse, aggregate pathologically, or reorganize only under specific cellular states? This Working Group will synthesize publicly available data to derive generalizable rules linking molecular features, interaction networks, cellular context, and emergent condensate behavior. The project will integrate existing datasets spanning scales: protein sequence features and low-complexity domains from UniProt and AlphaFold; protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks from BioGRID, STRING, ENCODE, eCLIP, and POSTAR; subcellular localization and protein abundance from the Human Protein Atlas and OpenCell; perturbation and morphology profiles from Cell Painting, LINCS, and image repositories such as the BioImage Archive and Image Data Resource; and transcriptomic and stress-response datasets from GEO, SRA, and single-cell atlases. No new experimental data will be generated. The central scientific question is: what combinations of molecular grammar, interaction topology, expression stoichiometry, and cellular state predict the emergence, material behavior, and functional consequences of mesoscale condensates? To address this, the team will build an open, harmonized condensate knowledge graph linking molecular components to imaging phenotypes, perturbations, disease associations, and cell-state variables. We will develop interpretable machine-learning models and causal network analyses to identify thresholds and nonlinear interactions that distinguish functional condensate formation from non-condensing assemblies or pathological aggregates. A major analytical innovation will be the integration of foundation-model-derived image embeddings with molecular interaction and sequence embeddings, allowing condensate-like mesoscale phenotypes to be compared across cell types, perturbations, laboratories, and imaging modalities. The project requires NCEMS support because it exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory: it demands coordinated expertise in cell biology, phase separation biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, artificial intelligence, statistics, network science, and open-science software engineering. The Working Group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, and national data-resource centers, with graduate students and postdoctoral fellows embedded in all stages of data curation, model development, reproducibility assessment, and community dissemination. Training activities will include hands-on workshops in FAIR data integration, reproducible workflow construction, biological image analysis, and responsible AI for molecular and cellular synthesis. Expected products include a public condensate data atlas, reproducible computational pipelines, benchmark datasets for predicting condensate emergence, interactive visualization tools, and community guidelines for annotating mesoscale cellular structures from heterogeneous public data. By synthesizing diverse existing datasets, this project will generate testable principles for how molecular-scale interactions give rise to emergent mesoscale cellular organization and how those mesoscale states influence cellular phenotypes. The resulting framework will advance fundamental understanding of cellular organization, provide reusable infrastructure for the broader community, and establish a model for open, collaborative synthesis research in emergent molecular and cellular systems.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates are a central example of mesoscale emergence: weak molecular interactions among proteins, RNAs, and chromatin can collectively generate dynamic compartments with properties not predictable from any single component. Yet a long-standing puzzle remains unresolved: why do some predicted phase-separating molecules form functional condensates in cells, while others do not, and when do condensates become pathological or phenotypically consequential? This working group will synthesize publicly available molecular and cellular datasets to develop a generalizable, data-driven framework linking molecular features to emergent condensate behavior and downstream cellular outcomes. The project will integrate existing resources including human and model-organism proteomes, intrinsically disordered region annotations, post-translational modification databases, RNA-binding and protein interaction maps, public proximity-labeling datasets, single-cell and bulk transcriptomic atlases, high-content microscopy repositories, CRISPR perturbation screens, disease variant catalogs, and curated condensate databases such as PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, and RNA granule resources. No new experimental data will be generated. Instead, the working group will harmonize heterogeneous datasets into an open, versioned knowledge graph describing condensate-associated molecules, their biophysical features, interaction contexts, cellular locations, perturbation responses, and phenotype associations. We will address three linked questions: (1) What combinations of molecular features and cellular context best predict condensate membership and mesoscale compartment identity? (2) Which emergent properties, such as compositional buffering, stress responsiveness, spatial co-localization, and dynamic exchange, can be inferred by integrating public imaging, proteomic, and perturbation data? (3) Which condensate states are associated with higher-order cellular outcomes, including stress tolerance, altered gene regulation, neurodegeneration-related toxicity, and cancer cell fitness? Analytically, the group will combine graph machine learning, interpretable multimodal models, causal inference from perturbation screens, and image-derived phenotype embeddings. A major methodological deliverable will be an open benchmark for condensate prediction and emergent-property inference, including negative controls, uncertainty estimates, and reproducible workflows. This synthesis requires NCEMS support because the necessary expertise spans biophysics, cell biology, RNA biology, microscopy, proteomics, machine learning, knowledge engineering, and open-science infrastructure, and because the data integration challenge exceeds the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will deliberately include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data repositories, and international open-data communities, with participation from graduate students and postdoctoral fellows as core analysts. Trainees will receive hands-on training through hackathons, reproducibility clinics, FAIR data curation sprints, and team-based manuscript and software development. All outputs, including harmonized metadata, analysis notebooks, trained models, benchmark datasets, and visualization tools, will be released publicly under permissive licenses with community governance. By transforming fragmented public datasets into a coherent synthesis framework, this project will provide mechanistic insight into how molecular interactions produce emergent mesoscale organization and how that organization shapes cellular phenotype.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates, including stress granules, nucleoli, transcriptional hubs, P bodies, nuclear speckles, heterochromatin domains, and signaling clusters, exemplify emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences. Their mesoscale properties arise from distributed, multivalent interactions among proteins, RNA, DNA, metabolites, post-translational modifications, and physical constraints of the cell. These compartments can concentrate reactants, buffer molecular noise, modulate biochemical kinetics, reorganize under stress, and influence gene expression, differentiation, aging, viral infection, cancer, and neurodegeneration. However, the field still lacks a predictive framework that explains why some molecules with intrinsically disordered regions, prion-like domains, low-complexity sequences, RNA-binding domains, or multivalent interaction motifs form functional cellular condensates, whereas others remain diffuse, participate only under specific contexts, or become pathological assemblies. This gap is a central mesoscale puzzle: component-level biophysical propensities are necessary but not sufficient to predict emergent cellular organization or phenotype.

The timing is ideal for synthesis research. Public repositories now contain large volumes of heterogeneous data relevant to condensate biology, including curated phase-separation databases, proteome-wide disorder and low-complexity annotations, protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction maps, proximity-labeling proteomics, post-translational modification catalogs, subcellular localization atlases, high-content microscopy images, single-cell transcriptomic atlases, genome-wide CRISPR perturbation screens, disease variant databases, and literature-derived condensate annotations. Individually, these datasets answer narrow questions. Integrated at community scale, they can reveal higher-order principles that are invisible to single-modality analyses. For example, a protein's condensate membership may be predictable only when sequence features are interpreted together with expression level, RNA availability, phosphorylation state, interaction neighborhood, cellular stress condition, and spatial localization. Similarly, pathological outcomes may depend not merely on phase separation propensity but on altered dynamic exchange, aberrant compositional recruitment, loss of buffering, or perturbation-sensitive network rewiring.

This project aligns directly with NCEMS priorities by using only publicly available data to address fundamental questions about emergent mesoscale biological organization. It requires collaboration among experts in condensate biophysics, RNA biology, proteomics, microscopy, cell biology, computational biology, knowledge graphs, machine learning, causal inference, and open-science infrastructure. No single laboratory can assemble, harmonize, validate, and interpret the necessary public datasets at the proposed scale. NCEMS support will enable a working group structure that combines community curation, cross-disciplinary synthesis, trainee-centered data science, and reproducible computational workflows. The anticipated outcome is not another isolated predictor, but an extensible synthesis framework that links molecular features, cellular context, emergent condensate properties, and phenotypic consequences. By transforming fragmented data into testable principles, the project will advance understanding of how weak molecular interactions generate mesoscale compartments and how those compartments influence cellular function and disease.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This working group will address three linked scientific questions. First, what combinations of molecular features and cellular contexts best predict condensate membership and mesoscale compartment identity? Existing predictors often emphasize intrinsic disorder, low-complexity sequence, charge patterning, aromatic residues, prion-like domains, or RNA-binding capacity. Yet these features alone produce many false positives and false negatives when compared with cellular observations. We hypothesize that accurate prediction requires multimodal context: sequence-derived biophysical features, domain architecture, post-translational modification potential, expression abundance, RNA or chromatin interaction profiles, interaction-network position, and cell-type or stress-state specificity. We further hypothesize that different condensate classes occupy distinguishable regions of this joint feature space; for example, stress granule proteins will show different combinations of RNA-binding, translation-state dependence, and stress-responsive phosphorylation than nucleolar, chromatin-associated, or signaling condensate components.

Second, which emergent condensate properties can be inferred from existing public proteomic, imaging, and perturbation data? Condensates are not defined solely by membership; their emergent behaviors include compositional buffering, selective recruitment, spatial co-localization, stimulus responsiveness, maturation, dissolution, dynamic exchange, and coupling to transcription, translation, or signaling. Direct measurements are incomplete across the proteome, but public data contain indirect signatures. We hypothesize that integration of proximity-labeling studies, subcellular imaging atlases, stress-response transcriptomics and proteomics, fluorescence microscopy features, and genetic or chemical perturbation screens can infer latent emergent properties. For example, proteins whose abundance, localization, and interaction neighborhoods remain stable despite perturbation may mark buffering condensates, whereas proteins showing coordinated relocalization and altered interaction partners under oxidative, heat, osmotic, or translational stress may indicate stress-responsive compartments. We also hypothesize that image-derived embeddings can capture mesoscale phenotypes that are poorly represented by manual annotations.

Third, which condensate states are associated with higher-order cellular outcomes, including stress tolerance, altered gene regulation, neurodegeneration-related toxicity, and cancer cell fitness? We hypothesize that phenotypically consequential condensates will be identifiable as network states in which molecular features, localization, interaction rewiring, disease variants, and perturbation effects converge. In neurodegeneration, pathogenic variants may preferentially affect condensate components with high disorder, RNA-binding capacity, aggregation propensity, and altered dynamic regulation. In cancer, fitness-relevant condensates may involve transcriptional coactivators, chromatin regulators, splicing factors, DNA damage response proteins, or signaling scaffolds whose perturbation effects are context dependent. We will test whether inferred condensate states improve prediction of CRISPR screen phenotypes, disease-gene enrichment, stress-survival signatures, and transcriptional regulatory changes beyond conventional gene-level features.

Collectively, the project's central hypothesis is that condensate emergence is predictable not from isolated molecular properties but from context-dependent, multiscale configurations of molecules, interactions, modifications, localization, and perturbation response. The working group will evaluate this hypothesis through transparent benchmarks, negative controls, uncertainty quantification, and cross-dataset validation across human and model-organism systems.

[Methods and Approach]
The project will be organized as a synthesis working group with coordinated data, modeling, validation, and training teams. All analyses will use existing public data; no new experimental data will be generated. During months 1 to 6, we will inventory and prioritize datasets, define metadata standards, and establish inclusion criteria. Core sources will include PhaSepDB, DrLLPS, LLPSDB, RNA granule resources, UniProt, Ensembl, DisProt, MobiDB, Pfam, InterPro, PhosphoSitePlus, BioGRID, IntAct, STRING, ENCODE, GTEx, Human Protein Atlas, OpenCell, PRIDE, ProteomeXchange, DepMap, BioGRID ORCS, Cell Painting repositories, Image Data Resource, Gene Expression Omnibus, Sequence Read Archive, Human Cell Atlas, ClinVar, gnomAD, COSMIC, and disease-specific variant catalogs. We will include human, yeast, Drosophila, mouse, and selected model-organism data when orthology mappings are reliable.

During months 4 to 12, we will construct an open, versioned condensate knowledge graph. Nodes will represent proteins, RNAs, genes, variants, domains, modifications, condensate types, cell states, perturbations, images, phenotypes, and publications. Edges will encode physical interactions, co-localization, proximity labeling, regulatory relationships, perturbation effects, orthology, disease associations, and evidence provenance. Harmonization will use stable identifiers, ontology mappings, evidence codes, confidence scores, and explicit license tracking. Negative and uncertain examples will be carefully curated, including proteins with high predicted phase-separation propensity but no evidence of cellular condensate membership, localization-matched controls, expression-matched controls, and shuffled or degree-preserved network controls.

During months 10 to 24, we will develop predictive and inferential models. Baseline models will use logistic regression, random forests, gradient boosting, and calibrated classifiers with interpretable features. Advanced models will include graph neural networks, heterogeneous network embeddings, multimodal transformers, and matrix factorization approaches that combine sequence, network, imaging, expression, and perturbation modalities. Image-derived phenotype embeddings will be extracted from public microscopy datasets using pretrained and self-supervised models, followed by quality control and batch-effect evaluation. Causal inference from perturbation screens will use methods such as doubly robust estimation, causal graph constraints, genetic interaction modeling, and sensitivity analyses to distinguish correlational associations from plausible downstream effects.

Validation will emphasize rigor rather than overfitting. We will use held-out condensate classes, organism-level splits, publication-date splits, and cell-type splits to evaluate generalizability. Performance metrics will include precision-recall area, calibration error, uncertainty estimates, enrichment over matched controls, and biological interpretability. Domain experts will review high-confidence predictions through structured annotation exercises. The group will also create an open benchmark for condensate membership, compartment identity, emergent-property inference, and phenotype prediction. Working meetings, hackathons, FAIR curation sprints, and reproducibility clinics will occur throughout the project, with trainees serving as core analysts and cross-institutional team members leading focused modules.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The project will deliver four major outcomes. First, we will produce a FAIR, versioned, publicly accessible condensate knowledge graph integrating molecular features, interaction context, localization, imaging signatures, perturbation effects, disease associations, and phenotype annotations. This resource will transform fragmented public datasets into a coherent synthesis platform for the condensate and mesoscale biology communities. Second, we will release an open benchmark for condensate prediction and emergent-property inference, including gold-standard positives, matched negatives, uncertain cases, metadata, evaluation scripts, and baseline models. This benchmark will reduce ambiguity in the field and enable rigorous comparison of future algorithms.

Third, we will generate mechanistic insights into the context dependence of condensate formation and function. Expected discoveries include feature combinations that distinguish condensate classes, molecular signatures of stress-responsive or buffering compartments, and network configurations that link condensate dysregulation to neurodegeneration, cancer fitness, transcriptional control, and stress tolerance. These results will help explain why phase-separation propensity alone is insufficient and will clarify how mesoscale organization emerges from molecular interactions embedded in cellular context.

Fourth, the project will train a cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral fellows in synthesis science, FAIR data stewardship, interpretable machine learning, causal inference, reproducible workflows, and collaborative team science. The impact will extend beyond condensate biology by providing reusable strategies for studying other emergent mesoscale systems, such as membrane-less organelles, signaling assemblies, cytoskeletal structures, and chromatin domains. NCEMS support will catalyze a community-scale collaboration that no individual laboratory could accomplish, advancing molecular and cellular biosciences while building open infrastructure and a data-savvy workforce.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Open science is central to the project design. All non-restricted outputs will be released under permissive licenses through public repositories, including GitHub or GitLab for code, Zenodo for citable releases, and appropriate domain repositories for datasets and metadata. The knowledge graph, benchmark datasets, harmonized metadata, analysis notebooks, trained models, model cards, documentation, and visualization tools will be publicly available. We will follow FAIR principles by using persistent identifiers, standardized ontologies, machine-readable metadata, provenance records, explicit license documentation, and versioned releases. Community governance will include transparent contribution guidelines, issue tracking, code review, data dictionaries, authorship policies, and procedures for external data corrections or annotation updates.

Reproducibility will be enforced through containerized computational environments, workflow managers such as Snakemake or Nextflow, continuous integration tests, locked software dependencies, and automated data validation checks. Each analysis will include executable notebooks, parameter files, input-data version identifiers, and archived outputs sufficient to reproduce figures, tables, benchmarks, and model evaluations. Model development will include preregistered benchmark splits, baseline comparisons, uncertainty estimation, calibration assessment, leakage checks, and robustness analyses across datasets, organisms, and cell types. We will document negative results and uncertain annotations to avoid publication bias and overconfident claims.

Training activities will include reproducibility clinics, FAIR curation sprints, hackathons, and trainee-led open-source development sessions. Trainees will learn not only computational techniques but also ethical data reuse, responsible AI practices, transparent reporting, and inclusive team science. Working group meetings will include open seminars and periodic community feedback sessions. Manuscripts will be posted as preprints when appropriate, and all publications will link directly to reproducible computational releases. These practices will ensure that the project produces durable, reusable, and trustworthy resources for the broader molecular and cellular biology community.

[Budget and Resources]
NCEMS support is essential because the project requires sustained coordination, computation, data engineering, trainee participation, and community engagement across institutions and disciplines. Requested resources will support working group meetings, travel for geographically diverse participants, trainee fellowships or analyst time, cloud and high-performance computing, data storage, software engineering, knowledge-graph infrastructure, and open-science dissemination. Funds will prioritize activities that enable synthesis rather than data generation; no budget will be used for new wet-lab experiments, sample acquisition, or new experimental assays.

The working group will include investigators from research-intensive universities, primarily undergraduate institutions, minority-serving institutions, national data repositories, and international open-data communities. Budgeted meetings will include an initial in-person scoping workshop, two annual synthesis meetings, quarterly virtual analysis sprints, and focused hackathons for knowledge-graph construction, imaging embeddings, perturbation-screen integration, and benchmark development. Travel support will ensure participation by early-career researchers, trainees, and investigators from institutions with limited discretionary research funds. Trainee support will enable graduate students and postdoctoral fellows to serve as core analysts, with mentorship from senior scientists and data engineers.

Computational resources will include secure cloud storage for harmonized public datasets, scalable processing for image-derived embeddings and graph learning, container registries, continuous integration services, and public web hosting for documentation and visualization. Software engineering support will be used to build maintainable pipelines, application programming interfaces, data validators, and user-facing query tools. NCEMS staff expertise in team science, reproducible workflows, data management, and open collaboration will be leveraged throughout the project. Existing institutional resources, including faculty effort, local computing clusters, repository expertise, and domain-specific curation experience, will provide substantial in-kind support. The proposed budget therefore creates the collaborative and technical infrastructure required for a rigorous community-scale synthesis project that exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence: An AI-Driven Synthesis of Multimodal Public Data to Uncover the Universal Rules of Biomolecular Condensate Assembly
title_norm: decoding mesoscale emergence an aidriven synthesis of multimodal public data to uncover the universal rules of biomolecular condensate assembly
abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—represent a paradigm-shifting example of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. These dynamic assemblies bridge the critical gap between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles, orchestrating essential cellular functions ranging from gene regulation to stress response. However, despite an exponential increase in individual laboratory studies, the universal biophysical rules and stoichiometric conditions that dictate the unexpected emergence of these mesoscale structures remain a long-standing mystery. Furthermore, predicting how localized condensate dynamics influence global, higher-order cellular outcomes remains beyond current capabilities. This gap in knowledge persists largely because existing experimental data—ranging from atomic-resolution structural biophysics to whole-cell spatial transcriptomics and high-content imaging—are highly siloed across disparate public repositories.

To address this, we propose the establishment of the "Meso-Condensate Synthesis Working Group" (MCS-WG), a transdisciplinary collaborative initiative designed to synthesize existing multimodal public datasets to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. By integrating fragmented data from PRIDE (mass spectrometry proteomics), GEO (transcriptomics), PhaSepDB (phase separation curation), AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (structural conformations), and the Image Data Resource (high-content cellular microscopy), our team will construct a massive, multi-scale biological knowledge graph. Crucially, this project will rely entirely on publicly available data, generating no new experimental data, thereby directly answering the NCEMS call for community-scale synthesis.

Our working group will leverage advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI), specifically geometric deep learning and multi-modal graph neural networks, to identify hidden patterns that drive mesoscale phase separation. Our research objectives are threefold: (1) Answer novel questions regarding the evolutionary conservation of disordered protein regions and their emergent phase-separation behaviors across distinct cellular stress states; (2) Solve the long-standing puzzle of how varied macromolecular concentrations dynamically trigger mesoscale assembly and disassembly; and (3) Develop an innovative, open-source AI analytical framework that predicts subcellular phenotypic outcomes based on molecular-level perturbations.

The complexity of this synthesis requires the unique support and resources of NCEMS, as it extends far beyond the computational or domain expertise of any single laboratory. The MCS-WG will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, data ontologists, and machine learning experts from varied geographic locations and institutional tiers. In strong alignment with NCEMS goals, our initiative places a heavy emphasis on workforce development. We will actively recruit and cross-train early-career researchers (graduate students and postdocs) from historically underrepresented backgrounds, equipping them with a dual skill set in molecular biology and advanced data science. Furthermore, committing strictly to open science principles, all curated datasets, harmonized ontologies, AI model architectures, and analysis pipelines will be released publicly via open-access community portals, ensuring reproducibility and providing a lasting resource for the molecular and cellular biosciences community. Through this transdisciplinary synthesis, we will unravel how mesoscale emergence dictates cellular fate.
