By integrating fragmented data from PRIDE (mass spectrometry proteomics), GEO (transcriptomics), PhaSepDB (phase separation curation), AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (structural conformations), and the Image Data Resource (high-content cellular microscopy), our team will construct a massive, multi-scale biological knowledge graph. Crucially, this project will rely entirely on publicly available data, generating no new experimental data, thereby directly answering the NCEMS call for community-scale synthesis.

Our working group will leverage advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI), specifically geometric deep learning and multi-modal graph neural networks, to identify hidden patterns that drive mesoscale phase separation. Our research objectives are threefold: (1) Answer novel questions regarding the evolutionary conservation of disordered protein regions and their emergent phase-separation behaviors across distinct cellular stress states; (2) Solve the long-standing puzzle of how varied macromolecular concentrations dynamically trigger mesoscale assembly and disassembly; and (3) Develop an innovative, open-source AI analytical framework that predicts subcellular phenotypic outcomes based on molecular-level perturbations.

The complexity of this synthesis requires the unique support and resources of NCEMS, as it extends far beyond the computational or domain expertise of any single laboratory. The MCS-WG will assemble a diverse team of structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, data ontologists, and machine learning experts from varied geographic locations and institutional tiers. In strong alignment with NCEMS goals, our initiative places a heavy emphasis on workforce development. We will actively recruit and cross-train early-career researchers (graduate students and postdocs) from historically underrepresented backgrounds, equipping them with a dual skill set in molecular biology and advanced data science. Furthermore, committing strictly to open science principles, all curated datasets, harmonized ontologies, AI model architectures, and analysis pipelines will be released publicly via open-access community portals, ensuring reproducibility and providing a lasting resource for the molecular and cellular biosciences community. Through this transdisciplinary synthesis, we will unravel how mesoscale emergence dictates cellular fate.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates represent a transformative paradigm in modern cell biology, offering profound insights into how cellular machinery organizes without membrane barriers. Formed primarily via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), these dynamic, membraneless organelles bridge a critical dimensional and conceptual gap—the mesoscale—between individual macromolecular interactions and higher-order, membrane-bound organelle behavior. They orchestrate a myriad of vital cellular processes, including spatiotemporal gene regulation, signal transduction, and acute cellular stress responses. Despite the exponential proliferation of single-laboratory experimental studies investigating these assemblies, the universal biophysical rules, evolutionary drivers, and exact stoichiometric thresholds that govern their sudden emergence remain elusive. This persistent knowledge gap highlights a fundamental limitation in the current research landscape: data are overwhelmingly siloed. High-resolution structural biophysics, mass spectrometry-based proteomics, whole-cell spatial transcriptomics, and high-content cellular imaging are generated at unprecedented rates but reside in disparate, unlinked public repositories such as PRIDE, GEO, AlphaFold databases, and the Image Data Resource (IDR). Consequently, the field lacks a cohesive, multi-scale understanding of how micro-scale molecular perturbations—such as alterations in intrinsically disordered region (IDR) composition or post-translational modifications—propagate to yield meso-scale phase transitions and ultimately dictate macro-scale cellular fates. The proposed "Meso-Condensate Synthesis Working Group" (MCS-WG) addresses this critical bottleneck by proposing a community-scale data synthesis initiative that aligns perfectly with the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mandate. We argue that the answers to long-standing questions regarding condensate assembly do not necessarily require new experimental data; rather, they require the intelligent integration and synthesis of the massive volumes of existing public data. The emergence of mesoscale properties cannot be deduced by examining singular data modalities in isolation. Instead, discovering the universal rules of condensate assembly demands a transdisciplinary approach that merges advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI)—specifically geometric deep learning and multi-modal graph neural networks—with rigorous biophysical and cell biology expertise. The significance of this proposal lies in its potential to entirely shift how researchers predict and interact with mesoscale biological phenomena. By constructing a comprehensive, multi-scale biological knowledge graph, we will map the topological and functional linkages from linear amino acid sequences to 3D structural ensembles, and up to organelle-level phenotypes. This synthesis will uncover hidden correlative and causal patterns driving biomolecular condensation across diverse species and stress conditions. Furthermore, this project is uniquely suited for NCEMS support because the computational magnitude and cross-disciplinary expertise required to harmonize such vast, heterogeneous datasets vastly exceed the capabilities of any individual laboratory. Ultimately, decoding mesoscale emergence will not only resolve a long-standing mystery in molecular biology but also provide the broader scientific community with revolutionary analytical frameworks and predictive models, catalyzing future innovations in bioengineering and synthetic biology while directly advancing the NCEMS vision of understanding complex, emergent biological properties.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The Meso-Condensate Synthesis Working Group (MCS-WG) will rigorously investigate the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates by testing hypotheses centered on three interrelated core research objectives. By exploiting AI-driven synthesis of multi-modal public datasets, we aim to answer novel questions, solve long-standing puzzles, and develop transformative analytical frameworks. Question 1: How are intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and their emergent phase-separation behaviors evolutionarily conserved to facilitate rapid cellular adaptation during distinct physiological stress states? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the sequence grammar—specifically the spacing and clustering of aromatic and charged residues—within IDRs is evolutionarily constrained not to maintain a static 3D structure, but to preserve specific mesoscale phase-separation propensities under specific biophysical triggers (e.g., pH shifts or temperature spikes). By synthesizing genomic, transcriptomic (GEO), and curated phase-separation data (PhaSepDB), we expect to reveal that stress-granule and nucleolar condensate proteins exhibit highly conserved phase-transition motifs across disparate eukaryotic lineages, representing a universal evolutionary mechanism for emergent stress resilience. Question 2: What are the universal stoichiometric and concentration-dependent thresholds that dynamically trigger the meso-scale assembly and disassembly of varied macromolecular complexes? Hypothesis 2: We postulate that localized cellular concentration thresholds required for condensate nucleation are not fixed, but are dynamically tunable by the multi-valent interaction networks of the surrounding proteome. By integrating mass spectrometry proteomics (PRIDE) with atomic-resolution structural conformations (AlphaFold), we hypothesize that we can define a universal thermodynamic rule-set governing these transitions. We predict that AI-driven graph analysis will demonstrate that specific, low-abundance scaffold proteins act as critical network hubs, nucleating condensates only when the local valency and concentration of surrounding client proteins reach a mathematically definable critical emergence threshold. Resolving this will solve the long-standing puzzle of why identical proteins phase-separate in vivo at concentrations significantly lower than those required in vitro. Question 3: How can we predict global subcellular phenotypic outcomes based on micro-scale, molecular-level perturbations in condensate-forming proteins? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that biomolecular condensates act as mesoscale information-processing hubs, meaning that micro-scale perturbations (such as single-amino acid mutations or targeted post-translational modifications) propagate through a predictable hierarchy to alter higher-order cellular phenotypes. We will test this by developing an innovative, multi-modal graph neural network (GNN). We predict that our AI analytical framework, trained on the synthesized biological knowledge graph encompassing molecular interactions and high-content cellular microscopy (Image Data Resource), will successfully predict structural cellular abnormalities (e.g., aberrant condensate rigidification linked to neurodegeneration) solely from primary sequence and basic transcriptomic input. Addressing these questions necessitates a synthesis approach because no single dataset captures the continuum from sequence to cellular phenotype. Validating these hypotheses will establish the first universal rules of condensate assembly, fulfilling the NCEMS goal of understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale.

[Methods and Approach]
The MCS-WG will execute a completely data-driven synthesis project, adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate of utilizing only existing, publicly available datasets and generating no new experimental data. Our methodology is structured around three consecutive phases: Data Harmonization, Knowledge Graph Construction, and AI-Driven Analysis. Phase 1: Multi-Modal Data Curation and Harmonization. The foundation of our approach is the systematic aggregation of siloed public databases. We will extract primary sequence and phase-separation behavioral data from PhaSepDB and UniProt. 3D structural conformations, specifically focusing on intrinsically disordered regions, will be sourced from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. Cellular concentration, stoichiometry, and interactome data will be synthesized from quantitative mass spectrometry datasets housed in PRIDE. Finally, transcriptomic profiles under varying stress conditions will be downloaded from GEO, while corresponding morphological phenotypes will be extracted from high-content imaging repositories like the Image Data Resource (IDR). Given the heterogeneous nature of these datasets, our data ontologists will develop automated pipelines to harmonize metadata, standardizing nomenclature, experimental conditions, and cellular contexts into a unified, machine-readable format. Phase 2: Construction of the Mesoscale Biological Knowledge Graph (MBKG). To bridge the gap between individual molecules and emergent cellular phenomena, we will map the harmonized data into a massive, multi-scale Biological Knowledge Graph. In this graph, nodes will represent entities at various scales (e.g., amino acid motifs, whole proteins, RNA molecules, stress conditions, and observable cellular phenotypes). Edges will denote the relationships between these entities, such as structural interactions, stoichiometric dependencies, and co-expression probabilities. This graph architecture natively supports the integration of disparate data types, allowing for the direct linkage of micro-scale atomic features to meso-scale phase behaviors and macro-scale cellular phenotypes. Phase 3: AI-Driven Analysis and Predictive Modeling. To identify the hidden patterns driving phase separation, our machine learning experts will deploy advanced Artificial Intelligence methodologies. Specifically, we will utilize Geometric Deep Learning to analyze the spatial and electrostatic topologies of protein surfaces and disordered regions derived from AlphaFold data. Concurrently, we will train Multi-Modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on the MBKG. The GNNs will perform link prediction and node classification to uncover the universal rules of condensate assembly. By performing graph convolutions across the diverse data modalities, the AI will learn how varying macromolecular concentrations dynamically trigger mesoscale assembly, effectively learning the grammar of phase separation. Furthermore, we will utilize attention mechanisms within the GNN to highlight which molecular features most strongly predict subcellular phenotypic outcomes. Team Integration and Feasibility. This approach is well beyond the capabilities of a single laboratory. It requires deep collaboration among structural biophysicists interpreting the AlphaFold data, cellular biologists contextualizing the IDR imaging, data ontologists building the MBKG, and AI experts designing the GNNs. The MCS-WG will hold bi-weekly virtual syncs and quarterly intensive, in-person hackathons supported by NCEMS. This transdisciplinary synthesis will ensure that our models are not only computationally robust but also deeply grounded in biological reality.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The proposed synthesis will yield transformative outcomes that fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence. The primary scientific deliverable will be the elucidation of the universal biophysical rules and sequence grammars that govern biomolecular condensate assembly. By deciphering these rules, we will solve the long-standing mystery of how cellular life organizes complex biochemical reactions in the absence of physical membranes. This foundational knowledge will catalyze novel research avenues across molecular and cellular biology, enabling researchers to predict condensate behavior under specific cellular stresses or mutations. Technologically, the project will result in two major deliverables: the Mesoscale Biological Knowledge Graph (MBKG) and the open-source, multi-modal Graph Neural Network (GNN) analytical framework. These tools will allow scientists worldwide to input molecular-level perturbations and predict higher-order subcellular phenotypes, drastically reducing the time and cost associated with experimental trial and error. This has profound implications for bioengineering, synthetic biology, and the development of therapeutics targeting condensate-linked pathologies, such as neurodegenerative diseases. Beyond scientific discovery, the MCS-WG will make a profound impact on workforce development, directly aligning with NCEMS goals. We will actively recruit and train a diverse cohort of early-career researchers, including graduate students and postdocs from historically underrepresented groups and varied institutional tiers. These trainees will be immersed in a highly collaborative, transdisciplinary environment, receiving rigorous cross-training in both molecular biology and advanced data science (AI/ML). By bridging the gap between biological theory and computational application, this project will cultivate the next generation of data-savvy scientists, equipped to tackle the complex, multi-scale biological challenges of the future.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The MCS-WG is deeply committed to the principles of open science, transparency, and reproducibility, recognizing them as essential pillars for maximizing the impact of community-scale synthesis research. Our approach will strictly adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles throughout the entirety of the project lifecycle. All curated datasets, harmonized metadata, and the fully constructed Mesoscale Biological Knowledge Graph (MBKG) will be made publicly available through established, open-access community portals such as Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF). To ensure seamless interoperability, our data ontologies will be documented and published according to community-created standards, allowing other researchers to easily query, append, or integrate our synthesis data into their own pipelines. Furthermore, the complete suite of AI model architectures, multi-modal Graph Neural Networks, data extraction scripts, and analysis pipelines will be released under a permissive open-source license (e.g., MIT License). We will host all source code in structured, well-documented public GitHub repositories. To guarantee computational reproducibility, we will provide containerized environments using Docker and Singularity, alongside Jupyter Notebooks that detail step-by-step analytical workflows. This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their computational infrastructure, can replicate our findings or adapt our AI models for their specific research questions. Finally, we will prioritize early and open dissemination of our research findings. We commit to publishing all manuscripts as open-access preprints on bioRxiv concurrently with peer review submissions. We will also host virtual workshops and webinars to train the broader molecular and cellular biosciences community on how to utilize our synthesized databases and AI frameworks, thereby fostering a culture of collaborative, reproducible, and team-oriented science.

[Budget and Resources]
The MCS-WG requires the unique infrastructure, administrative support, and funding provided by NCEMS, as the scale and transdisciplinary nature of this data synthesis project vastly exceed the typical resources of individual research laboratories. The requested budget is exclusively allocated to facilitate collaborative synthesis, computational infrastructure, and workforce development, with absolutely zero funds directed toward primary experimental data generation. A significant portion of the budget will support the personnel critical to this transdisciplinary effort. We request funding for two full-time postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students. These trainee positions will serve as the primary engines for data harmonization and AI model development, fulfilling our commitment to training a diverse, data-savvy workforce. Funds are also requested for a dedicated part-time project manager to coordinate the complex logistics of our multi-institutional team, ensuring milestones are met and open-science deliverables are properly curated. To stimulate rigorous cross-disciplinary collaboration, we allocate funds for bi-annual, intensive, in-person working group hackathons hosted at NCEMS facilities. These gatherings are essential for fostering deep intellectual integration among our geographically dispersed structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, data ontologists, and AI experts. Travel and accommodation support will ensure equitable participation across all career stages and institutional tiers. Computationally, while we will leverage existing open-source data, training multi-modal graph neural networks on a massive biological knowledge graph requires substantial computational power. Therefore, we request funds for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) and high-performance GPU cluster access to facilitate the training and optimization of our geometric deep learning models. Finally, a small budget is reserved for open-access publication fees and community outreach workshops to ensure our findings and AI frameworks are freely accessible to the global scientific community.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a paradigm-shifting example of emergent mesoscale organization in molecular and cellular biology. These membraneless compartments, including nucleoli, stress granules, and processing bodies, dynamically compartmentalize biochemical reactions, playing crucial roles in cellular homeostasis and stress responses. Despite their biological importance, a fundamental knowledge gap exists: how do nanoscale molecular interactions—specifically the sequence grammar of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and dynamic post-translational modifications (PTMs)—drive the emergent architectural and material properties of condensates at the mesoscale? Furthermore, how do these mesoscale properties subsequently dictate subcellular and cellular phenotypic outcomes, such as neurodegenerative protein aggregation?

Currently, the molecular and cellular biosciences are rich in publicly available, yet highly siloed, datasets spanning multiple biological scales. Nanoscale sequence and structural data reside in repositories like UniProt, DisProt, and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. In vitro mesoscale phase behaviors are cataloged in specialized databases such as LLPSDB and PhaSePro. Meanwhile, cellular-scale phenotypic and imaging data are distributed across the Image Data Resource (IDR) and high-throughput screening platforms like the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap). No individual research laboratory possesses the comprehensive expertise in molecular biophysics, spatial transcriptomics, artificial intelligence (AI), and cellular biology required to bridge these disparate data islands. Consequently, our understanding of cross-scale emergence remains fragmented, limiting our ability to predict cellular behavior from primary molecular inputs.

To overcome this fragmentation, the proposed 'Mesoscale Condensate Computome (MCC)' Working Group will conduct a community-scale synthesis project strictly utilizing existing, publicly available data. In perfect alignment with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS), this transdisciplinary effort will leverage advanced AI and data science to harmonize these isolated datasets. We hypothesize that emergent mesoscale phenomena, such as condensate viscosity and multiphase architecture, are predictable consequences of a decipherable 'molecular grammar' that propagates upward to influence cellular health and disease.

The significance of this synthesis project lies in its potential to solve long-standing puzzles regarding biological phase transitions. By eschewing de novo data generation in favor of integrating expansive, pre-existing datasets, the MCC Working Group will pioneer innovative analytical strategies. Our approach addresses the NCEMS vision of understanding unexpected biological properties at the mesoscale, positioned critically between biomolecules and higher-order cellular outcomes. By mapping this cross-scale emergence, we will provide the scientific community with a unified, predictive framework for LLPS, fundamentally advancing our understanding of cellular organization. Moreover, this project will catalyze cross-disciplinary collaboration, uniting diverse scientific perspectives to uncover broader insights into the non-linear emergence of complex cellular systems from simple molecular components. This synthesis will inherently require the collaborative power of multiple labs, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to assemble teams reflecting diverse scientific expertise, geographic locations, and institutional levels. Ultimately, this foundational knowledge will unlock new therapeutic paradigms for diseases rooted in aberrant phase separation, driving transformative impacts across the biosciences.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The Mesoscale Condensate Computome (MCC) Working Group will tackle compelling, novel research questions surrounding the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. By synthesizing existing datasets, we aim to bridge the molecular-to-mesoscale-to-cellular gap. Our research framework is driven by three primary research questions and corresponding hypotheses, perfectly aligned with the NCEMS mission to decode emergent properties at the mesoscale.

Question 1: What is the molecular grammar that dictates emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates, and how do dynamic alterations such as post-translational modifications (PTMs) modulate these properties?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the sequence features of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)—including charge distribution, hydrophobicity, pi-pi interaction potential, and specific PTMs—function as a combinatorial code that predictably dictates emergent mesoscale features like condensate viscosity, surface tension, critical concentration thresholds, and multiphase spatial architecture. By synthesizing data from UniProt, DisProt, and LLPSDB, we will reveal how nanoscale molecular inputs non-linearly generate complex mesoscale material states.

Question 2: How do specific emergent mesoscale features of biomolecular condensates propagate upward to influence subcellular dynamics and higher-order cellular phenotypes, particularly in the context of cellular stress and neurodegeneration?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the material state and multiphase architecture of mesoscale condensates act as direct mechanistic determinants of cellular-level outcomes. Specifically, we postulate that transitions from liquid-like to solid-like states (aberrant phase transitions) are the critical mesoscale events that trigger the formation of pathological stress granules and neurodegenerative protein aggregates. By integrating in vitro phase behavior data (PhaSePro) with mesoscale cellular imaging (IDR) and high-throughput phenotypic screens (DepMap), we expect to identify the critical tipping points where normal mesoscale compartmentalization collapses into disease-associated cellular phenotypes.

Question 3: Can artificial intelligence and data science methodologies effectively synthesize highly heterogeneous, cross-scale biological data to create a predictive computational framework for biological emergence?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that multimodal graph neural networks (GNNs) can successfully bridge highly siloed datasets to infer higher-order cellular phenotypes strictly from primary molecular sequences and available interactome topologies. Since condensates form via multivalent interaction networks, GNNs represent the ideal mathematical architecture to model the emergent topologies of these systems. We expect that our AI-driven approach will generate an open-source predictive algorithm capable of accurately forecasting cellular behavior based on nanoscale inputs, without the need for de novo experimental data generation.

These questions challenge the current reductionist paradigms in molecular biology by focusing explicitly on emergence and synthesis. By answering them, the MCC Working Group will solve long-standing mysteries surrounding biological phase transitions. The synthesis of vast, diverse datasets to answer these questions requires the multidisciplinary collaboration and computational resources that only NCEMS can facilitate, fundamentally advancing our understanding of how cellular complexity spontaneously arises from molecular simplicity. Furthermore, analyzing these questions through a synthesis lens allows us to evaluate the evolutionary conservation of the IDP grammar across diverse species, assessing whether the rules governing mesoscale emergence are universal biological constants or context-dependent variables. This approach will not only yield deep insights into cellular organization but also stimulate novel subsidiary questions regarding the role of energetic fluctuations and information transfer within membraneless organelles.

[Methods and Approach]
The MCC Working Group will execute a rigorous, community-scale data synthesis project, strictly utilizing existing, publicly available data without generating new experimental datasets. Our approach relies on assembling a transdisciplinary team of experts in molecular biophysics, spatial transcriptomics, AI, and cellular biology, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate for multi-lab collaboration. The methodology is divided into three integrated phases: Data Harmonization, AI-Driven Synthesis, and Predictive Modeling.

Phase 1: Multi-Scale Data Harmonization and Integration.
We will first construct a unified, cloud-based data repository by ingesting and harmonizing siloed datasets. Nanoscale molecular data will be sourced from UniProt, DisProt, and AlphaFold to map IDP sequence features, structural propensities, and known PTMs. Mesoscale in vitro phase separation data, including critical concentrations, droplet viscosity, and partition coefficients, will be extracted from LLPSDB and PhaSePro. Finally, macroscale cellular phenotypic and imaging data will be integrated from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and DepMap. We will develop automated natural language processing (NLP) pipelines to standardize metadata and curate missing functional annotations from the literature. This comprehensive knowledge graph will serve as the foundational dataset for all subsequent analyses.

Phase 2: AI-Driven Synthesis via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs).
To capture the non-linear emergence of mesoscale properties, we will develop novel multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Condensate formation is fundamentally a network phenomenon driven by multivalent interactions; thus, GNNs are optimally suited for this architecture. Nodes will represent individual proteins (with embedded sequence and structural features), while edges will represent interaction probabilities and interaction strengths derived from interactome databases (e.g., BioGRID, STRING). We will utilize self-supervised representation learning to extract latent features governing IDP interactions. These graph embeddings will then be mapped to mesoscale emergent properties (e.g., viscosity, multiphase architecture) using transformer-based attention mechanisms, allowing the model to weigh the contribution of specific sequence motifs to bulk mesoscale behaviors.

Phase 3: Predictive Modeling and Cellular Phenotype Inference.
The final analytical phase will link the predicted mesoscale properties to cellular outcomes. We will employ temporal graph networks to model the dynamic transition of stress granules from functional liquid states to pathological solid states, mapping these transitions against neurodegenerative disease phenotypes from DepMap and spatial transcriptomic atlases. The ultimate output will be the 'Condensate Computome,' an open-source algorithmic framework capable of receiving an inputted protein sequence or interactome network and predicting its phase behavior and corresponding cellular impact.

Team Structure and Training Integration.
This ambitious methodology far exceeds the capabilities of a single lab. The MCC Working Group will operate through bi-weekly virtual synthesis hubs and bi-annual in-person hackathons supported by NCEMS. Crucially, postdoctoral researchers and graduate students will be intentionally embedded as lead data architects. Co-mentored by AI specialists and molecular biologists, these trainees will receive unparalleled cross-disciplinary training. They will lead the development of the GNNs and data pipelines, emerging as the next-generation, data-savvy workforce capable of navigating the complex intersections of computational science and biological emergence.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The Mesoscale Condensate Computome (MCC) synthesis project is poised to deliver transformative outcomes that will profoundly impact the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, by decoding the molecular grammar of intrinsically disordered proteins and mapping it to mesoscale architectural properties, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how biological phase transitions are regulated in vivo. This will provide a unified framework that replaces the currently fragmented understanding of liquid-liquid phase separation.

Second, the project will generate highly innovative research and analytical strategies. The development of multimodal Graph Neural Networks specifically tailored for multi-scalar biological emergence represents a significant methodological breakthrough. The resulting 'Condensate Computome' predictive algorithm will allow researchers worldwide to infer mesoscale phase behaviors and higher-order cellular phenotypes strictly from primary molecular sequences, accelerating research in fields ranging from developmental biology to neuropharmacology.

Third, the project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By embedding trainees at the core of our data synthesis pipelines, we will actively cultivate a diverse, next-generation workforce of data-savvy scientists. These emerging leaders will possess rare, transdisciplinary fluency in molecular biophysics, AI, and cellular biology, positioning them to tackle future challenges in the biosciences.

Finally, the MCC Working Group will fundamentally alter how the scientific community approaches complex biological questions. By successfully demonstrating the power of community-scale synthesis—integrating diverse, pre-existing datasets across geographical and institutional boundaries—we will validate the NCEMS vision. The project will illuminate the non-linear rules governing biological emergence, shifting the paradigm from reductionist experimental data generation to holistic, AI-driven data integration, ultimately unlocking new avenues for understanding cellular organization in health and disease. Furthermore, defining the tipping points of aberrant phase transitions will unveil novel therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases, translating fundamental synthesis research into tangible clinical insights.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The MCC Working Group is deeply committed to the highest standards of open, team, and reproducible science, ensuring that all outputs provide enduring value to the community. In strict adherence to NCEMS policies, our project will be entirely transparent and accessible from inception to completion.

First, all harmonized and curated multi-scalar datasets—encompassing molecular sequences, in vitro phase behaviors, and cellular phenotypes—will be deposited in universally accessible, community-recognized repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Dryad) under FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. We will implement rigorous metadata standards and clear version control to ensure interoperability with future synthesis efforts.

Second, all code, algorithms, and machine learning models—specifically the multimodal Graph Neural Networks comprising the Condensate Computome—will be developed entirely in the open. Reproducible analysis pipelines, containerized via Docker and orchestrated with Nextflow, will be hosted on public GitHub repositories under permissive open-source licenses (e.g., MIT or Apache 2.0). This will allow researchers worldwide to easily deploy, validate, and build upon our analytical strategies.

Third, we will launch a dedicated, interactive web portal hosted by NCEMS. This platform will serve as an accessible interface for the biological community, allowing researchers without deep computational expertise to input protein sequences and visualize predicted mesoscale emergent properties and cellular interaction networks.

Finally, the working group will practice radical transparency in our collaboration. All meeting agendas, synthesis workflows, and decision-making processes will be documented using open laboratory notebooks. We will publish our findings in open-access peer-reviewed journals and utilize preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) to accelerate knowledge dissemination. By embedding these rigorous open science practices, the MCC project will democratize access to advanced AI-driven biological synthesis, fostering trust, accelerating discovery, and maximizing the return on investment for the scientific community.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed MCC Working Group requires the centralized support and resources of NCEMS, as the scale and complexity of this transdisciplinary synthesis project far exceed the capabilities of any single laboratory or traditional funding mechanism. Importantly, the budget is allocated exclusively for data synthesis, computational infrastructure, collaboration, and training; zero funds are requested for new experimental data generation.

The primary budget allocation will support personnel, specifically focusing on the next-generation workforce. We request funding for three full-time postdoctoral researchers and four graduate students, distributed strategically across the collaborating institutions. These trainees will serve as the operational core of our data science workflows, directly fulfilling the NCEMS mandate to train a data-savvy workforce. Faculty investigators will commit substantial time in-kind, supported by modest summer salary offsets to lead the synthesis hubs.

A critical portion of the budget is dedicated to computational resources. We require substantial cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud) to train the computationally intensive multimodal Graph Neural Networks, host the harmonized multi-scalar database, and maintain the public web portal. These resources are essential for executing the AI-driven synthesis of massive, disparate datasets.

Furthermore, the budget includes necessary funds to facilitate the deep collaborative partnerships that define a community-scale project. We request travel and logistical support for bi-annual, in-person working group hackathons and strategic planning retreats at the NCEMS headquarters. These intensive gatherings are crucial for breaking down disciplinary silos, integrating diverse scientific perspectives, and ensuring continuous alignment across geographic locations and career stages. Finally, modest funds are allocated for open-access publication fees and specialized data science training workshops for our trainees. This strategic resource allocation will empower the MCC Working Group to successfully pioneer a new era of AI-driven synthesis in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a paradigm-shifting example of emergent mesoscale organization. These membraneless compartments organize biochemical reactions dynamically, yet bridging the gap between nanoscale molecular interactions and their mesoscale architectural properties remains a critical challenge. While abundant public data exist detailing the sequence characteristics of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and the cellular phenotypes of their dysregulation, a unified framework mapping this cross-scale emergence is absent. Currently, critical datasets—such as sequence features (UniProt, DisProt), structural predictions (AlphaFold), in vitro phase behaviors (LLPSDB, PhaSePro), mesoscale cellular imaging (Image Data Resource), and high-throughput phenotypic screens (DepMap)—remain highly siloed. No individual research laboratory possesses the combined expertise in molecular biophysics, spatial transcriptomics, artificial intelligence, and cellular biology necessary to bridge these data islands. To address this compelling scientific puzzle, we propose the 'Mesoscale Condensate Computome (MCC)' Working Group. This highly collaborative, transdisciplinary team will synthesize entirely publicly available datasets to decipher the rules governing emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. We will employ advanced AI and data science methodologies, specifically developing multimodal graph neural networks, to seamlessly integrate cross-scale data. The project is structured around three core synthesis objectives: (1) Map the molecular grammar of IDPs and associated post-translational modifications to mesoscale emergent properties such as condensate viscosity, critical concentration thresholds, and multiphase spatial architecture; (2) Link these emergent mesoscale features directly to cellular-level outcomes, specifically focusing on stress granule dynamics and neurodegenerative protein aggregation pathways; and (3) Develop open-source predictive algorithms capable of inferring higher-order cellular phenotypes strictly from primary molecular sequences and available interactome topologies. This initiative goes far beyond the capabilities of an individual lab, necessitating the centralized support of NCEMS to unite diverse experts across geographic locations, institutional research levels, and career stages. The MCC Working Group will recruit diverse computational and biological scientists, intentionally embedding postdoctoral researchers and graduate students into the core data science workflows. This will provide unprecedented training opportunities, actively cultivating a data-savvy, next-generation workforce fluent in cross-disciplinary AI and biological synthesis. Furthermore, our initiative commits rigorously to community-created open science policies. We will release all harmonized multi-scalar datasets, machine learning models, and reproducible analysis pipelines via public GitHub repositories and a dedicated web portal, ensuring long-term utility for the molecular biosciences community. By decoding how simple molecular inputs trigger complex, non-linear mesoscale emergence, this synthesis project will answer long-standing mysteries regarding biological phase transitions, ultimately pioneering innovative analytical strategies for understanding cellular organization in health and disease.

[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where transient, multivalent interactions among thousands of biomolecules spontaneously give rise to highly organized, functional, membrane-less organelles. These mesoscale structures dictate critical subcellular outcomes, ranging from stress adaptation to gene regulation. However, the precise rules governing how molecular-level features—such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA secondary structures, and post-translational modifications (PTMs)—dynamically scale to produce emergent mesoscale physical properties remain a long-standing puzzle in cellular biology. Despite the exponential growth of publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, structural, and spatial imaging datasets, these rich resources remain deeply siloed across disparate repositories. Addressing this complex emergent phenomenon requires a community-scale data synthesis approach that far exceeds the computational and disciplinary capabilities of any individual research laboratory.

We propose the establishment of the Condensate Emergence Synthesis (CES) Working Group to decode the multiscale grammar of condensate formation. This transdisciplinary team will unite domain experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, cell biology, and multi-omics. Adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate, we will generate no new experimental data. Instead, we will synthesize massive public datasets, including molecular interaction networks (BioGRID), structural and disorder profiles (AlphaFold DB, DisProt), high-throughput proteomics (PRIDE), and mesoscale spatial imaging (Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Atlas). 

Our primary scientific objective is to develop an innovative, multimodal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework to uncover the hidden principles of mesoscale emergence. We will address a novel question: How do heterogeneous molecular inputs synergistically trigger the spatiotemporal emergence of specific condensates, such as stress granules, under shifting environmental pressures? By harmonizing these disparate, multi-scale data streams into a unified, dynamic knowledge graph, our AI-driven analytical strategy will predict how distinct molecular perturbations cascade upward to alter mesoscale properties—such as condensate size, viscosity, and composition—and ultimately influence cellular phenotypes.

Executing this transdisciplinary integration fundamentally relies on the unique infrastructure, computational resources, and collaborative ecosystem provided by NCEMS. By bringing together diverse scientific perspectives across career stages and institutional levels, we will translate fragmented biological data into a cohesive understanding of subcellular emergence. 

Crucially, the CES Working Group will adhere strictly to community-created open science policies. All integrated databases, AI models, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be distributed through open-source repositories following FAIR principles. Furthermore, this initiative will provide unparalleled training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through intensive, cross-disciplinary co-mentorship in advanced data science and systems biology, we will empower the future data-savvy workforce required to solve the next generation of biological mysteries.

[Background and Significance]
The fundamental concept of biological emergence posits that complex systems exhibit properties and behaviors that cannot be fully understood or predicted merely by analyzing their isolated components. A quintessential and highly impactful example of this phenomenon within modern cellular biology is the formation of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These mesoscale structures—lying precisely at the critical dimensional interface between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles—spontaneously self-assemble driven by transient, multivalent interactions among thousands of proteins and nucleic acids. Once formed, condensates such as stress granules, nucleoli, and transcriptional hubs exhibit emergent physical properties (e.g., specific viscosities, surface tensions, and selective permeabilities) that are entirely distinct from the properties of their constituent molecules. These mesoscale attributes profoundly influence downstream subcellular and cellular outcomes, dynamically regulating biochemical reaction rates, sequestering crucial signaling molecules during environmental stress, and reorganizing genomic architecture.

Despite a decade of intense experimental focus, a massive knowledge gap persists regarding the "multiscale grammar" of condensate formation. We fundamentally lack the predictive rules governing how microscopic, molecular-level features—such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), specific RNA secondary structures, and dynamic post-translational modifications (PTMs)—scale upward to dictate the emergent physical state and functional outcomes of the mesoscale condensate. This represents a long-standing puzzle in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Currently, the vast majority of research in this domain is conducted in highly compartmentalized silos. Structural biologists probe single-molecule IDR conformations; systems biologists map vast, static protein-protein interaction networks; and cell biologists generate immense volumes of high-content spatial imaging data documenting mesoscale condensate behavior under various physiological conditions. 

Consequently, the broader scientific community has accumulated an exponential wealth of publicly available, high-quality data residing in disparate repositories, including molecular interaction networks (BioGRID), high-throughput proteomics (PRIDE), structural and disorder profiles (AlphaFold DB, DisProt), and mesoscale spatial imaging libraries (Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Atlas). However, because these data streams span vastly different temporal and spatial scales—and exist in entirely different structural formats—they remain tragically disconnected. No single laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, transdisciplinary expertise, or human resources required to integrate these multimodal datasets into a cohesive, predictive model of mesoscale emergence.

This proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission by establishing the Condensate Emergence Synthesis (CES) Working Group. By assembling a transdisciplinary team of experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, molecular biology, and multi-omics, we will execute a community-scale data synthesis project that transcends the capabilities of conventional research silos. We will generate zero new experimental data. Instead, our synthesis will leverage AI to fuse fragmented, multi-scale public data into a unified, dynamic knowledge graph. By bridging the critical gap between molecular sequence and mesoscale emergent property, this research will not only decode the fundamental rules of condensate biology but will also pioneer an innovative analytical strategy for studying multi-scale emergence, ultimately catalyzing novel discoveries across the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The CES Working Group will leverage synthesized public datasets to answer three distinct, novel, and interconnected scientific questions regarding mesoscale emergence. By mapping the trajectory from molecular sequence to mesoscale physics to cellular phenotype, we will establish a comprehensive framework for understanding condensate biology.

Question 1: What is the defining "multiscale grammar" that translates dynamic molecular features (e.g., PTMs, IDR conformers) into emergent mesoscale physical properties (e.g., viscosity, composition)? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that emergent mesoscale physical properties are not merely the additive sum of individual molecular valencies, but rather arise from a complex, non-linear "grammar" of synergistic interactions. Specifically, we postulate that specific combinations of post-translational modifications (e.g., widespread phosphorylation of serine/arginine-rich domains) combined with distinct RNA structural motifs act as highly predictable, switch-like triggers. These molecular triggers abruptly alter the percolation network of the condensate, reliably dictating measurable mesoscale outcomes such as the transition from a liquid-like droplet to a solid-like hydrogel. By synthesizing mass spectrometry-derived PTM data with biophysical property datasets, our AI models will uncover these hidden combinatorial rules.

Question 2: How do heterogeneous, shifting intracellular environmental pressures drive the spatiotemporal emergence and dissolution of stress granules?
Hypothesis 2: Biomolecular condensates such as stress granules exhibit exquisite sensitivity to environmental fluctuations (e.g., oxidative stress, heat shock). We hypothesize that the spatiotemporal emergence of these structures is governed by threshold-based, synergistic integration of multiple stress-induced molecular inputs. Specifically, stress granules emerge only when a precise, multi-omic threshold is crossed: the simultaneous availability of exposed, untranslated mRNA (detectable in transcriptomic/Ribo-seq data) coupled with the altered interaction affinities of specific scaffolding proteins (detectable via structural/interaction databases). We propose that our dynamic knowledge graph will identify the precise environmental and molecular tipping points that precipitate this mesoscale emergence.

Question 3: How do the emergent mesoscale properties of distinct condensates ultimately dictate subcellular resilience and phenotypic outcomes?
Hypothesis 3: The emergent material state of a condensate directly modulates its biological function. We hypothesize that the mesoscale physical parameters (such as selective permeability and internal diffusion rates)—which we will infer from integrated high-content spatial imaging and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) datasets available in public repositories—predictably govern subcellular phenotypic outcomes. Specifically, we propose that the emergent viscosity of stress granules directly determines the survival probability of a cell under prolonged stress by precisely regulating the sequestration and delayed release of pro-apoptotic signaling complexes. 

By addressing these compelling, long-standing puzzles, our research will shift the paradigm from descriptive observations of phase separation to a predictive, systems-level understanding of mesoscale biological emergence. This highly focused, hypothesis-driven approach ensures that our synthesis project directly advances the core scientific vision of the NCEMS, demonstrating how unexpected biological system properties appear across scales of composition, space, and time.

[Methods and Approach]
The CES Working Group will employ a purely synthetic, computational approach, strictly generating no new experimental data. Our methodology relies on harmonizing massive, multi-modal public datasets through an innovative, AI-driven analytical strategy centered on Multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and computer vision frameworks.

Phase 1: Community-Scale Data Harmonization and Knowledge Graph Construction
We will extract, clean, and harmonize data from diverse public repositories to construct the dynamic Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph (CEKG). 
1. Molecular/Omic Nodes: Protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions will be sourced from BioGRID and IntAct. Dynamic PTMs under various cellular conditions will be integrated from PRIDE (mass spectrometry datasets) and PhosphoSitePlus. 
2. Structural/Biophysical Attributes: Intrinsically disordered region (IDR) annotations, sequence features, and structural embeddings will be derived from DisProt, MobiDB, and AlphaFold DB. 
3. Mesoscale/Imaging Data: High-content spatial imaging, time-lapse microscopy, and in vivo FRAP data documenting condensate size, shape, and viscosity will be computationally extracted from the Image Data Resource (IDR), the Allen Cell Atlas, and published supplementary datasets using automated scraping and curation pipelines. 
The CEKG will represent molecules as nodes containing rich structural/sequence embeddings, while edges will represent condition-specific interactions weighted by PTM status and environmental stress conditions.

Phase 2: Multimodal AI-Driven Synthesis and Feature Extraction
To bridge the massive gap between molecular data and spatial mesoscale properties, we will develop a novel, dual-stream deep learning architecture:
1. GNN Stream: A Spatiotemporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN) will process the CEKG. The ST-GCN will learn how perturbations at the molecular node level (e.g., a localized phosphorylation cascade) propagate through the interaction network over time, generating dynamic "mesoscale propensity" embeddings for specific protein-RNA sub-networks.
2. Computer Vision Stream: Concurrently, spatial imaging data of condensates will be processed using Vision Transformers (ViTs) to extract quantitative mesoscale physical features (e.g., aspect ratio, fusion kinetics, and internal heterogeneity). 

Phase 3: Predictive Modeling of Mesoscale Emergence
The critical innovation of our approach lies in the multimodal fusion of these two streams. Using contrastive learning techniques, we will align the graph-derived molecular embeddings with the vision-derived mesoscale physical parameters. This aligned latent space will allow our AI model to predict unobserved emergent properties. For instance, by inputting a specific transcriptomic profile and PTM state (molecular scale), the model will predict the corresponding stress granule size, viscosity, and spatiotemporal distribution (mesoscale).

Validation and Rigor
Because we cannot generate new wet-lab data, we will rigorously validate our models using retrospective, out-of-sample synthesis. We will train the models on public datasets published prior to 2021 and test their predictive accuracy against orthogonally generated datasets published from 2022 to the present. This ensures robust, unbiased validation of the model’s predictive power. The execution of this complex, computationally heavy multi-scale integration relies entirely on the collaborative synergy of our transdisciplinary working group and the high-performance computing infrastructure provided by NCEMS.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The CES Working Group will deliver transformative outcomes that directly fulfill the NCEMS mandate to decode mesoscale emergence and catalyze transdisciplinary synthesis.

Scientific and Methodological Outcomes:
1. The Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph (CEKG): We will produce the first unified, multi-scale, machine-readable database linking molecular sequence features, dynamic PTMs, and environmental triggers to mesoscale physical properties of condensates. 
2. Predictive AI Framework: The release of our multimodal GNN architecture will provide the broader scientific community with a powerful new tool capable of predicting emergent subcellular phenomena from widely available omics data.
3. Solving Long-Standing Puzzles: By defining the "multiscale grammar" of condensate formation, our synthesis will resolve critical ambiguities regarding how distinct molecular perturbations cascade to alter subcellular structures, generating highly specific, testable hypotheses for downstream experimental labs studying neurodegeneration and cancer, diseases intimately linked to aberrant phase separation.

Workforce Training and Broader Impacts:
This project will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. We will directly support and co-mentor a diverse cohort of postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. These trainees will be immersed in a truly transdisciplinary environment, receiving rigorous cross-training that bridges advanced deep learning, complex data harmonization, and molecular biophysics. Trainees will lead hackathons and data-jams within the NCEMS ecosystem, tapping into diverse new talent and promoting geographic and institutional inclusivity.

Ultimately, this synthesis project will shatter existing data silos, fundamentally altering how researchers approach the concept of biological emergence. By transforming fragmented, publicly available data into predictive, systems-level insights, we will establish a new gold standard for AI-driven, non-experimental biological discovery, cementing NCEMS’s role as the global leader in mesoscale synthesis research.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The CES Working Group is unequivocally committed to the highest standards of open science, reproducibility, and FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, adhering strictly to community-created policies.

Data Sharing and Accessibility:
The entirety of the Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph (CEKG), including all harmonized raw data, extracted features, and metadata, will be made publicly available immediately upon project completion. Datasets will be deposited in recognized, long-term repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad, accompanied by comprehensive data dictionaries and standardized ontologies to ensure seamless interoperability.

Code, Models, and Reproducible Workflows:
All analytical pipelines, GNN architectures, and computer vision models will be developed entirely in the open using GitHub. To guarantee absolute reproducibility, we will provide containerized environments (e.g., Docker) alongside detailed Jupyter and Google Colab notebooks. This will allow external researchers of varying computational skill levels to replicate our findings or apply our novel multimodal AI framework to their own distinct datasets. All source code will be released under a highly permissive open-source license (e.g., MIT License).

Open Access Dissemination:
We commit to making all findings accessible to the global community without paywalls. All manuscripts generated by the working group will be uploaded to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to peer review. Subsequent publications will be targeted exclusively at open-access journals or utilizing open-access publishing options.

Community Engagement:
We will actively maintain thorough documentation and host virtual workshops through the NCEMS platform to teach researchers how to navigate our integrated datasets and utilize our AI models. By establishing transparent, reproducible, and open team-science protocols, the CES Working Group will ensure that our synthesis efforts continually catalyze new discoveries across the molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Budget and Resources]
The successful execution of this highly complex, transdisciplinary data synthesis project requires resources, collaborative infrastructure, and computational power that far exceed the capabilities of any single research laboratory or traditional multi-PI collaboration. NCEMS support is fundamentally necessary to achieve these aims.

Personnel and Workforce Training:
The primary budget allocation will directly support the transdisciplinary workforce. We request full salary and fringe benefits for two Postdoctoral Synthesis Fellows and two Graduate Research Assistants for the duration of the project. These trainees will bridge the computational and biological disciplines, driving data harmonization and AI development. Their funding is directly tied to the NCEMS mission of training the next-generation, data-savvy scientific workforce.

Working Group Collaboration and Travel:
To stimulate transdisciplinary cross-pollination, funds are requested for biannual, intensive, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facility, bringing together our geographically diverse team of AI experts, biophysicists, and cell biologists. Additional travel funds will support trainee attendance at major national conferences (e.g., ASCB, NeurIPS) to disseminate findings and recruit diverse talent.

Computational Infrastructure and Data Storage:
Synthesizing massive, multi-terabyte public datasets (particularly high-content mesoscale spatial imaging from the Allen Cell Atlas and IDR) requires center-scale cyberinfrastructure. We request robust cloud computing credits (e.g., AWS/GCP) and dedicated access to high-performance GPU clusters essential for training the multimodal Graph Neural Networks and Vision Transformers. Funds are also allocated for long-term, high-capacity cloud storage to house the harmonized Condensate Emergence Knowledge Graph (CEKG) and ensure its uninterrupted availability to the global scientific community.

By leveraging the unique collaborative ecosystem and cyberinfrastructure provided by NCEMS, this budget will seamlessly transform deeply siloed public data into a unified, predictive understanding of mesoscale emergence.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where transient, multivalent interactions among thousands of biomolecules spontaneously give rise to highly organized, functional, membrane-less organelles. These mesoscale structures dictate critical subcellular outcomes, ranging from stress adaptation to gene regulation. However, the precise rules governing how molecular-level features—such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), RNA secondary structures, and post-translational modifications (PTMs)—dynamically scale to produce emergent mesoscale physical properties remain a long-standing puzzle in cellular biology. Despite the exponential growth of publicly available transcriptomic, proteomic, structural, and spatial imaging datasets, these rich resources remain deeply siloed across disparate repositories. Addressing this complex emergent phenomenon requires a community-scale data synthesis approach that far exceeds the computational and disciplinary capabilities of any individual research laboratory.

We propose the establishment of the Condensate Emergence Synthesis (CES) Working Group to decode the multiscale grammar of condensate formation. This transdisciplinary team will unite domain experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, cell biology, and multi-omics. Adhering strictly to the NCEMS mandate, we will generate no new experimental data. Instead, we will synthesize massive public datasets, including molecular interaction networks (BioGRID), structural and disorder profiles (AlphaFold DB, DisProt), high-throughput proteomics (PRIDE), and mesoscale spatial imaging (Image Data Resource, Allen Cell Atlas). 

Our primary scientific objective is to develop an innovative, multimodal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework to uncover the hidden principles of mesoscale emergence. We will address a novel question: How do heterogeneous molecular inputs synergistically trigger the spatiotemporal emergence of specific condensates, such as stress granules, under shifting environmental pressures? By harmonizing these disparate, multi-scale data streams into a unified, dynamic knowledge graph, our AI-driven analytical strategy will predict how distinct molecular perturbations cascade upward to alter mesoscale properties—such as condensate size, viscosity, and composition—and ultimately influence cellular phenotypes.

Executing this transdisciplinary integration fundamentally relies on the unique infrastructure, computational resources, and collaborative ecosystem provided by NCEMS. By bringing together diverse scientific perspectives across career stages and institutional levels, we will translate fragmented biological data into a cohesive understanding of subcellular emergence. 

Crucially, the CES Working Group will adhere strictly to community-created open science policies. All integrated databases, AI models, and reproducible analytical pipelines will be distributed through open-source repositories following FAIR principles. Furthermore, this initiative will provide unparalleled training opportunities for a diverse cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through intensive, cross-disciplinary co-mentorship in advanced data science and systems biology, we will empower the future data-savvy workforce required to solve the next generation of biological mysteries.
