[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. These non-membrane-bound organelles, spanning the critical scale between individual biomolecules and complex cellular organelles, orchestrate vital biological processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress response. Despite their fundamental importance, the rules governing how molecular-level properties translate into emergent mesoscale behaviors—such as condensate formation, material state transitions, and dissolution—remain a significant, long-standing puzzle in cellular biology. While the scientific community has generated vast amounts of data characterizing these phenomena, these resources remain deeply siloed. Biophysical databases detail the physicochemical properties of LLPS drivers, high-throughput transcriptomic datasets map cellular stress responses, and high-content imaging repositories capture spatio-temporal dynamics. However, the lack of integration across these disparate, multi-scale datasets prevents a unified, predictive understanding of mesoscale condensate emergence. This proposal addresses this critical gap through a community-scale data synthesis initiative that aligns perfectly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We will leverage existing, publicly available data—generating absolutely no new experimental data—to decode the emergent rules of biomolecular condensates. The complexity of mapping 1D molecular grammar and 3D structural conformations to higher-order cellular outcomes demands a transdisciplinary approach that far exceeds the capabilities of any single research laboratory. By integrating curated LLPS databases (such as PhaSePro and LLPSDB), AlphaFold3 structural predictions, single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) from diverse cellular stress models, and spatio-temporal proteomics and high-content microscopy imaging (e.g., Human Protein Atlas and Cell Painting datasets), we will bridge the gap between distinct biological scales. The significance of this project is twofold. First, it will establish a predictive, multi-scale framework elucidating how molecular features and transient cellular states cooperatively govern the emergence of mesoscale structures, addressing a fundamental question in cellular biology. Second, it will pioneer innovative AI-driven analytical strategies, specifically utilizing multi-modal graph neural networks (GNNs) to harmonize highly heterogeneous data types. This approach not only provides novel insights into condensate-driven pathologies, such as neurodegenerative diseases and cancer, but also exemplifies the NCEMS vision of leveraging AI to unlock the secrets of biological emergence. Furthermore, this project is uniquely positioned to stimulate robust cross-disciplinary collaboration by uniting experts in structural biology, computational biophysics, computer vision, and systems biology. By tapping diverse new talent and focusing heavily on the mentorship and training of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, we will cultivate the future data-savvy workforce necessary to navigate and decode complex biological systems. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will catalyze a paradigm shift in how we understand mesoscale emergence, transforming isolated datasets into a cohesive, predictive model of cellular organization under stress. In doing so, we will directly support the NCEMS mandate to explore the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at different scales of composition, space, time, energy, and information.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
To decode the emergent rules of mesoscale biomolecular condensates under cellular stress, our Working Group will focus on three fundamental research questions and their corresponding hypotheses. These questions are specifically designed to leverage the synthesis of publicly available data and advance our understanding of molecular and cellular emergence. Question 1: How do specific molecular grammars and 3D structural conformations predictably govern the emergent material properties and phase behaviors of biomolecular condensates across varying cellular stress states? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the integration of 1D sequence features (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, specific amino acid patterning) with AlphaFold3-predicted 3D conformational flexibilities will reveal distinct, quantifiable "interaction motifs." We further posit that these motifs act as a predictive molecular grammar that dictates the threshold and material properties (e.g., liquid-like versus gel-like states) of condensates under specific stress conditions, as reflected in high-throughput cellular imaging and spatio-temporal proteomics data. Question 2: In what ways do transient cellular states, specifically varying degrees and types of energy depletion and cellular stress, re-wire the interactome to trigger the assembly or dissolution of mesoscale condensates? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that cellular stress induces reproducible, state-specific transcriptional and translational shifts that alter the local concentration and post-translational modification profiles of key scaffold proteins. By synthesizing single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from cellular stress models with public LLPS interactome databases, we expect to uncover emergent, systems-level regulatory networks. These networks will demonstrate that condensate emergence is not solely a function of individual protein propensity, but rather a dynamic, system-wide phase transition driven by global cellular state changes. Question 3: Can a unified, AI-driven computational framework bridge biophysical, structural, transcriptomic, and visual data to accurately predict the spatio-temporal dynamics of mesoscale condensate assembly? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning can effectively map heterogeneous data modalities into a shared latent space. We project that this AI-driven synthesis will not only identify previously unrecognized condensate drivers but will also accurately predict the subcellular localization and morphological dynamics of these structures as observed in public Cell Painting datasets. These questions address long-standing puzzles regarding how micro-level molecular interactions scale to produce macro-level cellular responses. By exploring these inquiries purely through the synthesis of existing datasets, we align with the NCEMS mission to extract novel insights from the wealth of publicly available biological data. The hypotheses are constructed to force a transdisciplinary examination of emergence—demanding expertise from structural biology to computer vision. Answering these questions will provide a comprehensive, predictive understanding of biomolecular condensates, mapping the trajectory from individual molecular features to the emergent mesoscale phenomena that define cellular survival mechanisms. This rigorous framework will ultimately yield a reproducible blueprint for understanding complex subcellular organization. Furthermore, testing these hypotheses will necessitate the development of novel analytical metrics to quantify emergence, transitioning the field from descriptive biological models to predictive, quantitative rules. This will fundamentally reshape our understanding of biological complexity at the mesoscale.

[Methods and Approach]
Our transdisciplinary Working Group will utilize a robust, community-scale data synthesis methodology, strictly analyzing existing, publicly available datasets to generate novel insights without conducting new experiments. The approach is structured into three integrated phases: Data Aggregation and Harmonization, Multi-Modal AI Framework Development, and Emergent Property Inference. Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Harmonization. We will systematically harvest and curate data from diverse, established public repositories. Molecular and biophysical data will be sourced from curated LLPS databases (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS), extracting known drivers, clients, and thermodynamic parameters of phase separation. For structural data, we will utilize the AlphaFold3 database to extract both static 3D structures and conformational ensembles of intrinsically disordered regions critical for LLPS. Cellular-scale transcriptomic data will be drawn from public single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) archives (e.g., Gene Expression Omnibus, Human Cell Atlas), specifically selecting experiments modeling diverse cellular stress conditions (e.g., oxidative stress, heat shock, energy depletion). Finally, phenotypic and spatio-temporal data will be extracted from the Human Protein Atlas and large-scale, high-content public Cell Painting datasets (e.g., JUMP-CP). A critical first step for our Working Group will be standardizing metadata and ontologies across these highly siloed resources to enable seamless cross-modal integration. Phase 2: Multi-Modal AI Framework Development. The core analytical innovation of this project relies on developing advanced, multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning architectures. We will construct heterogeneous knowledge graphs where nodes represent distinct biological entities (e.g., proteins, RNA transcripts, cellular stress states, morphological features) and edges represent their structural, functional, or regulatory relationships. We will deploy representation learning to map 1D sequence grammar, 3D AlphaFold structural embeddings, and high-dimensional scRNA-seq profiles into a shared latent space. Simultaneously, we will utilize computer vision algorithms (e.g., convolutional neural networks and vision transformers) to extract quantitative morphological features of mesoscale condensates from the Cell Painting images, projecting these into the same latent space. Phase 3: Emergent Property Inference. With the multi-modal AI framework established, we will apply graph-based predictive modeling to decode the rules of emergence. We will train our GNNs to predict the formation, localization, and material properties of condensates based on the integrated input features. By applying deep learning interpretability techniques (e.g., GNNExplainer), we will reverse-engineer the AI’s predictions to identify the dominant molecular and systemic features driving phase separation under specific stress conditions. This step is crucial for answering our research questions and transforming black-box AI predictions into intelligible biological rules. This ambitious synthesis transcends the methodological capacity of any single lab. Our Working Group structure is intentionally designed to facilitate this transdisciplinary approach, featuring intensive, collaborative synthesis sprints. By uniting computational biophysicists, computer vision experts, AI developers, and cellular biologists, we ensure that every facet of the methodology is executed with unparalleled rigor, fully leveraging the NCEMS infrastructure to support this unprecedented scale of data integration.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This project will yield transformative outcomes that directly address the core mission of NCEMS, fundamentally advancing our understanding of mesoscale emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. The primary scientific outcome will be the establishment of a unified, predictive rulebook detailing how molecular grammar and transient cellular stress states collaboratively dictate the formation and dissolution of biomolecular condensates. By successfully mapping the trajectory from 1D sequence and 3D structure to complex phenotypic behaviors, we will solve a major, long-standing puzzle regarding subcellular organization and stress survival mechanisms. Methodologically, we will deliver a pioneering, open-source AI framework utilizing multi-modal Graph Neural Networks designed specifically for cross-scale biological data synthesis. This framework will serve as a versatile, reusable blueprint for future transdisciplinary research, enabling the broader scientific community to integrate biophysical, structural, transcriptomic, and imaging data to investigate other emergent mesoscale phenomena. Beyond scientific and technological advancements, this initiative will have a profound impact on workforce development. By embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a highly collaborative, multi-institutional Working Group, we will actively train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. These trainees will gain rare, hands-on experience in cross-disciplinary communication, advanced AI application, and large-scale data harmonization. Furthermore, our deliberate recruitment of researchers from diverse geographic locations, institutional tiers, and career stages ensures that a broad spectrum of scientific perspectives shapes the research. Ultimately, this community-scale synthesis project will catalyze a paradigm shift, proving that the deepest insights into complex biological emergence can be unlocked not by generating more data, but by intelligently synthesizing the vast, siloed datasets already at our disposal. This project will firmly establish NCEMS as the premier epicenter for uncovering the hidden rules of cellular life through innovative data science.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is unequivocally committed to the highest standards of open, team, and reproducible science, ensuring that all aspects of this synthesis project are fully accessible to the global scientific community. Adhering strictly to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, we will establish a comprehensive open science framework from the project's inception. All curated and harmonized datasets generated through our multi-scale synthesis will be deposited in established, widely accessible public repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Dryad) with comprehensive metadata and standardized ontologies. We will not wait until publication; rather, we will release intermediate data harmonization milestones to foster immediate community engagement. The AI-driven computational tools developed, including the multi-modal Graph Neural Networks and associated deep learning architectures, will be developed transparently. All source code, analysis scripts, and detailed computational workflows will be version-controlled and hosted on public GitHub repositories under permissive open-source licenses (e.g., MIT or Apache 2.0). To guarantee reproducibility, we will utilize containerization technologies (such as Docker and Singularity) and provide detailed, interactive Jupyter Notebooks that allow external researchers to seamlessly execute our pipelines, validate our findings, and apply our models to their own distinct biological questions. Furthermore, we are committed to open-access dissemination of our findings. All manuscripts resulting from this Working Group will be submitted as preprints to bioRxiv prior to peer review, and final publications will be published in open-access journals. We will also develop public-facing web dashboards that allow researchers without advanced coding expertise to interactively query our predictive condensate models. Through these rigorous open science practices, we will maximize the impact of NCEMS funding, ensuring our methodological innovations and biological discoveries broadly empower the entire molecular and cellular biosciences community.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed community-scale synthesis project requires NCEMS support and resources, as the sheer scale of data integration and the necessity of transdisciplinary collaboration far exceed the capabilities of any single laboratory or traditional funding mechanism. The requested budget is meticulously structured to facilitate intensive collaboration, advanced computational analysis, and comprehensive trainee development. A primary portion of the budget will support the logistical and travel requirements for the Working Group. We request funding for bi-annual, in-person synthesis sprints hosted at NCEMS facilities. These intensive, multi-day meetings are critical for bridging diverse scientific dialects—allowing structural biologists, computer vision experts, and systems biologists to collaboratively refine our AI models and interpret complex data outputs. Between in-person meetings, resources will support robust virtual collaboration platforms to maintain continuous project momentum. Crucially, the budget prioritizes the next generation of researchers by providing dedicated fellowship support for graduate students and postdoctoral trainees. This funding is essential to embed them fully into the cross-disciplinary matrix, ensuring they have the dedicated time and resources required to master diverse datasets and advanced computational techniques. To execute the multi-modal AI framework, we request support for high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The training of complex Graph Neural Networks on massive datasets—including large-scale Cell Painting imaging libraries and AlphaFold3 structural ensembles—requires significant GPU cloud-computing hours and scalable data storage solutions. Finally, funds are allocated for open science initiatives, including open-access publication fees, cloud hosting for our interactive, public-facing web dashboards, and professional data curation services. This targeted resource allocation guarantees that the Working Group can seamlessly synthesize disparate data silos, successfully decode the emergent rules of biomolecular condensates, and deliver on the ambitious scientific and workforce training mandates set forth by NCEMS.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates, such as stress granules and nucleoli, represent a quintessential example of emergent properties at the mesoscale. Arising from the dynamic, multivalent interactions of proteins and RNA, these membraneless organelles bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular functions. Despite their critical roles in cellular organization, stress adaptation, and disease pathogenesis, the fundamental rules dictating how physical interactions at the atomic and molecular levels scale up to govern mesoscale condensation and macroscopic cellular phenotypes remain a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Current biological research often captures these phenomena in isolated silos—producing disparate datasets on molecular structure, pairwise protein-protein interactions, or cellular imaging—leaving a critical knowledge gap in bridging these temporal and spatial dimensions.

To address this fundamental question of emergence, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis of publicly available biological data to decode the mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates. We will systematically integrate structural and sequence data (AlphaFold DB, DisProt, PDB), high-throughput interaction and proximity labeling networks (BioGRID, IntAct, PRIDE), transcriptomic profiles under distinct cellular stress states (GEO, SRA), and high-resolution spatial imaging data (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Crucially, this project will rely entirely on existing public data and will not generate any new experimental outputs.

Leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and data science, specifically multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and contrastive representation learning, we will develop an innovative analytical strategy to fuse these disparate, multi-scale data types. Our primary objective is to construct 'Mesoscale-CondensateNet,' a predictive foundation model that mathematically maps how molecular grammars (such as intrinsically disordered regions, amino acid spacing, and interaction valencies) dictate emergent mesoscale properties (including droplet formation, material state transitions, and biochemical partitioning) and their subsequent cellular outcomes like gene regulation and stress survival.

This ambitious synthesis project fundamentally exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. It necessitates the specialized resources, computational infrastructure, and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS. We have assembled a transdisciplinary team encompassing structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, AI/machine learning experts, and data ontologists. This diverse partnership deliberately bridges multiple geographic locations, career stages, and institutional types to ensure a breadth of scientific perspectives.

Committed to gold-standard open science principles, all curated multimodal datasets, AI architectures, and reproducible analytical workflows will be openly shared via GitHub and Zenodo, strictly adhering to FAIR data practices. Furthermore, this working group will serve as a premier training incubator for the future data-savvy workforce. Through dedicated hackathons and cross-disciplinary mentorship, graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will be cross-trained at the cutting edge of artificial intelligence and mesoscale biology. Ultimately, this synthesis will solve a critical mystery in molecular biology, providing a transformative, open-access computational framework to predict condensate-driven emergent behaviors across the cellular landscape.

[Background and Significance]
The concept of emergence in molecular and cellular biology is nowhere more vividly illustrated than in the formation and function of biomolecular condensates. These membraneless organelles, which include nucleoli, stress granules, and P-bodies, represent a profound mesoscale phenomenon. They spontaneously assemble via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), transitioning from individual, highly dynamic biomolecules into structurally organized, functional biochemical reactors. This mesoscale organization bridges atomic-level interactions with macroscopic cellular phenotypes, dictating vital processes such as stress adaptation, gene regulation, and cellular homeostasis. Despite an explosion of research surrounding biomolecular condensates over the last decade, a critical knowledge gap persists: we still do not fundamentally understand the comprehensive 'molecular grammar'—the complex set of rules dictating how sequence features, structural valency, and dynamic protein-protein/protein-RNA interactions collectively scale to produce emergent mesoscale properties like droplet viscosity, material state transitions, and specific biochemical partitioning.

Historically, biological research has addressed this puzzle in isolated silos. Structural biologists have generated vast repositories characterizing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and folded interaction domains. Systems biologists have mapped complex but static interactomes and transcriptomic networks. Cell biologists have compiled massive image datasets detailing the spatial and temporal localization of condensates under various physiological stressors. The grand challenge, and the central motivation for this synthesis proposal, is that these massive, multimodal datasets remain largely disconnected. The emergent properties of condensates cannot be deduced by examining molecular structures, transcriptomic profiles, or fluorescence images in isolation. Understanding mesoscale emergence inherently requires synthesizing these diverse spatial and temporal scales.

Aligned perfectly with the U.S. National Science Foundation National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) mission, our project proposes to break down these data silos through an unprecedented, community-scale data synthesis. Leveraging the massive volume of publicly available data—from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and DisProt, to BioGRID, IntAct, and the Image Data Resource (IDR)—we will employ advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) to construct a unified predictive framework. By focusing squarely on mesoscale emergence, this project tackles a phenomenon that defies reductionist approaches and requires the robust, multidisciplinary integration of biophysics, cell biology, and state-of-the-art data science. 

This synthesis effort exceeds the computational and collaborative capabilities of any single research laboratory. It necessitates the unique environment provided by NCEMS to foster a transdisciplinary Working Group capable of defining novel analytical strategies. The significance of this work extends beyond resolving long-standing biological mysteries regarding membraneless compartmentalization. By establishing a predictive foundation model linking molecular grammar to mesoscale emergence, we will provide the scientific community with an open-source paradigm that can be applied to understand pathological phase transitions—such as those driving neurodegenerative diseases like ALS—and to engineer synthetic condensates for biotechnology. Through this synthesis, we will fundamentally shift the paradigm of how we study mesoscale biology in the age of big data.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our multidisciplinary Working Group centers its synthesis project around three fundamental research questions, each addressing a distinct facet of mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates. By interrogating these questions through the large-scale integration of public data, we aim to map the entire continuum from molecular grammar to macroscopic cellular phenotypes.

Question 1: How do specific, distributed molecular features (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, amino acid spacing, charge distribution, and interaction valencies) synergistically combine to dictate the emergent mesoscale physical properties of biomolecular condensates? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that a universal, mathematically definable 'molecular grammar' governs mesoscale condensate assembly and material state (e.g., liquid-like versus solid-like). We postulate that this grammar cannot be identified through linear sequence analysis alone, but can be decoded by synthesizing structural data (AlphaFold, PDB) with known phase separation databases (LLPSDB, PhaSePro) into a multidimensional latent space. We predict that AI-driven synthesis will reveal hidden synergistic rules—such as specific spatial arrangements of pi-pi and cation-pi interaction motifs across multivalent networks—that accurately predict emergent physical properties.

Question 2: How do dynamic changes in the cellular environment, particularly diverse stress states, propagate through complex molecular networks to rapidly alter condensate composition, material state, and biological function? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that condensate phase transitions are not static but are highly responsive, tunable emergent properties driven by environment-specific interactome rewiring. By synthesizing time-resolved transcriptomic data (GEO, SRA) with high-throughput proximity labeling and protein-protein interaction networks (BioGRID, IntAct), we expect to identify dynamic 'mesoscale hubs.' We predict that under specific stress conditions, the transcriptomic upregulation of specific RNA species and the post-translational modification of hub proteins act as rheostats, fundamentally altering the interaction valency of the network and thereby driving the sudden emergence or dissolution of stress granules.

Question 3: Can a unified, AI-driven computational model, trained entirely on multi-modal, public biological data across multiple scales, accurately predict macroscopic cellular outcomes based solely on molecular-level inputs? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that bridging the spatial and temporal scales of biological data requires non-linear, multi-modal integration, which can be uniquely achieved using multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We posit that by constructing a vast knowledge graph where nodes represent biomolecules (annotated with structural and sequence features) and edges represent condition-specific interactions, a GNN can learn to predict not only the formation of a condensate but also its impact on cellular phenotypes (such as stress survival rates or transcriptomic shifts). 

Addressing these questions represents a paradigm shift from descriptive, siloed biology to predictive, synthesized biology. These hypotheses challenge the traditional reductionist view by asserting that mesoscale emergent properties can only be understood and predicted when the intricate, high-dimensional web of molecular interactions is analyzed collectively as an integrated, dynamic system. Testing these hypotheses relies entirely on synthesizing existing data, requiring precisely the community-scale collaborative effort that NCEMS is designed to catalyze.

[Methods and Approach]
Our research strategy relies strictly on the synthesis of existing, publicly available data, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental outputs. The approach is structured across three integrative phases: Multi-modal Data Aggregation, Graph-Based AI Modeling, and Biological Validation and Community Access. 

Phase 1: Multi-modal Data Aggregation and Harmonization
We will systematically ingest, curate, and harmonize multi-scale biological data. For the molecular scale, protein sequences, annotations of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and 3D structural data will be parsed from UniProt, DisProt, and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. RNA sequences and secondary structure predictions will be drawn from RNACentral. To capture the systems scale, we will mine extensive interactome datasets—including direct physical interactions, proximity-dependent biotinylation (BioID/APEX), and RNA-protein crosslinking (CLIP-seq)—from BioGRID, IntAct, and PRIDE. Cellular state context will be integrated using transcriptomic profiles of diverse stress conditions from GEO and SRA. Finally, phenotypic spatial data will be extracted from high-resolution microscopy datasets available in the Image Data Resource (IDR). A major methodological innovation of our Working Group will be the development of an ontological pipeline to standardize these heterogeneous formats, creating a massive, highly annotated 'Mesoscale Knowledge Graph' where molecules are nodes and interactions are edges, weighted by stress conditions and expression levels.

Phase 2: AI-Driven Modeling and Mesoscale-CondensateNet
To bridge these disconnected scales, we will deploy advanced artificial intelligence architectures, specifically developing 'Mesoscale-CondensateNet.' This model will utilize multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) combined with contrastive representation learning. First, protein and RNA sequences/structures will be encoded using large language models (e.g., ESM-2) into high-dimensional embeddings representing the 'molecular grammar.' These embeddings will serve as node features within our GNN. The GNN will process the knowledge graph through message-passing layers, allowing the network to learn how local molecular rules propagate through multivalent interaction networks to form dense clusters—representing mesoscale condensates. Contrastive learning will be utilized to align molecular graphs with phenotypic imaging data and transcriptomic states, teaching the model to correlate specific network topologies with emergent physical states (e.g., fluid droplets vs. solid aggregates).

Phase 3: Validation and Transdisciplinary Collaboration
We will validate Mesoscale-CondensateNet using highly curated, independent public databases of phase-separating proteins (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB, CD-Code) utilizing a rigorous hold-out testing framework. We will measure the model’s predictive accuracy in identifying novel mesoscale condensates, material states, and stress-dependent assembly rules.

To accomplish this beyond the scope of a single lab, we have assembled a distributed Working Group spanning multiple institutions. The team includes structural biophysicists, computational cell biologists, graph machine learning specialists, and data ontologists. Utilizing the collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS, the team will execute this methodology through integrated cloud-computing environments, regular virtual synthesis meetings, and intensive, in-person hackathons. This transdisciplinary convergence will ensure the synthesized AI framework is grounded in biological reality, mathematically rigorous, and fully capable of unlocking the rules of mesoscale emergence.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The successful execution of this proposal will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the fundamental understanding of mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences. The primary deliverable will be 'Mesoscale-CondensateNet,' a groundbreaking, AI-driven predictive foundation model capable of mapping molecular grammar to mesoscale phase separation and subsequent cellular phenotypes. Accompanying this tool will be the 'Mesoscale Knowledge Graph,' the largest harmonized, multimodal dataset of its kind, linking protein/RNA structures, condition-specific interactomes, and cellular imaging across multiple physiological stress states.

Scientifically, this synthesis will solve the long-standing puzzle of how membraneless organelles predictably assemble and function without lipid boundaries. By delineating the synergistic rules of multivalent interactions, we will shift the field from descriptive studies of isolated condensates to predictive models of whole-cell mesoscale organization. This has profound implications across the biosciences, providing the foundational knowledge necessary to understand condensate-driven pathologies, such as neurodegeneration and cancer, and empowering synthetic biologists to engineer custom condensates for therapeutic interventions.

Beyond scientific discovery, the impact on workforce development and collaborative infrastructure will be substantial. Aligned with the NCEMS mission, this project will act as a critical training incubator. Graduate students and postdocs involved in the Working Group will be uniquely cross-trained at the highly sought-after intersection of multi-modal artificial intelligence and biophysics. Through structured hackathons and cross-institutional mentorship, we will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists capable of leading transdisciplinary research.

Finally, the project will demonstrate the immense, untapped power of synthesizing existing public data. By showing that disparate, siloed datasets can be integrated to produce novel biological insights without generating new experimental data, this initiative will establish a scalable blueprint for future community-scale synthesis efforts in the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is unequivocally committed to the principles of Open Science and reproducible research, adhering strictly to gold-standard practices and the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. Because this project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, ensuring the transparency and reusability of our data ingestion, processing, and modeling pipelines is our highest priority.

All curated datasets, ontological mappings, and the final 'Mesoscale Knowledge Graph' will be deposited in recognized, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Figshare, accompanied by comprehensive metadata conforming to established biological and computational standards. To guarantee the reproducibility of our artificial intelligence models, the complete source code for 'Mesoscale-CondensateNet'—including data preprocessing scripts, GNN architectures, hyperparameter configurations, and model weights—will be maintained in a public GitHub repository under an MIT open-source license. We will utilize continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines to maintain code quality.

To facilitate immediate usability by the broader molecular and cellular biology community, we will containerize all computational environments using Docker and Singularity. This will allow researchers to deploy our models on local workstations or high-performance computing clusters with zero configuration overhead. Furthermore, we will provide interactive Jupyter and Google Colab notebooks serving as user-friendly tutorials, enabling biologists without advanced computer science backgrounds to run predictive queries on their proteins of interest.

All synthesis workflows will be documented extensively via openly accessible platforms (e.g., ReadTheDocs). By establishing community-created policies on open and team science within our Working Group, we will ensure that every phase of the project is transparent. Ultimately, the resulting open-access computational framework will empower a global community of researchers to continually test, refine, and expand upon our discoveries in mesoscale emergence.

[Budget and Resources]
In strict accordance with NCEMS guidelines, the proposed budget is entirely dedicated to data synthesis, collaborative team building, computational infrastructure, and workforce training; no funds are allocated for generating new experimental data. The budget requires NCEMS support because the scope of multi-modal data integration, advanced AI model training, and transdisciplinary coordination exceeds the resources of any single laboratory.

Personnel costs form the core of the budget, focusing heavily on training the future data-savvy workforce. We request support for two full-time Postdoctoral Fellows and three Graduate Research Assistants, deliberately distributed across our partnering institutions. These trainees will receive dual mentorship in structural biology and AI/ML, directly fulfilling the NCEMS goal of cultivating cross-disciplinary talent. Additionally, funds are allocated for a part-time Data Ontologist/Engineer to manage the complex harmonization of disparate public databases (AlphaFold, IDR, GEO, etc.) and ensure strict adherence to FAIR open-science standards.

Computational resources are a critical necessity. We request funding for cloud computing credits (AWS/GCP) and utilize NCEMS high-performance computing (HPC) clusters to train the resource-intensive multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (Mesoscale-CondensateNet) and manage the terabytes of required structural and transcriptomic data storage.

Finally, a significant portion of the budget is dedicated to Collaborative Partnerships and dissemination. We request travel and lodging funds to host three intensive, in-person 'Synthesis Hackathons' at NCEMS headquarters. These meetings are essential for deep intellectual integration, allowing biophysicists, cell biologists, and AI experts to collaboratively refine the model and troubleshoot data synthesis bottlenecks. Additional travel funds will support trainees presenting our open-source tools at major computational biology and biophysics conferences, ensuring broad community adoption. This budget intimately aligns with the NCEMS vision of fostering collaborative, large-scale data synthesis to unravel mesoscale biological mysteries.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, such as stress granules and nucleoli, represent a quintessential example of emergent properties at the mesoscale. Arising from the dynamic, multivalent interactions of proteins and RNA, these membraneless organelles bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular functions. Despite their critical roles in cellular organization, stress adaptation, and disease pathogenesis, the fundamental rules dictating how physical interactions at the atomic and molecular levels scale up to govern mesoscale condensation and macroscopic cellular phenotypes remain a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Current biological research often captures these phenomena in isolated silos—producing disparate datasets on molecular structure, pairwise protein-protein interactions, or cellular imaging—leaving a critical knowledge gap in bridging these temporal and spatial dimensions.

To address this fundamental question of emergence, our Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis of publicly available biological data to decode the mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates. We will systematically integrate structural and sequence data (AlphaFold DB, DisProt, PDB), high-throughput interaction and proximity labeling networks (BioGRID, IntAct, PRIDE), transcriptomic profiles under distinct cellular stress states (GEO, SRA), and high-resolution spatial imaging data (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Crucially, this project will rely entirely on existing public data and will not generate any new experimental outputs.

Leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and data science, specifically multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and contrastive representation learning, we will develop an innovative analytical strategy to fuse these disparate, multi-scale data types. Our primary objective is to construct 'Mesoscale-CondensateNet,' a predictive foundation model that mathematically maps how molecular grammars (such as intrinsically disordered regions, amino acid spacing, and interaction valencies) dictate emergent mesoscale properties (including droplet formation, material state transitions, and biochemical partitioning) and their subsequent cellular outcomes like gene regulation and stress survival.

This ambitious synthesis project fundamentally exceeds the capacity of any single laboratory or existing collaboration. It necessitates the specialized resources, computational infrastructure, and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS. We have assembled a transdisciplinary team encompassing structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, AI/machine learning experts, and data ontologists. This diverse partnership deliberately bridges multiple geographic locations, career stages, and institutional types to ensure a breadth of scientific perspectives.

Committed to gold-standard open science principles, all curated multimodal datasets, AI architectures, and reproducible analytical workflows will be openly shared via GitHub and Zenodo, strictly adhering to FAIR data practices. Furthermore, this working group will serve as a premier training incubator for the future data-savvy workforce. Through dedicated hackathons and cross-disciplinary mentorship, graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will be cross-trained at the cutting edge of artificial intelligence and mesoscale biology. Ultimately, this synthesis will solve a critical mystery in molecular biology, providing a transformative, open-access computational framework to predict condensate-driven emergent behaviors across the cellular landscape.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates, dynamic membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergence at the mesoscale. Arising from the multivalent interactions of proteins and nucleic acids, these mesoscale structures bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and complex cellular organelles, orchestrating critical subcellular processes ranging from stress response to gene expression. Despite the recent explosion of experimental data regarding LLPS, a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology remains: What are the fundamental, generalizable rules that govern the unexpected emergence of biomolecular condensates from constituent molecular features across dynamic cellular environments?

To address this gap, we propose the establishment of a transdisciplinary Working Group to synthesize massive, heterogeneous, publicly available datasets to uncover the multi-scale rules of mesoscale emergence. Our project strictly utilizes existing public data, bypassing new experimental data generation, to conduct a community-scale synthesis that integrates structural databases (PDB), intrinsically disordered protein repositories (DisProt, IDEAL), specialized LLPS databases (PhaSePro, LLPSDB), global protein-protein interactomes (BioGRID), and condition-specific spatial multi-omics (PRIDE, GEO).

Through the application of advanced artificial intelligence and data science techniques, specifically Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, our Working Group will construct a unified theoretical and computational framework. This framework will map the thermodynamic and kinetic emergence of condensates from microscale molecular properties—such as sequence grammar, post-translational modifications, and RNA-binding capacity—up to mesoscale structural properties and eventual cellular phenotypic outcomes. By integrating data across spatial, temporal, and energy scales (e.g., cellular homeostasis versus acute stress states), we aim to predict emergent mesoscale behaviors under diverse physiological contexts.

This synthesis initiative fundamentally requires the collaborative ecosystem and cyberinfrastructure of NCEMS. The sheer volume and dimensionality of the data, combined with the required integration of polymer physics, computational structural biology, multi-omics, and AI, place this effort far beyond the capabilities of any single research laboratory or traditional collaboration. Our team brings together a diverse assembly of molecular biologists, biophysicists, and data scientists from across geographic locations and career stages, encompassing both R1 universities and Minority Serving Institutions (MSIs) to ensure varied scientific perspectives and tap diverse new talent.

In strict adherence to Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, and analytical workflows will be made openly accessible via an interactive, open-source platform. Furthermore, this Working Group is deeply committed to training the future data-savvy workforce. We will host cross-disciplinary data synthesis workshops and provide dedicated mentorship programs for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, equipping them with the unique skills needed to navigate both molecular biology and advanced computational AI. Ultimately, this project will decode the principles of mesoscale emergence, providing a transformative, open-access resource that accelerates discovery across the molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Background and Significance]
The concept of emergence is central to understanding biological complexity, where novel properties arise at higher levels of organization that cannot be predicted solely from the individual components. A quintessential example of this phenomenon in molecular and cellular biology is the formation of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic, membraneless organelles represent a critical mesoscale transition, existing at the scale between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound cellular organelles. By compartmentalizing specific proteins and nucleic acids, condensates orchestrate a myriad of vital subcellular processes, including gene expression regulation, signal transduction, and acute cellular stress responses. Despite the profound biological importance of these structures, a significant gap remains in our fundamental understanding of how these mesoscale properties unexpectedly appear from microscale interactions across dynamic spatial, temporal, and energetic scales. In recent years, the molecular and cellular biosciences have witnessed an explosion of publicly available data related to phase separation. High-throughput sequencing, advanced structural biology, and spatial multi-omics have populated numerous independent databases with disparate information on protein sequences, intrinsically disordered regions, post-translational modifications, and protein-protein interaction networks. Repositories such as the Protein Data Bank (PDB), DisProt, IDEAL, PhaSePro, LLPSDB, BioGRID, and various multi-omic archives (PRIDE, GEO) represent a treasure trove of untapped potential. However, these datasets remain largely siloed. Traditional research approaches, often constrained to single-laboratory capabilities and specific biological models, are insufficient to synthesize this massive, heterogeneous data. Consequently, a long-standing puzzle remains: What are the fundamental, generalizable rules that govern the emergent formation, dissolution, and physical properties of biomolecular condensates across diverse physiological and pathological contexts? This proposal addresses this critical gap by establishing a transdisciplinary Working Group to conduct a community-scale synthesis of existing public data, directly aligning with the core mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We hypothesize that the integration of multi-omic, structural, and interactome data using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) will reveal the universal sequence grammar and thermodynamic principles underpinning condensate emergence. The significance of this project is twofold. First, scientifically, it will transition the field from a descriptive paradigm to a predictive one, enabling researchers to forecast mesoscale condensate behaviors based on microscale molecular signatures and cellular energy states. Second, methodologically, it will pioneer a robust AI-driven framework, specifically utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, tailored for multi-scale biological data integration. By capitalizing on the collaborative ecosystem of NCEMS, our synthesis project moves beyond the scope of a single laboratory, leveraging diverse expertise in polymer physics, computational structural biology, and machine learning. Through this synthesis, we will not only solve a long-standing mystery in molecular biology but also provide a revolutionary, transdisciplinary lens through which to view mesoscale emergence, significantly advancing the broader field of molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
To uncover the multi-scale rules governing the emergence of biomolecular condensates, our Working Group will focus on three fundamental research questions and their associated hypotheses. These questions are designed to synthesize publicly available microscale data to predict mesoscale emergent phenomena, strictly utilizing existing heterogeneous datasets in alignment with NCEMS objectives. Question 1: What is the universal 'sequence grammar' and structural architecture that dictates the mesoscale emergence of biomolecular condensates? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the propensity of proteins to undergo liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and their resulting mesoscale material properties (e.g., viscosity, surface tension) are encoded by a decipherable combination of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), specific multivalent interaction motifs, and dynamic post-translational modifications (PTMs). To address this, we will synthesize data from DisProt, IDEAL, PDB, PhaSePro, and LLPSDB. We expect to identify conserved patterns—such as charge distribution, pi-pi interactions, and spacer lengths—that act as a predictive grammar for phase separation across different proteomes. By integrating this microscale structural data, we aim to map how molecular flexibility and multivalency give rise to the unexpected appearance of mesoscale droplet formation. Question 2: How do dynamic cellular contexts, specifically varying temporal and energetic states, influence the thermodynamic and kinetic emergence of condensates? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the energetic and environmental shifts within a cell (e.g., acute stress versus homeostasis) alter the global protein-protein interactome and multi-omic landscape, driving the context-dependent emergence or dissolution of specialized condensates. This question tackles the time and energy scales of emergence. We will synthesize condition-specific spatial multi-omics from PRIDE and GEO with global interactome data from BioGRID. By tracking how transcriptomic and proteomic profiles change under stress, and mapping these changes onto known LLPS drivers, we can model the thermodynamic thresholds required for condensate nucleation. This will resolve the long-standing puzzle of how cells rapidly reorganize their mesoscale architecture in response to energetic perturbations without synthesizing new proteins. Question 3: Can an integrated Artificial Intelligence framework accurately predict the formation, composition, and phenotypic consequences of biomolecular condensates from disparate public data? Hypothesis 3: Deep representation learning and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), trained on synthesized multi-omic, structural, and interactome networks, will uncover hidden, non-linear relationships that traditional analytical methods miss, enabling highly accurate predictions of novel emergent condensates and their cellular functions. By defining biomolecules as nodes and their diverse interactions (physical, temporal, energetic) as edges, we hypothesize that AI can capture the high-dimensional complexity of the mesoscale. This methodological development addresses the urgent need for analytical strategies capable of handling community-scale biological data. The synthesized AI models will test whether the 'rules of emergence' derived from known condensates can accurately predict uncharacterized phase-separating systems. Ultimately, these integrated questions will transition our understanding of mesoscale emergence from isolated, descriptive observations to a generalized, predictive theoretical framework, answering critical mysteries in molecular biology through innovative data synthesis.

[Methods and Approach]
Our project will employ a purely computational, data-synthesis approach, rigorously adhering to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. The effort is beyond the capacity of a single laboratory, requiring a transdisciplinary Working Group comprised of experts in computational structural biology, polymer physics, multi-omics, and advanced AI. The workflow is divided into three distinct phases: Data Aggregation and Harmonization, AI-Driven Synthesis and Modeling, and Mesoscale Emergence Prediction. Phase 1: Community-Scale Data Aggregation and Harmonization. The foundation of our approach relies on integrating massive, heterogeneous, publicly available datasets. We will extract structural and sequence features of phase-separating proteins and their clients from dedicated LLPS databases (PhaSePro, LLPSDB, CD-CODE), linking them to high-resolution molecular data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and intrinsically disordered protein repositories (DisProt, IDEAL). To capture dynamic cellular contexts across different spatial and energetic scales, we will integrate global protein-protein interactomes (BioGRID, STRING) with condition-specific spatial multi-omics (transcriptomics and proteomics) sourced from PRIDE and GEO. A critical methodological innovation will be the development of a standardized ontological framework to harmonize these disparate data types—reconciling varying formats, biological conditions, and resolution scales—into a unified, multi-dimensional data matrix. Phase 2: AI-Driven Synthesis and Modeling via Graph Neural Networks. To synthesize this complex data matrix and extract the fundamental rules of mesoscale emergence, we will deploy state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence techniques. Specifically, we will construct heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In our graph architecture, nodes will represent biomolecules (proteins, RNAs) enriched with deep representation learning embeddings (e.g., utilizing protein language models like ESM-2 to capture sequence grammar and PTMs). Edges will represent varying types of interactions, weighted by thermodynamic probabilities derived from multi-omic expression levels and BioGRID interactome confidence scores. By training the GNN on known condensate-forming networks under diverse cellular conditions, the AI will learn the non-linear, multi-scale dependencies that bridge microscale molecular features with mesoscale droplet formation. This strategy will enable the model to capture the topological signatures and temporal dynamics of biomolecular condensation. Phase 3: Mesoscale Emergence Prediction and Validation. The finalized computational framework will be used to predict the formation, composition, and physical properties of novel condensates across uncharacterized physiological states. Because we cannot generate new experimental data, we will rigorously validate our AI models using a 'hold-out' temporal validation strategy. We will train our algorithms on historical datasets (e.g., pre-2020 public data) and test their predictive accuracy against newly published, independent experimental datasets (e.g., post-2020 literature and database additions) not seen by the model during training. Furthermore, we will use in silico biophysical simulations, specifically coarse-grained molecular dynamics guided by the AI-identified sequence grammar, to theoretically validate the thermodynamic feasibility of predicted emergent mesoscale structures. This integrated approach ensures a high standard of scientific rigor, yielding a robust analytical strategy capable of uncovering the fundamental rules of biomolecular condensates.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The proposed synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that directly address the core mission of NCEMS. Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the elucidation of a universal, predictive 'sequence grammar' and thermodynamic framework governing the emergence of biomolecular condensates. By solving this long-standing puzzle, we will empower the molecular and cellular biology community to predict how microscale mutations or cellular energy shifts cascade into mesoscale organizational changes and subsequent phenotypic outcomes. This represents a paradigm shift, transitioning the field from empirical observation to predictive modeling. Methodologically, we will produce a pioneering AI-driven analytical framework based on Graph Neural Networks and deep representation learning, specifically tailored for the synthesis of highly heterogeneous, multi-scale biological data. This innovative software infrastructure will be adaptable, providing a blueprint for future synthesis research tackling other complex emergent phenomena beyond phase separation. The broader impacts of this project are equally significant, focusing heavily on human capital and community building. By uniting researchers from diverse geographic locations, R1 universities, and Minority Serving Institutions (MSIs), we will tap into diverse new talent and stimulate unprecedented cross-disciplinary collaboration. A cornerstone of our expected impact is the comprehensive training of the future data-savvy workforce. Through immersive working group participation, cross-disciplinary data synthesis workshops, and specialized mentorship programs, graduate students and postdocs will acquire a unique, highly sought-after skill set at the intersection of biophysics, molecular biology, and advanced AI. Ultimately, this transdisciplinary effort will yield novel biological insights, cutting-edge analytical tools, and a newly minted cohort of scientific leaders, thereby profoundly accelerating discovery and innovation across the molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is resolutely committed to the highest standards of Open Science, reproducibility, and transparency, recognizing that community-scale synthesis relies fundamentally on accessible and reusable resources. To ensure compliance with community-created policies on open, team, and reproducible science, all aspects of our project will adhere strictly to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. First, all synthesized datasets, including the harmonized multi-omic matrices, structural embeddings, and interactome graphs, will be extensively documented with rich metadata and deposited into globally recognized, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Figshare. We will assign Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) to all dataset versions to ensure findability and permanent access. Second, all computational code, AI architectures (including our Graph Neural Networks), and analytical workflows will be developed openly via GitHub. To guarantee reproducibility, we will utilize containerization technologies such as Docker and Singularity, alongside workflow managers like Nextflow or Snakemake. This portal will allow the broader biological community—including researchers without advanced computational expertise—to query our synthesized models, input their own protein sequences of interest, and predict emergent mesoscale condensate properties. Open access preprints (e.g., bioRxiv) will precede all peer-reviewed publications, and all training materials developed for our workshops will be freely distributed under Creative Commons licenses. Through these robust Open Science practices, we will maximize the reuse, transparency, and collaborative impact of our synthesis research.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed synthesis project requires a level of integration, computational power, and collaborative infrastructure that fundamentally exceeds the capabilities of any single research laboratory or traditional funding mechanism, making NCEMS support indispensable. Our budget and resource requests are strategically aligned with facilitating Working Group dynamics, robust cyberinfrastructure, and comprehensive workforce training, with zero funds allocated for new experimental data generation. The primary budgetary request supports the logistical and travel requirements of the transdisciplinary Working Group. Funds will cover travel, accommodation, and per diem for all members—spanning molecular biologists, biophysicists, and data scientists from R1 universities and Minority Serving Institutions (MSIs)—to attend bi-annual, intensive, in-person synthesis meetings at the NCEMS facility. These face-to-face convenings are critical for fostering cross-disciplinary communication, brainstorming, and cohesive team science. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to training the next-generation, data-savvy workforce. We request stipend and tuition support for graduate students and postdoctoral fellows who will lead the day-to-day data synthesis and AI modeling. Additionally, funds are allocated for hosting open cross-disciplinary data synthesis workshops and specialized mentorship programs, ensuring trainees acquire vital skills spanning biological theory and advanced data science. The synthesis of massive global datasets (PDB, BioGRID, PRIDE) and the training of complex Graph Neural Networks demand high-performance computing (HPC) clusters, extensive cloud storage, and GPU acceleration that individual labs lack. NCEMS’s dedicated data management support and collaboration-enhancing software tools will provide the essential backbone for our Open Science web portal and rigorous version-controlled workflows. Through this tailored allocation of budget and computational resources, NCEMS will catalyze a transformative synthesis effort that could not otherwise be realized.

[
  "In molecular and cellular biology, biomolecular condensates emerge through the process of liquid-liquid phase separation. Despite abundant experimental multi-omic, structural, and interactome data, a critical gap remains in understanding the fundamental, generalizable rules governing the emergence, dissolution, and physical properties of these condensates from microscale interactions across dynamic cellular environments. The primary objective is to employ artificial intelligence in a purely computational data synthesis, utilizing graph neural networks, deep representation learning, protein language models, and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to uncover the multi-scale rules and sequence grammar dictating condensate behavior. To address limitations of heterogeneous and isolated datasets, public data from repositories such as PDB, DisProt, LLPSDB, BioGRID, and PRIDE will be harmonized using a standardized ontological framework into a multi-dimensional matrix modeled by heterogeneous graph neural networks that represent biomolecules as nodes and interactions as edges. This research significantly advances the field by shifting from descriptive observation to predictive modeling and pioneering an artificial intelligence-driven framework for integrating multi-scale biological data."
abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, dynamic membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergence at the mesoscale. Arising from the multivalent interactions of proteins and nucleic acids, these mesoscale structures bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and complex cellular organelles, orchestrating critical subcellular processes ranging from stress response to gene expression. Despite the recent explosion of experimental data regarding LLPS, a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biology remains: What are the fundamental, generalizable rules that govern the unexpected emergence of biomolecular condensates from constituent molecular features across dynamic cellular environments?

To address this gap, we propose the establishment of a transdisciplinary Working Group to synthesize massive, heterogeneous, publicly available datasets to uncover the multi-scale rules of mesoscale emergence. Our project strictly utilizes existing public data, bypassing new experimental data generation, to conduct a community-scale synthesis that integrates structural databases (PDB), intrinsically disordered protein repositories (DisProt, IDEAL), specialized LLPS databases (PhaSePro, LLPSDB), global protein-protein interactomes (BioGRID), and condition-specific spatial multi-omics (PRIDE, GEO).

Through the application of advanced artificial intelligence and data science techniques, specifically Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, our Working Group will construct a unified theoretical and computational framework. This framework will map the thermodynamic and kinetic emergence of condensates from microscale molecular properties—such as sequence grammar, post-translational modifications, and RNA-binding capacity—up to mesoscale structural properties and eventual cellular phenotypic outcomes. By integrating data across spatial, temporal, and energy scales (e.g., cellular homeostasis versus acute stress states), we aim to predict emergent mesoscale behaviors under diverse physiological contexts.

This synthesis initiative fundamentally requires the collaborative ecosystem and cyberinfrastructure of NCEMS. The sheer volume and dimensionality of the data, combined with the required integration of polymer physics, computational structural biology, multi-omics, and AI, place this effort far beyond the capabilities of any single research laboratory or traditional collaboration. Our team brings together a diverse assembly of molecular biologists, biophysicists, and data scientists from across geographic locations and career stages, encompassing both R1 universities and Minority Serving Institutions (MSIs) to ensure varied scientific perspectives and tap diverse new talent.

In strict adherence to Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, and analytical workflows will be made openly accessible via an interactive, open-source platform. Furthermore, this Working Group is deeply committed to training the future data-savvy workforce. We will host cross-disciplinary data synthesis workshops and provide dedicated mentorship programs for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, equipping them with the unique skills needed to navigate both molecular biology and advanced computational AI. Ultimately, this project will decode the principles of mesoscale emergence, providing a transformative, open-access resource that accelerates discovery across the molecular and cellular biosciences.
