full_text:
[Abstract]
The transition of individual biomolecules into mesoscale assemblies—particularly membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—represents a quintessential example of emergence in cellular biology. These biomolecular condensates exhibit unique material properties that govern critical cellular functions, from gene regulation to stress adaptation. Despite an explosion of single-discipline studies, predicting how mesoscale material properties (e.g., viscoelasticity, fluid-to-solid transitions) and subsequent cellular phenotypes emerge from localized molecular interactions remains a persistent enigma. Unlocking this puzzle requires transcending the capabilities of any single research laboratory through the large-scale integration of existing but highly siloed data. This Working Group proposes a transdisciplinary synthesis project to decode the emergence of biomolecular condensates at the mesoscale by integrating publicly available molecular, structural, and cellular imaging data. We will systematically synthesize intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequence data (DisProt), atomistic structural ensembles (AlphaFold DB, PDB), proteomics and protein-protein interaction networks (BioGRID, PRIDE), and high-resolution spatial imaging data (EMPIAR, Allen Cell Explorer, PhaSePro). By exclusively leveraging these vast open-access repositories with zero de novo experimental data generation, we will employ advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and multimodal data science to construct the first comprehensive 'Mesoscale Condensate Knowledge Graph.' Our project addresses three compelling scientific objectives: (1) Answer the long-standing puzzle of how the interplay between molecular grammar (sequence/structure) and cellular stoichiometry dictates the emergent mesoscale architecture of condensates; (2) Develop innovative, physics-informed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to predict condensate material states and aberrant transitions (which are frequently linked to neurodegeneration and cancer) under varying environmental cellular stresses; and (3) Map these mesoscale properties to their higher-order phenotypic outcomes. Because this effort requires bridging Angstrom-level biophysics with micron-level cell biology via sophisticated AI, it necessitates the transdisciplinary environment, collaboration, and infrastructural support unique to NCEMS. Our Working Group deliberately spans a diverse spectrum of expertise—incorporating computational biophysicists, molecular biologists, structural database engineers, and AI/machine learning scientists—across varied geographic locations, institution types, and career stages. Crucially, this project will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will be co-mentored by cross-disciplinary experts, gaining hands-on experience in multimodal AI, biological data harmonization, and cloud computing. Committed to gold-standard Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, and reproducible analytical workflows will be distributed under permissive licenses through GitHub and a dedicated, community-accessible web portal. By synthesizing existing data to reveal the hidden rules of mesoscale emergence, this project will not only answer fundamental biological questions but also establish a transformative methodological blueprint for community-scale synthesis in the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Background and Significance]
The spatial and temporal organization of the cellular environment relies fundamentally on the emergence of mesoscale structures from nanoscale molecular interactions. A quintessential example of this phenomenon is the formation of membraneless organelles, or biomolecular condensates, driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic assemblies partition specific proteins and nucleic acids, creating distinct biochemical microenvironments that orchestrate critical cellular processes, including gene regulation, signal transduction, and stress response. Condensates represent a fascinating manifestation of biological emergence: their macroscopic material properties, such as viscoelasticity, fluidity, and solid-like states, are not explicitly encoded in single molecules but arise collectively from multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and ordered domains.

Despite the explosion of research in this field over the past decade, a profound knowledge gap persists regarding how specific molecular grammars—the sequence features and structural ensembles of individual proteins—scale up to dictate the physical properties and functional outcomes of mesoscale condensates. Aberrant phase transitions, where fluid condensates mature into solid, amyloid-like aggregates, are central to the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases such as ALS and Alzheimer’s, as well as various cancers. Yet, our predictive understanding of these pathogenic transitions remains severely limited. This limitation stems largely from the highly siloed nature of modern biological research. Biophysicists characterize Angstrom-level interactions; structural biologists solve static nanoscale conformations; and cell biologists observe micron-scale phenotypic behaviors. The data generated across these scales is vast and publicly available, but it has never been comprehensively synthesized.

This fragmented landscape presents an unprecedented opportunity for community-scale synthesis, perfectly aligning with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). Unraveling the complex rules of condensate emergence is a challenge beyond the analytical and computational capabilities of any individual research laboratory. It necessitates a paradigm shift from reductionist experimentation to holistic, data-driven synthesis. By leveraging immense, publicly accessible repositories of molecular sequences, structural ensembles, protein-protein interaction networks, and spatial imaging data, we can transcend disciplinary boundaries.

Our proposed working group will execute a massive integration of these disparate datasets using cutting-edge artificial intelligence and multimodal data science. This approach embodies the NCEMS vision by interrogating the mesoscale—the critical bridge between biomolecules and organelles—without generating a single piece of de novo experimental data. The significance of this synthesis project lies in its potential to solve long-standing puzzles regarding the molecular grammar of LLPS and the stoichiometric drivers of phase transitions. By constructing a unified framework mapping molecular properties to emergent mesoscale behaviors and higher-order cellular phenotypes, this research will not only decode the fundamental rules of membraneless organelle formation but also provide a transformative methodological blueprint for future transdisciplinary investigations. Furthermore, understanding these mesoscale emergence phenomena is crucial for the rational design of synthetic condensates and targeted therapeutics. Harnessing this data through a collaborative, transdisciplinary team ensures diverse scientific perspectives are brought to bear on one of biology's most compelling mysteries, catalyzing a new era of predictive cellular biophysics.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
To decode the rules governing the emergence of biomolecular condensates, our working group will address three compelling, interconnected scientific questions that capitalize on the synthesis of disparate public datasets. These questions are designed to bridge the gap between nanoscale molecular grammar and mesoscale cellular phenotypes, testing overarching hypotheses regarding the predictive power of multi-omic data integration.

Question 1: How does the interplay between intrinsic molecular grammar (sequence and structural ensembles) and dynamic cellular stoichiometry dictate the emergent mesoscale architecture and baseline material state of biomolecular condensates?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the propensity for liquid-liquid phase separation and the resulting condensate viscoelasticity can be mathematically predicted by integrating intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequence features (charge distribution, pi-pi interactions) with spatial interaction network topologies. Specifically, we posit that specific combinations of highly connected scaffold proteins and variable client proteins within the interaction network act as stoichiometric tipping points, shifting the mesoscale state from fluid to gel-like.

Question 2: What are the mechanistic, data-driven rules governing aberrant phase transitions from functional fluid condensates to pathological solid-like aggregates under environmental cellular stress?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that aberrant phase transitions, frequently implicated in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer, are not random events but are deterministic outcomes of specific multi-omic signatures. By synthesizing proteomics data under stress conditions with atomistic structural predictions from AlphaFold DB, we expect to identify hidden 'transition motifs.' We propose that environmental stresses alter the localized cellular stoichiometry and post-translational modification landscapes, exposing these transition motifs and thermodynamically favoring solid-state aggregation. We will test this by deploying physics-informed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on integrated structural and interaction data.

Question 3: How can we map diverse mesoscale material properties of condensates to their higher-order phenotypic outcomes and cellular functions across diverse biological contexts?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that there is a conserved mapping function between the physical state of a condensate and its biological utility (e.g., rapid stress response vs. stable structural support) that transcends individual species and cell types. By synthesizing high-resolution spatial imaging data (e.g., from the Allen Cell Explorer and EMPIAR) with established protein networks, we predict that distinct mesoscale architectures correlate with specific transcriptomic or phenotypic states.

Addressing these questions requires the community-scale data synthesis championed by NCEMS. No single lab has the combined expertise in biophysics, structural biology, multi-omic analysis, and artificial intelligence needed to simultaneously interrogate these scales. Furthermore, the answers to these questions are embedded in existing datasets (DisProt, BioGRID, PRIDE, PhaSePro) but remain undiscovered due to the lack of cross-disciplinary integration. By computationally testing these hypotheses, our working group will solve the long-standing puzzle of mesoscale phase transition predictability, yielding a robust framework that explains how local molecular rules scale up to produce dynamic, emergent cellular phenomena. This hypothesis-driven synthesis will provide critical insights into the thermodynamic limits and evolutionary constraints of biomolecular condensates, identifying whether the rules of LLPS are universally conserved across domains of life or highly specialized, thereby transforming our conceptual understanding of cellular organization.

[Methods and Approach]
Our methodological approach strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate of community-scale synthesis, utilizing entirely pre-existing, publicly available data with zero de novo experimental data generation. Our transdisciplinary working group will synthesize molecular, structural, interactomic, and spatial imaging data to construct a 'Mesoscale Condensate Knowledge Graph' (MCKG) and deploy advanced artificial intelligence to decode emergent properties.

Phase 1: Data Identification, Harmonization, and Integration.
We will systematically harvest disparate datasets spanning multiple biological scales. Molecular grammar and sequence data for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) will be extracted from DisProt and MobiDB. Atomistic structural ensembles and multimeric predictions will be sourced from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold DB. To capture cellular stoichiometry and interactomics, we will parse extensive mass spectrometry and proteomics datasets from PRIDE, alongside validated protein-protein interaction networks from BioGRID and STRING. Finally, spatial and phenotypic imaging data will be integrated from EMPIAR, the Allen Cell Explorer, and PhaSePro. The most significant challenge in this phase is data harmonization—normalizing diverse formats, resolutions, and metadata standards. Our database engineers and computational biologists will develop automated, open-source pipelines to map these diverse data types onto a unified multi-relational framework, constructing the MCKG. In this graph, nodes will represent biomolecules, structural domains, and phenotypic states, while edges will encode physical interactions, stoichiometric ratios, and transitional probabilities.

Phase 2: Artificial Intelligence and Multimodal Data Science.
With the MCKG established, our AI and machine learning experts will develop and deploy physics-informed Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Unlike standard deep learning models, our GNNs will incorporate fundamental biophysical constraints (e.g., thermodynamic energy boundaries, polymer physics models of LLPS) into their loss functions. The GNNs will perform node classification and edge prediction to infer the material states of uncharacterized condensates. We will train these models to recognize the complex, high-dimensional patterns that dictate fluid-to-solid transitions. Through attention mechanisms, the AI will highlight specific molecular grammars (sequence motifs, charge patterning) and stoichiometric tipping points that trigger aberrant aggregation under simulated cellular stress conditions derived from the multi-omic data.

Phase 3: Cross-Disciplinary Synthesis and Validation.
Because we are not generating new experimental data, validation will rely on cross-referencing orthogonal datasets and historical literature held out from the training sets. The diverse expertise of our working group is critical here. Computational biophysicists will validate the thermodynamic plausibility of AI predictions, while molecular biologists will contextualize the findings within known phenotypic outcomes.

This comprehensive approach requires the unique infrastructural and collaborative support provided by NCEMS. It demands a highly coordinated effort among geographically dispersed experts in structural biology, biophysics, AI, and data science. Through iterative sprints and focused working group meetings, our team will synthesize these massive data streams into actionable, predictive models, demonstrating how multi-modal data science can effectively bridge the Angstrom and micron scales to reveal the hidden rules of mesoscale biological emergence.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This community-scale synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly align with the NCEMS mission to decode emergence in the molecular and cellular biosciences. First, the project will result in the creation of the 'Mesoscale Condensate Knowledge Graph' (MCKG), a first-of-its-kind, unified computational resource that links nanoscale molecular sequence and structural data to mesoscale biomolecular condensate material properties and macroscale cellular phenotypes.

Scientifically, the primary outcome will be the elucidation of a predictive molecular grammar governing liquid-liquid phase separation and aberrant phase transitions. By solving this long-standing puzzle, we will gain an unprecedented understanding of how neurodegenerative diseases and cancers exploit or disrupt these mesoscale emergence phenomena. The physics-informed Graph Neural Networks developed during this project will serve as a groundbreaking analytical strategy, allowing researchers worldwide to predict condensate behaviors in diverse biological systems without the need for exhaustive de novo experimentation.

Beyond scientific discovery, the impact on workforce development and community building will be profound. The project brings together a highly transdisciplinary team, tapping into diverse new talent across geographic locations, career stages, and institution types. Crucially, it serves as an elite training ground for the future data-savvy scientific workforce. Postdoctoral fellows and graduate students will be extensively cross-trained by experts in biophysics, multimodal AI, and software engineering. These trainees will emerge as bilingual scientists, fluent in both fundamental cellular biology and advanced data science. By bridging these historically siloed disciplines, this project will establish a new paradigm for synthesis research, demonstrating how AI-driven integration of public data can catalyze our understanding of emergent properties at the mesoscale. Ultimately, the frameworks and insights generated by this NCEMS Working Group will accelerate future discoveries, empowering the broader scientific community to rationally design synthetic condensates and identify novel therapeutic interventions.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the highest standards of Open Science, transparency, and reproducibility, recognizing that the true value of synthesis research lies in its accessibility to the broader scientific community. Following community-created policies on open and team science, every output of this project—including synthesized datasets, harmonized metadata, AI architectures, and analytical workflows—will be made strictly publicly available.

The 'Mesoscale Condensate Knowledge Graph' (MCKG) and all associated integrated datasets will be hosted on a dedicated, cloud-accessible web portal and deposited in recognized public repositories (e.g., Zenodo or Dryad) under a permissive CC-BY 4.0 license. This ensures that the data is FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable). Furthermore, to guarantee absolute reproducibility, all computational pipelines, data-cleaning scripts, and AI/machine learning models (including our physics-informed Graph Neural Networks) will be version-controlled and hosted on a public GitHub organization repository under an MIT open-source license.

We will utilize containerization technologies, such as Docker and Singularity, to package our complete analytical environments. This will allow any researcher to download, execute, and build upon our analytical workflows without facing complex software dependency issues. To support the community and train the next generation of researchers, we will provide detailed documentation, Jupyter Notebook tutorials, and video protocols detailing our data harmonization and AI training processes. Regular virtual workshops will be hosted to instruct external researchers on navigating the MCKG and utilizing our predictive models. All manuscripts resulting from this collaboration will be published in open-access journals and posted on preprint servers such as bioRxiv prior to peer review. Through these rigorous open science practices, we will maximize the reuse value of our work, foster ongoing collaborative inquiry, and ensure that our transdisciplinary synthesis yields an enduring legacy for the molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Budget and Resources]
The successful execution of this transdisciplinary synthesis project requires specific logistical, computational, and collaborative resources that fundamentally depend on NCEMS support. Because this project is beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory, the budget is strategically structured to facilitate cross-disciplinary collaboration, extensive data computation, and robust workforce training, strictly adhering to the guideline of zero de novo experimental data generation.

A primary portion of the budget will be allocated to support Working Group meetings and collaborative infrastructure. We request funding for bi-annual, in-person, intensive synthesis sprints at the NCEMS facility. These convenings are critical for bridging the communication gap between molecular biologists, structural database engineers, and AI scientists, fostering the deep intellectual synthesis required to tackle mesoscale emergence. Funds will cover travel, accommodation, and logistical support for all team members, ensuring equitable participation across geographic locations and career stages.

Secondly, substantial resources are allocated for computational infrastructure. Building and querying the 'Mesoscale Condensate Knowledge Graph,' and training complex physics-informed Graph Neural Networks requires significant high-performance computing (HPC) and cloud storage capabilities. The budget includes provisions for secure cloud computing instances (e.g., AWS or Azure) to manage petabyte-scale multi-omic and structural data harmonization, ensuring seamless, concurrent access for all geographically dispersed working group members.

Finally, a critical component of our budget is dedicated to training the next-generation data-savvy workforce. We request stipend and tuition support for two cross-trained graduate students and one postdoctoral researcher who will serve as the project’s analytical core. These trainees will receive dedicated mentorship from multiple co-investigators, gaining invaluable expertise at the intersection of AI and cellular biology. Additional modest funds are requested for open-access publication fees and open science dissemination efforts, ensuring our synthesized resources remain free and accessible to the global scientific community.

Our team is strategically assembled to reflect a broad spectrum of career stages, geographic locations, and institutional research levels (including primarily undergraduate and minority-serving institutions), ensuring diverse scientific perspectives.

A cornerstone of our proposal is the rigorous training of the next-generation, data-savvy scientific workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees embedded within the Working Group will undergo intensive cross-training at the intersection of molecular cell biology and advanced computational data synthesis, gaining essential, highly translatable skills in AI-driven biology.

Adhering strictly to Open Science principles, all synthesized datasets, AI architectures, analytical workflows, and educational materials will be made publicly accessible via FAIR-compliant repositories (e.g., Zenodo, GitHub) and disseminated through an interactive, community-facing web portal. By synthesizing disparate public data to map the continuous trajectory from molecular biophysics to emergent mesoscale architecture, the CESA Working Group will solve critical mysteries of cellular emergence, provide the community with transformative open-source analytical tools, and establish a new paradigm for transdisciplinary discovery in the biosciences.

[Background and Significance]
The biological mesoscale—the spatial and temporal domain bridging individual macromolecules and fully functional organelles—represents one of the most compelling and elusive frontiers in the molecular and cellular biosciences. Within this realm, biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) serve as the quintessential paradigm of mesoscale emergence. These dynamic, membraneless organelles compartmentalize cellular components, crucially regulating a myriad of biological processes ranging from stress response and chromatin organization to gene expression and signal transduction. Despite their foundational importance, a profound knowledge gap persists: the biophysical and molecular principles dictating how one-dimensional molecular sequence features (such as intrinsically disordered regions and interaction valency) collectively scale to generate complex, three-dimensional, emergent mesoscale behaviors remain poorly understood. While reductionist approaches have mapped individual biomolecular interactions, the unexpected appearance of new system properties at the mesoscale cannot be deciphered by examining components in isolation.

Over the past decade, the global scientific community has generated a massive volume of highly heterogeneous data on phase separation and condensate dynamics. These include extensive sequence and structural databases (e.g., DisProt, AlphaFold DB), specialized biophysical phase separation repositories (e.g., PhaSePro, CD-CODE), massive-scale stress-response proteomics (e.g., PRIDE, BioGRID), and high-resolution subcellular imaging (e.g., Image Data Resource). However, these vast datasets remain deeply siloed within disparate sub-disciplines. The fragmentation of these multimodal datasets impedes our ability to uncover the universal multiscale rules of condensate emergence. Addressing the sheer complexity of mesoscale phase separation far exceeds the capacity of any single research group or traditional collaborative network. It necessitates a paradigm shift toward community-scale, transdisciplinary data synthesis.

This proposal seeks to establish the 'Condensate Emergence Synthesis and Analytics' (CESA) Working Group to address this critical bottleneck. By strictly leveraging existing, publicly available datasets and generating no new experimental data, CESA perfectly aligns with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We will employ advanced artificial intelligence and data science frameworks to bridge the gap between distinct data modalities. Synthesizing these disparate data types will allow us to chart the continuous biological trajectory from fundamental molecular biophysics to emergent mesoscale architecture, and ultimately to cellular phenotypic outcomes like environmental stress resilience.

The significance of this synthesis project lies in its potential to solve long-standing puzzles regarding the deterministic versus stochastic nature of cellular organization at the mesoscale. By translating isolated, multidimensional datasets into a unified, predictive understanding of mesoscale emergence, this work will not only answer novel questions in molecular and cellular biology but also catalyze innovative research strategies. Furthermore, the CESA Working Group will establish a collaborative nexus of molecular biophysicists, cell biologists, and AI engineers, ensuring diverse scientific perspectives while concurrently training the next generation of data-savvy scientists in the rigorous practices of open, reproducible synthesis research.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching objective of the CESA Working Group is to synthesize multimodal, publicly available datasets to uncover the rules governing the emergence of biomolecular condensates and their impact on cellular fitness. To achieve this, our transdisciplinary synthesis research will be guided by three primary research questions (RQs) and corresponding hypotheses, designed to seamlessly span the continuum from molecular sequence to mesoscale emergent properties, and ultimately to cellular physiology.

RQ1: How do 1D sequence features and structural characteristics predictably dictate the emergent 3D biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the integration of intrinsically disordered region (IDR) signatures, sequence valency, and localized structural motifs (derived from DisProt and AlphaFold DB) can robustly predict emergent mesoscale biophysical parameters, such as condensate viscosity, critical concentration thresholds, and liquid-to-solid transition kinetics (curated from PhaSePro and CD-CODE). We anticipate that our synthesis will reveal universally conserved 'molecular grammar' rules across diverse biological domains that are currently obscured by single-modality analyses. By applying AI-driven pattern recognition across these synthesized datasets, we will identify the tipping points at which individual molecular interactions catalyze emergent mesoscale phase separation.

RQ2: What are the dynamic compositional architectures of stress-induced condensates, and how do transient protein-protein interactions drive their assembly and disassembly?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the integration of dynamic interactomics (from BioGRID) with massive-scale stress-response proteomics (from PRIDE) will unveil hidden, transient interaction networks that govern the spatiotemporal lifecycle of stress granules and other condition-specific condensates. We postulate that emergent condensate stability is not merely a function of core scaffold proteins but is heavily modulated by a dynamic periphery of transient 'client' proteins whose recruitment is triggered by specific cellular stress modalities. Synthesizing these datasets will answer the long-standing puzzle of how cells rapidly and reversibly reorganize their internal architecture in response to environmental fluctuations.

RQ3: How do the emergent biophysical and structural properties of mesoscale condensates quantitatively translate to macroscopic cellular fitness and stress resilience?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that spatial and temporal aberrations in condensate dynamics—extracted via advanced image analysis from high-resolution microscopy datasets (Image Data Resource, IDR)—correlate directly with quantitative cellular fitness outcomes. By linking subcellular imaging data with phenotypic datasets, we expect to demonstrate that optimal mesoscale emergence (e.g., maintaining liquid-like condensate states during acute stress) confers distinct survival advantages, whereas deviations (e.g., pathological transition to solid aggregates) compromise cellular resilience.

By addressing these interconnected questions, our synthesis approach directly tackles fundamental phenomena in molecular and cellular biosciences. These inquiries are completely untethered from the generation of novel experimental data; instead, they rely entirely on the systematic, AI-facilitated integration of existing, siloed knowledge. The scale and complexity of correlating molecular sequences with emergent mesoscale biophysics and cellular fitness represent a monumental challenge that can only be resolved through the collaborative synthesis of diverse data types and the combined expertise of our multifaceted Working Group.

[Methods and Approach]
The CESA Working Group will employ a rigorously structured, purely computational synthesis approach, utilizing solely existing, publicly accessible data. Our methodology is divided into three integrated phases: Data Ingestion and Harmonization, Multimodal AI Synthesis, and Collaborative Analytics and Validation.

Phase 1: Data Ingestion, Curation, and Harmonization. 
Our foundational step involves aggregating massive, highly heterogeneous datasets across four biological scales. Sequence and Structural Data will be harvested from DisProt, UniProt, and AlphaFold DB to extract 1D sequence features (e.g., intrinsic disorder, charge distribution) and 3D structural embeddings. Biophysical Phase Separation Data will be compiled from specialized repositories such as PhaSePro and CD-CODE, providing ground-truth measurements of condensate behavior (e.g., critical concentrations, material properties). Interactomic and Proteomic Data will be sourced from BioGRID and PRIDE, focusing on protein-protein interaction networks and expression profiles under varied physiological stresses. Finally, Subcellular Imaging Data will be retrieved from the Image Data Resource (IDR), providing high-resolution spatiotemporal visual evidence of condensate formation. To reconcile these siloed modalities, we will develop a unified graph-based ontology, transforming disparate biological formats into standardized, machine-readable matrices aligned by unique protein identifiers and cellular conditions.

Phase 2: Multimodal AI Synthesis and Predictive Modeling. 
To synthesize these interconnected data layers, we will engineer sophisticated artificial intelligence and data science architectures. First, we will develop Multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In this framework, nodes will represent individual proteins (embedded with sequence and structural attributes from Phase 1), and edges will represent physical interactions and co-localization propensities. The GNNs will learn to predict the collective, emergent phase-separation behaviors of entire protein ensembles, mapping the non-linear scaling from 1D molecular grammar to 3D mesoscale properties. Second, we will utilize Spatio-Temporal Deep Learning (e.g., 3D Convolutional LSTMs) to process the high-resolution imaging data from IDR. This pipeline will extract dynamic visual features of condensate assembly, fusion, and disassembly over time. We will utilize latent space alignment techniques to fuse the outputs of the GNNs with the imaging-derived features, enabling a continuous predictive mapping from molecular properties directly to emergent visual phenotypes and cellular fitness.

Phase 3: Collaborative Analytics and Transdisciplinary Validation. 
The implementation of these advanced methodologies is beyond the scope of a single laboratory. The CESA Working Group will utilize NCEMS support to host recurring hackathons, analytical workshops, and synthesis sprints. Our team—comprising molecular biophysicists, cellular biologists, computational scientists, and AI/ML engineers—will collaboratively guide the AI models, ensuring that the machine learning architectures remain biologically grounded. Domain experts will iteratively validate the AI-generated hypotheses against known biological phenomena, preventing algorithmic artifacts. Furthermore, graduate students and postdocs will be heavily involved in the data harmonization and modeling pipelines, receiving unprecedented cross-disciplinary training. They will learn to bridge the gap between abstract AI architectures and tangible molecular biology, fulfilling our core objective to cultivate a highly skilled, data-savvy scientific workforce equipped to pioneer the future of transdisciplinary synthesis research.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The CESA Working Group is uniquely positioned to deliver transformative outcomes that will fundamentally advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. First and foremost, we will generate a comprehensive, synthesized multimodal dataset mapping the continuum from protein sequence to emergent mesoscale condensate properties and cellular fitness. This unified compendium will resolve the profound fragmentation of current biological databases, providing the global research community with an unparalleled resource for exploring mesoscale phenomena.

Scientifically, our predictive Multimodal Graph Neural Network and Spatio-Temporal AI architectures will demystify the long-standing puzzle of biological emergence. By explicitly defining the 'molecular grammar' that dictates liquid-liquid phase separation, our models will allow researchers to predict emergent mesoscale behaviors and cellular stress resilience directly from primary sequence data. This deeper insight will catalyze novel questions regarding the evolutionary origins of membraneless organelles and inform innovative research strategies, such as the rational design of synthetic condensates for biotechnology and therapeutics.

Beyond scientific discovery, the impact of the CESA project extends to vital workforce development. Embedded graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will receive unparalleled, hands-on training at the critical intersection of molecular biology, data science, and artificial intelligence. This transdisciplinary immersion will mint a new generation of data-savvy scientists perfectly equipped to lead future community-scale synthesis initiatives.

Finally, by uniting diverse scientific perspectives from an array of institutional contexts—including minority-serving and primarily undergraduate institutions—this project will democratize access to cutting-edge computational biology. Ultimately, the CESA initiative will leverage NCEMS resources to establish a new paradigm for biological discovery, demonstrating that the synthesis of existing, publicly available data via advanced AI can successfully unlock the profound mysteries of mesoscale biological emergence.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
A foundational pillar of the CESA Working Group is our uncompromising commitment to the principles of Open Science, team-based collaboration, and uncompromising reproducibility. Aligning rigorously with NCEMS mandates and community-created policies, every facet of our synthesis project—from raw data ingestion protocols to finalized predictive models—will be transparently shared and extensively documented to ensure broad accessibility and immediate utility for the global scientific community.

All harmonized datasets synthesized during this project will adhere strictly to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. These comprehensive data compendiums will be deposited into established, long-term public repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad, accompanied by rich metadata and clear data dictionaries. 

To guarantee the reproducibility of our computational approaches, all artificial intelligence architectures, Multimodal Graph Neural Networks, data processing scripts, and analytical workflows will be developed using open-source frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, Python). The entire codebase will be maintained in public, version-controlled GitHub repositories. We will provide comprehensive Jupyter Notebooks and interactive Google Colab environments, coupled with detailed README documentation and step-by-step tutorials, allowing independent researchers to seamlessly replicate our findings, validate our models, and adapt our algorithms for their own novel research questions.

Furthermore, we will develop and host the 'Condensate Analytics Portal,' a community-facing, interactive web interface. This portal will allow molecular and cellular biologists lacking advanced programming expertise to effortlessly query our synthesized databases and utilize our AI models to predict mesoscale emergent properties for their proteins of interest. By democratizing access to our synthesized tools and findings, the CESA Working Group ensures that our collaborative efforts provide lasting, transformative value, setting a gold standard for reproducible, data-driven synthesis research in the biosciences.

[Budget and Resources]
The successful execution of the CESA project fundamentally requires the robust collaborative infrastructure, logistical support, and targeted funding provided by NCEMS. Because our proposal strictly utilizes publicly available data and generates absolutely zero new experimental data, our budget is exclusively dedicated to facilitating transdisciplinary synthesis, advanced computation, and comprehensive workforce training.

A primary portion of the budget will support Working Group convenings. We request funds to cover travel, accommodation, and logistical expenses for semi-annual, intensive, in-person synthesis meetings hosted at the NCEMS facility. These multi-day sessions are critical for bridging diverse scientific disciplines, allowing our team of biophysicists, cell biologists, and AI engineers to collaboratively review AI model outputs, debate biological interpretations, and steer the project’s analytical trajectory. Additionally, funds will support monthly virtual collaboration infrastructure to maintain uninterrupted momentum between physical meetings.

A substantial budgetary allocation is dedicated to training and personnel. We request stipend and tuition support for embedded graduate students and postdoctoral trainees. This investment directly addresses the NCEMS mandate to train the next-generation, data-savvy workforce. Trainees will be funded to participate in specialized data science boot camps and cross-disciplinary workshops, ensuring they acquire highly translatable skills in AI-driven biology.

Finally, resources are allocated for specialized computational infrastructure. While we leverage existing data, the multimodal integration and training of complex Graph Neural Networks require substantial computational power. Funds will be directed toward secure cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or similar platforms) capable of processing massive-scale subcellular imaging and proteomic datasets. Additionally, a minor portion of the budget will support the development, hosting, and long-term maintenance of the open-source 'Condensate Analytics Portal.' This strategic allocation of NCEMS resources will ensure the seamless execution of a community-scale synthesis project that is unequivocally beyond the capabilities of any single research laboratory.

[Background and Significance]
Understanding biological emergence—how complex, higher-order system properties arise from the dynamic interactions of simpler components—is one of the most profound challenges in the life sciences. The U.S. National Science Foundation National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) has astutely identified the mesoscale as the critical frontier for this inquiry. Bridging the nanometer scale of individual biomolecules and the micrometer scale of intact organelles, the mesoscale is where molecular potential translates into cellular function. The quintessential manifestation of mesoscale emergence is the formation of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic, non-membrane-bound compartments, such as stress granules and nucleoli, rapidly assemble and disassemble in response to environmental cues, compartmentalizing biochemical reactions and regulating cellular survival. 

Despite intense scientific interest, a long-standing mystery persists: What are the universal, emergent rules that dictate how atomic and molecular perturbations propagate to alter mesoscale condensate properties and ultimately dictate global cellular responses? Historically, investigations into LLPS have been highly localized. Individual laboratories focus on specific proteins, utilizing reductionist experimental approaches that cannot capture the system-wide complexity of emergence. Consequently, the field is awash in vast but fragmented datasets. Massive, publicly available repositories hold an unprecedented wealth of information. Transcriptomic and proteomic databases (e.g., GEO, PRIDE) catalogue global stress responses. High-resolution microscopy repositories (e.g., Image Data Resource) provide spatiotemporal cellular phenotyping. Structural databases (e.g., AlphaFoldDB, DisProt) map the intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) that drive multivalency. 

This landscape presents a paradigm uniquely suited for the NCEMS mission. The raw data required to decipher mesoscale emergence already exists in the public domain, but extracting these insights is beyond the capacity of any single investigator or traditional collaboration. It necessitates a community-scale synthesis utilizing cutting-edge artificial intelligence to harmonize multi-omics, structural, and imaging data. Our proposed transdisciplinary Working Group will address this fundamental question by synthesizing these disparate data streams. We aim to identify the precise biophysical and structural thresholds where molecular interactions collectively trigger mesoscale phase transitions. 

The significance of this proposal is multifold. First, it directly addresses a critical gap in molecular biology, transitioning the study of biomolecular condensates from descriptive observation to predictive, systems-level understanding. Second, it pioneers an innovative analytical strategy, utilizing AI-driven knowledge graphs to unite multi-scale biological data without generating any new experimental data. Third, it exemplifies the power of transdisciplinary synthesis, merging expertise from biophysics, data science, and cell biology. By cracking the code of mesoscale condensate assembly, this synthesis project will not only answer fundamental biological questions but also provide a methodological blueprint for studying other emergent phenomena, fulfilling the core mandate of NCEMS.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our Working Group seeks to unravel the complex mechanisms of mesoscale emergence by synthesizing public data through a transdisciplinary AI lens. We have structured our inquiry around three compelling scientific questions and their associated hypotheses, designed to solve long-standing puzzles regarding biomolecular condensate formation and cellular function.

Question 1: What are the universal biophysical rules linking molecular sequence and structure to emergent mesoscale condensate assembly? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that integrating intrinsic disorder predictions (DisProt, AlphaFoldDB) with interactome data (PRIDE, BioGRID) will reveal deterministic biophysical motifs—specifically quantifiable patterns of valence, charge distribution, and disorder—that act as universal triggers for mesoscale phase transitions. While single-lab studies have identified specific drivers (e.g., G3BP1 in stress granules), our community-scale synthesis will uncover generalizable physicochemical thresholds across the proteome. By synthesizing sequence data with phase separation databases (e.g., PhaSePro), our AI models will identify the hidden, complex network topologies that differentiate functionally diverse condensates, shifting the paradigm from protein-specific mechanisms to universal biophysical rules.

Question 2: How do emergent mesoscale networks dynamically reconfigure in response to distinct environmental stress states? 
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the macromolecular composition and mesoscale physical properties of stress condensates are not monolithic, but scale predictably with the nature, severity, and duration of the stressor. By harmonizing dynamic transcriptomic/proteomic datasets (GEO, PRIDE) corresponding to various stress conditions (e.g., oxidative, thermal, osmotic) with high-content imaging repositories (Image Data Resource), we will map how the mesoscale network dynamically rewires. We expect our data synthesis to reveal that distinct stressors induce specific emergent network typologies, effectively 'tuning' the liquid-to-solid phase transitions of condensates to buffer specific environmental shocks. 

Question 3: To what extent do the emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates predict global, macro-cellular fate? 
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the morphometric and biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates—such as their assembly rate, size distribution, and dissolution kinetics—serve as deterministic predictors of binary cellular outcomes, such as survival versus apoptosis. By leveraging computer vision and multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on public high-content imaging data paired with matched transcriptomic survival profiles, we will demonstrate that mesoscale physical states carry sufficient informational density to predict macroscopic cellular behaviors.

These questions are inherently transdisciplinary and cannot be answered via traditional reductionist biology. They demand the synthesis of structural biology, systems biology, thermodynamics, and computer science. By formulating these specific hypotheses, our Working Group will utilize the unique resources of NCEMS to transition the field from qualitative descriptions of localized LLPS events to a unified, predictive theory of mesoscale biological emergence, fundamentally altering our understanding of subcellular organization.

[Methods and Approach]
Our methodology strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate: it relies entirely on the synthesis of existing, publicly available datasets without generating new experimental data. We will achieve our objectives through a robust, transdisciplinary AI-driven computational framework executed by three highly integrated subgroups.

Phase 1: Data Acquisition, Harmonization, and Knowledge Graph Construction 
Our first objective is to build a Multi-Scale Biological Knowledge Graph (KG) that unifies molecular, mesoscale, and cellular data. We will programmatically ingest sequence and structural data focusing on intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) from AlphaFoldDB, DisProt, and MobiDB. Protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks will be sourced from BioGRID, IntAct, and PRIDE. Dynamic expression profiles under cellular stress will be acquired from GEO and ArrayExpress. Finally, phenotypic spatial data of condensates will be extracted from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Cell Atlas. A critical challenge in synthesis research is data harmonization. Our data science team will implement robust ontology mapping (e.g., Gene Ontology, Cell Ontology) and standardization pipelines to resolve metadata inconsistencies. The resulting KG, built on a Neo4j graph database architecture, will represent molecules as nodes and physical/functional interactions as edges, uniquely layered with metadata regarding spatial localization and temporal stress states.

Phase 2: Extracting Mesoscale Rules via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)
To address our first and second hypotheses, we will develop specialized multimodal GNNs. Traditional analytical methods fail to capture the non-linear, collective interactions driving LLPS. Our GNNs will traverse the KG to identify emergent topological patterns—subgraphs of highly connected, multivalent IDR-containing proteins that cross critical biophysical thresholds under specific stress conditions. By employing contrastive learning techniques, the GNN will distinguish between the interactomes of cells that successfully form protective stress granules versus those that fail. Biophysicists within our team will work iteratively with machine learning experts to interpret the hidden layers of the AI models, ensuring the extracted mathematical rules translate into meaningful physicochemical properties (e.g., critical concentration, percolation thresholds).

Phase 3: Linking Mesoscale Properties to Cellular Fate via Computer Vision
To test our third hypothesis, we will bridge structural interactomics with cellular phenomics. We will utilize advanced computer vision algorithms, including customized convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and segmentation models like Cellpose, to systematically analyze high-throughput microscopy datasets from the Image Data Resource. We will extract quantitative morphological features of stress granules (e.g., area, circularity, number per cell, spatial distribution). Using transformer-based predictive models, we will integrate the GNN-derived molecular embeddings with these computer vision-derived mesoscale features to predict macroscopic cellular outcomes reported in the corresponding phenotypic datasets. 

Throughout the project, we will employ rigorous statistical validation, including cross-study validation sets and hold-out test sets, to ensure our AI models generalize across different experimental lineages. This transdisciplinary approach—merging data engineering, advanced machine learning, and fundamental biophysics—is only possible through the collaborative framework of an NCEMS Working Group.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission of decoding molecular and cellular emergence. Scientifically, our synthesis will resolve the long-standing mystery of how molecular perturbations collectively yield mesoscale biomolecular condensates. By identifying universal biophysical rules governing phase separation across diverse stress states, we will shift the field from a localized, descriptive paradigm to a global, predictive one. This foundational knowledge will have cascading impacts across the biosciences, particularly in understanding stress-related pathologies, such as neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., ALS, Alzheimer’s), which are heavily implicated in aberrant condensate behavior.

Methodologically, we will deliver an innovative, AI-driven computational framework capable of bridging atomic, mesoscale, and macro-cellular data. Our Multi-Scale Knowledge Graph and custom multimodal Graph Neural Networks will represent a major leap in biological data synthesis. These tools will be broadly applicable to other emergence phenomena, providing the broader scientific community with a robust infrastructure to investigate complex systems.

Critically, this project is designed to tap diverse new talent and train the future data-savvy workforce. Our Working Group purposefully unites experts from varying career stages, geographic locations, and institutional levels. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will not be relegated to peripheral roles; they will be integrated into the core leadership of our analytical subgroups. Through hands-on, cross-disciplinary mentorship, trainees will gain unparalleled expertise in big data harmonization, advanced artificial intelligence, fundamental biophysics, and the principles of reproducible team science. By fostering this collaborative environment, NCEMS will catalyze the careers of the next generation of scientists, perfectly equipped to navigate and synthesize the ever-expanding landscape of biological data.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is unequivocally committed to the highest standards of open science and reproducibility, recognizing that community-scale synthesis relies inherently on transparency. We will strictly adhere to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles throughout the project's lifecycle.

All curated datasets, harmonized metadata, and the complete Multi-Scale Knowledge Graph will be made publicly available via a dedicated, user-friendly web portal and programmatic APIs, hosted in perpetuity through established repositories like Zenodo, which will assign permanent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). We will not hoard data or delay release; intermediate datasets and model checkpoints will be shared incrementally with the community.

To ensure complete computational reproducibility, all analytical workflows, data ingestion scripts, and AI model architectures (GNNs, computer vision algorithms) will be developed openly on a public GitHub repository under an MIT open-source license. We will utilize robust containerization technologies, such as Docker and Singularity, combined with workflow managers like Nextflow or Snakemake. This guarantees that any researcher, regardless of their local computational environment, can perfectly replicate our data synthesis pipelines and model training procedures.

Furthermore, we embrace modern team science practices. We have established clear governance and authorship guidelines modeled on the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) to ensure equitable recognition for all team members, particularly early-career researchers and data curators. All scientific findings will be published in open-access peer-reviewed journals, with early dissemination guaranteed through preprint servers such as bioRxiv. Through these rigorous open science practices, our NCEMS Working Group will ensure that our synthesis efforts serve as a transparent, enduring public good for the broader scientific community.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed synthesis project necessitates the specific collaborative infrastructure, computational resources, and administrative support uniquely provided by NCEMS. Our budget is strategically aligned with synthesis research, requesting no funds for experimental data generation or wet-lab supplies. 

The primary allocation of funds will support human capital, specifically dedicated postdoctoral fellows and graduate students. These trainees are the engine of our data synthesis; they will perform the rigorous data harmonization, code the AI models, and drive the cross-disciplinary analysis while receiving invaluable training in data-savvy team science. Support is also requested for a dedicated Data Steward to ensure strict compliance with FAIR principles, manage the open-source repositories, and maintain the Knowledge Graph infrastructure.

A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to computational resources. Community-scale synthesis of multi-omics and high-content imaging data requires substantial processing power. We request funds for cloud computing services (e.g., AWS or GCP) to support the high-memory requirements of our Neo4j graph database, as well as GPU-accelerated instances necessary for training the multimodal Graph Neural Networks and computer vision algorithms.

Finally, the success of this transdisciplinary Working Group depends on overcoming the silos of individual expertise. We request funds to support regular, intensive, in-person meetings at the NCEMS facility. These gatherings are critical for fostering the deep collaborative partnerships required to bridge biophysics, structural biology, machine learning, and cellular phenotyping. Travel and accommodation support will ensure equitable participation from diverse geographic locations and institutional research levels, allowing our team to synergize effectively and answer the fundamental questions of mesoscale biological emergence.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. These dynamic, membrane-less compartments bridge individual molecular interactions—specifically between intrinsically disordered proteins and RNAs—with organelle-level organization and cellular-scale outcomes. During environmental stress, condensates such as stress granules rapidly emerge to protect cellular viability. However, a fundamental long-standing puzzle remains: what are the universal, emergent rules governing how molecular-scale perturbations collectively propagate to alter mesoscale condensate properties and subsequent global cellular responses? Currently, the molecular and cellular sciences are rich with fragmented data concerning condensate formation. Massive, publicly available repositories house transcriptomic and proteomic profiles of stress responses (GEO, PRIDE), high-resolution microscopy of cellular compartments (Image Data Resource), and structural predictions of intrinsically disordered regions (AlphaFoldDB, DisProt). Yet, deciphering the emergent properties of these mesoscale structures is beyond the capability of any single research laboratory. It requires the community-scale synthesis of these disparate datasets using advanced artificial intelligence and transdisciplinary expertise. To address this compelling scientific question, our proposed NCEMS Working Group will synthesize diverse, publicly available multi-omics, structural, and high-content imaging datasets to uncover the rules of mesoscale emergence in stress condensates. We will develop a novel, AI-driven computational framework that integrates molecular sequence and structural disorder data with cellular-level phenotypic imaging. By employing multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and computer vision algorithms, we will map multi-scale relationships, identifying the precise biophysical thresholds where atomic and molecular interactions collectively trigger mesoscale phase transitions. Our project is defined by three primary objectives. First, we will construct a comprehensive, open-access multi-scale knowledge graph unifying public molecular, interaction, and cellular imaging data related to cellular stress states. Second, we will leverage machine learning to extract hidden physicochemical rules governing how emergent mesoscale networks dynamically reconfigure in response to distinct stressors. Third, we will develop predictive models linking mesoscale condensate behavior to macro-cellular fate. This synthesis necessitates the unique collaborative environment and computational resources provided by NCEMS. Our team brings together a diverse array of experts—spanning biophysics, structural biology, machine learning, and cellular imaging—from multiple geographic regions, career stages, and institutional research levels. Crucially, this initiative relies entirely on existing public data, requiring no new experimental generation. In strict adherence to open science principles, all integrated datasets, AI models, and analytical workflows will be publicly distributed following FAIR guidelines, ensuring complete reproducibility. Furthermore, this working group will serve as a premier training ground for the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will be integrated into the core leadership of the analytical subgroups, receiving cross-disciplinary mentorship in AI-driven data synthesis, biophysics, and reproducible team science. Ultimately, this collaborative effort will resolve critical mysteries regarding mesoscale biological emergence, catalyzing a paradigm shift in how we understand subcellular organization through the lens of big data.

[Abstract]
The emergence of biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—represents a profound paradigm shift in our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization. Bridging the critical spatial gap between individual biomolecules and functional membrane-bound organelles, these condensates regulate vital cellular processes, notably stress responses, RNA metabolism, and gene expression. Despite the recent explosion of isolated experimental datasets, a unified understanding of how nanometer-scale interactions of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and nucleic acids collectively drive the emergence of micrometer-scale mesoscopic phenotypes remains a major, unresolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Currently, vast amounts of heterogeneous, publicly available data exist in isolated silos: sequence-level IDP annotations (DisProt), large-scale proteomic profiles of isolated condensates (PRIDE), high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold DB), and mesoscale live-cell imaging datasets mapping spatial dynamics (BioImage Archive). No single research laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, diverse domain knowledge, or cross-disciplinary expertise required to harmonize these multi-modal, multi-scale datasets. Addressing this fundamental gap necessitates a community-scale data synthesis approach, aligning perfectly with the core mission of NCEMS. We propose a transdisciplinary Working Group to integrate disparate multi-omic, structural, biophysical, and spatial imaging datasets to decode the fundamental physicochemical rules governing condensate emergence. By leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and data science methodologies, specifically multi-modal graph neural networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, we will synthesize over 50,000 publicly available records spanning from the molecular to the cellular scale. Our collaborative synthesis project will address three compelling scientific questions: (1) What are the universal sequence and structural grammar rules that dictate multi-component, mesoscale condensate assembly? (2) How do emergent mesoscale biophysical properties, such as viscoelasticity and surface tension, arise predictably from the dynamic interactome of IDPs? and (3) How do these emergent mesoscale network properties dictate global cellular phenotypes, particularly cellular survival and adaptation during environmental stress? Crucially, this project will rely exclusively on the rigorous synthesis of existing public data, generating no new experimental data, but rather pioneering an innovative, AI-driven analytical framework for mesoscale biology. To achieve this, our Working Group convenes a diverse, multi-institutional collaborative team encompassing molecular biophysicists, structural biologists, AI/ML data scientists, and cell physiologists. This team spans early-career and established investigators from R1 institutions, Primarily Undergraduate Institutions (PUIs), and historically underrepresented institutions, ensuring a wide array of scientific perspectives and geographic diversity. Deeply committed to open science principles, our team will ensure all integrated datasets, trained AI models, and analytical workflows are disseminated through public repositories (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo) using reproducible, containerized pipelines. Furthermore, this initiative is highly dedicated to training the future data-savvy workforce. We will actively fund and integrate graduate students and postdoctoral researchers into the collaborative research efforts. Through specialized 'synthesis hackathons,' structured peer-mentorship networks, and intensive cross-training at the intersection of AI and molecular biophysics, we will equip early-career researchers with the transdisciplinary computational skills required to lead the next generation of emergence-focused biological synthesis research.

[Background and Significance]
The discovery of biomolecular condensates has fundamentally transformed our understanding of cellular organization, introducing a powerful new paradigm in which membraneless organelles assemble via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic structures represent a quintessential example of emergence at the mesoscale—bridging the critical spatial and temporal gap between individual nanometer-scale biomolecules and micrometer-scale functional organelles. By locally concentrating specific biomolecules, predominantly intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and nucleic acids, condensates dynamically regulate critical biochemical reactions, including RNA metabolism, gene expression, and cellular stress responses. Despite the profound biological importance of these mesoscale structures, the fundamental physicochemical rules governing their emergent properties remain a critical, unresolved puzzle in the molecular and cellular biosciences.

Over the past decade, there has been an unprecedented explosion of experimental data characterizing various aspects of biomolecular condensates. However, these data are currently trapped in disparate, specialized silos. For instance, sequence-level annotations of IDPs reside in databases like DisProt; large-scale proteomic profiles of isolated condensates are housed in PRIDE; high-resolution, static structural predictions are available via the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database; and mesoscale spatio-temporal dynamics are captured in high-throughput live-cell imaging repositories such as the BioImage Archive. This fragmentation prevents a holistic, systems-level understanding of condensate emergence. No single laboratory possesses the requisite computational infrastructure, comprehensive domain knowledge, or transdisciplinary expertise needed to harmonize these multi-modal, multi-scale datasets.

Addressing this monumental challenge requires a community-scale data synthesis approach, which aligns perfectly with the core mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We propose the formation of a transdisciplinary Working Group to integrate these distinct multi-omic, structural, biophysical, and spatial datasets. By eschewing the generation of new experimental data and strictly leveraging over 50,000 publicly available records, our project will synthesize existing knowledge to decode the rules of mesoscale condensate emergence.

Through the application of advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and data science methodologies, specifically multi-modal graph neural networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, we will bridge the gap between molecular interactions and mesoscopic phenotypes. This synthetic approach will not only catalyze novel scientific discoveries but also pioneer innovative research and analytical strategies for mesoscale biology. By uniting structural biologists, molecular biophysicists, data scientists, and cell physiologists, our working group will embody the collaborative spirit championed by NCEMS. Ultimately, this proposal represents a critical opportunity to transform isolated, fragmented data into a unified, predictive framework, illuminating how unexpected biological system properties spontaneously appear at the mesoscale and dictate higher-order cellular outcomes.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our community-scale synthesis project is driven by the overarching goal of understanding the mesoscale emergence of biomolecular condensates from molecular-level interactions. To achieve this, our transdisciplinary Working Group will address three compelling, well-defined scientific questions that tackle long-standing mysteries in molecular biology.

Question 1: What are the universal sequence and structural grammar rules that dictate multi-component, mesoscale condensate assembly?
Hypothesis: We hypothesize the existence of a universal, predictable 'grammar' within the primary sequences and conformational ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Specifically, we propose that the emergent assembly of multi-component condensates is dictated by mathematically definable patterns of 'sticker' (interactive) and 'spacer' (flexible) regions, which AI models can identify across diverse proteomes.
Rationale: While individual LLPS-driving proteins have been studied, a universal rulebook remains elusive. By synthesizing AlphaFold structural predictions, DisProt IDP annotations, and PRIDE proteomic data, we will use AI-driven deep representation learning to identify hidden combinatorial patterns across thousands of proteins. This will map how specific molecular signatures spontaneously give rise to higher-order mesoscale assemblies, answering a fundamental puzzle of biological emergence.

Question 2: How do emergent mesoscale biophysical properties, such as viscoelasticity and surface tension, arise predictably from the dynamic interactome of IDPs?
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the macroscopic biophysical properties of biomolecular condensates—such as their viscoelasticity, liquid-to-solid material state transitions, and droplet surface tension—are emergent properties that can be accurately modeled as a function of the underlying molecular network topology and transient non-covalent interactions.
Rationale: The material properties of condensates are critical for their cellular function, yet predicting these properties from primary sequence data is currently impossible for most individual research labs. By synthesizing multi-scale data, including biophysical measurements from the literature and spatial dynamics from the BioImage Archive, our multi-modal graph neural networks (GNNs) will construct predictive models. This will reveal how the dynamic interactome of constituent IDPs scales up to produce distinct physical properties at the mesoscale, creating an innovative analytical strategy.

Question 3: How do these emergent mesoscale network properties dictate global cellular phenotypes, particularly cellular survival and adaptation during environmental stress?
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the precise biophysical tuning of stress-induced biomolecular condensates acts as a primary, emergent sensor-effector system. Variations in condensate mesoscale properties directly regulate the kinetics of stress-response pathways, thereby dictating organismal and cellular adaptation and survival outcomes.
Rationale: Condensates like stress granules are known to form during environmental stress, but the systemic link between their biophysical properties and global cellular survival remains poorly integrated. By correlating our integrated molecular-biophysical models with phenotypic public data (e.g., transcriptomics and survival assays during stress conditions), we will elucidate how mesoscale emergence directly influences higher subcellular and cellular outcomes. Addressing this question provides novel insights into resilience mechanisms, fulfilling the NCEMS vision of understanding functional emergence across scales.

[Methods and Approach]
This project relies entirely on the synthesis of existing publicly available data and will generate no new experimental data. To execute this ambitious community-scale synthesis, we have designed a robust, AI-driven methodological framework executed by a diverse, transdisciplinary Working Group.

Working Group Composition and Collaboration:
The project demands expertise far beyond the capacity of a single laboratory. We will convene a transdisciplinary Working Group comprising 15 experts: molecular biophysicists, structural biologists, AI/ML data scientists, and cell physiologists. This team includes early-career and established investigators from R1 institutions, Primarily Undergraduate Institutions (PUIs), and historically underrepresented institutions, ensuring a wide array of scientific perspectives. The Working Group will collaborate through bi-monthly virtual meetings, continuous asynchronous communication, and three intensive, week-long, in-person 'synthesis hackathons' hosted at NCEMS facilities.

Data Acquisition and Harmonization:
The foundation of our approach is the systematic ingestion and harmonization of massive, disparate datasets. We will construct an automated data pipeline to extract over 50,000 records from four primary silos: (1) DisProt for sequence-level intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) annotations; (2) PRIDE for condensate-specific proteomic and interactomic profiles; (3) AlphaFold Protein Structure Database for structural conformations and predicted localized folding; and (4) the BioImage Archive for mesoscale live-cell imaging data capturing spatio-temporal dynamics. We will develop a unified multi-scale Knowledge Graph (KG) that seamlessly maps relationships between primary sequences, 3D structural motifs, physical interaction networks, and mesoscale spatio-temporal phenotypes.

AI and Data Science Methodologies:
To distill emergent rules from this complex KG, we will pioneer the use of multi-modal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning. Traditional analytical tools are insufficient for modeling the transition from molecular to mesoscale phenomena. Our ML architects will train GNNs to represent proteins as nodes and dynamic interactions as edges, enriched with multi-modal embeddings (sequence, structural, and biophysical features). The deep representation learning algorithms will project these high-dimensional data into a latent space to identify universal 'sticker' and 'spacer' grammars. Furthermore, computer vision models (e.g., 3D CNNs) will be applied to the BioImage Archive datasets to extract quantifiable mesoscale biophysical features—such as droplet fusion rates and morphology—which will then be correlated with the molecular KG.

Validation and Synthesis Rigor:
Because we are generating no new experimental data, the rigorous validation of our AI models is paramount. We will employ strict cross-validation techniques, holding out spatially and temporally distinct datasets to test the generalization of our predictive models. Furthermore, our team of domain experts will conduct iterative, biologically grounded reviews of the AI-generated hypotheses, ensuring that the synthesized physicochemical rules governing condensate emergence are physically plausible and biologically relevant. This continuous feedback loop ensures the highest standards of scientific rigor.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative scientific, methodological, and workforce development outcomes, perfectly aligning with the NCEMS mission.

Scientifically, we will solve a major puzzle in molecular biology by identifying the universal sequence and structural grammars that drive mesoscale condensate emergence. The resulting AI-driven predictive models will allow researchers to predict emergent properties—such as viscoelasticity and material state transitions—directly from primary amino acid sequences. This will catalyze a paradigm shift, enabling the rational design of synthetic condensates and providing deeper insights into how emergent mesoscale properties govern cellular stress responses and disease pathogenesis. Methodologically, we will provide the scientific community with an innovative, multi-scale Knowledge Graph and a suite of trained, multi-modal Graph Neural Networks tailored for mesoscale biology. These tools will break down existing data silos, establishing a new analytical strategy for transdisciplinary synthesis research.

Crucially, the impact on workforce development will be profound. By actively integrating graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, this project will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Through our specialized 'synthesis hackathons' and structured peer-mentorship networks, trainees will acquire highly sought-after cross-disciplinary skills at the intersection of AI, data science, and molecular biophysics. By intentionally including researchers from PUIs and historically underrepresented institutions, we will tap into diverse new talent, fostering a more inclusive and comprehensively skilled scientific workforce capable of leading future biological synthesis initiatives.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is uncompromisingly committed to the principles of open, team, and reproducible science. Recognizing that the value of synthesis research is maximized through broad accessibility, we will strictly adhere to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles throughout the entirety of the project lifecycle.

All harmonized datasets, unified Knowledge Graphs, and curated metadata synthesized during this project will be made freely available to the public. We will deposit these resources into recognized, long-term repositories such as Zenodo, ensuring they are assigned persistent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). To guarantee reproducibility and transparency in our analytical workflows, all developed code, AI/ML model architectures, and data processing scripts will be maintained in a public GitHub repository. We will utilize containerization technologies, specifically Docker and Singularity, to package our analytical pipelines. This ensures that any researcher worldwide can download our computing environments and seamlessly reproduce our findings or apply our AI-driven framework to their own synthesis queries, irrespective of their local hardware configurations.

In accordance with community-created policies, our Working Group will prioritize open-access dissemination. All manuscripts generated from this collaborative effort will be submitted as preprints to bioRxiv prior to peer review. [Budget and Resources]
Executing this ambitious, community-scale synthesis project strictly requires the unique support and resources provided by NCEMS, as it significantly exceeds the computational, financial, and logistical capabilities of any single research laboratory or standard collaborative grant.

A significant portion of the budget will be allocated to essential collaborative infrastructure. We request funding to support bi-monthly virtual coordination and to cover travel, lodging, and logistical expenses for three week-long, in-person 'synthesis hackathons' at the NCEMS facilities.
