We request full stipends and tuition support for three Ph.D. students and two postdoctoral researchers. These early-career scientists will serve as the operational engine of the data harmonization and AI modeling efforts, receiving unparalleled transdisciplinary training. Furthermore, we have allocated specific travel grants to ensure the active participation of trainees and faculty from Primarily Undergraduate Institutions (PUIs) and historically underrepresented institutions, fulfilling our commitment to tapping diverse new talent.

Given the massive scale of synthesizing over 50,000 multi-modal records and training complex Graph Neural Networks, robust cloud computing infrastructure and GPU access are required. abstract_original: The emergence of biomolecular condensates—membraneless organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation—represents a profound paradigm shift in our understanding of mesoscale cellular organization. Bridging the critical spatial gap between individual biomolecules and functional membrane-bound organelles, these condensates regulate vital cellular processes, notably stress responses, RNA metabolism, and gene expression. Despite the recent explosion of isolated experimental datasets, a unified understanding of how nanometer-scale interactions of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and nucleic acids collectively drive the emergence of micrometer-scale mesoscopic phenotypes remains a major, unresolved puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Currently, vast amounts of heterogeneous, publicly available data exist in isolated silos: sequence-level IDP annotations (DisProt), large-scale proteomic profiles of isolated condensates (PRIDE), high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold DB), and mesoscale live-cell imaging datasets mapping spatial dynamics (BioImage Archive). No single research laboratory possesses the computational infrastructure, diverse domain knowledge, or cross-disciplinary expertise required to harmonize these multi-modal, multi-scale datasets. Addressing this fundamental gap necessitates a community-scale data synthesis approach, aligning perfectly with the core mission of NCEMS. We propose a transdisciplinary Working Group to integrate disparate multi-omic, structural, biophysical, and spatial imaging datasets to decode the fundamental physicochemical rules governing condensate emergence. By leveraging advanced artificial intelligence and data science methodologies, specifically multi-modal graph neural networks (GNNs) and deep representation learning, we will synthesize over 50,000 publicly available records spanning from the molecular to the cellular scale. Our collaborative synthesis project will address three compelling scientific questions: (1) What are the universal sequence and structural grammar rules that dictate multi-component, mesoscale condensate assembly? (2) How do emergent mesoscale biophysical properties, such as viscoelasticity and surface tension, arise predictably from the dynamic interactome of IDPs? and (3) How do these emergent mesoscale network properties dictate global cellular phenotypes, particularly cellular survival and adaptation during environmental stress? Crucially, this project will rely exclusively on the rigorous synthesis of existing public data, generating no new experimental data, but rather pioneering an innovative, AI-driven analytical framework for mesoscale biology. To achieve this, our Working Group convenes a diverse, multi-institutional collaborative team encompassing molecular biophysicists, structural biologists, AI/ML data scientists, and cell physiologists. This team spans early-career and established investigators from R1 institutions, Primarily Undergraduate Institutions (PUIs), and historically underrepresented institutions, ensuring a wide array of scientific perspectives and geographic diversity. Deeply committed to open science principles, our team will ensure all integrated datasets, trained AI models, and analytical workflows are disseminated through public repositories (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo) using reproducible, containerized pipelines. Furthermore, this initiative is highly dedicated to training the future data-savvy workforce. We will actively fund and integrate graduate students and postdoctoral researchers into the collaborative research efforts. Through specialized 'synthesis hackathons,' structured peer-mentorship networks, and intensive cross-training at the intersection of AI and molecular biophysics, we will equip early-career researchers with the transdisciplinary computational skills required to lead the next generation of emergence-focused biological synthesis research.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. Formed via liquid-liquid phase separation, these membraneless organelles bridge the nanometer scale of individual biomolecules and the micrometer scale of cellular architecture. Despite their critical roles in regulating gene expression, stress responses, and metabolic compartmentalization, a fundamental puzzle remains: how do sequence-level molecular features, such as intrinsically disordered regions and transient post-translational modifications (PTMs), synergistically encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates (e.g., viscosity, multiphase organization, and dissolution dynamics) that ultimately govern cellular phenotypes? Addressing this complex multiscale challenge is beyond the capacity of any single laboratory and requires a community-scale synthesis of siloed, publicly available datasets. This Working Group proposes an ambitious, computationally driven data synthesis project to decode the rules of mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates. By adhering strictly to the use of existing public data, we will not generate new experimental results but will instead perform a massive integration of molecular, biophysical, and cellular databases. We will synthesize structural and sequence data (AlphaFold DB, DisProt), PTM annotations (PhosphoSitePlus), biophysical phase-separation registries (CD-CODE, PhaSePro), and cellular phenotypic and transcriptomic data (DepMap, GEO). To achieve this, our diverse, transdisciplinary team of biophysicists, computational biologists, machine learning experts, and cell biologists will develop an innovative, AI-driven analytical strategy. We will construct a multimodal Graph Neural Network (GNN) and leverage protein large language models (LLMs) to map how energy-dependent PTMs alter molecular motion and information transfer, triggering the spatial emergence of condensates. By modeling these mesoscale properties, our AI framework will predict higher-order subcellular and cellular outcomes across diverse stress conditions. This project perfectly aligns with the NCEMS mission to investigate emergent properties at the mesoscale, linking spatial and temporal dynamics from molecules to organelles. The proposed synthesis fundamentally requires the unique support and collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. The requisite integration of physical chemistry, structural biology, and multi-omic systems biology demands a sustained, cross-disciplinary Working Group environment that bridges geographic locations and institutional tiers. Our team deliberately incorporates researchers from varying career stages, ensuring a diverse array of scientific perspectives and expertise. Furthermore, this Working Group is deeply committed to open science and workforce development. All integrated datasets, AI architectures, and analytical workflows will be rigorously documented, version-controlled, and made freely available to the public following FAIR and open science principles. Crucially, the project will serve as a premier training ground for the next-generation data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees integrated into our team will receive unparalleled, cross-disciplinary mentorship in advanced data science, AI methodologies, and multiscale biological modeling. By illuminating the mesoscale rules of condensate emergence, this synthesis will solve long-standing molecular puzzles, pioneer novel analytical paradigms, and significantly advance our predictive understanding of cellular organization.

[Background and Significance]
Understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at different scales of composition, space, time, energy, information, and motion is the paramount challenge of modern biology. The U.S. National Science Foundation National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) emphasizes the critical nature of the mesoscale—the intermediate domain bridging individual biomolecules and higher-order cellular organelles. Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential, yet poorly understood, phenomenon of mesoscale emergence. These membraneless structures dynamically assemble and dissolve to compartmentalize biochemical reactions, filter cellular information, and mediate stress responses. 

Despite an explosion of research over the last decade, a critical knowledge gap remains: we lack a predictive understanding of how nanometer-scale, energy-dependent events—such as post-translational modifications (PTMs) on intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—catalyze the spatial and temporal emergence of these micrometer-scale condensates. While vast troves of high-throughput experimental data exist, they remain deeply siloed across distinct sub-disciplines. Structural biologists maintain repositories of protein sequences and intrinsic disorder (e.g., AlphaFold DB, DisProt); biochemists catalog PTMs and energetic modifications (PhosphoSitePlus); biophysicists track phase boundaries and material properties (CD-CODE, PhaSePro); and systems biologists map transcriptomic and phenotypic outcomes (GEO, DepMap). 

The complexity of integrating these disparate data sources to track emergent phenomena across scales far exceeds the capabilities of any single research laboratory. It requires the community-scale synthesis and multidisciplinary integration that NCEMS is uniquely designed to support. Current reductionist approaches have failed to yield a unified framework because they cannot encapsulate the highly non-linear, collective interactions that drive LLPS. 

This Working Group proposes an ambitious data synthesis initiative to bridge this gap. By strictly utilizing existing, publicly available datasets, we will investigate how modifications at the molecular scale scale up to dictate the rheological properties (viscosity, multiphase organization, dissolution dynamics) of mesoscale condensates, which in turn dictate overarching cellular phenotypes. This project is profoundly significant for three reasons. First, it directly answers the NCEMS call to address fundamental mysteries of mesoscale emergence by harmonizing multi-omic data. Second, it shifts the paradigm from descriptive molecular biology to predictive biological modeling, unlocking a new understanding of how life harnesses physics and chemistry to create order. Finally, by mapping the complex rules of condensate formation and dissolution, we provide the foundational knowledge necessary to eventually manipulate these structures in disease contexts, such as neurodegeneration and cancer. In sum, this transdisciplinary synthesis will resolve long-standing molecular puzzles and pioneer innovative analytical paradigms at the intersection of biophysics and data science.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This community-scale synthesis project is driven by three primary research questions that bridge the gap between nanometer-scale molecular characteristics and micrometer-scale cellular phenomena. Through the integration of diverse public datasets, our transdisciplinary Working Group will test the following hypotheses to decode the rules of mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates.

Question 1: How do sequence-level features, specifically intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), interact synergistically with transient post-translational modifications (PTMs) to dynamically dictate the phase boundaries and biophysical material properties of mesoscale condensates? 
We hypothesize that PTMs function as distributed, energy-dependent topological switches within IDR networks. Rather than acting in isolation, these modifications cooperatively alter the valency and interaction affinity of the network, thereby shifting the percolation threshold. By synthesizing data from PhosphoSitePlus and DisProt with phase separation registries like PhaSePro, we predict that distinct 'PTM codes' will predictably correlate with specific shifts in emergent material states—transitioning condensates from highly dynamic liquids to viscous gels or solid aggregates across different temporal and energetic scales.

Question 2: How does the multiphase spatial organization of condensates dictate the flow of biological information and enzymatic regulation within the cell during environmental stress? 
We hypothesize that the physical segregation provided by multiphase condensates creates tunable biochemical microenvironments that selectively filter molecular information. Specifically, we postulate that the spatial nesting within these membraneless organelles scales directly to altered transcriptomic outputs and cellular survival strategies. By integrating biophysical organizational data (CD-CODE) with transcriptomic stress response datasets (GEO), we aim to demonstrate that specific mesoscale condensate architectures are required to orchestrate complex, multi-step stress response pathways, acting as vital informational hubs that coordinate subcellular outcomes.

Question 3: Can a purely computational, multi-scale Artificial Intelligence framework predict cellular phenotypic outcomes solely from the primary sequence and transient modification states of condensate-forming proteins? 
We hypothesize that a sophisticated, multimodal Graph Neural Network (GNN), enhanced by state-of-the-art protein Large Language Models (LLMs), can successfully map the complex, non-linear trajectories from molecular composition to cellular phenotype. We anticipate that by training this AI architecture on harmonized, cross-disciplinary public datasets, it will uncover latent representations of mesoscale emergence that traditional statistical methods overlook. This framework will validate the premise that emergent properties are not random but follow decipherable biophysical rules encoded at the molecular level.

These research questions rigorously tackle novel and compelling puzzles in the molecular and cellular biosciences. By focusing on the integration of existing public data to evaluate these hypotheses, our Working Group will bypass the limitations of single-lab experimental designs. Instead, we will generate robust, community-level insights into how motion, energy, and information dynamically interact to generate emergent biological structures.

[Methods and Approach]
Our methodology strictly adheres to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data, focusing exclusively on the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets. To tackle the complex multiscale challenge of biomolecular condensates, our multidisciplinary team—comprising biophysicists, machine learning experts, cell biologists, and data scientists—will execute an innovative, AI-driven analytical strategy organized into three synergistic phases.

Phase 1: Community-Scale Data Harmonization and Curation
The foundation of our approach is the massive integration of highly heterogeneous, siloed databases. We will develop automated, open-source pipelines to ingest and harmonize multiscale data. Molecular and structural data will be sourced from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and DisProt to map intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Energetic and temporal modification data will be extracted from PhosphoSitePlus to annotate transient post-translational modifications (PTMs). Mesoscale biophysical characteristics—such as critical concentrations, viscosity, and phase boundary conditions—will be integrated from CD-CODE and PhaSePro. Finally, cellular phenotypic, survival, and transcriptomic data will be pulled from DepMap and GEO. A critical methodological innovation will be the creation of a unified, multi-dimensional relational database that maps each protein node not just by sequence, but by its spatial, temporal, and energetic state across diverse biological conditions.

Phase 2: AI-Driven Modeling of Mesoscale Emergence
To decode the rules of emergence, we will construct a bespoke, multimodal Artificial Intelligence architecture. First, we will leverage pre-trained protein Large Language Models (LLMs), such as ESM-2, to generate high-dimensional embeddings of protein sequences, fine-tuning them to recognize IDR features and PTM patterns. These embeddings will serve as input nodes for a sophisticated Graph Neural Network (GNN). The GNN is ideally suited for this synthesis because it naturally models relationships (edges) between interacting entities (nodes). We will program the GNN to represent biophysical interactions, allowing it to simulate how modifications alter molecular motion and network valency. By training the GNN on our harmonized biophysical datasets, the model will learn the non-linear rules that predict the emergent mesoscale properties of condensates—such as the transition from liquid to gel states—based solely on molecular inputs.

Phase 3: Phenotypic Prediction and Cross-Disciplinary Synthesis
In the final analytical phase, we will link the GNN-derived mesoscale features to higher-order cellular outcomes. We will employ advanced correlative machine learning techniques to map the predicted condensate states against transcriptomic signatures and cellular survival metrics from DepMap and GEO. This will establish a predictive pipeline from primary sequence to cellular phenotype.

The Working Group will convene through bi-weekly virtual sprints and biannual, intensive in-person hackathons hosted at NCEMS. This collaborative structure guarantees that the biophysicists will ground the AI models in thermodynamic reality, while the data scientists ensure mathematical rigor. This synthesis of diverse expertise is essential to transcend standard analytical methods and achieve novel insights into molecular emergence.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This community-scale synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that significantly advance the molecular and cellular biosciences. Scientifically, our primary outcome will be the establishment of a unified, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. By explicitly linking nanometer-scale protein modifications to micrometer-scale condensate behaviors and overarching cellular phenotypes, we will solve a fundamental puzzle regarding how cells dynamically reorganize internal structures in response to energetic and environmental cues. This will result in high-impact publications detailing the newly discovered 'rules' of biomolecular condensation.

Methodologically, we will pioneer a novel analytical strategy by releasing our AI-driven architecture, combining protein Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), specifically tailored for multi-omic spatial data integration. This modular AI framework will be highly adaptable, allowing researchers in other domains to synthesize disparate datasets to investigate different emergent phenomena across biological scales.

The broader impacts of this project are equally substantial, aligning directly with NCEMS's goal to train a data-savvy future workforce. Our Working Group deliberately integrates early-career researchers, including graduate students and postdoctoral scholars, providing them with unparalleled, cross-disciplinary mentorship. Trainees will not be siloed; instead, a biology postdoc will learn advanced graph theory, while a computational graduate student will master the thermodynamic principles of phase separation. 

Furthermore, by drawing together researchers from varying institutional research tiers and geographic locations, we will tap into diverse new talent pools, fostering equitable scientific partnerships. Ultimately, the predictive models and insights generated by this synthesis will offer a foundational resource for the broader scientific community, stimulating novel questions and providing rational design principles for future therapeutic interventions targeting dysregulated condensates in neurodegenerative diseases and cancers.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Adherence to Open Science and FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles is a foundational pillar of this Working Group. We are deeply committed to ensuring that all findings, synthesized datasets, and analysis workflows are transparent, reproducible, and immediately beneficial to the global scientific community. 

All harmonized datasets created during Phase 1 will be heavily annotated with standardized metadata ontologies and deposited into open repositories such as Zenodo under a CC-BY license. To prevent the phenomenon of 'data rot' and ensure interoperability, we will provide exhaustive documentation detailing the provenance, curation decisions, and normalization techniques applied to the original disparate public databases. 

Our computational workflows, including the AI and GNN architectures, will be developed transparently. All code will be written in Python and hosted on a public GitHub repository, utilizing continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines to ensure code reliability. To guarantee true reproducibility across different computational environments, all analytical pipelines will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. We will also provide comprehensive Jupyter Notebooks and Nextflow pipelines, acting as interactive, step-by-step tutorials that allow external researchers to recreate our figures and apply our models to their own datasets.

Furthermore, the Working Group will adopt community-created policies on team science. We will draft and publish a pre-registration of our methodological approaches and primary hypotheses on the Open Science Framework (OSF) prior to executing the final GNN models. By democratizing access to both our synthesized data and our cutting-edge AI methodologies, we will ensure that our project serves as a lasting, accessible resource that accelerates discovery and empowers the next generation of researchers in the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Budget and Resources]
To successfully execute this ambitious data synthesis project, we require the unique support, collaborative infrastructure, and resources provided by NCEMS. The requested budget is meticulously designed to support the collaborative synthesis, computational infrastructure, and extensive trainee development necessary for this transdisciplinary effort.

First and foremost, we request funding to support the core personnel driving the data synthesis, specifically allocating significant resources for the recruitment of two postdoctoral researchers and two graduate students. This aligns directly with the NCEMS mission to train the future data-savvy workforce. These trainees will be co-mentored by Principal Investigators across multiple disciplines (biophysics, machine learning, and cell biology), ensuring they receive comprehensive training at the intersection of AI and biological emergence.

Second, we request support for working group collaboration and travel. The complexity of integrating physical chemistry with multi-omic systems biology demands a sustained, highly interactive environment. We budget for biannual, in-person Working Group meetings hosted at the NCEMS facilities. These intensive 'hackathons' and synthesis sessions are vital for bridging geographic and disciplinary divides, fostering the transdisciplinary synergy required to interpret the GNN outputs correctly. 

Finally, we request computational resources to manage the massive scale of data integration and AI training. While the data is publicly available, the computational power required to harmonize these databases and train multimodal LLMs and GNNs is beyond the standard resources of individual labs. We request access to NCEMS cloud-computing credits and high-performance computing (HPC) clusters to ensure rapid iteration and training of our predictive models. 

This synthesis fundamentally requires the centralized, catalytic support of NCEMS; without the Center’s administrative coordination, physical meeting spaces, and computational backing, the synthesis of these siloed databases into a unified, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence would be impossible.

abstract_text: Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where individual macromolecules collectively phase-separate to form dynamic, functionally distinct membraneless organelles. Despite their critical roles in cellular organization, stress response, and disease—such as neurodegeneration and cancer—the fundamental rules governing how multi-scale biological properties cooperate to drive condensate emergence remain a long-standing puzzle. Specifically, the field lacks a holistic understanding of how changes in atomic-level structure, energetic states, and cellular information flows dictate the spatial and temporal emergence of these mesoscale assemblies. Currently, data capturing molecular properties and condensate behavior are highly fragmented across independent biophysical, structural, interactomic, transcriptomic, and imaging databases. [Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence, where individual macromolecules collectively phase-separate to form dynamic, functionally distinct membraneless organelles. Despite their critical roles in cellular organization, stress response, and disease—such as neurodegeneration and cancer—the fundamental rules governing how multi-scale biological properties cooperate to drive condensate emergence remain a long-standing puzzle. Specifically, the field lacks a holistic understanding of how changes in atomic-level structure, energetic states, and cellular information flows dictate the spatial and temporal emergence of these mesoscale assemblies. Currently, data capturing molecular properties and condensate behavior are highly fragmented across independent biophysical, structural, interactomic, transcriptomic, and imaging databases. This Working Group proposes to synthesize these vast, publicly available datasets to uncover the universal, predictable principles of mesoscale emergence. By integrating structural predictions (AlphaFold DB, PDB), biophysical phase separation databases (PhaSepDB, LLPSDB), interactomes (BioGRID, STRING), expression atlases (GEO, SRA), and high-content cellular imaging (Image Data Resource), we will construct a unified, multi-modal knowledge graph of condensate dynamics. Critically, in strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, this project will generate no new experimental data; rather, it relies entirely on the community-scale synthesis and integration of existing datasets using advanced data science. Our primary objectives are threefold. First, we aim to answer the novel question of how condition-specific cellular profiles (e.g., thermal shock, oxidative stress, or metabolic shifts) predict the emergent mesoscale material properties and compositional dynamics of condensates. Second, we will develop a novel analytical AI framework—an open-source 'Condensate Emergence Predictor' (CEP)—utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) capable of forecasting the spatial and temporal formation of these structures based solely on multi-omic and structural inputs. Third, we will explore how these emergent mesoscale properties are conserved or rewired across evolutionary time in diverse eukaryotic lineages. This massive data synthesis fundamentally requires NCEMS support and resources, as it far exceeds the computational and domain-specific capabilities of any single laboratory. Achieving our goals demands the cross-disciplinary convergence of experts in AI, bioinformatics, structural biophysics, and cell biology. Our Working Group deliberately convenes a geographically and institutionally diverse team—spanning R1 universities and primarily undergraduate institutions—to foster rich, collaborative partnerships. Furthermore, we are deeply committed to training the next-generation, data-savvy workforce. The Working Group will provide rigorous cross-training opportunities for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, who will co-lead the data harmonization and AI development phases under joint multidisciplinary mentorship. Adhering to the highest standards of open, reproducible science, all synthesized datasets, AI models, and analytical pipelines will be publicly disseminated via community repositories and a user-friendly interactive web portal. Ultimately, this synthesis project will illuminate how mesoscale architectural emergence bridges the gap between individual biomolecules and complex cellular outcomes.

[Background and Significance]
The concept of emergence is central to understanding the complexity of biological systems. At the mesoscale—the critical bridge between individual biomolecules and functional cellular organelles—emergent properties dictate how life sustains itself, adapts to stress, and succumbs to disease. One of the most profound manifestations of mesoscale emergence is the formation of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic, membraneless organelles, which include nucleoli, stress granules, and P-bodies, partition specific proteins and nucleic acids to create specialized biochemical environments. Despite intense global research over the past decade, a fundamental mystery remains: how do the multi-scale properties of individual macromolecules cooperate to spontaneously drive the emergence of these complex mesoscale assemblies across varying cellular states?

Currently, our understanding of condensate emergence is hindered by deep disciplinary silos and fragmented data landscapes. Structural biologists have cataloged atomic-level interactions and intrinsically disordered regions using tools like NMR and, increasingly, AlphaFold. Cell biologists have mapped the spatiotemporal dynamics of these condensates under specific stressors, depositing high-content imaging data into repositories like the Image Data Resource (IDR). Simultaneously, systems biologists have amassed vast transcriptomic (GEO, SRA) and interactomic (BioGRID, STRING) datasets capturing the flow of cellular information. However, no single laboratory has the capacity to synthesize these disparate, multi-scale datasets into a cohesive, predictive model of mesoscale emergence. The data are abundant, yet the insights remain elusive.

This gap presents an extraordinary opportunity for community-scale synthesis, perfectly aligned with the vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We propose to integrate these massive, publicly available repositories to uncover the universal biophysical and stoichiometric grammar that governs condensate formation. By leveraging AI and advanced data science, we will translate static, disconnected datasets into a dynamic, interconnected knowledge graph. 

The significance of this work extends well beyond basic cell biology. Dysregulation of mesoscale condensate emergence is increasingly implicated in devastating human pathologies. In neurodegenerative diseases like ALS and Alzheimer's, the aberrant phase transition of liquid-like condensates into solid, amyloid-like aggregates represents a pathological breakdown of mesoscale homeostasis. In oncology, condensates are now known to aberrantly concentrate transcriptional machinery to drive oncogene expression. Therefore, decoding the rules of condensate emergence under distinct cellular states is not merely an academic exercise; it is a critical prerequisite for identifying novel therapeutic vulnerabilities in diseases of mis-assembly. 

Ultimately, this proposal directly addresses the NCEMS mission to synthesize existing data to solve long-standing puzzles. By uniting experts across structural biophysics, bioinformatics, and AI, our Working Group will bypass the need for de novo experimental data generation. Instead, we will harness the untapped potential of existing community resources to achieve a paradigm-shifting synthesis, redefining our predictive understanding of mesoscale emergence and establishing a foundational framework for the next generation of cellular bioscience.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our Working Group seeks to resolve critical gaps in our understanding of mesoscale biological emergence through the synthesis of existing multi-omic and structural data. We have formulated three primary research questions, each paired with testable hypotheses that leverage advanced AI and data science to interrogate biomolecular condensate dynamics.

Research Question 1: How do condition-specific cellular profiles (e.g., thermal shock, oxidative stress, metabolic shifts) predict the emergent mesoscale material properties and compositional dynamics of condensates?
Hypothesis 1: Cellular stressors do not simply alter the concentration of individual proteins; they dynamically rewire the global energetic landscape of protein-protein and protein-RNA interaction networks. We hypothesize that by synthesizing transcriptomic data (GEO) with phase separation databases (PhaSepDB) and interactomes (BioGRID), we can identify conserved 'mesoscale stoichiometric signatures.' These signatures will mathematically predict the shift in condensate material properties—such as the transition from highly dynamic liquid droplets to rigid, gel-like states—demonstrating that condensate emergence is a predictable function of systemic cellular stress profiles rather than isolated biomolecular triggers.

Research Question 2: Can an Artificial Intelligence framework reliably forecast the spatial and temporal formation of membraneless organelles based exclusively on multi-omic, interactomic, and structural inputs?
Hypothesis 2: The complex, non-linear dependencies of mesoscale emergence cannot be captured by traditional statistical models. We hypothesize that Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can successfully model these phenomena. By constructing a multi-modal Knowledge Graph where nodes represent macromolecules (encoded with AlphaFold structural features and valency) and edges represent condition-dependent interactions, a GNN can learn the complex biophysical 'grammar' of phase separation. We posit that this 'Condensate Emergence Predictor' (CEP) will accurately forecast the de novo formation, composition, and dissolution of condensates under unseen cellular conditions, effectively bridging the gap between molecular inputs and emergent mesoscale phenotypes.

Research Question 3: How are the emergent mesoscale properties of biomolecular condensates conserved or rewired across evolutionary time in diverse eukaryotic lineages?
Hypothesis 3: While the primary amino acid sequences of scaffold proteins often diverge rapidly due to the low conservation of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), the topological and biophysical rules driving mesoscale emergence are deeply conserved. By synthesizing structural predictions and genomic data across distinct eukaryotic lineages (from yeast to humans), we hypothesize that evolutionary pressure acts at the mesoscale level rather than the molecular level. We predict our synthesis will reveal a conserved 'structural-valency network topology' that maintains emergent stress-resilience mechanisms across evolution, even as individual molecular components are heavily substituted.

These interconnected questions directly address the NCEMS mandate to tackle fundamental biological mysteries. By moving beyond isolated experimental observations to community-scale data synthesis, we will test these hypotheses using entirely publicly available datasets. The integration of sequence, structure, and cellular state data will yield unprecedented, predictive insights into how molecular parts coalesce to produce novel biological functions at the mesoscale.

[Methods and Approach]
This synthesis project relies exclusively on the integration of existing, publicly available datasets, rigorously adhering to the NCEMS mandate against generating new experimental data. Our approach bridges structural biophysics, systems biology, and artificial intelligence through a highly collaborative, geographically diverse Working Group. Our methodology is structured into three interconnected phases.

Phase 1: Multi-Modal Data Harmonization and Knowledge Graph Construction
The foundation of our project is the construction of a unified, multi-modal Knowledge Graph (KG) capturing condensate dynamics. We will systematically mine and synthesize data from diverse repositories. Structural and biophysical features of macromolecules will be extracted from AlphaFold DB, the Protein Data Bank (PDB), DisProt, and MobiDB. Verified phase-separating proteins and their material properties will be collated from PhaSepDB and LLPSDB. To capture cellular context, condition-specific transcriptomic and proteomic profiles (e.g., heat shock, oxidative stress) will be synthesized from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and PRIDE. Finally, spatial validation data will be sourced from high-content imaging repositories like the Image Data Resource (IDR).

Data harmonization will be executed by our bioinformatics sub-team. Proteins, RNAs, and specific cellular states will form the nodes of the KG. Edges will represent physical interactions (sourced from BioGRID and STRING), co-expression correlations, structural homology, and phase transition propensities. This KG will represent the most comprehensive, synthesized dataset of mesoscale condensate emergence ever created.

Phase 2: Development of the 'Condensate Emergence Predictor' (CEP) via AI
With the KG established, the AI/ML experts in our Working Group will develop the Condensate Emergence Predictor (CEP). We will employ advanced Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), specifically Graph Attention Networks (GATs), which are ideally suited for capturing the emergent properties of complex networks. The model will be trained to learn the non-linear mappings between individual molecular features (e.g., IDR length, charge distribution, structural valency) and their collective mesoscale behavior (e.g., droplet formation, dissolution, or gelation) under specific cellular contexts.

The CEP will be trained using a subset of well-characterized stress granule and nucleolus datasets, cross-validated using hold-out sets from divergent biological conditions. By extracting feature importances and attention weights from the GNN, we will transition AI from a 'black box' to an interpretable model, revealing the exact biophysical and stoichiometric tipping points that drive mesoscale emergence.

Phase 3: Evolutionary Network Analysis
To investigate the evolutionary rewiring of condensates, we will synthesize orthology databases (e.g., OMA, OrthoDB) with our newly developed AI tools. We will map the structural features of human condensate networks to orthologous networks in diverse eukaryotes (e.g., Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Caenorhabditis elegans, Arabidopsis thaliana). By applying network topology algorithms, we will quantify the conservation of emergent biophysical properties—such as node degree distribution and network percolation thresholds—testing our hypothesis that mesoscale architectural properties are conserved despite sequence divergence.

Collaboration Strategy
The project requires profound cross-disciplinary integration. The Working Group will convene for biannual in-person synthesis hackathons hosted at NCEMS, supplemented by bi-weekly virtual sprints. Postdoctoral researchers and graduate students will be assigned dual mentors (e.g., one biophysicist, one data scientist) to ensure rigorous cross-training, cultivating a deeply integrated, data-savvy workforce capable of navigating multiple biological scales.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This Working Group synthesis project will deliver transformative scientific, methodological, and workforce outcomes, fundamentally advancing our understanding of mesoscale biological phenomena. 

Scientifically, we will solve a long-standing puzzle by mapping the precise biophysical and contextual rules that dictate biomolecular condensate emergence. The creation of the multi-modal Knowledge Graph will provide the first unified view of how atomic-level structures and cellular-level information flows interact to produce membraneless organelles. By demonstrating that emergent mesoscale properties are conserved across evolutionary time, we will establish a new paradigm in evolutionary cell biology that prioritizes mesoscale architecture over simple sequence conservation.

Methodologically, the development of the 'Condensate Emergence Predictor' (CEP) will represent a major breakthrough in predictive biology. This innovative AI framework will allow researchers to accurately forecast spatial and temporal phase separations under diverse physiological and pathological conditions without relying on exhaustive de novo experimentation. By bridging the gap between structural prediction (e.g., AlphaFold) and cellular phenotype, the CEP will accelerate discovery in the molecular biosciences. This has profound translational impact; understanding these rules is a vital first step toward rationally designing therapeutics that target aberrant mesoscale emergence in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer.

Broader impacts are deeply integrated into our proposal. By convening a diverse mix of researchers from R1 institutions and Primarily Undergraduate Institutions (PUIs), across multiple geographic regions and career stages, we will foster a vibrant, inclusive research community. Crucially, the project serves as a premier training ground for the next-generation workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral trainees will receive unparalleled cross-disciplinary mentorship in deep learning, structural biophysics, and systems biology, addressing the critical shortage of data-savvy life scientists. Through NCEMS, this synthesis project will not only answer fundamental biological questions but will also equip a diverse scientific community with the tools to explore the next frontiers of cellular emergence.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Adherence to the highest standards of open science and reproducibility is a cornerstone of this Working Group's philosophy. We are fully committed to making all findings, synthesized datasets, and analytical workflows publicly accessible, fully aligning with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles and community-created policies on reproducible team science.

Data and Code Sharing: The complete, harmonized multi-modal Knowledge Graph generated in Phase 1 will be deposited in Zenodo under a Creative Commons (CC BY 4.0) license, ensuring open access to the scientific community. All source code, data parsing scripts, and the Condensate Emergence Predictor (CEP) AI architecture will be developed openly in a version-controlled GitHub repository. Code will be distributed under an open-source MIT license.

Reproducibility: To guarantee reproducibility across diverse computational environments, all data processing pipelines and machine learning training routines will be containerized using Docker and Singularity. We will utilize workflow management systems (e.g., Snakemake or Nextflow) to automate the synthesis of the diverse datasets, ensuring that any researcher can independently replicate our harmonization and AI-training processes from start to finish. Comprehensive documentation and interactive Jupyter/Quarto notebooks will be provided to guide users through the methodology.

Accessibility and Dissemination: To democratize access for biologists without extensive computational expertise, we will deploy a user-friendly, interactive web portal hosted on NCEMS or public cloud infrastructure. This portal will allow users to query the Knowledge Graph and input custom protein sequences and cellular conditions to visualize predicted mesoscale emergence dynamics. 

Publication Strategy: All manuscripts resulting from this working group will be posted as preprints on bioRxiv prior to peer review. Subsequent publications will be targeted to open-access journals to ensure barrier-free dissemination of our insights into mesoscale emergence.

[Budget and Resources]
To successfully execute this community-scale data synthesis, our Working Group requires NCEMS support that significantly exceeds the capabilities of any individual laboratory. In strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, exactly $0 is requested for laboratory supplies, reagents, or experimental data generation. Instead, the requested budget and resources are entirely dedicated to computational synthesis, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and workforce training.

Personnel and Training Support: The majority of the budget will fund the next generation of data-savvy scientists. We request salary and stipend support for two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students. These trainees will be the primary drivers of data harmonization and AI model development, benefiting from joint mentorship across our diverse, multi-institutional team. 

Collaborative Meetings and Travel: A critical component of this synthesis is fostering deep, transdisciplinary integration. We request funding for travel, lodging, and per diem for all Working Group members to attend biannual, week-long synthesis hackathons at the NCEMS headquarters. These intensive, face-to-face working sessions are essential for breaking down disciplinary silos, refining the Knowledge Graph, and troubleshooting the Condensate Emergence Predictor (CEP).

Computational Resources: While utilizing publicly available data, the synthesis of massive interactomic, structural, and transcriptomic databases requires substantial computational power. We require access to NCEMS cloud computing resources (or equivalent AWS/GCP credits) to support large-scale Graph Neural Network (GNN) training using high-performance GPUs. Additionally, we request long-term data storage allocations for the multi-modal Knowledge Graph and cloud-hosting resources to deploy and maintain the interactive CEP web portal for the broader scientific community.

Facilitation and Project Management: We request fractional support for an NCEMS project coordinator to assist with cross-institutional logistics, open science compliance, and meeting facilitation, ensuring the Working Group maintains high productivity and meets all open science dissemination milestones.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergent phenomena at the mesoscale. These membraneless organelles dynamically assemble from interacting networks of proteins and nucleic acids, fundamentally bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and complex subcellular organization. While recent years have seen an explosion of publicly available data on LLPS—ranging from intrinsic disorder profiles and high-throughput proteomics to live-cell imaging and mutational databases—these datasets remain heavily siloed across disparate platforms. Consequently, a long-standing puzzle remains: How do the sequence-level 'grammars' of thousands of distinct molecules interact collectively to drive the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates, and how do perturbations in these systems cascade into cellular dysfunction? 

To address this compelling question, we propose the 'Condensate Emergence Synthesis Network' (CESN), a multidisciplinary Working Group designed to synthesize massive, heterogeneous public datasets using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and data science. Our transdisciplinary team unites experts in computational biophysics, structural biology, multi-omics, machine learning, and cell biology. By integrating protein structure and disorder databases (e.g., AlphaFold DB, DisProt), phase separation repositories (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), large-scale interactomes (BioGRID), and clinical genomic datasets (ClinVar, TCGA), we will develop a unified, open-source computational framework. 

Our project will employ Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and multimodal deep learning to construct a predictive multi-scale model of condensate emergence. We aim to (1) define the molecular and thermodynamic rules governing the co-partitioning of multi-component mesoscale assemblies, (2) predict the emergent biophysical states of these condensates under varying cellular stress conditions, and (3) map how disease-associated mutations disrupt mesoscale homeostasis to drive pathological cellular phenotypes, such as neurodegeneration and oncogenesis. 

This community-scale synthesis project uniquely aligns with the NCEMS mission. It generates no new experimental data but rather extracts unprecedented value from existing repositories, a task computationally and intellectually beyond the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will leverage NCEMS resources to facilitate intensive, cross-disciplinary collaboration among researchers from diverse geographic, career-stage, and institutional backgrounds. 

Furthermore, this initiative places a strong emphasis on workforce development and open science. We will integrate graduate students and postdoctoral researchers as core drivers of the project, providing them with essential cross-training at the critical intersection of AI, big data management, and mesoscale biology. All integrated databases, machine learning pipelines, and analytical workflows will be rigorously documented and released through open-access portals following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will not only solve fundamental mysteries regarding mesoscale biological emergence but also establish innovative analytical strategies and cultivate a data-savvy workforce poised to lead the next generation of molecular and cellular sciences.

Understanding the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties is the central vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). Within this domain, biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represent a quintessential and critically under-mapped paradigm of mesoscale emergence. These dynamic, membraneless organelles—such as nucleoli, stress granules, and transcriptional hubs—dynamically self-assemble from dense networks of interacting multivalent proteins and nucleic acids. They fundamentally bridge the spatial and conceptual gap between the behavior of individual biomolecules and the highly organized complexity of whole cells. Despite the profound biological importance of condensates in regulating cellular homeostasis, gene expression, and stress responses, the universal rules governing their emergent properties remain an enduring mystery in molecular biology.

In recent years, the scientific community has generated an unprecedented volume of data relevant to biomolecular condensates. Advances in high-throughput biophysics, live-cell imaging, multi-omics, and structural prediction have populated numerous public repositories. We now have access to deep profiles of intrinsic disorder (DisProt), proteome-wide structural predictions (AlphaFold DB), compendia of known phase-separating proteins (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, LLPSDB), massive interactome mappings (BioGRID, STRING), and vast clinical databases cataloging human mutations (ClinVar, TCGA). However, this wealth of data remains heavily siloed. Individual laboratories generally lack the computational infrastructure, data-science expertise, and cross-disciplinary breadth required to synthesize these heterogeneous datasets into a cohesive, predictive model of mesoscale biology. Consequently, the field is data-rich but theory-poor, focusing predominantly on the descriptive analysis of single proteins or specific condensates rather than the universal 'grammar' of emergence.

To overcome this critical bottleneck, we propose the Condensate Emergence Synthesis Network (CESN), a community-scale synthesis project strictly utilizing existing, publicly available data. Aligning flawlessly with the NCEMS request for proposals, this Working Group will generate zero new experimental data. Instead, it will leverage advanced artificial intelligence and data science to execute a multi-disciplinary integration of these disparate databases. By breaking down existing silos, we aim to uncover the hidden thermodynamic and molecular principles that dictate how sequence-level features interact collectively to drive multi-component condensate assembly and biophysical behavior.

The significance of this transdisciplinary endeavor extends beyond fundamental discovery. Aberrant phase separation—where fluid condensates mature into solid, pathological aggregates—is now recognized as a core driver of numerous devastating human diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders (e.g., ALS, Alzheimer's) and various oncogenic transformations. By understanding how mesoscale emergence functions under physiological conditions, and how it fails under mutational or cellular stress, our synthesis will open entirely new therapeutic avenues. Furthermore, tackling a problem of this magnitude necessitates the collaboration of experts across computational biophysics, machine learning, clinical genomics, and cell biology, exactly the type of intellectual convergence NCEMS is designed to catalyze. Through this synthesis, we will answer long-standing puzzles, develop innovative analytical strategies, and fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale biological organization.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching objective of the Condensate Emergence Synthesis Network is to decipher the complex mapping between molecular sequence-level 'grammars' and emergent mesoscale biological phenomena. To achieve this, our transdisciplinary Working Group will utilize data synthesis to address three specific, compelling research questions and their corresponding hypotheses, deeply integrating biophysics, genomics, and cellular biology.

Research Question 1: What are the universal molecular and thermodynamic rules governing the co-partitioning and composition of multi-component mesoscale assemblies?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that a decipherable, predictive multi-scale grammar of transient interactions dictates the stoichiometric thresholds required for condensate emergence. We posit that this grammar is encoded primarily in the interplay between intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), structured interaction domains, and RNA-binding motifs. By synthesizing data from AlphaFold DB, DisProt, PhaSepDB, and BioGRID, we predict that advanced AI models can identify hidden topological network rules that dictate not only whether a single protein will phase separate, but the specific hierarchy of 'scaffold' and 'client' proteins necessary for the stable emergence of distinct, multi-component membraneless organelles in vivo.

Research Question 2: How do the emergent biophysical states of these condensates shift dynamically under varying cellular stress conditions and multi-omic perturbations?
Hypothesis 2: Condensates are not static entities; their mesoscale material properties (e.g., viscosity, liquid-to-solid transitions) are highly dynamic. We hypothesize that post-translational modifications (PTMs) and stress-induced transcriptomic shifts act as rapid, non-linear rheostats that alter valency networks and drive mesoscale phase transitions. By integrating heterogeneous datasets from stress-response transcriptomes (GEO), dynamic proteomics, and known biophysical state catalogs, we anticipate identifying the specific multi-omic signatures that govern adaptive (liquid-like) versus maladaptive (solid-like) phase behaviors. We propose that synthesizing these datasets will reveal exactly how changes in cellular environments shift phase boundaries across the entire interactome.

Research Question 3: How do disease-associated mutations disrupt mesoscale homeostasis to drive pathological cellular phenotypes across diverse tissues?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that a significant, yet currently unrecognized, proportion of pathogenic mutations mapped in clinical databases (e.g., ClinVar, TCGA) selectively alter critical nodes within the condensate interaction network, disrupting mesoscale homeostasis. We expect our synthesis to show that these mutations operate by either lowering the critical concentration for aberrant amyloid fibrillation, sterically hindering the recruitment of essential client proteins, or prematurely dissolving critical biomolecular hubs. By computationally superimposing clinical genomic data onto our AI-derived condensate networks, we will test whether mutational clustering in phase-separating domains directly predicts distinct disease etiologies, particularly in neurodegeneration and cancer.

These research questions represent long-standing puzzles in the molecular and cellular sciences. Because empirical validation of every possible multi-component interaction under all stress conditions is experimentally intractable, these mysteries can only be solved through the community-scale data synthesis and AI-driven predictive modeling proposed by this NCEMS Working Group. By addressing these questions, we will illuminate the fundamental principles of biological emergence at the mesoscale.

[Methods and Approach]
The CESN Working Group will rely entirely on the rigorous synthesis, integration, and computational analysis of existing, publicly available data. Our methodology is designed to translate siloed repositories into a unified predictive framework through three integrated phases: Data Harmonization, Artificial Intelligence Modeling, and in silico Synthetic Validation. This approach requires zero de novo experimental data generation, precisely fulfilling the NCEMS mandate for synthesis research.

Phase 1: Multi-Scale Data Harmonization and Integration
The initial phase entails constructing a cloud-based, multi-modal data lake. We will aggregate biophysical and structural molecular data (AlphaFold DB, DisProt, UniProt), phase separation databases (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, LLPSDB), vast interactome networks (BioGRID, STRING), and clinical mutation registries (ClinVar, TCGA). Due to massive data heterogeneity, we will develop a common ontological framework that standardizes nomenclature across these domains. Each biomolecule will be represented as a rich feature vector encompassing its predicted structure, disorder propensity, charge distribution, known post-translational modification sites, and interaction affinities. This harmonization effort alone will represent a monumental advance for the LLPS research community.

Phase 2: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence and Predictive Modeling
To capture the complex, non-linear topologies of multi-component condensate networks, we will employ advanced Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In our graph architecture, proteins and nucleic acids will function as nodes, while empirical interaction affinities and structural complementarities will define the edges. We will train spatial-temporal GNNs using well-characterized condensates (e.g., nucleoli, stress granules) as ground-truth labels. The GNNs will learn to identify the emergent network motifs and valency thresholds that drive phase separation. Furthermore, we will utilize multimodal deep learning (such as attention-based transformer architectures) to integrate these network graphs with dynamic transcriptomic and proteomic data. This will allow the model to predict how condensate composition and biophysical states (e.g., liquid-like vs. gel-like) evolve under different cellular stress paradigms, bridging the gap between molecular interactions and mesoscale emergence.

Phase 3: Synthetic Validation and Perturbation Mapping
Because we will not generate wet-lab data, we must rigorously validate our models computationally. We will achieve this through strict out-of-sample prediction using recently published, independent LLPS datasets and high-throughput screens intentionally withheld from the training phase. Subsequently, we will perform 'in silico perturbation mapping.' By introducing documented disease-associated missense mutations and truncations from ClinVar and TCGA into our modeled networks, we will predict how specific genetic variations shift phase boundaries and disrupt mesoscale homeostasis. We will validate these predictions against known clinical phenotypes and pathological records.

Working Group Execution
This methodology is far beyond the scope of a single laboratory. The project requires the combined expertise of our transdisciplinary team: computational biophysicists, machine learning scientists, and cell biologists. The Working Group will collaborate through bi-annual intensive synthesis meetings hosted by NCEMS, augmented by continuous virtual integration. Graduate students and postdocs will be embedded at every methodological step, driving the ML pipelines and receiving invaluable cross-training in biological data science.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The Condensate Emergence Synthesis Network (CESN) will deliver transformative outcomes that deeply align with the NCEMS mission to advance molecular and cellular biosciences through data synthesis. 

First, we will produce 'Condensate-AI', the first unified, multi-scale predictive model of biomolecular condensate emergence. This powerful computational framework will allow the global scientific community to input protein sequences, specific cellular conditions, or mutational profiles, and accurately predict the propensity for those molecules to partition into specific mesoscale organelles. This directly solves a long-standing puzzle regarding the 'grammar' of liquid-liquid phase separation.

Second, we will release a fully harmonized, open-access database that successfully merges previously siloed structural, biophysical, interactomic, and clinical genomic datasets. This resource will provide researchers with an unprecedented, panoramic view of the molecular drivers of phase separation, establishing an innovative analytical strategy for future investigations of mesoscale biological phenomena.

Third, we will generate a comprehensive landscape map detailing how specific human disease mutations disrupt mesoscale homeostasis. By computationally linking genetic variants to emergent biophysical dysfunction, this project will identify novel, previously obscured therapeutic vulnerabilities for devastating conditions such as ALS, Alzheimer's disease, and various oncogenic transformations, yielding significant clinical impact.

Beyond scientific discovery, this project will profoundly impact workforce development. By deeply integrating trainees into the Working Group, we will cultivate a new generation of data-savvy scientists. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers will gain critical, cross-disciplinary expertise at the nexus of artificial intelligence, big data management, and mesoscale biophysics. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will act as a catalyst for the scientific community, demonstrating the immense, untapped power of applying advanced AI to publicly available biological data, and setting a new gold standard for transdisciplinary collaboration in the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
A rigorous commitment to Open Science and reproducibility is the foundational cornerstone of the CESN Working Group. Our entire synthesis workflow will strictly adhere to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data principles, ensuring our findings benefit the broader scientific community and align with NCEMS community-created policies.

All raw aggregated datasets, intermediate processed files, and the final harmonized multimodal database will be permanently hosted on established public repositories, such as Zenodo and Dryad, accompanied by comprehensive, version-controlled metadata. To ensure absolute transparency and reproducibility, all machine learning architectures, GNN models, data harmonization scripts, and analytical workflows will be developed openly and maintained on GitHub under an open-source MIT license.

We will utilize modern containerization technologies, including Docker and Singularity, alongside reproducible computational environments such as Jupyter Notebooks and Snakemake. This guarantees that every analytical step—from data ingestion and preprocessing to AI model prediction—can be seamlessly downloaded, executed, and validated by external researchers on their own local or cloud infrastructure.

To maximize accessibility for researchers lacking advanced computational expertise, we will deploy Condensate-AI as a user-friendly, web-based open-access portal. This tool will allow experimental cell biologists and clinicians to easily query sequence properties and simulate mutational impacts on mesoscale phase separation through an intuitive graphical interface.

Furthermore, all resulting publications from the Working Group will be published in immediate open-access journals, with comprehensive preprints deposited on bioRxiv prior to formal peer review. We strongly endorse community guidelines on team science, ensuring transparent attribution of contributions and equitable authorship that highlights the critical work of our trainees. By fully embracing these gold-standard practices, we ensure that this NCEMS-supported synthesis becomes a highly accessible, foundational resource that sustainably empowers the global molecular biosciences community.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed budget is meticulously designed to support the collaborative and computational synthesis of existing public data, with absolutely no funds allocated for new experimental data generation or wet-lab equipment. This ensures complete alignment with the core funding requirements of the NCEMS program.

The primary allocation of funds will support the essential personnel required to drive this massive data integration effort. We request funding for two full-time postdoctoral fellows and three graduate students. These trainees will be the engine of the CESN Working Group, responsible for data harmonization, ontological mapping, and the development of the Graph Neural Network pipelines. This investment simultaneously fulfills our critical objective of training the future data-savvy scientific workforce. Additionally, partial summer salary support is requested for the co-Principal Investigators to facilitate their intensive leadership and cross-disciplinary mentorship throughout the synthesis process.

A crucial component of our budget is dedicated to fostering deep, transdisciplinary collaboration. We request travel, accommodation, and hosting funds to support bi-annual, in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facility. These intensive, week-long synthesis hackathons are absolutely vital for bridging the diverse scientific perspectives—spanning computational biophysics, machine learning, and clinical genomics—that cannot be effectively integrated through virtual meetings alone.

Finally, we require substantial support for cloud computing resources. Analyzing massive omics databases, training computationally intensive multimodal deep learning models, and securely hosting the open-access Condensate-AI web portal necessitates robust infrastructure (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud, or dedicated NCEMS-provided computing clusters). 

By leveraging NCEMS support, we establish a collaborative and computational infrastructure that vastly exceeds the capabilities of any single laboratory. This represents an exceptionally high return on investment, transforming previously siloed public data into profound, predictive insights regarding mesoscale biological emergence, while adhering strictly to the financial and scientific guidelines of the funding call.

abstract_original:
Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergent phenomena at the mesoscale. These membraneless organelles dynamically assemble from interacting networks of proteins and nucleic acids, fundamentally bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and complex subcellular organization. While recent years have seen an explosion of publicly available data on LLPS—ranging from intrinsic disorder profiles and high-throughput proteomics to live-cell imaging and mutational databases—these datasets remain heavily siloed across disparate platforms. Consequently, a long-standing puzzle remains: How do the sequence-level 'grammars' of thousands of distinct molecules interact collectively to drive the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates, and how do perturbations in these systems cascade into cellular dysfunction? 

To address this compelling question, we propose the 'Condensate Emergence Synthesis Network' (CESN), a multidisciplinary Working Group designed to synthesize massive, heterogeneous public datasets using advanced artificial intelligence (AI) and data science. Our transdisciplinary team unites experts in computational biophysics, structural biology, multi-omics, machine learning, and cell biology. By integrating protein structure and disorder databases (e.g., AlphaFold DB, DisProt), phase separation repositories (PhaSepDB, CD-CODE), large-scale interactomes (BioGRID), and clinical genomic datasets (ClinVar, TCGA), we will develop a unified, open-source computational framework. 

Our project will employ Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and multimodal deep learning to construct a predictive multi-scale model of condensate emergence. We aim to (1) define the molecular and thermodynamic rules governing the co-partitioning of multi-component mesoscale assemblies, (2) predict the emergent biophysical states of these condensates under varying cellular stress conditions, and (3) map how disease-associated mutations disrupt mesoscale homeostasis to drive pathological cellular phenotypes, such as neurodegeneration and oncogenesis. 

This community-scale synthesis project uniquely aligns with the NCEMS mission. It generates no new experimental data but rather extracts unprecedented value from existing repositories, a task computationally and intellectually beyond the scope of any single laboratory. The working group will leverage NCEMS resources to facilitate intensive, cross-disciplinary collaboration among researchers from diverse geographic, career-stage, and institutional backgrounds. 

Furthermore, this initiative places a strong emphasis on workforce development and open science. We will integrate graduate students and postdoctoral researchers as core drivers of the project, providing them with essential cross-training at the critical intersection of AI, big data management, and mesoscale biology. All integrated databases, machine learning pipelines, and analytical workflows will be rigorously documented and released through open-access portals following FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. Ultimately, this synthesis effort will not only solve fundamental mysteries regarding mesoscale biological emergence but also establish innovative analytical strategies and cultivate a data-savvy workforce poised to lead the next generation of molecular and cellular sciences.
