[Abstract]
The formation of membraneless organelles, such as stress granules and nucleoli, via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represents a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. While massive amounts of experimental data exist detailing the intrinsic disorder of individual proteins, in vitro biophysical properties, and phenomenological cellular imaging, a fundamental gap remains in understanding how molecular sequence grammar and dynamic cellular microenvironments integrate to predictably dictate the emergent material properties of these condensates. A critical, long-standing puzzle in cellular biology is how these finely tuned mesoscale phase transitions occasionally fail, leading to irreversible, aberrant aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Unraveling this multiscale complexity is beyond the computational and domain-specific capabilities of any single research laboratory. It requires synthesizing vast, disparate, and publicly available datasets—spanning transcriptomics, proteomics, structural biophysics (e.g., PDB, DisProt, PRIDE), metabolomics, and high-content cellular imaging (e.g., Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Currently, these multi-omic and multiscale datasets exist in isolated silos, severely limiting our ability to predict how biomolecular condensates assemble, function, and dissolve. To address this, we propose the establishment of the "Condensate Emergence Synthesis Working Group," requiring the unique collaborative infrastructure and support of NCEMS. This transdisciplinary initiative brings together researchers from six geographically diverse academic institutions, deliberately balancing early-career innovators with established pioneers across AI/machine learning, soft matter physics, structural biology, and cellular dynamics. The NCEMS infrastructure is essential not only for the logistical facilitation of intensive, hybrid synthesis meetings critical for cross-pollinating ideas among distinct disciplines, but also for standardizing community-scale data fusion. Using exclusively existing, publicly available data, our team will build an open-source data integration pipeline that harmonizes molecular features (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, valency, post-translational modifications) with spatial proteomics and quantitative live-cell imaging metrics. Building upon this integrated dataset, the Working Group will deploy advanced artificial intelligence methodologies, specifically geometric deep learning and multiscale graph neural networks, to bridge the spatial and temporal gaps between biomolecules and organelles. Our AI-driven models will predict how specific microenvironmental shifts (such as localized pH changes, molecular crowding, and ATP fluctuations) trigger mesoscale phase transitions, mapping the precise trajectory from monomeric proteins to functional mesoscale assemblies, and ultimately to higher-order cellular stress resilience. In strict adherence to community-created open science principles, all harmonized databases, predictive AI architectures, and analytical workflows will be publicly disseminated via open-access repositories (e.g., Zenodo, GitHub) ensuring complete FAIR compliance and reproducibility. Crucially, this working group will serve as an incubator for the future data-savvy scientific workforce. Trainees, including graduate students and postdoctoral fellows, will co-lead analytical sub-groups and participate in specialized cross-disciplinary hackathons focused on machine learning in the biosciences. By synthesizing siloed data to map the emergence of mesoscale properties, this project will answer novel questions about subcellular organization, pioneer innovative computational strategies, and provide an unparalleled collaborative training environment.

[Background and Significance]
Biological emergence at the mesoscale—the critical interface between individual biomolecular interactions and macroscopic cellular behavior—remains one of the most profound frontiers in the life sciences. A quintessential manifestation of this emergence is the formation of membraneless organelles, such as stress granules and nucleoli, driven by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic, mesoscale assemblies compartmentalize cellular matter without lipid bilayers, selectively concentrating specific proteins and nucleic acids to regulate diverse biological processes spanning gene expression to stress resilience. While the molecular drivers of LLPS, such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and multivalent interactions, are well documented, a massive knowledge gap persists in predicting how molecular sequence grammar and fluctuating cellular microenvironments integrate to dictate the emergent material properties of these condensates.

The scientific community has generated unprecedented volumes of multi-omic, structural, and phenomenological data. Databases such as DisProt and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) catalog the structural biophysics and intrinsic disorder of individual proteins, while repositories like PRIDE contain vast proteomics datasets detailing post-translational modifications. Simultaneously, high-content cellular imaging archives, including the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR), capture the spatial and temporal dynamics of these condensates in vivo. Despite this wealth of publicly available information, these datasets exist in isolated, discipline-specific silos. This fragmentation severely limits our capacity to map the multiscale trajectory from monomeric protein sequence to functional mesoscale assembly, and ultimately, to higher-order cellular phenotypic outcomes.

This fragmentation poses a significant barrier to solving a critical, long-standing puzzle in molecular biology: understanding how finely tuned mesoscale phase transitions occasionally fail. In healthy cells, condensates are highly dynamic and reversible; however, under chronic stress or genetic perturbation, they can undergo a deleterious phase transition into irreversible, aberrant solid-like aggregates. This aberrant mesoscale emergence is fundamentally linked to the pathogenesis of devastating neurodegenerative disorders, including Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer's disease. Predicting these pathological transitions requires a holistic, multiscale perspective that transcends the capabilities of any single research laboratory.

Addressing this profound challenge necessitates the unique collaborative infrastructure of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). We propose the establishment of the "Condensate Emergence Synthesis Working Group" to catalyze a community-scale synthesis of these vast, disparate datasets. By leveraging existing data exclusively, our transdisciplinary team of experts in artificial intelligence, soft matter physics, structural biology, and cellular dynamics will fuse isolated silos into a cohesive analytical framework. This project epitomizes the NCEMS mission, aiming to decode the unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale. Through the synthesis of multi-omic and high-content imaging data, we will not only illuminate the fundamental principles governing biomolecular condensate dynamics but also develop a predictive paradigm capable of forecasting their emergent behaviors under physiological and pathological conditions, fundamentally advancing molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching goal of the Condensate Emergence Synthesis Working Group is to decode the fundamental rules governing the mesoscale emergence of biomolecular condensates and their impact on cellular stress resilience. To achieve this, we have formulated three interconnected research questions that address longstanding puzzles in molecular and cellular biology, accompanied by specific, testable hypotheses derived from the proposed synthesis of disparate datasets.

Question 1: How do molecular sequence grammar and cumulative post-translational modifications (PTMs) dynamically integrate to dictate the emergent material properties of membraneless organelles?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that specific combinations of intrinsically disordered region (IDR) motifs and dense PTM clusters act as programmable “molecular rheostats.” By synthesizing structural biophysics data (DisProt, PDB) with global proteomics (PRIDE), we anticipate discovering a predictive combinatorial code where specific sequence features predictably tune the viscosity and liquidity of condensates at the mesoscale, dictating their functional capacity.

Question 2: In what ways do dynamic shifts in the cellular microenvironment—specifically localized pH, molecular crowding, and ATP concentration fluctuations—trigger and modulate mesoscale phase transitions?
Hypothesis 2: We postulate that biomolecular condensates function as highly sensitive microenvironmental biosensors, where multidimensional fluctuations (e.g., a drop in pH coupled with ATP depletion) non-linearly shift phase boundaries. By fusing metabolomic profiles with quantitative live-cell imaging metrics (IDR, EMPIAR), we predict the identification of distinct multivariable thresholds that trigger the sudden emergence or dissolution of stress granules, effectively modeling LLPS as a complex, environment-dependent mathematical topology rather than a simple binary switch.

Question 3: What are the precipitating multiscale events that drive the pathological transition from functional, liquid-like biomolecular condensates to irreversible, solid-like aberrant aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that aberrant aggregation is not solely a product of localized protein mutations, but rather an emergent failure of network-level homeostatic buffers at the mesoscale. We posit that by leveraging artificial intelligence to synthesize spatial transcriptomics, temporal proteomics, and high-resolution imaging, our models will reveal that chronic stress induces sequential failures in cellular chaperone networks and microenvironmental regulation. This systematic breakdown inevitably pushes condensates across a critical “point of no return” in their phase diagram, crystalizing into pathological aggregates.

To answer these novel questions, our working group will utilize exclusively publicly available data, bypassing de novo experimental generation. These questions cannot be addressed through isolated disciplinary lenses. They require the fusion of soft matter physics principles with molecular biology and advanced data science. By mapping the precise trajectory from monomeric proteins to functional mesoscale assemblies, and ultimately to higher-order cellular stress resilience or failure, this research will directly fulfill the NCEMS directive to understand how biological complexity arises. Our hypotheses are designed to move the field from descriptive phenomenology to quantitative prediction, fundamentally transforming our understanding of how molecular components interact to yield emergent structures and behaviors at the subcellular mesoscale.

[Methods and Approach]
To unravel the complexities of mesoscale emergence without generating new experimental data, the Condensate Emergence Synthesis Working Group will deploy a pioneering, highly collaborative data integration and artificial intelligence framework. Our methodology fundamentally relies on the synthesis of publicly available, yet historically siloed, multiscale datasets. The approach is divided into three interconnected phases: Community-Scale Data Harmonization, AI-Driven Multiscale Modeling, and Transdisciplinary Synthesis.

Phase 1: Community-Scale Data Harmonization and Integration. The foundation of our project is an open-source data integration pipeline designed to fuse disparate molecular and cellular databases. We will extract sequence grammar, intrinsic disorder metrics, and biophysical properties from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and DisProt. This will be integrated with comprehensive post-translational modification (PTM) and interaction data from PRIDE and BioGRID. Simultaneously, we will harvest quantitative spatial and temporal data regarding condensate dynamics from the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR). Because these datasets utilize heterogeneous formats, we will develop a standardized ontology for mesoscale condensate features. Using automated metadata extraction and semantic web technologies, we will map molecular features (e.g., valency, IDR charge distribution) directly to phenomenological cellular imaging metrics (e.g., condensate size, number, dissolution rate), creating the first unified, multiscale database of biomolecular condensates.

Phase 2: AI-Driven Multiscale Modeling. Building upon this harmonized dataset, we will implement state-of-the-art machine learning methodologies to bridge the spatial and temporal gaps between biomolecules and organelles. Specifically, we will utilize Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) and Multiscale Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). GNNs are uniquely suited for this task, as they can model proteins as nodes and interactions (both physical and environmental) as edges, allowing us to capture the complex topology of phase-separating networks. The models will be trained to predict emergent mesoscale properties—such as the transition thresholds for liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)—based on varying input parameters representing microenvironmental shifts (e.g., simulated pH changes, molecular crowding, ATP fluctuations extracted from public metabolomics data). Through deep learning, the AI will identify latent, nonlinear relationships across scales, predicting the precise trajectory of a protein from its monomeric state into a functional mesoscale assembly or an aberrant aggregate.

Phase 3: Transdisciplinary Synthesis and Collaboration. The success of this methodological approach hinges on the NCEMS-supported collaborative framework. Our team comprises researchers from six geographically diverse institutions, spanning AI/machine learning, soft matter physics, structural biology, and cellular dynamics. We will conduct intensive, hybrid synthesis meetings quarterly. These sessions are critical for contextualizing the AI outputs; physicists will interpret the thermodynamic feasibility of the model's phase boundary predictions, while cell biologists will validate the biological relevance of the predicted cellular stress responses. Sub-groups, co-led by trainees, will iterate on model architecture and data curation continuously. This continuous feedback loop between diverse scientific disciplines and advanced computational models will ensure the biological accuracy and robustness of our predictive framework, exemplifying the power of synthesis research to drive novel discoveries at the mesoscale.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The Condensate Emergence Synthesis Working Group anticipates delivering transformative outcomes that will fundamentally reshape our understanding of biological emergence at the mesoscale. Scientifically, our primary outcome will be the deployment of the first highly predictive, multiscale AI model capable of forecasting biomolecular condensate dynamics—from assembly and physiological function to pathological aggregation—based purely on molecular sequence grammar and dynamic microenvironmental factors. This will solve a critical, long-standing puzzle in molecular biology by providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how finely tuned phase transitions fail during the onset of neurodegenerative diseases.

In terms of community resources, we will release a fully harmonized, publicly accessible database that links multi-omic molecular profiles directly to high-content cellular imaging phenotypes. This unified dataset will break down existing silos, providing the broader scientific community with an unprecedented resource for exploring mesoscale biology. The innovative computational strategies developed, specifically the application of multiscale Graph Neural Networks to phase separation, will establish a new methodological gold standard for synthesis research in the biosciences.

Beyond scientific discovery, the impact on the future scientific workforce will be profound. By intentionally balancing early-career innovators with established pioneers across six diverse institutions, we will cultivate a vibrant, transdisciplinary ecosystem. Trainees, including graduate students and postdoctoral fellows, will be immersed in the intersection of artificial intelligence and cellular biology. Through their leadership of analytical sub-groups and participation in specialized cross-disciplinary hackathons, these trainees will emerge as the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Ultimately, this project will catalyze a paradigm shift, proving that the integration of diverse perspectives and the intelligent synthesis of existing data can unlock the fundamental rules of biological emergence, directly fulfilling the ambitious mandate of the NCEMS.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is uncompromisingly committed to the principles of open, reproducible, and team-driven science, aligning fully with the gold standard practices championed by NCEMS. We recognize that the true value of synthesis research lies not only in the discoveries generated but in the public accessibility and reusability of the methodologies and integrated data produced.

To ensure complete adherence to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles, all harmonized databases resulting from our multi-omic and imaging integration pipeline will be deposited in recognized open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad. Each dataset will be accompanied by comprehensive, standardized metadata, ensuring interoperability for future researchers seeking to leverage our synthesized resources.

All analytical workflows, data curation scripts, and predictive AI architectures—including the Multiscale Graph Neural Networks—will be developed transparently. The codebase will be hosted on public GitHub repositories under highly permissive open-source licenses (e.g., MIT or Apache 2.0). This includes funding for graduate student and postdoctoral fellow stipends to lead analytical sub-groups, as well as resources to organize and host specialized cross-disciplinary hackathons. These hackathons will serve as intensive, hands-on training environments focusing on the application of machine learning to biological synthesis. abstract_original: The formation of membraneless organelles, such as stress granules and nucleoli, via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represents a quintessential example of biological emergence at the mesoscale. While massive amounts of experimental data exist detailing the intrinsic disorder of individual proteins, in vitro biophysical properties, and phenomenological cellular imaging, a fundamental gap remains in understanding how molecular sequence grammar and dynamic cellular microenvironments integrate to predictably dictate the emergent material properties of these condensates. A critical, long-standing puzzle in cellular biology is how these finely tuned mesoscale phase transitions occasionally fail, leading to irreversible, aberrant aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Unraveling this multiscale complexity is beyond the computational and domain-specific capabilities of any single research laboratory. It requires synthesizing vast, disparate, and publicly available datasets—spanning transcriptomics, proteomics, structural biophysics (e.g., PDB, DisProt, PRIDE), metabolomics, and high-content cellular imaging (e.g., Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Currently, these multi-omic and multiscale datasets exist in isolated silos, severely limiting our ability to predict how biomolecular condensates assemble, function, and dissolve. To address this, we propose the establishment of the "Condensate Emergence Synthesis Working Group," requiring the unique collaborative infrastructure and support of NCEMS. This transdisciplinary initiative brings together researchers from six geographically diverse academic institutions, deliberately balancing early-career innovators with established pioneers across AI/machine learning, soft matter physics, structural biology, and cellular dynamics. The NCEMS infrastructure is essential not only for the logistical facilitation of intensive, hybrid synthesis meetings critical for cross-pollinating ideas among distinct disciplines, but also for standardizing community-scale data fusion. Using exclusively existing, publicly available data, our team will build an open-source data integration pipeline that harmonizes molecular features (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, valency, post-translational modifications) with spatial proteomics and quantitative live-cell imaging metrics. Building upon this integrated dataset, the Working Group will deploy advanced artificial intelligence methodologies, specifically geometric deep learning and multiscale graph neural networks, to bridge the spatial and temporal gaps between biomolecules and organelles. Our AI-driven models will predict how specific microenvironmental shifts (such as localized pH changes, molecular crowding, and ATP fluctuations) trigger mesoscale phase transitions, mapping the precise trajectory from monomeric proteins to functional mesoscale assemblies, and ultimately to higher-order cellular stress resilience. In strict adherence to community-created open science principles, all harmonized databases, predictive AI architectures, and analytical workflows will be publicly disseminated via open-access repositories (e.g., Zenodo, GitHub) ensuring complete FAIR compliance and reproducibility. Crucially, this working group will serve as an incubator for the future data-savvy scientific workforce. Trainees, including graduate students and postdoctoral fellows, will co-lead analytical sub-groups and participate in specialized cross-disciplinary hackathons focused on machine learning in the biosciences. By synthesizing siloed data to map the emergence of mesoscale properties, this project will answer novel questions about subcellular organization, pioneer innovative computational strategies, and provide an unparalleled collaborative training environment.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in cellular biology. Bridging the gap between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles, these dynamic, membraneless compartments orchestrate vital processes ranging from gene regulation to stress response. While individual molecular interactions driving LLPS are increasingly understood, a fundamental, long-standing puzzle remains: how do diverse, dynamic molecular properties collectively give rise to the emergent biophysical characteristics of condensates—such as viscoelasticity, multi-phase architecture, and compositional specificity—at the mesoscale? Despite the explosion of publicly available data encompassing protein sequences, structural ensembles, multi-omic interaction networks, and high-resolution live-cell imaging, these datasets remain largely siloed. To address this, we propose the MesoCondensate Synthesis Working Group to map the principles of mesoscale emergence by integrating massive, publicly available, yet disparate biological datasets. In strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, no new experimental data will be generated. Instead, we will synthesize data from specialized phase separation databases (e.g., LLPSDB, CD-Code), global structural repositories (AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-throughput interactomics (BioGRID, IntAct), transcriptomics, and open-source cellular imaging archives. Our transdisciplinary team—comprising structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, network theorists, and artificial intelligence experts across varied career stages and institutional contexts—will develop a novel analytical framework named MesoPhaser-AI. Using advanced multimodal deep learning, including graph neural networks, we will synthesize these multiscale datasets to decipher the hidden grammar of mesoscale emergence. Specifically, MesoPhaser-AI will predict how fundamental biomolecular features (intrinsically disordered regions, valency, electrostatic networks) integrate under varying thermodynamic and physiological conditions to yield emergent mesoscale properties. This community-scale synthesis requires the unique infrastructure and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS; synthesizing atomistic physics with cellular phenotypes is beyond the computational and intellectual scope of any single laboratory. The Working Group will stimulate cross-disciplinary collaboration by bringing together domain experts who traditionally do not intersect, fostering novel perspectives on mesoscale biophysics. Crucially, this project champions Open Science and workforce development. All synthesized databases, knowledge graphs, and MesoPhaser-AI source code will be released publicly under FAIR and open-source licenses, establishing a gold-standard community resource. Furthermore, the Working Group will host Data-to-Emergence bootcamps and synthesis hackathons tailored for trainees (graduate students and postdoctoral scholars). These initiatives will equip the next generation of scientists with cutting-edge skills in AI, data integration, and reproducible team science. By unifying disjointed molecular data into a cohesive predictive model of mesoscale emergence, this project will transform our understanding of subcellular organization, unlocking new paradigms for how life organizes itself between the scale of molecules and whole cells.

[Background and Significance]
Biomolecular condensates are membraneless organelles that form via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), representing one of the most profound examples of mesoscale emergence in contemporary cellular biology. Bridging the dimensional and functional gap between individual biomolecules and membrane-bound organelles, these dynamic compartments orchestrate critical cellular processes, including gene expression regulation, RNA metabolism, signal transduction, and cellular stress responses. Despite rapid advancements in our understanding of the singular molecular interactions that drive LLPS, a fundamental and long-standing puzzle remains: how do the diverse, dynamic, and transient molecular properties of individual proteins and nucleic acids collectively give rise to the emergent biophysical characteristics of condensates at the mesoscale? These emergent properties, such as viscoelasticity, multi-phase internal architecture, liquid-to-solid phase transitions, and compositional specificity, cannot be deduced simply by examining the isolated molecular components. Currently, the molecular and cellular biosciences are experiencing an unprecedented explosion of publicly available data. We possess vast repositories of protein sequences, structural ensembles (e.g., AlphaFold DB, PDB), high-throughput multi-omic interaction networks (e.g., BioGRID, IntAct), and specialized phase separation databases (e.g., LLPSDB, CD-Code), alongside extensive open-source cellular imaging archives. However, these datasets remain critically siloed by disciplinary boundaries. Structural biophysicists rarely integrate their atomistic models with the transcriptomic or global interactome data used by systems biologists, leaving the emergent mesoscale principles of biomolecular condensates largely obscured. Addressing this gap requires a community-scale synthesis approach, precisely aligning with the core mission of the U.S. National Science Foundation National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). The MesoCondensate Synthesis Working Group proposes to map the fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence by harmonizing and synthesizing these massive, disparate biological datasets. In strict accordance with the NCEMS mandate, our initiative will generate zero new experimental data. Instead, it will leverage existing public resources to uncover the hidden grammar of mesoscale emergence. By uniting structural biophysics, cellular biology, network theory, and artificial intelligence, our transdisciplinary team will overcome the inherent limitations of isolated, single-lab approaches. This synthesis is profoundly significant because understanding the rules of mesoscale emergence in condensates holds the key to deciphering how life organizes itself spatially and temporally. Furthermore, anomalous phase transitions are increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative diseases and cancers. Therefore, building a predictive, synthetic framework will not only answer fundamental biological mysteries regarding mesoscale emergence but also lay the groundwork for novel diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. Ultimately, this proposal champions the NCEMS vision by utilizing advanced data science and artificial intelligence to extract novel, emergent biological insights from the vast ocean of existing public data, moving the field from descriptive observation to predictive understanding of mesoscale biological phenomena.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The overarching objective of the MesoCondensate Synthesis Working Group is to elucidate the design rules that govern mesoscale emergence in biomolecular condensates. By synthesizing atomistic, molecular, and cellular data, we seek to answer long-standing puzzles regarding how microscale inputs dictate mesoscale biophysical properties. Our research framework is guided by three primary research questions and corresponding hypotheses. Question 1: How do specific molecular features, such as intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), multivalent interaction domains, and electrostatic charge distribution, synergistically encode the emergent material properties (e.g., viscoelasticity and surface tension) of biomolecular condensates? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the emergent viscoelastic properties of condensates are not merely additive but represent a non-linear emergent property encoded by a hidden grammar of molecular interaction networks. Specifically, we posit that the density of pi-pi and cation-pi interactions within IDRs, when synthesized with global protein-protein interaction network topologies, will predictably correlate with the liquid-to-solid phase transition thresholds observed in cellular imaging datasets. Question 2: What are the thermodynamic and physiological principles governing the compositional specificity and multi-phase architecture (e.g., core-shell organization) of mesoscale condensates? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that multi-phase compartmentalization arises from competitive and cooperative multivalent networking among scaffold and client proteins. By integrating structural data (AlphaFold DB) with high-throughput interactomics (IntAct, BioGRID) and specialized LLPS databases, we predict that distinct sub-compartments within condensates are driven by hierarchical binding affinities that can be modeled as modular sub-graphs within a broader mesoscale interaction network. MesoPhaser-AI will identify these modular sub-graphs, predicting multi-phase architectures across diverse cellular stress conditions. Question 3: How can artificial intelligence and advanced multimodal deep learning bridge the spatial and computational divide between atomistic physics and observable cellular phenotypes to predict condensate dynamics? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that a multimodal graph neural network (MesoPhaser-AI) capable of simultaneously processing one-dimensional sequence data, three-dimensional structural topologies, and highly dimensional omics data will successfully predict mesoscale emergence where traditional physics-based simulations fail due to computational bottlenecks. By embedding these disparate datasets into a unified latent space, the AI will identify previously unrecognized correlative and causal links between molecular sequence mutations and emergent mesoscale condensate dysregulation. To answer these compelling scientific questions, our transdisciplinary team will engage in rigorous community-scale synthesis. These questions are inherently beyond the scope of any single research laboratory because they require the simultaneous manipulation of structural biology data, global interactome networks, and advanced machine learning algorithms. Addressing these hypotheses requires the collaborative ecosystem provided by NCEMS, bringing together structural biologists who understand molecular valency, network theorists who can model multivalent interactions mathematically, and AI experts capable of building the necessary deep learning architecture. Through this transdisciplinary synthesis, we will solve long-standing puzzles surrounding condensate formation, transitioning the field from phenomenological observations to precise, AI-driven predictions.

[Methods and Approach]
In strict adherence to the NCEMS mandate, this project will generate zero new experimental data. Instead, our methodology centers entirely on the community-scale synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available data through a collaborative, transdisciplinary Working Group. Our approach is divided into three major phases: Data Harmonization, AI Architecture Development, and Emergence Modeling. Phase 1: Community-Scale Data Harmonization and Knowledge Graph Construction. The first challenge in predicting mesoscale emergence is the fractured nature of biological data. We will systematically extract, curate, and integrate data from specialized phase separation databases (LLPSDB, CD-Code), global structural repositories (AlphaFold DB, PDB), and high-throughput multi-omic interactome databases (BioGRID, IntAct, STRING). Additionally, we will mine open-source cellular imaging archives (e.g., Image Data Resource) to extract phenotypic metadata regarding condensate formation and material state under various physiological conditions. Our diverse team of data scientists and cell biologists will synthesize these disparate modalities into a unified, multi-relational Knowledge Graph (KG). In this KG, nodes will represent biomolecules (proteins and RNA), annotated with structural and sequence features, while edges will represent experimentally validated interactions, affinities, and spatial proximities. Phase 2: Development of MesoPhaser-AI. The sheer complexity of mesoscale emergence requires analytical strategies beyond traditional biostatistics. Our AI experts and structural biophysicists will collaboratively develop MesoPhaser-AI, a novel analytical framework leveraging multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). MesoPhaser-AI will process the multi-relational KG to learn the underlying topological and biophysical rules of LLPS. The GNN architecture is uniquely suited for this task, as it can capture the multivalent, non-linear interactions characteristic of mesoscale emergence. We will utilize advanced representation learning to embed 3D structural data (via AlphaFold predictions) and 1D sequence data (highlighting IDRs and electrostatic networks) into a shared latent space. The model will be trained to predict the emergent properties documented in our curated imaging and LLPS databases, such as critical concentration thresholds and viscoelastic states. Phase 3: Working Group Synthesis and Collaborative Validation. To ensure our computational models align with biological reality, the Working Group will hold bi-monthly virtual integration meetings and bi-annual in-person synthesis summits at the NCEMS facility. These gatherings will structurally mandate cross-disciplinary collaboration, forcing structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, network theorists, and AI specialists to interrogate the MesoPhaser-AI outputs collectively. We will use the model to solve the long-standing puzzle of compositional specificity by predicting the phase-separation behavior of novel, untested protein sequences based solely on their synthesized network and structural features. Through this methodology, we will synthesize atomistic physics with cellular phenotypes, a computational and intellectual feat impossible for a single laboratory. By leveraging NCEMS support, we will utilize publicly available data to develop innovative analytical strategies, ultimately deciphering the hidden grammar of mesoscale emergence.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The MesoCondensate Synthesis Working Group will deliver transformative outcomes that directly address the NCEMS mission to decode mesoscale emergence. Scientifically, our primary outcome will be the establishment of a cohesive, predictive model of mesoscale emergence for biomolecular condensates. By successfully linking disparate molecular data across sequence, structure, and interactomics, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how varied molecular inputs dictate the emergent biophysical characteristics of membraneless organelles. This will fundamentally shift the molecular and cellular biosciences from a descriptive paradigm to a predictive one, unlocking new frameworks for understanding subcellular organization. A major tangible deliverable will be the MesoPhaser-AI platform, a highly innovative analytical tool that the broader scientific community can utilize to predict liquid-liquid phase separation dynamics. This will allow researchers across diverse fields, from synthetic biology to neuropharmacology, to input protein sequences and environmental conditions to predict resulting mesoscale properties. Furthermore, the synthesized, multi-relational Knowledge Graph will represent the most comprehensive, integrated repository of phase-separation data in existence. This community-scale synthesis will eliminate existing data silos, providing an invaluable resource for future biological modeling. Beyond research, the project will have a profound impact on workforce development. By bringing together experts who traditionally do not intersect, we will stimulate lasting cross-disciplinary collaborations. Our integrated Data-to-Emergence bootcamps and synthesis hackathons will train the next generation of data-savvy scientists. Graduate students and postdocs will acquire highly sought-after skills in multimodal deep learning, knowledge graph construction, and transdisciplinary team science. Ultimately, this project will catalyze a new era of biological discovery, demonstrating how the synthesis of publicly available data, powered by AI, can reveal the fundamental rules of life organizing itself between the scale of molecules and whole cells.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The MesoCondensate Synthesis Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of Open Science, transparency, and reproducibility, recognizing them as essential pillars of modern team science and the NCEMS mandate. Our initiative is designed from the ground up to establish a gold-standard community resource. All data harmonization protocols, integrated datasets, and the finalized multi-relational Knowledge Graph will be made entirely accessible to the public in accordance with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles. Datasets will be deposited into established, stable public repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Dryad) with comprehensive metadata, persistent identifiers, and detailed data dictionaries to ensure interoperability and reuse by the broader biological community. Furthermore, the MesoPhaser-AI analytical framework and all associated source code will be developed transparently. We will maintain open-source repositories on platforms like GitHub, utilizing a version-controlled, highly documented workflow. The code will be released under a permissive open-source license, such as MIT or Apache 2.0. To guarantee reproducibility, we will provide containerized software environments using Docker and detailed Jupyter Notebooks that guide users step-by-step through our data processing, model training, and inference pipelines. This ensures that any researcher, regardless of their computational infrastructure, can replicate our findings and deploy our AI models. In alignment with community-created policies on open science, all resulting publications will be made available via open-access preprints (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to peer review, and final manuscripts will be published in open-access journals. Our Working Group will also develop a dedicated public web portal to host interactive visualizations of the synthesized datasets and model predictions. By institutionalizing these rigorous open science practices, we ensure that our synthesis efforts maximally benefit the global scientific community.

[Budget and Resources]
To successfully execute this community-scale synthesis project, the MesoCondensate Synthesis Working Group requires specific support and resources uniquely provided by NCEMS. Our budget is meticulously structured to facilitate transdisciplinary collaboration, computational innovation, and workforce training, adhering strictly to the mandate of utilizing only existing public data. The primary budget allocation will support collaborative infrastructure and team science activities. This includes travel, lodging, and per diem expenses for our diverse team of structural biophysicists, cellular biologists, network theorists, and AI experts to attend bi-annual, multi-day synthesis summits at the NCEMS facility. These in-person meetings are critical for overcoming disciplinary language barriers and driving the deep intellectual integration required to model mesoscale emergence. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to training the next-generation, data-savvy workforce. Funds are allocated for the organization and execution of the Data-to-Emergence bootcamps and synthesis hackathons. This covers travel and stipends for participating trainees, including graduate students and postdoctoral scholars, expert instructor compensation, and the provision of necessary educational materials. These initiatives will tap diverse new talent and equip them with cutting-edge skills in AI and data integration. Computational resources form the final core component of our budget. While we will leverage institutional computing where possible, dedicated funds are required for secure cloud computing infrastructure to host our massive synthesized knowledge graphs, train the MesoPhaser-AI multimodal graph neural networks, and host the public-facing interactive web portal. Additionally, we request support for open-access publication fees and professional data curation services to ensure strict adherence to FAIR data principles. This budget clearly demonstrates a need for NCEMS support that surpasses the capabilities of any single laboratory, providing the essential foundation for our ambitious, collaborative synthesis effort.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of emergence at the mesoscale. Bridging the critical gap between individual interacting biomolecules and higher-order cellular organization, these membraneless organelles dynamically partition proteins and nucleic acids to regulate essential cellular outcomes, from stress adaptation to gene expression. Despite an explosion of publicly available data characterizing intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, and phenotypic stress responses, a fundamental, long-standing puzzle remains: How do atomic and molecular-level 'grammars' predictably encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates, and how do these mesoscale structures subsequently dictate macroscopic cellular phenotypes? Solving this requires a scale of data synthesis and computational modeling far beyond the capability of any individual laboratory.

Bridging the critical gap between individual interacting biomolecules and higher-order cellular organization, these membraneless organelles dynamically partition proteins and nucleic acids to regulate essential cellular outcomes, from stress adaptation to gene expression. Our project has three distinct aims: (1) Synthesize molecular and biophysical datasets to construct a unified knowledge graph of condensate-forming proteins and their emergent physicochemical properties (e.g., viscosity, critical concentration thresholds). (2) Develop AI-driven analytical strategies to predict mesoscale condensate emergence based solely on input molecular features and environmental cellular conditions. (3) Map these emergent mesoscale properties to higher-order cellular outcomes by integrating stress-response transcriptomic and proteomic data, uncovering how condensate dynamics drive cellular survival and adaptation.

Crucially, this Working Group relies on the unique infrastructure and collaborative environment provided by NCEMS to foster cross-disciplinary synergy. The project will actively train the next generation of data-savvy scientists by embedding graduate students and postdoctoral researchers in a collaborative, team-science environment. Trainees will lead specific cross-disciplinary integration tasks and participate in data-science bootcamps, acquiring highly sought-after skills at the intersection of AI and biology. Furthermore, we are deeply committed to Open Science principles; all curated datasets, predictive models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available to the community via open-access repositories (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo) using reproducible workflows. Ultimately, this synthesis will not only resolve critical mysteries regarding mesoscale biological organization but will also provide the broader scientific community with groundbreaking open-source tools to predict emergent cellular phenomena.

[Background and Significance]
The concept of biological emergence at the mesoscale represents one of the most profound frontiers in modern molecular and cellular biosciences. At the heart of this frontier lies liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), a biophysical phenomenon driving the formation of biomolecular condensates. These membraneless organelles—such as stress granules, nucleoli, and processing bodies—dynamically partition proteins and nucleic acids in response to fluctuating intracellular environments. They bridge the critical gap between nanometer-scale interacting biomolecules and micrometer-scale higher-order cellular organization.

Despite a renaissance in LLPS research and an explosion of publicly available data characterizing intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks, a fundamental, long-standing puzzle remains: How do atomic and molecular-level rules—the 'grammar' of mesoscale emergence—predictably encode the emergent biophysical properties of these condensates, and how do these structures subsequently dictate macroscopic cellular phenotypes? The challenge stems from the inherent complexity of mesoscale phenomena. Traditional reductionist approaches cannot capture the collective behaviors of thousands of interacting molecules.

Concurrently, vast amounts of heterogeneous public data remain siloed. Databases like PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, and DisProt house critical biophysical and phase-separation annotations. Repositories such as GEO and PRIDE contain massive multi-omic (transcriptomic and proteomic) profiles of cellular states under varying stress conditions. Finally, structural interactome data are abundantly available via AlphaFold-DB and the PDB. However, these distinct layers of biological information have never been systematically synthesized to understand mesoscale emergence. This synthesis project aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission to catalyze multidisciplinary teams to leverage AI and data science.

We propose a community-scale data synthesis initiative that integrates these disparate public datasets without generating new experimental data. We hypothesize that hidden within the existing molecular and multi-omic data are deterministic principles governing condensate emergence and function. Unlocking this requires a scale of data synthesis and computational modeling far beyond the capabilities of any individual laboratory. By assembling a transdisciplinary Working Group comprising biophysicists, computational biologists, AI/machine learning experts, and cell biologists, we will leverage advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) to bridge these scales.

The proposed AI-driven synthesis will transition the field from descriptive biological models to predictive frameworks. This effort will uncover how unexpected systemic properties appear at the mesoscale and how they influence higher-order cellular outcomes, fulfilling the mandate to solve long-standing mysteries through the integration of molecular and cellular data. Ultimately, this comprehensive data synthesis will profoundly advance our understanding of how life organizes itself between the molecular and cellular scales, fundamentally transforming our grasp of mesoscale emergence.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project is driven by three interconnected research questions that target the fundamental mysteries of mesoscale emergence, designed specifically to capitalize on community-scale data synthesis and AI-driven methodologies.

Question 1: How do intrinsic molecular features and sequence grammars predict the emergent biophysical and material properties of biomolecular condensates?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the primary sequence of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and their structured interaction domains contain a decipherable 'grammar'—specific motifs, charge distributions, and interaction valencies—that deterministically encodes mesoscale properties such as critical concentration thresholds, viscosity, and viscoelasticity. By synthesizing data from DisProt, CD-CODE, and AlphaFold-DB, we expect our AI models to reveal non-linear dependencies between sequence composition and mesoscale emergent behaviors that current reductionist biophysical models fail to capture.

Question 2: How do dynamic changes in the intracellular environment (e.g., cellular stress) modulate this molecular grammar to trigger the targeted emergence or dissolution of specific mesoscale condensates?
Hypothesis 2: Mesoscale emergence is not purely sequence-dependent but is highly sensitive to the cellular state. We hypothesize that post-translational modifications (PTMs) and localized shifts in protein concentration during stress events act as biochemical switches that predictably alter the molecular grammar of LLPS. By integrating stress-responsive proteomic datasets from PRIDE with structural interactomes, we will test whether dynamic changes in the interaction network architecture accurately predict the spatiotemporal emergence of condensates.

Question 3: What are the governing rules that map the emergent dynamics of mesoscale condensates to specific, high-level macroscopic cellular outcomes, such as stress adaptation and survival?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that biomolecular condensates function as master regulatory hubs that orchestrate cellular stress responses, meaning their mesoscale material states are directly predictive of downstream transcriptomic and proteomic shifts. By synthesizing biophysical phase-separation data with matching multi-omic stress profiles from GEO, we anticipate identifying a conserved network of condensate-driven phenotypic responses. We posit that the AI-driven synthesis will uncover rules dictating how the physical properties of a condensate directly control cellular adaptation efficiency.

These questions represent a paradigm shift from traditional single-gene or single-condensate studies. Addressing them requires synthesizing millions of data points across molecular, mesoscale, and cellular levels—an endeavor strictly impossible for an individual research lab. Our hypotheses challenge the current limitations in understanding how the gap between individual proteins and complex cellular behaviors is bridged. Through rigorous AI-driven synthesis, this Working Group will uncover the universal rules of condensate-driven emergence. Moreover, by framing these questions around existing multi-omic and biophysical datasets, we adhere strictly to the NCEMS mandate of generating novel, deeper, and broader insights exclusively through the integration of publicly available data, without the generation of new experimental data.

[Methods and Approach]
To decipher the grammar of mesoscale emergence, this Working Group will employ a purely computational, community-scale data synthesis approach, fully compliant with the NCEMS restriction against generating new experimental data. Our methodology is structured around three integrated aims leveraging diverse, transdisciplinary expertise.

Aim 1: Construction of a Multiscale Knowledge Graph. We will synthesize heterogeneous, publicly available datasets into a unified, machine-readable Knowledge Graph (KG). Biophysical and LLPS-specific data will be curated from PhaSepDB, CD-CODE, and DisProt. Structural interactomes and 3D conformations will be sourced from AlphaFold-DB and PDB. Cellular state multi-omics (transcriptomics and proteomics) corresponding to various stress conditions (e.g., heat shock, oxidative stress) will be systematically downloaded from GEO and PRIDE. We will utilize semantic web technologies and biological ontologies to build a KG where nodes represent biomolecules, structural domains, condensates, and cellular phenotypes, while edges capture relationships such as interaction affinities, co-localization, and regulatory influence. This cross-disciplinary effort will require deep collaboration between data scientists for database integration and biophysicists for accurate biological ontology mapping.

Aim 2: AI-Driven Prediction of Mesoscale Condensate Emergence. Leveraging the KG, we will develop novel Artificial Intelligence architectures to predict condensate properties from molecular features. First, we will fine-tune advanced sequence-to-function Large Language Models (LLMs), such as ESM-2, specifically on IDP sequences from our curated synthesis to extract high-dimensional molecular embeddings that capture the 'grammar' of LLPS. Second, we will construct Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) utilizing the structural interactome data. The GNNs will integrate the LLM sequence embeddings with environmental parameters (e.g., stress-induced PTMs and concentration shifts) to predict the emergence of mesoscale physicochemical properties like phase boundaries and viscosity. AI experts will lead model architecture development, while molecular biologists will provide critical validation of the models' biological plausibility.

Aim 3: Mapping Mesoscale Properties to Cellular Outcomes. To bridge the gap from mesoscale condensates to macroscopic phenotypes, we will develop multi-modal machine learning pipelines. We will use deep learning regressors to correlate the AI-predicted condensate states (from Aim 2) with the temporal transcriptomic and proteomic stress signatures curated from GEO and PRIDE. This will elucidate how the dynamics of membraneless organelles govern cellular adaptation.

Training and Collaboration Strategy: This methodology relies on the diverse expertise assembled within our Working Group. Trainees (graduate students and postdocs) will be central to this effort, serving as the connective tissue between sub-groups. They will undergo cross-training via intensive data-science bootcamps hosted during Working Group meetings, learning to deploy LLMs and GNNs on biological data. This immersive training will produce a cohort of data-savvy scientists fluent in both computational AI and molecular biophysics. The NCEMS infrastructure will facilitate this transdisciplinary synthesis, providing the computational resources and collaborative framework necessary to execute this ambitious multiscale integration.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This synthesis project will yield transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to illuminate mesoscale emergence. The primary tangible outcome will be the release of the first comprehensive, multiscale Knowledge Graph linking intrinsic molecular grammar, biophysical condensate properties, and cellular stress phenotypes. This integrated resource will solve the long-standing problem of siloed data in LLPS research, enabling researchers to traverse seamlessly from atomic sequences to macroscopic cellular behaviors.

Our second major outcome will be the deployment of validated, open-source AI models (LLMs and GNNs) capable of accurately predicting the emergence of biomolecular condensates and their material properties based solely on sequence and environmental inputs. This represents a paradigm shift, transitioning the field from retrospective description to predictive modeling. By successfully mapping these mesoscale emergent properties to downstream multi-omic stress responses, we will provide the first predictive framework for how mesoscale biological organization dictates cellular survival.

Beyond scientific discoveries, the impact of this Working Group will profoundly shape the future workforce. By actively embedding graduate students and postdocs into a transdisciplinary synthesis environment, we will train a new generation of data-savvy scientists capable of bridging complex AI architectures and molecular biosciences. This cross-pollination of disciplines will tap diverse new talent, fostering collaborative partnerships across various career stages and institutional research levels.

Ultimately, this community-scale synthesis will resolve critical mysteries regarding how unexpected properties arise at the mesoscale. By providing the broader scientific community with groundbreaking open-source tools, methodologies, and synthetic datasets, this project will dramatically accelerate discovery across the molecular and cellular biosciences, firmly establishing NCEMS as a pioneering epicenter for AI-driven biological synthesis.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is deeply and uncompromisingly committed to the principles of Open Science, fully aligning with NCEMS community-created policies on open, team, and reproducible science. Given that this project relies entirely on synthesizing publicly available data, ensuring that our synthesized outputs remain highly accessible, transparent, and reusable is paramount.

All curated datasets, harmonized metadata, and the multiscale Knowledge Graph will be made freely available adhering strictly to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles. Data artifacts will be deposited in robust, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Figshare, accompanied by comprehensive, machine-readable metadata.

To guarantee computational reproducibility, all analytical pipelines, AI architectures (LLMs and GNNs), and data integration workflows will be developed in the open. Source code will be maintained in public GitHub repositories under highly permissive open-source licenses (e.g., MIT or Apache 2.0). We will utilize containerization technologies, such as Docker and Singularity, to package our models and dependencies, ensuring that any researcher worldwide can perfectly recreate our computational environments and reproduce our findings.

Furthermore, we will prioritize transparent research practices through pre-registration of our primary AI hypotheses and analytical protocols on platforms like the Open Science Framework (OSF). Detailed, interactive tutorials and Jupyter Notebooks will be published alongside our models to facilitate community adoption and lower the barrier to entry for non-computational biologists. All findings will be published in open-access peer-reviewed journals, and preprints will be uploaded to bioRxiv prior to submission. By democratizing access to these powerful AI tools and synthesized datasets, we will empower the global scientific community to further investigate mesoscale emergence.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed budget is strategically designed to support a collaborative, community-scale data synthesis effort, strictly adhering to NCEMS guidelines prohibiting funds for new experimental data generation (e.g., no wet-lab equipment or reagents). The budget primarily requests support for personnel, transdisciplinary collaboration, and high-performance computing infrastructure.

Personnel Support (45%): The majority of the budget is allocated to support two postdoctoral researchers and three graduate students. This reflects our core commitment to training the future data-savvy workforce. These trainees will be co-mentored by the Working Group's diverse experts, leading the hands-on data harmonization, AI model development, and phenotypic mapping.

Collaboration and Working Group Meetings (25%): To stimulate true cross-disciplinary collaboration, we request funds to host biannual, intensive in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facilities. These funds will cover travel, accommodation, and subsistence for our geographically and institutionally diverse team members. These meetings will feature data-science bootcamps for trainees and dedicated hackathons to accelerate Knowledge Graph construction and AI model integration.

Computational Resources and Cloud Infrastructure (20%): Developing and fine-tuning advanced LLMs and GNNs requires significant computational power. We request funds for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud) and access to high-performance GPU clusters essential for AI model training, data storage, and the hosting of our interactive web portals for the Knowledge Graph.

Open Science and Publication (10%): Funds are allocated to support Gold Open Access publication fees, ensuring all findings are freely accessible to the global community. Additionally, we budget for data storage fees in repositories like Zenodo to guarantee long-term hosting of our synthesized datasets.

This project demonstrates a clear need for NCEMS support, as the required logistical coordination, computational infrastructure, and transdisciplinary team-building vastly exceed the capabilities of any single research laboratory or standard grant mechanism.

abstract_text:
Biomolecular condensates, formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a quintessential example of mesoscale emergence in biology. These dynamic, non-membrane-bound organelles assemble from individual macromolecules to exhibit entirely new collective properties—such as tunable viscosity, selective permeability, and spatially restricted biochemical reactions. They effectively bridge the gap between single biomolecules and higher-order cellular phenotypes. Despite an explosion of single-lab experimental studies, the universal sequence grammar, biophysical parameters, and thermodynamic thresholds governing this mesoscale emergence across space and time remain a long-standing puzzle. Furthermore, predicting how these mesoscale properties dictate macro-cellular behaviors, such as survival mechanisms during cellular stress, is currently beyond the computational and analytical capacity of any individual research group.

To address this critical gap, we propose the Working Group 'Condensome-AI', a transdisciplinary team comprising structural biologists, biophysicists, machine learning experts, and cell biologists. We will leverage artificial intelligence and advanced data science methodologies to synthesize massive, publicly available, yet currently siloed datasets. Specifically, we will integrate biophysical droplet databases (e.g., PhaSePro, LLPSDB), high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold, PDB), global interactome datasets (BioGRID, PRIDE), and high-throughput cellular imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas, Image Data Resource). In strict adherence to NCEMS guidelines, this project will generate no new experimental data. Instead, it relies entirely on community-scale synthesis to construct a unified, predictive framework for mesoscale emergence.

Our project pursues three core scientific objectives: (1) Answer the novel question of how combinations of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and structured RNA-binding domains synergize to govern emergent rheological properties across different metabolic states; (2) Solve the long-standing mystery of how shifts in environmental energy and molecular composition trigger the sudden spatial and temporal appearance of these mesoscale structures; and (3) Develop 'MesoPredict,' an innovative, AI-driven analytical pipeline utilizing graph neural networks to predict condensate composition and subsequent cellular impacts directly from omics profiles.

Executing this synthesis requires the unique infrastructure and collaborative support of NCEMS. By bringing together diverse talent from distinct geographic locations and institutional tiers, we will foster a research environment impossible within traditional single-discipline grants. Our partnership emphasizes diversity and mentorship, deliberately pairing senior computational scientists with biology-focused graduate students and postdoctoral researchers. Through specialized computational bootcamps and collaborative working group sessions, we will actively train a data-savvy, next-generation workforce capable of navigating the intersection of AI and biological emergence.

Finally, our Working Group is deeply committed to rigorous open science practices. All synthesized datasets, AI/ML models, analytical workflows, and resultant code will be heavily documented, open-source, and distributed via community repositories like Zenodo and GitHub following FAIR data principles. By deciphering the complex language of mesoscale condensate emergence, this NCEMS-supported synthesis will fundamentally advance our understanding of cellular organization and provide a transformative, accessible resource for the entire molecular and cellular biosciences community.

Biomolecular condensates formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represent a profound paradigm shift in our understanding of cellular organization. Operating at the mesoscale—the critical bridge between individual biomolecules and functional organelles—these non-membrane-bound structures exhibit emergent properties that fundamentally cannot be predicted by studying their constituent macromolecules in isolation. When specific proteins and nucleic acids coalesce, they spontaneously generate unique local microenvironments characterized by tunable rheological properties, such as viscosity, surface tension, and selective permeability. These emergent mesoscale properties allow cells to dynamically compartmentalize biochemical reactions, sequester stress-related molecules, and precisely regulate gene expression in response to environmental fluctuations.

Despite the recent explosion of experimental studies characterizing individual condensates, the broader scientific community faces a critical bottleneck: these studies are largely siloed, focusing on single proteins or specific cellular conditions. Consequently, the universal sequence grammar, the overarching biophysical parameters, and the exact thermodynamic thresholds that govern this mesoscale emergence remain elusive. This fragmentation of knowledge represents a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences. Individual research laboratories lack the diverse computational infrastructure and transdisciplinary expertise required to synthesize these disparate datasets into a cohesive, predictive framework.
