[Abstract]
Biological systems exhibit profound emergent properties at the mesoscale, where dynamic, transient interactions between individual biomolecules give rise to higher-order functional structures like biomolecular condensates and membraneless organelles. Despite their critical roles in cellular regulation, stress response, and neurodegenerative diseases, the fundamental biophysical rules governing how these mesoscale properties emerge from atomistic and molecular features remain a long-standing puzzle. This project proposes a community-scale synthesis to elucidate the multiscale principles of stress-induced biomolecular condensation. By leveraging the vast, untapped wealth of publicly available structural, proteomic, and transcriptomic data, we aim to uncover the physical, spatial, and energetic drivers of mesoscale phase separation without generating any new experimental data. Our transdisciplinary Working Group will integrate distinct, heterogeneous public datasets—including AlphaFold-predicted and experimentally derived protein structures (PDB, EMDB), high-throughput interaction and stress-response proteomics (PRIDE, IntAct), and spatial and single-cell transcriptomics (GEO, Human Cell Atlas). We will utilize advanced artificial intelligence, specifically graph neural networks (GNNs) and large language models (LLMs) adapted for biological sequences, alongside multiscale physical modeling to bridge the gap between molecular-level properties (e.g., intrinsically disordered regions, valency, RNA-binding motifs) and cellular-level outcomes (e.g., stress granule assembly and disassembly). This synthesis demands a transdisciplinary effort far beyond the capabilities of a single laboratory. Our Working Group unites polymer physicists, structural biologists, artificial intelligence experts, and cellular physiologists representing a wide array of geographic locations, career stages, and institutional classifications. NCEMS support is absolutely essential to provide the computational infrastructure, collaborative networking, and data-science scaffolding required to harmonize these massive, multi-scale databases into a unified, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. By synthesizing these disparate data layers, the Working Group will address three compelling objectives: (1) map the dynamic "mesoscale interactome" of stress granules across different temporal cellular states and energy landscapes; (2) deploy machine learning models to identify the emergent biophysical and informational thresholds that trigger mesoscale condensation; and (3) predict how genetic mutations or transcriptomic shifts perturb these emergent structures, linking molecular alterations to cellular pathogenesis. Furthermore, this project is deeply committed to Open Science and the cultivation of a data-savvy workforce. All harmonized datasets, AI model architectures, and analysis pipelines will be released publicly through open-access repositories following FAIR data principles and reproducible workflows. To train the next generation, the Working Group will host specialized, hands-on data bootcamps for involved graduate students and postdoctoral scholars, providing them with unparalleled cross-training at the intersection of machine learning, open science practices, and molecular biology. By mapping the critical mesoscale space between biomolecules and organelles, this project will solve a major puzzle in molecular emergence, create innovative analytical strategies, and establish a scalable, open-source paradigm for future biological synthesis.

[Background and Significance]
Biological systems are defined by their emergent properties—characteristics that arise not from individual components alone, but from their complex, dynamic interactions across multiple scales of composition, space, time, and energy. At the mesoscale, positioned between individual biomolecules and large, membrane-bound organelles, one of the most profound examples of biological emergence is the formation of biomolecular condensates, such as stress granules. These membraneless organelles form via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), driven by multivalent, transient interactions among intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and nucleic acids. While these condensates are critical for cellular regulation, rapid stress adaptation, and are intimately linked to neurodegenerative pathologies when dysregulated (such as ALS and Alzheimer’s disease), the precise biophysical and informational principles governing their assembly and disassembly remain a long-standing puzzle in molecular biology. Historically, reductionist research paradigms have focused either on the atomistic structural details of isolated IDPs or on the macroscopic phenotypic observation of condensate formation via microscopy. However, the true rules of mesoscale emergence lie in the intermediate zone, requiring a highly integrated, multiscale understanding of how molecular features scale into collective, higher-order behaviors. Currently, a vast and rapidly expanding wealth of publicly available data exists across disparate biological domains: structural biology (e.g., PDB, EMDB, AlphaFold databases), interaction proteomics (PRIDE, IntAct), and transcriptomics (GEO, Human Cell Atlas). Yet, these datasets remain largely siloed. The lack of integration fundamentally limits our ability to identify the universal physical, spatial, and energetic thresholds that trigger condensation in vivo. This proposal addresses this critical knowledge gap through a highly collaborative, community-scale synthesis project. By harmonizing heterogeneous datasets without generating any new experimental data, our Working Group will decode the multiscale rules of stress-induced biomolecular condensation. This project aligns flawlessly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). It directly tackles fundamental questions about the unexpected appearance of biological system properties at the mesoscale, leverages AI and data science to synthesize massive volumes of public data, and brings together a diverse, multidisciplinary team of polymer physicists, structural biologists, AI experts, and cellular physiologists. The proposed synthesis is fundamentally beyond the capabilities of any single research group or existing collaboration. It specifically requires the specialized computational infrastructure, transdisciplinary networking, and collaborative environment uniquely provided by NCEMS. By integrating atomistic structural features—such as valency, electrostatic charge distribution, and RNA-binding motifs—with dynamic multi-omics data spanning various temporal cellular states, we will bridge the persistent gap between molecular biophysics and cellular physiology. The overarching significance of this work extends far beyond the study of stress granules; it establishes a generalized, predictive framework for mesoscale emergence, unraveling how the collective dynamics of macromolecules govern cellular life, pushing the boundaries of what is possible through data-driven biological synthesis.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This community-scale synthesis project is driven by the overarching goal of decoding the rules of mesoscale emergence. To bridge the gap between atomistic molecular interactions and cellular-level organelle outcomes, our transdisciplinary Working Group will address three compelling, interrelated scientific questions and rigorously test their corresponding hypotheses using synthesized public data. Question 1: How does the dynamic "mesoscale interactome" of stress granules evolve across different temporal cellular states and energy landscapes? Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that stress granule assembly follows a reproducible, hierarchical pathway of molecular recruitment driven by a stable core network of highly multivalent scaffold proteins, which subsequently recruit transient client proteins and RNAs based on dynamic, time-dependent changes in the cellular energy landscape and local transcriptomic availability. By synthesizing massive time-course proteomics from PRIDE and transcriptomic states from GEO, we will systematically map the spatiotemporal evolution of this interactome. We expect to identify distinct structural and energetic classes of condensates that correspond directly to specific cellular stress conditions and metabolic states. Question 2: What are the emergent biophysical and informational thresholds that trigger mesoscale condensation, and how can they be generalized across disparate biomolecular systems? Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that the onset of biomolecular condensation is governed by a predictable set of "molecular grammar" rules—involving specific combinations of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), electrostatic charge patterning, hydrophobicity, and RNA-binding motif valency—that must collectively cross a critical energetic threshold to initiate phase separation. Using AlphaFold-predicted structures alongside interaction databases like IntAct, integrated via artificial intelligence frameworks, we will extract the hidden biophysical thresholds of phase separation. We anticipate that large language models (LLMs) adapted specifically for biological sequences will reveal an underlying syntax that dictates emergent phase behavior without requiring any de novo experimental measurement. Question 3: How do genetic mutations or transcriptomic shifts perturb these emergent structures, and can these perturbations reliably predict cellular pathogenesis? Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that disease-associated mutations (e.g., those clinically linked to ALS or Alzheimer's) and aberrant transcriptomic shifts do not merely disrupt individual protein functions, but fundamentally alter the energetic landscape, valency, and stoichiometry of the entire mesoscale interactome, shifting dynamic liquid-like condensates into pathological solid-like aggregates. By correlating human genetic variation data (e.g., ClinVar) and single-cell transcriptomics (Human Cell Atlas) with our integrated biophysical models, we will predict how specific molecular perturbations cascade through the mesoscale to induce neurodegenerative pathogenesis. Addressing these questions requires a complete paradigm shift from reductionist biology to integrated synthesis science. None of these questions can be answered by interrogating a single dataset or relying on the expertise of a solitary laboratory. The hypotheses rely entirely on the cross-pollination of polymer physics theories with advanced machine learning, applied to harmonized multi-omics data. By leveraging the collaborative scaffolding fostered by NCEMS, this project will not only solve long-standing puzzles regarding stress granule regulation but also establish innovative analytical strategies capable of interrogating mesoscale emergence across any cellular system.

[Methods and Approach]
The proposed synthesis research will be conducted entirely through the integration and analysis of existing, publicly available data, strictly adhering to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. Our methodological approach is structured into three highly interconnected phases: Community-Scale Data Harmonization, AI-Driven Analytical Synthesis, and Multiscale Predictive Modeling. Phase 1: Community-Scale Data Harmonization. The foundation of this project is the integration of massive, inherently heterogeneous datasets. We will construct a unified, graph-based database mapping the stress granule interactome. Structural data will be sourced from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB), and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, specifically focusing on intrinsically disordered regions and the folded domains of known phase-separating proteins. Proteomic interaction data, capturing temporal cellular stress responses, will be extracted from PRIDE and IntAct. Transcriptomic data, providing the crucial spatial and expression context of RNA clients, will be synthesized from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and the Human Cell Atlas. A critical first step for our diverse team of data scientists and cellular biologists will be standardizing these disparate formats into a unified "Mesoscale Knowledge Graph." This ensures all nodes (proteins, RNAs, temporal stress states) and edges (physical interactions, expression correlations, energy potentials) are mathematically defined and interoperable. Phase 2: AI-Driven Analytical Strategies. To uncover the latent rules of mesoscale emergence, we will deploy advanced artificial intelligence methodologies. We will utilize Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operating directly on our Mesoscale Knowledge Graph to identify network motifs and topological features that are highly predictive of condensate recruitment. Furthermore, we will fine-tune Large Language Models (LLMs) specialized for biological sequences (e.g., ESM-2) to read the "molecular grammar" of disordered proteins. By feeding these LLMs structural features paired with phase-separation propensity data (derived from synthetic literature mining and databases like PhaSePro), the AI models will learn the complex multivalent, spatial, and energetic drivers of condensation. Phase 3: Multiscale Physical Modeling and Validation. AI predictions must be rigorously grounded in physical reality. Our polymer physicists will integrate the AI-derived molecular grammar into coarse-grained molecular dynamics and thermodynamic models. We will calculate the specific energetic landscapes, temperature dependencies, and interaction valencies required to trigger mesoscale phase transitions. This hybrid approach—combining powerful black-box machine learning with interpretable biophysical equations—represents a major methodological innovation. We will validate our predictive framework entirely in silico, using hold-out datasets of disease-linked genetic mutations to test if our multiscale models accurately predict the aberrant phase transitions documented in independent clinical and phenotypic databases. This multi-layered approach requires intense cross-disciplinary collaboration. Structural biologists will guide feature extraction, data scientists will construct AI pipelines, polymer physicists will oversee thermodynamic modeling, and cellular physiologists will contextualize biological relevance. NCEMS support is absolutely essential to provide the high-performance computing infrastructure necessary for large-scale AI model training, as well as the logistical scaffolding to host intensive, transdisciplinary Working Group synthesis sprints.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This community-scale synthesis project will fundamentally advance our understanding of mesoscale emergence, successfully transitioning the field of biomolecular condensation from a largely descriptive discipline to a highly predictive science. The primary expected outcome is the creation of a unified, multiscale predictive framework capable of mapping the energetic and physical drivers of stress granule assembly and disassembly. We will deliver a highly annotated, public-facing "Mesoscale Knowledge Graph" alongside open-source AI models (GNNs and fine-tuned LLMs) that accurately predict phase separation behaviors based solely on primary biological sequences and transcriptomic contexts. The impact of these deliverables is multifold and profound. Scientifically, it will solve the long-standing puzzle of how atomistic features translate into mesoscale organelle dynamics, offering unprecedented mechanistic insights into cellular stress responses and the pathological transitions underlying devastating neurodegenerative diseases like ALS and Alzheimer's. By demonstrating how to effectively combine machine learning with polymer physics, we will establish an innovative analytical strategy that can be seamlessly adapted for studying other emergent biological phenomena across the cellular biosciences. Broader impacts include the democratization of advanced computational biology tools. The predictive algorithms developed by our Working Group will allow researchers worldwide to screen genetic mutations for mesoscale disruptions entirely in silico, accelerating therapeutic discovery and precision medicine without relying on costly preliminary wet-lab experiments. Furthermore, this project will heavily impact the scientific community by bridging historically isolated disciplines, fostering a new paradigm where polymer physics, artificial intelligence, and cellular physiology operate as a unified investigative force. By strictly leveraging publicly available data, this project exemplifies the immense, untapped potential of synthesis science, fulfilling the NCEMS mission to catalyze novel discoveries, solve persistent mysteries, and push the very boundaries of the molecular and cellular biosciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The Working Group is fundamentally committed to the highest standards of Open Science and reproducible research, aligning fully with the NCEMS mandate and community-created policies on open, team-based science. Our strategy ensures that all harmonized datasets, analytical pipelines, AI architectures, and biophysical models will be entirely transparent, rigorously documented, and fully accessible to the global scientific community. All data synthesis efforts will strictly adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles. The "Mesoscale Knowledge Graph" and integrated multi-omics datasets will be deposited in recognized, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF), accompanied by rich metadata and standardized ontologies to ensure long-term usability. We will explicitly avoid proprietary data formats. To guarantee complete reproducibility, all code utilized for data cleaning, GNN/LLM model training, and thermodynamic simulations will be version-controlled and hosted openly on GitHub. We will utilize modern containerization technologies, such as Docker and Singularity, to encapsulate our exact software environments. This allows any external researcher to download our software containers and reproduce our computational workflows exactly, regardless of their local hardware configuration. Comprehensive Jupyter Notebooks will be provided as interactive, step-by-step tutorials detailing our analytical strategies. Furthermore, all significant findings will be disseminated rapidly through preprints (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to formal peer review, and all final publications will be submitted exclusively to open-access journals. The Working Group will also draft and publish a comprehensive "Best Practices Guide for Multiscale Biological Data Synthesis," providing a practical framework for future transdisciplinary teams attempting similar data integrations. By making our entire computational infrastructure open and fully reproducible, we will significantly lower the barrier to entry for computational biology, ensuring that the methodologies developed under this grant become a durable, community-driven resource.

[Budget and Resources]
The budget for this community-scale synthesis project is meticulously designed to support intensive transdisciplinary collaboration, robust computational infrastructure, and extensive workforce training, strictly excluding any costs associated with de novo experimental data generation. The primary resource requirement from NCEMS is the facilitation of our Working Group operations. We request funding to support bi-annual, in-person collaborative sprints at the NCEMS facility. These funds will thoroughly cover travel, accommodation, and logistical support for our diverse team of principal investigators, early-career researchers, and trainees, who are drawn from a wide array of geographic locations and institutional classifications, including R1, R2, and minority-serving institutions. A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to computational resources. We require NCEMS-supported access to high-performance computing (HPC) clusters and cloud-based GPU instances necessary for training complex machine learning models (GNNs and LLMs) and running extensive thermodynamic simulations. Funding is also strategically allocated for robust cloud storage to host and share the massive, harmonized multi-omics datasets and the Mesoscale Knowledge Graph. Central to the NCEMS mission of training a data-savvy workforce, a dedicated budget line is allocated for supporting the next generation of scientists. This includes stipend and tuition support for two postdoctoral fellows and three graduate students who will serve as the primary data integrators for the project. Furthermore, we request funding to host two specialized, hands-on "Data Bootcamps." These bootcamps will be integrated directly into the Working Group meetings, providing trainees with unparalleled, immersive cross-training at the cutting-edge intersection of artificial intelligence, open science practices, and molecular biology. Finally, modest funds are allocated for Open Access publication fees to ensure global, barrier-free accessibility of our findings. This budget relies heavily on the unique collaborative scaffolding and cyberinfrastructure provided by NCEMS, an absolute necessity for executing a synthesis of this unprecedented scale.

title: Decoding Mesoscale Emergence: A Multi-Omic and AI-Driven Synthesis of Biomolecular Condensate Dynamics

abstract_text: The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties—emergence—is a defining feature of the molecular and cellular biosciences. At the mesoscale, one of the most profound unresolved emergent phenomena is the formation of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic, membraneless compartments bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and functional subcellular organelles, playing critical roles in stress response, gene regulation, and disease pathogenesis. Despite a wealth of isolated molecular, structural, and phenotypic datasets, the overarching principles governing how atomic-level interactions scale to emergent mesoscale condensate properties remain largely elusive. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the spatiotemporal emergence of biomolecular condensates by integrating massive, disparate, publicly available datasets. We will synthesize structural data (AlphaFold, PDB), high-throughput interactomics (BioGRID, STRING), spatial transcriptomics and proteomics, and thousands of publicly deposited live-cell super-resolution microscopy datasets (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Because this undertaking vastly exceeds the computational and domain expertise of any single laboratory, it necessitates the transdisciplinary environment and resources uniquely provided by NCEMS. To solve this long-standing puzzle, our team of biophysicists, computational biologists, AI specialists, and cell biologists will employ advanced multimodal artificial intelligence and data science techniques. Specifically, we will develop novel Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to map multi-valent molecular interaction networks and integrate them with deep learning-based image analysis models capable of extracting biophysical mesoscale properties (e.g., viscoelasticity, droplet fusion rates) from archived imaging data. By synthesizing these scales, we will answer a critical, novel question: How do sequence-level variations and dynamic cellular conditions reliably encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates? Beyond scientific discovery, this Working Group is designed to foster a diverse, collaborative scientific community and train the future data-savvy workforce. Our team bridges varying career stages and geographical locations, integrating trainees (graduate students and postdoctoral fellows) directly into the core analytical pipeline. Trainees will benefit from dedicated mentorship, cross-disciplinary cross-training, and rigorous instruction in cloud computing, data synthesis, and machine learning. Furthermore, this project adheres strictly to Open Science principles. All aggregated datasets, curated metadata, trained AI models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available via public repositories, utilizing reproducible workflows (e.g., Jupyter Notebooks, Docker containers) to ensure maximum utility for the broader scientific community. Ultimately, this synthesis will yield a unified framework for mesoscale emergence, transforming isolated molecular observations into a holistic understanding of subcellular organization while establishing innovative analytical paradigms for future NCEMS initiatives.

Ultimately, this synthesis will yield a unified framework for mesoscale emergence, transforming isolated molecular observations into a holistic understanding of subcellular organization while establishing innovative analytical paradigms for future NCEMS initiatives.

[Background and Significance]
Emergence is the cornerstone of biological complexity, wherein the collective interactions of fundamental components give rise to novel, unpredictable system properties. Within the molecular and cellular biosciences, the mesoscale—the spatial and temporal domain bridging individual biomolecules and functional organelles—represents the most critical yet least understood frontier of emergence. The National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS) emphasizes this precise scale, recognizing that unraveling mesoscale phenomena is essential for a holistic understanding of cellular biology. The quintessential paradigm of mesoscale emergence is the formation of biomolecular condensates through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These membraneless organelles dynamically assemble to compartmentalize biochemical reactions, tightly regulating processes such as gene expression, signal transduction, and stress adaptation. When the precise balance of these condensates is perturbed, aberrant phase transitions occur, leading to the solid-like aggregates implicated in devastating neurodegenerative disorders, including Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer's disease. 

Over the past decade, the scientific community has amassed an unprecedented volume of publicly available data characterizing the components of these condensates. We have access to atomic-level protein structures via AlphaFold and the Protein Data Bank (PDB), comprehensive protein-protein interaction networks through BioGRID and STRING, and vast repositories of live-cell super-resolution microscopy in the Image Data Resource (IDR). However, these diverse datasets remain profoundly siloed. A critical knowledge gap persists: we do not understand the specific rules by which nanometer-scale, sequence-level variations and localized interactomic shifts propagate upward to dictate the micrometer-scale physical properties and functional behaviors of condensates. Individual research laboratories inherently lack the breadth of domain expertise—spanning biophysics, computational biology, advanced artificial intelligence, and structural biology—and the computational resources required to synthesize these disparate data types. 

This Working Group proposes a transformative, community-scale synthesis project to decode mesoscale emergence. By integrating massive multi-omic and imaging datasets using state-of-the-art multimodal artificial intelligence, we aim to bridge the gap between atomic interactions and mesoscale physical properties. This project aligns perfectly with the NCEMS mission: it relies entirely on the synthesis of existing public data, demands a collaborative, transdisciplinary approach beyond the capacity of a single lab, and tackles a fundamental, long-standing puzzle in cellular biology. The significance of this work extends beyond fundamental discovery; it will provide the community with predictive computational frameworks to model how genetic mutations or environmental stressors alter condensate biophysics. Furthermore, this initiative will recruit diverse talent and meticulously train a new generation of data-savvy scientists capable of operating at the intersection of machine learning and biophysics, thereby establishing a new standard for synthesis research in the molecular and cellular sciences.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
This synthesis project is driven by the overarching objective to understand how mesoscale emergent properties are encoded within molecular and cellular networks. By leveraging diverse public datasets, we will address three novel, compelling research questions and test their associated hypotheses to resolve long-standing mysteries regarding biomolecular condensates.

Research Question 1: How do sequence-level features and intrinsic molecular properties deterministically scale to encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates? 
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that the specific topological features of multivalent protein-protein interaction networks—predictable from sequence composition, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and AlphaFold-derived structural motifs—function as deterministic blueprints for the mesoscale material state (e.g., liquid-like vs. gel-like) of condensates. By synthesizing molecular structure data with phenomenological imaging data, we will demonstrate that critical valency thresholds and interaction affinities reliably predict the viscoelasticity and fusion dynamics of condensates in vivo. 

Research Question 2: How do dynamic fluctuations in cellular environments and stress conditions perturb established interaction networks to trigger pathological phase transitions? 
Hypothesis 2: Aberrant, disease-associated phase transitions (such as the liquid-to-solid transitions observed in neurodegeneration) are driven by identifiable 'tipping points' in the cellular interactome. We hypothesize that by integrating spatial transcriptomics, condition-specific proteomics, and live-cell imaging metadata, we can map how fluctuations in hub-protein concentrations and localized environmental stressors (e.g., pH, oxidative stress) push stable mesoscale condensates across critical biophysical thresholds. We anticipate finding that these pathological transitions follow predictable network-degradation pathways rather than random aggregation events.

Research Question 3: Can a generalized, multimodal artificial intelligence framework successfully bridge the scale gap by predicting emergent mesoscale properties exclusively from distinct, publicly available molecular datasets?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that isolated molecular datasets (sequence, structure, interactomics) and phenotypic datasets (super-resolution imaging) contain latent, complementary features that can be computationally synthesized. We posit that a multimodal deep learning architecture—combining Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for interactomics with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image feature extraction—can create a unified embedding space. This will allow the accurate prediction of condensate formation, localization, and biophysical dynamics without the need for generating de novo experimental data.

These questions directly target the NCEMS mandate to investigate emergence at the mesoscale. By translating structural and molecular data into biophysical, mesoscale predictions, this research will synthesize a fragmented field into a cohesive discipline. Furthermore, addressing these hypotheses requires deep integration across diverse scientific domains—spanning AI development, polymer physics, and cellular biology—necessitating the robust, cross-disciplinary Working Group environment that NCEMS is designed to support. The answers to these questions will not only decode the fundamental rules of condensate biology but also establish innovative analytical strategies for future multi-scale synthesis research.

[Methods and Approach]
Our methodology explicitly adheres to the NCEMS mandate: we will generate no new experimental data, relying entirely on the synthesis and integration of existing, publicly available datasets. Our approach is structured across three primary phases: Data Aggregation and Curation, Multimodal AI Development, and Cross-Scale Synthesis.

Phase 1: Data Aggregation and Curation
Our multidisciplinary team will construct a centralized, cloud-based data lake integrating multiple biological scales. For molecular and structural data, we will harvest proteome-wide sequences, intrinsically disordered region (IDR) predictions (e.g., IUPred, flDPnn), and 3D structural embeddings from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and the PDB. For network data, we will extract high-throughput protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks from BioGRID and STRING, focusing on interaction valency and affinity metrics. For phenotypic and biophysical data, we will mine the Image Data Resource (IDR) and the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive (EMPIAR) for live-cell, super-resolution microscopy datasets depicting condensate dynamics (e.g., FRAP recovery curves, droplet fusion events, morphological tracking). A dedicated team of data scientists and biophysicists will standardize metadata, ensuring distinct datasets are contextually aligned by cell type, stress condition, and temporal resolution.

Phase 2: Multimodal AI Development
To bridge the molecular and mesoscale, we will develop a novel artificial intelligence architecture. First, we will construct Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to represent the biological interactome. In these graphs, nodes represent individual proteins—embedded with their sequence features, AlphaFold structural data, and IDR profiles—and edges represent physical interactions weighted by binding affinity and valency. The GNN will learn the topological network representations of condensate-forming systems. Concurrently, we will deploy computer vision models, specifically deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs), to process the archived imaging data. These models will automatically segment condensates, track spatiotemporal dynamics, and extract critical mesoscale biophysical features, such as surface tension, viscoelasticity (derived from fusion rates), and sphericity.

Phase 3: Cross-Scale Synthesis and Integration
The core synthesis relies on aligning the molecular GNN embeddings with the phenotypic imaging embeddings. We will utilize cross-modal attention mechanisms and contrastive learning frameworks to map the latent space of molecular interactions directly to the latent space of physical properties. This will enable the model to learn how specific network topologies and sequence variations encode mesoscale behaviors. 

Collaboration and Execution
This approach requires a transdisciplinary Working Group. AI specialists will architect the neural networks; biophysicists will guide feature extraction and validate the physical plausibility of the AI predictions; and cell biologists will interpret the biological relevance of mapped disease-state phase transitions. Iterative, collaborative hackathons and synthesis working sessions will refine the models. By fusing these disparate data modalities through advanced AI, we will generate an unprecedented, predictive toolset that solves the complex puzzle of mesoscale emergence entirely through data synthesis.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
This proposed synthesis project will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission, bridging the gap between atomic interactions and mesoscale emergence. 

Scientific and Methodological Outcomes: We will produce the first unified, multimodal AI framework capable of predicting emergent biophysical properties of biomolecular condensates directly from publicly available sequence, structure, and interactomic data. By successfully synthesizing graph-based molecular networks with image-derived physical properties, we will solve the long-standing puzzle of how genetic and molecular variations dictate mesoscale phase transitions. This will yield profound insights into the foundational rules of cellular organization and provide predictive models for identifying pathological, disease-associated phase transitions (e.g., in neurodegeneration). Methodologically, we will establish an innovative, scalable analytical paradigm for multi-omic and image data integration that can be adapted for other mesoscale phenomena, significantly advancing the data science toolset available to the molecular biosciences.

Workforce Training and Broader Impacts: A cornerstone of our Working Group is the deliberate training of the future data-savvy workforce. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will be fully integrated into the project, receiving intensive cross-training at the intersection of biophysics, computer science, and molecular biology. Trainees will gain high-demand skills in cloud computing, advanced machine learning (GNNs, deep learning), and large-scale data synthesis through dedicated mentorship and hands-on workshops. Furthermore, by assembling a diverse team representing various geographic locations, career stages, and scientific disciplines, we will foster a collaborative network that breaks down traditional academic silos. Ultimately, the insights, methodologies, and newly trained scientists emerging from this project will heavily impact the broader biological community, proving the massive, untapped potential of utilizing public data synthesis to answer the most compelling questions in the life sciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the highest standards of Open Science, transparency, and reproducibility, ensuring that all outcomes serve as a gold-standard resource for the broader molecular and cellular biosciences community. We will strictly adhere to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles throughout the lifecycle of the project.

Data and Code Accessibility: Although we are not generating new experimental data, the curated, harmonized meta-datasets synthesized from disparate public sources represent a highly valuable community resource. All aggregated data lakes, standardized metadata files, and resulting databases will be deposited in stable, open-access repositories such as Zenodo and Dryad, minted with persistent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). The entire computational pipeline, including data ingestion scripts, Graph Neural Network (GNN) architectures, computer vision algorithms, and cross-modal synthesis models, will be developed openly on GitHub. 

Reproducibility Workflows: To guarantee the reproducibility of our complex AI workflows, we will utilize containerization technologies (e.g., Docker, Singularity). We will provide fully documented, interactive Jupyter Notebooks that allow external researchers to seamlessly execute our analytical pipelines, test our trained models on their own molecular data, and validate our findings. All model weights and training checkpoints will be made publicly available through platforms like Hugging Face.

Dissemination and Community Engagement: We will publish our findings in open-access, peer-reviewed journals and post all preprints to bioRxiv prior to submission. Furthermore, we will establish detailed data management plans (DMPs) and open-science charters during our initial Working Group meetings to ensure all team members and trainees are aligned with team science best practices. By making our methodologies, curated datasets, and predictive models entirely transparent, we will catalyze subsequent research and maximize the return on NCEMS funding.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed budget is meticulously designed to support the collaborative synthesis, computational demands, and workforce training inherent to this Working Group, entirely omitting any costs for de novo experimental data generation or wet-lab equipment. 

Personnel and Trainee Support (45%): The majority of our personnel budget is dedicated to training the next-generation workforce. We request stipend and tuition support for two graduate students and salary support for two postdoctoral fellows. These trainees will be the primary drivers of data curation and model development, benefiting directly from cross-disciplinary mentorship. Modest summer salary support is requested for early-career principal investigators to facilitate dedicated time for synthesis research and trainee mentorship.

Working Group Meetings and Collaboration (25%): To stimulate genuine cross-disciplinary synergy, we request funds for three in-person Working Group meetings at the NCEMS facilities. This budget covers travel, accommodation, and per diem for all team members—spanning biophysicists, data scientists, and cell biologists—from diverse geographic locations and institutional backgrounds. These intensive hackathons and strategy sessions are essential for bridging domain-specific knowledge gaps and iterative model refinement.

Cloud Computing and Data Infrastructure (20%): Synthesizing thousands of high-resolution live-cell imaging datasets and training complex multimodal AI models (GNNs and CNNs) requires substantial computational power. We request funds for cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS, Azure) and secure data storage to host our aggregated data lake. We will also leverage NCEMS-provided high-performance computing (HPC) clusters where available to optimize our budget.

Open Science and Dissemination (10%): Funds are allocated for open-access publication fees (APCs) to ensure all findings are freely available to the global scientific community. Additionally, we budget for software licensing, DOI minting for our public datasets, and long-term hosting of our interactive web portals and reproducible Docker containers, strictly adhering to community open-science mandates.

At the mesoscale, one of the most profound unresolved emergent phenomena is the formation of biomolecular condensates via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). These dynamic, membraneless compartments bridge the gap between individual biomolecules and functional subcellular organelles, playing critical roles in stress response, gene regulation, and disease pathogenesis. Despite a wealth of isolated molecular, structural, and phenotypic datasets, the overarching principles governing how atomic-level interactions scale to emergent mesoscale condensate properties remain largely elusive. This Working Group proposes a community-scale synthesis project to decode the spatiotemporal emergence of biomolecular condensates by integrating massive, disparate, publicly available datasets. We will synthesize structural data (AlphaFold, PDB), high-throughput interactomics (BioGRID, STRING), spatial transcriptomics and proteomics, and thousands of publicly deposited live-cell super-resolution microscopy datasets (Image Data Resource, EMPIAR). Because this undertaking vastly exceeds the computational and domain expertise of any single laboratory, it necessitates the transdisciplinary environment and resources uniquely provided by NCEMS. To solve this long-standing puzzle, our team of biophysicists, computational biologists, AI specialists, and cell biologists will employ advanced multimodal artificial intelligence and data science techniques. Specifically, we will develop novel Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to map multi-valent molecular interaction networks and integrate them with deep learning-based image analysis models capable of extracting biophysical mesoscale properties (e.g., viscoelasticity, droplet fusion rates) from archived imaging data. By synthesizing these scales, we will answer a critical, novel question: How do sequence-level variations and dynamic cellular conditions reliably encode the emergent biophysical properties of mesoscale condensates? Beyond scientific discovery, this Working Group is designed to foster a diverse, collaborative scientific community and train the future data-savvy workforce. Our team bridges varying career stages and geographical locations, integrating trainees (graduate students and postdoctoral fellows) directly into the core analytical pipeline. Trainees will benefit from dedicated mentorship, cross-disciplinary cross-training, and rigorous instruction in cloud computing, data synthesis, and machine learning. Furthermore, this project adheres strictly to Open Science principles. All aggregated datasets, curated metadata, trained AI models, and analytical pipelines will be made freely available via public repositories, utilizing reproducible workflows (e.g., Jupyter Notebooks, Docker containers) to ensure maximum utility for the broader scientific community. Ultimately, this synthesis will yield a unified framework for mesoscale emergence, transforming isolated molecular observations into a holistic understanding of subcellular organization while establishing innovative analytical paradigms for future NCEMS initiatives.

full_text:
[Abstract]
Biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represent a defining paradigm of emergent mesoscale organization. Bridging the critical gap between individual macromolecules and complex cellular organelles, these membraneless compartments orchestrate vital processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress response. Despite their biological ubiquity, the fundamental molecular grammar dictating how varied atomic-level interactions—particularly among intrinsically disordered proteins and RNA—scale up to govern mesoscale material properties and macroscopic cellular phenotypes remains a long-standing puzzle. Currently, structural biology, spatial proteomics, and cellular biophysics generate massive, high-fidelity datasets; however, these data remain highly siloed. Individual research laboratories lack the cross-disciplinary expertise and computational infrastructure required to unify these divergent streams into a cohesive, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. To address this, we propose a transdisciplinary Working Group to synthesize massive, publicly available molecular and cellular datasets to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. This community-scale synthesis project will leverage AI and advanced data science to integrate atomic-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold, Protein Data Bank), intrinsically disordered protein registries (DisProt), phase-separation databases (CD-CODE, PhaSePro), global interactomes (BioGRID, STRING), and bioimaging/Cryo-ET repositories (EMPIAR, Image Data Resource). Importantly, this project will generate no new experimental data, relying entirely on the computational synthesis and harmonization of these public resources. Our working group will pursue three primary objectives: (1) Unify and harmonize these highly heterogeneous datasets to construct the first multi-scale Condensate Graph, mathematically representing the relationships between sequence-level features and mesoscale assembly. (2) Develop and train novel geometric deep learning models to predict emergent mesoscale physical properties—such as condensate liquidity, valency, and viscoelasticity—directly from these synthesized omics and structural data. (3) Map these mesoscale phase behaviors to higher-order subcellular and phenotypic outcomes, specifically focusing on how the dysregulation of this emergent grammar correlates with known disease markers. This endeavor directly aligns with the core mission of NCEMS. The sheer scale and complexity of bridging atomistic biophysics with cellular phenomics via machine learning necessitate a collaborative, transdisciplinary approach that transcends the capabilities of any single research group. Our proposed Working Group deliberately brings together experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, structural biology, and spatial multi-omics from geographically diverse institutions and varying career stages. Central to our proposal is a steadfast commitment to workforce development and Open Science. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will be integrated as core analysts, receiving cross-training in AI-driven omics integration, biophysical modeling, and rigorous reproducible data science practices. Furthermore, in strict adherence to community-created open science policies, all integrated databases, machine learning codebases, and analytical workflows will be released publicly under FAIR principles. Ultimately, this data synthesis will solve fundamental mysteries of mesoscale biological emergence, providing the broader scientific community with a powerful new computational lens to understand subcellular organization.

[Background and Significance]
The unexpected appearance of new biological system properties at the mesoscale—the critical nexus between single biomolecules and complex cellular organelles—represents one of the most profound frontiers in modern molecular and cellular biosciences. Biomolecular condensates, formed through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), are a defining paradigm of this emergence. These membraneless compartments, driven by weak, multivalent interactions predominantly involving intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and RNA, orchestrate vital cellular processes from gene transcription to stress adaptation. However, how atomic-level interactions scale spatially and temporally to dictate mesoscale material properties, such as liquidity, viscoelasticity, and dynamically regulated valency, remains a fundamental biological mystery. Currently, the scientific community possesses massive, high-fidelity datasets generated by distinct biological disciplines. Structural biology offers atomic-resolution data via the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and predictive tools like AlphaFold; biophysics provides registries of intrinsic disorder (DisProt) and phase-separation behaviors (CD-CODE, PhaSePro); systems biology catalogs global interactomes (BioGRID, STRING); and cell biology maps spatial organization via bioimaging and Cryo-Electron Tomography repositories (EMPIAR, Image Data Resource). Yet, these data streams exist in disparate silos. Extracting the underlying 'molecular grammar' that bridges atomistic biophysics and cellular phenomics is an intractable challenge for isolated research labs, which generally lack the transdisciplinary expertise and computational infrastructure required for synthesis at this scale. This proposal directly addresses the strategic vision of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). By forming a collaborative, transdisciplinary Working Group, we will synthesize these vast public data repositories to construct a unified predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. Our approach relies entirely on the synthesis of existing publicly available data and will generate no new experimental data, making it a pure data science and AI-driven endeavor. The significance of this work is multifold. First, it solves a long-standing puzzle by decoding how micro-level sequence features emerge as macro-level subcellular architecture. Second, it develops innovative analytical strategies by applying geometric deep learning to disparate biological datasets, transforming a fragmented data landscape into a cohesive multi-scale Condensate Graph. Finally, the physiological implications are vast: the aberrant phase transitions of these condensates (e.g., from liquid droplets to solid pathological aggregates) are hallmarks of devastating neurodegenerative diseases and cancers. Uncovering this grammar will therefore not only advance fundamental molecular and cellular biology but will also yield computational lenses capable of identifying novel therapeutic targets. In alignment with NCEMS requirements, this ambitious synthesis project requires a synergistic team of AI specialists, structural biologists, and cellular biophysicists, leveraging diverse talent to train the next-generation, data-savvy scientific workforce.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
Our Working Group seeks to address three compelling scientific questions regarding mesoscale emergence, driven by specific, testable hypotheses formulated for AI-driven data synthesis. Question 1: How do heterogeneous atomic and sequence-level interactions—the 'molecular grammar'—encode the diverse emergent physical properties of mesoscale biomolecular condensates? We hypothesize that specific combinations of sequence motifs, spacer lengths, charge distributions, and RNA-binding domains within intrinsically disordered regions mathematically map to quantifiable mesoscale parameters (e.g., critical concentration, valency, and network connectivity). By synthesizing isolated databases (DisProt, CD-CODE, PDB), we hypothesize that these features can be successfully abstracted into a multi-scale Condensate Graph. In this graph, nodes represent molecular sub-domains and edges represent interaction valencies, allowing us to capture the emergent topology of condensate networks that linear sequence analysis currently misses. Question 2: Can AI, specifically geometric deep learning, reliably predict phase separation propensity and mesoscale material properties (e.g., liquidity vs. solid-like states) directly from synthesized structural and omics data? We hypothesize that spatially-aware geometric deep learning models—particularly Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)—trained on a harmonized corpus of AlphaFold structural predictions, global interactomes (BioGRID), and annotated phase behaviors (PhaSePro), will significantly outperform existing 1D sequence-based predictors. The rationale is that emergent properties at the mesoscale are dictated not just by linear amino acid sequences, but by the 3D conformational dynamics and spatial multivalency of the interacting networks. A GNN designed to process multi-modal, spatial biological data will identify the hidden non-linear relationships that govern liquid-liquid phase separation. Question 3: How does the dysregulation of this emergent grammar correlate with pathological subcellular organization and broader macroscopic cellular phenotypes? We hypothesize that known disease-associated mutations (synthesized from genomic and clinical databases) disproportionately disrupt key 'hub' nodes and high-valency edges within our established Condensate Graph. We expect our predictive AI models will show that these specific disruptions shift the mesoscale phase boundaries—for example, precipitating a liquid-to-solid transition that maps directly to the pathological protein aggregation observed in neurodegenerative disorders. Furthermore, by cross-referencing these predicted mesoscale shifts with bioimaging datasets (EMPIAR, Image Data Resource), we hypothesize that we can computationally validate how altered atomic grammar scales up to aberrant cellular phenotypes. Addressing these questions will completely transition the field from descriptive models of individual condensates to a generalized, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence.

[Methods and Approach]
To achieve our objectives, we will execute a transdisciplinary methodology focused entirely on the synthesis of publicly available data, utilizing advanced AI and data science. Our approach is structured into three integrated phases. Phase 1: Data Synthesis and Harmonization (The Multiscale Condensate Graph). We will systematically ingest and harmonize highly heterogeneous datasets. Sequence and structural data will be drawn from AlphaFold DB, PDB, and DisProt. Phase-separation properties and biophysical metadata will be extracted from CD-CODE and PhaSePro. Interaction networks will be mapped using BioGRID and STRING, while phenotypic and spatial context will be gathered from EMPIAR and the Image Data Resource (IDR). We will build an automated data-pipelining infrastructure to standardize molecular identifiers, extract biophysical parameters, and resolve conflicting metadata. The primary output of this phase will be a knowledge graph—the Multiscale Condensate Graph—where molecules, intrinsically disordered domains, and specific sequence motifs are nodes, and documented valencies, interaction strengths, and phase boundaries are edges. This harmonized graph will serve as the mathematical foundation for our modeling. Phase 2: AI and Geometric Deep Learning. Conventional machine learning approaches often fail in biology because they treat proteins as 1D strings rather than dynamic 3D entities. We will develop novel Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) architectures, specifically Equivariant Graph Neural Networks, designed to operate on the 3D structures and relational graphs generated in Phase 1. Our models will be trained to predict emergent mesoscale physical properties (such as condensate viscosity, critical concentration for phase separation, and droplet liquidity) directly from molecular data. We will utilize self-supervised learning techniques to handle the sparsity of experimentally annotated biophysical parameters, pre-training the models on the massive interactome and AlphaFold databases before fine-tuning them on the specialized condensate registries. Phase 3: Phenotypic Mapping and Validation via Synthesis. To map mesoscale phase behaviors to higher-order subcellular outcomes without generating new experimental data, we will employ computational cross-validation. We will project known disease mutations onto our trained models to predict shifts in mesoscale physical properties (e.g., predicting enhanced solid-like behavior in ALS-associated TDP-43 mutants). We will validate these predictions by correlating them with morphological data extracted from public bioimaging repositories (e.g., analyzing Cryo-ET tomograms in EMPIAR for the presence of fibrillar versus liquid-like dense phases). Team Science Approach: The Working Group will convene virtually bi-weekly and hold four intensive in-person synthesis hackathons at the NCEMS hub. By intentionally pairing AI specialists with structural biologists and cellular biophysicists, we will ensure that our computational models remain strictly grounded in biophysical reality, fulfilling the NCEMS mandate for cross-disciplinary collaboration.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The proposed Working Group will deliver transformative outcomes that resolve a major puzzle in molecular and cellular sciences: how atomic interactions encode emergent mesoscale organization. First, we will release the 'Multiscale Condensate Graph,' the most comprehensive, harmonized database bridging intrinsically disordered protein structures with mesoscale phase separation behaviors. Second, we will deliver an open-source suite of geometric deep learning models capable of predicting condensate properties from sequence and structural data. This tool will provide the broader scientific community with a powerful new computational lens to understand subcellular organization, facilitating virtual screens for therapeutics targeting aberrant phase transitions in diseases like cancer and neurodegeneration. Crucially, the impact extends beyond scientific discovery to robust workforce development. This project will train a cohort of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers at the intersection of AI, data science, and molecular biology. Trainees will not only co-author high-impact synthesis publications but will also acquire highly sought-after skills in machine learning, graph theory, multi-omics integration, and reproducible cloud computing. By deliberately recruiting early-career researchers and diverse participants from various institutional backgrounds, our Working Group will help cultivate the next generation of diverse, data-savvy scientific leaders. Ultimately, this community-scale synthesis will transition the study of biomolecular condensates from descriptive observation to a generalized, predictive discipline, perfectly fulfilling the NCEMS mission to catalyze discoveries of emergent phenomena at the mesoscale.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
Our Working Group is deeply committed to the principles of Open Science and will adhere strictly to community-created policies on open, team, and reproducible science. To ensure Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability (FAIR), all harmonized datasets, including the Multiscale Condensate Graph, will be hosted on public repositories such as Zenodo with comprehensive, machine-readable metadata. We will utilize GitHub/GitLab as the central hubs for all software development, ensuring version control and public visibility of our AI architecture, geometric deep learning models, and data-harmonization scripts. To guarantee reproducibility—a critical challenge in complex AI workflows—we will containerize all data processing pipelines and model training environments using Docker. These containers, alongside executable Jupyter and Google Colab notebooks, will allow researchers from diverse computational backgrounds to reproduce our findings with a single click or adapt the tools for their own target proteins. We will adopt a fully transparent dissemination strategy: all manuscripts will be posted to preprint servers (e.g., bioRxiv) prior to peer review, and final publications will be submitted to open-access journals. Furthermore, our project will establish detailed governance and data-sharing agreements among Working Group members at the onset to foster an equitable, inclusive, and transparent collaborative environment, serving as a gold-standard model for NCEMS synthesis science.

[Budget and Resources]
The proposed synthesis project requires a level of computational infrastructure, collaborative facilitation, and cross-disciplinary integration that far exceeds the capabilities of a single laboratory, thereby necessitating NCEMS support. The budget focuses heavily on human capital and computational resources rather than laboratory equipment. A major portion of the funds will support the recruitment and stipends for graduate students and postdoctoral trainees who will serve as the primary data analysts, executing the day-to-day harmonization and model training under the mentorship of our diverse Principal Investigators. To facilitate the deep transdisciplinary collaboration required, funds are allocated for travel, accommodation, and logistical support for four intensive, multi-day, in-person 'synthesis hackathons' to be held at the NCEMS headquarters. These crucial gatherings will build team cohesion and accelerate complex model-building tasks that are difficult to achieve asynchronously. Additionally, we request robust cloud computing resources (e.g., AWS or Google Cloud Platform credits) necessary for hosting large-scale structural databases and training computationally intensive geometric deep learning models on multi-GPU clusters. Finally, the budget includes allocations for Open Science activities, covering open-access publication fees, long-term cloud storage for our publicly released Docker containers and the Multiscale Condensate Graph, and software licensing as needed. This resource allocation directly maps to NCEMS priorities: funding the critical collaborative glue and computational firepower needed to synthesize existing public data into novel discoveries of mesoscale biological emergence.

abstract_original: Biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) represent a defining paradigm of emergent mesoscale organization. Bridging the critical gap between individual macromolecules and complex cellular organelles, these membraneless compartments orchestrate vital processes ranging from gene regulation to cellular stress response. Despite their biological ubiquity, the fundamental molecular grammar dictating how varied atomic-level interactions—particularly among intrinsically disordered proteins and RNA—scale up to govern mesoscale material properties and macroscopic cellular phenotypes remains a long-standing puzzle. Currently, structural biology, spatial proteomics, and cellular biophysics generate massive, high-fidelity datasets; however, these data remain highly siloed. Individual research laboratories lack the cross-disciplinary expertise and computational infrastructure required to unify these divergent streams into a cohesive, predictive framework of mesoscale emergence. To address this, we propose a transdisciplinary Working Group to synthesize massive, publicly available molecular and cellular datasets to decode the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. This community-scale synthesis project will leverage AI and advanced data science to integrate atomic-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold, Protein Data Bank), intrinsically disordered protein registries (DisProt), phase-separation databases (CD-CODE, PhaSePro), global interactomes (BioGRID, STRING), and bioimaging/Cryo-ET repositories (EMPIAR, Image Data Resource). Importantly, this project will generate no new experimental data, relying entirely on the computational synthesis and harmonization of these public resources. Our working group will pursue three primary objectives: (1) Unify and harmonize these highly heterogeneous datasets to construct the first multi-scale Condensate Graph, mathematically representing the relationships between sequence-level features and mesoscale assembly. (2) Develop and train novel geometric deep learning models to predict emergent mesoscale physical properties—such as condensate liquidity, valency, and viscoelasticity—directly from these synthesized omics and structural data. (3) Map these mesoscale phase behaviors to higher-order subcellular and phenotypic outcomes, specifically focusing on how the dysregulation of this emergent grammar correlates with known disease markers. This endeavor directly aligns with the core mission of NCEMS. The sheer scale and complexity of bridging atomistic biophysics with cellular phenomics via machine learning necessitate a collaborative, transdisciplinary approach that transcends the capabilities of any single research group. Our proposed Working Group deliberately brings together experts in artificial intelligence, computational biophysics, structural biology, and spatial multi-omics from geographically diverse institutions and varying career stages. Central to our proposal is a steadfast commitment to workforce development and Open Science. Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows will be integrated as core analysts, receiving cross-training in AI-driven omics integration, biophysical modeling, and rigorous reproducible data science practices. Furthermore, in strict adherence to community-created open science policies, all integrated databases, machine learning codebases, and analytical workflows will be released publicly under FAIR principles. Ultimately, this data synthesis will solve fundamental mysteries of mesoscale biological emergence, providing the broader scientific community with a powerful new computational lens to understand subcellular organization.
