[Abstract]
The unexpected appearance of higher-order biological properties from fundamental molecular interactions is most strikingly exemplified at the mesoscale, the critical nexus between individual biomolecules and functional organelles. Biomolecular condensates, which form via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), represent a paradigm-shifting emergent property at this scale, regulating essential cellular outcomes ranging from gene expression to stress adaptation. Despite an explosion of publicly available data characterizing intrinsically disordered proteins, biophysical phase boundaries, and cellular phenotypes, these datasets remain largely siloed. Consequently, a long-standing puzzle in molecular and cellular biosciences persists: How do the physicochemical properties and interaction networks of individual macromolecules predictably scale to dictate emergent mesoscale condensate dynamics and their subsequent cellular functions? To solve this, we propose the Predictive Rules of Emergent Condensates (PREC) Working Group. This transdisciplinary team will leverage AI and data science to synthesize existing, publicly available datasets spanning from the molecular to the phenotypic level. Our project strictly utilizes existing data, integrating biomolecular sequences and structural predictions from DisProt and the AlphaFold Database, specialized biophysical LLPS databases like PhaSePro and CD-CODE, and systems-level multi-omics and high-content imaging repositories such as the Human Protein Atlas and GEO. Integrating these disparate, multi-scale data sources to decode mesoscale emergence goes far beyond the capabilities of any single research lab, requiring the unique collaborative infrastructure and support provided by NCEMS. The PREC Working Group will bring together a diverse cohort of biophysicists, molecular biologists, AI researchers, and computational data scientists. By bridging these historically distinct fields, we will develop innovative analytical strategies, including multimodal Graph Neural Networks and transformer-based machine learning architectures. These models will be designed to map the multi-dimensional feature space of single molecules to the emergent properties of mesoscale condensates—such as rheology, stoichiometry, and spatiotemporal organization—and ultimately to their impact on subcellular and cellular health. Our synthesis project is driven by three core scientific objectives: First, to answer novel questions regarding the evolutionary conservation and divergence of condensate-driven emergent properties across different cellular lineages. Second, to solve the puzzle of how specific environmental stressors trigger widespread, synchronized mesoscale phase transitions by identifying hidden molecular grammars. Third, to develop and openly distribute a predictive algorithmic framework that maps molecular properties to mesoscale emergence. In strict adherence to open science principles, all curated datasets, AI models, and analytical workflows will be rigorously documented and made publicly available via community-standard repositories like GitHub and Zenodo to ensure complete reproducibility. Furthermore, this project serves as a premier training ground for the next generation of data-savvy scientists. We will actively recruit early-career researchers, graduate students, and postdocs from underrepresented backgrounds, providing them with unparalleled cross-training in molecular biophysics and advanced AI data science techniques. By synthesizing massive public datasets through a collaborative, community-scale effort, the PREC Working Group will illuminate the foundational rules of mesoscale emergence, transforming our understanding of cellular organization and establishing new computational paradigms for the biosciences.

[Background and Significance]
The emergence of higher-order biological properties from fundamental molecular interactions is a hallmark of living systems, yet it remains profoundly misunderstood. This gap in knowledge is most pronounced at the mesoscale—the critical organizational nexus bridging individual biomolecules and functional cellular organelles. Biomolecular condensates, dynamic membrane-less organelles formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), epitomize mesoscale emergence. These structures compartmentalize cellular matter, regulating essential processes from gene transcription and signal transduction to stress adaptation and metabolic flux. The unexpected appearance of these phase-separated droplets from the collective behavior of thousands of interacting macromolecules represents a paradigm shift in molecular and cellular biosciences.

Despite the critical importance of condensates, predicting their emergent behaviors from the physicochemical properties of their constituent molecules remains a monumental challenge. Historically, the field has approached this problem through reductionist, single-lab experimental paradigms. Consequently, while there has been an explosion of publicly available data, these datasets exist in isolated silos. We possess vast repositories of intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) sequences (DisProt) and high-resolution structural predictions (AlphaFold Database), alongside specialized biophysical databases cataloging LLPS boundaries and condensate constituents (PhaSePro, CD-CODE). Concurrently, massive systems-level multi-omics databases (GEO) and high-content subcellular imaging repositories (Human Protein Atlas) capture phenotypic and cellular states. Yet, the lack of community-scale integration across these multi-scalar datasets prevents us from decoding the foundational rules governing mesoscale condensate dynamics.

The Predictive Rules of Emergent Condensates (PREC) Working Group is proposed to directly address this long-standing puzzle. By synthesizing disparate multi-omics, structural, biophysical, and imaging datasets, PREC will uncover how individual macromolecular features predictably scale to dictate mesoscale condensate properties—such as rheology, stoichiometry, and spatiotemporal organization—and ultimately influence cellular health. This endeavor aligns perfectly with the mission of the National Synthesis Center for Emergence in the Molecular and Cellular Sciences (NCEMS). Transforming these siloed datasets into a cohesive, predictive algorithmic framework requires transdisciplinary collaboration far beyond the capabilities of any single laboratory. It necessitates the convergence of molecular biophysicists, cellular biologists, artificial intelligence experts, and computational data scientists.

The significance of this synthesis project lies in its potential to establish new computational paradigms for the biosciences. By leveraging advanced AI and data science techniques, PREC will bridge the gap between microscopic molecular interactions and macroscopic cellular phenotypes. Uncovering the 'molecular grammar' of mesoscale emergence will not only answer fundamental biological questions but also provide critical insights into condensate dysregulation, which is increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Furthermore, by strictly utilizing existing publicly available data, PREC will demonstrate the transformative power of data synthesis, maximizing the return on investment of previous experimental efforts. Ultimately, this working group will catalyze a leap forward in our understanding of subcellular organization, fulfilling the NCEMS vision of characterizing emergent properties at the mesoscale and empowering the broader scientific community with robust, openly accessible predictive tools and integrated datasets.

[Research Questions and Hypotheses]
The PREC Working Group will synthesize multi-scale datasets to address critical knowledge gaps concerning the emergent properties of biomolecular condensates. By deploying advanced artificial intelligence and data science methodologies across integrated public datasets, we aim to answer three compelling, interrelated research questions that probe the mesoscale organization of the cell.

Question 1: How are the rules governing condensate-driven emergent properties evolutionarily conserved or divergent across distinct cellular lineages?
Hypothesis 1: We hypothesize that while the primary amino acid sequences of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) undergo rapid evolutionary drift, the hidden 'molecular grammar'—specifically the spatial patterning of charged, aromatic, and hydrophobic residues—remains strongly conserved to maintain essential mesoscale phase separation capabilities. By synthesizing proteomic datasets across varied taxa (from yeast to humans) with biophysical databases like CD-CODE, we predict that our AI models will identify universally conserved interaction network motifs that dictate core condensate topologies, alongside lineage-specific adaptations that tune condensate rheology to specific physiological requirements or distinct cellular environments.

Question 2: What is the underlying molecular grammar that allows specific, disparate environmental stressors to trigger widespread, synchronized mesoscale phase transitions?
Hypothesis 2: We hypothesize that specific environmental perturbations (e.g., thermal shock, osmotic stress, oxidative damage) induce systemic shifts in the intracellular physicochemical environment (such as pH or ion concentration) that synchronously activate pre-existing, latent phase-separation propensities in distinct protein sub-networks. By integrating transcriptomic and proteomic stress-response data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) with molecular interaction maps and AlphaFold structural predictions, we expect to decode the specific multidimensional feature space (e.g., valence, flexibility, interaction affinity) that acts as a sensor and switch for LLPS. We anticipate finding that distinct stressors converge on a limited set of emergent mesoscale responses, governed by specific physicochemical threshold crossing within the cell.

Question 3: Can the multi-dimensional feature space of single molecules be computationally mapped to predict the emergent biophysical properties and subcellular functions of mesoscale condensates?
Hypothesis 3: We hypothesize that the emergent properties of condensates—such as internal stoichiometry, dynamic exchange rates, and viscoelasticity (rheology)—are deterministic functions of their constituents' structural ensembles and valency networks. Furthermore, we hypothesize that these mesoscale biophysical properties directly dictate the condensate's impact on broader cellular outcomes, such as stress survival rates or transcriptomic shifts. By developing multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to link molecular features (from DisProt and AlphaFold) with macroscopic phenotypic outcomes (from the Human Protein Atlas and phenotypic screening datasets), we will establish a predictive algorithm capable of accurately forecasting a condensate's physical state and functional cellular consequence based solely on the input sequences and environmental boundary conditions.

These questions are beyond the scope of traditional single-lab experimental designs, as they require the simultaneous analysis of evolutionary, biophysical, and systems-level data. By answering them through rigorous data synthesis, the PREC Working Group will solve long-standing puzzles regarding how cellular matter spontaneously organizes, fundamentally advancing our understanding of emergence in molecular and cellular biology.

[Methods and Approach]
The PREC Working Group's methodology is rooted in the rigorous, community-scale synthesis of publicly available data, explicitly adhering to the NCEMS mandate of generating no new experimental data. Our approach bridges the molecular, mesoscale, and phenotypic levels through an innovative computational pipeline that integrates disparate data silos using advanced artificial intelligence architectures.

Phase 1: Multi-Scale Data Curation and Harmonization
The foundation of our synthesis effort involves aggregating massive, multi-scalar datasets. Molecular and structural data will be harvested from DisProt, UniProt, and the AlphaFold Database to extract sequence features, intrinsically disordered region (IDR) profiles, and 3D structural ensembles. Biophysical phase boundary and condensate constituency data will be retrieved from PhaSePro, CD-CODE, and LLPSDB. Finally, systems-level transcriptomic, proteomic, and phenotypic data will be sourced from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and the Human Protein Atlas (HPA). The sheer volume and heterogeneity of these sources necessitate the unique collaborative infrastructure of NCEMS. Our computational data scientists will construct an automated, cloud-based harmonization pipeline to standardize metadata, resolve conflicting annotations, and map these varied data types into a unified, queryable relational database representing the molecular-to-phenotypic continuum.

Phase 2: AI-Driven Analytical Strategies
To decode mesoscale emergence, we will develop and train multimodal machine learning architectures. First, we will deploy Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) fine-tuned on protein sequences to extract the 'hidden molecular grammar' of phase-separating proteins. These models will identify predictive physicochemical patterns—such as the spacing of pi-pi and cation-pi interaction sites—that dictate LLPS. Second, to model the complex interaction networks that govern condensate stoichiometry and emergent rheology, we will construct multimodal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In these graphs, nodes will represent individual macromolecules (populated with AlphaFold and DisProt features), and edges will represent interaction affinities under specific environmental conditions. The GNNs will be trained to map these molecular interaction networks to mesoscale emergent properties (e.g., fluidity, phase boundaries) and subsequently to cellular phenotypes (e.g., stress survival derived from GEO data).

Phase 3: Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration and Execution
This methodological framework fundamentally requires the transdisciplinary expertise assembled in the PREC Working Group. Biophysicists will guide the parameterization of the GNNs to ensure thermodynamic plausibility. Molecular biologists will curate the functional annotations of stress responses and cellular phenotypes. AI researchers will design and optimize the neural network architectures, while data scientists will manage the cloud infrastructure and data harmonization. The group will convene through NCEMS-supported hybrid workshops, hackathons, and sustained virtual collaboration. These synthesis meetings will enable iterative model refinement, where biological intuition drives algorithmic adjustments, and AI-generated predictions spark novel biological insights.

By synthesizing millions of siloed data points through this integrated AI approach, we will construct a robust computational bridge across biological scales. This methodology not only addresses our specific research questions regarding evolutionary conservation and stress-induced phase transitions but also provides the broader scientific community with a pioneering analytical blueprint for utilizing machine learning to investigate mesoscale emergent phenomena.

[Expected Outcomes and Impact]
The PREC Working Group will deliver transformative outcomes that directly advance the NCEMS mission to illuminate emergence in molecular and cellular biosciences. Our primary scientific outcome will be the first comprehensive, multi-scale computational framework capable of predicting mesoscale biomolecular condensate dynamics—and their subsequent cellular impacts—directly from primary macromolecular sequences and environmental conditions. This will solve the long-standing puzzle of how individual physicochemical properties scale to govern higher-order, membrane-less cellular organization.

We expect to publish high-impact, peer-reviewed articles detailing the evolutionary conservation of condensate grammar and the mechanisms of stress-induced phase transitions. Crucially, the impact of PREC extends far beyond publications. We will release a unified, harmonized open-access database that bridges currently siloed molecular, biophysical, and phenotypic repositories, providing an unprecedented community resource for the study of LLPS. Furthermore, our open-source AI architectures (Transformer and GNN models) will establish a novel analytical paradigm, enabling researchers globally to predict mesoscale emergent properties in their own systems of interest.

Broader impacts will be realized through our robust commitment to training the future data-savvy workforce. Through the PREC Working Group, early-career researchers, graduate students, and postdoctoral fellows will receive unparalleled, transdisciplinary cross-training. By actively recruiting from underrepresented backgrounds and blending expertise in biophysics and advanced AI, we will cultivate a new generation of scientists uniquely equipped to tackle complex synthesis research. Ultimately, PREC will transform our understanding of cellular organization, providing the predictive tools necessary to understand condensate dysregulation in human disease while catalyzing a new era of AI-driven, synthesis-based discovery in the biosciences.

[Open Science and Reproducibility]
The PREC Working Group is unequivocally committed to the highest standards of Open Science, rigorously adhering to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) data principles to ensure absolute transparency and reproducibility. Because our synthesis project relies entirely on publicly available data, the democratization of our integrated outputs and analytical workflows is a cornerstone of our mission.

All curated datasets, harmonized metadata, and relational databases generated during this project will be comprehensively documented and deposited in stable, community-recognized repositories such as Zenodo and the Open Science Framework (OSF), assigned with persistent Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). Data dictionaries and detailed provenance logs will accompany every dataset, detailing exact source origins, extraction dates, and harmonization protocols.

Our algorithmic frameworks, including the multimodal Graph Neural Networks and Transformer-based models, will be developed openly. All source code, data processing scripts, and model training pipelines will be version-controlled and hosted on a public GitHub repository. To guarantee computational reproducibility, we will provide containerized environments using Docker and Singularity, alongside comprehensive Jupyter Notebooks that allow any researcher to seamlessly execute our pipelines, validate our findings, and apply our models to new datasets.

Furthermore, PREC will adhere to community-created policies on team science and reproducible research. We will implement transparent authorship and contributor guidelines based on the CRediT taxonomy, ensuring equitable recognition for all working group members, especially early-career trainees. Pre-prints of all manuscripts will be posted to bioRxiv prior to peer review, ensuring rapid dissemination of our findings. By integrating these rigorous open science practices at every stage of the project, PREC will ensure that our AI-driven synthesis tools become a lasting, reliable, and continuously evolving resource for the global molecular and cellular biology community.

[Budget and Resources]
The PREC Working Group requires the unique collaborative infrastructure, financial support, and computational resources provided by NCEMS to execute this community-scale synthesis. The ambitious scope of integrating multi-scalar data—from atomic resolution features to systems-level phenotypes—using advanced AI fundamentally exceeds the capacity, computational resources, and disciplinary scope of any single research laboratory or traditional grant mechanism.

The requested budget will primarily support the critical collaborative and training activities central to our proposal. Funds are allocated for travel, lodging, and logistical support to convene the transdisciplinary working group for three intensive, in-person synthesis meetings at the NCEMS facility over the project duration. These workshops are essential for cross-pollinating ideas between biophysicists, molecular biologists, and AI experts, fostering the team science required to tackle emergent mesoscale phenomena.

A significant portion of the budget is dedicated to supporting the next generation of data-savvy scientists. We request stipend support and travel funding for four early-career trainees (two graduate students and two postdoctoral fellows), actively recruited from underrepresented backgrounds. This funding ensures their dedicated participation in the synthesis research, providing them with critical cross-training in molecular biophysics and machine learning.

Furthermore, we request resources for robust cloud computing infrastructure necessary to train and optimize our multimodal Graph Neural Networks and Transformer models on massive, harmonized datasets. While no funds are requested for experimental data generation, modest support is allocated for open-access publication fees and professional data curation services to ensure strict compliance with FAIR data principles and our Open Science mandate. By leveraging NCEMS support, PREC will maximize the return on existing public data investments, delivering a transformative, community-scale predictive framework for the biosciences.
